That does not mean every hardship is persecution, or that we should go looking for trouble; much of our pain is ordinary, and some of it is our own fault. But where the pressure comes because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus, it is a mark of belonging, not of abandonment, and the right response is not panic but endurance.

How should I keep the Lord’s day? Keep it as the day of resurrection, centred on gathering with God’s people to worship, hear the word, pray, sing and share the Lord’s Supper. Christians differ over how strictly Sabbath rest applies, and the current view of this app is that the command is fulfilled in Christ, so the day is not a list of forbidden activities. But it is still a gift to be received rather than a gap to be filled: rest from ordinary work where you can, make room for fellowship, mercy and quiet, and do not let it become just another day for errands. If, like John, you are cut off from church by illness, work or distance, keep it anyway. The Lord is risen on Patmos too.

In a sentence. I, John, who share with you the suffering, the kingdom and the patient endurance that belong to those in Jesus, had been banished to Patmos for preaching God’s word and Jesus’ testimony; on Sunday, the Lord’s day, the Spirit took hold of me, and behind me a voice as loud as a trumpet told me to write down what I saw and send it to the seven churches, from Ephesus round to Laodicea.

On a Tuesday. Suffering for Christ, the kingdom of Christ and endurance in Christ come together. If you are under pressure for your faith, you are not off course; you are a partner with John. Ask which of the three you are least expecting this week. Most of us expect the tribulation and forget the kingdom, or expect the kingdom and resent the tribulation. Endurance is the ordinary virtue of staying where God has put you, one more day, under the load.

For worship. The Lord who rose on the first day found his old friend on a rock in the sea, keeping that day alone. Rome had shrunk John’s world to thirteen square miles, and the risen Christ used the exile to give the whole church the vision of his throne. No banishment can put a servant of his out of reach, and no island is so bare that the trumpet cannot sound behind it.
verseByVerse.note: Patmos is a small rocky island in the Aegean, about 40 miles off the coast of Asia. “The Lord’s day” is Sunday, the day of Jesus’ resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I turned to see the voice that was speaking to me, and on turning I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed with a long robe and with a golden sash around his chest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I turned to see the voice that was speaking to me, and on turning I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed with a long robe and with a golden sash around his chest.

Then I turned to see the voice. The ESV keeps the oddity rather than tidying it, and the oddity is the point. You do not see a voice. But this voice is so massive, so evidently coming from somebody, that John turns to look at it the way you would turn towards a shout in an empty house. It is a vivid way of saying he turned to see who was speaking.

I saw seven golden lampstands. What he sees first is not the figure. It is the furniture. Anyone raised on the Hebrew Scriptures would place it instantly. In the tabernacle and the temple there stood a lampstand of pure gold with seven branches, the menorah, and it burned continually in the holy place before the veil (Exodus 25:31–40). Zechariah saw it in a vision and was told what it meant: not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts (Zechariah 4:6). But something has changed, and the change is the point. In the temple there was one lampstand with seven branches. Here there are seven separate lampstands (lychnias), and verse 20 says they are the seven churches. The single light of Israel has been broken out and distributed: one in Ephesus, one in Smyrna, one in Pergamum, and so on up the road. The holy place is no longer a room in Jerusalem. It is a rented hall in a Roman market town, and another one sixty miles north, and the lamp is lit in both.

Golden. And they are gold. Small, struggling congregations in pagan cities, some of them compromised and one of them nearly dead, are in God’s sight precious metal. The world looked at a few dozen tradesmen meeting in a house and saw nothing worth counting. Christ looks and sees gold.

A lampstand makes no light. That quietly settles what a church is for. The stand holds the lamp up so the room can see. It is not admired; it is not the point; it is judged solely by whether the light is high enough to be useful (Matthew 5:14–16). The church is not the light itself; it holds up the light of Christ to the world. A congregation that has become impressive at everything except that has misunderstood the shape it was made in.

And in the midst of the lampstands. This phrase carries the weight of the whole vision (en mesō). Not above them, inspecting from a height. Not outside, waiting for results. Not far away in heaven, out of reach. In the middle of them, close enough to touch the gold. He walks among his churches (2:1), seeing all, tending the lamps, as the priest tended the lampstand. This is both comfort and warning: he is present to strengthen and to correct.

One like a son of man. Then, in the middle of them, a figure. The phrase (huion anthrōpou) comes from Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds into the presence of the Ancient of Days and receives a dominion that will never pass away. It is the title Jesus used of himself more than any other, and its power lies in its double edge. On the surface it means simply a human being. Underneath it means the figure Daniel saw receiving the worship of all peoples. He is truly human, and more than human.

Clothed with a long robe and with a golden sash around his chest. He is dressed. The long robe is podērēs, reaching to the feet, the very word the Greek Old Testament uses for the high priest’s garment (Exodus 28:4), and a golden sash was part of the priestly dress. The figure in Daniel 10:5 is clothed in linen with a belt of gold. Christ appears as the great high priest, ministering among the lampstands, and also as a king, since such robes signified dignity. The sash is not round his waist where a working man would knot it, but high across his chest, the way a man wears a sash when he is not labouring but presiding: dignity and rest, a task completed. The sacrifice is finished. What remains is the tending.

The priest at the lamps. The first thing John sees him doing is priestly work, and it is the humblest priestly work there was. Morning and evening in the holy place a priest trimmed the wicks and topped up the oil so that the flame never went out (Exodus 27:20–21; Leviticus 24:1–4). That is what the glorified Christ is doing among his churches. The one with eyes like fire and a face like the sun is first of all a lamp-tender.

What it does not mean. The details are not a physical portrait to be painted. They are symbols, each drawn from the Old Testament, to show who Christ is. Asking what he looked like misses the point; ask what each feature tells you about him.

Is Christ really present in my small, ordinary church? Yes. That is exactly what this vision says. Take the smallest, coldest gathering your church has had in the last year: the wet evening when eleven people came and the singing was thin and nobody could think of anything to say afterwards. He was standing in the middle of that room. He was not disappointed at a distance. He was there, doing what he does, keeping a wick alight that anybody else would have written off. He promised it where two or three gather in his name (Matthew 18:20), and the seven churches were not large. His presence is not measured by the size of the room or the quality of the music.

Is this vision about churches, or about me personally? Both, but in that order. The lampstands are congregations, and the picture is of Christ among his gathered people. Revelation does not imagine a Christian on his own with his private faith; it imagines believers held together in local churches, which is where Christ chooses to be found. Of course he is with each believer always (Matthew 28:20). But if you have drifted from church and kept your faith as a private thing, notice where John sees him standing: among the lampstands. To find him most clearly, go where he has said he walks.

In a sentence. When I turned to see who was speaking, I saw seven golden lampstands, and among them a figure like a son of man, dressed in a full-length priestly robe with a golden sash around his chest.

On a Tuesday. Next time you walk into your church, before you assess the turnout or the sound system, remember who is already standing in the middle of the room. Worship as those whose high priest is present. And ask the lampstand question about yourself and your congregation: is the light being held up where people can see it, or has the stand become the point?

For worship. The High Priest has not left the holy place. He has moved it. He walks now among a scattering of golden stands in market towns and back streets, trimming every wick, topping up every lamp, standing in the middle of the smallest gathering with the same care he gives the largest. The one before whom Daniel’s world bowed is the one who will not let a smoking flax go out (Isaiah 42:3).

verseByVerse.quote: The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire, his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters. In his right hand he held seven stars, from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in full strength.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire, his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters. In his right hand he held seven stars, from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in full strength.

The setting. Every feature here comes from the Old Testament, mostly from Daniel 7 and 10 and Ezekiel 1 and 43. The startling thing is that features belonging to the Ancient of Days, God himself, are now given to the Son of Man. John is showing, in pictures, that Jesus is God. He is not describing a face; he is assembling a theology out of the Old Testament’s greatest visions, and each feature tells a hard-pressed congregation something it needs to survive the week.

The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow. This is the most audacious sentence in the chapter, and it is easy to walk past. In Daniel 7 there are two figures in the throne room: the Ancient of Days, whose clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool (Daniel 7:9), and the son of man who is brought before him. John has taken the description of the first and put it on the second. He does not argue for the deity of Christ here. He simply hands the son of man the Ancient of Days’ own hair and moves on to the next clause. The white is not the white of decline. In Daniel it is the mark of one whose existence has no beginning to date: eternity, wisdom, dignity and purity. Christ shares the eternal majesty of God.

His eyes were like a flame of fire. The phrase (phlox pyros) comes from Daniel 10:6. Fire does two things at once: it illuminates and it consumes. Nothing survives it and nothing hides from it. In four of the seven letters that follow, this Christ will tell a church something about itself that it had managed not to know: Sardis thinks it is alive, Laodicea thinks it is rich. The eyes of flame are why. To Thyatira he introduces himself this way, as the one who searches mind and heart (2:18, 23). And the same fact lands two ways depending on where you are standing. To a believer keeping faith in a town where nobody notices, it means that nothing done in obscurity has gone unrecorded. To anyone maintaining a respectable front over something rotten, it means the front has never worked for a moment.

His feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace. Burnished bronze (chalkolibanō) is a rare word for a fine, glowing metal alloy, as in Daniel 10:6 and Ezekiel 1:7. Bronze glowing from the fire, and therefore bronze that has already been through it. These are feet that have stood in the heat and come out harder. Any reader who knows Daniel will remember three young men in a furnace and a fourth figure walking about in the flames with them, unbound and unburnt (Daniel 3:25). And these feet stand firm, in contrast to the feet of iron and clay on the statue of earthly empires in Daniel 2. Feet also crush; that image will return when the winepress is trodden (14:20; 19:15).

And his voice was like the roar of many waters. Ezekiel heard exactly this sound and named it: the sound of his coming was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with his glory (Ezekiel 43:2), the glory of God returning to a temple it had abandoned. For John on an island, the image is the endless crash of the sea on the rocks. Stand at the foot of a waterfall in spate and try to hold a conversation. You cannot. Every other sound in the valley is simply taken away. That is the volume at which this Christ speaks over the empire, the accuser, the rumour, and the voice in a believer’s head at three in the morning.

In his right hand he held seven stars. The right hand is the hand of power, authority and possession. The stars are not orbiting nearby; they are held. Verse 20 will say they are the angels of the churches. So the churches are in his hand: they are in his power, and they are safe, and no one will snatch them out of it (John 10:28). And Roman coins used stars to advertise imperial divinity; Domitian issued one showing his dead infant son as a god, seated on a globe among seven stars. John has seen the real hand.

From his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword. Not in his hand; from his mouth. The sword (rhomphaia) is a long one, and the weapon of this King is speech (Hebrews 4:12). Isaiah said the coming ruler would strike the earth with the rod of his mouth (Isaiah 11:4), and the Servant says that God made my mouth like a sharp sword (Isaiah 49:2). At the end, Christ defeats his enemies with this sword alone (19:15, 21). The Roman governor had the right of the sword, the power of execution; Christ’s word is greater. The church has therefore been given no other armament, and needs none: not political leverage, not cultural weight, not numbers, but the word, spoken by people with no power, which has outlived every empire that ever banned it.

And his face was like the sun shining in full strength. Three disciples, John among them, had seen it once before, on a mountain, for a short time (Matthew 17:2). Here it is not a glimpse permitted and withdrawn; this is simply what his face is like now, permanently, unbearable glory. And it is the last detail because nothing can be added after it. Every other feature has been an image drawn from somewhere. The face is just the face. He is the light that the lampstands were made to carry, standing in the middle of them, shining at full strength in a province that thought it had put the gospel out.

What it does not mean. This is not a description of a monster. Every image says something good and true about Christ: eternal, all-seeing, strong, authoritative, protective, powerful in word, glorious. The gentle Jesus of the Gospels is also this Jesus. Both are the same person.

Is this the same Jesus who took children in his arms? Yes, entirely. The Jesus who welcomed children, touched lepers and wept at a grave is the eternal Son, and this vision shows what was always true of him, now unveiled. The tenderness was never weakness; it was the kindness of the Lord of glory stooping. And the glory is never cruelty; it is the strength of the friend of sinners. If you know only the gentle Jesus, you will find him too small to trust in a crisis. If you know only the blazing one, you will be afraid to come near. The next verses put the two together: the same right hand holds the stars and rests on John’s shoulder.

Why should the eyes of fire comfort me rather than frighten me? Because they see everything, including what no one else sees. They see the faithfulness nobody thanks, the prayer nobody hears, the temptation resisted in private, the injustice done to you that no court will ever examine. Nothing is lost to him. They also see your sin, and that is meant to bring you to honest repentance, not despair, because the eyes belong to the one who died for the sins they see. For a believer, the searching gaze of Christ is the safest place there is to be known completely, because it is also the place where you are loved completely.

In a sentence. His head and hair were white as wool and snow, his eyes blazed like fire, his feet glowed like fine bronze fresh from the furnace, his voice thundered like a great waterfall, he held seven stars in his right hand, a sharp double-edged sword came out of his mouth, and his face shone like the sun at noon.

On a Tuesday. Let this vision correct small thoughts of Jesus. When you pray this week, picture not a vague kindly figure but this one, and see what it does to your requests, your fears and your excuses. When the loudest voice in your head is the old accusation, remember the voice like many waters. And when you are tempted to think the church needs some other weapon to make its way in the world, remember what comes from his mouth.

For worship. The friend of sinners is the Lord of glory. The hair of the Ancient of Days is on the head of the man from Nazareth; the eyes that wept at Lazarus’s tomb blaze through every disguise; the feet that were nailed are bronze from the furnace; the voice that said Little girl, arise drowns the sea. He holds the churches in his hand, he conquers by his word, and his face is the sun. This is who walks among the lampstands, and he is ours.

verseByVerse.quote: When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. But he laid his right hand on me, saying, "Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. But he laid his right hand on me, saying, “Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.

When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. This is the man who leaned back against Jesus at supper and asked him a question about the person sitting across the table (John 13:25). Sixty years later he sees the same person and his body simply stops holding him up. That reaction is the normal one, which is itself instructive. Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up and said, Woe is me! For I am lost (Isaiah 6:5). Ezekiel fell on his face (Ezekiel 1:28). Daniel fell into a deep sleep with his face to the ground (Daniel 10:9). Peter, in a boat with more fish in it than it could hold, said, Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord (Luke 5:8). Nobody in Scripture who actually sees the glory of God finds it comfortable. Holy fear is not a lack of faith; it is a true sight of who he is.

Near this Christ, or near a picture of him? Which raises a question worth putting honestly. If a congregation always leaves a service feeling pleasantly warmed and never once leaves it undone, has it been near this Christ, or near a picture of him scaled down to a size that would not disturb anybody? The answer is not to manufacture fear. It is to preach and sing the Christ of the Bible at his true size, and let him do the rest.

But he laid his right hand on me. Then the response, and every word of it counts. That is the hand from verse 16, the one holding the seven stars. He does not put them down to reach for John. The hand that governs the churches is the hand that steadies one frightened man on the floor, and it does both at the same time without strain. It is a hand of power and a hand of tenderness, as in Daniel 10:10, and as Jesus touched the frightened disciples on the mountain and told them to rise and have no fear (Matthew 17:7).

Saying, Fear not. Mē phobou: stop being afraid. The first words the glorified Christ speaks to his church in this book are the same words he used in Galilee to men in a sinking boat, and the most frequent command in Scripture. The voice like many waters says the gentlest thing in the vocabulary. And note the order carefully, because sentiment gets it backwards. The comfort does not arrive by reducing the glory. John is not told that he over-reacted. He is left flat on the ground, and lifted there. The awe remains, but the terror is removed. The glorious Christ does not destroy his own servant.

I am the first and the last. In Isaiah, twice, this is how God distinguishes himself from every rival: I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god (Isaiah 44:6; compare 48:12). It is not a phrase that can be shared out. Jesus takes it, unedited, and applies it to himself, the same divine title the Father used in verse 8 (Alpha and Omega). Jesus is not a lesser god; he is the one God, with the Father. And then he adds something Isaiah could not have said.

And the living one. Ho zōn. God is the living God, in contrast to dead idols, and Christ has life in himself (John 5:26). He does not merely have life, as we do, on loan. He is the one whose very definition is life, the source of it.

I died, and behold I am alive forevermore. Read that slowly, because no other being in existence can put those two clauses side by side. He does not say I was dead and now I am not, as though death had been an interruption to be got over. He says I am the living one, and then: I died. The Greek is literally I became dead (egenomēn nekros): a real death, in history, outside a city wall, with a spear to prove it. Life itself went into the grave. And came out, not restored to a life that could be lost again like Lazarus, but alive into the ages of the ages (eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn). His resurrection is not a return to ordinary life but entry into endless life. Death can never touch him again (Romans 6:9).

And I have the keys of Death and Hades. Keys (kleis) are not decoration; keys are authority. Whoever holds them decides who goes in and who comes out, and holds them because the door is his. Death here is the event and Hades is the realm, the state of the dead (hadēs, the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew Sheol): the two things every human being fears in different ways, the dying and the being dead. Jewish tradition said that only God holds the keys of death. Both sets of keys hang from one belt, and they were taken by the only man who has ever been inside and walked out under his own power. He will open the graves at the resurrection (20:13), and in the end Death and Hades themselves will be thrown into the lake of fire (20:14). For a church facing martyrdom, nothing could be more comforting: death has no power over those whose Lord holds its keys.

A locked room with the key in a loving hand. Which means this, exactly and without softening. A grave is not a locked room with the key lost. Somebody has the key, and he loves the person inside. For anyone who has stood at a graveside in the rain and heard the earth go down, that is not a decoration on a hard fact; it is the hard fact. The one holding the keys is not a stranger who might be persuaded. He is the one who wept at a tomb before he opened it (John 11:35, 43–44). And for anyone who lies awake afraid of their own dying, the fear is not answered by being told that death is small. It is not small. It is answered by the keys, and by whose hand they are in.

What it does not mean. The keys of Hades do not mean Christ went to hell to suffer further after his death. His suffering was finished on the cross (John 19:30). The keys mean authority over death, won by his death and resurrection. Nor does this support the idea of a second chance after death; the Bible gives none (Hebrews 9:27).

Does Fear not mean I should never fear God? It means you need never fear being destroyed by him if you belong to Christ. Scripture still calls believers to fear the Lord (Proverbs 9:10; 1 Peter 1:17), and that is not the opposite of this verse but the other half of it. The fear of the Lord is reverent awe: taking him seriously, trembling at his word, not daring to treat him lightly. What Christ removes is the terror of condemnation (1 John 4:18). John stays on his face, and he stays unafraid. That is the posture of a Christian before Christ: low, and safe.

What happens to a believer who dies? He goes to be with Christ at once. The soul does not sleep or wait in a holding place; to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23), and the souls of the martyrs in this very book are awake before the throne (6:9–11). There is no purgatory to pass through, because Christ’s blood has already freed us from our sins (1:5). The body rests in the grave until the resurrection, when he will use the keys and raise it, glorified, to be reunited with the soul (1 Corinthians 15:42–44, 52). So the grave is real, but it is temporary, and the one who holds the key is coming.

In a sentence. When I saw him I collapsed at his feet like a dead man, but he put his right hand on me and said, Do not be afraid: I am the first and the last and the one who lives; I was dead, but look, I am alive for ever and ever, and I hold the keys of death and of the grave.

On a Tuesday. Face death, your own and that of those you love, with this sentence: Jesus holds the keys. The grave is not locked against him, and he will open it. If you are sitting with someone who is dying, read them these two verses. If you are carrying a grief that has gone quiet but not away, say them over the grave in your mind. And if you are afraid, do what John did: stay low before him, and let him put his hand on you.

For worship. The first and the last once lay among the dead, in a new tomb in a garden, and the living one was counted with the corpses of Jerusalem. No one else in heaven or on earth can say I died, and I am alive for ever, and he says it to steady one fallen old man. All the authority death ever claimed over the human race has passed into the hands that were nailed. The grave keeps nothing he has not allowed it to keep for a while, and nothing it holds will stay there when he comes.

verseByVerse.quote: Write therefore the things that you have seen, those that are and those that are to take place after this. As for the mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands, the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Write therefore the things that you have seen, those that are and those that are to take place after this. As for the mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands, the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches.”

The setting. Christ repeats the command to write (v. 11) and explains two of the symbols. Where the book explains its own symbols, we follow it; where it does not, we look to the Old Testament, from which nearly every image comes.

Write therefore the things that you have seen. “Therefore” (oun) ties the command to what has just happened. Because Christ has conquered death and holds its keys, John is to write without fear. The man who was lying on the floor is put back on his feet and handed a pen.

Those that are and those that are to take place after this. “After this” (meta tauta) echoes Daniel 2:29 and 45, where Daniel tells the king what will be after this. The book concerns both present realities and future events, and both are mixed throughout. Many read this verse as a three-part outline: what John has seen (chapter 1), what is (chapters 2–3) and what will be after this (chapters 4–22). It is a serious reading of a genuine feature of the text, and 4:1 does open with almost the same words: come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this.

Where Christians differ: is this verse an outline of the book? Dispensationalists often take it as a strict outline, with chapters 4–22 entirely future, after the church is raptured at 4:1. Careful teachers in that tradition have worked it out at length, and any reader in a church shaped by it will have met it. Others hesitate, for two reasons that should also be given fairly. The same phrase, what must take place, is used in verse 1 of the entire book, chapters 2 and 3 included, so it is not obvious that it marks off a section beginning at chapter 4. And the contents resist the split in both directions: the letters to the seven churches are full of the future (a crown, a hidden manna, a pillar in the temple, the coming of Christ himself), while chapters 4 to 22 are full of the present (a throne that is occupied now, martyrs who are already under the altar, a Lamb who has already conquered). Verdict: the phrase is better read as describing the whole book: what John saw includes things that are and things still to come, all mixed together. Chapter 12, for example, goes back to Christ’s birth and ascension. The book is not a strict timeline but a series of visions, each showing the same age between Christ’s comings from a different angle, and each ending at or near the final judgement. Nothing essential about Christ rests on the question; readers who differ here can and do sing the same hymns, and where it changes the meaning of a passage the options are set out again at the verse itself.

As for the mystery. Then Christ explains his own symbolism, and that fact is more useful than the explanation. The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches. Twice in one sentence the pattern is: this image means that reality. A reader who wanted a rule for handling the rest of the book has just been given one by the author. The word mystērion in the New Testament never means a riddle nobody can solve. It means something that was hidden and has now been told (Ephesians 3:3–5). The visions are not locked; they are explained, sometimes on the spot, and almost always by the Old Testament.

The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches. Angels (angeloi) can mean messengers, and each of the seven letters is addressed to the angel of that church (2:1 and the others).

Where Christians differ: who are the angels of the churches? Some say they are human messengers carrying the letters, or the pastor of each church; they point out that each letter is addressed to the angel and then rebukes him and calls him to repent, which seems a strange thing to say to an unfallen angel. Others say they are guardian angels assigned to the churches. Others suggest they personify the spiritual life or heavenly counterpart of each church, its corporate character as heaven sees it. Verdict: they are most likely heavenly angels connected with each church, since every other use of “angel” in Revelation (over sixty) means a heavenly being, and Scripture speaks of angels watching over God’s people (Daniel 10:20–21; Matthew 18:10). Yet the letters are clearly aimed at the congregations themselves, who are rebuked and called to repent. The angel represents the church before God, so to address it is to address the church. In practice, the messages are for every believer (2:7).

And the seven lampstands are the seven churches. Christ calls the church to shine for him in the darkness. And in 2:5 he warns Ephesus that he could remove its lampstand: a church can lose its place as a witness if it will not repent. The lamp is his to light, and his to take away.

Held and surrounded. What is not ambiguous is where the stars are and where the lampstands are. The stars are in his right hand. The lampstands are around him, and he walks in their midst. Whatever pressure is coming in the next twenty-one chapters, and a great deal is coming, it will arrive at churches that are already held and already surrounded. That is the chapter’s last word before the letters begin, and it is the reason the letters can be as searching as they are. He can afford to tell Ephesus the truth. He is not going to lose it.

What it does not mean. The seven churches are not seven ages of church history, as some have taught (Ephesus the apostolic age, Laodicea the last days). Nothing in the text suggests it, and every church in every age needs all seven letters.

Does my church have its own angel? Possibly, though we should hold it lightly. Scripture says angels are sent to serve those who will inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14) and speaks of the angels of little ones (Matthew 18:10), and this verse most naturally pictures an angel connected with each church. But the Bible never invites us to identify, address or pray to such angels, and it forbids worshipping them (19:10; Colossians 2:18). The point for us is not the angel but the hand: the star is in Christ’s right hand. Your church is watched over, but it is Christ who holds it and Christ to whom it answers.

Can Christ still remove a church’s lampstand today? Yes. A congregation can lose its witness and even cease to be a true church if it abandons the gospel and refuses to repent, and history is full of buildings where Christ was once preached and is preached no more. Ephesus itself, the greatest church of Asia, is now a field of ruins. That does not mean any true believer is lost; Christ never lets go of his own (John 10:28). It means local churches are not guaranteed to last. The remedy he gives is simple: remember, repent and do the first works (2:5). The warning is given so that the lamp will not go out.

In a sentence. So write what you have seen, both the present and what is to come; and here is the meaning of the seven stars in my right hand and the seven golden lampstands: the stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the lampstands are the churches themselves.

On a Tuesday. Your local church, however small, is a golden lampstand that Christ holds and walks among. Love it, serve it and help it shine. When you are tempted to give up on it, remember he has not. And when you read the hard letters that follow, read them as words from the one who holds your church in his right hand: he rebukes because he intends to keep.

For worship. The Lord of the churches does not leave his servants guessing at what they are. He takes a star and a lamp, the brightest thing in the night sky and the humblest thing in the house, and says: this is you. The mystery hidden for ages is now told to his saints, and its heart is Christ himself among them, the hope of glory (Colossians 1:26–27). The one who died and holds the keys counts a few struggling congregations as stars worth holding, and the light they were lit to carry is his own.

2.title: Letters to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira
2.overview:
The seven letters of chapters 2–3 are the most immediately practical section of Revelation. Before the cosmic drama unfolds, the risen Christ pauses to speak personally to each congregation — by name, with specific knowledge, with diagnostic precision. These are not generic pastoral encouragements. They are surgical letters, each one calibrated to the exact spiritual condition of a real church in a real city.

Every letter follows a recognizable pattern: (1) a self-identification of Christ drawn from the vision of chapter 1; (2) “I know” — a statement of Christ’s comprehensive knowledge of the congregation’s situation; (3) commendation or absence thereof; (4) rebuke or absence thereof; (5) a call to repentance or endurance; (6) “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches”; and (7) a promise to “the one who conquers.” The word nikōn (conqueror/overcomer) is the key word of the seven letters. Every letter ends with a promise to the one who overcomes, and the nature of overcoming is not occasional spiritual performance but faithful endurance to the end.

The seven churches were not chosen arbitrarily. They formed a postal circuit in the Roman province of Asia, moving roughly in a clockwise direction from Ephesus. Any one of them could be a “hub” for distributing the letter to surrounding congregations. But the number seven also signals completeness — these seven represent the whole church of every age. Every congregation since the first century has found itself somewhere in these seven letters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — To the Church in Ephesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Ephesus was the first stop on the courier’s road: a harbour city of some quarter of a million people, home to the temple of Artemis, and the congregation Paul had spent three years building (Acts 20:31). Verse 1 addresses its angel and identifies the sender as the one who holds the seven stars and walks among the seven lampstands — both images sharpened from 1:13 and 1:16. He grips, and he is moving through the room.

Verses 2–3 are two full verses of commendation before a word of criticism, and it is genuine: works, toil to exhaustion (kopos), patient endurance, an unwillingness to bear with evil, false apostles tested and exposed, weight carried for his name’s sake, and no weariness after forty years. Paul had warned this very church that wolves would come (Acts 20:29–30) and they had acted on it.

Verse 4 turns: you have abandoned the love you had at first. The verb is not cooling but putting down and walking on. Everything in vv. 2–3 is visible from outside; what is missing can be seen only by the eyes of fire. Verse 5 gives the remedy in three ordered verbs — remember where you have fallen from, repent, and do the works you did at first — and then the threat: the lampstand removed from its place. Not salvation withdrawn; a congregation ceasing to give light. There is no church in Ephesus today.

Verse 6 returns to commendation before the letter ends: they hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which Christ also hates. Verse 7 sounds the refrain — he who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches — and promises the conqueror the tree of life in the paradise of God: the tree guarded since Genesis 3:24 and standing open in the street of the city at 22:2.
verseByVerse.theology:
Orthodox but Loveless

Ephesus had sound doctrine, hard work and endurance, but had abandoned its first love. The cure is to remember, repent and do the works it did at first.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A second-generation church kept the truth and lost the warmth.

Now: Ask what would remain of your faith if the things others can see were taken away.

verseByVerse.quote: "To the angel of the church in Ephesus write: 'The words of him who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“To the angel of the church in Ephesus write: ‘The words of him who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands.

Meaning first. Revelation 2 holds the first four of Christ’s seven letters to the churches of Asia. Each follows a pattern: Christ introduces himself with a feature from the vision of chapter 1; he says, I know your works; he praises and rebukes; he calls for repentance or endurance; he bids anyone who has an ear to hear what the Spirit says to the churches; and he makes a promise to the one who conquers. Ephesus is sound in doctrine and tireless in work but has abandoned its first love, and must repent or lose its lampstand; the conqueror will eat from the tree of life (vv. 1–7). Smyrna is poor, slandered and facing prison, and receives no rebuke, only the call to be faithful unto death and the promise of the crown of life (vv. 8–11). Pergamum, where Satan’s throne is, held fast when Antipas was killed, but tolerates the teaching of Balaam and the Nicolaitans, which permits idolatry and immorality; Christ will fight them with the sword of his mouth, and promises hidden manna and a white stone with a new name (vv. 12–17). Thyatira is growing in love, faith and service but tolerates a false prophetess, Jezebel, who leads believers into immorality and idol feasts; Christ, whose eyes are like fire, will judge her, and promises the faithful authority over the nations and the morning star (vv. 18–29). Together the letters show a Christ who knows his churches completely, loves them enough to rebuke them, and calls every believer to conquer by staying faithful.

The setting. Ephesus was the leading city of the Roman province of Asia, a great port of perhaps 200,000 to 250,000 people, with a theatre seating about twenty-four thousand. It was famous for the temple of Artemis (Diana), one of the seven wonders of the ancient world, and also had temples to the emperors. Paul spent nearly three years there (Acts 19; 20:31), and a riot broke out when the gospel threatened the trade in silver shrines of Artemis (Acts 19:23–41). He warned the Ephesian elders that fierce wolves would come in (Acts 20:29–30), and Timothy was left there to oppose false teaching (1 Timothy 1:3). Early tradition says John himself later lived and ministered in Ephesus. By now the church was perhaps forty years old, into its second generation.

The pattern of the seven letters. Every letter identifies its sender by lifting one feature out of the vision of chapter 1, and the feature chosen is always the one that particular congregation most needs to see. Once the pattern is in view, the variations start speaking. Two churches (Smyrna and Philadelphia) receive no rebuke at all. Two (Sardis and Laodicea) receive almost no praise, and Laodicea none. The rest are mixed. In every church, Christ’s knowledge is complete and his promises are rich.

To the angel of the church in Ephesus write. The angel (angelos, messenger) is most likely a heavenly angel who represents the church before God, but that question need not be resolved to read the letter, because the message is for the whole congregation and, beyond it, for all churches. The letter closes by telling whoever has an ear to hear what the Spirit says to the churches, plural. All seven letters were sent to all seven towns. Ephesus read Laodicea’s mail, and so do we.

The words of him who holds the seven stars in his right hand. “The words of” is tade legei, thus says: the formula the Old Testament prophets used for the LORD’s own speech, Thus says the LORD. Christ speaks with the authority of God. And both halves of his title come from 1:13 and 1:16, and both are sharpened. In chapter 1 he simply held the stars; the word here is stronger (kratōn): he grips them. To a church that may lose its lampstand, he presents himself first as the one who holds the churches firmly in his power.

Who walks among the seven golden lampstands. In chapter 1 he stood in the midst of the lampstands; here he walks among them (peripatōn), which is what an inspector does, and what a priest did as he went from lamp to lamp in the temple. He is not stationed at the front of the room. He is moving through it. He knows what goes on inside every congregation.

Where he is standing before he speaks. That is the picture a church needs before it is criticised, and the order is not accidental. Christ does not begin the correspondence by naming faults. He begins by saying where he is standing. Every hard sentence in the next twenty-eight verses is spoken from inside the room, by someone who has not left and is not going to. Correction from a stranger feels like an attack. Correction from the one who holds you in his right hand is love.

What it does not mean. The seven letters are not a forecast of seven eras of church history. Some teachers have said that Ephesus represents the apostolic church, Laodicea the lukewarm church of the last days, and the others the ages between. But these were real congregations with real problems, each letter is addressed to the churches (2:7), and the scheme only works by reading history in hindsight. They are messages to seven real congregations, and all seven speak to every church in every age.

Which of these letters is written to my church? Very possibly more than one. Any congregation that has ever existed will find itself somewhere in this chapter and the next: correct and cold, poor and hunted, compromised, tolerant of what it should have confronted, asleep, weak and faithful, or comfortable and self-satisfied. Before reading on for the interesting question of who the Nicolaitans were, ask the more useful one. Read all seven and notice which commendation you would most like to hear, and which rebuke makes you most uncomfortable. The discomfort is usually the clue. And remember that the letters are also personal, because each ends with a promise to the one who conquers, singular.

In a sentence. Write this to the angel of the church in Ephesus: These are the words of the one who grips the seven stars in his right hand and walks among the seven golden lampstands.

On a Tuesday. Christ walks among the churches today. Think of your church as he sees it, not as its reputation or its programme describes it. When you next sit in a service, remember that someone is walking the aisles whom nobody else can see, and that he is not there to count heads but to tend lamps.

For worship. The hand that grips the seven stars is the hand that was nailed to a Roman cross, and it has never once opened to let a church fall. The feet that walk among the lampstands walked to Golgotha first. He does not go through his churches as a landlord goes through a property, but as the one who loved the church and gave himself up for her, so that he might present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). Paul wrote those words to this very church, and every hard sentence that follows comes from that love.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the greatest city of Asia and home to the vast temple of Artemis. Paul had spent nearly three years there.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I know your works, your toil and your patient endurance, and how you cannot bear with those who are evil, but have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and found them to be false. I know you are enduring patiently and bearing up for my name's sake, and you have not grown weary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘I know your works, your toil and your patient endurance, and how you cannot bear with those who are evil, but have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and found them to be false. I know you are enduring patiently and bearing up for my name’s sake, and you have not grown weary.

The setting. Travelling preachers moved from church to church, and some claimed apostolic authority they did not have (2 Corinthians 11:13). Churches had to test them (1 John 4:1); an early church manual, the Didache, gives rules for doing so (Didache 11).

I know your works. Every one of the seven letters begins there (oida), and it cuts two ways depending on what is in the works. The fiery-eyed Christ knows everything, the good and the bad. Nothing is hidden from him: comfort for the faithful, warning for the compromising. To Ephesus it opens a commendation that runs for two full verses before a word of criticism.

Your toil and your patient endurance. What he commends is impressive by any measure. Toil is kopos, labour to the point of exhaustion: not activity, but the kind of work that leaves a person emptied. Patient endurance is hypomonē again: staying power under pressure, remaining under the weight. Ephesus was a hard-working, persevering church.

And how you cannot bear with those who are evil. “Cannot bear” (ou dynē bastasai) means they are unable to tolerate. They practised church discipline and did not tolerate evil in their midst, as Pergamum and Thyatira did.

But have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and found them to be false. “Tested” (epeirasas) means examined, put to the proof. “False” (pseudeis) means liars. They measured the claims of teachers against the apostolic gospel and exposed the frauds, and that took nerve, because rejecting a self-proclaimed apostle in the first century meant a public fight. This is exactly what Paul had asked of them. He had warned this very congregation, in tears, that after his departure fierce wolves would come in among them and that men would arise from their own number speaking twisted things (Acts 20:29–31). Ephesus took the warning and acted on it for forty years.

I know you are enduring patiently and bearing up for my name’s sake, and you have not grown weary. Then verse 3 says it again from a different angle, and the repetition is deliberate. There is a play on words: they cannot bear evil people, but they have borne (ebastasas, carried a load) hardship for Christ’s name. And another: they laboured (kopos) without growing weary (ou kekopiakes). They have carried the weight. They have done it for his name and not for their reputation. And they have not given up. Christ says all of it before he says anything else, and he means every word.

For my name’s sake. The motive Christ names is himself. Ephesus has carried its load for his name, and that name is not a label but a person, the one who first carried a heavier load for them. He endured the cross, despising the shame, and weary believers are told to consider him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that they may not grow weary or fainthearted (Hebrews 12:2–3). That is the secret of a church still on its feet after forty years. And the tests they ran on travelling apostles were tests of loyalty to him: false apostles are false because they preach another Jesus (2 Corinthians 11:4, 13).

Why the praise comes first. Which makes what follows in verse 4 far more serious than it would otherwise be. If Christ had opened with the fault, a reader could dismiss the commendation as softening. He opens with the commendation, at length, in detail, and it is genuine. The problem at Ephesus is not that the good things are unreal. It is that a church can have all of them and still be in danger.

What can be counted and what cannot. There is a warning here for anyone who has ever measured a congregation. Everything in these two verses is visible from outside: the workload, the doctrinal spine, the longevity, the discernment. A visitor could count all four in a single Sunday. What is about to be named cannot be counted at all, and only the eyes like a flame of fire could see it. That is why the same church can be commended by every observer and corrected by its Lord in the same letter.

What it does not mean. Christ’s praise shows that sound doctrine and discipline matter. The rebuke that follows does not mean Ephesus should have been less careful about truth. Christ commends their orthodoxy before he calls them back to love.

How do I test a teacher without becoming suspicious of everyone? Test what is taught, not the personality. Ask: does this teaching agree with the plain meaning of Scripture, read in context? Does it confess Jesus Christ as God come in the flesh, crucified and risen (1 John 4:2–3)? Does it lead to holiness, or make sin easy (Jude 4)? Is the teacher’s life consistent with what he says (1 Timothy 3:2–7)? And does he point people to Christ or to himself? You need not interrogate every sermon in a hostile spirit; most faithful teachers will make small mistakes. Testing is for protecting the flock from real error, and it should be done humbly, with Scripture open, in the company of your church and its elders.

In a sentence. I know what you have done: how hard you have worked, how you have persevered, how you refuse to put up with wicked people, and how you have examined those who claimed to be apostles and exposed them as liars; I know you have endured and carried burdens for my name, and have not given up.

On a Tuesday. Test what you hear, even from popular teachers, by Scripture. Christ praises a church that checks the claims of those who speak in his name. And take the things about your own Christian life that you would list if somebody asked how you were doing spiritually. Almost certainly they are things that can be observed: attendance, giving, service, sound convictions, a habit of Bible reading. Every one of them is good, and Christ commends every one of them here. Now ask what would be left if the thing that cannot be observed had quietly gone.

For worship. Nothing done for his name is lost on him. He knows every exhausting week, every hard conversation with a false teacher, every year of faithfulness that nobody thanked, and he names them one by one before he says anything else. The Lord who searches hearts is also the Lord who notices labour, and his praise, when he gives it, is never flattery.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first. Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first. If not, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first. Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first. If not, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.

The setting. Paul had praised the Ephesians for their love toward all the saints (Ephesians 1:15) and ended his letter to them with grace for all who love the Lord Jesus with undying love (Ephesians 6:24). Now, a generation later, that love has cooled. Jesus had warned that because lawlessness would increase, the love of many would grow cold (Matthew 24:12).

But I have this against you. One sentence, and it undoes the tone of everything before it. The praise is real, but so is the charge.

That you have abandoned the love you had at first. The verb matters. It is not that their love has cooled by degrees, the way a room cools when the fire goes out. Aphēkes is the word for leaving something behind, letting it go, releasing it, the same verb used of the disciples leaving their nets. Ephesus has not lost its first love in the way a man loses his keys. It has put it down and walked on.

What is first love? Two answers are usually given and there is no need to choose between them, because the letter itself refuses to. Love for Christ, plainly: the astonishment of a person who has just discovered he is forgiven and cannot get over it. And love for one another, which is what the same apostle spends his first letter insisting cannot be separated from it (1 John 4:20–21). A church that has stopped marvelling at grace will, in short order, stop being gracious. The two go together, and they leave together. The church kept doing the right things, and kept believing the right things, but the warmth of devotion that once drove it had gone. Its battles against false teachers may have left it suspicious and hard, defending the truth without the love that the truth produces.

Picture the difference. A young congregation in the fifties of the first century takes in a runaway slave and hides him at real legal risk, because they cannot get over the fact that they were themselves bought out of slavery. Forty years on, the same congregation, in the same city, correctly identifies a false apostle, writes a careful refutation, and is right in every particular, and nobody in the room would take a risk like that any more. Nothing has been believed that should not be. Nothing has been added to or removed from the creed. The doctrine is exactly what it was and the temperature is not.

Remember therefore from where you have fallen. Christ’s remedy is three verbs, and they are in a deliberate order. Remember (mnēmoneue, keep remembering): not try harder, but look back. Recovery begins with an honest comparison between what you were and what you are, and it is uncomfortable enough that most people skip it. And “fallen” (peptōkes) is a strong word: losing first love is a fall, not a small matter.

Repent, and do the works you did at first. Repent (metanoēson): the word means turn round, change your mind and direction, and it means this is a sin and not a phase. Coldness towards Christ is not a temperament or a season of life; it is something to be confessed. Then do the works you did at first: not wait for the feeling to return, but act. The cure has three steps: remember, repent, return.

The heart reached through the hands. That last instruction is the practical hinge of the letter, and it is enormously freeing. Anyone who has ever tried to manufacture affection for God by sheer effort knows that it does not work and that failing at it produces despair. Christ does not ask for the feeling directly. He asks for the deeds, and he identifies them from the record: the visit you used to make, the giving that used to cost you something, the praying you used to do before anyone was awake, the conversation about Christ you used to be willing to start. Do those. The heart is not reached by being lectured; it is reached through the hands.

The love that did not leave. Set the charge beside the one who makes it. Ephesus has let go of its first love, but its Lord has never let go of his. John, who wrote down this letter, had written in his Gospel that Jesus, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end (John 13:1). And he had told the churches where love begins: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). That is why the remedy starts with remembering. The way back to first love is not to stir up a feeling but to look again at the love that came first, his, which went to the cross and has not cooled for a single day since.

If not, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent. Then the threat, which is severe and precise. “Come” (erchomai) is not the final return here, but a coming in judgement on this church in history. Not I will remove your salvation: this is a letter to a church, and the lampstand is the congregation as a light-bearer (1:20). To remove it means the church would cease to be a witness and finally cease to exist as a church. A church that keeps its doctrine and loses its love does not immediately close; it can run for years on organisation and memory. But the light goes out, and eventually so does everything else. Orthodoxy without love is not enough to keep a church alive. Historically, the church at Ephesus did continue for centuries, which suggests it heeded the warning; but the harbour silted up, the city was abandoned, and Christianity there long ago disappeared. The lampstand stands in a field of ruins.

What it does not mean. Losing the lampstand does not mean true believers lose their salvation. Christ is speaking about the church as a community and its witness. True believers persevere because God keeps them (John 10:28–29); and one way he keeps them is by warnings like this one, which they heed.

How do I know if I have left my first love? Ask a few honest questions. Do I still marvel that I am forgiven, or has it become a fact I simply know? Is prayer something I want or something I manage? Do I love my fellow believers, especially the difficult ones, or mostly assess them? Am I quicker to spot error than to show kindness? Is my service still for Christ, or has it become habit and reputation? No one passes such a test perfectly, and the point is not to measure your feelings on a bad day. It is to notice drift over months and years, and the direction you are moving in.

What if I never had a dramatic first love to go back to? Then do not try to recover a feeling you never had. First love is not a particular emotional experience at conversion; many believers came to Christ quietly, as children or slowly over years. It is the love that answers grace: gratitude, delight in Christ, love for his people. The way into it is the same as the way back to it: look at what Christ has done for you, confess your coldness, and do the works of love. Read the Gospel accounts of the cross slowly. Serve someone in his name. Feelings often follow obedience; they rarely come before it.

In a sentence. But this is my complaint against you: you have walked away from the love you had at the beginning; so remember how far you have fallen, turn back, and do again what you did at first, or else I will come and take your lampstand out of its place, if you will not repent.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly whether your faith has become correct but cold. Remember what Christ’s love once meant to you, confess the drift, and do something today that love for him and for his people would do. Name one concrete work you did at first and have stopped doing, and do it this week.

For worship. The Lord of the churches wants to be loved, not merely obeyed and defended. He walks among the lampstands with the jealous love of the God whose name is Jealous (Exodus 34:14), and a church that is right about him but cold towards him wounds him more deeply than a pagan city can. And even his threat is mercy: he would rather wound Ephesus with the truth than leave it to go dark in comfort, and he gives it the way home in three words a child could follow, because he wants it back.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet this you have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet this you have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.’

The setting. The Nicolaitans are mentioned only here and in v. 15, where they are linked with the teaching of Balaam: eating food offered to idols and sexual immorality (v. 14). Early writers (Irenaeus) connected them with Nicolaus of Antioch, one of the seven in Acts 6:5, but this is uncertain, and later writers simply repeat him. They seem to have taught that Christians could join in pagan feasts and the trade guilds’ idolatrous life, perhaps claiming that what is done in the body does not matter. In Ephesus they were rejected; in Pergamum they were tolerated.

Yet this you have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. Christ returns to commendation before the letter closes, and this is a church he has just warned with the removal of its lampstand. The rebuke is not the last word even inside the same paragraph. What the text supplies about the Nicolaitans is more useful than the guesses: they were almost certainly not a doctrinal sect in the abstract. They were the party of accommodation, the people arguing that a Christian could keep his guild membership, attend the dinner, join the ritual, and privately not mean it.

Hate. Take the word seriously (miseis), because it is used twice and the second time Christ applies it to himself. This is a church commended for hating something. That sits awkwardly with a sentimental picture of Christian love, and it should. Love that cannot hate anything is not love; it is indifference wearing love’s clothes. A father who watched his child being fed poison and felt nothing would not be gentle. And the object of the hatred is stated with care: not the Nicolaitans, but the works of the Nicolaitans. Christ hates the works, not the people; some things are right to hate, whatever destroys his people. Ephesus has got that distinction right while getting first love wrong, and Thyatira will get first love right while getting this wrong. Neither church is asked to trade one for the other.

Whoever has an ear. Jesus often said, He who has ears, let him hear (Matthew 11:15; 13:9), after telling a parable. Here the call is to hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The words are Christ’s, yet John reports them as what the Spirit says: Christ speaks by his Spirit, and the two are not in competition. The sentence assumes a unity between them that no one in the room felt the need to explain. And it is churches, plural. Every letter is for every church.

To the one who conquers. The participle (nikōnti, from nikē, victory) ends every one of the seven letters. It is a fighting word, and it will be defined precisely later in the book: they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death (12:11). The Lamb conquered by being slain (5:5–6). Conquering, in Revelation, is not winning an argument or outlasting an opponent, and it is not winning battles by force. It is holding on to Christ, at cost, to the end. And the conquerors are not an elite class of super-Christians: everyone born of God overcomes the world through faith (1 John 5:4–5). Every true believer conquers. There is no other kind.

I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God. Trace the promise back and the reach of it becomes clear. The tree of life (xylou tēs zōēs) stood in the middle of the garden (Genesis 2:9), and after the fall a guard was set on the way to it so that fallen humanity could not reach out and take and live for ever in its ruin (Genesis 3:22–24). For the whole of Scripture after that, nobody eats from it. It reappears in the last chapter of the Bible, in the middle of the street of the city, with its leaves for the healing of the nations and no sword barring the path (22:2, 14). Paradise (paradeisos, a Persian word for a garden or park) is the word the Greek Old Testament used of Eden. Here in verse 7 the exile is declared over. Christ promises to restore what Adam lost: eternal life in the restored creation, in God’s presence.

The true tree and the true refuge. And see who opens the way back. It is the one who was himself hung on a tree. The goddess Artemis had a sacred tree at her temple, which was also a place of asylum where fugitives could claim protection. Christ offers the true tree, and the true refuge, and the cherub’s sword that barred the path to it fell on him.

What it does not mean. The promise is not a reward for a few especially victorious Christians, while others miss out. All who belong to Christ and persevere in faith will eat from the tree of life. The promise is meant to motivate perseverance, not to divide believers into ranks.

Am I a conqueror if I still struggle with sin? Yes, if you belong to Christ and keep coming back to him. Conquering in Revelation is not sinless perfection or a life of visible triumphs. It is persevering faith: trusting the blood of the Lamb, holding to his word and refusing to give up on him (12:11). A believer who falls, grieves, confesses and gets up again is conquering; the one who gives up on Christ is not. The victory belongs first to the Lamb, and you share it by faith (1 John 5:4). The struggle itself is a sign of life, because the dead do not fight.

Is it ever right for a Christian to hate? Yes, but only what God hates, and only in the way he hates it. Scripture calls us to hate what is evil and hold fast to what is good (Romans 12:9), and to hate even the garment stained by the flesh (Jude 23). That hatred is aimed at sin and the lies that destroy people, never at the people themselves, whom we are to love, even our enemies (Matthew 5:44). The test is simple: if your hatred of a false teaching makes you want to rescue its victims, it is godly; if it makes you enjoy the downfall of its teachers, it has gone bad.

In a sentence. Still, this is to your credit: you hate what the Nicolaitans do, as I do; whoever can hear should listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches; and the one who conquers I will allow to eat from the tree of life in God’s paradise.

On a Tuesday. Notice what kind of compromise you are being asked to make this week, and call it what Christ calls it. And when you are tired of holding on, remember what is at the end: not a reward for the few but a tree for every believer, and the way to it is open.

For worship. The garden gate that closed behind Adam has been opened by the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45). Every believer who holds on, the tired one, the one who falls and gets up, the one who dies unknown, will reach at last for the fruit no human hand has touched since Eden, and nobody will stop him. The tree will stand in the middle of the city, its leaves healing the nations, and the one who grants its fruit is the Lamb who conquered by being slain, who will be there in person to welcome his people home.
verseByVerse.note: The Nicolaitans are unknown outside Revelation; they seem to have taught that believers could take part in pagan feasts and immorality.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — To the Church in Smyrna
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Smyrna, thirty-five miles north, was the most beautiful and most loyal city on the coast — a temple to the goddess Roma from 195 BC and a temple to Tiberius won in competition against ten rival cities in AD 26. Verse 8 introduces Christ to this church as the first and the last, who died and came to life: of all the images in chapter 1, the two about death are handed to the congregation that is about to face it.

Verse 9 names three things he knows. Their tribulation. Their poverty — ptōcheia, the destitution of a beggar, in a wealthy city, and the invoice for their faith. And the slander of those who say they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan. Into the middle of that sentence Christ inserts three words: (but you are rich). Laodicea will receive the exact reverse (3:17).

Verse 10 forbids fear without denying the suffering. The devil is about to throw some of them into prison — and the purpose clause that follows, that you may be tested, does not belong to the devil. The word is the one used of assaying metal; the striking hand is his, the assaying is not (cf. Job 1:12; 1 Pet. 1:6–7). The ten days are a bounded stretch, and the boundary was not set by the persecutor. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life — stephanos, the victor’s wreath, in a city whose own skyline was called the crown of Smyrna.

Verse 11 closes with the refrain and a promise stated negatively: the conqueror will not be hurt by the second death, defined at 20:14 as the lake of fire. Everything Smyrna’s enemies can do to it falls inside the smaller of the two categories.
verseByVerse.theology:
Poor, and Rich

Christ, who died and came to life, knows Smyrna’s tribulation and poverty — and says they are rich. Suffering is coming, bounded and purposeful; the faithful will not be hurt by the second death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Polycarp, bishop of this church some sixty years later, served Christ to the fire.

Now: Grace for a trial is given on the day of the trial, not in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Smyrna write: 'The words of the first and the last, who died and came to life. "'I know your tribulation and your poverty (but you are rich) and the slander of those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And to the angel of the church in Smyrna write: ‘The words of the first and the last, who died and came to life. ‘I know your tribulation and your poverty (but you are rich) and the slander of those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.

The setting. Smyrna (modern Izmir) was a wealthy port about 35 miles (56 kilometres) north of Ephesus, a beautiful planned city that called itself the first of Asia, with a paved street running from the harbour to the temple of Zeus and a ring of public buildings along the ridge of Mount Pagos that visitors called the crown of Smyrna. It was fiercely loyal to Rome: it built one of the first temples to the goddess Roma (195 BC) and won the honour of a temple to the emperor Tiberius (AD 26) in a competition among eleven cities. Emperor worship was intense, and refusing it was seen as disloyalty. The city had a large and influential Jewish community. Destroyed around 600 BC and refounded three centuries later, it was said to have died and come back to life. Around AD 155, Polycarp, the elderly bishop of Smyrna, was burned alive for refusing to call Caesar lord.

The words of the first and the last, who died and came to life. Every letter takes its self-description from chapter 1, and this one takes the two clauses about death (1:17–18) and hands them to the church that is about to face it. To a congregation being told to prepare for prison, the credential offered is not power in the abstract. It is that he has been where they are going. The one giving the orders has been dead. As the city had, in a sense, died and lived again, the true Lord has truly died and risen.

I know your tribulation and your poverty. Tribulation (thlipsin) is pressure, persecution. The word for poverty is ptōcheia: not the modest means of a working family but destitution, the poverty of a beggar with nothing. In a rich city. That is not an accident of economics. A Christian who would not join the guild ritual lost the guild’s work, and a Jewish believer disowned by the synagogue lost the legal protection that exempted Jews from emperor worship. Some may have had their goods seized (Hebrews 10:34). Their poverty was the invoice for their faith.

(But you are rich). Into the middle of that sentence Christ inserts three words in brackets, and the parenthesis is the whole letter. He does not deny the poverty; he has just named it. He sets a second balance sheet beside the first and says the second is the real one. They are rich in the things that matter: in faith, and heirs of the kingdom (James 2:5). Laodicea, in the next chapter, will get the mirror image: rich in its own eyes, but wretched, pitiable and poor (3:17). Two churches, two account books, and the figures inverted in both.

Two instruments of measurement. Of the seven congregations, the two that receive no criticism whatever are Smyrna and Philadelphia, and both are poor and under pressure. The one that receives no commendation whatever is the wealthiest. Nothing in that pattern says money is evil or that hardship is holy by itself. It says that the instrument we habitually use to assess spiritual health is not the instrument Christ uses, and that the two readings can be exactly opposite.

And the slander of those who say that they are Jews and are not. Slander (blasphēmian) is abusive speech. Local Jews apparently denounced Christians to the authorities. Jews had legal tolerance in the empire and were excused from emperor worship; once they disowned the Christians as not Jews, Christians were exposed. In the account of Polycarp’s martyrdom, written by the church of Smyrna itself, the crowd gathered wood for the fire, and Smyrna’s Jews were said to have joined eagerly in it.

But are a synagogue of Satan. Synagogue (synagōgē) means assembly, gathering. Satan means the accuser, the adversary. The word is functional: by accusing God’s people, they were doing Satan’s work, for Satan is the accuser of the brothers (12:10), and whoever brings accusations against the people of God is doing the accuser’s work, whatever synagogue or church he attends. Christ says they are Jews in name but not in reality. As Paul says, the true Jew is one inwardly, by the Spirit (Romans 2:28–29); and all who belong to Christ are Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29).

What it does not mean. This is not antisemitism, and must never be used to justify it. Christ, John and the first church were Jews; the same apostle wrote that salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22). The words are aimed at a particular community that persecuted Christians, and the charge is spiritual, not ethnic: rejecting the Messiah and accusing his people. Reading this verse as a statement about Jewish people in general has done terrible damage in the history of the church, and it is a sin to be repented of. Scripture holds out hope for Israel’s salvation (Romans 11:25–29), and Christians are called to love their Jewish neighbours and pray for them.

Does this mean faithful Christians will always be poor? No. Scripture does not make poverty a badge of holiness, and it records faithful believers with property who used it for others (Acts 16:14–15; Romans 16:23). The point is that Christ’s accounts differ from ours. Faithfulness sometimes costs money, as it did in Smyrna, and when it does he counts the believer rich. Prosperity is not proof of his favour, and hardship is not proof of his displeasure. Ask not how much you have, but whether anything you have has been bought with compromise, and whether you are rich toward God (Luke 12:21).

In a sentence. To the angel of the church in Smyrna write: These are the words of the first and the last, who was dead and came back to life: I know what you are suffering and how poor you are, though in truth you are rich, and I know the slander of those who claim to be Jews but are not; they are a gathering that serves Satan.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ costs you money or reputation, he knows. In his account you are rich. If you are slandered for your faith, do not answer in kind; leave the accuser’s work to the accuser and keep doing your Lord’s. And if you are comfortable, ask whether your church’s instruments of measurement are Christ’s or the city’s.

For worship. The Lord who calls Smyrna rich knows poverty from the inside. Though he was rich, for our sake he became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9): laid in a manger because there was no room, owning no place to lay his head, slandered, falsely accused and stripped of his clothes at the end. Every coin his people lose for his name is entered in a book kept by one who gave up everything for them, and what he has made them heirs to no magistrate in Smyrna can confiscate.
verseByVerse.note: Smyrna (modern Izmir) was a wealthy port, loyal to Rome, with a large Jewish community, some of whom were slandering the church.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison, that you may be tested, and for ten days you will have tribulation. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison, that you may be tested, and for ten days you will have tribulation. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.

The setting. In the Roman world, prison was not usually a punishment in itself; it was a place to hold people before trial or execution. To be thrown into prison often meant death was coming.

Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Not do not fear, you will not suffer. The suffering is confirmed in the same sentence in which the fear is forbidden. “Do not fear” (mēden phobou) is literally fear nothing. Christ does not promise to stop the suffering; he tells them not to be afraid of it, as he told John (1:17). Whatever comfort this verse gives, it does not work by promising that the thing will not happen.
