Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison. The agent is named, and he is real. Devil (diabolos) means slanderer. This is not blind misfortune; somebody is doing it. Behind the slanderers and the Roman courts stands the devil, and persecution has a spiritual source. Some of you, not all, which is worse in one way, because it means the congregation will spend the coming months not knowing who. Yet even the devil can act only within the limits God allows, as in Job 1–2.

That you may be tested. Then the clause that turns the verse over. It is a purpose clause, and the purpose does not belong to the devil. He throws them in to destroy their faith; that is what he is for. The sentence says the imprisonment has another purpose running through the same event, and that purpose is the proving of something valuable (peirasthēte, tried, proved). The devil is permitted to strike, and while he strikes he is unwittingly doing the assayer’s work. Job was the first man to live inside that arrangement (Job 1:12), and Peter said the same to churches in this same province: the tested genuineness of your faith is more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire (1 Peter 1:6–7). The same event has two purposes, and only one of them will prevail.

Endurance, not stoicism. That clause is the difference between endurance and mere stoicism. A believer facing something frightening does not principally need to be told that it will end. He needs to know whether it means anything. This says it does: the thing coming at you has been given a purpose it did not choose, and the purpose is not your destruction.

And for ten days you will have tribulation. Ten days is short. In a book where numbers carry meaning, ten is the round figure for a complete but limited stretch; Daniel and his friends were tested for ten days (Daniel 1:12–14). Nobody should press it into a calendar. The point is the shape: the suffering is real, but it has a stated duration, and the one who states it is not the devil. There is a fence around this, and the fence was not built by the man who is about to be arrested.

Be faithful unto death. Faithful (pistos) means loyal, trustworthy. Unto death (achri thanatou) can mean faithful right up to the end of your life, and it can mean faithful even to the point of being killed. Both were true in Smyrna. Not just until you die naturally, but even if faithfulness costs your life.

And I will give you the crown of life. The crown is stephanos, the victor’s wreath of leaves given at the games, not the royal diadem. Every athlete in Smyrna knew that the wreath was brown within a week (1 Corinthians 9:25). And the citizens of Smyrna called the ring of buildings on their skyline the crown of the city. Christ takes the local word for a beauty that lasts a generation and a sporting trophy that lasts a week, and offers instead a crown that is life itself: eternal life (James 1:12). They may lose their earthly lives, but they will receive life that cannot end.

The faithful one asks for faithfulness. The command comes from the one who kept it first. He is the faithful witness (1:5), who became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8), and who introduced himself to this church as the one who died and came to life (2:8). He does not ask Smyrna to walk anywhere he has not walked. And the crown is his to give because he won it: the life he holds out is his own resurrection life, which the firstborn of the dead shares with all his younger brothers and sisters. Faithfulness unto death is following him to the place where death was beaten.

What it does not mean. Faithfulness unto death is not a work that earns salvation. It is the fruit and evidence of true faith, which God himself sustains. The crown is a gift (I will give).

Is the crown of life only for martyrs? No. It is eternal life itself, given to all who remain faithful to the end (James 1:12). The Smyrnaeans faced death, but the promise is for every faithful believer, including the one who dies quietly in a hospital bed after a long life of ordinary faithfulness. What the martyr shows openly, every believer shows in his own way: that Christ is worth more than life.

What if I am afraid I would deny Christ under pressure? Many are, and the fear is not a sign of unbelief. The question is not whether you feel you could face a prison. Nobody feels that, and Peter, who was certain he could, could not (Luke 22:33, 57). Grace is not issued in advance for a trial you are not in. It is issued on the day, in the cell, at the fire, which is exactly what Christ promised (Luke 21:14–15). Smyrna was not being asked to generate courage in the weeks before the arrests. It was being told who would be with them when they came. Your part today is faithfulness in the smaller costs; his part is the strength for the great ones.

In a sentence. Do not be afraid of what you are going to suffer: the devil will throw some of you into prison to test you, and you will be afflicted for a short time; stay faithful even if it costs your life, and I will give you life as your victor’s crown.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for believers in prison for Christ; there are many, in many countries, and they are your brothers and sisters. And ask him for the courage to be faithful in the smaller costs you face, the mockery, the missed promotion, the awkward silence, so that you are ready if greater ones come.

For worship. The devil keeps a prison, but the Lord of Smyrna sets the length of every stay, and the enemy cannot add a day to it. He takes the weapon aimed at his people’s faith and makes it the fire that proves it gold. And when the ten days are over, the one who holds the keys of Death and Hades will stand at the door the devil thought he had locked, and set on every faithful head the crown that does not wither, which is life with him for ever.
verseByVerse.note: “Ten days” probably means a short, limited time.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death.’

The Spirit’s word to Smyrna. As at the close of every letter, whoever has an ear is to hear what the Spirit says to the churches: Smyrna’s letter, too, is for every church. And then comes a promise phrased entirely in the negative.

The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death. “Will not be hurt” (ou mē adikēthē) is the strongest form of denial in Greek: will certainly never be harmed. The phrase second death occurs four times in Scripture and all four are in this book. Revelation explains it as the lake of fire, final and eternal punishment after the resurrection and judgement (20:6, 14; 21:8). The first death is physical death; the second is eternal separation from God under his judgement. Smyrna’s believers may suffer the first death, but they will never suffer the second.

The smaller of the two categories. Set that against the situation on the ground. The magistrate can compel the first death and has no jurisdiction whatever over the second. The devil can throw them into prison and cannot follow them past the grave. Everything the enemies of this congregation are able to do to it is contained inside the smaller of the two categories. Jesus had said it in one sentence: do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matthew 10:28; Luke 12:4).

What is not promised. Something is conspicuously not promised, and the honesty of it is part of the comfort. Smyrna is not told it will escape the first death. Several of them will not. Christ does not offer his most faithful church protection from the thing it fears; he offers immunity from the thing it has not thought about. It is the only kind of consolation that is actually true, and the only kind that holds when the cell door shuts.

Polycarp. Polycarp was bishop of this church about sixty years after this letter arrived, and he may well have heard it read as a young man. When the proconsul at Smyrna urged him to swear by the fortune of Caesar and revile Christ, he answered that he had served him eighty-six years and Christ had never done him wrong, and asked how he could blaspheme his King and Saviour. They burned him in the stadium. The account the church of Smyrna wrote afterwards says that when they came to nail him to the stake he asked them to leave him unfastened, because the one who gave him strength to endure the fire would give him strength to stay still in it. The letter to Smyrna had done its work.

Where Christians differ: is the second death the end of existence? Annihilationists hold that the second death means the wicked cease to exist after judgement. Verdict: Revelation describes the lake of fire as torment day and night for ever and ever (20:10; 14:11), and Jesus spoke of eternal punishment alongside eternal life (Matthew 25:46). The second death is called death because it is the final loss of all that makes life life: God’s presence and favour. It is conscious, eternal punishment, which is exactly why the promise here is so precious.

What it does not mean. The promise does not imply that some true believers may be hurt by the second death. All who are in Christ are safe from condemnation (Romans 8:1).

How can a loving God allow a second death? Because he is also just, and sin against an infinitely holy God is not a small thing. The second death is not God losing his temper; it is his settled, righteous judgement on those who refuse him to the end, and Scripture says it will be seen to be right (16:5–7; 19:1–2). But notice what this verse actually does with the doctrine: it turns it into comfort and invitation. The second death has no power over anyone in Christ, because Christ bore the judgement in their place (Romans 5:9; 1 Thessalonians 1:10). The way out is open to anyone who will come to him now.

In a sentence. Whoever can hear should listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches: the one who conquers will never be harmed by the second death.

On a Tuesday. When you are afraid of what people could do to you, measure it against this verse. The worst they can do is contained inside the smaller of the two deaths. And if someone you love does not yet know Christ, let the reality of the second death make you pray and speak, gently and soon.

For worship. The Lord of Smyrna has drunk to the bottom the cup of judgement his people deserved, and there is nothing left in it for them. The magistrate may take a believer’s first life; the second is guarded by the one who died and came to life, and no court on earth or in hell can reach it. He offered his most faithful church no escape from prison or the stake, and gave it something better: a death that cannot hurt them twice, and a life that the fire at Smyrna only hurried them into.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — To the Church in Pergamum
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Pergamum, inland on a cone of rock a thousand feet high, was the administrative capital of the province and the seat of the governor — the place where the right of the sword actually resided. Verse 12 accordingly introduces Christ as him who has the sharp two-edged sword. Verse 13 says I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is: the Great Altar of Zeus on its terrace, the serpent-emblemed healing shrine of Asklepios whose god was titled Saviour, and the province’s first temple to a living emperor, all on the same hill. In that city they held fast his name and did not deny the faith even when Antipas — given Christ’s own title from 1:5, my faithful witness — was killed among them.

Verses 14–15 bring the charge. Some there hold the teaching of Balaam, who could not curse Israel and so taught Balak to seduce it instead (Num. 22–24; 25:1–9; 31:16): eating food sacrificed to idols and practising sexual immorality, which in a guild town arrived in the same evening. Verse 15 adds the Nicolaitans — the very group Ephesus was commended for hating in v. 6. The accusation is not that the whole church holds this, but that the church has some there who hold it, unchallenged.

Verse 16 commands the whole congregation to repent, and the pronouns then separate ominously: I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth. A church that will not act against error is not exempted from the action; the action is simply taken by someone else, in the middle of the assembly.

Verse 17 sounds the refrain and gives three promises, each the reverse of what the compromisers wanted: hidden manna instead of guild meat (Ex. 16:33–34; cf. John 6:35), a white stone — a juror’s acquittal pebble, a victor’s banquet token, a guest’s ticket, the readings differ — and a new name known only to the one who receives it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Second Strategy

Pergamum held fast under the sword but tolerated the teaching of Balaam — the invitation to compromise at the idol-feast. The whole church is called to repent of its silence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Guild banquets tied a man’s livelihood to idol meat.

Now: The argument for compromise is always reasonable. Christ offers hidden manna and a new name instead.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Pergamum write: 'The words of him who has the sharp two-edged sword. "'I know where you dwell, where Satan's throne is. Yet you hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith even in the days of Antipas my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And to the angel of the church in Pergamum write: ‘The words of him who has the sharp two-edged sword. ‘I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is. Yet you hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith even in the days of Antipas my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells.

The setting. Pergamum, about 65 miles (105 kilometres) north of Smyrna, was the old capital of the province and probably still the seat of the Roman governor, who had the right of the sword: the power to execute. It stood on a huge cone of rock about a thousand feet above the plain, crowned with temples, among them the first in Asia to the emperor Augustus and the goddess Roma (29 BC), which made it the centre of emperor worship in the province. Its library was second only to Alexandria’s, and parchment (pergamēnē) is named after it.

The words of him who has the sharp two-edged sword. Christ introduces himself to this city, and only to this city, with the sword from 1:16. The governor of Asia held a sword by delegation and used it on Antipas. There is another sword in this letter. It comes out of a mouth, and its owner did not receive it from anyone. The governor has the sword of Rome, but Christ has the sword that really decides life and death: his word. And he will use it against the false teachers in the church (v. 16).

I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is. Three or four things in Pergamum have been proposed as the throne, and a first-century Christian climbing that hill would have seen them all. The Great Altar of Zeus stood on a terrace near the summit, its frieze carved with gods destroying giants, and from below it looked like a throne on a mountain. Below that lay the shrine of Asclepius, the most famous healing centre in Asia, whose god’s emblem was a serpent and who was worshipped under the title Saviour. The governor’s seat of judgement was there. And Pergamum had built the province’s first temple to a living emperor, which made it the birthplace of the imperial cult in Asia. The best explanation is the city’s leadership in emperor worship, combined with the governor’s power to condemn Christians: Satan’s power was concentrated there. Political power, false salvation and a serpent, all on one hill.

Where you dwell. The verb Christ uses of the church is katoikeis, the word for settled, permanent residence, not for lodging somewhere temporarily. And at the end of the verse he uses the same root of Satan: where Satan dwells. They live there. He lives there. Nobody is passing through. They did not choose the place, and Christ knows how hard it is.

Faithfulness on hard ground. That answers a question honest Christians ask about where they have ended up. Christ does not tell this congregation to move. He does not say that a believer should not be living in a place like that, or that their difficulty would be solved by relocation. He says I know where you dwell, and then commends them for what they have done while dwelling there. The address is not the problem. Faithfulness is measured on the ground a person is actually standing on, and some believers are standing on very hard ground by appointment rather than by mistake.

Yet you hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith. Two verbs, one positive and one negative, and in a city with a governor holding a sword they mean something specific. Hold fast (krateis) is to grip firmly: holding fast the name means still saying it in public. Deny (ērnēsō) is to disown: when the question came, and in this city it came formally, with a magistrate and a written record, they did not give the required answer. The test in the Roman world was rarely a demand to renounce Christ in a long speech. It was usually a demand to say Caesar is Lord and offer a pinch of incense, and perhaps to curse Christ, after which a man could believe whatever he liked in private. Pergamum would not do it. “My faith” (tēn pistin mou) means faith in me, or the faithfulness owed to me.

Even in the days of Antipas my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells. This is the only place in the Bible where the name occurs, and nothing else is known about him with any certainty; later tradition says he was roasted in a bronze bull. What is known is the title Christ gives him. In 1:5 Christ himself is the faithful witness (ho martys ho pistos). Here he hands his own description to a man from Pergamum who died in the same manner. Nobody remembers who the governor was. There is one name from that courtroom that the risen Christ has kept, and it is not the man who held the sword. Killed (apektanthē): martyrdom had already begun.

Among you. Two words remain, and they are among the most consoling in the letter. Not in your city, not in that period: among you. They had watched it happen, and Christ names their friend in front of everyone. Nothing done to the church at Pergamum happened out of sight.

What it does not mean. Satan’s throne does not mean Satan rules there in place of God. Christ holds the sword, and Satan’s power is borrowed and limited. Nor does living where Satan dwells excuse compromise; it calls for greater faithfulness.

Should I move away from a place, or a job, that is hostile to my faith? Not necessarily. Christ did not tell Pergamum to leave, and Christians are scattered into hard places on purpose, to be light there (Matthew 5:14; Jeremiah 29:7). Hostility alone is not a reason to go. But there are times when a wise believer should move: when staying would require you to sin, when your family is in real danger, or when a door opens elsewhere that does not depend on running from faithfulness (Matthew 10:23). Ask whether you are leaving to escape the cost of faithfulness or because faithfulness itself leads you on. Pray, take counsel, and wherever you are, hold fast his name.

In a sentence. To the angel of the church in Pergamum write: These are the words of the one who holds the sharp double-edged sword: I know where you live, in the place where Satan has his throne, and yet you keep a firm grip on my name and did not disown your faith in me, even when Antipas, my faithful witness, was put to death among you in the city where Satan lives.

On a Tuesday. You may live and work where unbelief seems to sit on a throne. Christ knows where you dwell. Hold fast his name there. When you are asked for your small pinch of incense, the sentence you do not believe, the silence that keeps the peace at your Lord’s expense, remember Antipas, whose name is known in heaven while the governor’s is forgotten.

For worship. The Lord of Pergamum once stood where Antipas stood, before a Roman governor who held the power of the sword, and he told the truth and was killed. He told that governor he would have no authority at all unless it had been given him from above (John 18:37; 19:10–11), and now the governor’s seat is empty and the crucified one holds the only sword that decides anything. The records of Rome lie in the dust, and the name of one faithful man from Satan’s hill is read aloud in every church on earth, because Christ chose to keep it.
verseByVerse.note: Pergamum was a centre of emperor worship and home to a great altar of Zeus — perhaps why it is called the place “where Satan’s throne is.”

verseByVerse.quote: But I have a few things against you: you have some there who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality. So also you have some who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I have a few things against you: you have some there who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality. So also you have some who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.

The setting. Balak, king of Moab, hired the prophet Balaam to curse Israel, but God turned the curse to blessing (Numbers 22–24). Balaam became the classic example of a prophet who leads God’s people into sin for profit (2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11).

But I have a few things against you. The commendation stops. A faithful church can still have serious faults. And the problem is not that Pergamum has denied Christ under pressure, because it has not. The problem is what it has permitted inside the room while standing firm at the door.

You have some there who hold the teaching of Balaam. The reference is to one of the strangest episodes in the Old Testament. Balaam tried four times to curse Israel and could not; every time he opened his mouth a blessing came out. Curses had failed. So, as Scripture states much later when Moses is accounting for a disaster, Balaam gave different advice (Numbers 31:16). Israel was invited to the Moabite festivals, ate the sacrifices, committed immorality with the women of Moab, bowed to Baal of Peor, and twenty-four thousand died in a plague (Numbers 25:1–9). What could not be cursed from outside was seduced from inside. And it is called teaching (didachēn): not merely bad behaviour but a doctrine that justified it, taught within the church. The sword did not work at Pergamum, so the strategy changed, and the second strategy was working.

Who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel. A stumbling block (skandalon) is a trap, the bait stick that springs it, something that makes people fall.

So that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality. The two specifics named were not two unrelated vices. In a Roman city they usually arrived in the same evening. Trade guilds were also religious associations; the carpenters, the dyers, the bakers each had a patron deity, and membership involved attending banquets held in the temple precincts, where the meat had been offered on the altar and where the later part of the evening often involved sexual licence. Refuse the dinner and you are outside the guild. Outside the guild there is no work. Food sacrificed to idols (eidōlothyta): eating meat that had once been offered to an idol was not wrong in itself, if bought in the market or eaten at a private meal (1 Corinthians 10:25–27). But eating it in the idol’s temple, as part of a feast in the god’s honour, was participating in idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:19–22), and the Jerusalem council had asked Gentile believers to abstain from both (Acts 15:29). Sexual immorality (porneusai) is any sexual relations outside marriage between a man and a woman. Possibly also spiritual unfaithfulness, as the Old Testament often calls idolatry adultery, but in context the literal sense is clear.

Two tables. Behind the guild dinner stands the question Paul had already put to another Greek city: whose table are you sitting at? The cup of blessing is a participation in the blood of Christ, and the bread a participation in his body (1 Corinthians 10:16), and a Christian cannot eat at the Lord’s table on the first day of the week and at the god’s table on the next feast day as though both meant nothing. The compromisers said the idol was nothing, so the meal was nothing. Christ’s answer is that his own table is not nothing. He gave his body and blood for his people, and no guild in Asia had anything to set beside that.

Balaam’s argument today. At that point the letter stops being about the first century. The party of accommodation in Pergamum was not arguing for wickedness. It was arguing that a man has to feed his family, that the ritual means nothing to a Christian anyway, and that God looks on the heart. Almost nobody reading this is being asked to burn incense. A great many people are being asked to say something in a meeting they do not believe, to stay quiet where speaking would cost a promotion, to let a client’s arrangements go unquestioned, to laugh at the table, to sleep with someone they are not married to because everyone does. And the argument that carries the day is always Balaam’s: it is only a formality, everyone does it, the alternative is your income, and God knows your heart. The stumbling block is not laid in front of people who want to fall. It is laid in front of people who need the work.

So also you have some who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans. “So also” (houtōs, in the same way): the Nicolaitans’ teaching is the same as Balaam’s, or very like it. And the parallel with verse 6 is exact and pointed. Ephesus hated the works of the Nicolaitans; Pergamum has some who hold their teaching. The same error, a hundred miles apart, met with rejection in one church and hospitality in the other. Between the two letters Christ has now criticised a church for being loveless and a church for being tolerant, which forecloses the comfortable assumption that one of these is the safe direction to err in.

You have some there. And the grammar of the accusation should not slip past. He does not say some of you hold this teaching, which would be a charge against individuals. He says you have some there who hold it: the charge is against the church for having them, unchallenged, in the membership. Pergamum’s sin is not that a few people were wrong. It is that nobody said anything.

What it does not mean. The problem was not that the church contained sinners; every church does. It was that the church tolerated teachers who taught that sin was acceptable, and did not discipline them. Pergamum had the opposite fault from Ephesus: love without truth, where Ephesus had truth without love.

Does this contradict Paul, who allows eating meat bought in the market? No. Paul allows eating market meat without asking questions (1 Corinthians 10:25), but he too forbids taking part in idol feasts: you cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons (1 Corinthians 10:21). Here the false teachers were leading Christians into idol feasts and the sexual immorality that went with them; that is what Christ condemns. For us the principle is the same. Ordinary things in an unbelieving world are not defiling in themselves. Taking part in worship of another god, or in sin dressed up as custom, is.

Where is the line between living in the culture and compromising with it? Ask three questions. Does this require me to do what God forbids, or to deny or hide Christ when faithfulness calls me to own him? Does it involve taking part in worship or celebration of something false, rather than simply being present among unbelievers? And is my real reason fear of loss, dressed up as wisdom? Christians can work in secular jobs, attend a colleague’s wedding, eat at a neighbour’s table and share in the common life of their town; Jesus ate with sinners. But when the price of belonging is sin, the answer must be no, even if it costs the job. Take counsel from mature believers when the case is not clear.

In a sentence. But I have some things against you: some among you hold to the teaching of Balaam, who showed Balak how to trap Israel into eating food offered to idols and committing sexual immorality; and in the same way, some of you hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.

On a Tuesday. Watch for teaching that makes compromise with the culture seem wise and safe, especially where your job or income is at stake. The pressure to fit in is often more dangerous than open hostility. Name the place in your week where Balaam’s argument is loudest, and decide now, before the moment, what faithfulness will look like there.

For worship. The Lord who could not be cursed out of loving his people will not let them be seduced out of it either. He sees through Balaam’s soft advice as clearly as through the governor’s sword, and he calls his church back because he will not share his bride with the idols of the market. His jealousy for his people is the jealousy of a husband, and it is love.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore repent. If not, I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore repent. If not, I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth.

The setting. Balaam himself was confronted by the angel of the Lord with a drawn sword (Numbers 22:23, 31).

Therefore repent. Two words (metanoēson), addressed to the whole congregation, including the majority who have done nothing wrong except let it happen. That is the first thing to see here. The people who held Balaam’s teaching are a faction; the command to repent goes to everyone. The church must repent of tolerating them, and the false teachers must repent of their teaching. A church is answerable for what it tolerates, and silence is a decision.

If not, I will come to you soon. “Come” (erchomai) is a coming in judgement on this church in history, not only the final return. And soon (tachy) carries the sense of speed rather than of the calendar. It does not necessarily mean next month. It means without delay once the decision is taken, and it means the matter is not going to be left indefinitely. God’s patience is real, and the next letter will show him giving a false prophetess time to repent, but it is patience with a purpose, not tolerance without a limit.

And war against them with the sword of my mouth. Then the wording is unexpected. He comes to you; he wars (polemēsō, makes war) against them. The pronouns separate, and the separation is deliberate and faintly terrifying. Christ will arrive at the congregation and conduct a battle inside it, against the false teachers, and the faithful majority will be standing in the room while he does. Refusing to act against error does not exempt a church from the action. It simply means the action is taken by someone else, in the middle of the assembly, without consultation. The faithful do not need to fear his sword, but they will see it used.

The sword of his mouth. The sword is the one from 1:16 and 2:12: his word of judgement, which exposes and condemns false teaching (19:15). That is how he fights. It is not a metaphor for something gentler; a sword is for cutting, and in 19:15 the same sword strikes the nations. But it does tell a church what the instrument of correction is, and therefore what its own instrument should have been. Pergamum was not asked to expel anyone by force or to organise against the faction. It was asked to say the true thing out loud, which is precisely what nobody there was doing.

The sword they could not see. There is an irony in the letter that a first-century reader in that city would have felt at once. Pergamum is where the sword of Rome lives. The believers there have already faced it and not flinched; Antipas went to his death rather than say the words. The sword they could see did not move them. The danger they had not noticed came from a sword they could not see, and it was pointed the other way: not at their bodies, which were brave, but at the purity of the church, which was unguarded.

Balaam’s end. Balaam himself is a warning attached to this. He is one of the few figures in Scripture who spoke true prophecy, blessed God’s people four times against his own financial interest, and predicted the star that would come out of Jacob (Numbers 24:17), a line this chapter picks up at verse 28. And he died by the sword, among the Midianites, fighting against the people he had blessed (Numbers 31:8). Getting the doctrine right and saying true things about Christ is not the same as being on his side, and a man can do the first for years while drifting into the second.

What it does not mean. This does not authorise Christians to fight false teachers with physical weapons or violence. Christ’s sword is his word. The church’s weapons are the truth, and church discipline (Matthew 18:15–20; 2 Corinthians 10:3–5).

Does Christ really fight against people inside his own church? Yes, against those who lead his people astray and will not repent. Not everyone on a church roll belongs to Christ (1 John 2:19), and he will not let wolves feed on his flock for ever. His war is waged by his word: the false teaching is exposed, consciences are troubled, judgement falls, and sometimes those who persist are removed. For the faithful this is protection, not threat. And for anyone who has been drawn into error, the first word of the verse is still open: repent. The sword is the last resort of a Lord who would much rather heal.

What should I do if my church tolerates false teaching? Begin with prayer and with your own heart, and make sure the issue is real error, not a matter of preference. Then speak, humbly and privately, to the elders, with Scripture open (Matthew 18:15; Galatians 6:1). Be patient; churches often move slowly. If the leaders themselves teach serious error about the gospel, or refuse to deal with open, unrepentant sin, and will not listen, you may in the end need to leave quietly for a faithful church, for your own sake and your family’s. But do not leave in a spirit of pride, and do not stop loving the people you leave.

In a sentence. So repent; otherwise I will come to you without delay and fight against those people with the sword that comes out of my mouth.

On a Tuesday. If you are tolerating a sin because confronting it would be uncomfortable, Christ calls you to repent. It is better to be corrected by his word now than fought by it later. The door that stands open in this verse is the same door that closes in verse 22. Walk through it while it is open.

For worship. The Lord of the church is not a distant inspector who files reports. He comes in person, and he fights for the purity of his bride with the same word that made the worlds. His patience waits, his warning calls, and his sword, when it falls, falls to save his people from those who would devour them.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it.’

The setting. Manna was the bread from heaven that fed Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16), and a jar of it was kept in the ark of the covenant (Exodus 16:33–34; Hebrews 9:4). Jewish tradition said that when the temple was destroyed, the ark and its manna were hidden by Jeremiah, and the Messiah would bring them out again.

Three promises against the guild. Here, as at the close of every letter, whoever has an ear is to hear what the Spirit says to the churches. Then come three promises, and every one of them is the reverse of something the compromisers in Pergamum were arguing for. They wanted the guild dinner; Christ offers hidden manna. They wanted the token of admission; Christ offers a white stone. They wanted to keep their standing in the city; Christ offers a new name.

To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna. Manna fell in the wilderness for forty years, and a jar of it was kept inside the ark as a permanent memorial, hidden in the sense that it was behind the veil where no one but the high priest could go, once a year. Set that against the issue in the letter and the promise lands exactly. The argument in Pergamum was about meat: eat what the temple provides, or lose your income. Christ answers with a different menu. Israel in the desert was fed by God alone, daily, for four decades, in a place with no fields and no guilds, and nobody starved. And the Lord who says this once said of himself, in a synagogue argument about manna, I am the bread of life (John 6:35, 48–51). Those who refuse to eat food offered to idols will eat the bread of heaven: Christ himself, and the feast of eternal life with him, the marriage supper of the Lamb (19:9). What they give up is nothing compared with what they will receive. What is hidden now is a Person, and the hiddenness is temporary.

And I will give him a white stone. This one is genuinely uncertain, and several proposals have been made by careful readers. A juror in a Greek court dropped a white pebble (psēphon leukēn) for acquittal and a black one for condemnation. A victor at the games could be given a token that admitted him to the celebration banquet. A guest at a feast received an inscribed ticket, and inscribed stones were also worn as amulets. Given the banquet in this verse, the most likely meaning is a ticket of admission to the messianic feast, combined with the sense of acquittal: the white stone of the verdict not guilty. Those shut out of the guilds’ feasts are admitted to Christ’s. What all the proposals share matters more than deciding between them: the stone is small, personal, handed to one individual, and it is the thing that gets him in.

With a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it. A new name (onoma kainon) in Scripture marks a changed identity and relationship conferred by God: Abram became Abraham, Jacob became Israel, Simon became Peter. Isaiah 62:2 and 65:15 promise God’s people a new name. Whose name is it? Possibly the believer’s new name, given by Christ, a personal and intimate sign of belonging; or Christ’s own name, which only those who know him truly understand (3:12; 19:12). Either way, the striking clause is the privacy of it. Nobody else knows it. Whatever else it means, it means that the knowledge Christ has of each of his people is particular and not generic. He is not handing out identical certificates to a crowd.

What the city takes and Christ gives. Consider what that says to the specific people being addressed. A tradesman in Pergamum who refuses the guild dinner loses, in order: his contracts, his standing, and eventually the way the city refers to him. He becomes the awkward one, the man who could not be reasonable. That is a real cost and this letter does not pretend otherwise. What it says is that a name is being kept for him which the city could not have given and cannot take, written on a stone, known to Christ and to him and to nobody else in the world.

What it does not mean. Nothing here supports secret knowledge for spiritual elites, as later Gnostic groups taught. The new name is known by the one who receives it, and every conquering believer receives one.

Does God really know me personally, or just love his people in general? He knows you personally, and this verse is the answer, deliberately intimate. For anyone who has ever felt that God’s love is a general policy rather than something addressed to them, that he saves crowds and might not have noticed one particular obscure believer in one particular unglamorous town, here is a private name, on a stone, in his hand, for you. The Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3), and he knew you before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). You are not lost in the crowd of the redeemed.

Will I lose my own identity in heaven? No. A new name in Scripture does not erase the person; it fulfils him. Abraham was still the man from Ur, and Peter was still the fisherman from Galilee, but each became more truly himself under the name God gave. In the new creation you will be you, healed, completed and free from sin, not dissolved into a crowd or turned into someone else. What will be gone is everything false that sin attached to your name: the shame, the labels, the reputation the world gave you. What remains is the person Christ redeemed and named.

In a sentence. Whoever can hear should listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches: to the one who conquers I will give a share of the hidden manna, and a white stone with a new name written on it that only the person who receives it knows.

On a Tuesday. If faithfulness is costing you a seat at someone’s table, a contract, a circle of friends, a good name in the office, remember the other table and the other name. Christ knows you by name, personally, and has a place for you at his table. No feast the world offers can compare.

For worship. The manna in the ark lay behind a curtain no ordinary Israelite could pass, and the true Bread from heaven opened the way through that curtain by giving his own flesh for the life of the world (John 6:51; Hebrews 10:19–20). What was hidden in the holiest place he now gives, himself, to tradesmen shut out of every dinner in the city. And he who has a name written that no one knows but himself (19:12) writes a name for each of his people, so that the Lord and each guest at his table share a secret the whole world cannot read.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of the white stone is uncertain; white stones were used as tokens of acquittal and as tickets of admission to feasts.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–29 — To the Church in Thyatira
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Thyatira was the smallest and least distinguished of the seven towns — no great temple, no governor, a valley with no defences, and more trade-guild inscriptions than any of the other six. Lydia, the first convert in Europe, dealt in its purple cloth (Acts 16:14). It receives the longest of the seven letters.

Verse 18 introduces Christ as the Son of God — the only use of that title in Revelation — with eyes like a flame of fire and feet like burnished bronze, in a town of metalworkers. Verse 19 gives the warmest commendation of the seven: love, faith, service and patient endurance, and latter works exceeding the first. Where Ephesus had gone backwards, Thyatira is growing, and love heads the list.

Verses 20–21 bring the charge: they tolerate a woman Christ calls Jezebel — a type, not a name (1 Kings 16:31; 18:4; 21:1–16) — who calls herself a prophetess and teaches Balaam’s programme over again. Nobody is accused of believing her; they are accused of letting her continue. Verse 21 adds that Christ gave her time to repent and she goes on refusing.

Verses 22–23 pronounce judgment, and every clause carries a distinction. The couch of the banquet becomes the sickbed. Those who commit adultery with her are threatened unless they repent — the door still open inside the sentence. Her children, in the Old Testament idiom, are those who have made her teaching their own. And all the churches will learn that he searches kidneys and hearts (Jer. 17:10) and repays each according to his works.

Verses 24–25 turn to the faithful remnant who never learned what some call the deep things of Satan — almost certainly the faction’s own boast about the deep things of God, with one noun replaced. To them: I do not lay on you any other burden. Only hold fast what you have until I come.

Verses 26–29 give the promise: authority over the nations, in the words of Psalm 2:8–9, handed on from the Son who received it from his Father; and then the morning star, which the book identifies as Christ himself (22:16; cf. Num. 24:17). Verse 29 closes with the refrain — and from this letter onward the refrain comes after the promise rather than before it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Warm but Undiscerning

Thyatira grew in love, faith, service and endurance, yet tolerated a self-appointed prophetess teaching compromise. Christ gave her time to repent; to the faithful he lays no other burden than to hold fast until he comes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a guild town, her teaching offered relief with a spiritual justification.

Now: The faithful in a compromised church are not asked to fix it, only to hold on — and they are promised the morning star.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Thyatira write: 'The words of the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like burnished bronze. "'I know your works, your love and faith and service and patient endurance, and that your latter works exceed the first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And to the angel of the church in Thyatira write: ‘The words of the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like burnished bronze. ‘I know your works, your love and faith and service and patient endurance, and that your latter works exceed the first.

The setting. Thyatira, about 40 miles (65 kilometres) southeast of Pergamum, was the smallest and least important of the seven cities. It had no great temple, no governor, no wonder of the world, and it sat in a valley with no natural defences. It was a centre of manufacturing and trade, with more trade guilds than any other city in Asia: wool, linen, dyeing, leather, pottery, slave trading and, especially, bronze-working. Lydia, the seller of purple cloth whom Paul met in Philippi, came from Thyatira (Acts 16:14). Each guild had a patron god and held feasts in the god’s honour, and membership was almost necessary for anyone who wanted to work. The city’s chief god was Apollo, worshipped as son of Zeus, and the emperor was honoured as son of god too.

The words of the Son of God. This is the only time this title (ho huios tou theou) appears in Revelation. In a city that honoured Apollo and the emperor as sons of Zeus, Christ declares himself the true Son of God. The title echoes Psalm 2, which is quoted in vv. 26–27: the LORD’s anointed, his Son, will rule the nations. And this smallest, dullest, most commercial town receives the longest of the seven letters, from the highest title in the book.

Who has eyes like a flame of fire. The image comes from John’s first vision (1:14). Eyes that see through every disguise, chosen for this church because Thyatira’s problem is hidden inside a congregation that looks healthy from outside. He will search minds and hearts (v. 23).

And whose feet are like burnished bronze. This too comes from the first vision (1:15). In a town of metalworkers, this is an image they would know exactly: refined bronze coming out of the furnace, shining, hard, and not to be argued with. Feet that stand firm and trample evil.

I know your works, your love and faith and service and patient endurance. Then the commendation, and it is the warmest given to any of the seven. Four qualities are named and they are paired. Love (agapēn) and faith (pistin, or faithfulness): the inward dispositions. Service (diakonian, practical ministry to people who need it) and patient endurance (hypomonēn): the outward expressions. The order is not accidental: love produces service; faith produces endurance. Read that against Ephesus and the contrast is almost surgical. The very things Ephesus lacked, Thyatira had in abundance. Thyatira is credited with love first in the list.

And that your latter works exceed the first. Unlike Ephesus, which had declined from its first love, Thyatira was growing. A church that was getting better, not worse, and doing more for its poor in the fortieth year than in the tenth.

Two churches, each rebuked where the other excelled. Which sets up the hardest lesson in the chapter, and it should be said before the criticism arrives so that it is not mistaken for a technicality. A congregation can be growing in love, growing in practical care, more useful this decade than last, warm, generous and well thought of, and be in serious danger. Warmth is not a substitute for discernment any more than discernment was a substitute for warmth at Ephesus.

What it does not mean. Growth in love and service does not mean all is well. Thyatira’s strength would also prove to be its weakness: a love that would not confront error.

Which is more dangerous, cold orthodoxy or warm tolerance? Both, and that is the point. Most Christians have a settled instinct here: some are sure the peril is cold orthodoxy, others are sure it is loose tolerance, and each is quietly confident that the failing they can see in others is the serious one. Chapter 2 rebukes both, in adjacent letters, in the same voice, from the same eyes of fire. Whichever of the two you find it easy to condemn is probably not the letter written to you. The goal is not a midpoint between truth and love but the fullness of both, as in Christ, who came full of grace and truth (John 1:14).

In a sentence. To the angel of the church in Thyatira write: These are the words of the Son of God, whose eyes blaze like fire and whose feet shine like fine bronze: I know your works, your love, your faithfulness, your service and your perseverance, and I know that you are doing more now than you did at first.

On a Tuesday. Christ sees and values your quiet acts of service and faithfulness. Keep growing in them. The meal taken to a neighbour, the hours with a struggling teenager, the faithfulness at a job nobody praises: the Son of God names these first. And if your church is warm and busy, thank God for it, and ask him to keep its eyes open as well as its doors.

For worship. The Son of God, before whom Apollo and Caesar are frauds, turns his blazing eyes on a small manufacturing town and finds love there, and says so first. He notices growth that no historian recorded. And because he loves this warm church, he will not leave it blind.
verseByVerse.note: Thyatira was a town of trade guilds, whose feasts honoured pagan gods. Lydia came from there.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have this against you, that you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and is teaching and seducing my servants to practice sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols. I gave her time to repent, but she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I have this against you, that you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and is teaching and seducing my servants to practice sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols. I gave her time to repent, but she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality.

The setting. Jezebel was the Phoenician wife of King Ahab of Israel (1 Kings 16:31). She promoted the worship of Baal, killed the LORD’s prophets, supported hundreds of prophets of Baal and Asherah at her own table, arranged a judicial murder to get a man’s vineyard, and led Israel into idolatry, which Scripture calls whoredom and sorcery (1 Kings 18:4, 19; 21:1–16; 2 Kings 9:22). She was the Old Testament’s great example of a powerful person leading God’s people into false worship, and she operated from inside the institution.

But I have this against you, that you tolerate that woman Jezebel. The verb aimed at the church is tolerate (apheis, let alone, permit). The church’s failure was not that she existed, but that it allowed her to go on teaching. Nobody in Thyatira is accused of believing what she taught. They are accused of letting her go on teaching it. And Jezebel is almost certainly a symbolic name, comparing this woman to Ahab’s queen, the way we might call someone a Judas. Every hearer in Thyatira would have caught it instantly. She was a real person in the church, possibly an influential and well-connected woman, and her teaching was having the same effect as the old Jezebel’s.

Who calls herself a prophetess. “Calls herself” (hē legousa heautēn): the claim is self-issued, and no one has tested it, which is precisely what Ephesus did do and was commended for (v. 2). She claimed to speak for God, which gave her teaching authority and made it hard to challenge.

And is teaching and seducing my servants. Teaching (didaskei) and seducing (plana, leading astray, deceiving). The same word is used of Satan, who deceives the whole world (12:9). False teaching misleads people who think they are being led to deeper truth. And notice whom she seduces: my servants. Christ’s own people.

To practice sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols. That is Balaam’s programme again, verbatim from verse 14, now with a prophetic authority claimed behind it. Probably she taught that Christians could join in the guild feasts with their idolatry and immorality, perhaps claiming that God had revealed this freedom to her, or that experiencing the deep things of Satan could not harm a truly spiritual person (v. 24).

The prophet who did not call himself. Set beside her the one who is speaking. Jezebel’s credentials were self-issued. Christ is the true Prophet, the one Moses said God would raise up (Deuteronomy 18:15; Acts 3:22), and he said of his teaching that it was not his own but the Father’s who sent him, and that the one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory (John 7:16–18). She offered a freedom that left people in their sins; he gives the freedom of the Son, who sets people free indeed (John 8:36). And she was seducing his servants, people he had freed by his blood (1:5). The anger in this letter is the anger of a Redeemer watching what he bought being stolen.

Why nobody confronted her. The reason is not hard to reconstruct in a guild town: her doctrine solved a real problem. If the sacrificed meat is nothing and the temple evening is a formality, then a dyer can keep his membership and his contracts. She was not offering vice. She was offering relief, with a spiritual justification attached, a way to keep one’s job and status without suffering. And it is very difficult to confront somebody who is telling frightened people what they urgently want to be true.

I gave her time to repent, but she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality. This is one of the most searching sentences in the chapter. Time (chronon): Christ had been patient, perhaps through warnings from the church or simply by his own forbearance (Romans 2:4). The delay was not indifference. The years in which the church did nothing and the false teaching flourished were years the Lord was holding open. What looked to the faithful remnant like God ignoring an outrage was God waiting for a woman to turn. But the verb in the second half is present and continuous: she refuses (ou thelei, does not want to). Her problem was not ignorance but an unwilling heart. She has been given room, she knows what it is for, and she is going on saying no. Mercy that is refused for long enough does not become permanent tolerance. It runs out, and the next verse is what that looks like.

Delay is not always absence. Hold on to that when a wrong goes unpunished for a long time and heaven appears to have no opinion. Peter wrote to churches in these same provinces that the Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but is patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). Sometimes the silence a believer finds unbearable is mercy being extended to somebody he has already written off. Sometimes it is being extended to him.

Where Christians differ: does this passage forbid women from teaching? Some use it to argue against women preaching; others say it shows women prophesied and taught in the church, and the problem was only false teaching. Verdict: Jezebel is rebuked for false teaching and immorality, not for being a woman who spoke. Scripture recognises women who prophesied (Acts 21:9; 1 Corinthians 11:5). This passage does not settle questions of church office; those are taught elsewhere. This app holds the complementarian view that the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church are given to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), while women serve in many vital ministries. The lesson here is for every church and every teacher, male or female: no claim to speak for God gives anyone the right to teach what contradicts his word. The same teaching was condemned at Pergamum six verses earlier with no reference to anyone’s sex, and the parallel Christ draws there is with Balaam, a man.

What it does not mean. Tolerance is not always a virtue. A church that loves its people will not let them be led into sin by any teacher, however gifted or powerful. Loving people sometimes means saying no.

Are there prophets like this today, and how should I treat someone who claims a word from God? The apostles and prophets laid the foundation of the church once for all (Ephesians 2:20), and with the canon of Scripture complete, this app holds, charitably, that the revelatory gift of prophecy has ceased; many sincere believers disagree, and they are brothers and sisters. Either way, the test is the same. Anyone who claims a word from God must be tested by the written word (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21; 1 John 4:1). If the supposed message makes sin acceptable, contradicts Scripture, or adds a requirement or a freedom the Bible does not give, it is not from God, however confident or impressive the speaker. You do not need to be unkind; you do need to say no.

In a sentence. But this is my complaint against you: you put up with that woman Jezebel, who claims to be a prophet and who is teaching my servants and leading them astray into sexual immorality and eating food offered to idols; I gave her time to repent, but she does not want to turn from her immorality.

On a Tuesday. Be wary of anyone who claims a special word from God that makes sin acceptable. And if you lead in your church, love your people enough to protect them from such teaching. If you find yourself drawn to a teacher mainly because he or she tells you what you want to hear about your money, your body or your comfort, take that as a warning sign rather than a confirmation.

For worship. The Lord is slow to anger, and he gives even a false prophetess time to repent. His patience outlasts our impatience and our despair, and it has been extended to every one of us. But he is also the Son of God whose eyes are fire, and he will not let his servants be seduced for ever. In him mercy and justice meet, and neither one is ever false to the other.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will throw her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her I will throw into great tribulation, unless they repent of her works, and I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart, and I will give to each of you according to your works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I will throw her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her I will throw into great tribulation, unless they repent of her works, and I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart, and I will give to each of you according to your works.

The setting. The old Jezebel’s end was terrible (2 Kings 9:30–37), and her family was destroyed (2 Kings 10). Christ’s judgement here is proportionate and fitting. These are the hardest two verses in the seven letters, but almost every clause contains a distinction that a quick reading loses.

Behold, I will throw her onto a sickbed. The Greek is a deliberate irony that the English cannot fully carry. The word for bed (klinēn) is the word used for the couch on which the guild banquets were eaten and the sin committed. The bed of immorality and the couches of the idol feasts, where people reclined to eat, will become a bed of sickness. The bed she chose becomes the bed she cannot leave. Judgement fits the sin. Compare 1 Corinthians 11:30, where abuse of the Lord’s Supper brought sickness and death. And the verb is throw, the same verb used of the devil throwing believers into prison at Smyrna in verse 10. Different hand, different purpose, and the reader is meant to feel the symmetry.

And those who commit adultery with her I will throw into great tribulation, unless they repent of her works. Those who commit adultery with her (moicheuontas) are those who follow her teaching, whether literally sleeping with her or joining in her spiritual unfaithfulness. And there it is: the door, standing open in the middle of the sentence of judgement. Unless they repent: there is still time. The threat is conditional for everyone except the woman who has already spent her allotted time refusing. Even at this point, with the verdict being pronounced, anyone who will turn may turn. Judgement in Scripture almost always arrives with that clause attached, and it is not decoration. Christ’s warnings are meant to bring people back.

And I will strike her children dead. This is the sentence that makes readers flinch, and it should not be waved away. Two things need saying. First, her children (ta tekna autēs) in the Old Testament idiom that Christ is using means her spiritual offspring, her followers, those who have taken her teaching so far into themselves that they now reproduce it, rather than her literal children. The verse has just distinguished two groups: those who commit adultery with her, who may still repent, and the children, who are hers. The wording marks a difference between people who have been drawn in and people who have become her. Strike dead (apoktenō en thanatō, literally kill with death) is a Hebrew way of saying kill with pestilence or plague: a severe judgement on those who refuse to turn. Second, this is what Scripture consistently says the end of persistent, chosen rebellion is, and it says it plainly rather than leaving the reader to discover it later. Christ is not more severe here than the New Testament is elsewhere; he is simply less indirect.

And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart. Searches (eraunōn) means examines, investigates. Mind and heart is literally kidneys and hearts (nephrous kai kardias). In Hebrew thinking, the kidneys, the organs furthest inside a body, were the seat of the deepest emotions, and the heart the seat of thought and will. And it is a straight quotation of the Old Testament’s claim about God alone: I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways (Jeremiah 17:10; compare Psalm 7:9). Christ takes the LORD’s own role. The claim is not that Christ is well informed. It is that he sees the part of a person that the person himself cannot get at, whatever outward show of spirituality people make, and this is said in a letter to a church that could not tell a prophetess from a fraud.

And I will give to each of you according to your works. A principle of judgement throughout Scripture (Psalm 62:12; Romans 2:6; 2 Corinthians 5:10). A reader who has grasped that salvation is by grace through faith alone will stop at that sentence, and the question deserves a straight answer. Scripture says both things without embarrassment: no one is justified by works of the law (Galatians 2:16), and each will be repaid according to what he has done. They are not in tension once the question each is answering is clear. Nobody is admitted on the strength of his works; the works are the evidence of whose he is, and they are the measure of what is given afterwards. A tree is not made alive by its fruit, and is identified by nothing else.

Each of you. The pronoun shifts at the end, and it changes who is being addressed. Verses 20 to 23 have been about her and them. The last clause turns and says each of you. The letter has been discussing a faction, and it ends the discussion by putting the whole congregation, one by one, in front of the eyes of fire.

What it does not mean. Judgement according to works does not mean salvation by works. We are saved by grace through faith, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9). But true faith always produces works, and the works reveal whether faith is real. On the last day, the works will show the truth about the heart (Matthew 25:31–46). Nor does this mean every illness is God’s judgement on a particular sin; Scripture warns against that conclusion (John 9:1–3). Here Christ announces a specific judgement.

Does God still send sickness as judgement today? He can, and Scripture records it (Acts 5:1–11; 1 Corinthians 11:30), but we are never given the right to read it into another person’s illness. Most sickness is simply part of living in a fallen world, and the godliest believers suffer it (2 Corinthians 12:7–9; 1 Timothy 5:23). If you are ill and your conscience is troubled about a specific, unrepented sin, confess it to God and put it right, and receive his forgiveness (James 5:15–16). If your conscience is clear, do not let anyone burden you with the idea that your illness is punishment. For those in Christ, even discipline is a Father’s love, never condemnation (Hebrews 12:6; Romans 8:1).

In a sentence. So I will throw her onto a bed of sickness, and those who commit adultery with her I will throw into terrible suffering, unless they turn away from what she does, and I will put her children to death; then all the churches will know that I am the one who examines people’s deepest thoughts and desires, and I will repay each of you as your works deserve.

On a Tuesday. Christ searches your mind and heart. Live before him without pretence, and turn quickly from anything you would not want him to find. The door in the middle of verse 22 is still open for anyone drawn into sin by a persuasive voice: unless they repent. Walk through it today rather than tomorrow.

For worship. Nothing is hidden from the Son of God. He sees to the kidneys and the heart, past every reputation and every spiritual performance. That is terror to the hypocrite, and rest to the believer, for the one who sees everything is the one who bore our sins and still holds the door of repentance open in the very sentence of judgement.

verseByVerse.quote: But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold this teaching, who have not learned what some call the deep things of Satan, to you I say, I do not lay on you any other burden. Only hold fast what you have until I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold this teaching, who have not learned what some call the deep things of Satan, to you I say, I do not lay on you any other burden. Only hold fast what you have until I come.

The setting. Gnostic groups in the second century boasted of knowing the deep things, secret spiritual knowledge reserved for the initiated. Some taught that the truly spiritual person could indulge the body without harm, or even should experience evil in order to master it. Jezebel’s teaching seems to have been an early form of this.

But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold this teaching. The tone changes completely. For the remainder of the letter Christ is speaking to the faithful. They exist. They have not been swept up. In a church whose besetting fault was tolerance, there were people who had quietly refused, and Christ addresses them directly and separately, which is itself a kindness. He knows exactly who in that congregation had said no.

Who have not learned what some call the deep things of Satan. The phrasing, what some call, suggests Christ is repeating the faction’s own slogan back at them with one word changed. They were very likely advertising the deep things (ta bathea) of God (1 Corinthians 2:10): a mature, advanced spirituality for people who had got beyond scruples, an inner freedom that let a believer walk through the guild feast untouched because he understood what the ordinary members did not. Christ calls it by its real name: the deep things of Satan. Alternatively, they claimed that to know Satan’s depths, to explore sin from the inside, was a mark of spiritual maturity. Either way, the supposed higher knowledge was demonic. Every generation produces some version of that offer, and it always flatters. Christ substitutes one noun and the whole thing collapses.

To you I say, I do not lay on you any other burden. This sentence ought to be read slowly by anyone who is tired. Burden (baros) means weight. This echoes the Jerusalem council’s letter, which said it laid no greater burden on Gentile believers than to abstain from idol food and sexual immorality (Acts 15:28–29). Christ adds no new requirements, no secret knowledge, no heavy rules. He does not give the faithful remnant a programme. He does not tell them to launch a campaign, purge the membership, or fix the church. He has already said what he will do about Jezebel and he will do it himself. To the people who have been holding on in a compromised congregation, the risen Christ says: nothing further is required of you.

The weight put where it belongs. That is an extraordinary pastoral moment, and it is aimed at a recognisable kind of exhaustion. There are believers in difficult churches who carry the whole thing on their shoulders, who feel personally answerable for every error nobody else is confronting, and who are being slowly ground down by a responsibility they were never actually given. The letter puts the weight where it belongs: on the one with the eyes of fire.

Only hold fast what you have until I come. That is the one thing. Not advance, not achieve, not reform: hold. Hold fast (kratēsate) is the same verb used of Pergamum holding fast his name in verse 13, a word for gripping something in a wind. Hold on to what you already have: the apostolic gospel, faithfulness to Christ. Nothing new is needed. And the time limit is stated: until I come (achris hou an hēxō), until his return. Holding on is not asked of anyone with no end in view, and this is the first mention in the letters of his final coming. There is a terminus. A believer is not being asked to grip in the dark for ever with no prospect of relief; he is being asked to grip until a specific person arrives, and that person has set out.

What it does not mean. Deep knowledge of God is not wrong; Paul prays for it (Ephesians 3:18–19). What is wrong is a claim to a secret deeper knowledge that goes beyond, or contradicts, the plain gospel. Maturity is growing deeper into what was taught from the beginning, not moving beyond it.

Should I stay in a church where error is tolerated, or leave? Christ did not tell the faithful in Thyatira to leave; he told them to hold fast, and said he would deal with Jezebel himself. So do not leave lightly, and do not make yourself responsible for fixing everything. Speak the truth where you have the opportunity, keep your own faith clean, pray for the church and wait. But if the church’s leaders themselves deny the gospel or require you to accept sin, and will not listen, it may become right to go to a faithful church, especially for the sake of your children. Thyatira still had a true congregation within it; not every building with a cross on it does.

How do I recognise a deep things offer today? It usually comes with three marks. It promises insight that ordinary Christians lack, available through a special teacher, technique, experience or method. It quietly makes the plain commands of Scripture seem childish or optional for the mature. And it flatters you: you are more advanced, freer, more enlightened than the people still worried about holiness. Real Christian growth looks different. It is deeper humility, simpler trust in Christ, greater love, and more obedience to the plain things, not less. If something new makes the old gospel seem small, it is not from God.

In a sentence. But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who have not taken up this teaching and have not learned what they call the deep secrets, which are really Satan’s, I say this: I will not put any further burden on you; just hold firmly to what you have until I come.

On a Tuesday. You do not need a new revelation or a secret key to the Christian life. Hold on to the gospel you have, and keep holding until Christ comes. Anyone worn down in a hard congregation, or in a hard household, or in a hard stretch of years, can take the instruction exactly as it stands. The requirement is not to fix it. The requirement is to still be holding on when he gets there.

For worship. The Lord who sees everything does not pile burdens on the weary. His yoke is easy and his burden is light (Matthew 11:30). He takes the judgement of the false teacher into his own hands, and asks of his faithful only that they keep holding what he has already given. And he has promised to come, so the holding has an end, and at the end of it is him.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers and who keeps my works until the end, to him I will give authority over the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron, as when earthen pots are broken in pieces, even as I myself have received authority from my Father. And I will give him the morning star. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who conquers and who keeps my works until the end, to him I will give authority over the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron, as when earthen pots are broken in pieces, even as I myself have received authority from my Father. And I will give him the morning star. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’

The setting. Psalm 2 describes the nations raging against the LORD and his anointed king, his Son. God says he will give the nations to his Son, who will break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel (Psalm 2:8–9).

The one who conquers and who keeps my works until the end. There is a condition, and it is repeated twice for emphasis. Keeps my works (ho tērōn achri telous ta erga mou): these stand over against Jezebel’s works in verse 22. They are the works Christ commands and produces, and the two sets of works are the two ways of getting through life in a guild town. The letter has now named both. Until the end: perseverance to the last. Conquering, in this book, is not a single dramatic act; it is defined by duration.

To him I will give authority over the nations. The promise to Thyatira is the longest of the seven and the strangest, and it is given to the church in the least important town on the road. Authority (exousian): Christians in Thyatira had no power at all; some of them had lost their guild membership and could not get work in a town where everything was guild work. They had just been told that their whole assignment was to hold on. To these people, Christ promises that they will share his rule over the nations. Believers will reign with Christ (3:21; 20:4–6; 22:5; 1 Corinthians 6:2–3).

And he will rule them with a rod of iron, as when earthen pots are broken in pieces. The wording of verses 26 and 27 is a direct quotation of Psalm 2, the great coronation psalm in which the nations rage and God installs his King on Zion and says to him: Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage (Psalm 2:8). Rule (poimanei) is literally shepherd: the Greek Old Testament translated Psalm 2:9 with that word, though in this context the shepherd’s rod is used in judgement. Rod of iron: unbreakable authority. Earthen pots: Thyatira’s potters knew that unfired clay can be reshaped but a fired pot can only be broken, and broken pots cannot be repaired. Opposition to Christ will be utterly broken.

Even as I myself have received authority from my Father. That psalm is about the Messiah. Christ quotes it, and then does something startling with it: he hands it over. Christ received this authority from the Father (Matthew 28:18). The authority the Father gave him, he gives to the ones who conquer, as the Son of God shares his inheritance with the sons of God (Romans 8:17).

And I will give him the morning star. Every other promise in the seven letters is a thing: a tree, a crown, a stone, a name, a pillar, a throne. This one is a person. The morning star (ton astera ton prōinon) is the planet Venus, which shines brightly before dawn, announcing the coming day, and the book says plainly who it is in its final chapter: I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star (22:16). Behind it stands Balaam’s own prophecy, which is a fine irony in a letter about Balaam’s teaching: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a sceptre shall rise out of Israel (Numbers 24:17). Christ is that royal star. Roman generals honoured Venus as the star of victory, but Christ is the true sign of triumph.

The star that means the sun is coming. The morning star is the one that rises last, when the sky is at its darkest, and it does not announce more night. It means the sun is coming. So the last word to Thyatira is not authority after all. Authority is promised, and then something better is added on top of it, and the something better is himself. To a congregation being urged to hold on until he comes, the final promise is that when he comes he will give them himself. Every other reward in these letters is something from his hand. This one is the hand.

The refrain after the promise. Then, for the fourth time, comes the call to hear what the Spirit says to the churches. In the first three letters it came before the promise; from Thyatira onwards it comes after. The change is small and probably deliberate. In the last four letters the promise is the last thing in the reader’s ear, and the call to hear stands over the whole of it. Whoever has an ear, and that is the point of the plural churches, this was written to be overheard.

Where Christians differ: when do believers rule the nations? Premillennialists see this fulfilled in a future thousand-year reign on earth after Christ returns. Verdict: believers already share Christ’s reign in a hidden way, as a kingdom of priests (1:6), and those who die in Christ reign with him now in heaven (20:4–6), which this app reads as the present age between Christ’s comings. The rule over the nations is completed at Christ’s return, when his enemies are judged (19:15) and his people reign with him for ever in the new creation (22:5). There is no separate future millennium on earth.

What it does not mean. Ruling with a rod of iron does not mean Christians now seek political power to impose the faith. Christ breaks his enemies by his word and at his coming. Our part now is faithful witness.

What does reigning with Christ look like now, in an ordinary life? Mostly it looks like what it looked like in Thyatira: faithfulness without power. Believers are already seated with Christ in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6), and they share his rule as his word goes out and the nations are discipled (Matthew 28:18–20).
