In practice that means praying with authority for the world, refusing to bow to the idols of the market, standing for truth, serving others as Christ served, and overcoming evil with good (Romans 12:21). It does not look like dominance. The authority is real, but for now it wears the shape of the cross, and it will be seen openly when he comes.

Will the saints really judge and rule? Yes. Scripture says the saints will judge the world and even angels (1 Corinthians 6:2–3), and will reign with Christ for ever (22:5). We do not know all that this will involve, but it means that the weak and despised of this age will be honoured with responsibility in the age to come, under Christ and in perfect agreement with his justice. It is not revenge. It is the restoration of humanity to the dominion God gave Adam at the beginning (Genesis 1:28; Psalm 8:6), now held in Christ, the true and better Adam.

In a sentence. To the one who conquers and keeps doing my works to the end, I will give authority over the nations, to shepherd them with an iron rod and shatter them like clay pots, just as I have received authority from my Father; and I will give him the morning star; whoever can hear should listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches.

On a Tuesday. If you feel powerless, unnoticed, holding on in a small place, remember who is speaking to you and what he has promised. Keep doing his works today, the plain obedient things, until the end. And when the night feels darkest, look for the morning star: he rose while it was still dark, and the day is coming.

For worship. The King of Psalm 2 did not take the nations by breaking them first. He let himself be broken, and the Father gave him the nations as the reward of his obedience to death (Philippians 2:8–9). Now he shares that inheritance with dyers and potters who lost their guild places for his name, and above the inheritance he gives the one gift that makes it worth having. The star Balaam saw far off, which rose over an empty tomb, will rise over every faithful church at the end of its night, and it will not set.

3.title: Letters to Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea
3.overview:
The final three letters of the seven complete the range of pastoral diagnosis the risen Christ brings to his churches. Sardis has a reputation for life but is spiritually dead. Philadelphia is small and weak but receives no rebuke and the most lavish promises. Laodicea is wealthy and self-satisfied and receives the most devastating rebuke of all.

Together the seven letters form a kind of mirror in which every church and every believer can find themselves. There is no congregation in history that does not exist somewhere on the spectrum these letters describe. The genius of John’s use of seven churches is that seven is the number of completeness: these seven letters are the full portrait of the church in every age, not just the church of Asia Minor in the first century.

The chapter ends with Christ standing at the door and knocking. The cosmic drama of the throne room is inseparable from the intimate pastoral reality of the local congregation. The one who will come with the clouds of heaven (1:7) is the same one who stands at the door of Laodicea and knocks (3:20). The book does not let us choose between the cosmic and the personal, the eschatological and the pastoral. Both are always in play.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — To the Church in Sardis
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Sardis had been the capital of Lydia and the seat of Croesus, and the first coins ever struck were minted there. By John’s day it was a comfortable provincial town with a magnificent past and no importance. Verse 1 introduces Christ as the one who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars — the Spirit and the messengers both in his hand — and then delivers the shortest, harshest assessment in the seven letters: you have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead. The word for reputation is onoma, a name. No heresy is named here and no persecution; Sardis is one of only two churches with no enemies mentioned at all.

Verse 2 issues the remedy: wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die, for I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God. The works are not wrong but unfinished — finished enough for the province, not for God. Verse 3 adds three more commands, remember what you received and heard, keep it, repent, and then the threat: I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come against you. Sardis stood on a spur thought impregnable and fell twice, in 546 and 214 BC, both times to a night climber up the cliff while the garrison slept.

Verse 4 turns: you have still a few names in Sardis, people who have not soiled their garments. The word is names again — the church has a name and is dead; these have no name and are alive. Verse 5 gives them three promises: white garments, a name never blotted out of the book of life (a city kept a citizen register and struck names from it at death or conviction), and confession of that name before the Father and the angels (cf. Matt. 10:32). Verse 6 sounds the refrain.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Name for Being Alive

Sardis had a reputation for life and was dead. Christ calls it to wake up, strengthen what remains, remember and repent, and he counts the few who have not soiled their garments.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The city had twice fallen to a night climb while the guards slept.

Now: Ask whether the reasons you would give for your church’s health are reasons Sardis could have given.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Sardis write: 'The words of him who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. "I know your works. You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And to the angel of the church in Sardis write: ‘The words of him who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. ‘I know your works. You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead.

Meaning first. Revelation 3 contains the last three of Christ’s seven letters. Sardis has a reputation for life but is dead; Christ calls it to wake up, strengthen what remains, remember the gospel and repent, or he will come like a thief; yet a few have kept their clothes clean, and the conqueror will walk with him in white, never be blotted out of the book of life, and be acknowledged before the Father (vv. 1–6). Philadelphia has little strength but has kept Christ’s word; he who holds the key of David has set before it an open door no one can shut, will make its persecutors acknowledge his love for it, and will keep it in the hour of trial; the conqueror will be a pillar in God’s temple, bearing God’s name, the name of the new Jerusalem and Christ’s new name (vv. 7–13). Laodicea is lukewarm, neither hot nor cold, and Christ is about to spit it out; it thinks itself rich but is wretched, poor, blind and naked, so Christ counsels it to buy from him refined gold, white clothes and eye salve; he disciplines those he loves, stands at the door knocking, and will eat with anyone who opens; the conqueror will sit with him on his throne (vv. 14–22). The chapter shows that Christ’s verdict on a church can be the opposite of its reputation: the dead church looked alive, the weak church was strong in faithfulness, and the rich church was poor.

The setting. Sardis, about 30 miles (50 kilometres) southeast of Thyatira, had once been the capital of the kingdom of Lydia, whose king Croesus was proverbial for his wealth; the first coins ever minted were struck there. Its acropolis stood on a steep hill, thought impregnable, yet it was captured twice by surprise: by Cyrus of Persia in 546 BC and by Antiochus III in 214 BC, both times when soldiers climbed the cliffs at night and found the walls unguarded. The city was destroyed by an earthquake in AD 17 and rebuilt with help from the emperor Tiberius. By John’s day it was prosperous but living on its past glory: a comfortable provincial town with a magnificent history and little importance. It had a large and wealthy Jewish community, and a great temple of Artemis.

The words of him who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. Both phrases have been used already, the sevenfold Spirit at 1:4 and the stars at 1:16, 20, and putting them together says something precise to a dying church. The seven spirits are the Holy Spirit in his fullness, who gives life, and a dead church needs nothing so much as the life-giving Spirit, and Christ has him to give. The seven stars are the churches held in his hand: this church is still his. He holds the Spirit, and he holds the messengers. Everything a church needs in order to come alive is in the hands of the person writing the letter. The remedy is not somewhere else.

I know your works. Christ knows more than the reputation; he knows the reality. And then comes the shortest and most devastating assessment in the seven letters.

You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead. The word for reputation is onoma, a name. Sardis has a name for being alive. That is not gossip or misunderstanding; it means the congregation is genuinely well regarded, perhaps busy, respected and admired by other churches, and that the regard is based on something observable. Something is going on at Sardis that reads, from outside, as life. Yet it is dead (nekros): spiritually lifeless. And nothing in the letter suggests heresy. There is no false teacher here, no Jezebel, no Balaam, no persecution, and that last absence tells its own story, because Sardis is one of only two churches with no enemies mentioned at all. Nobody was troubling them; there was nothing worth attacking. That, it turns out, was the problem. It was comfortable, conformed and asleep. Paul describes people who have the appearance of godliness but deny its power (2 Timothy 3:5).

A full building. Consider what the diagnosis actually means in practice, because dead church has become a phrase people throw at congregations they dislike. Christ is not describing an empty building. He is describing a full one. There are services; there is a name; there is enough activity to sustain a reputation across a whole province. And there is nothing inside it. A body can be laid out with its clothes arranged and its hands folded and look, from the doorway, very much like a man asleep.

Living inside the reputation. The gap between the two verdicts is the whole letter. Sardis’s reputation and Sardis’s condition are opposites, and the congregation is living inside the reputation. Nobody in that room thought they were dead. They had the reviews to prove otherwise. And of all the seven churches, this is the one whose situation is hardest to detect from inside, because the very evidence a member would reach for, look at our history, look at what people say about us, is the thing being contradicted. The eyes that wrote this letter are the eyes of flame from 1:14, and they do not read reviews.

What it does not mean. Dead does not mean every member was unconverted; there were a faithful few (v. 4). It means the church as a whole had lost spiritual life: going through the motions, without the power of the Spirit, the reality of repentance or the warmth of love. Nor is a church alive just because it is busy, large or popular.

How can I tell whether a church, or my own faith, is alive? Not by activity or reputation, which is exactly what Sardis had. Look instead for the marks the Spirit produces. Is Christ himself loved and spoken of, or only the church’s programmes and history? Is the word of God believed, preached and obeyed? Is there real repentance when sin is exposed, rather than management of appearances? Is there prayer that expects God to act? Is there love that costs something, and are people being brought to faith and growing? None of these is measured on a single Sunday. But if they are absent for years, the name is outliving the life.

In a sentence. To the angel of the church in Sardis write: These are the words of the one who has the sevenfold Spirit of God and the seven stars: I know your works; you have a name for being alive, but you are dead.

On a Tuesday. A reputation is not a life. Ask Christ to show you whether your faith is living or only looks it, and ask for his Spirit to bring life. And the honest question here is not whether some other congregation is Sardis. It is whether the reasons you would give for your own church’s health, or your own, are reasons of the kind Sardis could have given: a record, a name, a general impression, held by people who have not looked closely, that things are basically fine.

For worship. The Lord who holds the Spirit of life in his hand does not leave a dead church to its funeral. He tells it the truth, because he alone can raise it. He who called Lazarus out of the tomb can call a sleeping congregation to its feet, and he is speaking to Sardis because he has not finished with it.
verseByVerse.note: Sardis had been a great royal city. Its seemingly impregnable citadel was taken by surprise more than once in its history.

verseByVerse.quote: Wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die, for I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God. Remember, then, what you received and heard. Keep it, and repent. If you will not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come against you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die, for I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God. Remember, then, what you received and heard. Keep it, and repent. If you will not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come against you.

The setting. Twice in its history, Sardis fell because its watchmen were asleep. Everyone in the city would have known the story. Jesus had warned his disciples to stay awake because the thief comes when no one expects him (Matthew 24:42–44), and Paul used the same image (1 Thessalonians 5:2–6).

Wake up. Five commands come in a rush, and the first one governs the rest. “Wake up” (ginou grēgorōn) is literally become watchful, keep on being alert: a present imperative, a summons to a state, not a single act. Start being watchful and keep at it. Spiritual sleep is the condition of a church that is not watching for Christ, not praying, not on guard against sin. And it is an odd thing to say to a corpse, which is the first hint that the death of verse 1 is a verdict on the congregation as a body rather than on every individual in it. Verse 4 will confirm it: a few names in Sardis are still very much alive.

And strengthen what remains and is about to die. There is something left. That is genuinely good news arriving in the middle of the worst assessment in the chapter, and its placement is deliberate. Strengthen (stērison) means to make firm, to prop up, to brace. What remains (ta loipa) is the things that are left. Christ does not tell Sardis to start something new; he tells it to put its weight under what is still standing. Not everything is dead yet. There are embers that can be fanned into flame: a handful who still pray, a half-abandoned practice, a doctrine still confessed without conviction. Strengthen them before they too go out.

For I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God. Not wrong. Not false. Incomplete: peplērōmena means filled up, brought to fullness. Their works are begun and not finished: outwardly correct but inwardly empty, lacking the reality of faith and love. And the phrase in the sight of my God is the whole difficulty in six words. In the sight of the province of Asia, the works of Sardis were finished enough to build a reputation on. Two audiences, two verdicts, and only one of them is looking at the part that counts.

Remember, then, what you received and heard. The remedy at Ephesus was also memory (2:5), and here as there it points backwards to something specific. Received (eilēphas) and heard (ēkousas) are the standard vocabulary for the apostolic gospel handed on from person to person (1 Corinthians 15:1–3): the gospel they were first taught, and the grace they were given. Sardis does not need a new message. It needs the old one to mean something again. The cure for a dead church is not a new technique but the old gospel.

Keep it, and repent. Catch the order: hold on to it (tērei, keep on keeping), and turn round (metanoēson, a decisive turning). First a decisive break with their sleep, and then a lasting faithfulness. The verbs together describe a church that still possesses the truth and has stopped being changed by it. Repentance here is not the abandonment of a false position but the recovery of a true one that had gone quietly inert.

If you will not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come against you. For anyone who knew the city, this was a piece of local history used as a weapon. Sardis was built on a spur of rock with sheer cliffs, and it was considered impregnable. It fell twice, the same way. In 546 BC, so the historian Herodotus tells, a soldier of Cyrus watched a defender climb down the rock face to retrieve a dropped helmet, noted the route, and led a party up it; the city was taken while its garrison trusted its walls. In 214 BC, under Antiochus III, a Cretan climber did much the same thing at night. Twice in three centuries, Sardis lost everything because nobody was watching the one place that did not seem to need watching. The congregation would have felt that instantly. Christ is not making a general point about vigilance. He is telling a church in that particular town that its besetting civic sin has become its spiritual one.

Like a thief. Hōs kleptēs: unexpectedly, without warning. This may refer to a judgement on Sardis in history, or to Christ’s final return, which will be a disaster for those found asleep (16:15). And note the object of the coming: I will come against you. Elsewhere in these letters his coming is the church’s hope, the thing worth holding on for (2:25; 3:11). Here the same arrival is a threat. It is the same event; what differs is which side of the wall you are on when it happens. For the watchful, the thief image is no threat at all (1 Thessalonians 5:4).

What it does not mean. Coming like a thief does not mean Christ’s return will be secret or invisible. It means unexpected. Every eye will see him (1:7); but those who are not watching will be caught unprepared, as Sardis was by its enemies.

What does staying awake look like in an ordinary week? It is not anxious date-setting or constant emotional intensity. It is the steady habits of someone who expects his Lord. Pray regularly, and include his coming in your prayers (22:20). Keep listening to God’s word, privately and with his people. Deal with sin while it is small, before it hardens into habit. Notice where comfort is making you careless. And stay among believers who will tell you the truth about yourself (Hebrews 3:13). Spiritual sleep rarely starts with a decision to stop believing. It starts with a hundred small neglects that each seemed harmless.

What if I have already drifted asleep? Then this letter is for you, and it begins with hope: something remains, and Christ is speaking to you because he means to wake you. Do not wait to feel alive before you act. Do what he says, in his order. Remember the gospel you first received: that Christ died for your sins and rose again. Hold on to it, and turn back to him in plain repentance, naming what put you to sleep. Then strengthen what is left: go back to church, open the Bible again, pray even briefly, and tell a mature Christian where you are. Sleepers are woken one call at a time.

In a sentence. Wake up, and shore up what is left before it dies too, for I have not found your works complete in my God’s eyes; so remember what you received and heard, hold on to it and turn back; if you do not wake up, I will come on you like a thief, at an hour you do not expect.

On a Tuesday. Spiritual sleep begins with neglecting prayer and Scripture, and with comfort. Go back today to the gospel you first received, and strengthen whatever in your life with God is weak. Ask where your unguarded cliff is: the one area of your life you have assumed needs no watching.

For worship. The Lord of the church will not let his people sleep through their own fall without shouting a warning from the walls. His coming is the hope of every watchful servant and the alarm of every sleeping one, and in his mercy he sounds the alarm before he comes, so that the thief’s hour may become the bridegroom’s.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet you have still a few names in Sardis, people who have not soiled their garments, and they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy. The one who conquers will be clothed thus in white garments, and I will never blot his name out of the book of life. I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet you have still a few names in Sardis, people who have not soiled their garments, and they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy. The one who conquers will be clothed thus in white garments, and I will never blot his name out of the book of life. I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’

The setting. Sardis was famous for its wool and dyeing industry. White garments were worn at festivals, at victories and by citizens on special occasions, and in the ancient world a soiled robe could disqualify a worshipper from entering a temple. Ancient cities kept registers of citizens, and a name was erased when a citizen died or was disgraced. The idea of God’s book goes back to Exodus 32:32–33, Psalm 69:28 and Daniel 12:1, where those whose names are written in the book will be delivered.

Yet you have still a few names in Sardis. Not a few people: a few names (onomata), which is the same word used in verse 1 of the church’s reputation. A play on words. The congregation has a name for being alive and is dead; a handful of individuals have no name at all in the province and are alive. Christ knows them individually, and the shepherd who calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3) is counting them one at a time in a church he has just pronounced dead.

People who have not soiled their garments. Soiled (emolynan) means stained, defiled. Clothing in Scripture often pictures a person’s life and conduct (Jude 23; Zechariah 3:3–5). These few had not been stained by compromise with the culture’s sin and idolatry. What exactly they refused is not stated, and the silence should be respected. No heresy is named in this letter and no persecution; whatever kept these few clean was probably unremarkable and certainly unrewarded. Nobody was watching. Their reward, three times over, is that somebody was.

And they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy. Three promises follow, and each one answers something the letter has already raised. The first is fellowship and white garments. Walk with me: they will share the company of Christ. White: purity, victory and festival joy. Throughout this book white clothing is the dress of heaven: the martyrs under the altar (6:11), the great multitude (7:9), the armies that follow him (19:14). Worthy (axioi) should not be read as a claim about merit. Four chapters later the same book will say that the white robes were washed and made white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14), which is a deliberately impossible image and settles where the whiteness comes from. Their worthiness is that their lives fit the gift, not that they earned it (19:8).

The one who conquers will be clothed thus in white garments. The robe of righteousness, given by Christ (Isaiah 61:10), and the purity of a life washed in his blood. Every conqueror wears it, not only the few in Sardis.

And I will never blot his name out of the book of life. The second promise. Never (ou mē) is the strongest negative in Greek: certainly not, never, no never. The book of life (biblou tēs zōēs) is God’s register of those who belong to him and will have eternal life, and Revelation says these names were written before the foundation of the world (13:8; 17:8). Every hearer in Sardis knew what an erased name on a city register meant. The promise is a strong assurance, stated negatively: I will certainly not erase it. And it is given precisely to people whose names carried no weight in the town at all. The register that matters is not kept in Sardis, and there is no scribe anywhere with authority to reach it.

I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels. The third promise, and the best. Confess (homologēsō) means acknowledge, declare openly, literally say the same thing: stand up and agree. This is a direct echo of what Jesus said in Galilee: everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven (Matthew 10:32; Luke 12:8). So a believer in an unimportant town, whose faithfulness nobody recorded and whose congregation had ceased to notice him, will one day hear his name said aloud by Jesus Christ in front of the Father and the assembled angels. Those who confess Christ on earth, at great cost, will be confessed by Christ in heaven.

Names that matter. Let that stand as it is written, because it is the whole answer to a church living on reputation. Sardis had a name and no life. These few had life and no name. And the one with the eyes of flame, who reads no reviews and misses nothing done in the dark, will himself speak their names in the only place where a name is worth having. He is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

Where Christians differ: can a name be blotted out of the book of life? Arminian Christians read this verse as implying that believers who fail to persevere can have their names erased and lose their salvation, and they point to texts that speak of blotting out (Exodus 32:33; Psalm 69:28; Revelation 22:19). Verdict: the verse is a promise, not a threat. Christ never says he blots anyone out; he says he will never do it. Names in the Lamb’s book were written before the foundation of the world (13:8; 17:8), so those who belong to Christ cannot be removed. Those who never persevere show that they were never truly written (1 John 2:19). The warnings in these letters are the means God uses to keep his people persevering; the promises assure them that he will.

What it does not mean. Worthy does not mean that some believers are good enough to deserve heaven. All are saved by grace. Their worthiness is the fitness of a life that has received and lived by that grace.

How can I know my name is written in the book of life? You cannot read the book, but you can see its fruit. Names were written by God’s free choice before the world began (Ephesians 1:4), and the evidence that yours is there is that you have come to Christ: you trust him alone for forgiveness, you love him, however weakly, and you want to follow him (John 6:37; 2 Peter 1:10). Do not look for assurance in a feeling or a past decision alone; look at Christ, and at whether you are looking at him. Jesus told his disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). That joy is meant for ordinary believers.

What if I have been ashamed of Christ in the past? Then remember Peter. He denied Jesus three times with oaths, and Jesus restored him three times by a charcoal fire (John 21:15–19), and he went on to confess Christ before the council and, at the last, in his death. The promise of being acknowledged before the Father is not for those who have never failed, but for those who come back and keep confessing him. If you have kept quiet about Christ out of fear, confess that to him; he forgives it. Then take the next opportunity to own him, gently and plainly. Your past silence does not cancel his present welcome.

In a sentence. Even so, there are a few people in Sardis who have not stained their clothes, and they will walk with me dressed in white, because they are fit to do so; the one who conquers will be clothed in white like them, I will certainly not erase his name from the book of life, and I will acknowledge him by name before my Father and his angels; whoever can hear should listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches.

On a Tuesday. If you are one of the few in a sleepy church, or a sleepy family, or a workplace where no one else follows Christ, keep your garments clean in the small unrecorded choices of this week. Nobody may notice. He does. And let the assurance that your name is written make you bold to confess him: the one who will say your name before his Father is not asking you to earn the mention, only not to be ashamed of his.

For worship. Your name is written in the Lamb’s book of life, and it will never be erased. The register of heaven is kept by the hand that was pierced, and no clerk on earth can reach it. One day the Son of God will stand before his Father and the angels and say the names of his people aloud, one by one, the forgotten and the obscure among them, and he will not be ashamed of a single one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — To the Church in Philadelphia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Philadelphia was the youngest of the seven cities, founded as a missionary outpost of Greek culture on the edge of the uplands, and it sat on a fault line. The earthquake of AD 17 destroyed it, aftershocks went on for years, and people camped outside the walls rather than sleep under a roof. Twice the city took a new name to thank an emperor who paid for its rebuilding.

Verse 7 introduces Christ with four descriptions, none of them drawn from the vision of chapter 1: the holy one, the true one (alēthinos, the genuine article as against the counterfeit), and the holder of the key of David who opens and no one shuts — quoted from Isaiah 22:22, where the key of the royal house is laid on the shoulder of a new steward. Verse 8 sets before them an open door no one can shut, and gives the most encouraging assessment in the seven letters: I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name.

Verse 9 promises that the accusers who deny them a share in the promises will come and bow before them — and the sentence ends not with humiliation but with they will learn that I have loved you. Verse 10 is the disputed one: I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world, where both the hour of trial and keep from are argued over, and the readings are set out at the verse. Verse 11 gives the instruction: I am coming soon. Hold fast what you have, so that no one may seize your crown.

Verse 12 answers the city’s history point by point: a pillar in the temple of God, never to go out of it, for people who had lived in tents outside their own walls; and three names written on him — God’s name, the name of the new Jerusalem, and Christ’s own new name (cf. 19:12) — for a town that had twice taken a new name and twice seen it fade. Verse 13 closes with the refrain.
verseByVerse.theology:
Little Power, No Rebuke

Christ holds the key of David and sets an open door before a weak church that has kept his word. Its accusers will learn that he has loved it; the faithful will be pillars in the temple of God and bear his names.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A small congregation in an earthquake town had been told it had no share in the promises.

Now: Christ measures a church by faithfulness, not size.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: 'The words of the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens. "I know your works. Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut. I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: ‘The words of the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens. ‘I know your works. Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut. I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name.

The setting. Philadelphia, about 28 miles (45 kilometres) southeast of Sardis, was the youngest of the seven cities, founded in the second century BC by Attalus II, whose love for his brother earned him the nickname Philadelphus, brother-lover. It stood at the gateway to the high plateau of Phrygia, on an important road, and was founded to spread Greek culture into the east: a city with an open door. It sat on a fault line, and it was badly damaged in the earthquake of AD 17; aftershocks went on for years, and many residents lived outside the city for fear of falling buildings. After Tiberius helped rebuild it, it was renamed Neocaesarea, New Caesar. Like Smyrna, the church faced hostility from the local synagogue. In Isaiah 22:20–22, the LORD gives Eliakim, the new steward of King Hezekiah’s palace, the key of the house of David, so that what he opens no one shuts and what he shuts no one opens. This is a small town that knows what it is to have the ground move, to live outside the walls, and to be given a new name by somebody powerful.

The words of the holy one, the true one. Christ introduces himself with descriptions that, unlike the other six letters, do not come from the vision of chapter 1. The holy one (ho hagios) is in the Old Testament the title of God himself: to whom then will you compare me, says the Holy One (Isaiah 40:25). The true one (ho alēthinos) means not merely truthful, but genuine, real as against counterfeit, faithful. To a congregation being told by the synagogue across the street that it was not the real people of God, the sender identifies himself as the Real One. Christ is the true Messiah, whatever the synagogue says.

Who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens. This is quoted almost word for word from Isaiah 22, where a steward named Shebna is stripped of office and the key of the house of David is laid on the shoulder of Eliakim (Isaiah 22:22). The key is the steward’s badge of office: authority over who is admitted to the king’s house. Christ, David’s greater son, has authority over the house and kingdom of David, and he decides who enters. In chapter 1 he held the keys of Death and Hades; here he holds the key of admission to the kingdom. If the synagogue shuts out the Christians, saying they are not God’s people, Christ opens the door to them, and no one can shut it. Whoever else in Philadelphia claimed the right to decide who was in and who was out, the decision was being made elsewhere.

Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut. Two meanings fit, and both are defensible. First, the door into the kingdom (thyran ēneōgmenēn), guaranteed by Christ, held open for a congregation being told by its neighbours that it had no right of entry. Second, a door of opportunity for the gospel, as Paul used the phrase, a door for the word (1 Corinthians 16:9; 2 Corinthians 2:12; Colossians 4:3), which fits a city founded to spread Greek culture eastward and sitting on the road inland. As the city was a gateway for Greek culture, the church would be a gateway for the gospel. The two are not in competition: the church put out of the synagogue has been given a door nobody in that synagogue can close, and a door out into the world besides.

I know that you have but little power. Then the assessment, and it is the most encouraging sentence spoken to any of the seven churches. Little power (mikran dynamin): small in numbers, influence and resources. Christ does not rebuke them for this. He does not say you have little power, but never mind. He does not tell them to grow. He names the weakness as a simple fact, a small congregation in a small town with no influence and no leverage. Weakness is not failure.

And yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name. Then he puts the words and yet in front of everything that matters. Small, and faithful. The smallness is not the story. They kept his word (etērēsas mou ton logon): faithful in what matters. They held on to the truth and did not disown Christ under pressure. What Christ values is not size or power but faithfulness. Of the two churches he finds nothing to criticise in, one was poor and hunted and the other was small and weak.

What it does not mean. The open door does not mean that weak churches will automatically grow, or that faithfulness guarantees success by the world’s measures. It means Christ has opened the way, and no opposition can close it.

Is a small church a failing church? No. That sentence of Christ’s belongs to a very large number of believers and congregations. There are churches of thirty people in places nobody has heard of, holding on, keeping the word, not denying the name, and quietly convinced that whatever God is doing in the world is happening somewhere else with more resources. Philadelphia is the letter written to them, and it contains no rebuke of any kind. Size is not the measure Christ uses. A small church should still pray for growth and walk through the doors God opens, but it should not despise itself. Christ does not.

How do I know which door God has opened for me? Usually by looking at the people and opportunities already in front of you, rather than waiting for a dramatic sign. Paul saw open doors in places where people were ready to listen, even when there were many adversaries (1 Corinthians 16:9). Ask: who in my life is asking questions, going through a hard time, or open to friendship? Where do I have a natural reason to be and speak? Pray for opportunities (Colossians 4:3), then take the small ones: an invitation, an honest answer, an offer of help in Christ’s name. If one door closes, it was not the only door. Christ holds the key, and he does not run out of doors.

In a sentence. To the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: These are the words of the Holy One, the True One, who holds the key of David, so that what he opens no one can shut and what he shuts no one can open: I know your works; look, I have put in front of you an open door that no one can close; I know you have little strength, yet you have kept my word and have not disowned my name.

On a Tuesday. You may feel small and weak. Christ asks for faithfulness, not strength. Look for the door he has opened for you to speak of him, and walk through it. And when someone tells you, in words or by their manner, that you are not really part of what God is doing, remember who holds the key.

For worship. The Holy One, the True One, carries the key of David’s house at his belt, and what he opens stays open. No synagogue, no council, no empire can shut the door he has set before his people. He does not measure his churches by their strength, and he has never yet lost a small congregation that kept his word.
verseByVerse.note: Philadelphia was a small city often shaken by earthquakes.

parallels.desc: he shall open, and none shall shut

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will make those of the synagogue of Satan who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie—behold, I will make them come and bow down before your feet, and they will learn that I have loved you. Because you have kept my word about patient endurance, I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world, to try those who dwell on the earth. I am coming soon. Hold fast what you have, so that no one may seize your crown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I will make those of the synagogue of Satan who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie—behold, I will make them come and bow down before your feet, and they will learn that I have loved you. Because you have kept my word about patient endurance, I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world, to try those who dwell on the earth. I am coming soon. Hold fast what you have, so that no one may seize your crown.

The setting. Isaiah prophesied that the nations who had oppressed Israel would come and bow down at Israel’s feet, acknowledging that the LORD had loved his people (Isaiah 45:14; 49:23; 60:14). Here the roles are startlingly reversed: Jewish persecutors will bow before a mostly Gentile church, acknowledging that Christ has loved it.

Behold, I will make those of the synagogue of Satan who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie. As at Smyrna (2:9), and the phrase needs the same guard: this is not a statement about Jewish people. John is a Jew, so is his Lord, and the same apostle wrote that salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22). Satan means accuser, and the charge is functional: a particular group in one town was denouncing its Christian neighbours and telling them they had no share in the promises. By rejecting the Messiah and persecuting his people, they had forfeited the right to the name of God’s people. Lie (pseudontai): their claim is false.

Behold, I will make them come and bow down before your feet. What makes this verse remarkable is where the imagery comes from. The Old Testament repeatedly promises that the nations will come and bow down before Israel. Christ takes that promise and applies it to a small congregation of Gentile and Jewish believers in Philadelphia, with the roles the other way round. He is not abolishing the promise; he is saying who the true Israel turns out to be, the same argument Paul makes at length in Romans 9 to 11. Bow down (proskynēsousin, prostrate themselves) is not worship of the church, but acknowledgement that the church is God’s true people. This may happen through their conversion, as Paul hoped (Romans 11:11–14), or at the final judgement, when every knee bows (Philippians 2:10–11).

And they will learn that I have loved you. The point of the bowing is not humiliation. The sentence does not end with before your feet; it ends with this. Loved (ēgapēsa) echoes Isaiah 43:4, where the LORD says to Israel that they are precious in his eyes and he loves them. The love once claimed exclusively by the synagogue belongs to the despised church. The vindication being promised is not that its opponents will be crushed. It is that they will find out the truth, and the truth they will find out is not that Philadelphia was right, but that Philadelphia was loved.

Because you have kept my word about patient endurance. My word about patient endurance (ton logon tēs hypomonēs mou) is the command to endure as Christ endured, or the message of his endurance.

I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world. Keep from (tērēsō ek) means keep out of, guard from. There is a play on words: because you have kept my word, I will keep you. The hour of trial (tēs hōras tou peirasmou) is a time of testing coming on the whole world, which the rest of Revelation describes in the seals, trumpets and bowls. And the ground of the promise is not in dispute: Philadelphia is kept because it kept his word, and the keeping is his doing. A church with little power is not asked to survive the hour on its own strength under any reading of the verse.

To try those who dwell on the earth. Throughout Revelation this phrase (tous katoikountas epi tēs gēs) means unbelievers, the world in rebellion against God (6:10; 13:8; 17:8). The trial is aimed at them, not at the church.

Where Christians differ: is this a promise of a pre-tribulation rapture? Dispensationalists read “keep you from the hour of trial” as a promise that the church will be removed from the earth before a final seven-year tribulation. Teachers such as John Walvoord and Charles Ryrie argued it with care, and the argument has real force: the promise is deliverance from an hour, not merely from harm within it, and the trial is explicitly worldwide. Verdict: the same words appear in John 17:15, where Jesus prays not that the Father would take his disciples out of the world, but that he would keep them from the evil one. To keep from is to protect within, not to remove from. Revelation consistently shows God’s people sealed and protected in the midst of the judgements (7:3; 9:4; 12:6, 14), while they still suffer at the hands of the beast. The promise was made to a church in the first century, which was never raptured; it was preserved. God protects his people from his wrath and from losing their faith, not from all suffering. There is one visible return of Christ, not a secret rapture.

I am coming soon. Soon (tachy) means quickly. It is the promise that sustains endurance, and the book ends with it three times (22:7, 12, 20).

Hold fast what you have, so that no one may seize your crown. The instruction to the weakest church is the same as to the compromised one at Thyatira: hold on. Not achieve, not expand: hold (kratei, grip). And the danger named is not that the crown will be lost by failure but that someone may seize it (labē, take), the language of an athlete’s wreath (stephanon) being taken by a rival. Whatever else that means, it means the crown is already theirs and is worth guarding. Not that someone could steal their salvation, but that they must persevere to receive the prize. The warning is one of the means by which Christ keeps them.

What it does not mean. This passage does not support replacing love for Jewish people with contempt. The point is the vindication of a persecuted church, and the hope is that its persecutors will learn Christ’s love. Many in Philadelphia’s synagogue may have come to faith.

If Christ keeps his people in the hour of trial, why do Christians still suffer? Because the keeping is not exemption from all pain but protection from the things that would destroy them. The believers in Revelation are sealed so that God’s judgements do not fall on them (7:3; 9:4), yet they are hated and sometimes killed by the beast (13:7). What Christ guarantees is that no suffering will separate them from his love (Romans 8:35–39), that their faith will not finally fail (Luke 22:32), and that they will never face God’s wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9). So if you are suffering, you have not been left out of the promise. You are being kept inside the storm, as the disciples were kept in the boat.

Could someone really take my crown? Not by force against Christ’s will, since no one can snatch his sheep out of his hand (John 10:28–29). The warning works the way a parent’s warning works: it is one of the means by which Christ keeps his people holding on. A crown can be seized only by letting go of the one who gives it, which is what false teachers, persecutors and the lure of an easier life invite us to do. The true believer hears the warning and grips harder, and that gripping is itself the evidence of the grace that keeps him. So take the warning seriously, and take the promise more seriously still.

In a sentence. Look, I will make those in Satan’s synagogue, who claim to be Jews but are lying, come and bow at your feet and recognise that I have loved you; because you have kept my command to endure, I will keep you safe through the hour of testing that is coming on the whole world to test the earth’s inhabitants; I am coming soon; hold on to what you have, so that no one takes your crown.

On a Tuesday. If you are opposed for your faith, Christ will vindicate you. Do not strike back. Hold fast, and trust him to show your opponents that he loves you, and pray that they will learn it by coming to love him too. And when a hard season comes, do not ask why God has not removed you from it. Ask him to keep you in it, and he will.

For worship. The love that the despised church could not prove to its accusers, Christ will one day prove himself, before their eyes. He keeps those who keep his word, in the hour of trial and through it, and he is coming soon. The crown he has given he will guard, and the hand that holds it out is the same hand that holds his people fast.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God. Never shall he go out of it, and I will write on him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from my God out of heaven, and my own new name. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God. Never shall he go out of it, and I will write on him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from my God out of heaven, and my own new name. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’

The setting. In a city shaken by earthquakes, where buildings collapsed and people fled outside the walls, a pillar was the part of a building that stood firm. Columns often remained standing in ruined temples. Cities sometimes honoured a distinguished citizen or priest by setting up a pillar inscribed with his name in a temple. And Philadelphia had twice been renamed after emperors (Neocaesarea and Flavia); Christ gives a greater name.

Every promise aimed at a wound. A reader who knows what Philadelphia had lived through can watch the promises in this verse land one after another.

The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God. A pillar (stylon, column) speaks of permanence, stability and honour. This is spoken to people whose city had been shaken flat in AD 17, whose aftershocks went on for years, and who had spent seasons living in the fields outside the walls because no roof could be trusted. A pillar is the part of a building that does not move. Those with little power and shut out of the synagogue will be pillars in God’s own temple. Paul called church leaders pillars (Galatians 2:9); here every conqueror is one.

Not architecture but presence. The image needs one clarification, because it can be read as though a person becomes masonry. The last chapters of this book say plainly that the new Jerusalem has no temple building in it, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (21:22). So the promise is not a job in a building. To be a pillar there is to belong permanently in God’s presence: a place in what does not shake.

Never shall he go out of it. And this is the clause that would have stopped the room. Never (ou mē … eti) is certainly never again. In an earthquake city, people had to flee again and again. No more running into the fields at three in the morning. No more coming back to see what is left standing. In God’s temple, no one will ever have to leave. Eternal security and permanent belonging, fixed in a building that cannot fall.

And I will write on him the name of my God. Then three names, written on him. A name marks ownership. The high priest wore the name of the LORD on his forehead, on a gold plate engraved Holy to the LORD (Exodus 28:36–38). Believers bear God’s name, as his servants (14:1; 22:4), in contrast to those who bear the beast’s mark (13:16–17). In the ancient world a slave was branded and a soldier marked; here the mark is not degradation but belonging to God himself.

And the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from my God out of heaven. The new Jerusalem is the city of God, the bride of the Lamb, coming down from heaven in the new creation (21:2, 10). This is citizenship, given to a congregation put out of its synagogue and told it had no home. Believers are citizens of that city (Philippians 3:20; Hebrews 12:22), whatever earthly citizenship they lose. And Philadelphia had twice taken a new civic name to flatter an emperor, and the names faded when the dynasties did; this one is written on the person, not on a milestone.

And my own new name. Last and least expected. Not a name for the believer this time, but Christ’s own (19:12, 16), expressing his full revelation and victory at his return. Whatever it is, it is not yet fully disclosed; the book will say at 19:12 that he has a name written that no one knows but himself. There is more of Christ still to be revealed than has yet been revealed, and believers will share in his glory. The ones who get to know it include a handful of people with little power in a town on a fault line.

Sardis and Philadelphia side by side. Chapter 3 has now made its point twice. Sardis had a name and no life. Philadelphia had no standing, no strength and no name worth keeping, and receives three names and a pillar. The church with the reputation is warned; the church with no reputation is told its name is being written by the hand of God.

He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The refrain, coming after the promise rather than before it, as in all the last four letters.

What it does not mean. The three names are not literal tattoos, any more than believers will be literal pillars of stone. They are pictures of belonging to God, his city and his Son, for ever.

Is the new Jerusalem a place, or the people of God? Both, and Revelation holds them together. The city is described as the bride, the wife of the Lamb (21:9–10), so it pictures the redeemed people themselves in their final glory. But it is also the home where God dwells with his people on a renewed earth (21:1–3), a real place in a real new creation, not a cloud or a mood. To bear the city’s name now means you already belong to that people and are on your way to that home. Your citizenship is held in heaven even while your passport says something else (Philippians 3:20).

In a sentence. The one who conquers I will make a pillar in my God’s temple, and he will never have to leave it; I will write on him my God’s name, the name of my God’s city, the new Jerusalem that comes down out of heaven from my God, and my own new name; whoever can hear should listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches.

On a Tuesday. When the ground moves under you this week, a diagnosis, a redundancy, a family upheaval, remember the promise made to a city that knew earthquakes. You have a permanent place in God’s presence that no aftershock can reach. Live as someone who bears God’s name: it is written on you, and others are reading it.

For worship. In a shaking world, the holy and true one has promised his weak people a place that will never shake. He writes his Father’s name on them, and the name of the city, and his own, and he does not lose small congregations in obscure towns. The ground under Philadelphia moved again and again. Everyone in that little church who held on is a pillar in a temple that has never shifted an inch.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — To the Church in Laodicea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Laodicea sat at the junction of three trade roads and made its money three ways: banking, a glossy black wool exported across the empire, and a medical school producing a famous eye ointment. When an earthquake levelled it in AD 60 it refused imperial relief and rebuilt at its own expense — Tacitus records it, and the city was proud of it. Every line of this letter is written against that fact.

Verse 14 gives three titles, each a rebuke before any criticism: the Amen (the God of Amen, Isa. 65:16; cf. 2 Cor. 1:20), the faithful and true witness, and the beginning of God’s creation — archē, origin and source, not first creature.

Verses 15–16 turn on local geography. Hierapolis six miles north had hot healing springs; Colossae ten miles east had cold mountain water; Laodicea had to pipe water in and it arrived tepid and unpleasant. So cold is not indifference on a scale. Cold water is good and hot water is good; the charge is uselessness. I will spit you out of my mouth renders emeō, to vomit — the involuntary reaction to a cup of Laodicean tap water.

Verse 17 quotes the church’s own words, the only congregation permitted to speak in these letters: I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing — not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. The last three answer the three industries exactly. Verse 18 responds with an offer rather than a command — I counsel you to buy from me — gold refined by fire for the bank, white garments for the wool town, eye salve for the medical school (cf. Isa. 55:1).

Verse 19 reframes everything: Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline (Prov. 3:12; Heb. 12:5–11), using phileō, the warmer word. Verse 20 has Christ knocking outside his own church, offering the evening meal to whoever opens — and the invitation narrows to the singular, if anyone. Verse 21 gives the last and largest promise of the seven, a seat on his own throne, grounded on a conquest already finished. Verse 22 closes the letters with the refrain for the seventh time.
verseByVerse.theology:
Useless, Not Merely Lukewarm

Laodicea’s water was neither hot nor cold and good for nothing, and so was its church. Rich and self-sufficient, it did not know it was poor, blind and naked. Christ counsels it to buy from him, disciplines because he loves, and knocks at the door.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A city that refused imperial relief produced a church that said, “I need nothing.”

Now: Ask who in your town is helped because your church exists — and open the door to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Laodicea write: 'The words of the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God's creation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And to the angel of the church in Laodicea write: ‘The words of the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God’s creation.

The setting. Laodicea, about 40 miles (65 kilometres) southeast of Philadelphia, stood in the Lycus valley at the junction of three trade roads, about 10 miles (16 kilometres) from Colossae and 6 miles (10 kilometres) from Hierapolis. It was the richest town on the circuit: a banking centre, famous for a glossy black wool, and home to a medical school known for an eye salve made from a local powder. When an earthquake devastated it in AD 60, it refused help from Rome and rebuilt itself from its own wealth, as the historian Tacitus records, and the city was proud of it. Hold that fact; every line of this letter is written against it. Its weakness was water: it had no good supply of its own and piped water in through an aqueduct. Paul mentions the church at Laodicea in Colossians 2:1, 4:13–16, and asked the Colossians to share letters with it. The church was probably founded by Epaphras.

Three titles, each a rebuke. Christ introduces himself with three titles, and every one of them is a rebuke before a word of criticism is spoken.

The words of the Amen. A strange thing to call a person. Amēn is the Hebrew word for it is firm, it is so, the word a congregation says at the end of a prayer to put its weight behind what has been said. Isaiah 65:16 speaks of the God of truth, literally the God of Amen: the one who can be relied on absolutely. And Paul says that all the promises of God find their Yes in Christ, and that is why it is through him that we utter our Amen (2 Corinthians 1:20). Christ is God’s Amen. To a church that will shortly be described as neither one thing nor the other, the sender identifies himself as the one who is definitively, unwaveringly what he is.

The faithful and true witness. Faithful was already his title at 1:5, and here true is added. A witness who is faithful will not lie; a witness who is true reports what is actually there. He tells the truth, even when it hurts. And this is being said immediately before the most unflattering assessment given to any of the seven churches, addressed to a congregation whose own opinion of itself is about to be quoted back at it. If the testimony that follows is unwelcome, the credentials of the witness have been stated in advance.

The beginning of God’s creation. The Greek is archē: origin, source, ruler, the root inside our word architect, the one from whom a thing begins. Colossians, a letter Laodicea had heard read (Colossians 4:16), says that by Christ all things were created, that he is before all things, and that he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:15–18). Christ is the origin and ruler of everything God made, including Laodicea’s banks, its wool and its medicine. This congregation had already been given the meaning in writing.

Where Christians differ: does this mean Christ was created? The ancient Arians, and Jehovah’s Witnesses today, read “the beginning of God’s creation” as meaning that Christ was the first being God created. Verdict: the word archē can mean the beginning in the sense of the source or ruler, and that is its meaning here. Revelation gives Christ the titles of God: the first and the last (1:17), the Alpha and the Omega and the beginning and the end (22:13), worshipped with the Father (5:13). John’s Gospel says all things were made through the Word, and without him nothing was made (John 1:1–3); so he cannot himself be a made thing. Christ is the uncreated source of creation, not its first product.

The one thing with weight. So before the letter says anything at all about lukewarmness, it has set three immovable things in front of a church that has drifted: the Amen, the true witness, and the source of everything that exists. Laodicea’s problem is that nothing in its life has any weight. The remedy begins by naming the one thing that does.

What it does not mean. The Amen is not just a word to close prayers. As a title for Christ, it means that he is God’s final, unshakeable yes.

How do I answer someone at my door who says this verse proves Jesus was created? Gently, and from the Bible they are holding. Show that archē means source or ruler as well as first in a series, just as we speak of the principal of a school. Then turn to the same book: the Lord God is the Alpha and the Omega in 1:8, and Jesus takes that very title, with the beginning and the end, in 22:13. If the Father is the beginning without being created, so is the Son. Add John 1:3: everything that was made was made through him, so he cannot be among the things made. Then, more important than winning, speak of why it matters: only God can save, and the one who died for us is God the Son.

In a sentence. To the angel of the church in Laodicea write: These are the words of the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the source and ruler of God’s creation.

On a Tuesday. Say Amen with understanding. When you end a prayer this week, remember that you are not adding a full stop but leaning your weight on the one who is God’s Yes to every promise. And when someone tells you the truth about yourself that you did not want to hear, ask whether the faithful and true witness is speaking through them.

For worship. Christ is God’s Amen, and every promise is sure in him. He is the witness who has never told a lie, not even a kind one, and the source from whom every grain of the universe began. When everything else has been shaken and every human boast has been answered, he will still be standing, the final and unshakeable Yes of God.
verseByVerse.note: Laodicea, about ten miles from Colossae, was a wealthy banking and textile city. Rebuilt without imperial aid after an earthquake in AD 60, it prided itself on needing nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: "I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were either cold or hot! So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were either cold or hot! So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth.

The setting. Nearby Hierapolis, six miles north, had famous hot springs, used for healing; the white terraces they left behind are visible from Laodicea across the valley. Colossae, ten miles east, had cold, pure, refreshing water. Laodicea’s water was piped in from a distance, arriving tepid and full of minerals; the remains of its pipes show thick deposits of calcium carbonate. The water was notoriously nauseating, the kind of water that makes people want to spit it out.

I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. This is the verse everyone remembers and the one most often misread, and the local geography settles it. Cold (psychros) and hot (zestos, boiling): the image comes from the local water, not from a scale of spiritual temperature. Hot water heals and cold water refreshes, and the two neighbouring towns were known for exactly those two services. Both are useful. Lukewarm water is useless.

Would that you were either cold or hot! Christ is not saying that it would be better to be against him (cold) than half-hearted. In the light of the water image, both cold and hot are good: either healing like Hierapolis or refreshing like Colossae. The problem is that Laodicea is neither; its works do nothing for anyone. The complaint is not that the church is half-hearted on a scale from zero to ten. The complaint is that it is useless: a city with everything, supplying nothing. He would rather have anything than this, and of all the conditions in these seven letters, the one hardest to do anything with is the one doing no harm and no good. Ephesus could be told to remember. Pergamum could be told to repent of something specific. Sardis could be told to strengthen what remains. There is nothing in Laodicea to take hold of.

A more searching charge. That is a far more searching charge than the usual reading, and much harder to escape. A congregation examining itself for lukewarmness in the popular sense asks about the temperature of its feelings, and any honest person will find some warmth somewhere and take comfort. The question this verse actually asks is different: what is your church for? Who in your town is helped because you exist? If the doors closed on Sunday and the building were sold, who outside the membership would notice, and what exactly would they miss?

So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth. Lukewarm (chliaros) is tepid. The verb (emesai) is to vomit, to spew. Most English versions soften it, and the softening loses the picture: this is the involuntary reaction of a body to something it cannot keep down. Nobody decides to do it. It is the reaction of a man handed a cup of Laodicean tap water. A violent, disgusted image: Christ finds this church nauseating. Yet the tense, literally I am about to spit, leaves time for repentance (v. 19).

Where Christians differ: what do hot and cold mean? The common reading takes hot as spiritually zealous, cold as openly hostile, and lukewarm as half-hearted; on that reading Christ would prefer open hostility to half-heartedness. Verdict: the local water explains the image better. Both hot and cold water are good; lukewarm water is useless and sickening. Christ does not want anyone to be cold toward him. He wants his church to be useful, either healing or refreshing, by real faith and love. Laodicea’s self-satisfied religion did no good to anyone.

What it does not mean. Being spat out does not mean that true believers lose their salvation. Christ is warning a church as a whole, much of which, like Sardis, may never have been truly converted. The response he wants is repentance (v. 19).

Am I lukewarm? One thing should be said plainly, because this verse frightens sensitive readers and hardly troubles the people it was written for, which is itself the pattern the letter describes. A Christian who reads verse 16 and is alarmed by it is, by that reaction, showing that it is probably not describing him. Lukewarmness is not a state that worries about itself. Laodicea was entirely comfortable. So the better questions are these: is my faith doing anyone any good? Does anyone find healing or refreshment because of my prayers, my words, my time, my money? Have I come to feel that I need nothing from Christ? If the honest answer troubles you, do what verse 19 says, and you will not stay lukewarm.

In a sentence. I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot, and I wish you were one or the other; but since you are tepid, neither hot nor cold, I am about to spit you out of my mouth.

On a Tuesday. Ask whether your faith does anyone any good, bringing healing or refreshment to others. Comfortable religion that serves no one is what Christ finds hardest to stomach. Name one person this week whom you could refresh like cold water or help to healing like the hot springs, and do it in his name.

For worship. The Lord of the church will not swallow a church that is useless, because he gave himself to make his people a blessing to the world. He is the fountain of living water, healing and refreshing, and he cannot be content with a bride who offers the thirsty nothing. His disgust is the disgust of love that will not settle for less than our good.
verseByVerse.note: Often explained from local water: hot springs at nearby Hierapolis and cold water at Colossae, while Laodicea’s piped-in water arrived tepid. Both hot and cold are useful; lukewarm is not.

verseByVerse.quote: For you say, "I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing," not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire, so that you may be rich, and white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be seen, and salve to anoint your eyes, so that you may see.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you say, ‘I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing,’ not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire, so that you may be rich, and white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be seen, and salve to anoint your eyes, so that you may see.

The setting. Each part of Christ’s counsel aims at one of Laodicea’s sources of pride: its banks and gold, its famous black wool, and its eye medicine. The proud city that refused Rome’s help after the earthquake had a church with the same attitude toward God.

For you say, I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing. Christ quotes the church’s own sentence back at it, and it is the only place in the seven letters where a congregation is allowed to speak. It echoes Hosea 12:8, where Ephraim boasts that it is rich and has found wealth, and no one can find sin in it. Three clauses, and the third is the fatal one. Being rich is not a sin. Having prospered is not a sin. Needing nothing is the end of the Christian life, because the whole of it runs on asking. Self-sufficiency is the root problem. The church thought it needed nothing, so it did not need Christ.

The town seeps through the walls. They had grounds for the boast. Laodicea had turned down an emperor’s earthquake relief and rebuilt itself out of its own reserves. It is very hard to be a self-sufficient city for a generation without becoming a self-sufficient church, and nobody in the congregation would have felt a decision being made. The town’s civic virtue simply seeped through the walls.

Not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. Five words, and the first two are the diagnosis of the other three. Wretched (talaipōros) is the word Paul uses of himself in Romans 7:24. Pitiable (eleeinos) means fit to be pitied, and Laodicea, which pitied nobody and needed nothing, is the object of pity in the only court that matters. Then the three that answer the three industries: poor (ptōchos, a beggar) to the banking town, blind (typhlos) to the town with the eye clinic, naked (gymnos, shamefully exposed) to the town that clothed the empire in black wool. The richest church was spiritually a naked blind beggar.

You do not know. And the governing phrase (ouk oidas, you do not know) is the whole tragedy of the letter. Christ says, I know your works (v. 15); they do not know their own condition. Laodicea is not a church that knows it is failing and cannot summon the energy to change. It is a church that has read its own accounts and concluded that everything is fine. Smyrna was poor and rich; Laodicea is rich and poor (2:9). Two congregations, two balance sheets, and both of them wrong in the world’s eyes about which column they were in.

I counsel you to buy from me. Then verse 18, and its tone lands before its content does. Counsel (symbouleuō) means advise. Not I command. To the church he has just threatened to spit out of his mouth, Christ offers advice, as a friend, in the manner of a merchant making an approach to a buyer. There is even a trace of humour in it, and it is not cruel: the wealthiest church in Asia is being invited to go shopping. Buy from me echoes Isaiah 55:1, where the LORD invites those who have no money to come, buy and eat, without money and without price. They must come to Christ for what they need, admitting they have nothing to pay with. The cost is not cash. It is the admission that you have none.

Gold refined by fire, so that you may be rich. The bank has no money. What is offered is gold that has been through the furnace (pepyrōmenon ek pyros): purified gold, the true riches of faith tested by trials, exactly the image Peter used (1 Peter 1:7), and the treasure of Christ himself.

And white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be seen. White, in a town whose fortune was built on glossy black. The white garments are the righteousness Christ gives (3:4–5; 19:8). In Scripture, nakedness is a picture of shame and judgement (Ezekiel 16:37), and from the first garden only God could cover it (Genesis 3:7, 21). The one thing Laodicea could not manufacture is the one thing it needed to wear.

And salve to anoint your eyes, so that you may see. Salve (kollourion) is eye ointment. Laodicea’s medical school made a compound for weak eyes, sold across the province. Laodicea could sell sight to strangers and could not see itself. They need spiritual sight, which only Christ’s Spirit can give, to see their real condition and his glory (Ephesians 1:18). Whatever the remedy, it is applied by him and not compounded locally, and its first effect would be that the congregation finally reads verse 17 as a description of itself.

Three purchases, one first move. Every one of them requires the same thing: coming to him with empty hands and asking. That is what I need nothing makes impossible, and it is why this is the most dangerous condition of the seven.

What it does not mean. Wealth is not itself the sin. The sin is trusting in it, and thinking that prosperity proves God’s favour. A church can be well-funded and spiritually bankrupt. Nor does buying from Christ mean earning salvation; it is the kind of buying Isaiah describes, without money and without price.

How should a well-off Christian live in the light of this letter? Gratefully, generously and watchfully. Paul tells the rich not to be haughty or to set their hopes on uncertain riches, but on God, who richly provides everything to enjoy, and to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–19). In practice: give regularly and sacrificially, not just from what is left over; use your home and resources for others; keep praying daily for what you seem not to need, because you do; and notice the moment comfort makes you feel that church, prayer or Scripture are optional. Wealth is a trust, not a verdict. The poorest believer and the richest come to Christ the same way: as beggars.

In a sentence. You say, I am rich, I have done well and I need nothing, without seeing that you are miserable and pitiful, poor, blind and naked; so I advise you to buy from me gold purified in the fire, to make you truly rich, white clothes to put on and cover your shameful nakedness, and ointment for your eyes, so that you can see.

On a Tuesday. Watch for the thought that you need nothing. Comfort can make you blind. Come to Christ as a beggar, every day. Begin your prayers this week by naming what you cannot provide for yourself: forgiveness, righteousness, sight, a heart that loves him. You will find you need everything.

For worship. The Lord who owns every bank and every flock and every herb in the valley offers himself to a church that thinks it needs nothing, and he names the price: empty hands. His gold is tried in the fire, his white garments cover every shame, his salve opens blind eyes. He sells without money, because he has already paid, and he counsels as a friend those he could have simply condemned.

verseByVerse.quote: Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent. Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent. Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me.

The setting. Proverbs 3:12 says that the LORD reproves the one he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights, a verse also quoted in Hebrews 12:5–6. In the Song of Songs 5:2, the beloved knocks at the door, saying, open to me. In the ancient world, eating together was a sign of friendship and acceptance.

Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline. After everything that has been said, this. The verb for love here is not the usual agapaō but philō, the warmer word for affection between friends, the word used of the Father’s love for the Son and of Jesus’ love for Lazarus (John 5:20; 11:36). To the worst church on the road, Christ uses the fondest word in the chapter. Reprove (elenchō) means expose, convict. Discipline (paideuō) means train, correct, as a parent trains a child. Even this sickening church is loved. Christ’s harsh words are the wounds of a friend (Proverbs 27:6).

The rebuke explained. The sentence comes from Proverbs, the same text Hebrews takes up at length to explain why hard providences are not evidence of rejection (Hebrews 12:5–11). And it reverses the entire meaning of the letter’s severity. The threat to spit them out was not the sound of Christ washing his hands of Laodicea. It was the sound of him refusing to leave it alone. The rebuke came first and the declaration of love came after, and the second explains the first rather than softening it. The churches that received no rebuke were not the better loved. Indifference does not bother to correct.

So be zealous and repent. Two commands, and the first is present and continuous: keep on being zealous (zēleue, be earnest, burn with zeal), a word from the same family as the word for hot, zestos, in verse 15. To the lukewarm church, the cure for tepid is not warm. It is boiling. The second command is a single decisive act: repent (metanoēson), once, now.

Behold, I stand at the door and knock. Then the best-known sentence in the seven letters, and it is almost always quoted out of position. Stand (hestēka) is I have taken my stand and remain standing; knock (krouō) is keep knocking. Christ is standing outside a church: the congregation that thinks it needs nothing, and has managed the remarkable feat of conducting its life with its Lord on the wrong side of the door. Stay with the picture, because it is almost unbearable. He is not far off. He is not waiting for Laodicea to travel. He is on the step, and he is knocking, which means he intends to be heard.
