And the church inside is in session, and busy, and has no idea. There is nothing in this letter about the congregation losing its doctrine or its attendance. It simply carried on without him and did not notice the difference.

If anyone hears my voice and opens the door. Note that it is singular (ean tis, if anyone). The letter has been addressed to a congregation throughout, and at the decisive moment it narrows to one person. A whole church may be lukewarm; the door is opened by individuals. Even if the church as a whole does not respond, any one person can. Nobody in Laodicea had to wait for a majority.

I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me. What he offers on the other side of the door is not a rebuke but a meal. The word (deipnēsō) is the evening meal, the unhurried one at the end of the day, not food snatched standing up but the table where a household sits and talks. In the ancient world, eating with someone was the public sign of accepting them; it is what got Jesus into trouble repeatedly (Luke 15:2), and he shared meals with his disciples after rising (Luke 24:30; John 21:12). To the church he has just called wretched, pitiable, poor, blind and naked, the offer is dinner. And he with me: the reciprocity is the last touch. Christ does not come in as an inspector who eats and leaves. He comes as a guest and stays as the host, and this book will end with a wedding supper (19:9). This is fellowship, friendship, communion with Christ, and a foretaste of that marriage supper.

Where Christians differ: an invitation to unbelievers? This verse is often used in evangelism, as Christ knocking at the door of an unbeliever’s heart, waiting to be invited in. Verdict: in context it is addressed to a church, calling professing believers to repent and restore fellowship with Christ. It can rightly be applied to unbelievers, since the gospel calls everyone to turn to Christ, and many professing members of Laodicea were probably not truly converted. But the verse does not mean that Christ is helpless until a sinner decides to let him in. Scripture teaches that the dead sinner can respond only because God first gives new life (John 6:44; Ephesians 2:1–5). When Christ knocks, his voice is powerful: it opens deaf ears, and his sheep hear his voice (John 10:27). The free invitation and God’s sovereign grace stand together.

What it does not mean. Christ’s discipline is not anger at people he has rejected. It is the opposite: the discipline of a father who loves. Nor is this verse about a once-for-all decision only; it calls for ongoing, renewed fellowship with Christ.

Is the hardship in my life God’s discipline? It may be, and if you belong to Christ, it is never his rejection. Discipline in Scripture is broader than punishment: it is training, the way a father shapes a son, and it can come through rebuke, through the consequences of sin, or through hardships that have no link to any particular sin (Hebrews 12:7–11). You do not need to identify the exact reason for every trial. Ask instead what God may be teaching you, confess any sin you know of, and trust that he is treating you as a beloved child. The evidence of his love is not the absence of correction but the cross, and the promise that it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness.

What does opening the door look like for a believer? Hearing his voice in his word and doing what it says. In practice: admit, in plain words to him, that you have been carrying on without him; repent of the specific things that crowded him out, whether busyness, comfort, a habit or a grudge; and make room for him again, in unhurried prayer, in reading Scripture to meet him rather than to tick a box, and in gathering at his table with his people. He has not been waiting with folded arms. He has been knocking, and he is eager to come in.

In a sentence. I correct and discipline everyone I love, so be earnest and turn back; look, I am standing at the door knocking, and if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in and share a meal with him, and he with me.

On a Tuesday. Listen for the knock this week: in the passage that unsettles you, the sermon that names your comfort, the friend who asks a hard question. Do not wait for your church to respond; open the door yourself. And at the Lord’s Supper, remember that Christ invites himself to eat with his people. Open to him, and enjoy his company.

For worship. The Lord of glory stands on the doorstep of a church that has forgotten him, and he does not break the door down or walk away. He knocks, and keeps knocking, and his voice is the voice of a friend. The door of the richest church in Asia is answered from inside one person at a time, and what is standing on the step is not a summons but Christ himself, with the evening free and the table ready.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’”

The setting. The final promise of the seven letters is the highest of all, and it is given to the worst church. It leads directly into chapters 4–5, where John sees God’s throne and the Lamb who conquered.

As I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne. Read the second half of the sentence first, because it is the ground of the first. Christ conquered (enikēsa, past tense: a finished victory), and the word is the same one used of the believer throughout these letters. He conquered by his death and resurrection (5:5–6), and then he sat down at the Father’s right hand (Hebrews 1:3; 12:2). That is a statement about what has already happened. The victory is not pending. The seat is not empty. Every promise made to the seven churches rests on a conquest that is finished and a throne that is occupied. And Christ’s throne and the Father’s throne are one (22:1, 3).

The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne. Then the astonishing clause. Grant (dōsō) is give: a gift, not an earned right. The conqueror is to sit with me on my throne. Not near it. Not in front of it. On it, sharing Christ’s royal rule. In the next chapter John will see the throne room and be unable to describe the one seated there except in jewels and colours, and twenty-four elders will fall down before it and cast their crowns before it. This verse says that ordinary Christians will be seated on that throne with Christ. Jesus promised the Twelve that they would sit on thrones (Matthew 19:28), and believers will reign with him (2:26–27; 20:4; 22:5; 2 Timothy 2:12). Paul said the same thing in a flat sentence that most readers hurry past: God raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6). The church that thought it was rich, and was offered the riches of Christ, is promised more than it ever imagined.

What conquering has meant. Consider how the word conquer has been defined by these two chapters, because it decides who this promise is for. It has not once meant achievement. At Ephesus it meant recovering a love that had been put down. At Smyrna it meant not denying him in a cell. At Pergamum it meant refusing a dinner invitation. At Thyatira it meant holding on. At Sardis it meant keeping a garment clean when nobody was looking. At Philadelphia it meant keeping his word with very little strength. And here at Laodicea it means getting up and opening a door. That is the whole list. The throne of the universe is promised to people whose great victory was answering a knock.

The seven promises together. The seven letters are finished, and the pattern of the promises is complete: the tree of life, escape from the second death, hidden manna and a new name, authority over the nations and the morning star, white garments and a name confessed before the Father, a pillar in the temple that never shakes, and now a seat on the throne. Every single one is given to the same people: ordinary believers in seven unremarkable towns, most of whose names nobody wrote down. And every one is, in the end, Christ himself and life with him.

He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The final call, for the seventh and last time. The plural has been there every time. Seven congregations read all seven letters, and so does every church since. The next words in the book are after this, and a door opens in heaven.

What it does not mean. Sharing Christ’s throne does not mean believers become gods or share his divine nature. It means they share in his reign as redeemed human beings, kings and priests under him (1:6; 5:10).

I am so weak; how can I conquer? By trusting the one who already has. The promise is grounded in his victory, not yours: I conquered. Your conquering is joined to his, the way a soldier shares the triumph of a general who has already won the war. It looks like the small things these letters have named: coming back to Christ when you have drifted, saying no to compromise, holding on, opening the door. Philadelphia had little power and received no rebuke at all. And he does not leave you to do it alone; he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). Weakness is not disqualification. It is the place where his strength is seen (2 Corinthians 12:9).

In a sentence. To the one who conquers I will give a seat with me on my throne, just as I conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne; whoever can hear should listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches.

On a Tuesday. Whatever your church is like, these letters are for you. Find yourself in them, hear the rebuke, take the promise, and conquer by staying faithful to Christ. Pick the one letter that most describes you, and do this week the one thing it tells you to do.

For worship. He conquered. That is the sentence the rest of the book will spend nineteen chapters unfolding, and it is already in the past tense. The Lamb who was slain has sat down beside his Father on the throne of heaven, and there is nothing left to be won that he has not already won. The dragon is coming, and the beast, and the harlot city, and the long ranks of the martyrs, and every one of them arrives after this verse, on the far side of a finished victory. And the Victor has made room on his throne for those who answered his knock.

You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead.<sup>2</sup>Wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die, for I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God.<sup>3</sup>Remember, then, what you received and heard. 4.title: Holy, Holy, Holy: The Throne Room of Heaven
4.overview:
After the letters to the seven churches, the scene shifts dramatically. John is drawn up through an open door in heaven and finds himself standing before the throne of God. Everything changes. The pastoral specificity of the seven letters gives way to cosmic, overwhelming, dazzling vision. Before any seal is opened, before any trumpet sounds, before any judgment falls, John must see — and the church must see with him — what actually governs history. The answer is: this throne. This worship. This God.

Chapters 4 and 5 together form the interpretive center of the entire book. Chapter 4 answers the question: Who is God? Chapter 5 answers the question: How has God chosen to rule? The answer to the first is: the Creator of all things, infinitely holy, eternally worshipped, Almighty. The answer to the second is: through the slaughtered Lamb who has conquered. Everything that follows in Revelation — every seal, every trumpet, every bowl, every beast, every judgment, every promise — flows from these two chapters as from a spring.

Interpretive flag — “Come up here” (v. 1): Dispensational premillennialists have often read “Come up here” as a prophetic picture of the Rapture — the moment at which the church is caught up to heaven before the tribulation begins. The supporting observation is that the word “church” (ekklēsia) does not appear again in Revelation after chapter 3 until 22:16, suggesting the church has been removed from the scene. The amillennial/idealist reading understands “Come up here” as the commission given specifically to John for his visionary experience — John, not the church, is called up to receive the vision. The church’s absence from the term ekklēsia in chapters 4–22 is explained by the fact that the church is addressed throughout these chapters under other designations: the 144,000, the two witnesses, the great multitude, the bride, the new Jerusalem. The amillennial reading is followed here, with genuine respect for the dispensational position.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Throne Room of Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2 open the vision: a door standing open in heaven, the trumpet voice of 1:10 calling come up here, John at once in the Spirit, and then the sentence the whole book turns on — a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne. The word throne occurs some forty-seven times in Revelation and about fifteen times in the whole of the rest of the New Testament. Nothing else in the room is described first.

Verse 3 describes the one seated with three colours and nothing else: jasper (clear as crystal, 21:11), carnelian (blood-red), and around the throne a rainbow like an emerald. Carnelian was the first stone of the high priest’s breastpiece and jasper the last (Ex. 28:17–20). The rainbow is the sign given after the flood, a warrior’s bow hung up and pointed away (Gen. 9:13–16). No face is described, and the restraint is the point.

Verse 4 sets twenty-four elders on twenty-four thrones around it, in white garments with golden crowns — every reward promised to the seven churches, already being worn. Verse 5 fills the room with Sinai: lightning, rumblings and peals of thunder out of the throne itself (Ex. 19:16–19), and seven burning torches which John identifies as the seven spirits of God.

Verse 6 gives the floor — a sea of glass, like crystal, chaos frozen solid in front of the throne (cf. Ex. 24:10; 21:1) — and introduces four living creatures, nearer than the elders, covered in eyes. Verse 7 names them: lion, ox, the face of a man, and an eagle in flight, drawn from Ezekiel’s cherubim (Ezek. 1:5–11).

Verse 8 gives them Isaiah’s six wings and Isaiah’s song — Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come (Isa. 6:2–3) — sung without ceasing, day and night. Verses 9–11 close the chapter with a repeated movement: whenever the creatures give glory, the twenty-four elders fall down, cast their crowns before the throne, and say Worthy are you, our Lord and God… for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Throne Comes First

Before any seal is opened, John is shown an occupied throne, ringed by a rainbow and surrounded by unceasing worship: holy, holy, holy. The Creator of all things is worthy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Domitian liked to be called “our Lord and God”; the elders give those words to the true throne.

Now: Lay down every crown you were given before the one who gave it.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven! And the first voice, which I had heard speaking to me like a trumpet, said, "Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this." At once I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven! And the first voice, which I had heard speaking to me like a trumpet, said, “Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this.” At once I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne.

Meaning first. Revelation 4 takes John, and the reader, into the throne room of heaven, before any judgement or beast appears. John sees a door open in heaven and is called up to see what must happen (v. 1). At the centre is a throne, and one seated on it, shining like precious stones and surrounded by an emerald rainbow (vv. 2–3). Around it are twenty-four elders on thrones, in white with golden crowns; from the throne come lightning and thunder; before it burn seven torches, the Spirit of God, and spreads a sea like crystal (vv. 4–6a). Four living creatures, full of eyes, like a lion, an ox, a man and an eagle, never stop crying, Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty (vv. 6b–8). Whenever they give glory to God, the elders fall down, cast their crowns before the throne and praise him as worthy because he created all things (vv. 9–11). Before John sees anything of the world’s chaos, he sees that the universe has a centre, and it is a throne that is occupied. Everything that follows in the book flows from this throne.

The setting. The vision draws on the great throne visions of the Old Testament: Isaiah 6, where the Lord sits on a high throne and the seraphim cry Holy, holy, holy; Ezekiel 1, with its four living creatures, wheels, rainbow and crystal expanse; Daniel 7, where thrones are set and the Ancient of Days sits in judgement; and 1 Kings 22:19, where Micaiah sees the LORD on his throne with the host of heaven. For readers living under the emperor, whose court ceremonies were grand and whose subjects were expected to hail him as lord and god, this chapter declares who truly sits on the throne of the universe.

The camera lifts. The letters are finished. Seven congregations have been examined by a Christ who walks among them, and the verdict on most of them was uncomfortable. Now the view rises from the road in Asia to the room where the world is governed.

After this I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven! “After this” (meta tauta) means after John saw these things, not necessarily after the events of chapters 2 and 3 in history. It is John’s way of marking a new vision, and he will use it repeatedly (7:1, 9; 15:5; 18:1). It marks the order of John’s seeing, not necessarily the order of events. What follows is not the next instalment of a timetable; it is the next thing shown to him. And the door has been opened (thyra ēneōgmenē, a door that has been opened, and stands open). Heaven is not closed; God opens it to reveal himself. Philadelphia was promised an open door that no one could shut (3:8); Laodicea had Christ knocking at a closed one (3:20). Now heaven’s own door stands open.

And the first voice, which I had heard speaking to me like a trumpet. The voice of Christ from 1:10. The same Lord who walked among the lampstands now calls John up to the throne.

Said, Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this. “Come up here” (anaba hōde): John is summoned, in vision, into heaven, to see earth’s history from heaven’s point of view. “Must” (dei) is God’s sure plan, as in 1:1. Nothing that John is about to see is improvised.

At once I was in the Spirit. The same phrase as 1:10, and the second of four times John uses it to mark a new stage of the book (1:10; 4:2; 17:3; 21:10): a new level of prophetic vision. He is not describing a technique. Something is being done to him.

And behold, a throne stood in heaven. Then the sentence the whole book turns on. Nothing else is described first. Not the walls, not the light, not the attendants. A throne (thronos), and somebody on it. The word occurs again and again in chapters 4 and 5, and about forty-seven times in Revelation, far more than in all the rest of the New Testament together; it is the single most repeated image in the book, and its central symbol: God rules. Rome’s throne, and Satan’s throne (2:13), are rivals that will fall. And its position here is deliberate. Before one seal is opened, before a single horseman rides, before the dragon appears or the beast rises out of the sea, John is shown a throne that is occupied.

With one seated on the throne. Seated (kathēmenos): God is not anxious or pacing; he sits, at rest, in sovereign control. Sitting is the posture of a ruler whose work is not in danger and who is not going to be moved from his chair. John does not describe God himself in human form, only his radiance (v. 3), in reverent restraint. He is called, throughout the book, simply the one seated on the throne.

A location, not an explanation. Consider what that meant for the congregations who first heard it read. They had just been told to expect prison, poverty, slander and execution. The reply is not an explanation and not a promise of rescue. It is a location. There is a throne. It is not empty, it is not being contested, and the one on it is seated. Whatever is coming in the next eighteen chapters arrives in a universe with that furniture in it.

Where Christians differ: is John’s ascent the rapture of the church? Dispensationalists often read “Come up here” as a picture of the church raptured before the tribulation, noting that the word “church” does not appear on earth from chapter 4 until 22:16. That observation is a real feature of the text, and the reading is held by many believers who love this book. Verdict: the call is to John alone, to receive a vision; nothing suggests the whole church is taken up. Ezekiel and Isaiah were taken up in vision in much the same way. The church appears throughout chapters 4–22 under other names: servants of God (7:3), saints (13:7), those who keep God’s commandments and hold the testimony of Jesus (12:17), the bride (19:7). The saints are under the altar (6:9), sealed (7:3) and conquering by the blood of the Lamb (12:11). The word church is absent because the visions use symbolic language, not because the church has gone. There is one visible return of Christ, not a secret rapture.

What it does not mean. Heaven is not described here in a way that can be mapped or measured. The vision uses symbols to communicate God’s majesty and rule, not the floor plan of heaven.

Is this where believers who have died are now? In a real sense, yes. The throne room is the presence of God, and Scripture says that to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). Revelation shows the souls of the martyrs before the throne (6:9–11) and a great multitude serving God day and night in his temple (7:15). So when a believer dies, he goes to be with Christ in this presence, conscious and at rest, awaiting the resurrection of the body and the new creation (21:1–4). The symbols are not a map, but the reality behind them is where your believing loved ones are.

How does a throne in heaven help me when my life is falling apart? It does not explain your trouble, and it was not meant to. It tells you who is in charge of it. The churches hearing this were facing prison and death, and the first thing God showed them was not a way out but a throne that was occupied. Nothing in your life is outside his rule: not the diagnosis, the betrayal, the loss, or the news. He is not pacing; he is seated. When you pray, begin there, as the Lord’s Prayer does: Our Father in heaven. The ground under you may shake. The throne does not.

In a sentence. After that I looked and saw a door standing open in heaven, and the trumpet-like voice I had heard before said, Come up here, and I will show you what has to happen next; immediately the Spirit took hold of me, and I saw a throne in heaven, and someone sitting on it.

On a Tuesday. When the news is frightening and your own life feels chaotic, remember that before John saw any of the troubles, he saw the throne. Begin there. Before you read the headlines tomorrow, read this chapter. Let the first thing you see in the day be the one who is seated.

For worship. The universe has a centre, and it is not empty. Before the seals, before the trumpets, before the beast and the dragon and the burning city, there is a throne, and the one on it is seated, at rest, in perfect command. He opened the door of heaven to show a frightened church where the world is ruled from, and he has never once stood up in alarm.

verseByVerse.quote: And he who sat there had the appearance of jasper and carnelian, and around the throne was a rainbow that had the appearance of an emerald.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he who sat there had the appearance of jasper and carnelian, and around the throne was a rainbow that had the appearance of an emerald.

The setting. Ezekiel saw a rainbow-like brightness around the throne of God (Ezekiel 1:28). The rainbow first appeared after the flood, as the sign of God’s covenant never again to destroy the earth by water (Genesis 9:12–17). On the high priest’s breastpiece, with its twelve stones for the twelve tribes, the sardius (carnelian) is the first stone and the jasper the last (Exodus 28:17–20); in the foundations of the new Jerusalem jasper is the first and carnelian the sixth (21:19–20), and the city has the glory of God, its radiance like jasper, clear as crystal (21:11).

The most remarkable restraint in Scripture. John has been given a sight no living man has had, and when he comes to describe the one seated on the throne he describes no face, no form, no figure, no size. He gives three colours and stops.

And he who sat there had the appearance of jasper and carnelian. “Appearance” (horasei) means look, aspect. John describes God only by comparison with dazzling light through gems. Jasper (iaspidi) in the ancient world was a name for various precious stones, not only the opaque stone the modern name suggests; 21:11 describes it as clear as crystal, which points to something like a diamond: brilliant, colourless, throwing light in every direction. Purity and brilliant glory. Carnelian (sardiō) is a fiery red stone, named after Sardis: deep and burning, perhaps God’s blazing holiness, even his wrath. Blazing white light and blood-red fire, and no shape between them.

The first and the last of his people’s stones. The two stones may well not be chosen at random. On the high priest’s breastpiece, where the names of Israel’s tribes were carried before God, carnelian was the first of the twelve stones and jasper the last. The one on the throne is bounded, as it were, by the first and the last of the stones that bore his people’s names before him, and the first and the last is exactly what Christ called himself in 1:17. The God of this throne has always carried his people on the heart of their high priest.

Why no face? Not because there was nothing to see. Scripture is consistent that no one may look on God and live (Exodus 33:20). God is light, dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see (1 Timothy 6:16). Every prophet who came close reported the same difficulty. Ezekiel piles up qualifiers until the grammar buckles: the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD (Ezekiel 1:28). Isaiah described the train of a robe and the smoke (Isaiah 6:1–4). Even here, the two most searching words in the verse are the appearance of, and John uses them twice.

The mercy of restraint. That restraint is itself a mercy, and there is a warning inside it for anyone who wants a picture. Every attempt to draw God ends in something smaller than God, which is the reason the second commandment exists. What the vision gives instead is what light does when it strikes a stone: a description of an effect, because the cause cannot be looked at.

And around the throne was a rainbow that had the appearance of an emerald. Then the third colour, and it changes everything. A rainbow (iris, a halo or rainbow), emerald green (smaragdinō). Around the throne. Encircling it completely, so that no one can approach from any direction without coming through it. The rainbow entered Scripture at the end of the flood, when God set his bow in the cloud and called it the sign of a covenant. The picture there is of a warrior hanging up his weapon, the bow turned away from the earth: When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant (Genesis 9:16). It was a promise given after judgement had fallen, to a world that deserved it and had just seen what God can do.

The order is the theology. So set the three colours together in the order John gives them. Blazing holiness. Burning judgement. And around the whole throne, without a gap, a covenant promise. Around the blinding, fiery majesty of God is a sign of his covenant mercy. The throne of judgement is surrounded by grace. Chapters of trumpets and bowls and plagues are about to be poured out from this room, and every one of them will come out from inside a rainbow. Everything that follows, including the terrible judgements, happens within the circle of God’s faithfulness to his promises.

What it does not mean. The stones do not give God a physical form; God is spirit (John 4:24). The point is overwhelming, beautiful glory that words can only point to.

Will we ever see God’s face? Yes, in Christ. The last chapter of this book promises that his servants will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads (22:4). Jesus said the pure in heart will see God (Matthew 5:8), and John wrote that when Christ appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Even now, God’s glory is seen in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6): whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). What sinful eyes cannot bear now, glorified eyes will see with joy. That sight, theologians have long said, is the highest happiness of heaven.

Why does the rainbow matter if God is about to judge the world? Because it tells you what kind of judge he is. The rainbow does not mean there will be no judgement; Revelation is full of it. It means God’s judgements come from a throne bound by covenant faithfulness. He keeps his promises to his people even while he judges a rebellious world, and every judgement serves his purpose of rescuing and renewing. For a believer, the rainbow says: the storm you see coming out of the throne will not touch the promise around it. God has bound himself to you, in Christ, at his own initiative, and he cannot go back on it.

In a sentence. The one seated there shone like brilliant jasper and red carnelian, and a rainbow glowing like an emerald encircled the throne.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to picture God in a way that makes him manageable, a kindly grandfather or a stern headmaster, remember that John would not draw his face. And when you fear that his holiness leaves no room for you, look at the rainbow. Thank him today for one promise he has kept to you, and trust him with the ones still waiting.

For worship. The one seated on the throne is holy beyond describing and terrible beyond looking at, and he has bound himself in a covenant, in writing, at his own initiative, to a people who had nothing to offer. His majesty and his faithfulness belong together. The bow is hung up and turned away, and it is green as an emerald, and it was around the throne long before John arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and seated on the thrones were twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads. From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings and peals of thunder, and before the throne were burning seven torches of fire, which are the seven spirits of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and seated on the thrones were twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads. From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings and peals of thunder, and before the throne were burning seven torches of fire, which are the seven spirits of God,

The setting. King David divided the temple priests into twenty-four divisions (1 Chronicles 24:3–19), and the temple musicians into twenty-four groups (1 Chronicles 25). At Sinai, God’s presence came with thunder, lightning and a thick cloud (Exodus 19:16). Daniel saw thrones set in place around the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:9).

Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and seated on the thrones were twenty-four elders. Elders (presbyterous): they sit on thrones, so they share in God’s rule. They wear white, so they are pure. They wear golden crowns (stephanous, victors’ wreaths), so they have conquered.

Where Christians differ: who are the twenty-four elders? Some see them as an order of angels, a heavenly council around God (Psalm 89:7), since they appear alongside the living creatures and are distinguished from the redeemed multitude of 7:9. Others see them as representing the whole people of God, Old Testament and New: the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles. A third reading notes that David divided the priests into twenty-four courses, so that twenty-four could stand for the whole priesthood. Verdict: the second view is the most likely. The new Jerusalem bears the names of the twelve tribes on its gates and the twelve apostles on its foundations (21:12–14), a clear twelve plus twelve. The elders receive what the seven letters promise to conquering believers: white robes, crowns and thrones. They represent the one people of God, redeemed from both covenants, already worshipping in heaven. The church on earth is represented before the throne.

Clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads. White garments: exactly what was promised to the conquerors at Sardis (3:5). Golden crowns: the victor’s wreath promised at Smyrna (2:10). Thrones of their own: the promise made to Laodicea at the end of the letters (3:21). Every reward held out to the seven churches is already visible in the throne room, being worn, before the first seal is opened. The promises are not aspirations. They are furniture.

From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings and peals of thunder. This is Sinai. When God came down on the mountain there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud and a very loud trumpet blast, and the people trembled (Exodus 19:16–19). It speaks of God’s awesome majesty and coming judgement. The same sequence of lightning, rumblings and thunder appears at the climax of each series of judgements (8:5; 11:19; 16:18), each time intensified, linking them to this throne. Each time it means that God is about to act.

Not a quiet room. Which is a necessary corrective to the way this scene is usually imagined. The throne room of Revelation 4 is not serene in the way a library is serene. There is a storm coming out of the middle of it. Whatever the peace of heaven is, it is not the peace of a quiet room; it is the peace of people standing perfectly still in the presence of something that could level a mountain.

And before the throne were burning seven torches of fire, which are the seven spirits of God. Torches (lampades). John interprets the symbol himself, as he did at 1:20, and the sevenfold Spirit has already been named at 1:4 and 3:1. Zechariah’s lampstand stands behind the image again (Zechariah 4:2–6): the Holy Spirit in his fullness. Fire speaks of holiness, light and purifying power. And note where the Spirit is: before the throne, ready to be sent out into all the earth (5:6). The Spirit at work in seven struggling congregations on a road in Asia is the Spirit blazing in front of the throne of God, and he is not two Spirits.

Everything placed by the throne. The arrangement of the whole scene repays attention. Everything in this chapter is described by its position relative to the throne: around the throne, from the throne, before the throne, on each side of the throne. Nothing in heaven is described in its own terms. Every creature, every object, every light in the room is located by reference to the one fixed point, and there is no other way of giving directions in that place.

What it does not mean. The elders on thrones do not mean that believers share God’s divine authority. They reign under him, as the next verses show when they cast their crowns before his throne (v. 10).

If lightning comes from the throne, how can I approach it with confidence? Through the High Priest who sits at its right hand. Hebrews says that because we have a great high priest who sympathises with our weakness, we may draw near to the throne of grace with confidence, to receive mercy and find grace in time of need (Hebrews 4:14–16). The lightning is real: God is holy, and no sinner can stand before him on his own merits. But the elders sit there in white, near the storm, unafraid, because their robes have been washed in the blood of the Lamb (7:14). You come the same way. Not cautiously hoping to be tolerated, but welcomed for Christ’s sake.

In a sentence. Around the throne were twenty-four other thrones, with twenty-four elders seated on them, dressed in white and wearing golden crowns; from the throne came lightning, rumbling and thunder, and in front of it seven torches blazed, which are the sevenfold Spirit of God.

On a Tuesday. When you gather with your church this Sunday, however small it is, remember that the whole people of God, from every age, is already represented before God’s throne. When you worship, you join them. And when you pray alone on a weekday, you are not shouting into the dark; you are coming, in Christ, to a throne surrounded by your brothers and sisters in white.

For worship. The throne of God is a storm of holiness, and around it sit the redeemed in white, crowned and unafraid. The promises made to struggling churches are already being worn in heaven. The Spirit who burns before the throne is the Spirit who lives in the weakest believer, and the God of Sinai has made a place in his presence for the people he has washed.
verseByVerse.note: Twenty-four may combine the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles — the whole people of God.

verseByVerse.quote: and before the throne there was as it were a sea of glass, like crystal. And around the throne, on each side of the throne, are four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind: the first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and before the throne there was as it were a sea of glass, like crystal. And around the throne, on each side of the throne, are four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind: the first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight.

The setting. In Ezekiel 1:5–22, four living creatures, each with four faces (man, lion, ox and eagle), carry God’s throne-chariot, with wheels full of eyes, beneath an expanse like awesome crystal; Ezekiel later identifies them as cherubim (Ezekiel 10:20). In Isaiah 6:2, seraphim with six wings stand above God’s throne. In Solomon’s temple, a huge bronze basin called the sea stood in the court for the priests to wash in (1 Kings 7:23–26). In the ancient Near East, the sea was a symbol of chaos and evil; in Revelation, the beast rises from the sea (13:1), and in the new creation there is no more sea (21:1).

And before the throne there was as it were a sea of glass, like crystal. Two qualifiers in a few words, as it were and like, and they are the marks of a man describing something for which no word exists. A floor before the throne, flat and shining and utterly still. The sea of glass (thalassa hyalinē) would have struck the first hearers, because ancient glass was usually cloudy, so glass as clear as crystal was rare and precious.

What stands behind the sea. Three things stand behind the image. When the elders of Israel went up Sinai and saw the God of Israel, there was under his feet as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness (Exodus 24:10), the same doubled hesitation. Possibly the sea speaks of God’s transcendence, the vast distance between his throne and creation. In Solomon’s temple the bronze Sea stood in the courtyard for washing before the priests could serve; the way to God always ran past water. And in the ancient imagination the sea was chaos itself, restless and dangerous and full of what could not be tamed, which is why the beast will come up out of it in chapter 13, and why the new creation is announced with the words and the sea was no more (21:1).

The chaos is a floor. Here the sea is glass. Still, transparent, motionless, with the light going straight through it. The forces of chaos and evil lie calm and still before God’s throne: no storm reaches him. The chaos is not raging in front of the throne; it is a floor. Whatever threatens the church in the chapters ahead is in this room already, and it is being walked on. In 15:2, the conquerors stand beside the sea of glass mingled with fire, like Israel beside the Red Sea after the exodus, singing.

And around the throne, on each side of the throne, are four living creatures. Living creatures (zōa, living beings) are not beasts; that is a different word, thēria, used for the evil beasts of chapter 13. They are high angelic beings, combining features of Ezekiel’s cherubim and Isaiah’s seraphim: John’s creatures have Ezekiel’s faces and Isaiah’s wings and song. They are nearest of all, nearer than the elders. Four is the number of the earth (four corners, four winds, 7:1). They represent the whole of creation, worshipping its Creator.

Full of eyes in front and behind. Eyes speak of ceaseless watchfulness and knowledge. Nothing escapes their sight, nor God’s. Whatever else these beings are, they are unresting perception. Nothing in the created order goes unobserved by the creatures closest to the throne, and they have been looking at it from every angle for as long as there has been anything to see.

The first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight. Each represents the highest of a kind of creature: the lion, the noblest of wild animals; the ox, the strongest of domestic animals; man, the wisest of all; the eagle, the swiftest of birds. Ancient rabbis said much the same. Together they show all creation, at its best, worshipping God. In Ezekiel each creature had all four faces; here each has one.

Adoration, not administration. And the practical point of the whole arrangement is easily lost among the animals. The nearest beings to the throne of God are not administrators. They are worshippers covered in eyes, whose entire function is to see and to say what they see. Nearness to God does not produce mere activity; it produces adoration. That is the direction the whole book is travelling, and the church is being shown its destination before it is shown its road.

What it does not mean. The four creatures were later linked by church tradition with the four Gospels (Matthew the man, Mark the lion, Luke the ox, John the eagle), a link first made by Irenaeus in the second century, though this pairing is Jerome’s, which is why medieval churches put a lion beside Mark and an ox beside Luke. This is an ancient and memorable devotional association, but it is not what the text means. The creatures represent creation worshipping God. The instinct behind the tradition is sound, all the same: creation and the gospel both come from this room.

Does all creation really worship God? Yes, in its own way. The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1), and the psalmist calls sea creatures, fire, hail, mountains, trees, beasts and birds to praise the LORD (Psalm 148:7–10). They do it by being what he made them to be, displaying his wisdom and power. In the next chapter every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea joins the song (5:13). Creation now groans under the curse, waiting for the freedom of God’s children (Romans 8:19–22), but it was made for praise and will be renewed for it. When you look at a hawk or a field of cattle, you are looking at worshippers. Humans are the ones who were made to put that praise into words.

In a sentence. In front of the throne was something like a sea of glass, clear as crystal, and around the throne, on every side, were four living beings covered with eyes in front and behind: the first was like a lion, the second like an ox, the third had a human face, and the fourth was like an eagle in flight.

On a Tuesday. When the chaos of the world threatens to swamp you, remember that before the throne it is a sea of glass. And let the next lion, ox, eagle or human face you see remind you what they are for. Your highest purpose, and theirs, is to praise him. Take a walk this week and give thanks for what you see, out loud if you like.

For worship. All creation exists to worship God. The fiercest, the strongest, the wisest and the swiftest of his creatures stand nearest his throne, covered in eyes, and they have never seen anything that made them want to stop praising him. The sea that terrified the ancient world lies still as glass before him, and the beings closest to his glory are the ones most taken up with it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never cease to say, "Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never cease to say, “Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!”

The setting. In Isaiah 6:2–3, the seraphim, each with six wings, cover their faces and feet and call to one another: Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory. Isaiah, seeing it, cried out, Woe is me! For I am lost. He heard it in the year King Uzziah died, the year the political certainty of his lifetime came to an end (Isaiah 6:1).

And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings. Six wings, like the seraphim: two to cover their faces, in reverence; two to cover their feet, in humility; two to fly, in service (Isaiah 6:2).

Are full of eyes all around and within. Ceaseless awareness of God, and of all his works. They see everything, inside and out.

And day and night they never cease to say. “Never cease” is literally they have no rest (anapausin ouk echousin). Not a burden but a joy. Their worship is ceaseless because God’s holiness is inexhaustible. In contrast, those who worship the beast have no rest day or night in torment (14:11). The same phrase describes the two destinies of creatures: endless joy in worshipping God, or endless restlessness in refusing him.

Holy, holy, holy. Isaiah heard this song some eight hundred years earlier. It is the same three words, and the fact that they have not changed in eight centuries, or in the centuries since, is part of the point. Empires have come and gone in the interval. The song has not been revised. Holy is hagios, in Hebrew qadosh: set apart, utterly other, pure. Hebrew has no endings for more and most; to intensify a word you repeat it. Twice means emphasis. Three times is the superlative: God is the holiest possible, holy beyond all measure. And there is only one attribute of God that Scripture ever trebles like this. Nobody sings loving, loving, loving or mighty, mighty, mighty. God is love and God is almighty and both are said plainly, but the word said three times before the throne, day and night, without ceasing, is holy. Christians have long seen in the threefold Holy a hint of the Trinity, Father, Son and Spirit, though the main point is God’s infinite holiness.

What holiness means. Holy means separate, cut off, other. It is not first a moral word but a word about distance: God is not a larger version of us, not the best example of anything on our scale. He is in a category with one member. The moral meaning follows from that: because he is wholly other, he is wholly pure. Teachers such as R. C. Sproul spent a lifetime on this one word, and rightly: get it wrong and every other doctrine sags, because sin stops being an outrage and grace stops being a miracle.

Is the Lord God Almighty. Almighty (pantokratōr, ruler of all), as in 1:8. The God of armies, the God who holds every power.

Who was and is and is to come! As in 1:4, 8, with the order changed. There it was who is and who was and who is to come, beginning with the present. Here it begins with the past. From the throne room, where eternity is the vantage point rather than a struggling church in Asia, the sequence runs in ordinary order: God’s eternity, and his coming to judge and renew. And the middle term is the one being sung over: he is.

What it does not mean. Holiness is not only moral purity, though it includes that. It means God is utterly distinct from everything he has made, in a class of his own. It does not make him distant and uncaring; the holy God comes near in Christ, so that sinners can stand before him.

Is God vain to want endless praise? No, and the question deserves a straight answer. First, praise is not something God lacks and needs topping up. He was not lonely or unadmired before there was a universe; Father, Son and Spirit have delighted in one another from eternity, and nothing was made to fill a gap. Second, praise is what happens when anything true is seen clearly. Nobody watching a sunrise over water has to be commanded to say something; the praise is not a tax levied on the viewer but the completion of the seeing. To ask people who are looking at God to stop praising him would be to ask them to look at him and not notice. What is happening in this room is not flattery. It is accuracy. And it is for our good: we were made to find our joy in him.

Won’t heaven be boring if it is endless worship? Not if worship is what this chapter shows. Boredom is what happens when a thing is exhausted, when you have seen all there is and the eye has nowhere further to go. The creatures nearest the throne are covered in eyes, have been looking without pause, day and night, and have not yet come to the end of the first word. It is not that they must keep saying it. It is that they cannot stop. Worship in heaven is not a never-ending church service as we know it; it is the whole of life, work, fellowship and joy, lived in the open presence of the God who is infinitely worth knowing (22:3–5). The only way it could bore us would be for God to be smaller than he is.

In a sentence. Each of the four living beings had six wings and was covered with eyes, all round and even under the wings, and day and night they never stop saying, Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was, who is and who is coming.

On a Tuesday. Sing Holy, holy, holy with understanding. You join the worship that has never stopped around God’s throne. When you next confess your sin, start where Isaiah started, with God’s holiness, and you will find your sin is more serious and his grace more astonishing than you had thought.

For worship. He is holy, holy, holy, in a category with one member, and the creatures who have looked at him longest have found nothing in him that is less than holy. Empires have risen and fallen since Isaiah first heard the song, and not one word of it has needed changing. He was, he is, and he is coming, and the praise that surrounds him is not flattery but the truth, sung by those who see him clearly and cannot stop.

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever, the twenty-four elders fall down before him who is seated on the throne and worship him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne, saying, "Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever, the twenty-four elders fall down before him who is seated on the throne and worship him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne, saying, “Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.”

The setting. When a king was defeated or became a client of Rome, he might lay his crown before the conqueror as a sign of submission; the historian Tacitus describes Tiridates of Armenia taking the royal diadem from his head and laying it at the foot of the emperor Nero’s statue. And the emperor Domitian liked to be addressed as our lord and god (dominus et deus noster), as the Roman historian Suetonius reports. The elders give this very title to the only one who deserves it.

A movement. The chapter ends with a movement, and it is the most eloquent gesture in the book.

And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne. Glory (doxan), honour (timēn), thanks (eucharistian): creation praises God for who he is and gives thanks for what he has done. And the word whenever makes it a pattern rather than a single event. Every time the creatures begin, the elders go down.

Who lives forever and ever. In contrast to emperors who live and die. Domitian was dead within a year or two of this book, murdered in his own palace. The one on this throne has no successor.

The twenty-four elders fall down before him who is seated on the throne and worship him. Two things happen: they fall, and they throw. Fall down (pesountai) and worship (proskynēsousin, prostrate themselves). Worship involves the body: they lie face down before God. Falling is what people do in the presence of God: Ezekiel, Daniel, John himself in chapter 1.

They cast their crowns before the throne. Throwing the crown is different. That is a decision about what to do with a reward. Cast (balousin) is throw. These crowns were given. Nobody in that room manufactured one. They are the victor’s wreaths promised to the conquerors of Smyrna and Philadelphia, handed over by Christ himself, and the elders will not keep them on in front of the throne. Whatever honour God gives his people, they give back to him. Their victory was his. In the Roman world a client king laid his crown at the emperor’s feet to acknowledge where his authority came from. Heaven does the same thing with far better cause.

Saying, Worthy are you, our Lord and God. Worthy (axios) means deserving, of equal weight. The word was used in acclaiming the emperor at his arrival. Only God is worthy. And a first-century hearer would have flinched at the next phrase. Our Lord and God (ho kyrios kai ho theos hēmōn) was precisely the title Domitian liked to hear, and Suetonius records that it came to be used of him as a matter of course. The congregations hearing this letter were under pressure to say those words to a man in Rome. John gives them the same words to say, and a different throne.

To receive glory and honor and power. God does not need these from us; he is worthy of them, and to give them is right.

For you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created. The ground of the worthiness is stated. Created (ektisas). By your will (dia to thelēma sou, because of your will). God is worthy of worship because he is the Creator. Not merely because he is strong, and not merely because he will win, but because everything that exists does so at his pleasure and would stop existing if he stopped willing it. Nothing exists by chance or of necessity. And take the order seriously: they existed comes before and were created. Perhaps they existed in his purpose and then came into being; or they exist now because they were created. Either way, the intention preceded the act. Nothing in the universe is an accident or an afterthought, including the small congregation in Thyatira and the person reading this sentence. The Creator has the right to rule, judge and redeem his creation, which is what the rest of the book shows.

A song deliberately incomplete. That is where chapter 4 stops, and it is deliberately incomplete. The song here is about creation, and creation alone is not enough to save anybody; the world he made is the world in rebellion against him. In the next chapter a scroll will appear that nobody in heaven or earth is able to open, and John will weep. The answer to that will be a new song, and the new song will not be about creation but about redemption, sung to the Lamb who was slain.

What it does not mean. Casting crowns does not mean believers’ rewards are worthless. It means that their highest joy is to give all glory to God. Nor does creation by God’s will mean God needed to create. He created freely, out of love and for his glory.

What crowns do I have to cast down now? Anything you are tempted to wear as though you earned it. There is a very practical question in the elders’ gesture for anybody who has ever done anything well. What are you holding that was given to you and is being worn as though it were your own achievement? A capacity, a competence, an upbringing, a marriage, a body that still works, thirty years of faithful service in a church, a ministry others admire. None of it was self-generated (1 Corinthians 4:7). Cast it down by thanking God for it specifically, by using it for others rather than for your reputation, and by refusing to compare yourself with those who seem to have less. What is worn in this life is thrown down in the next, and the sooner a person starts throwing, the less it will cost him at the end.

If God made everything by his will, where did evil come from? Not from God’s creating. Everything he made was very good (Genesis 1:31). Evil entered through the rebellion of creatures, angelic and human, who turned from him (Genesis 3; Jude 6). God is not the author of sin, yet nothing escapes his sovereign rule, and he governs even evil for his good purposes, as he did supremely at the cross (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). Scripture does not explain everything about this, and we should not pretend it does. But it shows us what God has done about evil: the Creator entered his creation to bear its curse, and the next chapter shows him on the throne as the Lamb who was slain.

In a sentence. Whenever the living beings give glory, honour and thanks to the one seated on the throne, who lives for ever and ever, the twenty-four elders fall down before him and worship the eternal one, and lay their crowns in front of the throne, saying, You are worthy, our Lord and God, to receive glory, honour and power, because you created everything, and it is by your will that everything came to be and exists.

On a Tuesday. Lay down whatever crowns you have, your achievements, gifts and successes, before God. He made you, and everything you have came from his will. And when you are asked this week, in whatever form, to give to someone or something else the loyalty that belongs to God alone, say the elders’ words under your breath: our Lord and God. There is only one throne that title belongs to.

For worship. Before the scroll, before the seals, before the horsemen and the martyrs and the long war, there is a throne, and it is occupied, and the one seated on it is holy, holy, holy. He was before anything was. He is, while everything shakes. He is coming, and the storm going out from his throne is fenced by a rainbow. Worthy is he to receive glory and honour and power, for he made all things, and they exist because he willed them, and the crowns of all his conquering people lie at his feet.
