And the first voice, which I had heard speaking to me like a trumpet, said, “Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this.”<sup>2</sup>At once I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne.<sup>3</sup>And he who sat there had the appearance of jasper and carnelian, and around the throne was a rainbow that had the appearance of an emerald.<sup>4</sup>Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and seated on the thrones were twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads.<sup>5</sup>From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings and peals of thunder, and before the throne were burning seven torches of fire, which are the seven spirits of God,<sup>6</sup>and before the throne there was as it were a sea of glass, like crystal. And around the throne, on each side of the throne, are four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind:<sup>7</sup>the first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight.<sup>8</sup>And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never cease to say, “Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!”<sup>9</sup>And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever,<sup>10</sup>the twenty-four elders fall down before him who is seated on the throne and worship him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne, saying,<sup>11</sup>“Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.”

5.title: The Scroll and the Lamb
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is perhaps the most emotionally dramatic chapter in the entire Bible. It begins with a crisis — a sealed scroll that no one can open — passes through grief — John weeps uncontrollably — and arrives at an explosion of worship that fills all of heaven and earth. The transition from weeping to worship is accomplished by a single announcement: the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered, and he can open the scroll. And when John looks for the conquering Lion, he sees — a Lamb, standing as though slaughtered.

The scroll sealed with seven seals is the interpretive key to the chapter. A scroll sealed with seven seals in the ancient world was typically a legal document of great importance: a will, a deed of purchase, or a covenant document. Most scholars understand it as the scroll of history — God’s redemptive plan for the world, the title deed to creation, the covenant document of the new age. Seven seals indicates absolute sealing: only the one who is truly worthy can break them and open what they guard. The entire drama of Revelation — the seals, the trumpets, the bowls — is the Lamb opening this scroll.

The Lion who is the Lamb — the great reversal at the heart of chapter 5 — is the christological center of Revelation and, in a sense, of the entire New Testament. John is told to look for a conquering Lion. He looks and sees a slaughtered Lamb. The conquest was accomplished through the cross. The power that governs history is the power of self-giving love. The one who has the authority to open the seals of history is the one who was willing to be the sacrifice that history required. This is the theological answer to every form of worldly power: the crucified one reigns.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Scroll and the Lamb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2 put a scroll in the right hand of the one on the throne, written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. Writing on both sides meant the contents were complete; seven seals was the number required for a Roman will, openable only by the rightful heir. A mighty angel heralds one question across creation — not who is strong enough but who is worthy?

Verses 3–4 answer it: nobody, in heaven or on earth or under the earth. Not the elders, not the living creatures, not Abraham or Moses or David. And John breaks down — I began to weep loudly — the only tears anyone sheds in the throne room of this book, and they are not rebuked. An unopened scroll means a world with no resolution: the martyrs never answered, Rome for ever, history running down like a clock nobody winds.

Verse 5 stops the weeping with an announcement rather than an argument: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered (Gen. 49:9–10; Isa. 11:1–10). The verb is the past tense of the word that ends every one of the seven letters. Whatever the churches are being asked to do, he has already done.

Verses 6–7 are the hinge of the book. John is told a Lion and sees a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain — arnion, the diminutive, a lambkin, which becomes John’s main name for Christ twenty-eight times over. The participle is perfect: a past slaughter whose marks are still present. Seven horns are complete power, seven eyes complete knowledge (Zech. 4:10). Then, without ceremony, he went and took the scroll.

Verses 8–10: the creatures and elders fall before the Lamb — worship no creature in this book may receive (19:10; 22:8–9) — holding harps and golden bowls of incense which are the prayers of the saints (cf. Ps. 141:2). The new song grounds his worthiness in his death: you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, made them a kingdom and priests, and they shall reign on the earth.

Verses 11–12 widen the circle to myriads of myriads of angels (cf. Dan. 7:10) with a sevenfold ascription: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing. Verses 13–14 widen it to every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea, addressing one doxology to the throne and the Lamb together; the living creatures say Amen, and the elders fall down and worship in silence.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lion Is the Lamb

No one is worthy to open the sealed scroll of God’s purpose until the Lion of Judah is announced — and John sees a Lamb standing, as though slain. He takes the scroll, and heaven and earth worship him who ransomed a people by his blood.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: John wept at a world with no resolution; his tears were answered by a person, not an argument.

Now: No prayer offered in faith is lost; the prayers of the saints are held in golden bowls before the throne.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, "Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, “Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?”

Meaning first. Revelation 5 continues the throne-room vision of chapter 4 and introduces the Lamb. In God’s right hand is a scroll sealed with seven seals, and a mighty angel asks who is worthy to open it (vv. 1–2). No one in all creation is able, and John weeps (vv. 3–4). An elder tells him to stop: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered and can open it (v. 5). John looks and sees, not a lion, but a Lamb standing as though it had been slain, with seven horns and seven eyes, the Spirit sent into all the earth, and the Lamb takes the scroll (vv. 6–7). Then heaven erupts in worship. The living creatures and elders, holding harps and bowls of incense, which are the saints’ prayers, sing a new song: the Lamb is worthy, because he was slain and by his blood ransomed people for God from every tribe, language, people and nation, and made them a kingdom and priests who will reign on the earth (vv. 8–10). Countless angels join in: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain (vv. 11–12). Finally every creature everywhere praises the one on the throne and the Lamb together, and the elders fall down and worship (vv. 13–14). The chapter answers the question behind the whole book: who can carry God’s plan for history through to its end? Only the crucified and risen Christ, who conquered by dying.

The setting. In the ancient world important documents such as wills, contracts and title deeds were written on scrolls, rolled up and sealed. Under Roman law a will was sealed with seven seals, one for each of the seven witnesses required, and it could be opened only by the rightful heir in their presence. A sealed book was also a familiar prophetic picture. Ezekiel was handed a scroll written on the front and the back, full of lamentation and mourning and woe (Ezekiel 2:9–10). Daniel was told to shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4, 9). John’s vision is built out of both.

The camera has not moved. John is still in the throne room of chapter 4, still looking at the one seated on the throne, the Creator before whom the elders have just cast down their crowns. Nothing in heaven has changed, and yet the whole chapter will turn on what he now notices: something in that hand.

Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll. The right hand is the hand of power, authority and action in Scripture: your right hand, O LORD, shatters the enemy (Exodus 15:6). The scroll (biblion) is not lying on a table in the corner of heaven waiting to be consulted. It is held, gripped, in the hand of the God who made all things. Whatever is written in it is his, and it is not out of his reach for a moment.

Written within and on the back. Ancient scrolls were normally written on one side only, because the papyrus fibres on the reverse ran the wrong way and caught the pen. A document written on both sides, what scholars call an opisthograph, meant one thing: the contents were complete. There was no room for anything further. Nothing can be added to this plan, and nothing has been left out. God is not drafting history as he goes, waiting to see how things turn out before he writes the next chapter. It is written, front and back, to the edges.

Sealed with seven seals. The word (katesphragismenon) means sealed up tight. Seven, in this book, is the number of completeness. The seals do not mean the plan is uncertain. They mean it is closed. It exists, it is finished and it is in God’s hand, and at the opening of this chapter it is shut.

Feel it before you explain it. That is the situation the chapter begins in, and it should be felt before it is explained. The plan of God for the world exists. It is finished, in writing, in his hand. And it is not happening, because nobody has opened it.

And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals? The verb for proclaiming is the herald’s word, and the voice is loud enough to reach, as the next verse shows, heaven and earth and under the earth. This is a summons to the entire creation, and it asks one question.

Notice which question. Not who is strong enough, and not who is clever enough. Who is worthy? The word (axios) means deserving, qualified, of the right weight. The issue is not capability but standing. Anyone can break a seal; a seal is wax. What the moment requires is somebody with the right to break it, and the whole tension of the chapter, and arguably of the book, is that the future of the world waits not on power but on the moral qualification of a person.

What is the scroll? Many suggestions have been made: the Old Testament, the book of life, a title deed to the world waiting for its heir, a last will and testament with the inheritance of the saints. The text itself only shows what happens when it is opened, and what happens is the sweep of history from the cross to the new creation. The best answer is that it contains God’s plan to judge evil and redeem his creation, his purpose for history from the cross to the end. Opening it means not only revealing that plan but carrying it out. As the seals are broken in chapter 6, events happen on earth.

What it does not mean. The sealed scroll does not mean God’s plan is uncertain, or that God is unable to act. The question is who among creatures can carry it out on God’s behalf, as Lord of history and Redeemer of the world. The answer will be one who is both creature and more than creature.

Is the scroll the same as the book of life? Probably not, though they are related. The book of life (3:5; 13:8; 20:12) is the register of those who belong to the Lamb, and it is never described as sealed. This scroll is the unfolding of God’s purpose in history, judgement and salvation together. But the two are bound up with each other, because the purpose that the scroll carries out is the bringing home of every name written in that other book. The plan of history and the list of the redeemed are in the same hands.

In a sentence. Then I saw a scroll in the right hand of the one seated on the throne, with writing on both sides, sealed with seven seals, and I saw a powerful angel calling out in a loud voice, Who is worthy to break the seals and open the scroll?

On a Tuesday. History is not random. It is written in a scroll held in God’s right hand, written to the edges, with nothing missing. Whatever happens this week, at work, in the hospital waiting room or on the evening news, is within his plan, and none of it has caught him with a blank page. And when you find yourself asking who is in charge of where this world is going, notice the question heaven asks. Not who has the most power, but who is worthy. The people and movements that promise to put the world right usually answer the first question. Only one person has ever answered the second.

For worship. The God of this chapter holds the whole story of the world in one hand, every page of it written, every line of it his. He is not waiting on events; events are waiting on him. Before a single seal is broken, before a horse rides out or a trumpet sounds, the plan is complete in his grip. And the question his herald asks is the most hopeful question in the universe, because the God who wrote the scroll had already provided the answer to it before the foundation of the world (13:8).

verseByVerse.quote: And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it, and I began to weep loudly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it, and I began to weep loudly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.

And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth. The three-tier phrase is the ancient way of saying everywhere: heaven, with its angels and powers; earth, with the living; and under the earth, the realm of the dead. It is a complete search of the universe, and it returns nothing.

Was able to open the scroll or to look into it. “Able” (edynato) means had the power, was competent. Consider who was in the room while that search was conducted. Twenty-four elders. Four living creatures who have never taken their eyes off God. Presently, myriads of myriads of angels. Not one of them was worthy. On earth, the whole roll of human greatness, every philosopher, reformer, general and king, and not one. And under the earth, the dead, including every saint who had died in faith. Abraham was not worthy. Moses was not worthy. David, who wrote half the songs sung in that room, was not worthy. No creature has the worthiness to bring history to God’s good end, to defeat evil and redeem the world. Not even to look inside.

And I began to weep loudly. The verb (eklaion) is emphatic and continuous: John did not become quietly emotional; he broke down and sobbed, and the tense suggests he kept on doing it until somebody stopped him. These are the only tears in heaven. Nowhere else in this book does anyone in the throne room weep, and two chapters from the end God himself will wipe away every tear from every eye (21:4).

Why so extreme a reaction? Because John has grasped what the closed scroll means. If nobody opens it, the plan stays shut. The martyrs under the altar are never answered (6:10). Rome goes on for ever. The seven churches keep meeting in borrowed rooms until they die out one by one, and nothing in the sealed purposes of God ever comes to anything. An unopened scroll is a world with no resolution: evil never judged, suffering never ended, God’s promises never fulfilled, the persecuted church never vindicated, and history simply running down like a clock nobody winds. His tears are the right response to a world without a redeemer.

Because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it. “Found worthy” (axios heurethē). The problem is not power but worthiness. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). No sinner can redeem sinners, and no unfallen angel can stand in for a human race he does not belong to. The search fails, not because the universe is short of strength, but because it is short of righteousness.

That grief is not exotic. Any honest believer has felt a version of it. It is what settles on a person reading the news for the fortieth year and noticing that the same things keep happening. It is what a woman feels standing in a cemetery in a country where nobody was ever tried for what was done. It is the specific despair of suspecting that the world is not going anywhere: that there is no scroll, or that if there is one, it will never be opened.

Note what John does not do. He does not tell himself that it will probably work out. He does not console himself with the throne he has just seen, though the throne is still there in front of him. He weeps, in heaven, in the presence of God, and Scripture records it without embarrassment and without rebuking him. There is no verse in this book telling the reader that grief over a world out of joint is a failure of faith. And the weeping is answered, but not by an argument. Nobody in the following verse tells John he was overreacting.

What it does not mean. John’s tears are not a lack of faith. They show how great the need is. He has not yet seen the answer. Christians, too, can weep over the brokenness of the world while knowing the answer; Jesus himself wept at the tomb of a friend he was about to raise (John 11:35).

If the plan was always going to be carried out, why make John weep at all? Because God wants us to know what the answer is worth. A rescue is only understood by someone who has looked at the drop. If John had seen the Lamb first, he would have admired him; having seen the empty universe first, he worships him. The same is true for us. The gospel is not meant to be received as pleasant extra information by people who were managing quite well. It is meant to land on people who have seen, for one honest moment, that without Christ there is no one, anywhere, who can put the world right, or put them right.

Is it wrong for me to feel this despair? No. To feel the weight of a world that has not been put right is to see it truly, and Scripture is full of believers who cried out how long (Psalm 13:1; Habakkuk 1:2; Revelation 6:10). What would be wrong is to stay there as though the elder had never spoken. Weep, and then listen. The Christian is not the person who never feels the darkness, but the person who has been told who walked into it.

In a sentence. No one anywhere, in heaven, on earth or under the earth, could open the scroll or even look inside it, and I wept and wept because no one was found who was worthy to open it or look into it.

On a Tuesday. Let John’s tears teach you how hopeless the world would be without Christ. No politician, movement, technology or reform can bring history to its good end, and every one of them that promises to will in the end be searched and found wanting. So when the news drives you to despair this week, do not hide the despair from God, and do not paper over it with optimism. Take it into his presence as John did, and let it become the place where you hear the next verse.

For worship. Heaven was searched and earth was searched and the grave was searched, and the only being found worthy was the one who did not need to be searched for, because he had come looking for us. The universe could not produce a redeemer. God gave one. Every tear John shed in that room was an honest measure of the size of the gift, and the God who let him weep for a moment is the God who will wipe away every tear for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the elders said to me, "Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And one of the elders said to me, “Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals.”

The setting. Two great messianic titles from the Old Testament stand behind this verse. Dying Jacob calls Judah a lion’s cub and says the sceptre shall not depart from Judah until tribute comes to him, and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples (Genesis 49:9–10). Isaiah promises a shoot from the stump of Jesse, David’s father, on whom the Spirit of the LORD would rest, who would judge the poor with righteousness and strike the earth with the rod of his mouth; the root of Jesse would stand as a signal for the peoples (Isaiah 11:1–4, 10). Jewish writings of the time used both images for a warrior Messiah who would destroy Israel’s enemies.

And one of the elders said to me, Weep no more. “Weep no more” (mē klaie) is literally stop weeping. Not you were wrong to weep. Not compose yourself. The tears are not criticised; they are ended, and they are ended by an announcement about a person, not by advice. That is the shape of every real Christian comfort. Nobody is talked out of grief by being told that things are not so bad. Grief stops when somebody walks into the room.

Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah. The lion (leōn) is royal, powerful and conquering. Jesus was born of the tribe of Judah (Hebrews 7:14), the tribe of kings, and he is the King promised to Judah on Jacob’s deathbed nearly two thousand years before. Between them these two titles carry the whole hope of Israel: the royal lion, and the living root of a dynasty that had been cut down to a stump.

The Root of David. The word is rhiza, root. Not only David’s descendant but David’s root, his source (22:16). Jesus once asked the Pharisees how, if David calls the Messiah Lord, he can be his son (Matthew 22:41–45). Here is the answer: he is both David’s offspring and David’s Lord, the branch that grew from the family tree and the root from which the whole tree drew its life. A stump looks dead. This root was never dead.

Has conquered. The verb is enikēsen, the same word that ends every one of the seven letters as a promise to the one who conquers (2:7, 11, 17, 26; 3:5, 12, 21). Whatever the churches of Asia are being asked to do, he has already done, and the doing is finished. The tense is past: not he is conquering, not he will conquer, but he conquered, and the matter is closed. Christ conquered first, and his people conquer through him (3:21).

So that he can open the scroll and its seven seals. Observe the logic of the sentence, because it is easy to slide past. He can open the scroll because he has conquered. The right to unroll the purposes of God was not given to him as a courtesy of rank. It was won. Somewhere in history a battle was fought, and the outcome of it is the reason anything at all is about to happen in this book.

Hold the Lion in mind. Here the reader is at the exact hinge of Revelation, and everything depends on reading the next two verses in the right order. What John is told is a Lion. What John then sees is something else entirely. Hold the Lion in mind for one more sentence, because the elder has just announced, in the most muscular language the Old Testament has, that the conqueror has arrived and the scroll is as good as open.

What it does not mean. The Lion’s conquest is not the military victory many expected the Messiah to win. John is about to see how he won it (v. 6). Revelation never pictures the Messiah’s victory as violence against his enemies on the way to his throne; he conquered by being slain.

Conquered whom, and when? Christ conquered sin, death and Satan at the cross and in his resurrection. At the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15); through death he destroyed the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14); and he rose as the firstborn of the dead (1:5). The battle that decides history is not still to be fought at the end of the age. It was fought outside Jerusalem around AD 30, and everything in Revelation from here on is the outworking of a victory already won.

If Christ has already conquered, why is the world still so dark? Because a war can be decided before it is over. The decisive battle has been won, the enemy’s doom is sealed, and the remaining fighting is real but cannot change the outcome. That is exactly what the rest of this book shows: seals, trumpets and bowls of real suffering, a dragon who is furious because he knows that his time is short (12:12), and through it all the Lamb holding the scroll. The darkness is not a sign that the victory failed. It is the last struggle of an enemy who has already lost.

In a sentence. Then one of the elders said to me, Stop weeping; look, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has won the victory, so he is able to open the scroll and break its seven seals.

On a Tuesday. When grief over the world or over your own life comes, do not wait for an argument to make it lift. Look at a person. Turn to Christ as he is described here, and say his titles to him: Lion of Judah, Root of David, the one who has conquered. You are not fighting to win a war that is still undecided. You are standing firm in a war that is already won, and the one who won it is the one opening the scroll of your days.

For worship. The elder does not offer John a programme or a hope or a reason to cheer up. He points to a King. The promise made over Judah by a dying man in Egypt, the shoot Isaiah saw rising from a dead stump, the Son and Lord of David: every thread of Israel’s hope runs to one person, and he has already won. Christ did not come to try. He came and conquered, and the verb is finished. Weep over the world, but never without hope, because the Lion has prevailed.

verseByVerse.quote: And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne.

The setting. The Passover lamb was killed and its blood put on the doorposts, so that the LORD passed over Israel when he judged Egypt (Exodus 12). Isaiah describes the Servant of the LORD led like a lamb to the slaughter, bearing the sin of many (Isaiah 53:7, 12). John the Baptist pointed to Jesus as the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). In Jewish apocalyptic writing a horned ram sometimes represented a conquering leader (Daniel 8:3; 1 Enoch 90). Zechariah speaks of the seven eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth (Zechariah 4:10).

And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb. He was told a Lion. He sees a Lamb. That single substitution is the interpretive key to the whole book, and everything that follows must be read through it. Revelation will go on speaking the language of conquest, warfare, thrones and armies for seventeen more chapters, and this verse has just defined what every one of those words means. The Lion conquers as a Lamb. The victory the elder announced was won by dying. Power has been redefined by sacrifice. This is the heart of Revelation, and of the gospel.

A little lamb. The word John uses is arnion, and it matters. It is not the more usual sacrificial term amnos used of Christ elsewhere (John 1:29; Acts 8:32); arnion is a diminutive in form, a little lamb, a lambkin. John uses it twenty-eight times of Christ in this book, and it becomes his main name for him. In the most violent, cosmic, thunderous book in the Bible, the name of the conqueror is the smallest and most defenceless word available.

At the centre. Notice where he stands: between the throne and the four living creatures, among the elders. That is the very centre of heaven, the place nearest to God. The Lamb does not appear on the edge of the throne room as a guest or petitioner. He is in the middle, and later John will speak of the Lamb in the midst of the throne (7:17) and of the throne of God and of the Lamb (22:1). He shares God’s throne.

Standing, as though it had been slain. Two impossible things in one clause. “Standing” (hestēkos) is alive, risen, upright. And the word behind slain is esphagmenon, from a verb used for cutting a sacrificial animal’s throat: butchered, not merely killed. It is a perfect participle, which in Greek means a past action whose result is still in force. The wounds are not a memory. They are present tense. This Lamb is standing, which is resurrection and life, and is at the same time visibly, permanently, a slaughtered animal.

The marks are the credential. Stay with that, because it is the centre of the Christian faith rendered as a picture. The one thing that will never be erased from the new creation is the evidence of what it cost. When Thomas needed proof, the risen Christ did not produce a restored body but a scarred one: put out your hand, and place it in my side (John 20:27). Heaven’s throne room is not a place where the crucifixion has been tidied away and forgotten. His death is not a past event he has moved beyond; it is the permanent ground of his authority and of our salvation, and the whole company falls down in front of it.

Does Jesus still suffer in heaven? No. The perfect tense means the effect of his death remains, not that the dying goes on. Christ died once for all (Hebrews 9:26–28; Romans 6:9–10), and his sacrifice is finished (John 19:30). He is standing, not lying on an altar. The marks are like the scar on a soldier who has come home: they are no longer pain, they are proof. And this is why the Lord’s Supper is a remembrance and not a repetition. We do not offer Christ again; we feed on a sacrifice that was completed, and whose marks he carries into eternity.

With seven horns. A horn in the Old Testament is strength (Deuteronomy 33:17; Psalm 18:2), the weapon of a strong animal and the emblem of a king. Seven of them is complete power. The Lamb is not weak. All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (Matthew 28:18).

And with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. Seven eyes is complete knowledge, seeing everything; the phrase is quarried from Zechariah, where the seven eyes of the LORD range through the whole earth (Zechariah 4:10). The seven spirits are the Holy Spirit in his fullness (1:4). And notice whose eyes they are: the Spirit is the Spirit of the Lamb, sent out by him into all the earth (John 15:26; 16:7; Acts 2:33). The Lamb is all-powerful, all-knowing, and present everywhere by his Spirit: fully God. The picture is deliberately impossible to draw. It is not meant to be sketched. It is meant to be believed.

And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne. The sentence is flat, almost domestic, and the room has been holding its breath for six verses. “Took” (eilēphen) is perfect tense again, a decisive act with lasting result. Nobody stops him. There is no challenge, no ceremony, no coronation first. He walks up and takes it, and the reaching out of that hand is the moment the future of the world is unlocked. It echoes Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man comes to the Ancient of Days and is given dominion and glory and a kingdom. The Lamb receives authority to carry out God’s whole plan for history.

No one else could have done it. Heaven was searched, and earth, and the place of the dead, and every candidate failed on the same question: not strength, but worth. And then a Lamb with its throat cut walks out from among the elders and takes the scroll out of the hand of God, and every creature in the room goes down on its face. He conquered. He was slaughtered, and he is standing, and the wounds are still visible, and history has begun to move again.

What it does not mean. The Lamb is not a sign of weakness. He has seven horns. Nor does his gentleness cancel his justice; the same book speaks of the wrath of the Lamb (6:16). Revelation’s Christ is the slain Lamb who conquers, and the conquering Lamb who was slain.

Why does the Lamb take the scroll from the Father, rather than having it already? Because the picture is of the Son receiving, as the risen Messiah, the authority he won. As God the Son he shares the Father’s rule eternally. As the incarnate Son who obeyed to the point of death, he is given the name above every name (Philippians 2:8–11) and all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). There is no rivalry here. The Father gives and the Son takes, in perfect agreement, and the plan of the Father is carried out by the hand of the Son.

So is the Lamb a picture of how Christians should live? Yes, and that is one of the most practical things in the book. The Lamb’s way of victory, through sacrifice, truth-telling and faithful suffering rather than force, is the way he calls his people to walk. The saints conquer the accuser by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death (12:11). That does not make Christians doormats, and it does not forbid lawful government its sword (Romans 13:4). It means the church never advances Christ’s kingdom by coercion, manipulation or worldly power, and that faithfulness which looks like losing is often how the Lamb wins.

In a sentence. Then I saw a Lamb, standing at the centre, between the throne with its four living beings and the circle of elders; it looked as though it had been slaughtered, and it had seven horns and seven eyes, which are the sevenfold Spirit of God sent out into the whole world; and the Lamb came and took the scroll from the right hand of the one seated on the throne.

On a Tuesday. When you think of power, think of the Lamb. In the meeting where you could win by bending the truth, in the family argument where you could crush by being cleverer, in the moment when you are wronged and could get even, ask what the Lamb would look like here. Christ’s way of victory, through sacrifice, self-giving and faithful suffering, is the way he calls you to walk too. It will often look like losing. So did the cross.

For worship. In the middle of heaven, at the very centre of all that is, stands a Lamb with the marks of slaughter on him, and all power and all knowledge are his. The wounds that the world inflicted on him are the credentials by which he rules it. The Lion of Judah did not conquer by roaring but by bleeding, and the hand that reaches out to take the scroll of history is the hand that was pierced for us. There is no other face at the centre of the universe, and there never will be. Behold, the Lamb of God.
verseByVerse.note: The Lion of v. 5 turns out to be a slain Lamb. Horns stand for power and eyes for knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. And they sang a new song, saying, "Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. And they sang a new song, saying, “Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth.”

The setting. Harps, or lyres, were used in temple worship (1 Chronicles 25:1; Psalm 33:2). Incense was burned twice a day on the golden altar in front of the veil, and its smoke was a picture of prayer rising to God: let my prayer be counted as incense before you (Psalm 141:2). The Psalms and prophets often call for a new song, celebrating a new act of salvation (Psalm 96:1; 98:1; Isaiah 42:10).

And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb. The response to the taking of the scroll is immediate and total. The same posture given to the one on the throne in chapter 4 (4:10) is given here to the Lamb, without a word of explanation and without anyone objecting. And in this book angels twice refuse worship outright, telling John to worship God (19:10; 22:8–9). No creature may receive it. The Lamb receives it in the presence of God the Father, and the room approves. This is a clear statement that Jesus is God.

Each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. They are holding two things. The harp is for the song about to be sung. The bowls need dwelling on. “Saints” (hagiōn, holy ones) means all believers, not a special class of the especially devout. What John sees is the Psalm’s image made literal. The prayers of ordinary Christians are in golden bowls in the throne room of the universe, held by the highest beings in creation, at the moment the scroll is opened.

None of them evaporated. Take that as concretely as it is meant. Every desperate prayer prayed by a believer in Smyrna the night before a hearing. Every prayer of a slave in Laodicea that nobody else in the household knew about. Every muttered, distracted, badly worded prayer said by anyone reading this at the kitchen table before work: the ones that felt as though they hit the ceiling and slid down the wall. None of them evaporated. They were collected. They are in golden bowls, and the bowls are full, and an elder is holding them in front of the throne.

And some of it was explosive. There is more in the picture. At 8:3–5 those same prayers, mixed with incense, are offered on the golden altar, and then fire from the altar is thrown onto the earth, and there are peals of thunder, lightning and an earthquake. The persecuted church’s cries for justice (6:10) are heard, and prayers that seemed to accomplish nothing come down again as the opening act of God’s judgement on the world that ignored them. Nothing prayed in faith is wasted, and some of it turns out to have been explosive.

What about prayers that were never answered? Two things are true together. First, God does not always give what we ask, because he is wiser than our requests; Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed and was given grace instead (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Second, no prayer of faith is lost. It is kept before God and woven into his purposes in ways we often cannot see in this life. A mother who prayed for thirty years for a son who was converted after her funeral did not pray in vain; her prayers were in the bowl the whole time. Keep asking. The bowls are not yet full, and nothing put into them is thrown away.

Does this mean the elders pray for us, or that we should pray to saints in heaven? No. The elders present the prayers; they do not produce them or receive them as the ones prayed to. The prayers are the saints’ own prayers, offered to God. Scripture nowhere invites believers to address their prayers to departed saints or angels, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Pray directly to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit. What this verse adds is not a new channel for prayer but an assurance about where every prayer arrives.

And they sang a new song. “New” (kainēn) means new in kind, not merely recent. The Old Testament calls for a new song whenever God does something unprecedented, and a new act of redemption, greater than the exodus, calls for a new song. Chapter 4 ended with a song about creation. This one has a different subject.

Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals. There is the answer to the herald’s question in verse 2. Who is worthy? You are.

For you were slain. “Slain” (esphagēs). The ground of the worthiness is not his power, though he has seven horns, nor his knowledge, though he has seven eyes. It is his death. Heaven’s argument for the Lamb is a wound.

And by your blood you ransomed people for God. “Ransomed” (ēgorasas) is the slave-market word: to buy a person out of ownership by paying the price. The price is named in the same clause: by your blood. The people bought belong to God. This is substitutionary atonement: Christ paid the price that set us free. You were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:20), ransomed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19).

From every tribe and language and people and nation. Four terms, the number of the whole earth. John will use this fourfold phrase seven times in this book, each time in a slightly different order, as if to stop anyone turning it into a fixed list. The redeemed come from every ethnic and linguistic group, and the church is gloriously multinational. This fulfils God’s promise to Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Nobody is outside the reach of it. And nobody is ransomed as a nation or a category: the purchase is of people, out of every group there is.

And you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God. The same phrase as 1:6, and both are lifted from Sinai (Exodus 19:6). Notice the tense: you have made, already done, not pending. A kingdom means they belong to the King and share his rule. Priests means they have direct access to God and serve him in worship, intercession and witness. What Israel was called to be at Sinai, the ransomed of every nation now are in Christ.

And they shall reign on the earth. “Reign” (basileusousin). The redeemed share in Christ’s rule, and their rule is on the earth: the renewed earth of the new creation (21:1; 22:5). Whatever a reader concludes about the thousand years, a question taken up where the text raises it at chapter 20, the destination of the redeemed in this book is not an escape from the material world into a spiritual one. It is this earth, renewed, with the ransomed reigning on it. Salvation is not escape from creation but the renewal of it.

Where Christians differ: did Christ die for every person, or for his people? Many Christians hold that Christ died equally for every person, making salvation possible for all, so that it becomes actual when people believe. Verdict: the song says that Christ’s blood actually ransomed people for God, not that it made a ransom possible. And it ransomed people from every tribe, language, people and nation, not every person in every nation. This is definite atonement: Christ died with the intention of actually saving those the Father gave him (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25), and his death secures their salvation. Its value is infinite, sufficient for all, and the gospel is to be offered freely to everyone. But its design is to save a people chosen from every nation, and it does not fail.

Can I then tell anyone that Christ died for them? You can tell every person, without hesitation, that Christ died for sinners, that he is able and willing to save all who come to him, and that whoever believes in him will not perish (John 3:16; 6:37). That is the gospel the apostles preached, and it is a sincere offer, because the sacrifice is of infinite worth and the invitation is God’s own. What definite atonement adds is not a limit on the offer but a certainty about the result: the Lamb’s blood did not merely make salvation available and then wait to see who would take it. It bought a people, and the Spirit will bring every one of them home. That is why missionaries can go to the hardest places with confidence.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “redeemed us” and “made us kings and priests, and we shall reign”, making the elders sing about themselves. The best manuscripts read “ransomed people” (or simply ransomed for God from every tribe) and “made them … they shall reign”. Some manuscripts also read they reign (present tense) rather than they shall reign. Both are true: believers reign now with Christ in a hidden way (1:6), and will reign fully in the new creation.

What it does not mean. Reigning on the earth does not mean a future thousand-year political reign before the final state. The promise is fulfilled in the new heaven and new earth, where God’s servants will reign for ever and ever (22:5).

How do I reign now, when my life feels so small? Not by holding office or winning arguments, but by belonging to the King and sharing his victory. You reign when sin no longer has dominion over you (Romans 6:14), when you pray and heaven’s purposes move, when you refuse to be ruled by fear, money or the opinion of others, and when you suffer faithfully rather than giving in. The reign is hidden now, as Christ’s own reign was hidden on the cross, but it is real; and one day it will be revealed on a renewed earth. The widow praying in a care home is not less a royal priest than the preacher on a platform.

In a sentence. When he had taken the scroll, the four living beings and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each with a harp and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of God’s people, and they sang a new song: You are worthy to take the scroll and break its seals, because you were slaughtered, and with your blood you bought for God people from every tribe, language, people and nation, and made them a kingdom of priests to serve our God, and they will reign on the earth.

On a Tuesday. Pray this week as someone whose prayers are kept in golden bowls. The short prayer before a hard phone call, the half-sentence for a friend in hospital, the prayer you have prayed for years without a visible answer: none of them is wasted. And look around your church on Sunday. If there are people there whose language, background or skin is not yours, you are looking at what the Lamb bought. Make a point of learning one of their names, and praying for one place in the world where the gospel has not yet reached a tribe or language.

For worship. The Lamb is worthy, and heaven gives one reason: he was slain. He went to the slave market of a race that had sold itself to sin, and he paid with his own blood, and the people he bought now belong to God. He bought them from every tribe and tongue, he made them kings and priests, and he will set them reigning on a renewed earth. And not one of their prayers, from the first cry of a new believer to the last breath of a dying saint, has ever fallen to the ground. Every one is in a golden bowl before the throne of the Lamb who loved them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and I heard around the throne and the living creatures and the elders the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice, "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I looked, and I heard around the throne and the living creatures and the elders the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!”

The setting. Daniel describes the Ancient of Days with a thousand thousands serving him and ten thousand times ten thousand standing before him (Daniel 7:10). At Jesus’ birth, a multitude of the heavenly host appeared with the shepherds, praising God (Luke 2:13–14).

Then I looked, and I heard around the throne and the living creatures and the elders the voice of many angels. The circle of worship widens: first the living creatures and elders, now countless angels. The singing has been going on out there the whole time John was weeping.

Numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands. A myriad (myrias) is ten thousand, the largest number Greek had a single word for. Ten thousand times ten thousand is a hundred million, but myriads of myriads is not a count; it is the language running out. Daniel used exactly the same expression of the throne of the Ancient of Days, and John has been quarrying Daniel 7 since chapter 1. The point is not arithmetic. It is that the ring of worshippers extends beyond the range of counting.

Saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb who was slain. The angels speak of the Lamb rather than to him. Perhaps that is because he did not die for them, though they join in praising what he did. And there is something the angels are doing here that they cannot do in the fullest sense. The song of verse 9 is sung by those ransomed by his blood; the angels in verse 12 sing about a redemption they have watched but not received. Peter says these are things into which angels long to look (1 Peter 1:12). Whatever the honour of an unfallen angel, it does not include being bought. The forgiven sinner in the back row of an ordinary congregation has a line in this song that Gabriel cannot sing.

Two songs, one throne. Set the two songs side by side, because the difference between them is the gospel. In chapter 4 the elders sang worthy are you, our Lord and God, and the ground was creation: you created all things (4:11). Here the angels sing worthy is the Lamb, and the ground is the cross: he was slain. Two songs, one throne, and the second could not have been sung by anyone before Calvary.

To receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing! Seven qualities, the complete set: “power” (dynamin), “wealth” (plouton), “wisdom” (sophian), “might” (ischyn), “honor” (timēn), “glory” (doxan), “blessing” (eulogian). In Greek a single article governs all seven, joining them as one whole. Everything there is to give is given, and it is given to a slaughtered lamb.

Every currency of Rome. Note the order of the seven. Power comes first and blessing last, and in between are wealth, wisdom, might, honour and glory: every currency the Roman world traded in, everything that kings and emperors claimed. A congregation that had been shut out of the guilds, fined, boycotted and in some places killed is being told where all seven actually belong. And wealth is in the list. The one who though he was rich, yet for your sake became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9), who was laid in a borrowed tomb, is worthy of all the riches of the universe.

What it does not mean. The Lamb does not receive these because he lacks them. As God, he has them eternally. As the slain Lamb, he is now acknowledged and honoured with them as the reward of his obedience (Philippians 2:8–11).

Why do the angels worship, if Christ did not die for them? Because they love God’s glory, and in the cross they have seen it more clearly than in anything else. Through the church the manifold wisdom of God is made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places (Ephesians 3:10). The angels watched the Son of God make worlds; they watched him leave heaven, sleep in a manger, sweat in Gethsemane and die. They had never seen holiness and love meet like that. Their worship is a rebuke to any believer who finds the cross dull. If beings who were never lost cannot stop singing about it, how much more should those who were.

In a sentence. Then, as I looked, I heard the voices of angels beyond counting, thousands upon thousands and millions upon millions, surrounding the throne, the living beings and the elders, and they called out with a loud voice: The Lamb who was slaughtered is worthy to receive power, riches, wisdom, strength, honour, glory and praise!

On a Tuesday. When you sit down in a small church on a wet Sunday with a thin congregation and an out-of-tune piano, remember that you are not the whole choir. You are joining a song that has been going on around the throne beyond counting, and your voice is wanted in it. And look at the seven words this week: power, wealth, wisdom, might, honour, glory, blessing. Which of them are you tempted to keep for yourself? Your money, your reputation, your cleverness? Give that one back to the Lamb on purpose.

For worship. Worthy is the Lamb. Not worthy to be pitied, not worthy merely to be remembered, but worthy to receive everything there is. And the reason given by the whole of heaven is not that he is strong, though he holds seven horns, and not that he sees everything, though he has seven eyes. The reason is that he was slaughtered. Ten thousand times ten thousand voices, and the argument they make is a wound; and the song that angels can only admire, ransomed sinners get to sing as their own.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, "To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!" And the four living creatures said, "Amen!" and the elders fell down and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, “To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!” And the four living creatures said, “Amen!” and the elders fell down and worshiped.

The setting. Paul says that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11).

And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them. The circle widens one last time, and this time it takes in everything that exists. “Every creature” (pan ktisma) means all created things. Those are the same three regions searched in verse 3, with the sea added. There, the search found nobody worthy; here, the whole of it is singing. The chapter has come full circle. What began with a silence that made a man weep ends with every created thing, the living, the dead, the powers above, and whatever is in the deep, making one sound. John sees ahead to the end, when all creation acknowledges God and the Lamb.

Saying, To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever! The climax: one doxology, two recipients, no distinction between them. Chapter 4 praised God as Creator; chapter 5 has praised the Lamb as Redeemer; now both are worshipped together in a single sentence, in exactly the same words, and nobody in the room regards that as a problem. The doctrine of the Trinity is not argued anywhere in Revelation. It is simply what worship in heaven looks like. This is the clearest picture in the book of the Son’s full equality with the Father.

Blessing first. Four attributes here rather than seven, and the first of them is blessing, which is not something a creature can add to God. To bless God is to speak well of him, to say back to him what he is. That is the last thing all creation does in this vision, and it is the only thing it can do that God has not already got.

And the four living creatures said, Amen! “Amen” means so be it, it is true. The beings nearest the throne, who have been singing holy, holy, holy without pause, do not add anything. They agree.

And the elders fell down and worshiped. The worship ends where it began, with the living creatures and elders. The last movement in the chapter is a silence: twenty-four figures on their faces with their crowns already on the floor, and John does not record a single further word.

Look back at where this chapter started. A sealed scroll, a challenge nobody could answer, and a man weeping loudly in the middle of heaven because it looked as though the world would never be put right. Fourteen verses later the same man is listening to every creature in existence say the same thing at once. Nothing changed in between except that a Lamb walked forward and took a scroll.

Where Christians differ: will every creature be saved? Universalists read this verse, with Philippians 2:10–11, as meaning that all creatures, including those now in rebellion, will finally be reconciled and saved. Verdict: universal acknowledgement is not universal salvation. Revelation clearly teaches that some will be thrown into the lake of fire for ever (14:9–11; 20:10, 15; 21:8). Every creature will confess that God and the Lamb are worthy; for the redeemed it is joyful worship, and for the lost it is the forced admission of a truth they rejected. God’s glory will be acknowledged everywhere, in mercy and in justice.

What it does not mean. Worshipping the Lamb with the Father does not mean there are two Gods. Revelation is strictly monotheistic. The Father and the Son share one throne (22:1, 3) and receive one worship.

How can creatures in the sea and under the earth praise God? In the way the heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1) and the trees of the field clap their hands (Isaiah 55:12): by being what God made them to be, under his rule, and showing his glory. John sees the whole created order brought into harmony with its Maker, the creation that now groans (Romans 8:19–22) set free and giving voice to praise. For rational creatures it is conscious praise; for the rest of creation it is the praise of a world put right. Nothing God made is left out of the song.

What comes next. The seven seals are about to be broken, and the four horsemen are behind the first four of them. Conquest, war, famine and death are coming, and after them the souls under the altar and the sky rolling up like a scroll. Every one of those seals is opened by the hand that was pierced. Whatever rides out of this scroll rides at the word of the Lamb who was slain, and it goes no further than he permits. That is the comfort a reader must carry into chapter 6.

In a sentence. Then I heard every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea, everything in the whole creation, saying: To the one seated on the throne and to the Lamb be praise, honour, glory and power for ever and ever! And the four living beings said, Amen, and the elders fell down and worshipped.

On a Tuesday. Worship Jesus as you worship the Father, with the same words and the same whole heart. When you pray, it is right to address the Son directly, as heaven does; the first martyr did (Acts 7:59). And when the world looks as though it will never be put right, read verse 3 and verse 13 side by side. The search that found no one has become the song that includes everyone. Say Amen to that, out loud if you need to, before you open the news.

For worship. Worthy is the Lamb. He was searched for through heaven and earth and the grave and not found, because he was not looking like a lion; he was standing among the elders with his throat cut and his hands open. He took the scroll. He is opening it still. To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb belong blessing and honour and glory and might for ever, one throne, one worship, one God. And when the last seal is broken and the last trumpet has sounded and the last enemy is gone, the song that all creation is singing here will not have changed a word. Amen.

6.title: The Opening of the Seals
6.overview:
The Lamb begins to open the seven seals, and with each seal a new dimension of history is revealed. The first four seals release the famous Four Horsemen — one of the most powerful images in Western literature. The fifth seal lifts the veil on the souls of the martyrs beneath the heavenly altar and their agonizing cry: “How long, O Lord?” The sixth seal unleashes cosmic convulsion on a terrified earth. The seventh seal — which will bring complete silence in heaven — is withheld until chapter 8.

Interpretive flag — Sequential or Recapitulatory? This is the second major structural decision point of Revelation. The sequential reading (predominant in dispensational premillennialism) understands the seals, trumpets, and bowls as three successive series of events: the seals run their course, then the trumpets begin, then the bowls pour out — covering the seven-year tribulation in ascending severity. The recapitulatory reading (predominant in amillennial/idealist interpretation) understands the three series as parallel sweeps, each covering the same period (the church age and/or the final tribulation) from different vantage points and with increasing intensity. Several features of the text favor recapitulation: (1) the sixth seal already appears to describe the final judgment (vv. 12–17), yet the narrative continues; (2) the sixth trumpet and sixth bowl also appear to describe the same climactic events; (3) the interludes (chapters 7, 10–11) break the sequential pattern; (4) the phrase “the great day of their wrath has come” (v. 17) sounds like a finale, yet much remains. The seals are read here as the first of three parallel sweeps, with the sequential reading noted respectfully.

The Four Horsemen are among the most theologically misread images in Revelation. They are not four distinct events in a future tribulation timeline. They are the recurring instruments of divine governance that have marked history since the fall: war, internecine conflict, famine, and death. They describe the ongoing reality of a fallen world under the Lord’s providential judgment — not unprecedented novelties but the intensified concentration of what the church has always known. The question the martyrs ask — “How long?” — is the question the church has been asking since Abel’s blood first cried from the ground.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: the Lamb opens the first seal, a living creature calls Come! with a voice like thunder, and a white horse rides out whose rider has a bow and a crown that was given to him. Whether that rider is Christ, the gospel’s advance, or conquest itself is genuinely disputed and is set out at the verse. Verses 3–4: a bright red horse, whose rider is permitted to take peace from the earth so that people should slay one another — mutual killing, the neighbour with the knife — and is given a great sword.

Verses 5–6: a black horse, its rider holding scales, and a voice from the midst of the living creatures quoting the price list. A denarius was a day’s wage; a quart of wheat was one man’s daily ration. A labourer in full work can feed himself and nobody else. Do not harm the oil and wine sets a limit on the famine and also describes its injustice: bread is rationed while the luxury trade goes on undisturbed.

Verses 7–8: a pale horse — chlōros, the green of a corpse — and the only rider who is named. Death rides, and Hades follows to collect. They are given authority over a fourth of the earth, with the four instruments of Ezekiel 14:21. The fraction matters: the trumpets will touch a third, and only at the end does anything become total.

Verses 9–11 break the pattern: no horse, no rider. Under the altar, where the blood of every sacrifice was poured out (Lev. 4:7), are the souls of those slain — esphagmenōn, the word used of the Lamb at 5:6. They cry how long? like a third of the psalter. Verse 11 answers with a white robe each, permission to rest, and a reason for the delay that is very hard: until the number of their brothers who are to die in the same way is complete.

Verses 12–14: the sixth seal removes every fixed point in the universe — earthquake, sun black as sackcloth (goat hair, so the comparison is exact), moon like blood (Joel 2:31), stars falling like the winter figs a gale brings down, the sky rolled up (Isa. 34:4), every mountain and island moved. Verses 15–17: seven classes of people, from kings down to slaves, hide in caves and beg the mountains to fall on them — choosing burial over being looked at — and the chapter ends on an unanswered question: who can stand?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Seals in the Lamb’s Hand

Conquest, war, famine and death ride out only when the Lamb opens the seals, and every one of them is given or permitted within a limit. The martyrs cry “How long?” and are robed and told to rest; the sixth seal removes every fixed point but the throne.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The churches met the red horse and the pale one without being told why.

Now: Crying out for justice is not unbelief; handing vengeance to God is obedience. And who can stand? Those washed in the Lamb’s blood.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, “Come!” And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer.

Meaning first. Revelation 6 shows the Lamb opening the first six seals of the scroll, and what happens on earth as he does. Four horsemen ride out at the command of the four living creatures: a white horse whose rider conquers (vv. 1–2), a red horse that takes peace from the earth (vv. 3–4), a black horse bringing famine and high prices (vv. 5–6), and a pale horse named Death, followed by Hades, killing a quarter of the earth by sword, famine, plague and wild beasts (vv. 7–8). At the fifth seal, the souls of martyrs under the altar cry out, How long until you judge? They are given white robes and told to wait until the number of their fellow martyrs is complete (vv. 9–11). At the sixth seal, the universe itself comes apart: earthquake, a black sun, a blood moon, falling stars, the sky rolled up, mountains and islands moved (vv. 12–14). Everyone, from kings to slaves, hides and begs the mountains to fall on them, to hide them from the face of God and the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand (vv. 15–17)? The chapter shows that the wars, famines and deaths of history are not out of control: they are released by the Lamb, limited by God, and leading to the final day of judgement.

The setting. Zechariah saw horses of different colours, red, black, white and dappled, sent out to patrol the earth (Zechariah 1:8–11; 6:1–8). Jesus, in his teaching about the end, spoke of wars and rumours of wars, nation against nation, famines and earthquakes as the beginning of the birth pains, followed by persecution, and then the sun darkened, the moon not giving its light, and the stars falling from heaven (Matthew 24:6–29; Luke 21:9–26). The seals follow the same order. In the first century Rome feared the Parthians, an empire to the east whose mounted archers had defeated Roman armies and who were famous for their skill with the bow.

The scroll is opened. History begins to move. Before the first horse rides, three things about the mechanics of this chapter need saying, because they govern how everything after it is read.

Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals. First, who is doing it. Not an angel, not fate, not an enemy. Every horror in this chapter is released by the hand that was pierced, and the reader who has just watched chapter 5 knows exactly whose hand that is. Everything that follows is under his authority. The disasters are not outside his control; they are part of his plan.

And I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, Come! Second, the summons. “Come” (erchou) is a command to the horseman, calling him out. One of the beings nearest the throne speaks, and the horseman comes. Heaven speaks first; earth responds. And there is something fitting in who calls. The living creatures represent creation in its fullness, and they summon the judgements that must come before creation is set free and renewed.

Third, the grammar. Watch for the passive verbs through the next seven verses: a crown was given, the rider was permitted, he was given a great sword, they were given authority. Four times. “Was given” (edothē) is a phrase that recurs through Revelation for God’s permission. Even evil powers act only as God allows. Nothing here takes itself.

How the seals fit the rest of the book. The seals are the first of three sevens, followed by trumpets (8–11) and bowls (15–16), and how a reader relates them shapes the whole book. On the reading followed in this commentary, held by Augustine, William Hendriksen, G. K. Beale and the amillennial tradition generally, the three series are not one long timeline but parallel passes over the same stretch of history, each running from the cross to the last day, each more intense than the last. What favours it is that all three series end at the same place: the sixth seal brings the sky rolling up and the kings hiding (6:12–17); the seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord (11:15); the seventh bowl is followed by a voice saying It is done (16:17). Futurist readers, such as John Walvoord, take the sevens as consecutive events in a future tribulation. The point of this chapter is the same either way: whatever these riders are, the Lamb sends them. See the verdict at vv. 12–14.

And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him. The bow (toxon) was the weapon of the Parthian cavalry, the horsemen who haunted Rome’s eastern frontier. The crown (stephanos) is the victor’s wreath. And it was given to him: even the conqueror rides on a permission.

And he came out conquering, and to conquer. “Conquering” (nikōn). Military conquest, invasion, empire-building. He is not content with one victory; he rides out to win the next one too. Every empire in history has had this horseman at its head.

Where Christians differ: who is the rider on the white horse? Some identify him with Christ, since Christ rides a white horse in 19:11, and they read the first seal as the gospel going out and conquering; white is the colour of holiness elsewhere in the book, and the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations (Mark 13:10). Others see him as the antichrist or false messiahs, imitating Christ. Others take him as military conquest in general. Verdict: the rider is conquering war, aggression and empire, like the other three horsemen, who all bring disaster. The four belong together as a set of judgements, following Jesus’ teaching (wars, then famines and death). Christ in chapter 19 has many crowns and a sword from his mouth, not a bow; and Christ is the one opening the seals, not one released by them. The white colour may suggest a deceptive imitation of Christ, as conquerors always promise peace and glory, or the white horses of victorious generals.

The order in which they come. Either way the four ride together as one picture: the ordinary, recurring furniture of a fallen world. Conquest, then war, then famine, then death, in that order, because that is the order in which they actually arrive. Every war in history has run that sequence, and the four have been riding since the first century without a break.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “Come and see”, as if the living creature were speaking to John. The best manuscripts read simply “Come!”, addressed to the horseman.

What it does not mean. The four horsemen are not one-time future events only. They describe what happens throughout the age between Christ’s comings: conquest, war, famine and death. They were real in John’s day and are real in ours. Nor does God’s permission make him the author of human evil. He limits it, uses it and will judge it.

Should I try to match the horsemen to current events? No. Every generation has done it, and every generation that named this war or that dictator as the fulfilment has been wrong, because the seals are not a coded timetable of one decade but a description of the whole age. That is a relief, not a disappointment. It means you do not need to decode the news to understand it. When armies invade, you already know three things: this was foretold, it is under the Lamb’s authority, and it is not the end of the story. Read the newspaper with Revelation 6 open, not to calculate dates, but to remember whose hand is on the seal.

Why would a loving God release such things at all? Because the world is in rebellion against him, and judgement on sin is part of his goodness, not an exception to it. A God who let evil run on for ever unchecked and unpunished would not be loving. But notice how these first judgements work: they are partial, limited and early, and their purpose is stated later in plain words: they did not repent (9:20–21). They are warnings loud enough to be heard, given while there is still time to turn. The God who sends the horsemen is the same God who, in the previous chapter, sent his Son to die for people from every nation.

In a sentence. Then I watched as the Lamb broke the first of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living beings call out in a voice like thunder, Come! and I saw a white horse, whose rider carried a bow; he was given a crown, and he rode out as a conqueror, bent on conquest.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of invasions and wars, remember that they are not outside Christ’s control. Pray for peace, for rulers and for the people caught in the path of armies (1 Timothy 2:1–2). And notice your own response to the news: is it panic, as though nobody were in charge, or indifference, as though it did not matter? The Christian response is neither. It is grief, prayer and steady trust in the Lamb who holds the scroll.

For worship. The first thing heaven wants the suffering church to know about the troubles of history is the identity of the one who opens them. Not chance, not Caesar, not the devil: the Lamb who was slain. Every crown the conquerors wear was given, and can be taken back. Every empire that rides out bent on conquest rides under the eye of the one who conquered by dying. The kingdoms rise and fall, and the Lamb is not shaken, because the scroll in his hand was written by his Father and sealed with his own blood.
verseByVerse.note: The four horsemen draw on Zechariah’s visions. Some take the white rider to be Christ (compare 19:11); many see him as conquest, the first of four judgments.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, "Come!" And out came another horse, bright red. Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth, so that people should slay one another, and he was given a great sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, “Come!” And out came another horse, bright red. Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth, so that people should slay one another, and he was given a great sword.

The setting. In John’s day the empire boasted of the Pax Romana, the peace of Rome, kept by its legions. Yet the first century saw civil war in AD 68–69, the year of the four emperors, the Jewish war that destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70, and endless bloodshed on the frontiers.

And out came another horse, bright red. The word is pyrros, fiery red, the colour of fire and blood, and its association is unmistakable in a chapter about slaughter. The first rider went out to conquer. What follows conquest is not peace.

Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth. Two things in that clause. The rider does not bring war; he takes peace away, which assumes that peace was there and was a gift. Ordinary quiet, a town where the shops open, a night without sirens, children walking to school, is not the natural state of things that occasionally breaks down. It is a mercy being extended, and it can be withdrawn. The false peace of empire is fragile. Without the true peace that Christ gives (John 14:27), human peace does not last.

On a leash. And he was permitted. The verb (edothē, it was given) is a divine passive, the second of the chapter’s four, and it is the hinge of the whole vision. Nothing here is out of control. That is a hard comfort rather than an easy one, and it should be given as it stands: Scripture does not say that God is doing his best against forces he cannot restrain. It says that even the horse of war rides on a permission, and therefore on a leash.

So that people should slay one another. Then the specific horror. Not so that armies should destroy nations; the Greek is reciprocal, one another, mutual killing. This is civil war, the neighbour with the knife, the country that turns on itself. And the twentieth century, which killed more people than any century before it, did much of its killing exactly that way: not chiefly invaders against defenders but citizens against their own, in Rwanda, in Cambodia, in the Soviet countryside, in the Balkans. “Slay” (sphaxousin, slaughter) is the same verb used for the Lamb who was slain (5:6). Human sin, released and allowed to run, destroys itself, and it does to people what it did to the Son of God.

And he was given a great sword. The word is machaira, the short blade a Roman soldier actually carried for close combat, and the word used for the sword of the state’s authority in Romans 13:4. It is not the long ceremonial weapon of a general. It is the instrument of ordinary official violence, and here it has been handed to a horseman whose only business is that men should kill each other.

If God permits this, is he responsible for it? Scripture holds two things together without flinching and refuses to release either. God is never the author of evil, and no man who takes up a sword can plead that heaven made him do it. And nothing happens outside God’s governance, including this. Joseph said both in one sentence about the worst thing his brothers ever did: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). The brothers were guilty. God was not idle.
