Both clauses stand (Westminster 5.4).

Why the difference matters. The practical difference is not small. A believer watching the news from a war can hold one of two things. Either the world has slipped its moorings and God is somewhere off-stage hoping for the best, in which case there is nothing to pray for and no reason to expect an end. Or the red horse rides on a permission granted in the throne room, in front of a rainbow, by a Lamb with the marks still on him. The second is far harder to look at, and it is the only one with any hope in it.

What it does not mean. God does not cause people to hate and kill. The violence comes from human hearts: what causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not your passions at war within you (James 4:1–2)? The judgement is that God removes the restraint and lets sin bear its own fruit, as Paul describes in Romans 1:24–28, where God gives people up to what they desire.

Does this mean Christians may never serve as soldiers? No. The sword here is wielded for slaughter, but Scripture also says the governing authority does not bear the sword in vain and is God’s servant to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4). John the Baptist told soldiers to be honest and content, not to leave the army (Luke 3:14), and the first Gentile convert was a centurion (Acts 10). The historic Reformed view is that Christians may lawfully wage war upon just and necessary occasions (Westminster 23.2). Many Christians in good conscience hold otherwise, and should be honoured. What this verse forbids is not the defence of the innocent but the lust for blood, and it warns that even just wars are fought in a world where the red horse rides.

In a sentence. When the Lamb broke the second seal, I heard the second living being say, Come! and another horse came out, fiery red; its rider was allowed to take peace away from the earth, so that people would slaughter one another, and he was handed a huge sword.

On a Tuesday. Every outbreak of violence shows that human beings cannot make lasting peace on their own. Thank God tonight for the ordinary peace you enjoy: the street without checkpoints, the sleep without shelling. It is a gift, and it can be withdrawn. Then be a peacemaker (Matthew 5:9) in the small wars nearest you, at home, at work and in church, where the same sin that fuels the red horse is at work on a smaller scale. And point people to the Prince of Peace.

For worship. There is only one peace that no horseman can take away, and it was made by the blood of a cross (Colossians 1:20). The Lamb was slaughtered by men who had taken peace from the earth, and by that slaughter he made peace between God and sinners, and between sinners who had been enemies. The red horse rides on a leash held by the Prince of Peace. One day the leash will be pulled in for ever, and they shall beat their swords into ploughshares, and the nations shall learn war no more (Isaiah 2:4).

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a black horse! And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand. And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying, "A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, “Come!” And I looked, and behold, a black horse! And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand. And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying, “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine!”

The setting. A denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer (Matthew 20:2). A quart (a choinix, about a litre) of wheat was roughly one person’s daily ration. Normally a denarius would buy eight to sixteen times as much. So a whole day’s wage would buy only enough wheat for one person, or enough barley, a coarser grain, for a small family. Nothing would be left for anything else. Around AD 92 there was a grain shortage in Asia, and the emperor Domitian ordered half the vineyards in the provinces to be cut down to grow more grain; the order provoked such protest that he withdrew it.

And I looked, and behold, a black horse! War has ridden through; now comes what always follows an army. Fields trampled, men conscripted off the land, granaries emptied, roads unsafe for carts. Famine is not usually a separate disaster. It is the second half of a war. “Black” (melas) is the colour of mourning, hunger and death; Lamentations speaks of faces blacker than soot and skin hot as an oven with the burning heat of famine (Lamentations 4:8; 5:10).

And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand. The scales (zygon, a balance) are the point. Grain sold by weight rather than by the sackful is grain being rationed, and the prophets used exactly this image: when I break your supply of bread, ten women shall bake your bread in a single oven and shall dole out your bread again by weight (Leviticus 26:26); they shall eat bread by weight and with anxiety (Ezekiel 4:16). A man watching his food weighed out in front of him knows precisely how bad things have become.

And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures. A voice from the very centre of heaven, near the throne. God himself sets the limits of the famine. The famine is not a gap in his attention. The boundary around it was drawn in the throne room.

A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius. The voice gives the market prices, and the figures are exact enough to be checked. Famine prices: roughly ten times the normal cost. Do the arithmetic the way a first-century hearer would have done it instantly. A man works from dawn to dusk and earns enough to feed himself, and nothing for his wife or his children. If he switches to barley, coarse and cheap, what you fed animals, he gets three days’ worth, and the family eats badly and is still hungry. This is not a picture of mass starvation with bodies in the street. It is something more familiar and more grinding: a working man in full employment who cannot feed his household, and who knows there is nothing further he can do about it. The poor would suffer most, spending everything just to eat.

And do not harm the oil and wine! “Oil” (elaion, olive oil) and “wine” (oinon). Olive trees and vines have deep roots and survive drought better than grain. The judgement is limited: severe, but not total. It is a warning, not yet the end. Limits are set everywhere in this chapter.

The cellar and the street. But there is also irony in the line. Oil and wine were the produce of estates rather than smallholdings, the goods of the comfortable. What the prohibition describes is the specific injustice of every food crisis in history: the price of bread soars and the luxury trade goes on undisturbed. The rich man’s cellar is untouched while a labourer counts out grain by weight in the street outside. Name that plainly, because it is the shape the world still takes. Famines are rarely a simple absence of food; they are ordinarily a failure of access, and the people who die are the people who cannot pay. The third seal does not describe it in the abstract. The voice quotes the price list.

What it does not mean. The scales are not a sign of justice here, but of scarcity. Nor is this a forecast of one particular famine. It describes the economic hardship that recurs throughout history, until Christ returns.

What should a Christian do when prices soar and money is tight? Three things. Trust, first: your Father knows what you need, and he feeds the birds who neither sow nor reap (Matthew 6:25–33). That does not promise luxury, but it does promise that you are not forgotten. Then share: the early church met famine by sending relief to believers in need (Acts 11:28–30), and those with oil and wine in the cellar are called to open it. And be honest about which side of the street you are on. If the rise in the price of bread is an inconvenience rather than a crisis for you, this verse is asking you what you are doing for the person for whom it is a crisis.

In a sentence. When the Lamb broke the third seal, I heard the third living being say, Come! and I saw a black horse whose rider held a pair of scales; and I heard what sounded like a voice from among the four living beings, saying, A day’s pay for a single ration of wheat, a day’s pay for three rations of barley, but do not damage the olive oil and the wine.

On a Tuesday. Hunger is still real for millions, and in many places it is the hunger of the working poor. Look at your own spending this month and choose one specific, regular gift to relieve it, through your church or a trustworthy agency. And when your own budget is squeezed, turn the anxiety into prayer rather than letting it settle into bitterness. Remember that God has set limits even on famine, and that the voice naming the prices speaks from beside the throne.

For worship. The voice that set the price of bread in the famine is the voice of the God who rained bread from heaven in the wilderness, and who in the fullness of time sent the true bread from heaven. Jesus said: I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger (John 6:35). He was hungry in the desert and did not turn stones to bread; he was thirsty on the cross. And he will spread a table on the renewed earth where they shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more (7:16). The black horse does not have the last word over the poor. The Lamb does.
verseByVerse.note: A denarius was a day’s wage; a quart of wheat was about one person’s daily ration — famine prices.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! And its rider's name was Death, and Hades followed him. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, “Come!” And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! And its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed him. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth.

The setting. In Ezekiel, God speaks of sending his four disastrous acts of judgement on Jerusalem: sword, famine, wild beasts and pestilence (Ezekiel 14:21). The fourth horseman brings all four. John is not inventing a scenario. He is using the standing vocabulary of covenant judgement that every reader of the prophets already knew.

And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! The word is chlōros, pale green, greenish-grey, the root of our words chlorine and chlorophyll. Elsewhere in the New Testament it means the green of grass (8:7; Mark 6:39). Used of a body, it is the colour of a corpse, of sickness and decay. Here it means the green of a face.

And its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed him. This rider is the only one of the four who is named. The first three were anonymous forces; this one has a name, Death (ho Thanatos), personified, and behind him walks a second figure. Hades (ho Hadēs) is the realm of the dead, the place that receives what Death takes. The image is of a reaper and a cart: one kills, and the other collects.

Whose keys? A reader of this book has heard both words before, and John expects him to remember. In the first chapter the risen Christ said: I have the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). The two figures riding out at the fourth seal are the two whose keys are on the belt of the one who opened the seal. They ride only at his word, and the man who holds their keys is the man who let them out. And at 20:14 the same two are thrown into the lake of fire.

And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth. The fourth divine passive of the chapter, and this time an explicit fraction. A fourth. Not half, not all. Stay with that limit, because it is easy to read past a number in a list of horrors. Every rider so far has been permitted, and now the permission is quantified. Death is given a portion and not the whole. Later in the book the trumpets will touch a third (8:7–12), and only with the bowls does anything become total (16:1). The judgements in Revelation escalate, and they escalate because they are being measured out by somebody, in stages, with a purpose. These are not the death-throes of a world God has abandoned. They are warnings loud enough to be heard.

To kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth. “Pestilence” translates thanatō, literally death, a common word in the Greek Old Testament for plague. The fourth horseman sums up the first three and adds disease and wild animals. These are the great killers of human history.

The four are complete. Stand back and look at what has actually been shown. Not a coded map of the twenty-first century. Not a set of clues about a particular decade. The ordinary, terrible furniture of human history: empires that conquer, nations that turn on themselves, hunger that follows the armies, and death that gathers what is left. And every one of the four riding out at the word of the Lamb, on a permission, within a fraction, in front of a throne. The four horsemen match the order of Jesus’ own warnings: wars, famines and earthquakes, which he called the beginning of the birth pains (Matthew 24:6–8). That supports the reading of the seals as troubles that mark the whole age before the end, not only a final period.

The hand on the seal. That is not a comfortable doctrine and it was never meant to be. It is, however, the only alternative to the thought that these things ride at nobody’s word at all. The churches in Asia were about to meet the red horse and the pale one personally. What they were given was not an explanation of why. It was the identity of the hand on the seal.

What it does not mean. Every death in war, famine or plague is not a specific punishment for that person’s sin. The four horsemen show that the world as a whole lives under God’s judgement because of sin (Romans 8:20–22), and that these sufferings are warnings to repent (Luke 13:1–5). Believers suffer them too, but for believers, death has lost its sting (1 Corinthians 15:55).

If Christians die in the same plagues, what difference does faith make? All the difference, though not always the difference we would choose. The same disease may strike a believer and an unbeliever, but it does not do the same thing to them. For the one who is not in Christ, death is the end of every opportunity and the entrance to judgement. For the believer, Death and Hades ride under the authority of his own Saviour, who has already been through death and come out holding its keys. Death can take his body; it cannot keep it. It can end his life here; it delivers him to Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). The pale horse is a thief to the world and, for the Christian, only a servant opening a door.

Was a pandemic God’s judgement? In the broad sense, yes: every plague belongs to a world under the curse, and every one is a summons to repent, as Jesus said of a tower that fell on eighteen people (Luke 13:4–5). In the narrow sense, we are not told which specific sins of which specific people a particular disaster answers, and anyone who claims to know is speaking beyond Scripture. The right response to a plague is not to point at others, but to examine ourselves, care for the sick at cost as Christians have done since the plagues of the Roman empire, and remember how short life is.

In a sentence. When the Lamb broke the fourth seal, I heard the fourth living being say, Come! and I saw a pale, sickly horse; its rider was named Death, and the grave came close behind him; they were given power over a quarter of the earth, to kill by war, famine, disease and wild animals.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of pandemics and disasters, let them remind you how short life is, and turn to the one who holds the keys of Death. Ask the question the horseman forces: if death came for me this year, where would it take me? Settle that with Christ today. Then, if there is someone in your life who has never settled it, let the next headline become the opening of a conversation.

For worship. Death rides out, and Hades follows with its cart, and the keys of both are on the belt of the Lamb. He is the one who went into death on purpose, who let it swallow him and then broke it from the inside: I died, and behold I am alive forevermore (1:18). The pale horse has a fourth of the earth for a season. It does not have Christ, and it will not keep those who are his. Death will be thrown into the lake of fire, and the last enemy will be destroyed, and the Lamb who holds the keys will lock the door behind it for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne. They cried out with a loud voice, "O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne. They cried out with a loud voice, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?”

The setting. In the temple, the blood of sacrifices was poured out at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7), and Leviticus says the life of the flesh is in the blood (Leviticus 17:11). Paul spoke of his coming death as being poured out like a drink offering (2 Timothy 4:6; Philippians 2:17). The cry How long? is the cry of suffering believers throughout the Psalms (Psalm 13:1–2; 79:5–10; 94:3) and the prophets (Habakkuk 1:2; Zechariah 1:12). The blood of Abel cried out to God from the ground (Genesis 4:10).

The fifth seal breaks the pattern. There is no horse, no rider, no thundered Come! The camera turns away from the earth altogether, and what John sees is a congregation.

When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar. The altar (thysiastērion) is the place of sacrifice. Why under the altar? In the temple the blood of a sacrifice was poured out at its base, so the place where the life of every offering collected was the foot of the altar. These people are lying exactly where the blood of the offerings went. Their deaths were not waste; they were an offering, and heaven has put them where an offering belongs. What looked like defeat was worship.

The souls of those who had been slain. “Souls” (psychas) means persons, lives. They have died, but they are alive and conscious in God’s presence, waiting for the resurrection. And the verb for slain is esphagmenōn, the same word used of the Lamb at 5:6. What was done to Christ has been done to them, and Scripture says so with a single deliberate word. They share his death.

For the word of God and for the witness they had borne. As John himself was on Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus (1:9). They died because they would not stop believing and confessing Christ. Antipas of Pergamum, the faithful witness who was killed where Satan dwells (2:13), is one of them.

Where are they now? The verse settles, in passing, a question ordinary Christians ask constantly at funerals. Between death and resurrection, believers are conscious, recognisable, in the presence of God, capable of speech, and not yet finished, because the body is still in the ground and the resurrection has not happened. Paul says the same: my desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better (Philippians 1:23). Not unconscious. Not yet complete. With him.

They cried out with a loud voice, O Sovereign Lord, holy and true. Then they speak, and what they say is startling. “Sovereign Lord” is despotēs, the word for an absolute master over a household, a title chosen because their complaint is precisely that he has the power to act and has not. Holy and true: because God is holy and true, he must judge evil. Their prayer appeals to his character.

How long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? “How long” (heōs pote) is literally until when. This is the cry of the psalms of complaint, in substance word for word: how long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever (Psalm 13:1)? Something like a third of the Psalter is made of it. “Judge” (krineis) and “avenge” (ekdikeis, vindicate, see justice done). “Those who dwell on the earth” is, in Revelation, a standing name for unbelievers in rebellion against God (3:10). They do not ask for personal revenge, but for God to act as judge and put things right publicly. It is a prayer for justice, which God promises to answer: will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? (Luke 18:7–8; Romans 12:19).

Should believers pray for vengeance? A careful Christian will raise it, and it deserves a real answer rather than a nervous one. Did not Christ tell us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us (Matthew 5:44), and did not Stephen die asking that the sin not be held against them (Acts 7:60)? Four things settle it. First, they are not asking to do anything; they are asking God to do it. Vengeance belongs to him and nobody else: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Romans 12:19), and that command is a command to hand the matter over, not to pretend the matter does not exist. Second, they do not name individuals or ask for a particular punishment. They ask the judge to judge. Third, what they are asking for is not private satisfaction but justice, which God has promised and the world urgently needs. A universe in which murder is finally shrugged at is not a kind universe. Fourth, the two prayers are not rivals: Christ prayed for his executioners’ forgiveness (Luke 23:34) and also promised that every hidden thing would be brought into the open (Luke 12:2–3). The one who repents is forgiven. The one who does not is judged. Praying for both is not confusion; it is the whole gospel with nothing left out.

The second burden lifted. That frees a believer from something needless. Anyone who has been genuinely wronged, assaulted, defrauded, lied about, bereaved by somebody who was never charged, often carries a double burden: the injury itself, and the guilt of still minding about it. This verse takes the second one away. The holiest company in Scripture, standing in the immediate presence of God, wearing the marks of martyrdom, are asking out loud how long justice is going to take. Nobody tells them to stop.

Where Christians differ: do the dead sleep until the resurrection? Some groups teach soul sleep: that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection, or that the soul does not exist apart from the body. Verdict: the martyrs are conscious, speaking, praying and comforted, while their bodies are in the grave. Scripture teaches an intermediate state in which believers are with Christ at once when they die (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). They are not yet in their final state, which comes at the resurrection, but they are with the Lord, at rest (v. 11). Nor is there any purgatory; they are under the altar, in God’s presence, not being purified.

What it does not mean. Praying for God’s justice is not hatred or a lack of love. Jesus prayed for his enemies’ forgiveness (Luke 23:34), and so did Stephen (Acts 7:60). Both prayers belong together: we pray for our enemies to repent, and we pray for God to judge evil and vindicate his people if they do not. We leave vengeance to God.

Do the dead in Christ know what is happening on earth? This verse shows they know enough to know that justice has not yet been done, and that is as far as Scripture takes us. It does not teach that departed loved ones watch over us, hear our words, or can be spoken to, and we should not try. What it does teach is better: they are with Christ, at rest, conscious, and joined with us in longing for his coming. The communion of saints is real, but it runs through Christ, not around him. You can thank God for them and look forward to seeing them; you do not need to talk to them.

How do I pray this prayer without becoming bitter? Pray it to God, out loud, in the words of the Psalms if you need them, rather than rehearsing it privately against the person. Tell him exactly what was done and that it was wrong. Then leave the verdict with him, and ask him for the grace to bless the person if they repent. Bitterness is justice held in your own hands too long. The martyrs’ prayer is justice handed over to the only Judge who will get it exactly right, and that is why it can be prayed by someone who also forgives.

In a sentence. When the Lamb broke the fifth seal, I saw beneath the altar the souls of those who had been killed because of God’s word and the testimony they had held to, and they cried out loudly: Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how much longer before you judge the inhabitants of the earth and avenge our blood?

On a Tuesday. Pray for persecuted Christians today, by name and by country if you can, and pray with them for God’s justice. The prayers of the suffering church are heard (8:3–5). And if you are carrying a wrong that has never been put right, bring it to God this week in a how long prayer. You are not being unspiritual. You are standing with the martyrs.

For worship. The God of this verse lets his people cry how long in his own presence and does not rebuke them, because he is holy and true and the cry is a cry for him to be what he is. He has placed his martyrs at the foot of his altar, where the blood of the sacrifices was poured, beside the one great sacrifice of the Lamb, slain with the same word. Not one drop of their blood has been forgotten. The Judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25), and every saint who died for his name is already alive in his presence, waiting for the day he does it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they were each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they were each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.

Two parts, neither expected. The answer comes in two parts, and neither is what the question asked for. They asked how long, and they are given a garment and a word.

Then they were each given a white robe. Before anything is explained, something is handed over. The white robe (stolē leukē) means purity, victory, vindication. It is the promise made to the conquerors in Sardis (3:4–5), worn by the elders (4:4) and by the great multitude (7:9), and 7:14 will say where the whiteness comes from: they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. That is a deliberately impossible image, and it settles that the robe is not a reward for dying well. It is the verdict of the court delivered in advance. Before the final judgement, God gives them his verdict: they are righteous, and their cause is just. Whatever the world’s courts said about these people, and several of them were executed as criminals under due process, heaven has dressed them in the colour of innocence.

Each. Note the word. Not a general amnesty issued to a category; a robe apiece, handed to individuals. This is the same God who counts a few names in Sardis one at a time (3:4).

And told to rest a little longer. The first thing in the word is rest. The verb (anapausontai) means to cease from labour, to stop. It is not a command to be patient in the sense of gritting the teeth; it is permission to stop working. Their part is finished. Whatever is still to be done about the injustice done to them is not their assignment any more. Not a rebuke of their prayer, but comfort while they wait. Their rest contrasts with the restless torment of those who worship the beast, who have no rest, day or night (14:11). Blessed indeed are the dead who die in the Lord, that they may rest from their labours (14:13).

A little longer. There is an end, and God has an opinion about the length of the wait. He does not say indefinitely. He calls it short, which, said to people already dead and already in his presence, is a measurement taken from a place where the arithmetic looks different from the way it looks in a cell.

Until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete. “Complete” (plērōthōsin, be filled up, fulfilled). God has a set number of martyrs, as he has a set number of the elect, the fullness of the Gentiles coming in (Romans 11:25). The end will come when his purposes are complete, not before. History moves on God’s timetable. And the number is not a casualty estimate but a roll. Nobody in it is an accident, and nobody outside it will be taken by mistake.

Who were to be killed as they themselves had been. This is the third thing in the sentence, and it is very hard. “Were to be” (mellontes, about to). More martyrdoms are coming. The church was not promised escape from suffering. The delay in judgement is not administrative. God is waiting because there are more still to come, and they will die in the same way. The answer to how long until you avenge our blood is: until the rest of your brothers have shed theirs. Nothing softens that, and it should not be softened.

The patience that produced Paul. But consider what the delay is doing on the other side of the ledger. God is patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9), and his plan includes the faithful witness of the church through suffering. Every year the judgement is postponed is a year in which somebody who is currently an enemy of God can be brought in. The man who wrote half the New Testament’s letters about grace had held the coats at the first martyrdom (Acts 7:58; 8:1). Paul was in the number of the persecutors before he was in the number of the persecuted. The patience the martyrs are being asked to accept is the patience that produced Paul.

What it does not mean. The fixed number does not mean God enjoys the death of his people. Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints (Psalm 116:15). It means that even martyrdom is not random; it is within his loving and wise plan, and each death matters to him.

Should I expect to be martyred? Most Christians in history have not been, and most readers of this page will not be. But every Christian is called to be ready, and in parts of the world today the number is still being filled. What this verse forbids is the assumption that faithfulness will be safe. Jesus said that if they persecuted him they would persecute his followers (John 15:20), and the costs in the West are usually smaller: a lost promotion, a broken friendship, mockery. Prepare for those now, because the courage to die for Christ is ordinarily built from a thousand small refusals to be ashamed of him.

If God has fixed the number, why pray or evangelise? Because God fixes the ends and the means together. The same God who knows the full number of his people has appointed that they be gathered through preaching, prayer and the witness of the church, often at the cost of suffering. A fixed number does not make the work pointless; it makes it certain. Paul kept preaching in Corinth because the Lord told him, I have many in this city who are my people (Acts 18:10). The roll is full of names not yet called, and your witness may be how one of them is.

So the fifth seal is honest. It does not answer the question of timing at all, and it does not pretend it has. It gives three things instead: a verdict delivered early, an end that is fixed, and a reason for the wait that is not indifference. For a congregation in Smyrna expecting arrests, that was the whole of the comfort available, and it turned out to be enough for sixty generations.

In a sentence. Each of them was given a white robe, and they were told to rest a little while longer, until the full number of their fellow servants, their brothers and sisters who were going to be killed just as they had been, was complete.

On a Tuesday. If you are waiting on God for something that has not come, a healing, a justice, a prodigal’s return, notice that God’s answer to the martyrs was not an explanation but a robe and rest. Ask him for those first. Receive his verdict over you in Christ, and stop carrying what he has told you to put down. And pray this week by name for one persecuted church, that they may be faithful, and that those who persecute them may become like Paul.

For worship. Those who have died for Christ are at rest and honoured, dressed in white by the hand of God himself, robed in the righteousness of the Lamb whose death they shared. The world condemned them; heaven acquitted them before the trial was over. And the God who counts them one by one is counting still, patient with his enemies, faithful to his friends, and certain of the end. Not one name on his roll will be missing when the number is complete. Precious in his sight is the death of his saints.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the sixth seal, I looked, and behold, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood, and the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale. The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and every mountain and island was removed from its place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he opened the sixth seal, I looked, and behold, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood, and the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale. The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and every mountain and island was removed from its place.

The setting. The Old Testament prophets described the Day of the LORD in terms of cosmic collapse: the sun and moon darkened, the stars falling, the heavens rolled up like a scroll, the mountains shaking (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4; Joel 2:10, 31; Haggai 2:6). Jesus used the same language for his coming (Matthew 24:29–30). Sometimes this language described the fall of earthly empires: Isaiah 13 is about Babylon, Ezekiel 32:7–8 about Egypt, Isaiah 34 about Edom. But here its universal scope points to the end of the age.

The world comes apart. The sixth seal is opened, and six things go, in order, from the ground upward: the earth quakes, the sun goes black, the moon turns to blood, the stars fall, the sky rolls up, and every mountain and island is moved out of place. The whole stage is struck.

There was a great earthquake. “Earthquake” (seismos). In Scripture, earthquakes accompany God’s coming in power: the whole mountain trembled greatly at Sinai (Exodus 19:18), and yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens (Hebrews 12:26–27). Asia was earthquake country. Sardis and Philadelphia had been flattened in AD 17, and every reader would have understood the terror.

And the sun became black as sackcloth. Sackcloth (sakkos) was coarse cloth woven from black goat hair and worn in mourning, so the comparison is exact and not merely poetic. The sun itself puts on mourning.

The full moon became like blood. As in Joel 2:31: the sun shall be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes. Peter quoted it at Pentecost (Acts 2:20).

And the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale. The one detail that is unmistakably John’s own is the fig tree, though it echoes Isaiah 34:4. Late figs (olynthous) that never ripened hang on through the winter, hard and green and useless, and the first real storm brings them down in a shower. It is a small, domestic, almost homely image dropped into the middle of a cosmic catastrophe, and it reduces the stars to windfall. The lights that sailors steered by and astrologers consulted and emperors were named after come down like unripe fruit off a tree in a gale, and the tree does not notice.

The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up. “Vanished” (apechōristhē) means was split apart, removed. Isaiah says the skies roll up like a scroll (Isaiah 34:4). The created order as we know it passes away: the heavens will pass away with a roar (2 Peter 3:10), and from the presence of him who sits on the great white throne earth and sky flee away (20:11).

And every mountain and island was removed from its place. The most solid things on earth are moved. Nothing is left to hide behind.

The fixed points removed. That is the actual argument of these three verses, and it is aimed at people under pressure from something that looks immovable. Everything humanity has ever used as a fixed reference point is in this list. The ground, which does not move. The sun, which always rises. The stars, which are how you find your way home when nothing else is visible. Mountains, which are the standing definition of permanence. Every one of them, in three verses, gone. And the throne is not in the list. Chapter 4 established where the one fixed point is, and chapter 6 now removes every rival. When the sky is rolled up like a scroll there will be one thing left standing in the universe, and it will be the thing that was described first.

Where Christians differ: is this the end, or a stage on the way? Many futurist readers place the sixth seal early in a future tribulation, with many more judgements to follow in a strict sequence. Verdict: the sixth seal describes the final day of judgement itself, when Christ returns. The language is the language Jesus used for his coming, and the people cry that the great day of wrath has come (v. 17). This shows that Revelation is not one long timeline but a series of parallel visions, each ending at or near the end. The seals take us to the end; the trumpets and bowls go over the same ground again from other angles, with growing intensity. This is called recapitulation, and it fits the amillennial reading of the book.

What it does not mean. The cosmic language is not a scientific description of astronomical events. It is the prophets’ way of describing the shaking and passing away of the whole created order at God’s coming. It may be literal in part, and it is certainly real; but its main point is that nothing in creation can stand before its Creator.

Will the world really end, or be renewed? Both, in the biblical sense. The present order, scarred by sin, will pass away; but God does not throw his creation away and start from nothing. He makes all things new (21:5). As the flood purged the old world without abolishing the earth (2 Peter 3:6–7), so the fire of the last day will purify and transform creation, which waits with eager longing to be set free from its bondage to corruption (Romans 8:19–21). The sky rolling up is not the end of everything God made. It is the end of everything that stood between creation and its glory.

Should I be afraid of the end of the world? If you are in Christ, no. For the believer, the day the sky is rolled up is the day of his redemption: when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near (Luke 21:28). The fear that grips people over world events, war, climate, economic collapse, is answered not by pretending nothing will be shaken, but by knowing the one who cannot be. Christians should care for the world, work for the good of their neighbours and take real dangers seriously. But they do not need to panic, because the end of the world is in the same hands as its beginning.

In a sentence. When the Lamb broke the sixth seal, I looked and saw a great earthquake: the sun went black like mourning cloth, the full moon turned red as blood, and the stars fell to earth like unripe figs shaken from a tree in a storm; the sky split open and rolled up like a scroll, and every mountain and island was moved out of its place.

On a Tuesday. Everything that seems permanent will be shaken. Make a short list of the things you lean on hardest for a sense of security: savings, health, a job, a relationship, a reputation, a country. None of them is wrong to have. Every one of them is on the list of things that will be moved out of its place. Build your life on the one kingdom that cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:27–28), and hold the rest with an open hand.

For worship. When the sun is clothed in sackcloth and the stars fall like windfall figs and the sky is rolled up like a finished book, the throne will still be there, exactly where John first saw it, and the one seated on it will not have moved. He made the sun and he will put it out; he hung the stars and he will gather them in. The God of this verse is the only fixed point in the universe, and he is the one his people have trusted all along. They will not be shaken, because he is not.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains, calling to the mountains and rocks, "Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains, calling to the mountains and rocks, “Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?”

The setting. Isaiah describes people fleeing into the caves of the rocks and the holes of the ground from before the terror of the LORD, when he rises to terrify the earth (Isaiah 2:19–21). Hosea says they shall say to the mountains, Cover us, and to the hills, Fall on us (Hosea 10:8). Jesus quoted Hosea on his way to the cross (Luke 23:30). Malachi asks who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears (Malachi 3:2), and Nahum asks who can stand before his indignation (Nahum 1:6).

From the cosmos to faces. The last three verses of the chapter turn from the sky to people, and they are the most searching in it.

Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful. Seven classes of people, which in this book means the complete list, the whole of humanity. Five of them are the top of the pyramid. “Kings” (basileis) are the same kings of the earth over whom Christ is ruler (1:5). “Great ones” (megistanes) are nobles, top officials. “Generals” (chiliarchoi) are commanders of a thousand. Then the rich (plousioi) and the powerful (ischyroi). Those who seemed untouchable, who persecuted the church, are the first to flee.

And everyone, slave and free. Then the sentence widens to take in everybody, and finishes with the two words that in the Roman world divided the whole human race. The order is deliberate and it starts at the top. Every category that ordinarily protects a person is named first and named uselessly. A king has an army. A general has the army itself. A rich man can buy his way out of most things and a powerful one can arrange them. On this day the list of people who cannot help themselves runs from the throne down to the labour gang, and the emperor and the man he owns end up behind the same rock. No one is exempt. Status means nothing on that day.

Hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains. The mountains have just been moved (v. 14); there is nowhere to hide.

Calling to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us and hide us. This is the terrible part. They are asking mountains to crush them. Given the choice between being buried alive and being looked at, they choose the burial. Not repentance, but terror. They do not ask for mercy; they ask to be hidden.

From the face of him who is seated on the throne. Sit with what they are hiding from, because it is not fire and it is not an army. It is the face (prosōpou). Moses asked to see that face and was told that no man could see it and live (Exodus 33:20). The great blessing of Israel was that the LORD would make his face shine upon you (Numbers 6:25). The whole hope of this book is that his servants will see his face (22:4). The same face that the redeemed long to see is what the lost cannot bear, and here men are begging geology to spare them from it.

And from the wrath of the Lamb. The phrase ought to stop every reader. “Wrath” (orgē) is settled, righteous anger. Put the two words side by side and they should not fit. Lambs do not have wrath. That is the point, and it is the exact counterpart of 5:5–6: there John was told a Lion and shown a Lamb, and here the Lamb turns out to be what men flee from. This is not a mild Christ who has finally lost his temper. It is the same Lamb, with the same wounds, and the wrath is the other face of the love that bore them. The Lamb is gentle, but he is not soft. Those who reject the Lamb’s sacrifice will face the Lamb’s anger. The one who died for sinners will judge those who refuse him (John 5:22, 27; Acts 17:31). Nothing is more terrible than mercy that has been refused for long enough, and the only thing left to meet is the one who offered it.

For the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand? “The great day” (hē hēmera hē megalē) is the Day of the LORD, the final judgement (Joel 2:11, 31; Zephaniah 1:14). “Their wrath” is the wrath of God and the Lamb, one wrath. “Who can stand” (tis dynatai stathēnai): who is able to stand firm, survive and be acquitted? The question is the last word of the chapter, and it is left hanging deliberately. It is not rhetorical despair; it is a real question, and the whole of the next chapter is the answer. Before the seventh seal is opened, John will be shown a hundred and forty-four thousand sealed on the forehead and a multitude nobody can count, standing, standing, before the throne and before the Lamb (7:9).

Two places to stand. So the honest question this chapter leaves with a reader is not whether the world is going to be shaken. It says plainly that it is, and that the shaking has been going on since the first horse rode out. The question is where a person will be standing when the last of the fixed points goes, and there are only two options in the text: behind a rock, or in front of the throne in a white robe.

The difference is the blood. And the difference between them is not courage or achievement. Every one of the seven classes hiding in the caves failed for the same reason, and every one of the multitude in the next chapter succeeded for the same reason, and it is the reason given in 7:14: they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. The wrath they are spared is the Lamb’s, and so is the blood that spares them.

What it does not mean. God’s wrath is not uncontrolled rage or a bad temper. It is his holy, just and settled opposition to evil, which he has delayed in patience. And it is not the whole picture of God. The same Lamb whose wrath is feared offers to bear wrath in our place: we shall be saved by him from the wrath of God (Romans 5:9), Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come (1 Thessalonians 1:10).

Will people get another chance on that day? No. These people know exactly who they are hiding from, and they still do not repent; they ask to be hidden, not forgiven. That is the frightening thing: seeing God does not by itself change a heart that has refused him. Scripture holds out no second chance after death or after his coming. It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgement (Hebrews 9:27). That is why the invitation is so urgent now: behold, now is the favourable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2). The only time to run to the Lamb is before the day of his wrath.

How can I be sure I will stand? Not by examining your courage or your record, but by looking where the multitude in chapter 7 looked: to the blood of the Lamb. If you have turned from your sin and trusted Christ, his death has already borne the wrath you deserved, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Your assurance rests on his finished work, confirmed by the Spirit’s witness that you are God’s child (Romans 8:16) and by the fruit of a changed life. If your faith is weak, it is still faith in a strong Saviour. Those he has sealed will stand, not because they are strong, but because he holds them.

In a sentence. Then the kings of the earth, the nobles, the military commanders, the rich and the powerful, and everyone else, slave or free, hid in caves and among the mountain rocks, calling out to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us and hide us from the face of the one seated on the throne and from the anger of the Lamb, for the great day of their anger has come, and who can survive it?

On a Tuesday. No one can hide from God. The only safe place on that day is in Christ, under the blood of the Lamb. Run to him now, and do not wait for the sky to roll up before you settle it. Then think of one person you know who is hiding, behind busyness, wealth, cleverness or simply never thinking about it, and pray for an opening to tell them where the only shelter is. Urge them while it is still called today.

For worship. The wrath of the Lamb is real, and the Lamb is the one who drank it. On the cross the face of the Father was turned away from his Son, so that the face which the kings of the earth cannot bear could shine on sinners in peace. He bore the darkness so that the redeemed might see his face; he was crushed so that they need never ask the mountains to fall. Who can stand? Only those who stand in him. And everyone who stands in him will stand for ever, robed in white, before the throne and before the Lamb.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, “Come!”<sup>2</sup>And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer.<sup>3</sup>When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, “Come!”<sup>4</sup>And out came another horse, bright red. Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth, so that people should slay one another, and he was given a great sword.<sup>5</sup>When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, “Come!” And I looked, and behold, a black horse! And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand.<sup>6</sup>And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying, “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine!”<sup>7</sup>When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, “Come!”<sup>8</sup>And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! And its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed him. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth.<sup>9</sup>When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne.<sup>10</sup>They cried out with a loud voice, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?”<sup>11</sup>Then they were each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.<sup>12</sup>When he opened the sixth seal, I looked, and behold, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood,<sup>13</sup>and the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale.<sup>14</sup>The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and every mountain and island was removed from its place.<sup>15</sup>Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains,<sup>16</sup>calling to the mountains and rocks, “Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb,<sup>17</sup>for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?”

7.title: The Sealed and the Standing: God's People in the Storm
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is the first great interlude of Revelation — a pause between the sixth and seventh seals that answers the question that ended chapter 6: “Who can stand?” The answer comes in two scenes that together present the whole people of God from two perspectives. The 144,000 sealed from the twelve tribes of Israel (vv. 1–8): the church as it endures on earth, the complete and protected people of God in the midst of judgment. The great multitude from every nation (vv. 9–17): the church as it will appear before the throne, the redeemed in their innumerable fullness, already standing where the kings of the earth could not.

The 144,000 has generated more interpretive controversy than almost any other passage in Revelation. A strictly literal reading — exactly 144,000 ethnic Jewish males from the twelve tribes of Israel — faces several difficulties: (1) Dan is missing from the list and Manasseh (Joseph’s son) substituted, while Levi (not a territorial tribe) is included, making this no straightforward census; (2) the twelve tribes as distinct ethnic communities had not existed since the Assyrian deportation of the northern tribes in 722 BC; (3) the number 12 × 12 × 1,000 is conspicuously mathematical — in a book where seven means completeness, twelve means the people of God, and 1,000 means an immense completeness, 144,000 is the fullness of the fullness of God’s people. The majority Reformed/amillennial reading understands the 144,000 as the complete church of both testaments, the spiritual Israel (Romans 2:28–29; Galatians 3:29; 6:16; Philippians 3:3), sealed for protection through the tribulation. The dispensational reading understands them as 144,000 literal Jewish evangelists who will be saved and minister during the tribulation.

The great multitude of verses 9–17 is most likely the same group seen from a different vantage point — not a second group that supplements the 144,000 but the 144,000 as they appear before the throne, their number now seen to be “a great multitude that no one could number.” The innumerable quality is not a contradiction of the 144,000 but its complement: both “complete” and “uncountable” describe the fullness of the redeemed. The scene before the throne anticipates the final state, giving the church a vision of its own destiny as it endures the trials of the present.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 6 ended with the sky rolled up and a question hanging: who can stand? The seventh seal is not opened until 8:1, and everything here sits in that gap, answering the question before the last seal breaks.

Verse 1: four angels at the four corners of the earth hold back the four winds, so that no wind blows on earth or sea or against any tree. The stillness before a storm — destruction under restraint. Verse 2: a fifth angel ascends from the rising of the sun with the seal of the living God, and outranks the four. Verse 3 gives his order: Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads. Judgment is not cancelled; it is delayed until God’s people are marked (cf. 2 Pet. 3:9).

The picture behind it is Ezekiel 9:4, where a man with a writing case marks the foreheads of those who sigh and groan over what is being done in Jerusalem, and the executioners are told to touch nobody who carries the mark. A seal marked ownership, gave protection, and guaranteed authenticity; all three apply.

Verse 4 gives the number: 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel. Verses 5–8 list the twelve, twelve thousand each — Judah, Reuben, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin. The list matches no tribal register in the Old Testament: Judah heads it rather than Reuben the firstborn; Dan is missing; Levi, which had no territorial allotment, is counted; and Manasseh is listed alongside Joseph, his own father. Who the 144,000 are is set out at the verse, with the evidence on both sides.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sealed Before the Storm

The winds of judgement are held back until God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads, as in Ezekiel 9. Whether the 144,000 are ethnic Israel or the whole people of God, God knows the number exactly.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The seal did not exempt them from the tribulation; it marked them as God’s within it.

Now: The text caps nobody’s hope: the next scene is a multitude no one could number.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, that no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree. Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, with the seal of the living God, and he called with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm earth and sea, saying, "Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, that no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree. Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, with the seal of the living God, and he called with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm earth and sea, saying, “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads.”

Meaning first. Revelation 7 is a pause between the sixth and seventh seals, and it answers the question that ended chapter 6: who can stand? Four angels hold back the winds of judgement until God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads (vv. 1–3). John hears the number of the sealed: 144,000, twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes of Israel (vv. 4–8). Then he looks and sees a great multitude that no one could count, from every nation, tribe, people and language, standing before the throne and the Lamb in white robes, waving palm branches, crying that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb (vv. 9–10). All the angels fall down and worship (vv. 11–12). An elder explains: these are the ones coming out of the great tribulation, who have washed their robes white in the Lamb’s blood (vv. 13–14). So they are before God’s throne, serving him day and night; he shelters them with his presence; they will never again hunger, thirst or be scorched; the Lamb will shepherd them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes (vv. 15–17). The chapter shows the church twice: on earth, sealed and protected as God’s true Israel before the storm; and in heaven, a countless multitude safe for ever after it.

The setting. In Ezekiel 9:4–6, before Jerusalem was judged, God told a man with a writing case to put a mark on the foreheads of those who sigh and groan over the abominations committed in the city, so that the executioners would spare them. At the first Passover the blood on the doorposts marked the houses God would pass over (Exodus 12:13). In the ancient world a seal on a document or object marked ownership and protection; slaves and soldiers were sometimes branded with their master’s or general’s mark.

The gap between the seals. Chapter 6 ended with the sky rolled up and seven classes of people hiding in caves, and with a question left hanging in the air: who can stand? The seventh seal is not opened until 8:1. Everything in this chapter sits in the gap between the sixth and the seventh, and its whole business is to answer that question before the last seal breaks.

After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth. Four angels, four corners, four winds: four is the number of the created world in this book, its compass points and its extent (Jeremiah 49:36). The winds are destructive forces of judgement, perhaps the four horsemen of chapter 6 under another image, since Zechariah links the horses and the four winds of heaven (Zechariah 6:1–5). “Holding back” (kratountas) means gripping firmly. Judgement is restrained by God’s angels until his purpose is done.

That no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree. Anyone who has stood outside before a storm knows that stillness. The air stops. The leaves do not move. Nothing has happened yet, and everything is about to. That is the atmosphere of the first three verses, and the reader is meant to feel it: all creation waits. The winds have not been cancelled. They are being held.

Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun. “Rising of the sun” (anatolēs hēliou) is the east, the direction of dawn and, in Ezekiel, the direction from which the glory of God returns to his temple (Ezekiel 43:2). Hope comes before judgement. And this fifth angel outranks the four, because he gives them orders.

With the seal of the living God. The seal (sphragis) is a signet ring, a stamp. It is the seal of the living God, in contrast to idols that are dead. A seal in the ancient world did three things. It marked ownership, like a brand or a signet pressed into wax. It gave protection, because tampering with a sealed item was an offence against the owner. And it guaranteed authenticity. All three are in play here.

Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads. That is the shape of the whole chapter in one sentence. The judgement is not cancelled; it is delayed, and it is delayed for one reason: God’s people are not marked yet. The winds of the world are held on a leash until the last of the servants has been sealed. Every year of history since is an instance of the same arrangement, and the reason is stated elsewhere in one line: the Lord is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9).

What the seal is. The seal marks God’s ownership and guarantees his protection. In 14:1 the 144,000 have the name of the Lamb and his Father’s name written on their foreheads. The seal is God’s name, which means they belong to him. In the New Testament believers are sealed with the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 1:22; Ephesians 1:13; 4:30).

Who was marked in Ezekiel. The picture behind it is Ezekiel 9, and John expects the reader to know it. The executioners were told to touch nobody who carried the mark. And note who was marked: not the strong or the successful, but the people who were grieved by what was happening around them.

Whose name is on you? One more thing, and the whole book turns on it later. The mark goes on their foreheads. In chapter 13 another power will demand a mark on the right hand or the forehead, and nobody will be able to buy or sell without it (13:16–17). Everyone alive is marked by somebody. The only question in this book is whose name is on you, and the sealing happens first, six chapters before the counterfeit is even offered.

What it does not mean. Sealing does not protect believers from all suffering or from death; many will be martyred (6:11; 13:7). The four winds are eventually released. The very next scene shows this same company coming out of the great tribulation, which means they went through it. The seal is not a shield against suffering. It is a mark of ownership that suffering cannot remove. It protects them from the wrath of God that falls on unbelievers (9:4), and above all from losing their faith and their place in God’s kingdom. Their bodies may suffer; their souls are safe. What is guaranteed is not an easy passage but a safe arrival.

How do I know whether I am sealed? The seal is the Holy Spirit himself, given to everyone who believes: in him you also, when you heard the word of truth and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13). So the question is not whether you have had a special experience but whether you have trusted Christ. The Spirit’s presence shows itself in a faith that keeps looking to Jesus, in a growing hatred of sin and love of holiness, in love for other believers, and in his inward witness that you are a child of God (Romans 8:15–16). These may be faint at times. The seal does not depend on your feeling it.

Can the seal be broken? No. God seals his own for the day of redemption (Ephesians 4:30), and no one can snatch them out of the Father’s hand (John 10:28–29). A believer may grieve the Spirit, fall into serious sin, and lose for a time the joy of his salvation, but he cannot lose the Spirit’s seal. This is the doctrine of perseverance: those God has truly called he keeps to the end (Philippians 1:6). It is not a licence for carelessness, because a person who is happy to live in sin has reason to ask whether he was ever sealed at all. It is a comfort for the weak, who fear that their grip will fail. Your grip is not what holds you.

In a sentence. After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the earth’s four winds so that no wind would blow on land or sea or on any tree; then I saw another angel coming up from the east with the seal of the living God, and he shouted to the four angels who had been given power to harm land and sea: Do not harm the land or the sea or the trees until we have put a seal on the foreheads of the servants of our God.

On a Tuesday. If you belong to Christ, you are sealed by his Spirit. Whatever storms come this week, the diagnosis, the redundancy, the slander, God has marked you as his own, and he does not lose what he owns. And notice who was marked in Ezekiel: those who grieved over sin around them. Ask whether the evils of your culture and your own heart grieve you, or merely annoy you. Grief over sin is one of the Spirit’s fingerprints.

For worship. The winds of judgement strain against the hands of angels, and the whole earth holds its breath, and God will not let them blow until every one of his servants has his name on them. That is the patience and the tenderness of the God of this chapter. He holds back the storm of the ages for the sake of his people. He seals them with his own Spirit, the living God marking them as his living possession, and nothing in heaven or earth can tear that name off. Before the counterfeit mark is ever offered, the true one has been given. We are his.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel: 12,000 from the tribe of Judah were sealed, 12,000 from the tribe of Reuben, 12,000 from the tribe of Gad, 12,000 from the tribe of Asher, 12,000 from the tribe of Naphtali, 12,000 from the tribe of Manasseh, 12,000 from the tribe of Simeon, 12,000 from the tribe of Levi, 12,000 from the tribe of Issachar, 12,000 from the tribe of Zebulun, 12,000 from the tribe of Joseph, 12,000 from the tribe of Benjamin were sealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel: 12,000 from the tribe of Judah were sealed, 12,000 from the tribe of Reuben, 12,000 from the tribe of Gad, 12,000 from the tribe of Asher, 12,000 from the tribe of Naphtali, 12,000 from the tribe of Manasseh, 12,000 from the tribe of Simeon, 12,000 from the tribe of Levi, 12,000 from the tribe of Issachar, 12,000 from the tribe of Zebulun, 12,000 from the tribe of Joseph, 12,000 from the tribe of Benjamin were sealed.

The setting. Israel was made up of twelve tribes descended from the sons of Jacob. The Old Testament lists them about twenty times, in many different orders. By John’s day ten of the tribes had been scattered since the Assyrian conquest in 722 BC, and Jews looked forward to God gathering all twelve tribes in the last days (Isaiah 11:12; Ezekiel 37:15–28). Before a war, Israel took a census of the tribes to count its fighting men (Numbers 1). Jesus chose twelve apostles, who would sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes (Matthew 19:28), signalling that he was reconstituting Israel around himself.

And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000. John hears a number. And then twelve tribes, twelve thousand each, named one after another with a deliberateness that slows the reading right down. 144,000 is 12 × 12 × 1,000: twelve (the tribes of Israel) times twelve (the apostles), times a thousand (a vast, complete number). In a book where seven means fullness and myriads of myriads means beyond counting, that is how numbers work. It is a symbolic number for the complete people of God, the whole of God’s true Israel.

Sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel. Organised like an army, counted by tribes as in the census of Numbers 1. In 14:1–4 the 144,000 stand with the Lamb on Mount Zion, follow him wherever he goes, and are called firstfruits for God and the Lamb, redeemed from mankind. They are God’s army, which conquers not by fighting but by following the Lamb.

12,000 from the tribe of Judah. The list is strange in four ways at once, which is the strongest evidence of what it means. Judah is first, though Reuben was the firstborn, because the Messiah, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, has just been introduced (5:5). Dan is missing altogether, and Dan was the tribe that set up an idol and became a byword for apostasy (Judges 18:30–31; 1 Kings 12:29–30). Levi, which normally received no land and was left out of such lists, is counted as a tribe, perhaps because all God’s people are now priests (1:6). And Joseph is listed alongside Manasseh, Joseph’s own son, while Ephraim disappears. The result is a list that matches no tribal register in the Old Testament. It is twelve names arranged theologically rather than genealogically: the new Israel, gathered around the Messiah.

Where Christians differ: who are the 144,000? Dispensationalists usually see them as literal ethnic Jews, converted during a future tribulation after the church has been raptured, who then evangelise the world; what favours this in their eyes is that the text names the tribes one by one, which is a great deal of trouble to go to for a symbol. Jehovah’s Witnesses teach that exactly 144,000 people form a heavenly class, while other believers live on earth. Others take them as Jewish Christians in the church, distinct from Gentile believers. Verdict: the 144,000 are the whole church, the true Israel of God, Jew and Gentile together, seen on earth, sealed and protected. Four reasons. First, John hears a number (v. 4) and then sees a countless multitude from every nation (v. 9), just as in 5:5–6 he heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb: the two are the same reality, described first in Old Testament terms and then in its fulfilment. Second, the sealing is for all God’s servants (v. 3), and in 9:4 everyone without the seal is harmed, so the sealed must be all believers. Third, the New Testament calls the church the Israel of God (Galatians 6:16), the twelve tribes in the dispersion (James 1:1), and Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29). Fourth, the tribe list itself has been deliberately altered, which signals a symbolic, not a literal, Israel. Nothing in the text supports a special class of 144,000 with a different destiny.

Counted and countless. If John is doing here what he did in chapter 5, then the numbered army of Israel and the uncountable multitude of the nations are one company seen from two sides: as God counts them, exact and complete with nobody missing; and as they actually appear, beyond counting and drawn from everywhere. And the point that matters most is agreed on every side: God knows the number. There is no rounding here and no estimate. It is a figure that has been counted, and the counting was done before the winds were released.

What it does not mean. This does not mean God has forgotten ethnic Israel. Jewish believers are part of the 144,000, as they were the first members of the church. And Paul looks forward to a great turning of Israel to Christ (Romans 11:25–27). But in Christ there is one people of God, not two.

If the 144,000 are the church, what of God’s future for the Jewish people? The two do not conflict. The 144,000 picture the whole people of God, sealed and counted, and the great multitude of v. 9 is the same people seen as they are, from every nation. Paul’s hope for a great turning of Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11:25–26) is part of that people being gathered; the elect of Israel are included in God’s complete number, not set apart from it. Christians differ over how and when that turning will come, and whether it is a great end-time conversion or the steady gathering of the Jewish remnant through the age, but all agree that it will be by faith in Jesus the Messiah, into the one olive tree.

What do I say when someone at the door says only 144,000 go to heaven? Point gently to the next verse. The teaching that only 144,000 people go to heaven while the rest of the saved live for ever on earth cannot be got out of this chapter. In the same vision John sees a multitude that no one could number, standing before the throne in white robes, and later they are said to serve God in his temple (v. 15). Whatever one thinks of the 144,000, the text does not cap the number of the redeemed. It does the opposite: it names a number and then immediately shows a crowd too large to count. Then turn to the deeper question, who Jesus is, because that is where the real difference lies.

Do I need to know which tribe I belong to? No. The chapter never asks anyone to work out his tribe. What it says about the sealed is that they are the servants of our God (v. 3), and what it says about the multitude is that they washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb (v. 14). Those are the two descriptions given, and neither of them is a bloodline. If you belong to Christ, you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29). Your place in God’s Israel is secured by faith, not by ancestry.

Why is Dan left out, and does that mean Danites are lost? No individual is excluded from salvation by his ancestry. The omission is a warning, not a verdict on bloodlines: the tribe that led Israel into idolatry stands as a picture of what idolatry does, in a book that calls Christians again and again to refuse the idols of their age. Some early writers speculated that the antichrist would come from Dan, but the text says nothing of that. The lesson for us is simpler: no heritage, however privileged, protects a person who turns to idols, and no heritage, however compromised, keeps out a person who turns to Christ.

In a sentence. Then I heard how many were sealed: 144,000 from all the tribes of Israel, twelve thousand each from Judah, Reuben, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph and Benjamin.

On a Tuesday. You are not a statistic to God. When you feel lost in a crowd, overlooked at work, forgotten by friends, invisible in a large church, remember that God counts his people one by one, by name, and the number is complete with no one missing. And if you are ever tempted to think your background makes you a second-class Christian, notice that God has rewritten even Israel’s family tree around his Son. In Christ, the only lineage that counts is his.

For worship. The God who numbered the stars and called them all by name has numbered his people too, and not one is missing. He has drawn up his army, tribe by tribe, and set the Lion of Judah at its head. He has taken the old names of Israel and filled them with people from every nation, so that the promise made to Abraham’s family is kept to the last syllable. You are not lost in the crowd. You are counted, sealed and known, numbered among God’s Israel by the hand that holds the scroll.
verseByVerse.note: The tribe list is unusual: Judah comes first, Dan is missing, and both Joseph and his son Manasseh appear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — A Great Multitude from Every Nation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 9–10: John looks and sees a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages — the fourfold phrase of 5:9, so that this chapter is the receipt for that purchase. They are standing, which answers 6:17 directly, in white robes and holding palm branches (Lev. 23:40–43; John 12:13), and they cry Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb! Not a syllable of the song is about what they did.

Verses 11–12: all the angels stand in the outer ring — the redeemed are nearer the throne than the angelic host — and fall on their faces with a sevenfold doxology bracketed by Amen. It matches the ascription to the Lamb in 5:12, with thanksgiving replacing wealth. Heaven falls down because a crowd of forgiven human beings has just sung.

Verses 13–14: an elder asks who they are and where they have come from, and John answers Sir, you know (cf. Ezek. 37:3). The answer has two halves: these are the ones coming out of the great tribulation — a present, continuous participle, a stream still emerging — and they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Blood does not whiten cloth; the image is deliberately impossible.

Verse 15: therefore they are before the throne, serving him day and night in his temple in priestly service (latreuō), and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence — literally, will spread his tent over them (cf. Ex. 40:34; John 1:14; Rev. 21:3). Verses 16–17 close with five promises quoted from Isaiah 49:10: no hunger, no thirst, no sun, no scorching heat; the Lamb in the midst of the throne as their shepherd, guiding them to springs of living water; and God wiping away every tear from their eyes.
verseByVerse.theology:
Washed in the Blood of the Lamb

A multitude from every nation stands before the throne and sings that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb. They came out of the great tribulation, washed their robes in the Lamb’s blood, and are sheltered by God’s presence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Hunger, thirst and scorching heat were the daily lot of many first hearers.

Now: God himself will wipe away every tear — every one, by name.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands, and crying out with a loud voice, "Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
