After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands, and crying out with a loud voice, “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!”

The setting. God promised Abraham that his offspring would be as numerous as the stars of heaven, too many to count (Genesis 15:5; 22:17). At the Feast of Tabernacles Israel waved palm branches and lived in booths, remembering how God had sheltered them in the wilderness (Leviticus 23:40–43). When Jesus entered Jerusalem, the crowds waved palm branches and shouted Hosanna, which means save us (John 12:13). Palm branches were also used to celebrate military victories (1 Maccabees 13:51).

After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number. “Great multitude” (ochlos polys). Set that beside what John has just heard. A moment ago there was a precise figure and a list of twelve names. Now there is a crowd nobody can count. And no one could number is a deliberate phrase, because it takes the reader back to a promise made to a childless old man standing outside his tent at night: look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them; so shall your offspring be (Genesis 15:5). That promise has been kept, and this is what it looks like when it is. Heaven will not be thinly populated.

From every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages. Four terms, as in 5:9: all humanity. The Lamb’s blood ransomed people from every group, and here they are. This chapter is the receipt for that transaction. The purchase was made in chapter 5; here are the purchased, standing in the room.

Standing before the throne and before the Lamb. “Standing” (hestōtes). This answers the question of 6:17: who can stand? These can, because the Lamb stands for them. While kings and generals crawled into caves, here is the answer, and it is not a class of person anyone would have picked: a crowd with no rank, no army and no leverage, drawn from every obscure corner of the world, upright before the throne while the great ones of the earth are face down under the rocks.

Clothed in white robes. Purity, victory, washed in the Lamb’s blood (v. 14). The robes have been promised since 3:5 and given since 6:11.

With palm branches in their hands. “Palm branches” (phoinikes) mean victory and joyful celebration, like a heavenly Feast of Tabernacles. That was the week each autumn when Israel moved out of its houses and lived in booths made of branches to remember the wilderness, a festival of harvest home, of a journey finished. God will shelter them (v. 15), and the wilderness journey is over. And palms were what the crowd waved on the road into Jerusalem, shouting save us.

And crying out with a loud voice, Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb! That makes the cry the answer to the shout on that road. They asked save now; they are here saying that salvation (hē sōtēria, deliverance, rescue) belongs to him. It is his, it comes from him, it is his to give and nobody else’s to supply. They give all the credit to God and the Lamb. Salvation is entirely his work: planned by the Father, accomplished by the Son. As Jonah said from the belly of the fish, salvation belongs to the LORD (Jonah 2:9).

Not one syllable about themselves. Take the word belongs seriously, because everything in the Christian life depends on it. The multitude has come out of the great tribulation. Some of them died under torture. Every one of them held on when it would have been easier not to. And when they open their mouths in front of the throne, not one syllable of the song is about what they did. They do not sing we endured. They sing that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb, and there is no second clause. That is the test of whether a person has understood the gospel, and it can be run quietly at any moment. If everything you are were suddenly explained out loud in front of the throne, whose name would the account turn on? The people who have suffered most for Christ are, on the evidence of this verse, the least inclined to mention it.

What it does not mean. This is not a separate group from the 144,000, one Jewish and one Gentile. It is the same people of God, seen first as God’s Israel, sealed and counted on earth, and then as the countless multitude from all nations, safe in heaven.

Will we keep our nations and languages in heaven? It seems so. John does not see a crowd in which every distinction has been erased, but people still recognisable as from every nation, tribe, people and language. At the end of the book the kings of the earth bring the glory and honour of the nations into the new Jerusalem (21:24–26). The gospel does not flatten cultures into one; it redeems people within them and gathers them around one throne. What will be gone is everything sinful in our cultures: the pride, the hostility, the walls. What remains is a unity so rich that it needs every tongue to sing it.

Does no one could number mean that most people will be saved? Scripture does not tell us the proportion, and Jesus warned that the gate is narrow and few find it (Matthew 7:13–14). But neither should we imagine heaven as a tiny remnant huddled in a corner. From the perspective of the end, gathered from every age and nation, the redeemed are a countless multitude. Both truths matter. The narrowness of the gate makes us urgent about our own soul and our neighbours’; the size of the crowd makes us confident that the gospel will not fail. God is not saving a few survivors from a lost world. He is gathering a world.

In a sentence. After this I looked and saw an enormous crowd that no one could count, from every nation, tribe, people and language, standing in front of the throne and the Lamb, dressed in white robes and holding palm branches, and shouting loudly: Salvation comes from our God, who sits on the throne, and from the Lamb!

On a Tuesday. Give God all the credit for your salvation, out loud, this week. When you tell someone how you became a Christian, notice how much of the story is about you and how much is about him, and change the proportions. And let the diversity of heaven shape your love for believers of every nation now. Seek out a Christian from a different background in your church, or pray by name for a church in another land, because you are going to stand beside them for ever.

For worship. Salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb. All of it: the choosing, the ransoming, the calling, the keeping, the bringing home. The promise made to Abraham under the stars has become a crowd that no one can count, from every language that has ever been spoken, robed in white and waving the palms of a journey finished. And not one of them takes the credit. The whole multitude, with one voice, gives it to the one who sits on the throne and to the Lamb, and every one of them is right.
verseByVerse.note: John hears a number (v. 4) but sees a multitude no one can count — likely the same people seen from two angles.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God, saying, "Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God, saying, “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen.”

And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures. Note the seating plan, because John gives it carefully. In the middle, the throne. Around it, the living creatures and the elders. And in the outer ring, all the angels, the myriads of myriads from 5:11. But the multitude of verse 9 is described as before the throne and before the Lamb, which seems to put the redeemed nearer than the angelic host. Ransomed sinners stand closer to God than the beings who never fell.

And they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God. They have been standing throughout; now they go down. What has just happened to prompt it? The multitude sang. The angels of God hear a crowd of forgiven human beings say that salvation belongs to God, and they put their faces on the floor. Jesus said there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10); here is joy over a countless multitude.

Saying, Amen! They agree with the multitude’s cry. The word means it is firm, it is so, and it is the only word in the verse that is not itself a gift. To say Amen is to agree with what somebody else has said.

Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen. Seven ascriptions, as in 5:12: complete praise, everything there is to give, given. Every item has the definite article in Greek: the blessing, the glory, all of it, belongs to God. And the list is almost the same as the sevenfold ascription to the Lamb in 5:12, with thanksgiving (eucharistia) here in place of wealth. The change is not accidental. Wealth is what a conqueror receives; thanksgiving is what a redeemed people offer. The angels thank God for salvation, though they have not been redeemed themselves.

Bracketed by Amen. The whole doxology begins and ends with Amen, wrapping the praise in agreement. The angels open and close by adding their agreement to a song they cannot sing on their own account, because nobody has ever ransomed an angel.

The redeemed sing, and heaven agrees. There is something in that arrangement that is easy to miss and difficult to get over once seen. The order of events in these two verses is: the redeemed sing, and then heaven agrees. The song that sets the whole company of angels on their faces was started by people who had been slaves, shopkeepers, soldiers, prostitutes and thieves, out of every language on earth. Peter says these are things into which angels long to look (1 Peter 1:12). Here they are looking, and this is what looking does to them.

What it does not mean. Angels do not need salvation in the way humans do. The holy angels never fell, and Scripture offers no redemption for fallen angels: it is not angels that he helps, but the offspring of Abraham (Hebrews 2:16). They worship God for his saving work among human beings.

Do we worship with the angels now? Yes. When the church gathers, it comes not only to a building but to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, to innumerable angels in festal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn (Hebrews 12:22–23). That does not mean we pray to angels or seek their presence; they are fellow servants who point away from themselves (19:10). It means that the smallest gathering of believers on a Sunday morning is joined to a worship far larger than itself. Your Amen at the end of a prayer is the same word the angels say here, and it belongs in the same song.

In a sentence. All the angels standing around the throne, the elders and the four living beings fell face down before the throne and worshipped God, saying: Amen! Praise and glory, wisdom and thanks, honour, power and strength belong to our God for ever and ever. Amen!

On a Tuesday. If angels rejoice over your salvation, how much more should you? Choose one of the seven words this week, wisdom perhaps, or power, and each time something happens that shows it, a problem solved, a temptation resisted, a provision you did not expect, say it back to God: the wisdom is yours. And mean your Amens. Do not let the word become punctuation. It is agreement with the whole of heaven.

For worship. He was on that throne when the seals were breaking and the horses were riding and the winds were straining against four angels’ hands. He is on it still. And everything that exists in heaven, from the creatures covered in eyes to the last angel in the outermost ring, is on its face in front of him, saying it is so. Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honour and power and might be to our God for ever and ever. Amen.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, "Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?" I said to him, "Sir, you know." And he said to me, "These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, “Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?” I said to him, “Sir, you know.” And he said to me, “These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

The setting. Daniel speaks of a time of trouble such as never has been, and at that time God’s people will be delivered, everyone whose name shall be found written in the book (Daniel 12:1). Jesus spoke of great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world (Matthew 24:21). When God asked Ezekiel whether the dry bones could live, the prophet answered, O Lord GOD, you know (Ezekiel 37:3).

Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come? An elder turns to John and asks him a question he cannot possibly answer. It is a teacher’s question, asked to give the answer rather than to get one, and John knows it. The elder wants John, and us, to understand.

I said to him, Sir, you know. “Sir” (kyrie, my lord) is a title of respect. Sir, you know is not evasion; it is the honest reply of a man who has been asked something beyond him and does not intend to guess. Ezekiel gave the same answer standing in a valley full of dry bones. There is a kind of ignorance that is a form of faith, and Scripture records both men practising it. Revelation interprets itself here.

These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. The answer comes in two halves, and each half settles something. First, the tense. “Coming out” (hoi erchomenoi) is a present participle: the ones who keep coming. Not a single group arriving at once, but a steady stream of believers coming out of tribulation, as each one dies or as the age ends. Second, the article: the great tribulation (tēs thlipseōs tēs megalēs). John has already called himself their partner in the tribulation in the first chapter (1:9), using the same word of his own present situation, and Jesus said plainly that in the world you will have tribulation (John 16:33).

Where Christians differ: what is the great tribulation? Dispensationalists understand it as a specific seven-year period at the end of history, after the church has been raptured, and see this multitude as those converted during that time. Verdict: the great tribulation describes the suffering of God’s people throughout the whole age between Christ’s comings, which John and his readers were already in (1:9; 2:9–10), and which will intensify toward the end in a final climax of persecution (Matthew 24:21–22; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–4). The multitude is the whole number of the redeemed, from every nation, coming out of that tribulation through all history. The present tense, “coming out”, suits a continuing stream. The church is not removed from tribulation; it is brought through it.

So will Christians go through the tribulation? Yes, and we are in it now. Scripture nowhere promises a secret removal of the church before trouble comes. Jesus prayed not that the Father would take his people out of the world, but that he would keep them from the evil one (John 17:15). Paul told new converts that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). For most believers in history, and many today, that has meant prison, poverty or death; for others it means quieter pressures. Christ will return once, visibly, to gather his people and judge the world (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). Until then, the promise is not escape but keeping.

They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Then the second half of the answer, and it is the sentence the whole chapter has been walking toward. “Washed” (eplynan) and “made white” (eleukanan). Read that slowly, because it is an impossible sentence, and it is meant to be. Blood does not whiten cloth. Anyone who has ever tried to get blood out of a shirt knows exactly what it does, and every first-century hearer had killed animals with his own hands and knew better still. The image is deliberately, flagrantly wrong, and that is the point. There is one substance in the universe that reverses its own nature at this one job, and the effect is not a stain but a colour nothing else produces. The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7); though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow (Isaiah 1:18). Israel washed their garments to meet God at Sinai (Exodus 19:10, 14); these have washed theirs in something better.

Their action, his detergent. And the verb is active: they washed. Not their robes were washed for them. There is something a person must do, and Revelation is not shy about it: the whole book is an appeal to repent, hold fast, conquer, come. But look at what the washing consists of, because the sentence contains its own safeguard: they washed in the blood of the Lamb. The action is theirs; the detergent is entirely his. Nobody in that multitude contributed a drop of what makes them white. Their white robes are not their own achievement but the result of Christ’s death applied to them by faith. They washed their robes by trusting in his blood.

From where have they come? That is the answer to the elder’s second question, and it is the more important one. He asked not only who are these but from where have they come. They came from every nation on earth, and out of the great tribulation, and from under the executioner’s sword in some cases, and none of that is the answer. They came from the blood of the Lamb. Every person in a crowd nobody can count arrived there by the same road, and there is no second road, and no one of them can tell a better story about the journey than the person next to him.

What it does not mean. Washing their robes is not a work that earns salvation. It is faith, trusting in what the Lamb has done. Their robes are white because of his blood, not because of their sufferings.

How do I wash my robe in the Lamb’s blood? By coming to Christ as a sinner and trusting that his death was for you. That is how it begins: you admit that your own robe is stained beyond your power to clean, and you rest your whole weight on his sacrifice. And it continues, because the Christian keeps coming back to the same fountain: if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). So when you sin this week, do not try to scrub the stain out yourself with good resolutions before you dare approach God. Go straight to the blood. It is the only thing that has ever made anyone white.

In a sentence. Then one of the elders asked me, Who are these people dressed in white, and where have they come from? I answered, Sir, you are the one who knows; and he told me, These are the ones who are coming out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

On a Tuesday. If you are suffering for Christ, at work, in your family, in your country, you are part of the stream coming out of the great tribulation. That is not a sign that God has forgotten you; it is the normal road of his people. Your robe is white not because of what you endure but because of the blood of the Lamb. So when you are tempted to think your sufferings make you more acceptable to God, or your sins make you less, look again at what the robes were washed in.

For worship. Blood does not make cloth white, except this blood. The Lamb poured out his life, and everything it touches is made clean: the stained robe of the thief, the persecutor, the coward, the respectable sinner. A stream of people is coming out of the great tribulation even now, and each one has the same testimony and the same garment, white in the blood of the Lamb. No one in that crowd will ever say I made myself clean. Every one of them will say he did, and it will be the truest thing they ever said.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence.

The setting. In the wilderness God’s glory dwelt in the tabernacle, a tent among his people, and he sheltered them with the pillar of cloud by day and fire by night (Exodus 40:34–38). Isaiah promised that the LORD would create a cloud by day and fire by night over Zion as a canopy and a shelter (Isaiah 4:5–6). John’s Gospel says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, literally pitched his tent among us (John 1:14).

Therefore they are before the throne of God. “Therefore” (dia touto, for this reason) carries the entire logic of the gospel. Not because they endured, though they did. Not because they were faithful under torture, though many were. Therefore: because of the washing in the previous verse, and because of nothing else, they are standing where they are standing. Their access to God rests on Christ’s sacrifice, not on their merit.

And serve him day and night in his temple. “Serve” (latreuousin) is not general helpfulness but priestly service, the word for what a priest did at the altar. In the temple in Jerusalem only priests entered the holy place, and only one man went behind the veil, once a year, with blood, having washed. Here a crowd from every nation on earth is inside, permanently, doing priestly work. The promise of 1:6 has arrived: he made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father. “Temple” (naos) is the sanctuary, the inner shrine: they are in the very place where God dwells. In the new Jerusalem, God and the Lamb are the temple (21:22).

Day and night. The phrase should not be hurried past. It is the phrase used of the living creatures who never cease (4:8). But there is no night in the city at the end of this book (21:25; 22:5), which means the expression is not measuring hours. It means without interruption. Nothing ever again breaks it off: no fatigue, no distraction, no sin, no need to stop and earn a living, no Monday.

And he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence. The English can only half carry this clause. The Greek is skēnōsei ep’ autous: literally, he will spread his tent over them. It is the word for the tabernacle, the tent God pitched in the middle of Israel’s camp so that he could live among them in the wilderness (Exodus 25:8; 40:34). It is the same word John used in the first chapter of his Gospel. And it is the word that will be used at 21:3, when the loud voice from the throne announces that the dwelling place (skēnē) of God is with man, and he will dwell (skēnōsei) with them.

Proximity, not distance. So the picture is not chiefly of protection from something. It is of nearness. God puts his tent over these people, the way a father pulls a blanket over a child, the way the cloud stood over the tabernacle in the desert. They are not being kept at a safe distance from the throne and defended; they are being covered by the one on it. The people who were driven out by persecution, who perhaps had no home, are given God himself as their home.

The same throne, two companies. Set that beside where the previous chapter ended. In 6:16 the great ones of the earth begged the mountains to fall on them and hide them from the face of him who is seated on the throne. Here, the same throne, the same one seated on it, and a crowd with no rank at all is being sheltered under him. The identical presence is the thing one company cannot bear to look at and the thing the other company lives inside. And the difference between the two, once again, is not in the people. It is in verse 14.

What it does not mean. Serving day and night does not mean heaven is exhausting or monotonous. There is no tiredness there (22:5), and the service is perfect freedom and delight.

Will heaven be boring? Only to someone who imagines it as an endless church service he did not enjoy on earth. The service here is the joyful activity of people made perfect, in the presence of the most interesting being there is, God himself, whose glory is inexhaustible. Elsewhere Revelation speaks of reigning (22:5), of the glory of the nations brought in (21:26), and of a city with streets and a river. Service in Scripture includes worship, but it also includes work: Adam was put in the garden to work it (Genesis 2:15). Whatever heaven holds, it will not be less than the best of this life. Boredom is a symptom of a fallen heart, and it will not be there.

In a sentence. That is why they stand before God’s throne and worship him day and night in his temple, and the one who sits on the throne will spread his tent over them.

On a Tuesday. Your worship on earth is a rehearsal for heaven, and so is your work done for God. Serve God gladly now, in the meeting and in the kitchen, at the desk and at the bedside, as a priest in his temple. And when you feel exposed, homeless in the world, or far from God, remember the tent. You are not being held at arm’s length until you prove yourself. You were brought near by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 2:13).

For worship. The God who once pitched his tent in the middle of a wandering people, and then pitched it in human flesh in the person of his Son, will at last spread it over a multitude from every nation, and never fold it up again. The throne that the kings of the earth could not bear to look on becomes the shelter of the poor and persecuted. He who was without a home for our sake becomes our home for ever. We shall dwell in the house of the LORD, and he will dwell over us.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat.

The setting. The words come almost directly from Isaiah 49:10, where God promises the exiles returning home that they shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them. John takes the promise made to a people in exile and gives it to a multitude out of every nation. He sees the final fulfilment of the promise of a new exodus.

They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore. “No more” (ou … eti) means never again. Notice how specific and how bodily the list is. Hunger. Thirst. Sunstroke. These are not spiritual metaphors to the people first hearing them. The black horse rode out with a pair of scales in chapter 6, and a labourer’s whole day bought one man’s ration of wheat (6:5–6). Believers under economic boycott in Smyrna were poor in the beggar’s sense (2:9). Hunger and thirst, the daily fears of the poor and the punishments of persecution, are over for ever. Jesus promised that whoever comes to him shall not hunger, and whoever believes in him shall never thirst (John 6:35).

The sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat. “Strike” (pesē) is literally fall on, and “scorching heat” (kauma) is burning heat: exposure, exhaustion, suffering. A slave working a field in Asia Minor in August knew precisely what scorching heat does to a man who cannot stop. In the Middle East the sun was a real danger to travellers, and the Psalm promises that the sun shall not strike you by day (Psalm 121:6). In 16:8–9 the fourth bowl scorches the wicked with fire from the sun; the redeemed are spared.

Item by item. So the promise is not vague comfort about a better place. It answers, item by item, the exact things that had made their lives hard: the empty stomach, the dry throat, the sun on the back of the neck at the end of a long day.

Deliverance of the body. That plainness is doing theological work, and it cuts against an instinct most Christians have absorbed without noticing. Ask a congregation what heaven will be like and the answers come back weightless: light, peace, spirits, somewhere else. The Bible almost never talks that way. It promises a body that works, food, water, shade, a city with streets in it, and a Lamb who has to lead people to springs, which means there is somewhere to walk and something to arrive at. The Greeks wanted deliverance from the body. Scripture promises deliverance of it.

Why negatives? There is a reason the promises are stated as negatives: no hunger, no thirst, no striking sun. A negative is the only honest way to describe a condition nobody alive has experienced. No one can picture a body that never tires, because everybody reading this has been tired every day of his life. What can be pictured is the absence of a specific misery, and that is what John gives: not an abstraction, but the removal, one by one, of things the reader could name from this week.

Your own line in the verse. Try the same move with whatever is currently wearing you down: the diagnosis that has to be managed daily, the pain that decides what you can and cannot do, the arithmetic at the end of the month that never quite works, the exhaustion that sleep no longer touches. Each of those is a hunger of some kind, and each has its own line in this verse. The promise is not that you will stop minding about them. It is that they will not be there.

What it does not mean. This is not only a promise for the future. Believers already taste it in Christ, the bread of life and the living water. But its full reality comes after the tribulation, in God’s presence.

Will we eat and drink in heaven? Scripture gives good reason to think so in the resurrection. The risen Jesus ate fish in front of his disciples (Luke 24:42–43), he spoke of drinking the fruit of the vine new in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29), and the end of the age is pictured as a feast, the marriage supper of the Lamb (19:9; Isaiah 25:6). We should not press details we are not given. But the hope of the Christian is not to become a ghost. It is to be raised in a body like Christ’s, on a renewed earth, where eating will be joy and not survival, and hunger will never come again.

In a sentence. They will never again be hungry or thirsty, and the sun and its burning heat will never beat down on them.

On a Tuesday. If you are weary, poor, ill or suffering, this is God’s promise to you: one day it will be over for ever, and the thing you could name this morning will have its own line crossed out. Say it to yourself specifically: there will be no more of this. Meanwhile, be the foretaste of that promise for someone else. Care for those who are hungry and thirsty now (Matthew 25:35), because the King counts what you do for the least of his brothers as done for him.

For worship. Every one of the four clauses describes something being taken away, and none of them names what is put in its place. That comes in the next verse, and it is not a condition or a climate. It is a person. But even here the God of this promise is plain: he has pity on his people, he knows the hunger of the poor and the heat on the labourer’s back, and he has sworn that none of it will follow them home. The one who was hungry in the wilderness and thirsty on the cross has made sure of it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

The setting. Psalm 23 begins, The LORD is my shepherd. Ezekiel promised that God himself would search for his sheep, and would set over them one shepherd, his servant David (Ezekiel 34:11–16, 23). Jesus said, I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). Isaiah promised that God will swallow up death for ever, and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces (Isaiah 25:8).

For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd. The last verse of the chapter contains three promises, and the first of them is a sentence no one but John would have dared write. “In the midst of the throne” (ana meson tou thronou) means at the centre, sharing God’s throne. “Shepherd” (poimanei) is will shepherd them. The Lamb will be the shepherd. Lambs are shepherded; they do not shepherd.

The third reversal. This is the third of the great reversals in this book: the Lion who is a Lamb (5:5–6), the Lamb who has wrath (6:16), and now the Lamb who is a Shepherd. Every one of them works the same way: the image that ought to be weak turns out to be the strong one, and the strength is of a kind nobody was looking for.

And the shepherd is one of us. That is the force of it. Psalm 23 says the LORD is my shepherd, and Ezekiel promised that God himself would come, and Jesus said that the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. Here all of it arrives at once: the shepherd who leads this flock is the one who was himself led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7). He has been where they have been. He knows what they have suffered because he suffered it. He is not directing the flock from a height; he is walking in front of it, and he has scars.

And he will guide them to springs of living water. “Guide” (hodēgēsei) is to lead on the way. The Greek for the water is literally springs of waters of life (zōēs pēgas hydatōn): not a cistern, not a well that has to be drawn from, but water coming up out of the ground under its own pressure and not stopping. It is eternal life flowing from God himself, the fountain of living waters (Jeremiah 2:13). It is the offer he made to a woman at a well at noon (John 4:14) and cried out on the last day of the feast (John 7:37–39), and it is where this book will finish, with the river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb (22:1).

And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes. “Wipe away” (exaleipsei) means to wipe out completely, and “every tear” is pan dakryon. Think about what that sentence requires. It requires that there be tears in the first place: the promise is not that nothing bad happened but that something is done about it afterwards. It requires that God knows which ones and whose: every tear, not the general average of human sorrow. And it requires that he does it himself. Not an angel with a cloth. Not time healing it. God, personally, close enough to touch a face. The image is of a parent drying a child’s eyes. It is repeated in 21:4: death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore.

Take it as it is written. Anyone who has sat with somebody dying, or stood at a small grave, or gone on getting up in the morning after the worst thing, should take this verse exactly as it is written and not one degree weaker. The tears were real, and they were counted, and every one of them will be dealt with by the hand of God on a human face. And the hand doing it belongs to the Lamb who was slaughtered, who is the shepherd, who has come through worse and has the marks to prove it.

What it does not mean. Wiping away tears does not mean that the sufferings of this life did not matter or will be forgotten as if they had never happened. It means they will be fully comforted and healed. The Lamb still bears his wounds (5:6), and the suffering of his people is honoured, but tears will be no more.

Will I remember my sorrows in heaven? Scripture does not say that our memories will be erased, and the Lamb’s own wounds suggest that the past is not simply deleted. But it will be transformed. The sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed (Romans 8:18), and what was once only pain will be seen as part of a story that ended in God’s glory and our joy. Joseph could say of his worst years that God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). In heaven every believer will be able to say that of everything, and say it without a tear.

What about loved ones who did not believe? This is the hardest question a grieving Christian asks, and Scripture does not answer every part of it. What it does promise is that God will wipe away every tear, which means that nothing, not even this, will spoil the joy of the redeemed. We will see then with perfect clarity the holiness and justice of God, and we will be wholly at one with him. Until then, do not presume to know the final state of anyone whose last hours you did not see, since God can save to the last breath, and do not let the question keep you from trusting his goodness. The Judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25).

The answer complete. The question at the end of chapter 6 was who can stand? Here is the answer, and it has taken seventeen verses: a crowd nobody can count, from every nation and tribe and people and language, sealed before the winds were let loose, washed in blood that makes cloth white, standing before the throne with palm branches, sheltered under the tent of God, led by a Lamb to water that never runs dry, with a Father wiping their faces. They can stand. And there is nothing in the list that any of them did.

In a sentence. For the Lamb at the centre of the throne will be their shepherd and lead them to springs of living water, and God himself will wipe every tear from their eyes.

On a Tuesday. Read this verse at funerals and in times of grief, and read it to someone who is grieving this week, slowly, without explaining it away. And if you are the one weeping, do not be ashamed of the tears. They are not a failure of faith; they are the very thing God has promised personally to deal with. Let the Lamb shepherd you now, through his word, his people and his table, to the springs he has already opened.

For worship. The Lamb is the Shepherd. The one who was led to the slaughter now leads his flock, and he walks in front of them with scars, to springs that never run dry. And at the end of the long road the God of all the universe will stoop and, with his own hand, wipe away every tear from every eye, every one counted, every one remembered, every one ended. There is no comfort in the world like it, and it is not a hope only. It is a promise sworn by the one who sits on the throne, and the Lamb has already paid for it.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, that no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree.<sup>2</sup>Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, with the seal of the living God, and he called with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm earth and sea,<sup>3</sup>saying, “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads.”<sup>4</sup>And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel:<sup>5</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Judah were sealed, 12,000 from the tribe of Reuben, 12,000 from the tribe of Gad,<sup>6</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Asher, 12,000 from the tribe of Naphtali, 12,000 from the tribe of Manasseh,<sup>7</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Simeon, 12,000 from the tribe of Levi, 12,000 from the tribe of Issachar,<sup>8</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Zebulun, 12,000 from the tribe of Joseph, 12,000 from the tribe of Benjamin were sealed.<sup>9</sup>After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands,<sup>10</sup>and crying out with a loud voice, “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!”<sup>11</sup>And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God,<sup>12</sup>saying, “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen.”<sup>13</sup>Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, “Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?”<sup>14</sup>I said to him, “Sir, you know.” And he said to me, “These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.<sup>15</sup>Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence.<sup>16</sup>They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat.<sup>17</sup>For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

8.title: The Seventh Seal and the First Four Trumpets
8.overview:
The seventh seal does not release a horseman or a cosmic catastrophe. It releases silence. “When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.” After the unceasing worship of chapters 4–7, after the thunder and lightning of the throne room, after the cries of the martyrs and the acclamation of the great multitude — silence. Heaven holds its breath. The silence of the seventh seal is more terrifying than any of the sounds that preceded it, because it signals that something of ultimate gravity is about to happen.

Out of the silence, seven trumpets are given to seven angels. Before the trumpets sound, another angel offers incense before the altar — and the prayers of the saints rise with the incense before God. This is the answer to the martyrs’ prayer of 6:10 (“How long, O Lord?”): the prayers of God’s people are not lost. They have been gathered. They are being presented before the throne. And now fire from the altar is thrown to the earth — the prayers of the saints become the fire of divine judgment.

The trumpets follow the pattern of the Exodus plagues, but escalated. Hail, fire, blood — the first trumpet echoes the seventh plague of Egypt. The sea turning to blood — the second trumpet echoes the first plague. Darkness — the fourth trumpet echoes the ninth plague. The Exodus pattern is deliberate: the God who judged Egypt to liberate his people is now judging the new Egypt (Rome, Babylon) to liberate the new Israel (the church). The judgments of Revelation are not arbitrary cruelties; they are the exodus of the new covenant people on a cosmic scale.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Seventh Seal and the Golden Censer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: the last seal is opened and nothing happens. There was silence in heaven for about half an hour. Everything the reader has heard for four chapters — the ceaseless holy, holy, holy of the living creatures (4:8), the myriads crying Worthy is the Lamb (5:12), a multitude nobody could number (7:10) — stops. Scripture repeatedly commands exactly this silence before God acts in judgment (Hab. 2:20; Zeph. 1:7; Zech. 2:13), and the crowd outside the temple prayed in silence while the incense was offered (Luke 1:10). Both are probably in view.

Verse 2: seven angels who stand before God are given seven trumpets — the second of the book’s three sevens. A trumpet in Israel sounded at Sinai (Ex. 19:16), brought down Jericho (Josh. 6:16–20), raised the alarm (Joel 2:1), announced Jubilee (Lev. 25:9) and will sound at the resurrection (1 Cor. 15:52).

Verses 3–4: before a trumpet sounds, another angel stands at the altar with a golden censer and is given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints, and the smoke rises before God. This is the payoff of 5:8, where the elders held golden bowls which John identified as those prayers. Three details matter: all the saints; the incense is added from the other side, so the prayers do not go up on their own account; and they arrive.

Verse 5 turns everything over. Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, followed by thunder, rumblings, lightning and an earthquake — the Sinai signs of 4:5 with an earthquake added. The same censer that carried the prayers up now carries fire down. The trumpets are the answer to the church’s praying.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer and the Censer

Heaven falls silent, and the prayers of all the saints rise with much incense given at the altar. Then the same censer is filled with fire and thrown to the earth: the trumpets are God’s answer to his people’s prayers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The martyrs’ “How long?” is being answered.

Now: Prayers that seem to do nothing are gathered, perfected, and answered in God’s time.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.

Meaning first. Revelation 8 opens the seventh seal and begins the seven trumpets. When the last seal is broken, heaven falls silent for half an hour (v. 1). Seven angels receive seven trumpets, and another angel offers incense with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar, and the prayers rise before God (vv. 2–4). Then the angel fills the censer with fire from the altar and throws it on the earth, with thunder, lightning and earthquake: the saints’ prayers are being answered in judgement (v. 5). The first four trumpets strike a third of creation: hail and fire burn a third of the land (vv. 6–7); a burning mountain turns a third of the sea to blood (vv. 8–9); a star called Wormwood makes a third of the fresh water bitter (vv. 10–11); and a third of the sun, moon and stars is darkened (v. 12). An eagle cries woe, woe, woe to the earth’s inhabitants because of the three trumpets still to come (v. 13). The trumpets are warning judgements, echoing the plagues on Egypt: partial, so that people may repent, and sent in answer to the prayers of God’s suffering people.

The setting. Trumpets in the Old Testament announced God’s presence (Exodus 19:16), summoned Israel to worship and war (Numbers 10:1–10), brought down the walls of Jericho after seven priests blew seven trumpets on the seventh day (Joshua 6), and warned of coming judgement (Joel 2:1; Ezekiel 33:3–6). The trumpets of Revelation recall the ten plagues on Egypt: hail and fire, water turned to blood, darkness, locusts. As the plagues judged Pharaoh’s Egypt and freed Israel, so the trumpets judge the world that persecutes God’s people, while his sealed servants are protected (9:4).

When the Lamb opened the seventh seal. The last seal. The scroll is now fully open. Everything in this book has been building to the opening of the last seal, and what happens is nothing. No trumpet, no throne, no announcement. Heaven stops. What does the scroll contain? The seventh seal seems to unfold into the seven trumpets, as the seventh trumpet unfolds into the seven bowls. Each series ends at the final judgement, and then the next goes over the same ground with greater intensity.

There was silence in heaven. “Silence” (sigē). Consider what has to stop for that sentence to be true, because the reader has been in this room for four chapters. The four living creatures have been saying holy, holy, holy day and night without ceasing (4:8). Myriads of myriads of angels have been crying Worthy is the Lamb (5:12). A multitude nobody could number has been shouting that salvation belongs to God (7:10). All of it goes quiet. The most continuous sound in the universe is interrupted, and John, who has been describing thunder and voices and songs for four chapters, has nothing to write down.

Why the silence? Three explanations fit together. Awe, first, and this is the most probable: it is the silence Scripture repeatedly commands before God acts in judgement. The LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him (Habakkuk 2:20). Be silent before the Lord GOD, for the day of the LORD is near (Zephaniah 1:7). Be silent, all flesh, before the LORD, for he has roused himself from his holy dwelling (Zechariah 2:13). In all three the silence is the hush before a verdict, and in all three what follows is God rising to act. Prayer, second: in the temple, incense was offered while the people prayed outside, the whole multitude praying at the hour of incense (Luke 1:10), and what happens immediately after this silence is an angel offering incense with the prayers of all the saints. On that reading heaven falls silent so that the prayers of the church can be heard (vv. 3–4). And third, the stillness before a storm: judgement is about to fall. Either way, the silence is not empty. It is loaded.

For about half an hour. A short but noticeable time, suspense before what follows. The vagueness of about in a book of exact numbers is itself striking; John is describing what it felt like, the way a man says a wait went on for about twenty minutes. And half an hour is long. Try it. Half an hour of silence in a room is close to unbearable, and it is very much longer than any pause in any human ceremony. Whatever is coming, heaven considers it worth stopping everything for. Half of an hour may also hint at incompleteness: this is not yet the end.

What it does not mean. The silence does not mean worship has stopped for good, or that God is absent. It is a deliberate pause, full of meaning, and the praise resumes (11:15–18).

What do I do when God is silent to my prayers? There is something here for the believer who has been on the other end of a silence: who has prayed for a year about the same thing and heard nothing back, and drawn the natural conclusion. This verse does not explain that experience away, but it does say something about the nature of heaven’s quiet. The silence here is not absence and it is not indifference. It is the pause of a court before sentence, and it comes immediately before the prayers of the saints are carried up and then answered. God being quiet and God being idle are not the same thing, and this half hour is the proof. So keep praying through the silence. Tell him honestly that he seems silent, as the Psalms do (Psalm 22:2). And hold on to what he has said, in his word, while you wait for what he has not yet said.

Should our worship include silence? It is wise and biblical to make room for it. Be still, and know that I am God (Psalm 46:10). Much modern worship, and much modern life, is afraid of quiet, filling every gap with music or words. A pause after the reading of Scripture, or before confession, or at the Lord’s Table, is not dead time. It is a way of saying with the whole of heaven that God is about to speak or act, and that we have stopped to listen. Silence is not a form of worship that needs special techniques; it is simply reverence with the noise turned off.

In a sentence. When the Lamb broke the seventh seal, heaven went silent for about half an hour.

On a Tuesday. Find ten minutes of real silence today: no phone, no music, no background noise. Read a psalm, and then stop, and be still before God. If the silence makes you uncomfortable, notice that, and ask why. And if God has been silent toward you for a long time, do not read his silence as his absence. Heaven went quiet just before it acted.

For worship. The God of this verse is so great that the whole of heaven falls silent before him, the ceaseless song of the creatures, the myriads of angels, the countless multitude, all hushed in awe of what he is about to do. He does not need our noise to be glorious. He is the LORD in his holy temple. And the silence before him is not empty, because it is the silence of a Judge who has heard every prayer and is rising to answer. Let all the earth keep silence before him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them. And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne, and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them. And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne, and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel.

The setting. In the tabernacle and temple a golden altar of incense stood in the Holy Place, before the curtain of the Most Holy Place (Exodus 30:1–10). Twice a day a priest burned incense on it while the people prayed outside (Luke 1:8–10). The rising smoke pictured prayer going up to God: let my prayer be counted as incense before you (Psalm 141:2). Jewish tradition named seven archangels who stand before God, among them Gabriel, who said, I am Gabriel, who stand in the presence of God (Luke 1:19).

Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them. The definite article, the seven angels, suggests a particular known order. “Stand before God” (enōpion tou theou hestēkasin): angels of the highest rank, ready to serve. “Were given”: the trumpets come from God. Their trumpets are the second of the book’s three sevens.

What a trumpet meant. A trumpet in Israel was never a musical instrument in the modern sense. It sounded at Sinai, so loud that the people trembled (Exodus 19:16). It brought down the walls of Jericho on the seventh day (Joshua 6:16–20). It was the alarm blown when an army was coming (Joel 2:1). It announced the year of Jubilee, when debts were cancelled and slaves went free (Leviticus 25:9). And it will sound at the end, when the dead are raised (1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16). A trumpet means: attention, something is about to happen, and you cannot sleep through it.

And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer. But before a single trumpet is blown, the vision stops and does something else entirely. The censer (libanōtos) is a firepan for carrying burning coals and incense. This is the fulfilment of 5:8, where the elders held golden bowls of incense which John explained were the prayers of the saints. Now the incense is being burned.

And he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints. Three details in these verses deserve slowing down for. The first is all the saints: every believer, not only the martyrs. Not the prayers of the notable ones, not the prayers that were well phrased or persevered in longest. All of them, which includes prayers prayed by people who did not know how to pray, in the dark, badly, and then forgot about.

Much incense, given. The second detail is the incense (thymiamata polla), and it is given to him. The prayers do not go up on their own account. Something is added to them at the altar, from the other side, before they rise, making them acceptable and fragrant before God. Any honest person who has prayed knows that his prayers are not impressive; the mind wanders, the motives are mixed, the words run out. What this verse says is that they are not offered as they left the mouth. The incense is not yours.

On the golden altar before the throne. In heaven the altar is right before the throne. In the earthly temple the altar of incense stood outside the curtain, and only the high priest went beyond it once a year. Here there is no curtain. The prayers of God’s people go straight into his presence.

And the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel. The third detail is the direction. “Rose” (anebē, went up). They arrive. That is stated flatly, as a fact about what John saw. The prayers of persecuted believers in small churches across Asia rise to the throne of the universe, not as a general principle, not as an encouragement, but as a thing happening in front of a man’s eyes while he watches. Not one is lost. The cry of the martyrs, How long? (6:10), is part of this.

Something has occurred. Consider what that does to the ordinary experience of praying. A believer kneels by a bed at eleven at night, says something short and inadequate about a son who is not speaking to him, and gets up feeling that nothing has occurred. On the evidence of this verse, something has occurred. The words went up. They were mixed with much incense from the hand of another, and they stood before God, and God is not deaf and does not mislay things.

Where Christians differ: should we pray to angels or saints, or through them? Roman Catholic and Orthodox traditions have used passages like this to support asking angels and departed saints to present our prayers to God. Verdict: the angel serves as part of the heavenly worship, offering the prayers before God, but he is not prayed to, and the saints on earth do not address him. Scripture teaches that there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and that believers may come boldly to the throne of grace through him (Hebrews 4:14–16). The incense that makes our prayers acceptable is the intercession and merit of Christ, our great High Priest, who always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25). Pray to God alone, through Christ alone.

Is this angel Christ? Some have taken him so, since he does a high priest’s work. But John calls him simply another angel, and Revelation never calls Christ an angel; elsewhere in the book Christ is the Lamb on the throne, receiving worship, not a servant at the altar. The more likely reading is that he is an angelic servant in the heavenly worship, showing that the saints’ prayers rise before God and are answered in his judgements. Yet the reality the picture points to is Christ’s own intercession: it is because of him that any prayer of ours is accepted at all.

What it does not mean. The angel does not make prayers acceptable by his own merit, or decide which prayers are heard. He serves God’s purposes. The scene shows how precious our prayers are, not that they need a heavenly middleman.

Why do my prayers need incense? Because even our best prayers are mixed with sin, distraction and self-interest, and a holy God could not receive them on their own merits. That is not a reason to stop praying; it is the reason Christ prays for us. Whatever you ask in my name, Jesus said, this I will do (John 14:13). To pray in his name is not to add a formula at the end, but to come trusting that he has made you welcome and that his perfect intercession covers your imperfect words. The Spirit, too, helps us in our weakness, interceding with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26). Your prayer does not have to be good to be heard. It has to be offered through him.

In a sentence. Then I saw the seven angels who stand in God’s presence, and they were given seven trumpets; another angel, holding a golden censer, came and stood at the altar, and he was given a large amount of incense to offer, together with the prayers of all God’s people, on the golden altar in front of the throne; and the smoke of the incense went up before God from the angel’s hand, along with the prayers of the saints.

On a Tuesday. Your prayers, however weak they feel, rise before God’s throne. Keep praying, especially for persecuted believers, and do not wait until you can pray well. Pray the short, tired prayer at the end of the day, and believe that it arrived. If it helps, keep a simple list of what you have asked, and look back at it in six months; you will be surprised how many of the prayers you forgot God has remembered.

For worship. The God of the universe has set an altar before his throne for the prayers of his people, and he has given the incense himself. Every whispered, stumbling, unfinished prayer of every believer in every age has risen before him, perfumed with the merit of his Son, who ever lives to intercede for us. He does not merely tolerate our praying. He has built it into the centre of heaven’s worship. Heaven falls silent, and the prayers of the saints go up, and the Lord of all creation bends to hear.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.

The setting. In Ezekiel a man clothed in linen is told to fill his hands with burning coals from between the cherubim and scatter them over Jerusalem in judgement (Ezekiel 10:2). The coal from the altar that touched Isaiah’s lips brought cleansing (Isaiah 6:6–7); here fire from the altar brings judgement.

Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar. And then the verse turns, and it is one of the great surprises of the book. The same censer. The one that a moment ago was carrying the prayers of all the saints up to God is now filled with fire from that same altar. The same altar is the source of both.

And threw it on the earth. “Threw” (ebalen, cast). What went up as incense comes back as fire. The trumpets that follow are the answer to the church’s praying, and the answer arrives in the form of judgement on the world that made the praying necessary. The prayers of the persecuted church are not ignored; they move heaven to act. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working (James 5:16).

How long is answered. Go back and hear what those prayers had been. Under the altar in chapter 6, the martyrs cried O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? (6:10). They were told to rest a little longer. This is the little longer coming to an end. The how long of chapter 6 is answered by the censer of chapter 8, and the seven trumpets are the answering.

Operating the levers from their knees. Take that as concretely as John means it. Prayer, in this book, is not a private spiritual exercise with private spiritual effects. It is one of the means by which the judgements of God are set in motion. The most powerless people in the Roman empire, slaves, widows, boycotted tradesmen, prisoners awaiting a hearing, are shown to have been moving history from their knees the whole time, without knowing it and without seeing a single result. Set that against the way praying usually feels. The commonest objection a Christian raises against his own prayer life is not doctrinal; it is that it appears to do nothing. This verse answers that with a picture rather than an argument. The prayer that seemed to evaporate went into a golden bowl. The bowl went to an altar. The altar had fire on it. And the fire came back down.

And there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake. These are the Sinai signs from 4:5, where they came out of the throne, the signs of God’s throne and presence, now with an earthquake added. John will use this same list twice more, more intensely, at 11:19 and 16:18–21, each time at a hinge in the book, each time with something added. Each series of judgements ends with this sign, showing that each reaches the final judgement. The earthquake is his standing signal that God has begun to act.

Who never leaves the room. The angel offers the incense, the angel fills the censer, the angel throws it; but the fire is from the altar, and the altar is before the throne. The seven trumpets do not begin because an angel decided something. They begin because the prayers of ordinary Christians reached the throne of God, and God answered.

What it does not mean. This does not mean Christians should pray for the destruction of their enemies. We pray for God’s kingdom to come and his will to be done, which includes the defeat of evil, and we pray for our enemies’ repentance. God decides how to answer, and his judgements are always just.

If God is sovereign, why does he need our prayers? He does not need them in the sense of being unable to act without them. But he has chosen to work through them, as he works through preaching and through all the means he appoints. The God who decreed the end also decreed the prayers that would lead to it, and he gives his people the dignity of taking part. That is why Elijah prayed for rain after God had promised it (1 Kings 18:1, 41–45; James 5:17–18). Sovereignty does not make prayer pointless; it makes it effective, because we are asking the one who actually governs the world, not a God who is hoping things work out.

What should I pray for, then? Begin where Jesus taught us: hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven (Matthew 6:9–10). Those three petitions contain everything in this verse, the defeat of evil, the vindication of God’s people and the coming of his reign. Then pray for persecuted believers by name, for the salvation of the lost, including those who oppose the gospel, and for justice where it has been denied. Bring your own needs too; he cares about them. But let the big prayers have a place, because they are the ones the golden bowls are full of.

In a sentence. Then the angel took the censer, filled it with fire from the altar and hurled it down on the earth, and there came thunder, rumbling, lightning and an earthquake.

On a Tuesday. Pray Your kingdom come today, slowly, and mean it, knowing that God hears and will answer. History is shaped not only by governments and armies but by the prayers of his people. The next time you feel that your prayer meeting is small and pointless, remember the censer. Ten tired people in a church hall praying for the persecuted church are doing something that echoes in thunder.

For worship. The altar that receives our prayers is the same altar from which the fire of judgement falls, because the God who hears the cry of his people is the God who acts to put the world right. He does not let the prayers of the weak go unanswered. He gathers them, perfumes them, weighs them, and answers them with thunder. And the fire that falls on the earth does not fall on those who pray, because for them the fire of the altar fell long ago on the Lamb, who bore the judgement in their place.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 6: the seven angels prepare to blow. Verse 7: the first trumpet brings hail and fire mixed with blood, and a third of the earth, a third of the trees and all green grass are burned. Verses 8–9: the second brings something like a great mountain, burning, thrown into the sea — the image Jeremiah used of Babylon as a burnt mountain (Jer. 51:25) — and a third of the sea becomes blood, a third of its creatures die, a third of the ships are destroyed. For seven churches on the coast of Asia the sea was the economy, not the scenery.

Verses 10–11: the third trumpet drops a blazing star, Wormwood, on the fresh water, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter. Apsinthos is bitter rather than poisonous, and it is the prophets’ standing image for judgment that makes the sweet unswallowable (Jer. 9:15; 23:15; Lam. 3:19) — most pointedly in Amos, where men turn justice to wormwood (Amos 5:7) and here find their own wells undrinkable.

Verse 12: the fourth strikes a third of the sun, moon and stars, so that a third of the light is darkened — the ninth plague on Egypt (Ex. 10:21–23), aimed at a nation whose chief god was the sun and whose Pharaoh was his son.

Verse 13 closes with an eagle at the zenith, where everyone can see it, crying Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth — one woe for each trumpet still to come. Four trumpets have struck earth, sea, fresh water and sky, the whole created order. The remaining three will fall on people.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trumpets Are the Plagues of Egypt

Hail and fire, water turned to blood, bitterness and darkness strike earth, sea, fresh water and sky — each limited to a third. As in Egypt, the aim is to expose false gods and bring God’s people out.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: For coastal churches, a stricken sea meant a stricken economy.

Now: Do not decode these as headlines; see in them the failure of every false security, and the warning to repent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them. The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them. The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.

The setting. The seventh plague on Egypt was hail mixed with fire, which struck down every plant and broke every tree of the field (Exodus 9:23–25). Joel speaks of blood and fire and columns of smoke before the day of the LORD (Joel 2:30).

Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them. “Prepared” (hētoimasan, made ready). One verse of pure anticipation. Seven angels lift seven trumpets. Everything is ordered and deliberate. And then the first sounds, and what follows is the plagues of Egypt happening again on a larger stage.

The plagues of Egypt again. That parallel governs the whole trumpet sequence and should be established at the start. The first trumpet brings hail and fire, the seventh plague (Exodus 9:23–25). The second turns a third of the sea to blood, the first plague (Exodus 7:20–21). The fourth darkens the lights, the ninth plague (Exodus 10:21–23). The fifth trumpet will bring locusts (Exodus 10:12–15), and the sixth will end with people refusing to repent, exactly as Pharaoh did.

Why Egypt? The point of the parallel is not decoration. The plagues on Egypt were not random cruelty; they had two purposes, both stated in Exodus. They were aimed at the gods of Egypt: on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgements (Exodus 12:12), each plague striking at something Egypt worshipped. And they were aimed at getting a people out: let my people go. So when John dresses the trumpets in the clothes of the exodus, he is telling seven small congregations something enormous. The empire that is grinding you is Egypt. The God who broke Egypt is not retired. And the purpose of what is coming is the same purpose it was then: to expose the gods that cannot save, and to bring his people out.

The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood. Like the plague on Egypt, but worse: blood is added. A terrifying picture of destruction from the sky.

And these were thrown upon the earth. “Thrown” (eblēthē) is a divine passive: God throws them.

And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up. Three things are struck: the land, the trees, the grass. And two of the three are measured. “A third” (to triton). The seals struck a quarter (6:8); the trumpets strike a third; the bowls will strike everything (16). Ezekiel spoke of judgement on Jerusalem by thirds (Ezekiel 5:2, 12). The judgements escalate in stages, and the escalation is the argument: these are not the end. They are warnings that get louder because they are not being heard, and chapter 9 will say so in as many words: the rest of mankind did not repent (9:20). “All green grass” perhaps means all the grass in the third that is burned.

A fraction is a mercy. It is easy to read past. Two thirds of the earth is not burned. Somebody is holding the line at a third, and the same hand that holds it wrote the number down. Judgement that stops is judgement that still intends to be answered.

Where Christians differ: are the trumpets literal events? Some read the trumpets as literal future events, perhaps nuclear war or asteroid strikes. Historicists match each trumpet to an event in church history (invasions of the Roman Empire by Goths, Vandals and others). Verdict: the trumpets are symbolic pictures of God’s judgements on a rebellious world throughout the age between Christ’s comings, drawn from the plagues of Egypt. They include natural disasters and ecological catastrophes, which are real and recur through history, as warnings to repent. Their purpose is stated in 9:20–21: to call people to turn from idols. They are not a timeline to be decoded, but they are real, and they may also intensify before the end.

Not from the newspaper. One caution about reading these verses, and it applies to the whole trumpet sequence. Every generation has matched them to its own headlines, volcanic ash, wildfire, chemical warfare, industrial pollution, and every generation has been confident and wrong. The images here are quarried from Exodus, not from the newspaper. What is permanent about them is not the mechanism but the argument: the created order itself turns against a humanity in rebellion against its Maker, the things people depend on become the things that fail them, and none of it happens outside the throne room. That was true in Egypt, it was true under Rome, and it has been true in every century since without needing to be decoded.

What it does not mean. These judgements do not mean God does not care about his creation. The new creation will be its renewal (21:1–5). Creation suffers now because of human sin (Romans 8:20–22), and God uses even its suffering to warn the world.

If God burns the earth in judgement, should Christians care for the environment? Yes. The earth is the LORD’s (Psalm 24:1), and Adam was set in the garden to work it and keep it (Genesis 2:15). That mandate has never been withdrawn. The fact that God judges creation because of human sin is not permission for us to abuse it; if anything, it shows how seriously God takes what happens to his world. Christians care for creation not because they think they can save the planet, but because it belongs to God and he means to renew it. Look after it as a steward looks after his master’s estate, knowing the master is coming back.

When a wildfire or a storm destroys a town, is that a trumpet? In the broad sense, yes: every disaster in a fallen world is a trumpet blast, a warning that the world is not as it should be and that life is short. Jesus said so when a tower fell on eighteen people: unless you repent, you will all likewise perish (Luke 13:4–5). But we are not told which disaster answers which sin, and Christians suffer them too. The right response is to grieve with the bereaved, help generously and practically, examine our own hearts, and point people to the only shelter that no fire can reach.

In a sentence. Then the seven angels holding the seven trumpets got ready to blow them; the first angel blew his trumpet, and hail and fire mixed with blood rained down on the earth, and a third of the land was burned up, along with a third of the trees and all the green grass.

On a Tuesday. When you see wildfires, storms and disasters, let them be trumpets calling you and others to repent and turn to God (Luke 13:1–5). Do not scroll past them. Pray for the people affected, give if you can, and ask yourself whether the things you depend on most are the kind that can burn.

For worship. The God who broke Egypt is not retired. He still judges the gods that cannot save, and he still brings his people out. And even in his judgements he measures: a third, not the whole, because he would rather warn than destroy, and he holds back his hand to give time for repentance. The Lord is a God of justice, and the Lord is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. Both are true of the hand that holds the trumpets, and both are seen most clearly at the cross, where the fire fell on his own Son so that it need not fall on us.
verseByVerse.note: The trumpet plagues echo the plagues on Egypt, but each strikes only a third — judgment still held back.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood. A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood. A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.

The setting. The first plague on Egypt turned the Nile to blood, so that the fish died (Exodus 7:20–21). Jeremiah calls Babylon a destroying mountain, which God will roll down from the crags and make a burnt mountain (Jeremiah 51:25). In AD 79 the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in Italy buried Pompeii, and stories of a burning mountain and the sea would have been fresh in readers’ minds.

And something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea. “Something like” (hōs, as it were). Note the hesitation in the wording. John is again describing what he has no vocabulary for, and he says so rather than pretending. Whatever it was, it looked like a burning mountain and it went into the sea. The image may suggest a volcanic eruption, or a falling empire like Babylon, since a mountain in prophetic language is often a kingdom: something immovable, dominating the landscape, permanent. The burning mountain thrown down is an empire coming to an end. But the main point is catastrophe on the sea.

And a third of the sea became blood. As in the plague on the Nile, on a greater scale.

A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed. What is struck this time is the sea, and for the seven churches on the coast of Asia the sea was not scenery. It was the economy: trade, food, transport. Ephesus and Smyrna were harbours. Grain came from Egypt by ship, and so did every luxury on the list that chapter 18 will read out over the fall of Babylon. A third of the sea life dead and a third of the ships destroyed is not primarily an ecological note; it is a commercial collapse. Trade routes fail, cargoes are lost, and the merchants of the earth, who in chapter 18 will stand weeping at a distance because no one buys their cargo any more (18:11, 17–19), discover that the system they trusted was never load-bearing.

The sea in this book. And the sea carries a further weight. It is where the beast comes from (13:1).
