It is the ancient image of chaos, restless and untameable, which is why the throne room has a sea of glass, like crystal, still and calm before God (4:6), and why the new creation is announced with the words and the sea was no more (21:1). The second trumpet strikes the thing the world sails on and the thing the beast rises out of, and does it with a measured third.

What has any of this to do with me? A working reader will ask it, and it should be answered rather than avoided. The answer is in what gets hit. The trumpets do not fall on temples and armies. They fall on the earth a man farms, the sea a man trades on, the water a man drinks and the light a man works by. God’s judgements in this chapter land on the ordinary infrastructure of confidence: the things that make it possible to believe that tomorrow will be much like today. Anyone who has watched a business fail, or a pension shrink in a crash he did not cause, has met the second trumpet in miniature. The point is not that such an event is a punishment aimed at that person; Scripture is careful about that (Luke 13:4–5). The point is what it reveals. Every one of these systems is holding up somebody’s confidence, and every one of them can be taken down by a third in a single afternoon. The only thing this book has shown that cannot be taken down is the throne, and it was shown first, on purpose, before any of this began.

What it does not mean. This is not a prediction of a particular volcano or meteor. It is a picture of God’s judgement on the sea and on the commerce of a world that lives without him.

Is it wrong, then, to save, invest or run a business? No. Scripture commends work, diligence and wise provision (Proverbs 6:6–8; 1 Timothy 5:8), and trade is part of the ordinary good life God gives. What this trumpet warns against is trust: as for the rich in this present age, charge them not to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). Use money; do not lean on it. Be generous with it, because generosity is the surest sign that your heart is not anchored to the ships.

In a sentence. The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a huge mountain on fire was hurled into the sea; a third of the sea turned to blood, a third of the creatures living in the sea died, and a third of the ships were wrecked.

On a Tuesday. The world’s economy is not as secure as it seems. Look honestly at what you would feel if a third of your savings disappeared this afternoon. Concern is natural. Panic would tell you where your trust really lies. Do not trust in trade and wealth; trust in God, who holds even the seas in his hand, and give something away this week as a small declaration of independence from the ships.

For worship. The sea that terrified the ancient world, home of chaos and the beast, lies like glass before the throne of God. He made it, he sets its boundaries, he can turn it to blood with a word, and one day he will abolish it altogether. And the God of the sea is the God who walked on it, who stilled its storm with a rebuke and told his frightened disciples, take heart; it is I. The economies of the world can sink in an afternoon. He cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.

The setting. Wormwood (apsinthos) is a shrub of the Middle East with an intensely bitter taste, related to the plant used to make absinthe. In the Old Testament it pictures bitterness, sorrow and God’s judgement: I will feed this people with bitter food, and give them poisonous water to drink (Jeremiah 9:15; 23:15; Lamentations 3:15, 19). Amos accuses those who turn justice to wormwood and cast down righteousness to the earth (Amos 5:7). At Marah God made bitter water sweet for Israel (Exodus 15:23–25); here, sweet water is made bitter. Isaiah describes the king of Babylon as a day star fallen from heaven (Isaiah 14:12).

The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch. “Star” (astēr). In Revelation stars can represent angels (1:20; 9:1). This may be an angel carrying out God’s judgement, or simply a burning, meteor-like object.

And it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. Fresh water this time, rivers and springs, the thing no settlement can exist without. Fresh water is essential for life.

The name of the star is Wormwood. The name tells us its meaning: bitterness. Those who turn away from the living water of God, and drink the poisoned waters of idolatry, find life bitter. My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water (Jeremiah 2:13; 9:13–15).

A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter. This is the first trumpet where the text says plainly that people died. Wormwood is not normally deadly; the image is intensified. The waters of life become the waters of death.

The judgement matches the crime. That line in Amos is the key to the trumpet. In Amos, men make justice bitter, and here God makes their water bitter. A society that has poisoned what should have refreshed people finds its own wells undrinkable. This is the shape of divine judgement throughout Scripture: not an arbitrary penalty attached to an offence, but the offence itself, served back.

A third again. Two thirds of the springs are still sweet. The restraint in this chapter is monotonous by design: a third, a third, a third, a third. Somebody is counting, and the counting is happening on the earth as well as in heaven.

What it does not mean. Wormwood is not a code word for a specific modern disaster, such as the Chernobyl nuclear accident. It has been widely repeated that Chernobyl is the Ukrainian word for wormwood and that the 1986 disaster is therefore this verse. The linguistic claim is roughly right, since the name relates to a variety of the plant, and the interpretation is not. On that logic any place in the world named after a bitter herb becomes a candidate, and the verse would have nothing to say to the churches John actually wrote to, or to any generation between them and 1986. Revelation’s symbols draw on the Old Testament, not on modern place names. The trumpet is the standing biblical picture of a world whose own water turns against it, and it has been true in every century, including that one.

What if I am the one who has been made bitter? There is a plain application here for anyone in that condition. A person can live for decades on water that has been made bitter, by an injustice never put right, by a marriage that went wrong, by a betrayal nobody was ever called to account for, and go on functioning, and never taste anything sweet again. Scripture takes that condition seriously enough to name a trumpet after it, and warns that a root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled (Hebrews 12:15). The way out is not to pretend the wrong did not happen, but to hand it to God the Judge, as the martyrs did (6:10), and to drink from a different spring. The God who made the waters of Marah sweet can do the same in a soul. It is often slow, and it usually begins with honest prayer about the very thing that poisoned the well.

In a sentence. The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star blazing like a torch fell from the sky onto a third of the rivers and springs; the star is called Wormwood, and a third of the waters turned bitter, and many people died from drinking the water because it had been made bitter.

On a Tuesday. Life without God turns bitter in the end. Notice what you are drinking from for refreshment this week: entertainment, approval, achievement, alcohol, grievance. Some of those are harmless gifts and some are broken cisterns. Drink from Christ, the spring of living water (John 4:14), in his word and in prayer, and offer it to someone else who is plainly thirsty.

For worship. The God who turns sweet water bitter in judgement is the God who threw a log into the bitter waters of Marah and made them sweet, and who at last hung on a tree to make the bitterest thing in the world sweet for sinners. He drank the cup of wormwood that was ours. And this book ends with a river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and free to anyone who is thirsty (22:1, 17). Let the one who is thirsty come.
verseByVerse.note: Wormwood is a bitter plant, used by the prophets as a picture of bitter judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night. Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, "Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night. Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!”

The setting. The ninth plague on Egypt was darkness that could be felt over the land for three days, so that no one rose from his place, though the people of Israel had light where they lived (Exodus 10:21–23). God created the sun, moon and stars on the fourth day, to give light and to mark times (Genesis 1:14–18). The Egyptians worshipped the sun god, so the darkness was a judgement on their gods. Hosea says, set the trumpet to your lips, for one like a vulture (or eagle) is over the house of the LORD (Hosea 8:1).

The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars. “Struck” (eplēgē, smitten; the word for plague, plēgē, comes from the same root). God strikes the lights he created. The world that worships created things instead of the Creator (Romans 1:25) loses part of the light it takes for granted.

So that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night. The word third occurs repeatedly in one verse. The repetition is not clumsy writing; it is the drumbeat of the whole sequence, and by now a reader hearing this read aloud would be waiting for it. Darkness pictures judgement, sorrow and the absence of God. Like the first four seals, the first four trumpets strike the natural world: land, sea, fresh water, sky.

The sun god cannot keep his lamp lit. The gods being judged in the ninth plague were unmistakable: Egypt worshipped the sun. Ra was the head of the pantheon, and Pharaoh was his son. To darken the sun over Egypt was to demonstrate publicly that the chief god of the empire could not keep his own lamp lit. The same argument runs in the province of Asia. The emperor was often associated with the sun in imperial art and poetry; Nero had himself portrayed with rays around his head. And the heavenly bodies were what everyone in the ancient world steered by, planted by, and read their fortunes by. The fourth trumpet strikes the calendar, the compass and the horoscope in a single stroke.

Reliable light. What is being taken away, in other words, is not light in general but reliable light: the confidence that the day will behave as days have always behaved. There is something more disturbing about a sun that is a third dimmer than about no sun at all. Total darkness announces itself as a catastrophe. A partial failure of the light is worse in its way, because it says that the machinery is not as fixed as everyone assumed, and nobody can be sure what it will do next.

Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead. The chapter ends with a warning nobody could sleep through. The Greek word (aetos) covers both the eagle and the vulture, and both associations are working: the eagle was the standard of the Roman legions, and the vulture is the bird of prey circling over what is about to die. Jesus used the same ambiguity: wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather (Matthew 24:28). “Directly overhead” (en mesouranēmati) is mid-heaven, the highest point of the sky, where everyone on the ground can see and hear.

Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth. “Woe” (ouai, alas) is a cry of grief and doom. Three woes, one for each of the three trumpets still to come (9:12; 11:14). And the phrase the eagle uses is one to watch, because it becomes a technical term in this book: those who dwell on the earth. It occurs about ten times, and it never means simply everyone alive. It means unbelievers in rebellion against God, the people whose whole account is settled here, who have no other citizenship and want none: the ones who, in 6:16, would rather be crushed by a mountain than look at the face on the throne. The saints in this book live on the earth too. They are never called earth-dwellers.

At the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow! The last three trumpets will be worse, and the escalation is explicit. Four trumpets have struck the earth, the sea, the fresh water and the sky, the whole created order in the four-part division the ancient world used. The remaining three will not fall on the environment. They will fall on people directly, with demonic torment and death, and chapter 9 opens the shaft of the bottomless pit.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “an angel flying” instead of “an eagle flying”. The two Greek words (angelou and aetou) look somewhat alike. The best manuscripts read “eagle”.

What it does not mean. The darkening of a third is not a scientific description of how sunlight would be reduced. It is a picture: part of creation’s light withdrawn as a warning, before the deeper darkness of the bowls (16:10).

A mercy in the shape of a threat. So the eagle’s cry is announced in advance, in daylight, at the top of the sky, in a loud voice, to people who still have time to do something about it. Every warning in Revelation is an act of patience, and the God who sends an eagle across the sky before the fifth trumpet is not a God who wants anybody caught unawares.

Can a Christian be an earth-dweller? Not in John’s sense, because the phrase describes where a person’s heart lives, not where his feet stand. But Christians can drift toward it, living as though this world were all there is, anxious about what earth-dwellers are anxious about and hoping for what they hope for. The test is simple and searching: if everything in this chapter happened, the land, the sea, the water and the light, what would you have left? Our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Saviour (Philippians 3:20). Live here fully, love your neighbours, work hard; but keep your passport in the right place.

Are we near the last trumpets? On the reading followed here, the trumpets sound throughout the age between Christ’s comings, and they may grow louder as the end approaches; so in one sense every generation hears them. We are not told the date of the end, and Jesus said that no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36). What we are told is that the end is always near enough to matter. The right question is not how close the last trumpet is, but whether you are ready if it sounded tonight.

In a sentence. The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun, a third of the moon and a third of the stars were struck, so that a third of them went dark, and a third of the day and of the night were without light; then, as I watched, I heard an eagle flying high overhead and crying out loudly: Woe, woe, woe to the people of the earth, because of the trumpet blasts that the other three angels are about to sound!

On a Tuesday. God’s warnings grow louder. If you have been putting off turning to him, or speaking to others about him, do not delay. Name the person you have meant to talk to about Christ for the longest time, and ask God for the opportunity this week. The eagle shouts in daylight so that no one is caught by surprise; the church is meant to do the same, but with tears.

For worship. The God who made the sun and moon and stars on the fourth day can dim them with a word, and the gods that men worship cannot keep their own lamps lit. He alone is the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change (James 1:17). And the one whom the darkness of the cross covered for three hours from noon is the light of the world, and in the city to come there will be no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb (21:23).

9.title: The Fifth and Sixth Trumpets: The Demonic and the Deadly
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is among the most vivid and terrifying in Revelation. The fifth trumpet releases demonic locusts from the abyss — creatures drawn from Joel 2 and shaped like scorpions, with the faces of humans and the hair of women and the teeth of lions. The sixth trumpet releases four angels bound at the great Euphrates river, who command an army of two hundred million mounted troops. The devastation escalates from the bounded third of the earlier trumpets to something more comprehensive and more personal: now humanity itself is directly targeted.

The two woe-trumpets of chapter 9 share a common theme: demonic power unleashed. The fifth trumpet releases the army of the abyss, led by “the angel of the bottomless pit” whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon and in Greek Apollyon — “Destroyer.” The sixth releases an army from beyond the Euphrates — the frontier from which Israel’s ancient enemies (Assyria, Babylon) had always come. The locust-army of the fifth trumpet torments but does not kill; the cavalry of the sixth kills a third of humanity. The escalation is purposeful: God is turning up the pressure on a world that refuses to repent.

The chapter’s most sobering verse is its final one: “The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent.” The purpose of the trumpet judgments — like the purpose of the Exodus plagues — was to break the hardness of heart that keeps humanity from turning to God. Pharaoh’s hardness repeated in every generation: even faced with the unmistakable signs of divine judgment, even watching a third of their companions die, the survivors “did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons.” The judgment does not automatically produce repentance; only grace can break what judgment cannot.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Fifth Trumpet: The Locusts from the Abyss
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a star fallen from heaven — a perfect participle, an event already complete — who is immediately a he, and who was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. He opens it, and before anything comes out the light goes: smoke like the smoke of a great furnace darkens the sun and the air (cf. Gen. 19:28).

Verses 3–4: locusts come up out of the smoke with the power of scorpions — and are told not to touch grass, plant or tree, which is the one thing locusts exist to do. Their only target is those who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads: the first cash-out of chapter 7, and the doorpost of the Exodus Passover moved from the house to the person (cf. Ex. 8:22; 10:23).

Verses 5–6: they are allowed to torment for five months — about the life cycle of a locust swarm — but not to kill. And then the hardest sentence in the chapter: people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them (cf. Job 3:21; Jer. 8:3).

Verses 7–10 describe them in eight comparisons, each introduced by like: horses prepared for battle (Joel 2:4), what looked like crowns of gold, human faces, women’s hair, lions’ teeth (Joel 1:6), iron breastplates, wings like many chariots, and scorpion tails in which their power to hurt resides.

Verses 11–12: Proverbs 30:27 says locusts have no king; these have one — the angel of the bottomless pit, named in both languages, Abaddon (Hebrew for destruction, Job 26:6; 28:22; Prov. 15:11) and Apollyon (Greek for destroyer). Then a line of bookkeeping: the first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.
verseByVerse.theology:
On a Permission

A fallen star is given the key to the abyss; the locusts are told whom they may not touch and allowed five months. Their king is Abaddon, Apollyon, the destroyer — a creature on a leash, not God’s rival.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The torment fell on those without God’s seal, and it ended when the season ended.

Now: If you have longed to die, you are in the company of Job, Moses and Elijah, not under condemnation — tell another believer.

verseByVerse.quote: And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. He opened the shaft of the bottomless pit, and from the shaft rose smoke like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened with the smoke from the shaft.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. He opened the shaft of the bottomless pit, and from the shaft rose smoke like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened with the smoke from the shaft.

Meaning first. Revelation 9 describes the fifth and sixth trumpets, the first two woes, in which judgement moves from nature to people, and from natural forces to demonic ones. At the fifth trumpet, a fallen star opens the bottomless pit, and smoke darkens the sky (vv. 1–2). Out of the smoke come locusts with the sting of scorpions, allowed to torment, but not kill, those without God’s seal for five months, so that people long to die (vv. 3–6). They are described as monstrous war horses with human faces, women’s hair, lions’ teeth, iron breastplates and scorpion tails (vv. 7–10), and their king is the angel of the pit, Abaddon or Apollyon, the Destroyer (vv. 11–12). At the sixth trumpet, a voice from the altar releases four angels bound at the Euphrates, prepared for this very hour, to kill a third of mankind (vv. 13–15). An army of two hundred million cavalry appears, with fire-coloured breastplates and lion-headed horses breathing fire, smoke and sulphur, with tails like serpents (vv. 16–19). Yet the rest of mankind still does not repent of worshipping demons and idols, or of murder, sorcery, immorality and theft (vv. 20–21). The chapter shows the horror of a world given over to the demonic powers it has chosen, God’s protection of his sealed people, and the terrible hardness of the human heart.

The setting. The eighth plague on Egypt was locusts, which covered the land and darkened it (Exodus 10:12–15). The prophet Joel described a locust plague as an invading army: like horses, with a sound like chariots, with teeth like a lion’s, darkening the sun and moon, a picture of the Day of the LORD (Joel 1:4–7; 2:1–11). In the ancient Near East a locust swarm could strip a whole region bare in hours. In Jewish thought the abyss was the prison of evil spirits (Luke 8:31; 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6).

The target changes. Four trumpets have struck the earth, the sea, the fresh water and the sky. An eagle has crossed the sky crying three woes. Now the fifth sounds, and the target changes: from here on the trumpets fall on people.

And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth. The grammar does half the work. John does not say he saw a star fall; he saw a star fallen. “Fallen” (peptōkota) is a perfect participle, describing a completed event whose result is still standing: having fallen, and lying there. The falling is not happening in front of him. It happened, and this is the aftermath. And the star is immediately a he: the pronoun switches from an object to a person in the same sentence. A star in Revelation can represent an angel (1:20).

Who is the fallen star? Many take him to be Satan, and the case is strong. Jesus said, I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18); Isaiah’s taunt against the king of Babylon, how you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn (Isaiah 14:12), has been read that way since the early church; and in 12:9 this book will describe the dragon being thrown down to the earth. Others take him to be one of God’s angels on commission, since 20:1 shows an angel coming down from heaven with the key of the bottomless pit and a great chain, and that one is plainly no enemy. This is probably a fallen angel, possibly Satan himself. The text does not settle it, and on the point that matters it does not need to.

And he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. “Was given” (edothē): permission from God. Whoever holds the key received it, and there is only one place in this book where keys are kept. Christ said: I have the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). Any other key is borrowed. Even the opening of the abyss is a delegated act. Nothing gets out of that shaft on its own authority.

The abyss. The bottomless pit is abyssos, the abyss, the deep. In the Greek Old Testament it is the word for the primeval deep of Genesis 1:2 and for the waters under the earth. In the New Testament it is where demons are kept and where they do not want to go: the legion in the Gerasene man begged Jesus not to command them to depart into the abyss (Luke 8:31). Peter and Jude both describe rebel angels kept in chains of gloomy darkness until the judgement (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). It is the prison from which the beast also rises (11:7; 17:8) and in which Satan will be bound (20:1–3). And it has a shaft (phrear), a well, a narrow neck, which means it has a mouth, and a mouth can be shut. It is shut except when it is opened, and it is opened by permission.

He opened the shaft of the bottomless pit, and from the shaft rose smoke like the smoke of a great furnace. The comparison is to a furnace, and the reader is meant to hear Sodom, where Abraham looked down and saw the smoke of the land going up like the smoke of a furnace (Genesis 19:28), and Sinai, wrapped in smoke like the smoke of a kiln (Exodus 19:18). Hell’s darkness is rising into the world.

And the sun and the air were darkened with the smoke from the shaft. Before anything comes out, the light goes. That is the first effect of the abyss being opened, and it is exactly right as a description of what evil does. It does not usually arrive arguing. It arrives as a haze: things that were clear stop being clear, distinctions that used to be obvious go soft, and after a while nobody can see far enough to be sure of anything. The god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel (2 Corinthians 4:4). The fourth trumpet darkened a third of the sun by direct judgement. The fifth darkens it by pollution from below. Both take the light; only one of them comes up out of a hole.

What it does not mean. The abyss being opened does not mean evil has escaped God’s control. Every detail stresses that the key was given, the locusts were given power, they were told what to harm, and they were allowed only five months. God uses even demonic forces as instruments of judgement on those who have chosen them.

Is the devil real, or only a symbol of evil? Real. Revelation uses symbols to describe him, a star, a dragon, a serpent, but the symbols point to a personal being, a fallen angel who deceives the whole world (12:9). Jesus spoke to him in the wilderness and named him a murderer and a liar (John 8:44). C. S. Lewis observed that there are two opposite errors about devils: to disbelieve in them, and to feel an excessive and unhealthy interest in them. Scripture avoids both. It takes Satan seriously and never makes him the centre. He is real, he is hostile, and he is on a chain held by Christ.

In a sentence. When the fifth angel blew his trumpet, I saw a star that had fallen from the sky to the earth, and it was given the key to the shaft of the abyss; when it opened the shaft, smoke poured up like smoke from a huge furnace, and the sun and the sky went dark with it.

On a Tuesday. Spiritual evil is real, but its key is borrowed. Do not be fascinated by the demonic: stay away from the occult, from horror that glamorises it, and from curiosity that wants to look into the pit. And do not fear it either. Fear and trust the one who holds all the keys. When your thinking goes hazy about right and wrong, when things that were plain start to look complicated, suspect smoke, and go back to the light of God’s word.

For worship. The keys of the abyss hang on the belt of the Lamb. Every power of darkness that has ever troubled the world has come up through a door that he unlocked and will go back through a door that he will lock. Satan fell like lightning; Christ rose like the sun. The smoke from the pit can darken the air for a season, but it cannot reach the throne, and the light of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ shines on in the hearts of his people, where no smoke can come.

verseByVerse.quote: Then from the smoke came locusts on the earth, and they were given power like the power of scorpions of the earth. They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then from the smoke came locusts on the earth, and they were given power like the power of scorpions of the earth. They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.

Then from the smoke came locusts on the earth. “Locusts” (akrides). Locusts were the standard ancient image of total devastation, and Joel had built a whole prophecy on them: an army that darkens the land, runs like war horses, leaps over walls, and leaves a garden of Eden looking like a desert behind it (Joel 1:4–7; 2:1–11). Anyone who has seen a swarm knows why the image works. There is nothing to fight. They come as a shadow on the horizon, and when they lift there is nothing green left standing.

Wrong in every particular. But these locusts are wrong in every particular, and the wrongness is the point. They come out of the abyss rather than off the fields. They are given the power of scorpions, which locusts do not have. And the next clause tells them not to touch a single blade of grass, which is the one thing locusts exist to do. Whatever John is describing, it is not an infestation. They are demonic powers, pictured as a locust plague: what comes up when the pit is opened, wearing the shape of the most feared plague in the ancient world.

And they were given power like the power of scorpions of the earth. “Scorpions” (skorpioi). A scorpion’s sting is rarely fatal to a healthy adult, and it is agonising. Rehoboam threatened Israel with it as an image of intensified cruelty (1 Kings 12:11). Jesus gave his disciples authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy (Luke 10:19), linking scorpions with demonic power. The comparison sets the terms for the whole trumpet: this is a judgement that does not kill, and it is not therefore a lesser judgement.

They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree. Three restrictions in one verse, and the pattern of the whole book is in them. They were told (errethē, it was said to them): the divine passive again, which has governed every judgement since chapter 6. There is a fence around the vegetation. Ordinary locusts eat plants; these are forbidden to. Their target is people.

But only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads. And there is a fence around people, drawn along one line: the seal of God. This is the first time the sealing of 7:3 is cashed out. God’s people are protected from this demonic torment, as Israel in Goshen was protected from the plagues on Egypt: I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies shall be there (Exodus 8:22; see also 9:4, 26; 10:23). When the destroyer went through at the Passover, the doorposts of the sealed households were marked with blood. The seal on the forehead in Revelation is the doorpost of Exodus, moved from the house to the person. And notice that this protection covers all who have God’s seal, which confirms that the 144,000 sealed in chapter 7 are all believers.

What the seal does and does not do. It does not exempt anybody from the great tribulation; 7:14 said they came out of it. It did not spare the martyrs under the altar. What it does is set a limit on what can be done to a sealed person and by whom. The powers that come up out of the abyss have a list, and the list has a boundary, and the boundary was drawn before the shaft was opened. The evil one does not touch him who is born of God (1 John 5:18).

What it does not mean. Protection from the locusts does not mean believers never face spiritual attack. Satan attacks them through temptation, accusation and persecution (12:10–17). But they cannot be possessed or destroyed by demonic power, and the judgement of the locusts is not for them.

What does the seal actually protect, when Christians still suffer? This is where a believer’s honest fear should be answered rather than flattered. The seal is not a promise that nothing will happen to you. Christians get cancer, lose jobs, are lied about, go to prison, and die. What the seal guarantees is that nothing can reach past it to touch what you actually are: your union with Christ, your adoption, your inheritance. There are torments in this chapter that go on for five months and cannot be escaped, the torment of a soul handed over to the darkness it chose, and a marked person is not on the list. And the reason is not his courage. It is the name on his forehead.

Can a Christian be troubled by demons? Troubled, yes; owned, no. Believers are told to resist the devil (James 4:7) and to put on the whole armour of God against the schemes of the devil (Ephesians 6:11), which only makes sense if he attacks them. He tempts, accuses, deceives and stirs up persecution. But a Christian is the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19), and the house cannot be possessed by another master. If you are a believer in spiritual distress, you do not need a special ritual. You need what every Christian has: the word of God, prayer in Jesus’ name, the fellowship and oversight of your church, and confidence that he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4).

In a sentence. Out of the smoke came locusts onto the earth, and they were given power like that of scorpions; they were told not to damage the grass or any plant or tree, but only the people who did not have God’s seal on their foreheads.

On a Tuesday. When you feel spiritually attacked this week, by an accusing thought that will not leave, a temptation that feels unusually strong, a darkness in your mind, do not panic, and do not try to fight it in your own strength. Remind yourself whose name is on your forehead. Say it out loud if you need to: I belong to Christ. Then do the ordinary things that the devil hates most: pray, read the word, tell a Christian friend, and get some sleep.

For worship. The same God who drew a line through Egypt around the land of Goshen has drawn a line around his people, and the hordes of the abyss stop at it. They have power like scorpions, and they cannot touch one sealed forehead. The blood on the doorposts has become the Spirit on the soul, and the destroyer passes over. The powers of the abyss cannot claim you, because you have been claimed already, bought with blood, sealed by the Spirit, held by the Father’s hand.

verseByVerse.quote: They were allowed to torment them for five months, but not to kill them, and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings someone. And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were allowed to torment them for five months, but not to kill them, and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings someone. And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them.

The setting. The life cycle of a locust is about five months, and the locust season ran roughly from spring to late summer, about five months. Job speaks of those who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures (Job 3:21). Jeremiah said the survivors of a judged nation would prefer death to life (Jeremiah 8:3).

They were allowed to torment them for five months, but not to kill them. “Allowed” (edothē, it was given): permission again. And two boundaries: a duration and a limit. They may torment; they may not kill. Five months, and not a day more. “Torment” (basanisthēsontai) is torture, intense pain.

Why five months? The most likely answer is the plainest one: the life cycle of a locust swarm, from hatching to death, is about five months, roughly May to September. The number is not a code. It means one locust season: a real, bounded, recognisable stretch of time with a beginning and an end that everybody in an agricultural society could measure. It will feel endless while it lasts. It is not endless. God limits the time, and he does not allow them to kill. The purpose of the torment is to bring people to repentance (v. 20).

And their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings someone. Agonising but not fatal. What might this torment be? Perhaps the spiritual and psychological misery of life under demonic deception: despair, emptiness, fear, addiction, the inner torment of a life without God that has given itself to the powers of darkness.

And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them. This is the most terrible sentence in the chapter and one of the hardest in the Bible. “Seek” (zētēsousin). “Long” (epithymēsousin, desire intensely). “Flee” (pheugei). This is the condition in which existence itself has become the punishment, and there is no exit, because the one exit a person would take has been closed. People would rather die than go on, but even death escapes them. And still they do not turn to God.

A state worse than dying. The horror of the verse, rightly read, is not that God is cruel. It is that there is a state worse than dying, and that human beings can arrive at it by their own steady choosing. The most merciful thing in the passage is that it has a five-month fence around it, and that the fence was put there by God.

What it does not mean. This verse should never be used to suggest that a person in despair or with suicidal thoughts is under God’s judgement. Believers, too, can suffer deep depression and long for death, as Elijah did (1 Kings 19:4). The picture here is of judgement on those who reject God, and the right response to anyone in despair is compassion, care and the hope of the gospel.

Is this verse about me, if I have wished I would not wake up? Some readers will read it from the outside as a description of a future horror. Others will read it and recognise the country. There are Christians who have lain awake and wished quite specifically not to wake up. If that is you, this verse is not describing your condemnation, and it should not be allowed to sound as though it is. Wanting to die is not the same as being abandoned by God, and Scripture proves it by the company: Job wanted it, Moses asked God to kill him (Numbers 11:15), Elijah sat under a tree and asked to die the day after the greatest victory of his life (1 Kings 19:4), and Jonah asked twice. God did not reject one of them for it. He fed Elijah and let him sleep. And look at who is in this verse and who is not: the torment falls expressly on those who do not have the seal of God (v. 4).

What should I do if I am in that dark place? Tell someone, this week, out loud: a pastor, a Christian friend, your doctor. If you are in immediate danger, contact emergency services or a crisis line today. That is not weakness or lack of faith; it is what the body of Christ, and the ordinary means of medicine God gives, are for. Despair says the darkness is permanent and there is no door. This whole book is the announcement that there is a door, that it has been opened from the other side at enormous cost, and that the one who opened it personally holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). Your life is in his hands, and he has not finished with it.

In a sentence. They were permitted to torment those people for five months, but not to kill them, and the agony was like the pain of a scorpion’s sting; in those days people will look for death and not find it, they will long to die, but death will run away from them.

On a Tuesday. Many people around you live with quiet despair, some of them behind cheerful faces at work or in church. Do not judge them; point them to the Christ who gives rest to the weary (Matthew 11:28), and be the kind of person they could tell. Ask one person this week how they are really doing, and wait for the real answer.

For worship. The Lord who sets a five-month fence around the torment of the abyss is the Lord who went into the deepest torment himself and came out the other side. He knew what it was to be sorrowful even to death (Matthew 26:38). He was forsaken so that no one who trusts him ever will be. For those outside him, there is a misery worse than death; for those in him, death itself has been turned into a door, and beyond it no one will ever again long for an end, because the life he gives is life to the full.
verseByVerse.note: Five months is roughly the life span of a locust, or the season in which they swarm.

verseByVerse.quote: In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle: on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold; their faces were like human faces, their hair like women's hair, and their teeth like lions' teeth; they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle. They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle: on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold; their faces were like human faces, their hair like women’s hair, and their teeth like lions’ teeth; they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle. They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails.

The setting. Joel says the locusts look like horses and run like war horses, with a noise like chariots (Joel 2:4–5). A locust’s head does look rather like a horse’s; the Italian word for a grasshopper, cavalletta, means little horse, and the German Heupferd means hay horse. Joel says the invader has the teeth of a lion (Joel 1:6). The Parthians, Rome’s feared eastern enemy, were famous mounted archers who wore their hair long.

Impossible to draw. Now the description, and it is deliberately impossible to draw. John piles up comparisons in four verses, nearly every one introduced by like. He is not filing a report on a species. He is telling a congregation what it felt like to look at.

In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle. “Like” (homoiōmata, likenesses). He is describing something beyond ordinary experience in the best images he has. Not a portrait to be drawn, but a series of impressions: unstoppable, terrifying, intelligent and cruel.

On their heads were what looked like crowns of gold. Not crowns: what looked like crowns. This is a counterfeit, and John will not let it pass for the real thing: a show of authority and conquest. They seem victorious. Everything in this book that is genuinely crowned is crowned by God.

Their faces were like human faces. Three details follow in ascending order of menace, and the human face is the worst of them. Whatever this is, it has intelligence and intention, and it looks back at you. These are not mindless insects.

Their hair like women’s hair. Long, flowing hair. It suggests the streaming antennae of a locust and perhaps, to a first-century ear, the long hair of the Parthian warriors. Seductive, perhaps, as well as wild.

And their teeth like lions’ teeth. Ferocious, destructive. It is Joel again, of the locust nation with the teeth of a lion.

They had breastplates like breastplates of iron. There is no attacking them; nothing gets through. The locust’s armoured body, invulnerable, hard to resist.

And the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle. Overwhelming, terrifying (Joel 2:5). A locust swarm is heard before it is seen, a dry roar that fills the whole sky, and people who have lived through one describe the sound as the thing they never forgot.

They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails. The sting is in the back end, and the sixth trumpet will repeat it: those horses too have power in their tails (v. 19). Twice in one chapter the injury comes from behind, after the thing has apparently passed. That is a fair description of how a great deal of evil actually works. The damage is rarely done at the moment of the encounter. It is done afterwards, by what was left in the wound. And limited again: five months.

Every category slips. Stand back from the portrait and the effect is exactly what John intends. It has a man’s face and a lion’s teeth. It wears armour and a crown that is not a crown. It is a locust that will not eat grass and a horse that is not a horse. Every category the mind reaches for slips. That is what comes up out of the abyss.

Where Christians differ: what are the locusts? Some popular writers have identified them with modern weapons, such as attack helicopters with rotor blades, tail guns and armoured cockpits. Historicists have identified them with the Muslim Arab armies of the seventh century. Others take them as literal demonic creatures to be unleashed in a future tribulation. Verdict: the locusts are demonic powers, released by God’s permission to torment those who have rejected him, pictured with images drawn from Joel’s locust army. John uses “like” again and again, signalling symbols, not technical descriptions. Reading modern technology into them ignores how the first readers would have understood the book. The locusts describe demonic torment, real and terrible, wherever people give themselves over to evil, throughout the age and especially toward its end.

Left behind by the next generation. That is why every generation that has tried to identify these creatures with a particular weapon, cavalry, cannon, helicopters, drones, has been confident and has been left behind by the next generation’s equally confident identification. What is permanent here is not the mechanism. It is the anatomy of spiritual evil given a body: intelligent, armoured, unkillable by the people it torments, crowned with an authority it did not earn, deafening, and stinging from behind. A congregation in Pergamum living under the shadow of Satan’s throne (2:13) did not need the picture decoded. They needed to be told that it comes up on a permission and goes down on a timetable.

What it does not mean. The details are not to be decoded one by one, as though each feature were a separate clue. Together they build a single picture of overwhelming, intelligent, demonic hostility.

What does this look like in ordinary life? Usually not monsters. It looks like something that seems glorious and wears a crown: an ideology that promises liberation, a pleasure that promises freedom, a habit that looks harmless in the first year. It has a human face, so it seems reasonable. It is armoured, so argument bounces off it. And it stings from behind: the pornography that seemed private and later poisons a marriage, the gambling that was fun until the debts arrived, the bitterness nursed for years that finally isolates a man from everyone. The way to resist is not to study the creature but to stay near Christ, who has already disarmed the powers (Colossians 2:15).

In a sentence. The locusts looked like horses equipped for battle; they wore what seemed to be gold crowns, their faces looked human, their hair was long like a woman’s, their teeth were like a lion’s, their chests were armoured as if with iron, and their wings roared like a mass of chariots and horses charging into battle; they had tails with stings like scorpions, and the power to hurt people for five months was in their tails.

On a Tuesday. Evil often looks impressive, crowned and armoured. Do not be taken in, and do not be afraid. It serves its time and is gone. Ask yourself this week whether there is anything in your life that looked harmless at the front and has started to sting from behind. Name it to God, and to one trusted Christian, before the five months are up.

For worship. Every crown in this vision is a counterfeit, and there is only one head on which the true crowns rest. The Lamb who wears many diadems needs no armour of iron, because he took the sting of death into his own body and drew its poison. The locusts roar like chariots, but the Lord of hosts is not impressed by noise. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15:55–57).

verseByVerse.quote: They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon. The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon. The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.

The setting. Proverbs says that the locusts have no king, yet all of them march in rank (Proverbs 30:27). These locusts do have a king. In the Old Testament Abaddon (Hebrew for destruction) is a name for the place of the dead, linked with Sheol and death: Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering (Job 26:6; 28:22; Psalm 88:11; Proverbs 15:11). The Greek god Apollo was sometimes symbolised by the locust, and emperors since Augustus had linked themselves with Apollo; Domitian liked to be seen in that light.

They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. “King” (basilea). It is one of the things that makes a swarm so unnerving: a vast coordinated destruction with nobody in charge. These locusts have one. The chaos is organised, and it has a commander. The demonic powers are organised under a ruler. The angel of the abyss is either Satan himself or a high-ranking demonic spirit under him.

His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon. John gives his name twice so that neither half of his congregation misses it. “Abaddon” means destruction. “Apollyon” (Apollyōn) is the Greek participle meaning the destroyer, the one who ruins. The two names say the same thing in two languages, which is John’s way of saying that this figure is not a local problem. The name sums up his nature: the thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy; Christ came that they may have life and have it abundantly (John 10:10).

A barb in the name. There is very probably a barb in the Greek name that the first hearers would have caught at once. Apollo was one of the great deities of the Greek world, and one of his emblems was the locust. Imperial propaganda freely associated the emperors with him. So when John names the king of the abyss Apollyon, a Christian in Ephesus hearing it read out would have made the connection without being told: the god the empire boasts in has a name very like destroyer, and the thing he actually rules is a pit.

His only competence. And that is the only thing this figure can do. Not create, not build, not make anything at all. His entire competence is destruction, and his name is his job description. Set that beside the one seated on the throne, whose song in chapter 4 is you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created (4:11), and the asymmetry is total. One of these two makes things out of nothing. The other unmakes what somebody else made, and can be shut in a shaft.

The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come. A single verse of bookkeeping, and it does two things. It confirms that the eagle’s three woes in 8:13 map onto the fifth, sixth and seventh trumpets. Worse is coming. And it says has passed. The five months ended. Whatever came up out of that shaft went back down, and John is already speaking of it in the past tense while two more are still to come. That is not a small thing to say to people who are inside something. Every affliction in this book is announced, measured, and then reported finished. The one who keeps the register is the one who holds the keys, and he has never once lost count.

What it does not mean. Abaddon’s power, like the locusts’, is limited. He is a king, but not the King. Christ is King of kings (19:16), and Abaddon’s kingdom is the abyss into which Satan will finally be bound and then thrown into the lake of fire (20:3, 10).

Are God and Satan two equal powers fighting it out? No, and this fear troubles thoughtful Christians more than they usually admit: the sense that good and evil are two roughly matched forces wrestling for the world, with the outcome genuinely uncertain. Revelation never allows it. The destroyer is a subject in a passive sentence: he is given a key, he is allowed five months, he is told what he may not touch. He is not the opposite number of God. He is a creature with a leash and a name. His true opposite, if he has one, is an archangel like Michael (12:7), not the Creator. God has no rival.

Is this the Apollyon of The Pilgrim’s Progress? Yes. John Bunyan took the name from this verse for the monster that meets Christian in the Valley of Humiliation, claiming him as his subject and trying to frighten him back. Christian is wounded, thrown down, and loses his sword; then he recovers it and, with a word of Scripture on his lips, gives Apollyon a thrust that sends him flying away. It is a fine picture of the point of this verse. The destroyer is real and fierce, and he claims what is not his; but the believer resists him with the word of God and the promise of victory, and he flees (James 4:7).

In a sentence. Their king was the angel who rules the abyss, whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon and in Greek Apollyon, both meaning Destroyer; the first woe is past, but look, two more woes are still to come.

On a Tuesday. Satan’s name tells you what he does: he destroys. Whatever he promises, his end is destruction. When a temptation comes this week dressed up as freedom, success or pleasure, ask what it builds and what it destroys. Christ’s name is Saviour, and everything he touches he makes new. If you are in the middle of something hard, say the bookkeeping verse to yourself: this, too, will be reported as passed.

For worship. The destroyer can only unmake; the Lord can make out of nothing, and remake what was ruined. The king of the pit rules a hole in the ground; the King of kings rules heaven and earth from a throne before which the elders cast their crowns. Every woe is counted and every woe will pass, and the one who counts them is the one who said, Behold, I am making all things new (21:5). Abaddon’s name means destruction. Jesus means the LORD saves.
verseByVerse.note: Abaddon means “destruction” and Apollyon “destroyer.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Sixth Trumpet: The Army from the Euphrates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 13–14: the sixth trumpet, and a voice from the four horns of the golden altar — the incense altar, where the prayers of all the saints were offered in 8:3–4 and from which fire was thrown down in 8:5. The order it gives is Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates. They are bound; they must be released; the order comes from the altar where the church prays. The Euphrates was the empire’s eastern frontier and the direction every invasion of Israel had come from.

Verse 15: the four had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year — one article in the Greek governs all four, so this is a fixed moment rather than a duration — and are released to kill a third of mankind. The fraction has moved from things to people. Verse 16 gives the number of mounted troops as twice ten thousand times ten thousand, with the telling clause I heard their number, exactly as at 7:4.

Verses 17–19: breastplates the colour of fire, sapphire and sulfur — the same three things the horses breathe. Lions’ heads; fire, smoke and sulfur from their mouths, the substance of Sodom (Gen. 19:24) and of the lake of fire (19:20; 20:10). A third of mankind killed by these three plagues. And the power is in mouths and in tails, the tails being like serpents with heads — the word John reserves for the dragon (12:9; 20:2).

Verses 20–21 give the verdict the whole sequence was building toward. The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent — not of the works of their hands, not of worshipping demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood which cannot see or hear or walk (Ps. 115:4–8), and not of their murders, sorceries, sexual immorality or thefts.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Order Comes from the Altar

The voice that releases the four angels comes from the altar where the saints’ prayers are offered. They were prepared for the hour, day, month and year. Yet the survivors did not repent of their idols, sorceries and sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Beyond the Euphrates lay the invader every Roman province feared.

Now: Judgement alone does not change hearts; we become like what we worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, "Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.”

The setting. The Euphrates was the great river of Mesopotamia, the north-eastern boundary of the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18). Israel’s great enemies, Assyria and Babylon, had come from beyond it. In John’s day it was the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire, beyond which lay the Parthians, Rome’s most feared enemy, whose cavalry had destroyed a Roman army at Carrhae in 53 BC. The altar of incense had a horn at each corner (Exodus 30:2–3).

Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God. Of all the places a command could come from, this is the one that matters. The golden altar is the incense altar, and the reader has been there twice already. In 8:3–4 an angel stood at it and offered much incense with the prayers of all the saints. In 8:5 the fire from that altar was thrown down on the earth. Now a voice speaks out of its four horns, and what it says releases the sixth trumpet. The voice from the altar links this judgement too to the prayers of God’s people.

The horns of the altar. The horns of an altar were the four projections at its corners, and they were the part a man grasped when he fled to the sanctuary claiming protection (1 Kings 1:50–51). Blood was put on them at the great atoning sacrifices (Leviticus 4:7, 18). They were the place of refuge and the place of blood. Those who reject the atonement face judgement from the same altar.

Where the prayers went. That is the third time in two chapters the same connection has been made, and it is the argument the trumpets exist to make. The judgements of God on the world are not arbitrary spasms. They are the answer to the praying of his people, issued from the place where that praying is received. A congregation that has prayed for years about wickedness that nobody seems to be doing anything about is being told where its prayers went and what they are doing.

Saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates. Two things. They are bound. “Bound” (dedemenous) is perfect tense: having been bound and remaining bound, presumably for a long time, since somebody had to bind them. These are evil angels, held in check by God until now, as fallen angels are kept in eternal chains (Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4). And they must be released (lyson, loose), by an order, from an altar, at a specified moment. The reader is now four chapters into a pattern that does not vary: nothing hostile in this universe moves except on a permission, and every permission is issued from the throne room. God holds back the forces of destruction, and releases them at his chosen time.

The direction the end comes from. To say the Euphrates to a first-century reader was to say what the border says in any country that has been invaded across one. Every great invasion that threatened Jerusalem came from beyond it: Assyria, then Babylon. In John’s own day the terror on that frontier was Parthia, the one power Rome had never subdued, whose mounted archers were the standing nightmare of the eastern provinces. The Euphrates, the ancient boundary from which invasion came, pictures the terror of foreign invasion and war. And on the far side of that river, in this vision, are four angels who have been tied up and are now being untied by order. Whatever a reader thinks about the invasions of history, this verse says something specific about all of them: the horde crossing the border was on a rope, and the rope was in God’s hand, and the hand let go at a moment of its own choosing.

Textual note. Some important manuscripts read “a voice from the horns of the golden altar”, without the word “four”. The meaning is unchanged.

What it does not mean. The Euphrates here is not necessarily a prediction of armies literally crossing that river in the future, though it may include that. In Revelation place names often carry symbolic meaning: Babylon, Sodom, Egypt, Armageddon. The Euphrates stands for the frontier from which the terror of invasion comes.

What holds evil back now? God does, through means he has appointed. Paul speaks of something that restrains lawlessness until the appointed time (2 Thessalonians 2:6–7), and Christians have usually understood that to include the ordinary restraints God gives in his common grace: lawful government, which bears the sword against evil (Romans 13:4), conscience, the family, the presence and prayers of the church, salt in a decaying world (Matthew 5:13). We rarely see how much is being held back. Every peaceful year, every war that did not happen, every evil plan that failed, is the four angels still bound. That is why we pray for those in authority, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life (1 Timothy 2:1–2).

In a sentence. Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice coming from the horns of the golden altar in God’s presence, telling the sixth angel with the trumpet, Set free the four angels who are bound at the great River Euphrates.

On a Tuesday. God restrains evil far more than we know. Thank him tonight for every day of peace, and pray by name for one country living under war or invasion. And pray for your own rulers, whether you voted for them or not. Your prayers go to the same altar this voice comes from.

For worship. The altar of God is the place of refuge and the place of blood, and it is also the place from which judgement goes out. Those who grasp its horns in faith, sheltering under the blood of the Lamb, are safe for ever. Those who refuse it find that the same altar speaks against them. And every power of destruction in the world, from the ancient empires beyond the Euphrates to the bound angels of the abyss, waits on a word from the God who hears the prayers of his people. He holds the rope. He has never once let go by accident.
verseByVerse.note: The Euphrates was the eastern frontier of the Roman world, beyond which lay the feared Parthians.

verseByVerse.quote: So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind. The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind. The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.

So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year. Four units of time, and the Greek has a single article governing all four, which makes them one appointed moment rather than a span. Not for a year and a month and a day and an hour, as though the killing lasted that long. For the hour, which falls on the day, in the month, of the year. This is a diary entry. “Prepared” (hētoimasmenoi) is a perfect participle again: made ready and standing ready. God has appointed the exact moment.

The most steadying sentence. Sit with the implication, because it is the single most steadying sentence in the chapter. There is a moment fixed for this, and it was fixed before the angels were bound. The catastrophe that arrives without warning and appears to prove that nobody is steering has a time stamp on it, and the stamp was applied in advance. That is not the same as saying the catastrophe is good, and Scripture never says so. It is saying that history is not a series of accidents interrupted occasionally by providence. Even its catastrophes come at the hour, the day, the month and the year God has fixed. Every hour in it has been counted, including the ones nobody would have chosen.

Were released to kill a third of mankind. The fraction moves again. The horsemen of chapter 6 had a fourth (6:8). The first four trumpets took a third of the earth, the sea, the water and the light. Now a third of mankind. This is the first time the trumpets kill people directly. Under the fifth trumpet they longed for death; now it comes. The judgements are escalating from things to people, and still, still, two thirds are untouched, and the reason will be stated with brutal clarity in verse 20.

The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand. “Twice ten thousand times ten thousand” (dismyriades myriadōn, two myriads of myriads): two hundred million, if it is arithmetic. It is almost certainly not. A myriad, ten thousand, was the largest number Greek had a single word for, so a myriad of myriads is the language reaching its ceiling, and John has used it already of the angels around the throne (5:11), as Daniel did before him of the attendants of the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:10). Doubling it is not a census; it is a way of saying, and then twice that again. The whole Roman army had perhaps three hundred thousand soldiers, and the population of the entire empire was perhaps sixty million. The number means an army beyond counting, overwhelming.

I heard their number. The detail that fixes it is the last clause. John did not count them and does not claim to have. He was told, and he is reporting what he was told, exactly as he did with the 144,000: I heard the number of the sealed (7:4). The two numbers are given the same way, and a reader who takes one as a figure of overwhelming completeness should take the other the same way. The two armies stand in contrast: God’s army, sealed and counted, and the demonic army, vast and destructive.

A matter of proportion. What the number is doing is a matter of proportion. The church in Asia was a few thousand people in seven towns, meeting in houses, with no standing whatever. The forces arrayed against them are described in a figure that runs off the end of the counting system. And the whole of that host was on the wrong side of a river, tied up, waiting for a word from an altar.

Where Christians differ: is this a literal army of two hundred million? Some popular writers have identified it with a future Chinese army, after China claimed it could field two hundred million soldiers. Verdict: the number is symbolic of an overwhelming, uncountable host, a demonic army more than a human one, as the description of the horses that follows makes clear. Its point is the terror of war and destruction let loose, not a prediction about any particular nation. Readings that tie it to modern nations have repeatedly had to be revised as world politics changed.

What it does not mean. The fixed hour does not mean God takes pleasure in death. He has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but would rather that they turn from their way and live (Ezekiel 33:11). The fixed hour means that even judgement is under his wise and just control.

Should I be afraid of dying in some catastrophe? If you belong to Christ, your hour is fixed too, and it is fixed by your Father. My times are in your hand (Psalm 31:15). No bomb, virus, accident or army can take you a moment before he calls you home, and none can keep you a moment after. That does not make Christians careless; we take sensible precautions, because God works through means. But it does free us from the dread that hangs over people who think their lives are at the mercy of chance. Whether death comes in old age or in a catastrophe, for the believer it comes on an appointment kept by a Saviour.

In a sentence. So the four angels, who had been kept ready for that very hour, day, month and year, were set free to kill a third of humanity; the number of their cavalry was two hundred million; I heard the number.

On a Tuesday. No disaster in the news happens outside God’s appointed hour. That does not make it less terrible, but it means it is not meaningless. When the next headline frightens you, say Psalm 31:15 out loud, for yourself and for the people you love. And let the size of the enemy’s host drive you, not to despair, but to the one who has twice as many angels and needs none of them.

For worship. The God of this verse keeps a diary, and every hour of history is written in it. Nothing surprises him, nothing overtakes him, nothing comes early or late. The hosts of the enemy may be numbered in myriads of myriads, but they wait on his word like dogs on a chain. And the same God who fixed the hour of judgement fixed another hour, the one Jesus spoke of when he said, Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son (John 17:1). Because that hour came, no hour of judgement need ever be ours.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them: they wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur, and the heads of the horses were like lions' heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths. By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur coming out of their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them: they wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur, and the heads of the horses were like lions’ heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths. By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur coming out of their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.

The setting. Fire and sulphur (brimstone) rained down on Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24). In Revelation they are the elements of the lake of fire (14:10; 19:20; 20:10; 21:8). The Parthian cavalry were famous for shooting arrows backwards over the horse’s rump as they rode away, so that their power seemed to be in their tails.

And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them. “In my vision” (en tē horasei). John reminds the reader, in the middle of the description, that this is a vision. He is not claiming to have watched cavalry through a telescope.

They wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur. Three colours: red (fire), dark blue (hyakinthinous, the colour of hyacinth, of smoke), and the sickly yellow of brimstone. And they are the colours of the three things that come out of the horses’ mouths in the next clause: fire, smoke and sulphur. The riders are wearing what the horses breathe.

And the heads of the horses were like lions’ heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths. Monstrous, demonic horses, like dragons. Lions’ heads speak of ferocity. Sulphur is theion, brimstone, and in Scripture it has one address: the LORD rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the LORD out of heaven. It is the smell of judgement. What comes out of these mouths is the substance of hell itself breaking out into the world.

By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed. “Plagues” (plēgōn, blows, strokes) is the Exodus vocabulary, which has governed the whole trumpet sequence: fire, smoke and sulphur. And the killing is done by what proceeds out of a mouth, which in this book is never accidental. The weapon of Christ is the sharp sword that comes from his mouth (1:16; 19:15). Two mouths, two kinds of word, and both of them decisive. What comes out of a mouth kills or saves.

For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound. Twice now the tail has been the dangerous end: the scorpion-locusts of verse 10 and these horses. And here the tails are given heads of their own. It is a grotesque image and a precise one: the thing bites in both directions, and the second bite comes after you have decided it has gone past. These horses kill from the front and wound from behind. Demonic power is deadly in every direction.

John has signed the picture. The word for serpents is opheis, and in this book that word has a single owner: the great dragon is that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan (12:9; 20:2). Whatever historical shape this army takes, and the Parthian archers shooting backwards would have come to mind at once for any reader in Asia, the tail that stings from behind belongs to the serpent.

Evil does its worst work with its back turned. That is a fair description of how ruin actually arrives in a life, and it should be said plainly for the reader who is living in the aftermath of something. The moment of the encounter is rarely the moment of the damage. The affair ended years ago; the consequences are only now walking through the door. The drink was put down; the liver was not consulted. The words were said in one bad evening; the son has not called since. Evil does its worst work with its back turned, and the person it wounds usually thought the danger had passed.

What it does not mean. This is not a description of modern tanks or military aircraft, as some have suggested. It is a vision of demonic destruction, drawing on the images of Sodom’s judgement and the lake of fire.

Is there hope when I am living with the sting of my own past sin? Yes. The consequences of sin may remain for a time, and God does not always remove them; David was forgiven, and still his household suffered (2 Samuel 12:13–14). But the guilt is gone the moment you confess it, and the serpent’s sting has been drawn at the cross: the sting of death is sin, but thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15:56–57). Do the repairing you can do: apologise, make restitution, keep faith with those you hurt. Then refuse to let the accuser keep stinging you with what God has forgiven. God is able to bring good even out of the wreckage (Romans 8:28), and he often does it slowly.

How do I pray against spiritual powers without becoming obsessed with them? By keeping your eyes on Christ rather than on the enemy. Paul tells us that we wrestle not against flesh and blood but against the spiritual forces of evil (Ephesians 6:12), and then the armour he describes is almost entirely ordinary: truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word of God, and prayer at all times in the Spirit. You do not need to name or map demons, or address them in prayer. Pray to the Father, in the name of the Son who has already triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15), for his kingdom to come and for deliverance from evil. That is how Jesus taught us to pray (Matthew 6:13).

In a sentence. This is how the horses and their riders looked in my vision: the riders wore breastplates that were fiery red, smoky blue and sulphur yellow, the horses had heads like lions, and fire, smoke and sulphur came out of their mouths; these three plagues, the fire, smoke and sulphur pouring from their mouths, killed a third of humanity; for the horses’ power was in their mouths and in their tails, which were like snakes with heads that they used to wound people.

On a Tuesday. War and violence are not only human; they are also demonic. Pray against the spiritual powers behind them (Ephesians 6:12), especially when you hear of atrocities. And be watchful for the tail in your own life: before you make a choice this week, ask not only what it will do now, but what it will leave behind when it has passed.

For worship. Fire and smoke and sulphur pour from the mouths of the horses of the abyss, and a sword proceeds from the mouth of the Lamb, and his word is stronger. The ancient serpent stings from behind, and the seed of the woman has crushed his head, though his own heel was bruised in doing it (Genesis 3:15). The weapons of hell are fearsome, and they are all on a leash. The weapon of Christ is the truth, and it will have the last word over every lie the serpent has ever told.
