verseByVerse.quote: The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk, nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk, nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.

The setting. Pharaoh hardened his heart again and again under the plagues on Egypt (Exodus 8:15, 32; 9:34). The Old Testament mocks idols that have mouths but do not speak, eyes but do not see, ears but do not hear (Psalm 115:4–7; 135:15–17; Daniel 5:23). Paul taught that behind idols are demons (1 Corinthians 10:20).

The sentence the sequence has been building toward. And now the sentence the whole trumpet sequence has been building toward, and it is the most sobering diagnosis of the human heart in the New Testament.

The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent. Start with the two words that carry the weight: the rest. Two thirds of mankind survived. Every fraction in the last four chapters, a fourth, a third, a third, a third, existed for the sake of the people who were left, and this verse says what the survivors did with the mercy of being alive. “Did not repent” (ou metenoēsan). This is the purpose of the trumpets: they were warnings, calling people to repent. And this is the tragedy: they did not. The same words return in 16:9, 11.

Suffering does not automatically produce repentance. That is the answer to a question a great many people carry, usually unspoken: surely if God made himself unmistakable, people would believe. Send a real catastrophe, something undeniable, and the world would turn. Revelation says it has been tried. The sky has gone dark, the water has turned bitter, a third of the human race has died, and the survivors go back to what they were doing. Suffering by itself does not change the heart. It hardens as often as it softens, and Pharaoh, whose plagues these are, is the standing proof: after plague after plague he hardened his heart, and the last thing he did was drive into a sea that had opened.

Of the works of their hands. Idols made by human hands. What they will not give up is listed in two groups, and the order is not accidental. First, the idols.

Nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk. John pauses to describe them with what can only be called contempt. It is a quotation of the Psalms almost word for word: they have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see; those who make them become like them (Psalm 115:4–8). The last clause of that psalm is the sting. You become like what you worship. Worship something blind and deaf, and in the end you cannot see or hear either, which is exactly what this chapter has just described. Gold, silver, bronze, stone, wood: idols for the rich and the poor alike.

Behind the idols, demons. “Demons” (daimonia). Idolatry is not harmless. Paul said the same about meat sacrificed in temples: what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God (1 Corinthians 10:20). The statue is wood. What is being served through it is not nothing. And the very powers that tormented them in this chapter are the ones they keep worshipping. Idols include anything people trust and serve in place of God: money, power, pleasure, status; covetousness, which is idolatry (Colossians 3:5).

Nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts. Then the second list, and it is startlingly ordinary. Four sins, breaking the commandments of the second table: murder (sixth commandment), sexual immorality (seventh), theft (eighth). The second needs a word. “Sorceries” (pharmakōn, from pharmakeia) is the use of drugs and potions in magic and the occult; our word pharmacy comes from it. What it names is the attempt to control life, luck, love and death by technique rather than by trusting God: pay the right practitioner, use the right substance, say the right words, and bend reality your way.

Root and fruit. Set the two lists together and the diagnosis is complete. Idolatry, breaking the first table of the law, always leads to breaking the second (Romans 1:21–32). Idolatry is the root; murder, manipulation, immorality and theft are the fruit. A person who has replaced God will end up destroying his neighbour’s life, body, marriage or property, because there is nothing left to stop him. And none of these four is exotic. Every one of them is available on an ordinary Tuesday.

Where Christians differ: can people repent whenever they choose? Many hold that people always have the natural ability to repent and believe if they choose to. Verdict: this verse shows the terrible bondage of the human will apart from grace. Even under overwhelming judgement, people do not repent, because their hearts are enslaved to sin and they love darkness (John 3:19). Scripture teaches that sinners are dead in sin (Ephesians 2:1) and unable to come to Christ unless the Father draws them (John 6:44). Repentance is God’s gift (Acts 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25). This does not excuse unbelievers; they are responsible for refusing. But it shows why we pray for God to give new hearts, and why we preach the gospel, which is God’s power to save (Romans 1:16).

Did not, not could not. Because the whole chapter is finally about a door that stayed open and was not used. The judgements were fractional so there would be somebody left to turn. The trumpets were warnings and not the end. An eagle flew overhead in daylight shouting three woes before the first of them landed. God went to extraordinary lengths to be heard, and the last word of the chapter is that they did not repent. The bondage of the will is real, and it is a bondage they love; the refusal is theirs, and so is the guilt.

What it does not mean. It does not mean no one ever repents through suffering. Many do (11:13). But suffering alone does not save; only God’s grace through the gospel does.

The test in this verse. There is a test here that a reader can run on himself, and it is more searching than it looks. It is not do I own a statue? An idol is whatever you would be unable to give up. Take the thing you have already been warned about, by your body, by your bank, by your wife, by a friend who took a risk in saying it, and notice how expertly you have explained the warning away. That is verse 20 happening in a life, at a scale where it can still be repented of.

Is my unbelieving friend beyond hope, if even disasters do not move people? No. What disasters cannot do, God can. The same Paul who was dead in sin was turned around in a moment on the Damascus road. Hardness of heart is a reason to stop relying on arguments and circumstances to do the work, and to rely instead on the Spirit, who gives new hearts (Ezekiel 36:26). So keep praying for them by name, keep loving them, and keep telling them the gospel plainly when the door opens. God often uses suffering as the occasion of conversion, but it is always grace, not the suffering, that saves.

Are horoscopes, tarot and crystals harmless fun? Scripture treats them as anything but. They belong to the family of sorceries named here: attempts to know or control the future and the self apart from God. Israel was forbidden every form of divination (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), and the new believers in Ephesus burned their magic books publicly at great cost (Acts 19:19). Even when they are meant lightly, they train the heart to look for guidance and security somewhere other than the Lord. A Christian has no need of them. Your future is not in the stars; it is in the hands of the one who made them.

Does pharmakeia mean Christians should avoid medicine? No. The word here is about magic and the occult, not about medicine, and reading it that way is a misuse. Scripture treats medical care as a good gift: Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), Luke was a physician (Colossians 4:14), and Jesus said that those who are sick need a doctor (Luke 5:31). Taking prescribed medication, including for mental illness, is not a lack of faith. What is condemned is using substances to manipulate spiritual powers, or to escape into darkness, rather than receiving God’s gifts with thanksgiving.

In a sentence. Yet the rest of humanity, those who were not killed by these plagues, still did not turn away from what they had made with their own hands; they did not stop worshipping demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood, which cannot see, hear or walk, and they did not turn from their murders, their magic arts, their sexual immorality or their stealing.

On a Tuesday. Pray for unbelieving friends and family, asking God to do what suffering alone cannot: give them new hearts. And keep sharing the gospel with them. Then run the test on yourself. Name the warning you have been explaining away, and do one concrete thing about it before the week is out: delete the app, make the phone call, cancel the subscription, confess the sin. Repentance is not a feeling. It is a turning, and it can begin today.

For worship. The God of this chapter goes to extraordinary lengths to be heard. He measures his judgements, he sends warnings in daylight, he holds back the hosts of the abyss to leave room for repentance. And when the human heart still refuses, he does what no trumpet can do: he gives a new heart, and puts his Spirit within, and turns the rebel into a son. Every believer is a living proof that God can soften what disasters only harden. Salvation belongs to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb, for even our repentance was his gift.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit.<sup>2</sup>He opened the shaft of the bottomless pit, and from the shaft rose smoke like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened with the smoke from the shaft.<sup>3</sup>Then from the smoke came locusts on the earth, and they were given power like the power of scorpions of the earth.<sup>4</sup>They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.<sup>5</sup>They were allowed to torment them for five months, but not to kill them, and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings someone.<sup>6</sup>And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them.<sup>7</sup>In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle: on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold; their faces were like human faces,<sup>8</sup>their hair like women’s hair, and their teeth like lions’ teeth;<sup>9</sup>they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle.<sup>10</sup>They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails.<sup>11</sup>They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon.<sup>12</sup>The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.<sup>13</sup>Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God,<sup>14</sup>saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.”<sup>15</sup>So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind.<sup>16</sup>The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.<sup>17</sup>And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them: they wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur, and the heads of the horses were like lions’ heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths.<sup>18</sup>By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur coming out of their mouths.<sup>19</sup>For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.<sup>20</sup>The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk,<sup>21</sup>nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.

10.title: The Angel and the Little Scroll
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is the second great interlude of Revelation — this one inserted between the sixth and seventh trumpets (as chapter 7 was inserted between the sixth and seventh seals). The interlude performs the same function: it pauses the judgment sequence to reorient the reader to the prophetic commission of the church. Before the seventh trumpet sounds and the final woe arrives, John is given a little scroll to eat and recommissioned to prophesy.

A mighty angel descends from heaven clothed with a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, his face like the sun, his legs like pillars of fire — imagery that deliberately echoes the description of Christ in chapter 1. He stands on sea and land (claiming sovereignty over the whole earth), holds a little open scroll, and cries out with a loud voice like a lion’s roar. Seven thunders respond — and John is told not to write what the thunders said. This is the only thing in Revelation that is sealed rather than revealed: some of God’s purposes remain hidden until their time.

John eats the little scroll at the angel’s command. It is sweet in his mouth but bitter in his stomach — an echo of Ezekiel’s commissioning (Ezekiel 2:8–3:3) and Jeremiah’s experience of the word (Jeremiah 15:16). The word of God is sweet to receive — it is the good news of grace, the promise of the kingdom, the comfort of the gospel. But the prophetic task is bitter: to speak God’s word to a world that does not want to hear it, to witness to the truth in the face of hostility, to suffer for the testimony of Jesus. The whole book of Revelation is this little scroll: sweet with the glory of the Lamb, bitter with the suffering of faithful witness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Angel and the Little Scroll
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Six trumpets have sounded; the seventh does not sound until 11:15. Everything between is an interlude, exactly as chapter 7 stood between the sixth and seventh seals — a repetition that is itself an argument about how John builds his sevens.

Verses 1–2: another mighty angel comes down wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, a face like the sun and legs like pillars of fire — every detail borrowed from the descriptions of God and of Christ (1:7, 15, 16; 4:3; Ex. 13:21). He holds a little scroll, and it is already open, unlike the sealed scroll of chapter 5. He sets his right foot on the sea and his left on the land: the conqueror’s posture (Josh. 1:3), with one foot on each of the two places the beasts of chapter 13 will rise from.

Verse 3: he calls out like a lion roaring — the prophets’ image for God speaking (Amos 3:8; Hos. 11:10; Joel 3:16) — and the seven thunders sound, the definite article suggesting a known set, most likely the sevenfold voice of the LORD in Psalm 29. Verse 4: John, pen in hand and about to write, is stopped: Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down.

Verses 5–7: the angel raises his right hand and swears — the posture of Daniel 12:6–7 — by the one who lives for ever and who made heaven, earth and sea, that there would be no more delay, and that at the seventh trumpet the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.

Verses 8–10: John is sent to take the open scroll and told Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey — Ezekiel’s commission exactly (Ezek. 2:9–3:3; cf. Jer. 15:16). He eats, and reports the tastes in the order he met them: sweet first, bitter after. Verse 11 sends him back to work: You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sealed Thunders and the Swallowed Scroll

A mighty angel in his master’s glory stands on sea and land. What the seven thunders said is sealed — the one sealed sentence in an unsealed book. The angel swears there will be no more delay, and John must eat the little scroll: sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An exiled old man was recommissioned to prophesy to peoples, nations and kings.

Now: Do not claim to know what God has withheld; and expect the gospel to be sweet to receive and costly to carry.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, and his face was like the sun, and his legs like pillars of fire. He had a little scroll open in his hand. And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, and his face was like the sun, and his legs like pillars of fire. He had a little scroll open in his hand. And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land,

Meaning first. Revelation 10 is a pause between the sixth and seventh trumpets, as chapter 7 was between the sixth and seventh seals. A mighty angel comes down from heaven, robed in cloud, crowned with a rainbow, shining like the sun, with a little open scroll in his hand, and plants his feet on sea and land (vv. 1–2). He roars like a lion, and seven thunders speak, but John is told to seal up what they said and not write it (vv. 3–4). The angel raises his hand and swears by the eternal Creator that there will be no more delay: when the seventh trumpet sounds, the mystery of God announced by the prophets will be fulfilled (vv. 5–7). John is told to take the little scroll and eat it; it is sweet as honey in his mouth but bitter in his stomach (vv. 8–10). Then he is told that he must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages and kings (v. 11). The chapter renews John’s commission as a prophet, like Ezekiel’s, and prepares for chapter 11. God’s word is sweet to receive and bitter to carry, because it brings both salvation and judgement, and the church that proclaims it must suffer. And over the whole chapter stands the God who made sea and land and everything in them, who has sworn that his plan will be finished exactly as he promised.

The setting. In Ezekiel 2:8–3:3, God gives Ezekiel a scroll written on front and back with lamentation, mourning and woe, and tells him to eat it; it is sweet as honey in his mouth, and then he is sent to prophesy to Israel. In Daniel 12:4–9, Daniel is told to seal up his vision until the end, and a man clothed in linen raises both hands to heaven and swears by him who lives for ever that it will be for a time, times and half a time. Revelation 10 echoes both, and John’s first readers, who knew those books far better than most of us do, would have recognised the scene before a word was spoken in it.

John does not rush his sevens. Six trumpets have sounded. The seventh does not sound until 11:15, and everything between is an interlude, exactly as chapter 7 stood between the sixth and seventh seals. That repetition is itself an argument. Twice now, at the very point where a reader is braced for the end, the vision stops and turns to look at the church. God does not hurry past his people on the way to the finish. Before the last trumpet, he shows them where they stand and what they are for.

Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven. Every detail of this figure is one the reader has already met, and that is what has made him controversial. He is wrapped in a cloud, and the cloud is what God travels in and what Christ returns on (1:7). The rainbow over his head was around the throne in 4:3, the sign of God’s covenant faithfulness since the days of Noah. His face like the sun is precisely how the risen Christ was described in 1:16. His legs like pillars of fire recall the feet like burnished bronze in 1:15, and the pillar of fire that led Israel through the wilderness by night (Exodus 13:21). It is not surprising that some readers, including serious ones, have concluded that this is Christ himself.

Where Christians differ: is the mighty angel Christ? Some identify him with Christ himself, because of the cloud, the rainbow, the sun-like face and the fiery legs. Three things tell against it, and they should be given plainly. The word is allos: another mighty angel, another of the same kind as the mighty angel of 5:2, which puts him in a category with the angels. In verse 6 he swears by the one who lives for ever and ever, and swearing by a higher authority is not something Christ does or needs to do; when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself (Hebrews 6:13). And Revelation never once calls Christ an angel, though it names him a hundred other things; he is the one the angels worship (5:11–12). Verdict: he is most likely a powerful angel who reflects Christ’s glory and represents him. Angels who come from God’s presence share something of his glory, as Moses’ face shone after he had been with God (Exodus 34:29).

A herald in his master’s livery. That is the more useful reading, and it explains the borrowed glory. When an ambassador arrives wearing the king’s colours, the point is not that he is the king. The point is whose message he is carrying. Every ray of light on this angel’s face is reflected light. He shines because he has come from the one who is himself the light, and the reader who sees the angel is meant to think at once of Christ.

What it does not mean. The angel’s glory does not make him an object of worship. When John later falls at an angel’s feet, he is told not to: worship God (19:10; 22:9). The more glorious a servant of God appears, the more firmly he points away from himself.

He had a little scroll open in his hand. Two things about it. It is little: the Greek uses a diminutive, biblaridion, a different word from the great sealed scroll of chapter 5. And it is open. The scroll in chapter 5 had seven seals and nobody in heaven or on earth could break them, until the Lamb who was slain took it from the hand of him who sat on the throne. This one is already unrolled, lying open in an angel’s hand, and in a few verses John will be told to walk over and take it. It is probably closely connected with the scroll of chapter 5, which the Lamb has now opened: God’s revealed purpose, now handed to a man to proclaim. Whether it is a portion of the great scroll or a separate commission is not stated. What is stated is that it is small enough to hold, open enough to read, and about to be given to a man. What the Lamb alone could open, the Lamb now gives away.

And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land. The posture is a claim. Land and sea are the ancient way of saying everywhere, and planting a foot on something is what a conqueror does to territory: every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you (Joshua 1:3). This is not a figure standing beside the world. He is standing on it, a gigantic figure astride the earth, because his message concerns the whole of it. And he has one foot on the element the beast will rise out of (13:1) and one on the element the second beast will rise out of (13:11).

Before the beasts appear. Hold that picture when the next three chapters grow dark. Before the dragon appears, before either beast comes up, a messenger from heaven has already been shown standing with a foot on each of the places they come from, holding an open scroll, wrapped in a cloud, with a covenant rainbow over his head. The order of the visions is itself a comfort. Evil will rise out of the sea and out of the earth, and it will look for a time as though it owns them. But God has already shown his church whose feet are on that ground.

What is the rainbow doing here, in a chapter about judgement? It is a reminder of what God has promised, worn over the head of the one bringing his message. After the flood God set his bow in the cloud as a sign that he would never again destroy the earth by water (Genesis 9:13–16), and in Revelation the same bow encircles his throne (4:3). So even the heralds of judgement come with mercy over their heads. The judgements of Revelation are real and terrible, but they are not the outbursts of a God who has forgotten his covenant. They are the acts of a faithful God clearing the ground for a new creation, and keeping every promise to his people while he does it.

In a sentence. Then I saw another powerful angel coming down from heaven, clothed in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, a face shining like the sun and legs like pillars of fire; he held a small scroll lying open in his hand, and he planted his right foot on the sea and his left foot on the land.

On a Tuesday. God’s word is for the whole world, sea and land. Your part of the world is included, the street, the office, the family table, and your part in passing it on matters. And when the news is frightening, when powers rise that seem to own the earth and the sea, remember the order of these chapters: the messenger’s feet were on that ground before the beasts came up out of it. You do not have to pretend the darkness is not dark. You only have to remember who stood there first.

For worship. Blessed be the God whose servants shine with borrowed light, because his own glory is so great that even his messengers glow with it. Before the beast ever rose from the sea, he had planted his claim upon the sea; before the second beast ever came up from the earth, his herald stood upon the earth. The rainbow of his faithfulness is over every word he sends. And the scroll that no one in heaven or on earth could open lies open now, because the Lamb was slain and is worthy, and what he opened he has given to his people.

verseByVerse.quote: and called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring. When he called out, the seven thunders sounded. And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, "Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring. When he called out, the seven thunders sounded. And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down.”

The setting. Amos 3:8 says the lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken; who can but prophesy? Hosea 11:10 says the LORD will roar like a lion, and Joel 3:16 that the LORD roars from Zion. Psalm 29 describes the voice of the LORD seven times as thunder over the waters. Paul was caught up into paradise and heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter (2 Corinthians 12:4).

And called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring. The verb, mykatai, means to roar or bellow, a voice of power that demands attention. A lion’s roar is not a warning shot. It can be heard for miles, and its purpose is to announce possession of territory. Amos used it of God speaking, and Hosea and Joel use it the same way. And in this book there is one Lion, of the tribe of Judah, who turned out to be a Lamb (5:5–6). The angel standing on sea and land roars with his master’s voice, and the roar says: this ground is claimed.

When he called out, the seven thunders sounded. The definite article is odd and deliberate: not seven thunders but the seven thunders, hai hepta brontai, as though John expects his readers to know which ones. The likeliest background is Psalm 29, where the voice of the LORD sounds over the waters seven times in eleven verses, breaking the cedars, flashing forth flames of fire, shaking the wilderness, and ending with the whole temple crying Glory! In that psalm the thunderstorm is the voice of God himself. So this is a further series of seven, arriving between the trumpets and the bowls, and the reader is by now trained to recognise it: seven seals, seven trumpets, seven thunders. The pattern says that a full sequence of divine speech has just been uttered.

They spoke words. John hears them, and he understands them. That is clear from the next verse, since a man does not reach for a pen to write down noise. Whatever the thunders said, it was articulate, it was complete, and it came from the same source as everything else in this book.

And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write. John has been faithful to the command to write what he saw (1:11, 19). And then it is taken away from him, and from every reader since.

But I heard a voice from heaven saying, Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down. This is the strangest instruction in the book, and it is the exact reverse of every other one John receives. He has been told to write from the beginning: write what you see in a book and send it to the seven churches (1:11); write therefore the things that you have seen (1:19); and at the end, write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true (21:5). Again and again in this book he is told to write. Once he is told not to. And notice the timing. The pen is already in his hand. He was about to write: he had heard it, understood it, judged it worth recording, and started to move. The prohibition arrives mid-action.

The one sealed sentence. Seal up (sphragison) is the reverse of what happens everywhere else in Revelation. Daniel was told to seal his book until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4, 9). At the close of this book John is explicitly told not to seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near (22:10). Revelation is the unsealed book. There is exactly one sealed sentence in it, and we do not have it.

Why were the thunders sealed? Several answers have been offered. Perhaps they were further judgements that God has chosen to cancel or cut short, so that the end comes without more warnings, and the very next verse says there will be no more delay. Perhaps they are held back to show that the warnings already given are enough. Or perhaps they are sealed simply to teach that God has not told us everything. None of the first answers can be proved, and the honest position is that nobody knows, because the whole point of the verse is that we were not told. What is certain is the last lesson: the secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law (Deuteronomy 29:29).

A boundary God has set. Two categories, in Moses’ sentence, and both are God’s decision. And note what the revealed things are for in that verse: not so that we may know, but so that we may do. That has a very practical edge for anyone who reads Revelation the way it is most often read. There is an appetite, and it is not always a healthy one, for more than has been given: the date, the identity, the exact sequence, the name behind the number. This verse says that the appetite has a limit and that God set it. John, an apostle, in the Spirit, on assignment, with the information in his ears and his pen moving, was refused permission to pass it on.

What it does not mean. The sealed thunders do not invite speculation, or claims by later teachers to have discovered what they said. Some groups have claimed that their founders revealed the seven thunders. Anybody who claims to have recovered what the thunders said is claiming something John himself was forbidden to give. What God has sealed, no one may unseal, and the canon is closed (22:18–19). We have everything we need for life and godliness in what is written (2 Peter 1:3; 2 Timothy 3:16–17).

Does this mean the Bible is incomplete? No. It means the Bible is complete for its purpose, which is not the same as exhaustive. God has not told us everything he knows; he has told us everything we need, to know him, to be saved, and to live for him until Christ returns. A father does not tell a child everything about the family finances, and the child is not the poorer for it; he is told what he needs, by someone who loves him and knows the rest. The sealed thunders are a reminder that Scripture’s silences are as deliberate as its words, and that a believer who keeps to what is written is not missing anything God meant him to have.

When God does not answer my question. There is a gentler application here too, for a believer who has spent years asking God something that has never been answered. Why did that happen? Why was there no child? Why did the prayer of a good man seem to come to nothing? This verse does not say the answer does not exist. The thunders spoke; there was content; John understood it. It says the answer exists and has not been given, and that the withholding is deliberate and comes from heaven in a voice. Being told no by God about a piece of information is not the same as there being nothing there. And the God who withholds it is the same God who did not withhold his own Son (Romans 8:32). He can be trusted with what he keeps.

In a sentence. He shouted with a loud voice like a lion roaring, and when he shouted, the seven thunders spoke; when they had spoken, I was about to write it down, but I heard a voice from heaven say, Keep secret what the seven thunders said; do not write it.

On a Tuesday. You do not need to know everything about the future. Be content with what God has revealed, and trust him with what he has not. When a book, a video or a preacher offers you the hidden key to the end times, the date or the name or the sequence the rest of the church has missed, remember that an apostle with the pen in his hand was told to stop. And when your own unanswered question returns in the night, bring it to God honestly, and then put beside it the things he has plainly said: that he works all things together for good for those who love him, that nothing can separate you from his love, and that he will wipe away every tear. Those are revealed, and they are yours.

For worship. The voice of the LORD is upon the waters, the God of glory thunders, and his voice is full of majesty. He speaks in sevens and is never exhausted; he says more than any man could write and keeps back what he chooses, and he owes no one an explanation. Yet this God, who has secrets he will not share, has not kept back the one thing we could not live without. What the thunders said we do not know. What the cross said we know by heart: that he so loved the world, that he gave his only Son. Let him keep his secrets. He has given us himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it, that there would be no more delay, but that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it, that there would be no more delay, but that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.

The setting. In Daniel 12:7, a man clothed in linen raised his hands to heaven and swore by him who lives for ever that it would be for a time, times and half a time, and that when the shattering of the power of the holy people came to an end, all these things would be finished. Raising the hand was the gesture of a solemn oath (Genesis 14:22; Deuteronomy 32:40). The martyrs had asked, How long? (6:10), and were told to rest a little longer (6:11).

And the angel raised his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever. The gesture is a formal oath, and the whole scene is quarried from Daniel 12. John’s readers who knew Daniel, and he has been using Daniel since chapter 1, would have recognised the posture before the content arrived. “Swore” (ōmosen) is the most solemn guarantee human speech has. Men swear by something greater than themselves, and in oaths the final confirmation ends every argument (Hebrews 6:16). This angel swears by the greatest there is: the eternal God, the highest authority in the universe.

Who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it. The one sworn by is described in a single long clause: he lives for ever and ever, and he made heaven, earth and sea and everything in all three. That is not decoration. The angel is standing on the sea and the land, and he swears by the one who made the sea and the land. Whatever the beasts about to come out of them may claim, the ground under this oath belongs to somebody else. And because God made it all, he has both the right and the power to bring it to its end. A maker may finish what he began.

That there would be no more delay. The older translations rendered it there should be time no longer, and generations of readers took it to mean the abolition of time itself. The Greek chronos can mean either time or delay, and the context settles it. This is the answer to a question asked four chapters earlier by the souls under the altar: O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long (6:10)? They were told to rest a little longer. Here, under oath, standing on the whole world, an angel announces that the little longer has run out. God’s patience, which delayed judgement to give time for repentance, will come to an end.

Textual note. The King James Version translates “that there should be time no longer”, which some have taken to mean the end of time itself. The Greek word chronos can mean delay, and the context, answering the martyrs’ How long?, shows that this is the meaning here.

The hardest thing is the waiting. The waiting has been the hardest thing in this book, and it is the hardest thing in the Christian life. Not the suffering itself so much as its open-endedness: the not knowing whether it goes on for another month or another forty years. This verse does not tell the church when. It tells the church that the when has been fixed and sworn to, on oath, by the Creator of everything, and that the postponement is over. A prisoner who knows the date of his release can bear a great deal. A believer who knows that the date has been sworn to by God can bear more.

What it does not mean. “No more delay” does not mean the end came in John’s lifetime. It means that when the seventh trumpet sounds, the end will come without further postponement. Until then, God’s patience continues, giving time for repentance (2 Peter 3:9).

But if there is no more delay, why has it been two thousand years? Because the oath concerns what happens when the seventh trumpet sounds, not a stopwatch started in John’s day. Revelation shows the whole age between Christ’s first and second comings from several angles, and each cycle of sevens ends at the edge of the last judgement. This oath says that when God’s moment arrives there will be no further postponement, no last extension, no second thoughts. Peter answers the same question directly: the Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but is patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:8–9). Every year that passes is not God forgetting. It is God gathering the last of his elect, and the day he has fixed will not move.

But that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel. The seventh trumpet (11:15) announces the coming of God’s kingdom in full: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.

The mystery of God would be fulfilled. Mystery (mystērion) in the New Testament never means a puzzle nobody can solve. It means something once hidden that has now been disclosed: a secret told. In the New Testament the mystery is God’s plan of salvation in Christ, including the gathering of Gentiles with Jews into one people (Ephesians 3:3–6; Colossians 1:26–27), and its completion at the end, when all things are united in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth (Ephesians 1:9–10). The mystery of God is his whole purpose for the world: that in Christ he would gather up everything, judge evil, redeem a people out of every nation, and put the creation right. And the verb, etelesthē, means completed, brought to its goal, finished off. It belongs to the same family as the cry from the cross: it is finished.

Just as he announced to his servants the prophets. The last clause guards the promise against novelty. Nothing new is being introduced. What the seventh trumpet will complete is the same programme God published through Isaiah and Daniel and Amos and the rest; for the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets (Amos 3:7). And the word for announced, euēngelisen, is the verb behind gospel and evangelise. He preached the good news of it to them in advance. God’s final victory is not a threat that he has kept up his sleeve. It is good news, and he has been telling it for centuries.

The reassurance at exactly the right moment. This is what a reader most needs at this point in the book. Six trumpets have sounded and the world has grown worse; the rest of mankind has refused to repent (9:20–21); the beasts have not even arrived yet. And an angel with a foot on the sea and a foot on the land raises his hand and swears that God’s plan will be finished, on time, exactly as advertised, and that the delay is over.

How should this change the way I read the news? It should make you sober without making you frantic. The headlines are not the whole story, and they are not the last word. The world will not drift on for ever, nor collapse by accident, nor end when men decide; it will be brought to its goal by the God who made it, at a moment he has fixed and sworn to. So you do not need to decode current events to know where history is going. You need to know who is finishing it. That frees you to grieve real evils without despair, to work for good without imagining that everything depends on you, and to pray, as the church always has, Come, Lord Jesus.

In a sentence. Then the angel I had seen standing on sea and land lifted his right hand to heaven and swore by the one who lives for ever and ever, who created heaven, earth and sea and everything in them, that there would be no more waiting: when the seventh angel blows his trumpet, God’s hidden plan will be completed, just as he announced it as good news to his servants the prophets.

On a Tuesday. Think of the thing you are waiting on God for, the healing, the justice, the prodigal, the end of a long loneliness, and ask what you have been telling yourself about the delay. That God has forgotten? That he cannot? That he has changed his mind? Then set beside it this oath. God has not told you when, but he has sworn that his purpose will be completed and that he will not postpone it one moment beyond the time he has set. You may still have to wait. You do not have to wait wondering whether he means it.

For worship. God has sworn, and there is no one greater by whom he could swear. He lives for ever and ever; he made the heavens and all their hosts, the earth and all that fills it, the sea and every creature in its depths; and he will bring all things to their good end, just as he promised. The mystery hidden for ages is told now in the gospel: Christ, the Lamb who was slain, gathering a people from every nation and uniting all things in himself. What God began in a garden he will finish in a city, and not one word he preached to his prophets will fall to the ground. Worship him, the Creator who is also the finisher, and whose patience with sinners is the only reason the trumpet has not yet sounded.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, "Go, take the scroll that is open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land." So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, "Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey." And I took the little scroll from the hand of the angel and ate it. It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, “Go, take the scroll that is open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land.” So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, “Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey.” And I took the little scroll from the hand of the angel and ate it. It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter.

The setting. Ezekiel ate a scroll full of lamentation and woe, and it was sweet as honey in his mouth (Ezekiel 3:1–3); afterwards he went in bitterness, in the heat of his spirit, and sat among the exiles seven days, overwhelmed (Ezekiel 3:14–15). Jeremiah said, your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart (Jeremiah 15:16), and yet his ministry brought him great suffering. Psalm 19:10 and 119:103 call God’s words sweeter than honey.

Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, Go, take the scroll. The same voice that told him not to write now tells him to move. John is not just to look at the scroll but to take it: God’s word must be received personally. And John does something rather charming. He went to the angel and told him to give him the little scroll. He does not snatch it. He walks across and asks. The whole exchange has the texture of an errand, and a mighty angel with his feet on the world hands a book to an old man who asked for it.

Take and eat it. The verb, kataphage, is strong: devour it, eat it up. Ezekiel was given this exact commission some seven hundred years earlier, and John expects it to be recognised. A hand held out a scroll written on both sides with words of lamentation and mourning and woe, and the prophet was told to eat it and go and speak to the house of Israel, and he ate it, and it was in his mouth as sweet as honey (Ezekiel 2:9–3:3).

Why eating? Eating is the picture, and it is chosen carefully. A messenger could be handed a script and read it out; that is what a herald does. This is not that. Nobody delivers a message by digesting it. What eating does is make a thing part of you, slowly, internally, irreversibly. To eat a scroll means to take God’s word inside, to absorb it and make it part of oneself, before speaking it to others. God’s word is not first material to be transmitted. It is food to be taken into a person until it is in his blood, and only then does he speak. A prophet cannot pass on what he has not first taken in. Our Lord said the same of himself in a deeper way: man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matthew 4:4).

It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey. Bitter (pikranei) and sweet (glyky), and both are true of the gospel at once. Why sweet? Because it is the word of God, and there is nothing better. The psalmist said God’s rules were sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb (Psalm 19:10). It is his word, full of grace, and it tells of his victory and the salvation of his people. To be handed something from the throne room and told it is for you is the sweetest thing that can happen to a human being.

Why bitter? Because of what is in it. It brings judgement on the unrepentant, and those who proclaim it will suffer, as chapter 11 is about to show. John is about to be shown two witnesses killed in the street, a dragon hunting a woman, a beast making war on the saints and conquering them, and a city drunk on the blood of the martyrs. A man cannot take that in and feel nothing. Ezekiel left his commission in bitterness and sat stunned among the exiles for a week. The word that saves is also the word that judges, and nobody who loves people can carry the second half of that sentence lightly.

And I took the little scroll from the hand of the angel and ate it. It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter. John obeys, and experiences both, and he reports it in the order he experienced it: sweet first, bitter after. The angel had warned him in the reverse order, bitter then sweet, as though preparing him for the sting; the experience arrived the other way round.

The order of the two tastes. The order is the point, and it describes something every honest Christian eventually recognises. The gospel is sweet on the way in and costly on the way down. Nobody is converted by being told what it will require; they are converted by being told they are loved and forgiven, and it is honey. The bitterness comes later, and it is not a sign that something has gone wrong. It is the taste of a truth being taken in by a person who now has to live in a world that does not want it.

The taste of ministry. And it is specifically the taste of bearing witness. Anyone who has had to say a true thing that would cost him a friendship knows the exact sequence: the delight of knowing it, and then the churning at two in the morning before the conversation. A preacher who finds Scripture only sweet has not yet noticed what is in it. One who finds it only bitter has forgotten why he started. The prophet gets both, in that order, from the same scroll.

What it does not mean. The bitterness does not mean God’s word is harmful. It means that taking God’s word seriously brings grief as well as joy: grief over sin and judgement, and the cost of faithful witness. A preacher or Christian who only ever finds the word sweet may not have digested all of it.

Why is Revelation so hard to read? This verse is the honest answer. Partly because it was never meant to be a comfortable read. It is sweet as honey: the Lamb reigns, the martyrs are vindicated, God wipes away every tear. And it is bitter, because the road to those things runs through everything in chapters 11 to 20. John was given both, and he was made to swallow before he was allowed to speak. If you find parts of this book troubling, you are reading it as its first reader did. Keep reading to the end. The bitterness is real, but it is not the last taste.

What does eating the word look like for an ordinary Christian? It is the difference between reading the Bible and taking it in. Read a passage slowly, more than once. Ask what it shows you of God, what it says to you, and what it asks of you. Turn it into prayer before you put it down. Carry one verse with you through the day and come back to it at odd moments, the way you return to a conversation that mattered. Memorise some of it, because what is in you cannot be taken away. You will not do this perfectly, and God does not require that you do. But a short passage chewed is worth more than a long one swallowed whole and forgotten by lunch.

What if the Bible has only felt bitter to me lately? Then you may be in exactly the place this verse describes, and it is not a sign that God has left you. Sometimes the bitterness is the cost of obeying, or the grief of seeing sin and judgement clearly, and that is the word doing its work. Sometimes it is that you have been reading the commands without the promises, the law without the gospel. Go back to the honey: read a Gospel, a psalm of trust, Romans 8, Isaiah 53, and look at Christ for yourself, not only at your duty. The scroll is sweet first. Ask God to let you taste that again, and he will.

In a sentence. Then the voice I had heard from heaven spoke to me again: Go and take the open scroll from the hand of the angel standing on the sea and the land; so I went to the angel and asked him for the little scroll, and he said, Take it and eat it; it will turn your stomach sour, but in your mouth it will taste as sweet as honey; I took the little scroll from his hand and ate it, and it was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had swallowed it, my stomach turned bitter.

On a Tuesday. Read the Bible not just for information but to take it in, slowly, prayerfully, until it becomes part of you. Expect it to bring both delight and grief, and let both shape how you speak to others. If you have a hard true thing to say to someone this week, a word of warning, an honest correction, the gospel to a friend who does not want it, expect the churning before you say it, and do not take the churning as proof you should stay silent. Say it with the sweetness still in your mouth: as someone who has been forgiven, speaking to someone you want to see forgiven too.

For worship. How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! The word of the Lord is the bread of heaven, and he feeds his servants with it before he sends them. And the bitterness, too, he knows from the inside. The Word who became flesh took the whole scroll of lamentation and mourning and woe into himself; he drank the cup that was bitter beyond all others, so that the word his people carry could be, at its heart, the sweetest news in the world. He tasted death for everyone he came for, and he gives them honey from the rock.
verseByVerse.note: Like Ezekiel, John eats God’s message: sweet to receive, bitter because it announces judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And I was told, "You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I was told, “You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.”

And I was told. The Greek is literally they say to me, legousin moi, an indefinite plural, probably meaning the heavenly voice and the angel together.

You must again prophesy. Consider who is being told this. An old man on a bare island of a few square miles, under Roman banishment, with no congregation, no property, no pulpit and no way home. He has already written the seven letters. He has already been shown the throne, the Lamb, the seals and the trumpets. By any ordinary reckoning his work is behind him. You must again prophesy. The word “must” is dei: it is necessary, a divine command, the same word used in 1:1 of the things that must soon take place, and the word Jesus used of his own suffering. This is not an invitation and it is not a career step. It is a commission, and John is not asked whether he would like it. “Again” (palin): John’s commission is renewed. He has already prophesied; now he must go on, with the second half of the book.

About many peoples and nations and languages and kings. The scope is enormous. The fourfold phrase is the one John has used since 5:9 and 7:9 for the whole human race, with kings substituted for tribes, because from chapter 11 onward the book turns to the powers of the earth: the kings of the earth in chapters 13 to 19. A prisoner with no legal standing has just been given a preaching commission covering every nation on earth and their rulers, and the only equipment he is issued is a small scroll he has eaten. The message concerns the fate of the nations and their rulers, for judgement and for salvation.

About, or against. The preposition, epi, matters too. He is to prophesy about them, or possibly against them; the Greek can bear either. Prophecy in Scripture is very rarely prediction for its own sake. It is God’s verdict on the present, delivered out loud, usually to people who did not ask for it. Emperors who thought themselves gods are about to hear what heaven thinks of them, from a man they had exiled.

What it does not mean. This does not mean that John will literally travel and preach to all nations. His prophecy, written in this book, goes to them. And the church, taking up his commission, prophesies to the nations through the gospel (11:3–6).

Are there prophets like John today? Not in John’s sense. John received new revelation directly from God, and what he received is now written down as the last book of the Bible, with a warning against adding to it or taking from it (22:18–19). That kind of prophecy has ceased, because the canon is complete. But the prophetic task of the church goes on. Every faithful preacher who opens this book, and every believer who tells a neighbour what God has said in Scripture, is declaring God’s word to peoples and nations and kings. We do not receive new thunders. We carry the scroll that has already been opened, and it is enough.

When my useful years seem over. There is something here for any Christian who has concluded that his work for God is finished, because of age, or illness, or a job that ended, or a church that no longer asks. John’s circumstances were worse than most: exiled, elderly, isolated, and already the author of a Gospel and three letters. Heaven’s assessment was again. The most extraordinary assignment of his life arrived after everything that looked like his ministry had been taken away from him. The work may look different now: prayer instead of travel, a letter instead of a sermon, faithfulness in a small room instead of influence in a large one. But no one who belongs to Christ is ever discharged from his service while he still has breath.

The shape of the chapter. Look at it as it closes. A messenger comes down wearing his master’s glory and plants his feet on the whole world. Seven thunders speak and are sealed, so that the church learns there is a limit to what it will be told. An oath is sworn by the Creator of everything that the waiting is over and the mystery of God will be finished exactly as he promised his prophets. And then a scroll is handed to a man, and he eats it, and it is honey and it is bitterness, and he is sent back to work. That is the pattern of every real commission God has ever given. He does not hand out information to be relayed. He feeds a person with his own word until it is inside him, and then sends him out to say it, and the sweetness and the bitterness both come from the same source, and neither of them is a mistake.

In a sentence. Then I was told, You must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages and kings.

On a Tuesday. The gospel concerns every nation and every ruler. Pray for kings and all who are in high positions (1 Timothy 2:1–2), and support the spread of the gospel to all peoples. Then bring it closer: who in your own small world needs to hear what God has said, and has no one else to tell them? You do not need John’s visions to do it. You need the scroll he ate, which is open on your table, and the willingness to say again what you have said before.

For worship. The Lord of the nations is not finished with his servants when the world has finished with them. He found an old man on a prison island and sent him to the kings of the earth, and the emperors who exiled him are dust, while his book is read in every language under heaven. All the peoples and nations and tongues belong to the Lamb who was slain, who ransomed people for God from every one of them by his blood. His word runs swiftly, and it will not return to him empty. Blessed be the King of the nations, who feeds his servants with his word and sends them out again.

11.title: The Two Witnesses and the Seventh Trumpet
11.overview:
Chapter 11 is the most compressed chapter in Revelation, covering the entire church age from two angles: the measuring of the temple (the church’s preservation), the ministry of the two witnesses (the church’s prophetic witness), their death and resurrection (the church’s apparent defeat and vindication), and the seventh trumpet (the declaration of the kingdom consummated). It is also one of the most contested chapters in the book.

The measuring of the temple in vv. 1–2 has generated enormous debate. Dispensationalists understand it as a prophecy of a literal rebuilt temple in Jerusalem during the tribulation, the outer court given over to Gentile domination for 42 months. The amillennial reading understands the temple as the church (following Paul’s regular use of temple-language for the believing community — 1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21; 2 Corinthians 6:16) and the measuring as God’s preservation of his people. The outer court “given over to the nations” represents the church’s visible vulnerability to worldly power — it will be trampled — while the inner sanctuary (the true community of the redeemed) is preserved.

The two witnesses of vv. 3–13 are the most important image in the chapter. Their identity has been debated endlessly: Moses and Elijah (because of the specific powers: turning water to blood = Moses, shutting the sky = Elijah), Elijah and Enoch (the two who did not die), or — the majority Reformed reading — the whole witnessing church across the church age. The number two is the number of legal testimony (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15; Matthew 18:16); the two witnesses represent the complete testimony of the church to the gospel of Jesus Christ. Their supernatural powers (fire from their mouths, power over rain and waters) are the powers of the prophetic word: proclamation that both judges and saves.

The seventh trumpet of vv. 15–19 does not release a new woe but sounds the final declaration of the kingdom: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.” This is the answer to the Lord’s Prayer (“Your kingdom come”) and the goal toward which all of history moves. The kingdom is announced as already accomplished — the aorist tense of the verb (“has become”) indicates a completed action. What will still unfold in chapters 12–22 is the working out of what has already been declared from the throne.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: John is given a measuring rod and told to measure the temple, the altar and the worshippers — but expressly not the outer court, which is given over to the nations to trample for forty-two months. Measuring in the prophets is a legal owner marking out what is his (Ezek. 40–42; Zech. 2:1–5). Something is claimed and something is deliberately left out, and both are God’s decision.

Verses 3–4: two witnesses are granted authority to prophesy 1,260 days in sackcloth — the coarse black goat hair of mourning, not the uniform of a triumphant movement. They are the two olive trees and the two lampstands of Zechariah 4, where two olive trees feed oil straight into a lampstand and the governing word is not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit (Zech. 4:6).

Verses 5–6 give their powers, and they are two men’s résumés side by side: fire from the mouth (cf. Jer. 5:14), shutting the sky so that no rain falls — Elijah, for three and a half years (1 Kings 17:1; Luke 4:25) — and turning water to blood and striking with plagues, which is Moses in Egypt (Ex. 7:17–20).

Verses 7–8: when they have finished their testimony, the beast from the bottomless pit makes war on them, conquers them and kills them, and their bodies lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified. John supplies the interpretive key himself: pneumatikōs, symbolically. Verses 9–10: for three and a half days the world gazes at the bodies, refuses them burial, and throws the only party in the book — making merry and exchanging presents, because these two prophets had been a torment.

Verses 11–12: a breath of life from God enters them and they stand on their feet (Ezek. 37:10), and a loud voice says Come up here! — the words spoken to John at 4:1 — and they go up in a cloud and their enemies watched them. Verse 13: an earthquake takes a tenth of the city and seven thousand people, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. Verse 14 closes the section: the second woe has passed.
verseByVerse.theology:
Measured, Trampled, Raised

God measures his temple and leaves the outer court to be trampled for a bounded time. His two witnesses prophesy in sackcloth, are killed when their testimony is finished, lie unburied while the world celebrates, and are raised and called up in their enemies’ sight.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Plagues had not moved the world; the witnesses’ death and vindication did.

Now: No faithful witness is cut off before his testimony is finished, and a witness that troubles nobody may not be one.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, "Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there, but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, “Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there, but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.

Meaning first. Revelation 11 shows the church’s life and witness in this age, and then the sounding of the seventh trumpet. John is told to measure God’s temple, its altar and its worshippers, but to leave out the outer court, which is given to the nations, who will trample the holy city for forty-two months (vv. 1–2): God’s people are protected in their inner life, while exposed outwardly to persecution. Two witnesses, clothed in sackcloth, prophesy for 1,260 days; they are the two olive trees and two lampstands, and like Elijah and Moses they have power to devour enemies with fire, shut the sky and strike the earth with plagues (vv. 3–6). When their testimony is finished, the beast from the abyss kills them, and their bodies lie unburied in the great city, spiritually Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified, while the world celebrates (vv. 7–10). After three and a half days, God’s breath enters them, they stand up, and they are taken up to heaven in a cloud as their enemies watch (vv. 11–12). An earthquake strikes, seven thousand die, and the rest give glory to God (vv. 13–14). Then the seventh trumpet sounds: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ; the elders give thanks that God has begun to reign, judged the dead, rewarded his servants and destroyed the destroyers; and God’s temple in heaven opens to show the ark of the covenant (vv. 15–19). The chapter pictures the whole church age: a witnessing church, protected yet suffering, apparently defeated, finally vindicated, and the kingdom of Christ coming in full. It is the story of the Lord Jesus told again in the lives of his people: witness, death, resurrection, ascension, and a kingdom that cannot be shaken.

The setting. Ezekiel 40–48 describes a man measuring a new temple, a vision of God’s restored dwelling among his people. Zechariah 2:1–5 describes a man measuring Jerusalem, which God will protect as a wall of fire all around. Measuring in the Old Testament can mean protecting and preserving what belongs to God (Zechariah 2), or marking out for judgement (2 Kings 21:13; Lamentations 2:8). Daniel spoke of a period of a time, times and half a time (three and a half years) during which a hostile king would persecute God’s holy people (Daniel 7:25; 12:7). Jesus said that Jerusalem would be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled (Luke 21:24).

Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff. The rod (kalamos) is a reed, a measuring stick about three metres long. Measuring in the prophets is not surveying. It is the act of a legal owner marking out what is his and what he intends to protect. Ezekiel was shown a man with a measuring reed who measured a temple chapter after chapter. Zechariah saw a man with a measuring line going to measure Jerusalem, and was told the city would be so full that it needed no walls, because the LORD himself would be a wall of fire around her and the glory in her midst. To be measured is to be claimed.

Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there. The word for temple, naos, is the sanctuary, the inner shrine, not the whole complex of courts. And notice the third item on the list: those who worship there. You can measure a building and an altar with a reed. You cannot measure worshippers with one, unless the temple is made of them. People are in view, not just a building. In the New Testament the temple of God is the church, God’s people in whom he dwells: do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you (1 Corinthians 3:16–17; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Ephesians 2:19–22; 1 Peter 2:5)? Measuring the temple means God marks out his people as his own and guarantees their protection, as the sealing did in chapter 7. The two visions say one thing in two figures.

But do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations. “Leave that out” is literally throw it outside, ekbale exōthen. The outer court was where Gentiles could come in Herod’s temple. Here it stands for the church’s outward, visible life in the world, which is exposed to attack. Something is measured, and something is deliberately left unmeasured, and both are God’s decision. He does not say the outer court is beyond his reach. He says leave that out, and then it is given over: the trampling is permitted, and the permission comes from him.

Protected and exposed. That is the pastoral heart of the passage, and it should be stated carefully. The church is not promised that nothing can be trampled. It is promised that what the trampling can reach is not the temple. Buildings burn, reputations are ruined, denominations collapse, believers are imprisoned and killed. None of that touches the sanctuary, the altar, or the worshippers, and God has drawn the line himself with a measuring rod. The church is safe in its inner relationship with God, but outwardly vulnerable to persecution. Both halves are true at once, and a Christian who expects only the first will be bewildered when the second arrives.

And they will trample the holy city for forty-two months. “Trample” (patēsousin) is tread underfoot. The holy city is God’s people, the church, the new Jerusalem in the making (21:2). This is the first appearance of the book’s most repeated number, and it comes in three interchangeable forms: forty-two months (11:2; 13:5), 1,260 days (11:3; 12:6), and a time, and times, and half a time (12:14). All three are three and a half years. They come from Daniel, where the little horn wears out the saints for a time, times, and half a time (Daniel 7:25; 12:7), and they recall the three and a half years of drought in Elijah’s day (Luke 4:25; James 5:17).

Half of seven. In a book where seven is the number of completeness, half of seven is the number of a period that is real, severe, and definitely not complete: broken off before it can run its course. In Revelation it is the whole period between Christ’s first and second comings, when the church witnesses and suffers. Its message is the reason John keeps repeating it: this is a bounded time. Somebody has already written down when it stops.

Where Christians differ: is this a literal temple in Jerusalem? Dispensationalists hold that a third temple will be rebuilt in Jerusalem before Christ returns, with sacrifices restored, and that this passage describes it during a literal three-and-a-half-year period. This view has the merit of wanting to take the words plainly, and those who hold it love the Scriptures. But on the usual dating John wrote around AD 95, a quarter of a century after the temple was destroyed, so a literal reading requires a temple that does not yet exist. Verdict: the temple is the church, the people of God. The New Testament never anticipates a rebuilt temple with renewed sacrifices; Hebrews teaches that Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice has made the temple and its sacrifices obsolete (Hebrews 8:13; 10:11–18). Revelation itself shows no temple in the new Jerusalem, because God and the Lamb are its temple (21:22). The worshippers are measured with the temple, showing that people are in view. And the number forty-two months is drawn from Daniel’s symbolic times, used in Revelation for the whole church age.

What it does not mean. The trampling does not mean that God has abandoned his people or lost control. He measures and protects; he sets the time limit. The outer court is given over by his permission, for a set time.

If I am measured and protected, why do Christians still suffer and die? Because the protection promised here is not protection from all harm but protection of what you truly are in God. The outer court is trampled, and that is real: believers lose jobs, health, property and sometimes life. What cannot be touched is your belonging to God, your access to him, and your final salvation. Jesus said the same in one breath: some of you they will put to death, yet not a hair of your head will perish (Luke 21:16–18). Both are true. The world can reach your body and your circumstances. It cannot reach the place where God has measured you as his own, and it cannot keep you there beyond the time he has fixed.

In a sentence. Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff and told: Go and measure the temple of God and the altar, and count those who worship there; but leave out the courtyard outside the temple and do not measure it, because it has been handed over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.

On a Tuesday. The world may trample on the church outwardly, mocking, marginalising and persecuting it. But God has measured you as his own. Your inner life with him is safe. So when your reputation is attacked for following Christ, or the church you love is shrinking, or the culture treats your faith as a joke, do not conclude that the sanctuary has fallen. Go to the altar. Pray. Worship with God’s people on the Lord’s day. That is the measured ground, and nothing outside it can take it from you.

For worship. The Lord knows those who are his, and he has measured them with his own rod. Not one worshipper is missing from his count; not one is left in the outer court by oversight. He has set a wall of fire around his people and his glory in their midst. Let the nations trample what they are permitted to trample for the days he has numbered. The sanctuary is his, the altar is his, the worshippers are his, and the Lamb who was slain has written down the day the trampling ends.
verseByVerse.note: Forty-two months, 1,260 days (v. 3) and “a time, and times, and half a time” (12:14) are all three and a half years — Daniel’s limited time of trouble.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth." These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth.” These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.

The setting. In Zechariah 4, the prophet sees a golden lampstand with two olive trees beside it, supplying oil; they are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth, Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, a king and a priest who rebuilt the temple, not by might nor by power, but by God’s Spirit. In the law, two witnesses were required to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus sent his disciples out two by two (Luke 10:1). Sackcloth was worn in mourning and repentance, as by the prophets (Isaiah 20:2; Jonah 3:5–6).

And I will grant authority to my two witnesses. Witnesses (martysin): witness is the church’s calling throughout Revelation (1:2, 9; 2:13; 6:9; 12:11, 17), and the word would in time give us our word martyr, because so many who bore witness died for it. Two is the legal number for valid testimony: only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established (Deuteronomy 19:15). Their whole activity in this chapter is testimony, and it is true, and it will stand in God’s court. And the authority is granted. They do not take it, earn it or vote it to themselves. It is given by the one who calls them my witnesses.

And they will prophesy for 1,260 days. 1,260 days is forty-two months, the same period as the trampling of the holy city (v. 2). The church witnesses through the whole time of its suffering. The trampling and the testimony run side by side for exactly the same length of time, which means there is never a day when the church is being trampled and has nothing to say.

Clothed in sackcloth. Coarse black goat hair, the dress of mourning and repentance, worn by Jacob for a son he thought was dead and by the whole city of Nineveh at Jonah’s preaching. Their message is a call to repentance, and they mourn over the world’s sin. This is not the uniform of a triumphant movement. It is the clothing of people who are grieved by what they see, and it tells you the tone of the church’s testimony in this age. Not swagger. Mourning. The witnesses do not gloat over the world they warn; they weep over it, as their Lord wept over Jerusalem.

These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth. The image is lifted whole from Zechariah 4, where two olive trees beside a lampstand feed oil directly into the lamps. In 1:20, the lampstands are the churches. So the two witnesses are the church, in its role of witness. The olive trees in Zechariah are a king and a priest, empowered by the Spirit; the church is a kingdom of priests (1:6), and its witness depends on the Spirit, not on might or power. In Zechariah there is one lampstand; here there are two, perhaps for the two witnesses required by law, or for the church drawn from Jews and Gentiles. And it may be no accident that of the seven churches, two, Smyrna and Philadelphia, received only praise: faithful witnesses.

Not by might, nor by power. The word the Zechariah vision turns on is the sentence spoken to Zerubbabel in the middle of it: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts (Zechariah 4:6). That is the point of the olive trees. A lampstand cannot make light and cannot make oil; it holds up what is poured into it.
