The church testifying in sackcloth for 1,260 days is not running on its own reserves, and never was. And that is the answer to a discouragement common to every serious Christian: the sense that the church is too small, too tired and too compromised to say anything the world will hear. The two witnesses are two, in mourning dress, in a city that will kill them. They are also connected to an inexhaustible supply, and the authority they have was granted.

Where Christians differ: who are the two witnesses? Many futurists see them as two individual prophets in a future tribulation, often Moses and Elijah returned, because the powers described in the next verses are precisely theirs and because those two stood with Christ on the mount of transfiguration (Matthew 17:3); or Enoch and Elijah, the two men in Scripture who did not die (Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2:11). Others suggest Peter and Paul, martyred in Rome. Verdict: the two witnesses symbolise the witnessing church throughout this age. Revelation tells us the lampstands are churches (1:20). Their ministry lasts for the same period as the church’s trampling, the whole age. The whole world sees their deaths (v. 9), which suits a worldwide church better than two individuals. And the beast makes war on them (v. 7), as it makes war on the saints (13:7). They are pictured with the powers of Moses and Elijah, the law and the prophets, because the church carries on the prophetic witness of the Old Testament, in the power of the Spirit. On any reading the substance of the passage is unchanged: God has witnesses, they are given authority, they speak for a bounded time, they are killed, and they are raised.

What it does not mean. The two witnesses are not a special class of Christians while others are spectators. All believers are called to be faithful witnesses to Christ, in word and life (Acts 1:8).

Are the 1,260 days a literal three and a half years? Futurist readers take them as the second half of a future seven-year tribulation. But John uses the three forms interchangeably for the same period (11:2–3; 12:6, 14; 13:5), drawn from Daniel, during which the church witnesses, is nourished in the wilderness and is persecuted by the beast. The more likely reading is that they describe the whole age between Christ’s comings: a limited time, cut short, under God’s control. That means you are living in the 1,260 days now. This chapter is not about someone else at the end of history. It is about the church you belong to, this week.

I am not a preacher. How am I a witness? A witness is simply someone who tells what he knows to be true. You know that Christ died for sinners, that he rose, and that he has forgiven you. You bear witness when you live honestly at work, when you speak of God without embarrassment in ordinary conversation, when you explain why you hope, when you invite a friend to church, when you refuse to join in what dishonours Christ, and when you suffer patiently. Most witness is not a sermon. It is a life lived in the open with a reason for it, and the reason given gently and respectfully when someone asks (1 Peter 3:15). The Spirit supplies the oil. You hold up the lamp.

In a sentence. And I will give my two witnesses authority to prophesy for 1,260 days, dressed in sackcloth; these witnesses are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand in the presence of the Lord of the earth.

On a Tuesday. You are part of the witnessing church. Not by might nor by power, but by God’s Spirit, your words and life point people to Christ. When you feel small and ineffective, remember that a lampstand is not meant to be impressive; it is meant to hold the light where it can be seen. And when you speak of Christ to someone, let it carry something of the sackcloth: not superiority, but sorrow for sin, your own included, and longing for the other person to come home.

For worship. He stands before the Lord of the whole earth, and so do his witnesses. The oil that never runs dry is his Spirit, poured into frail lamps that could never light themselves. He sent his first witnesses out two by two with nothing in their hands, and he has kept a testimony alive in the world through every century of trampling since. Blessed be the Lord of the lampstands, who walks among his churches, who grants authority to weak people in mourning clothes, and whose light the darkness has never overcome.

verseByVerse.quote: And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed. They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed. They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.

The setting. Elijah called down fire from heaven on soldiers sent to arrest him (2 Kings 1:10–12), and announced a drought that lasted three and a half years (1 Kings 17:1; James 5:17). Moses turned the Nile into blood and struck Egypt with plagues (Exodus 7–11). God told Jeremiah, I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people wood, and the fire shall consume them (Jeremiah 5:14).

And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. From their mouth, ek tou stomatos autōn: not from heaven, as in Elijah’s case, and not from the hand, but from the mouth. In this book that is a settled image: the sharp two-edged sword comes from the mouth of Christ (1:16; 19:15). The weapon is the word. What these witnesses do is speak. The word of judgement they proclaim will finally consume those who reject it.

If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed. The sentence is stated twice, which is unusual and deliberate. It reads like a standing legal rule rather than a description of a single event: harm them, and this is what follows. “Doomed” is dei, must, the word of divine necessity. Those who oppose God’s witnesses are opposing God, and will be judged by the word they rejected: the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day (John 12:48). The witnesses are not the executioners. They speak; the judgement falls from somewhere else.

They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying. That is Elijah exactly, who told Ahab there would be neither dew nor rain except by his word, and there was not, for three and a half years (1 Kings 17:1; Luke 4:25). And notice that Luke and James both attach that very duration to Elijah’s drought: the number of this chapter, arriving in the source material. The church’s prayers and witness have real power in the world: the prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working, and James makes the point with Elijah, a man with a nature like ours (James 5:16–18).

And they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire. That is Moses in Egypt (Exodus 7:17–20). The plagues of the trumpets are linked to the church’s witness and prayers (8:3–5): the prayers of the saints rise before God, and fire from the altar is thrown on the earth. The witnesses’ word announces God’s judgements, and their prayers call them down.

Moses and Elijah. Moses and Elijah stand behind the two witnesses, and the pairing is not random. They are the law and the prophets, the two halves of the Old Testament, and they are the two figures who appeared with Christ on the mountain and spoke with him about his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:30–31). What the church testifies to is the whole word of God, and it is doing what Moses and Elijah did: standing in front of a Pharaoh and an Ahab and saying the true thing.

As often as they desire. The phrase is startling and should not be softened. God does not give his witnesses a rationed supply of authority for approved occasions. But hold it beside verse 7, which is coming, and the shape of the whole passage appears: these are people with power to shut the sky, and they are about to be killed in the street, and both of those things are true at once. That combination is the actual experience of the church in every century. The word of God in the mouth of believers has real, world-altering force, and the people who carry it are frequently overpowered, humiliated and killed. Anyone who has only been told the first half will be shattered by the second. Anyone who has only seen the second will not believe the first. John gives both, two verses apart.

Where Christians differ: should the church expect such miracles today? Some read these verses as promising that end-time believers will perform Elijah-like and Moses-like miracles, and some charismatic groups expect such signs as normal. Verdict: the images are symbolic of the power of the church’s witness, which comes through the word of God and prayer. The miraculous signs of Moses, Elijah and the apostles served to confirm new revelation at key moments in redemptive history (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). This app holds, charitably, that such sign gifts have ceased with the completion of the canon. God still answers prayer powerfully, and still judges the world; but the church’s fire is the word it speaks, not miracles performed at will.

What it does not mean. This does not authorise Christians to call down judgement on their enemies. When James and John wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village, Jesus rebuked them (Luke 9:54–55). The fire is God’s, through the word; we preach and pray, and leave judgement to God.

So how should I pray about evil in the world? Pray boldly, because the prayers of the saints are taken up into the purposes of God (8:3–5), and pray as Jesus taught, first for God’s name, his kingdom and his will. Ask God to stop the wicked, to defend the oppressed, to bring down unjust rulers and to bring justice for the persecuted, as the psalms do. But pray also for the conversion of those who do evil, as Stephen did for the men stoning him, and as Christ did from the cross. Leave the manner and the timing of judgement to God. The witnesses’ fire is a word spoken, not a grudge nursed. Your part is to speak truly and to pray; his part is to judge rightly, and he will.

In a sentence. If anyone tries to harm them, fire comes out of their mouths and burns up their enemies; anyone who wants to hurt them must die like this; they have power to shut up the sky so that no rain falls while they are prophesying, and power to turn water into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague whenever they want.

On a Tuesday. The word of God is powerful. When you speak it faithfully and pray, you are doing more than you know. The Bible verse you send to a struggling friend, the honest answer you give when a colleague asks what you believe, the prayer you offer for your nation’s leaders on an ordinary evening: none of it is small. Heaven treats the prayers of the saints as incense before the throne, and the word in the mouth of an ordinary believer is the same fire that was in the mouth of Elijah.

For worship. The word of the LORD is a fire, and it is in the mouths of his people. He who shut the heavens in Elijah’s day and turned the Nile to blood in Moses’ day has not grown weaker. He is the God of the law and the prophets, and the law and the prophets spoke of his Son, who spoke with Moses and Elijah on the mountain about the death he would die. The fire that consumes his enemies is the same word that kindles faith in his elect. Blessed be the God whose word does not return empty, whose people pray and the heavens answer.
verseByVerse.note: Their powers recall Elijah (fire, drought) and Moses (water to blood, plagues).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them, and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them, and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.

The setting. In Daniel 7:21, the horn of the fourth beast made war with the saints and prevailed over them. To leave a body unburied was the greatest dishonour in the ancient world (Psalm 79:2–3). Sodom was the Old Testament’s symbol of wickedness (Genesis 19; Isaiah 1:10); Egypt was the land of slavery and oppression of God’s people.

And when they have finished their testimony. Four words carry the whole verse, and the first of them changes everything. “Finished” (telesōsin) means completed. The beast does not interrupt them. Until then, nothing could harm them. He cannot touch them until the testimony is complete. God’s witnesses are immortal until their work is done, and only when God allows it can the beast touch them.

A promise you can put weight on. It is not the promise most people want. It does not say the witness will be protected. It says the witness will be finished. Nobody in God’s service is cut off mid-sentence by accident, and the man who dies at forty with half his work apparently undone has, on the testimony of this verse, completed it. The missionary who dies in her first year on the field, the young pastor buried before his church was built, the mother who did not live to see her children grown: each was given a testimony to bear, and each was allowed to finish it. The length was God’s decision, and so was the completion.

The beast that rises from the bottomless pit. “Beast” (thērion) is a wild animal. This is his first appearance in the book, introduced casually with the definite article, as if already known from Daniel 7, two chapters before he is described in full in chapter 13. He rises from the abyss, the realm of demons opened in 9:1–2, and he represents the power of the state, or of any human system, when it sets itself against God and persecutes his people. And that origin places him: he is not a rival power from somewhere outside God’s rule. He comes up out of a pit that had to be unlocked with a key that somebody was given.

Will make war on them and conquer them and kill them. Here is the word that ought to stop a reader. “Conquer” (nikēsei) is the verb that ends every one of the seven letters as a promise to the faithful, the verb used of Christ himself in 5:5. Here it is used of the beast, against the saints, successfully, and it will be used that way again at 13:7. Revelation will not pretend the church always wins its battles. It says plainly that the church loses, visibly, in public, at the hands of a power that is permitted to defeat it.

Same verb, opposite direction. And the whole book exists to redefine what that defeat means, because the definitive instance of somebody conquering by being killed is the Lamb standing in the middle of the throne, looking as though it had been slain (5:6). The beast conquers by killing witnesses. The Lamb conquered by being killed. The beast seems to conquer, but the church conquers by being faithful unto death, as the Lamb did: they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death (12:11). Apparent defeat is real victory.

And their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city. In Revelation, the great city (tēs poleōs tēs megalēs) is always Babylon (16:19; 17:18; 18:10), the world system opposed to God. The holy city (v. 2) and the great city stand opposed, and the whole book is a tale of these two cities. Their bodies lie in the street. Not in a prison, not in a tomb: in the open, where the traffic goes. Whatever public humiliation looks like in a given century, that is what is being described, and John does not spare the reader a single detail of it.

That symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt. John supplies the key himself. “Symbolically” is pneumatikōs, spiritually, in the manner the Spirit speaks. He is telling the reader outright that these names are not addresses. It is Sodom in its wickedness, Egypt in its oppression of God’s people. Sodom is the byword for depravity, and Isaiah had already addressed Jerusalem’s rulers as rulers of Sodom (Isaiah 1:10). Egypt is the house of slavery that would not let God’s people go.

Where their Lord was crucified. This points to Jerusalem, where Jesus died. But Jerusalem in rejecting him became like Sodom and Egypt (Isaiah 1:9–10). And the great city is wherever the world rejects Christ and persecutes his witnesses. Piling four identities onto one city is the point: wherever the people of God are opposed, that place becomes Sodom and Egypt and Babylon and the city that killed the Lord. It is one city under many names, and it has a branch in every generation. Jerusalem crucified the Lord; the world system kills his witnesses. As their Lord was treated, so are they: if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (John 15:18–20).

What it does not mean. The great city is not just one city on a map. It is the world in its rebellion against God, which showed its true face by crucifying Christ, and which shows it again whenever it persecutes his people.

If the beast can conquer the church, how is Christ winning? He is winning the way he won at the cross: by what looks like defeat. The beast has power over bodies, but not over souls (Matthew 10:28). He can kill the witnesses only after their testimony is finished, only in the place and time God permits, and only to send them where their Lord has gone. Every martyr’s death is a testimony completed, not a testimony stopped. And the story does not end in the street. Read on two verses: breath from God, a voice from heaven, a cloud. The beast’s victories are real, temporary and already reversed in the counsel of God. Christ’s victory is real, permanent and already won.

In a sentence. When they have finished giving their testimony, the beast that comes up out of the abyss will wage war on them, overpower them and kill them, and their corpses will lie in the main street of the great city, which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, the city where their Lord was also crucified.

On a Tuesday. You cannot be stopped until your work is done. And if faithfulness costs you, you are walking where your Lord walked. So do not live as though your life were fragile in God’s hands. It is fragile in the world’s hands, and secure in his. Do today what he has given you to do, and leave the length of your days to him. And pray this week for Christians in places where the beast is openly making war: they are not losing; they are finishing their testimony.

For worship. He who holds the keys of death and Hades decides when each witness has finished. The beast is a creature on a leash, let up from the pit by permission, and the pit is not his own. The street where the bodies lay is the street where the Lord was led out to die, and he went that way first, so that no witness of his would ever walk it alone. The Lamb who was slain is standing. He conquered by dying, and every one of his people who dies faithful conquers in him. Glory to the Lamb, who has turned the beast’s victories into his own.

verseByVerse.quote: For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb, and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb, and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.

For three and a half days. A short time compared with their 1,260 days of witness. Three and a half again: limited, cut short. Three and a half days against three and a half years everywhere else in the chapter, and the proportion is the message: the humiliation is real and it is brief. It has the same shape as the ministry and none of the length. The world’s triumph over the church is brief.

Some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies. The four terms are the ones used for all humanity (5:9; 7:9), and in 5:9 they described the ransomed multitude. Now they describe the spectators. The same world that the Lamb bought is standing in the street looking at the bodies. People from every nation see, which points to a worldwide reality: the church’s suffering is seen by the whole world, not just one city. And the verb, blepousin, is to look at, to watch. They come and stand and look. There is a particular kind of public appetite being described here, and any generation that has watched a humiliation circulate for days will recognise it exactly.

And refuse to let them be placed in a tomb. Denial of burial was total contempt, the final insult. In the ancient world burial was owed even to an enemy; refusing it was a way of saying that a person did not count as human. The psalmist’s lament over Jerusalem was exactly this: they have given the bodies of your servants to the birds of the heavens for food, and there was no one to bury them (Psalm 79:2–3).

And those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents. “Rejoice” (chairousin) and “make merry” (euphrainontai). “Exchange presents” (dōra pempsousin, they will send gifts) is the language of a festival, as at Purim (Esther 9:19, 22). It is a grotesque parody of a holiday: the world celebrates the silencing of God’s witnesses. Every other celebration in these chapters is in heaven; this one is on the earth, and it is held because two preachers are dead. Somebody declares a day off. People send each other gifts. Compare the joy of heaven when Babylon falls (18:20; 19:1–3): the book has two parties in it, and they are held by different people for opposite reasons.

Those who dwell on the earth. Note the phrase, twice in one verse. It is John’s technical term, established at 8:13, for people whose whole account is settled here: not merely people who live on the earth, as every Christian does, but people whose home and hope and heart are nowhere else.

Because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth. “Torment” (ebasanisan) is the word used of the locusts tormenting people in 9:5. The witnesses had no army and no legal standing; what they had was a message, and the message was intolerable. Calling people to repent, and warning them of judgement, tormented the consciences of the world. People hate the light, because it exposes their deeds (John 3:20). Ahab said it to Elijah’s face: is it you, you troubler of Israel (1 Kings 18:17)?

A warning and a comfort in one sentence. The warning: if the world is entirely comfortable with what your congregation says, it is not saying what these two were saying. A witness that troubles nobody is probably not a witness. The comfort: when Christians find themselves treated as a problem to be removed rather than an opinion to be debated, that is not evidence that something has gone wrong. It is the treatment the two witnesses received, and the treatment their Lord received in the same city.

What it does not mean. The world’s rejoicing does not mean the church has failed. Its witness was so powerful that its silence brought relief to its enemies. The world rejoiced over Jesus’ death too, but only for three days.

Should I try to be offensive, then, so that I know I am faithful? No. The torment comes from the truth, not from the manner. The witnesses are in sackcloth, not armour; they mourn over the world, they do not sneer at it. Peter tells Christians to make sure that if they suffer, it is for doing good and for the name of Christ, not for being meddlers or for doing wrong (1 Peter 4:15–16), and to give their reasons with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). A Christian who is rude and is resented for it has not been persecuted; he has been rude. Aim to be kind, honest and clear, and let any offence be the offence of the cross.

In a sentence. For three and a half days, people from every people, tribe, language and nation will stare at their bodies and will not allow them to be buried; the inhabitants of the earth will gloat over them, celebrate and send each other gifts, because these two prophets had tormented them.

On a Tuesday. If the world celebrates when Christians are silenced or disgraced, do not be surprised. The truth always troubles a guilty conscience. Hold on: the world’s party is short. And when you see a Christian publicly humiliated, whether justly for a real fall or unjustly for faithfulness, refuse to join the crowd that gazes. Do not pass the story on for the pleasure of it. Pray, and if the person belongs to Christ, stand with them.

For worship. The party in the street lasts three and a half days, and the next verse begins with but. The world sent gifts to celebrate the death of God’s witnesses; God sent his only Son to die for the world. Men rejoiced over the body of Jesus for three days, and then the stone was rolled away. The Lord laughs at those who think they have silenced him, for he sees that their day is coming. And the feast he is preparing is not three days long. It is the marriage supper of the Lamb, and it never ends.

verseByVerse.quote: But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them. Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, "Come up here!" And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them. Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, “Come up here!” And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.

The setting. In Ezekiel 37:5, 10, God says to the dry bones that he will cause breath to enter them and they will live, and breath came into them, and they lived and stood on their feet, an exceedingly great army. Elijah was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11). Jesus ascended in a cloud while his disciples watched (Acts 1:9).

But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them. The wording is Ezekiel’s, and any reader who knows the valley of dry bones will hear it at once. The prophet was set down in a valley full of bones, very many and very dry, and asked whether they could live; he was told to prophesy, and breath came into them. “Breath of life” is pneuma zōēs, spirit of life, and the same word means breath and spirit, in the Hebrew of Ezekiel as in the Greek here. As in Ezekiel 37 and Genesis 2:7, God gives life by his breath. The witnesses are raised by God, as their Lord was. What a public that had refused them burial declared finished stands up in the street.

And they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them. “Great fear” (phobos megas). The detail John records is the reaction of the crowd. The party stops mid-sentence. Three and a half days of gazing at corpses, and then the corpses stand up. The celebration turns to terror. The resurrection of God’s people is their vindication, and their enemies’ dismay.

Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, Come up here! The same call John heard in 4:1. They are summoned into God’s presence. Every phrase in this sentence has been used before in this book or in the Gospels, and the effect builds as it goes.

And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them. In a cloud is how Christ ascended, a cloud taking him out of the disciples’ sight (Acts 1:9), and how he will return (1:7). The witnesses are given their Lord’s death, in his city, and then their Lord’s resurrection and his ascension, in that order. And the last clause is not decoration. When Jesus rose, the world did not see it; the guards saw an empty tomb and were paid to say something else, and the risen Christ appeared only to his own. Here the vindication is public, and the people who arranged the deaths are standing in the street with their gifts still in their hands. God vindicates his witnesses openly.

Vindication comes after, and in public. This is where the passage does its real work for an ordinary believer. The pattern it describes is not that faithful witness avoids humiliation. It is that vindication comes afterwards, and in front of the same audience. Every Christian who has been written off, misrepresented, quietly removed, or made ridiculous for saying something true is being shown the end of that story, and the end of it is not a private consolation. It is a summons heard out loud and a departure the accusers have to watch.

What the witnesses do not do. They do not argue, retaliate, or explain. They stand up, and they are called, and they go. Vindication in Scripture is almost never something a person achieves; it is something done to him by somebody else, usually later than he would have chosen. Peter told churches in these same provinces exactly that: humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you (1 Peter 5:6).

Where Christians differ: is this the rapture? Some read this as a mid-tribulation rapture of two individual prophets, or of the church. Verdict: if the two witnesses are the church, their resurrection and ascension picture the resurrection of believers at Christ’s return, when the dead in Christ rise and the church is caught up to meet the Lord in the clouds (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). It is public, seen by their enemies, not secret. It follows the church’s whole period of witness and suffering, and it is followed at once by the final judgement and the seventh trumpet (v. 15), which Paul also links with the last trumpet (1 Corinthians 15:52). There is one visible return, with one resurrection of the righteous and the gathering of the church at that time.

What it does not mean. The church is not raised to escape the world’s judgement before it suffers. It is raised after it has finished its witness, after its death. Vindication comes through suffering, not instead of it.

Will my body really be raised? Yes. The breath of God that entered the witnesses is the picture of a real promise: the same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead will give life to your mortal body (Romans 8:11). The Christian hope is not that the soul escapes the body for ever, but that the body itself is raised, changed and glorified, like Christ’s own body (Philippians 3:21). When a believer dies, his soul goes at once to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23), and his body rests in the grave, still united to Christ, until the last trumpet. Then the dead in Christ will rise, and those alive will be changed, and together they will meet the Lord, in full view of the world that buried them.

In a sentence. But after three and a half days, the breath of life from God came into them, and they stood up, and terror gripped everyone who saw them; then they heard a loud voice from heaven calling to them, Come up here! and they went up to heaven in a cloud while their enemies looked on.

On a Tuesday. Whatever happens to you for Christ’s sake, God will have the last word, and it will be resurrection. So you do not have to win every argument, clear your name in every circle, or have the last word yourself. Tell the truth, do what is right, and leave your reputation with God. And stand by the graveside of a believer differently: not pretending death is nothing, but knowing it is not the end of the story. The Lord who called Come up here has not lost the address.

For worship. The breath that moved over the waters at creation, that filled Adam’s nostrils and swept through the valley of dry bones, is the breath that raised the Lord Jesus from the tomb, and it will raise every one of his people. He who was called up into the cloud before the eyes of his disciples will call his church up in the same way, before the eyes of the whole world. The grave cannot keep what he has claimed. Glory to the God who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist.

verseByVerse.quote: And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.

The setting. In Elijah’s day, God kept seven thousand in Israel who had not bowed the knee to Baal (1 Kings 19:18). Here the number is reversed: seven thousand die. In the Old Testament, giving glory to God sometimes means confessing the truth and turning to him in repentance (Joshua 7:19; Jeremiah 13:16).

And at that hour there was a great earthquake. Earthquakes accompany God’s coming in judgement (6:12; 8:5; 16:18). At that hour: the vindication of the witnesses and the shaking of the city are one event. Heaven does not let the ascension pass without the earth feeling it.

And a tenth of the city fell. The proportions are the first thing to notice, because they run the opposite way from everything in the book so far. In chapter 6 a fourth of the earth was struck. In chapters 8 and 9 it was a third, repeatedly. Here it is a tenth: a further step beyond the quarter of the seals and the third of the trumpets, but still partial, and much smaller. A tithe, perhaps: a portion given up in judgement, while the rest is spared to repent.

Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake. Literally, seven thousand names of men. A tenth of the city, perhaps symbolic of a city of seventy thousand; seven speaks of completeness. And the number carries an echo. When Elijah, who stands behind these witnesses, complained that he alone was left, God told him he had kept seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that had not bowed to Baal. There, seven thousand were the remnant preserved. Here, seven thousand fall and the great majority are spared. The arithmetic of grace has been turned the other way up.

And the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. “Gave glory” (edōkan doxan). Set that against 9:20, two chapters earlier: the rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent. Same phrase, opposite outcome. The trumpets of chapter 9 struck a third of mankind and produced nothing. Two witnesses prophesied in sackcloth, were killed, and were raised, and nine tenths of a city gave glory to God. What judgements alone could not do, the church’s witness, death and vindication achieve. This is the purpose of the church’s suffering witness: the conversion of the nations. Then only a remnant was saved; here only a remnant is judged, and most are saved.

Where Christians differ: is this genuine repentance? Some take “gave glory” as a terrified, forced acknowledgement of God, not true conversion. Verdict: the phrase in Revelation is used for true worship and repentance: in 14:7 the angel calls the nations to fear God and give him glory, and in 16:9 those who did not repent refused to give him glory. Here, unlike 9:20–21, the response is positive. It points to the fruit of the church’s faithful witness: many from the nations turning to God. This fits the great multitude from every nation (7:9) and the nations walking by the light of the new Jerusalem (21:24).

How the world is actually reached. If that reading is right, and it is, the chapter has made an argument about how the world is reached, and it is not the argument most churches would have made. Plagues did not do it. Cosmic catastrophe did not do it. A third of mankind dying did not do it. What did it was two witnesses in mourning dress, refusing to stop speaking, being killed for it, and being raised. Tertullian put it in a line the church has never forgotten: the blood of Christians is seed.

The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come. The bookkeeping verse again, matching 9:12. The eagle’s three woes of 8:13 are the fifth, sixth and seventh trumpets. The second woe is the sixth trumpet with its interlude (9:13–11:14). The third woe is the seventh trumpet, the final judgement. It is announced as soon, and the very next verse sounds the seventh trumpet, which turns out to contain no plague that John describes, only the announcement of a kingdom.

What it does not mean. The conversion of many does not mean everyone will be saved. Seven thousand died under judgement. But it shows that the gospel will triumph among the nations.

Then why do disasters not bring people to God? Sometimes they do, for a while; churches fill after a catastrophe and empty again within months. This chapter explains why that is not enough. Fear of judgement by itself hardens as often as it humbles (9:20–21; 16:9). What turns hearts is the word of God, carried by witnesses whose lives and deaths make it credible, and applied by the Spirit. That is why the church must not wait for a crisis to do its evangelism for it. Crises shake people. Christ, preached by people who love him more than their own lives, saves them.

In a sentence. At that very moment there was a violent earthquake, and a tenth of the city collapsed; seven thousand people died in the earthquake, and the survivors were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven; the second woe has passed, and look, the third woe is coming quickly.

On a Tuesday. The church’s faithful witness, even through suffering, bears fruit. Do not lose heart: many will yet turn to God. Think of the person you have prayed for and spoken to for years without visible result. This chapter does not promise you will see the harvest, but it does tell you how harvests come: through faithful, patient, costly witness that does not stop. Keep speaking. Keep praying. The seed is in the ground.

For worship. The God of heaven is not content with a remnant when he could have a multitude. He who kept seven thousand in Elijah’s day turns the arithmetic over and gathers the nine tenths. He uses the weakest things, two witnesses in sackcloth, a murdered testimony, a body left in the street, to bring proud cities to their knees. And all of it is the pattern of his Son, who was lifted up and draws all people to himself. Glory to the God of heaven, whose kindness leads to repentance and whose witnesses, even in death, are seed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 15: the seventh trumpet sounds and brings no plague at all, only an announcement — The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever. Singular kingdom, not plural: one worldly system under many governments, and it has changed hands. And the verb is aorist, a completed act: not will become but has become.

Verses 16–17: the twenty-four elders come off their own thrones onto their faces, giving thanks to Lord God Almighty, who is and who was — and the threefold title of 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8 has lost its third term. The one who is to come has come, and the future tense drops out of the name of God. You have taken your great power and begun to reign: not been given, but taken. He was always sovereign; what changes is that the reign becomes visible and unopposed.

Verse 18 quotes Psalm 2:1 in the past tense — the nations raged, and it is over — and lists what the moment contains: wrath; the dead judged; the servants rewarded, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great; and destroying the destroyers of the earth, an exact reciprocity using the same root twice.

Verse 19 opens the temple in heaven, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple — the object that stood behind the veil, seen by one man once a year, and lost when Babylon destroyed the temple in 586 BC. Then the storm signs, now five of them: lightning, rumblings, thunder, earthquake and heavy hail.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Kingdom Has Come

The seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. God is now praised as the one who is and who was — the one to come has come — and the ark of his covenant is seen in his temple.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The outcome was declared with eleven chapters still to run.

Now: Believers live inside a victory already won and not yet seen; small and great alike will be rewarded.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever." And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying, "We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.” And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying, “We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.

The setting. Psalm 2:2 speaks of the kings of the earth setting themselves against the LORD and against his Anointed. Daniel 2:44 and 7:14, 27 foretell a kingdom that God will set up that will never be destroyed, given to the Son of Man and to the saints of the Most High, an everlasting kingdom. Exodus 15:18, the song of Moses, ends: The LORD will reign forever and ever.

Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet. The last trumpet, the third woe (11:14), announced in 10:7 as the moment when the mystery of God would be fulfilled. Paul speaks of the last trumpet at which the dead are raised (1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16). Six trumpets brought hail, blood, wormwood, darkness, locusts and cavalry. The seventh does not describe new plagues. It brings an announcement, and it is the sentence the whole book has been climbing towards.

And there were loud voices in heaven, saying, The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. Any reader who knows Handel has heard these words sung, and the singing can carry a person past what they actually say. “The kingdom of the world” (hē basileia tou kosmou) is singular, not plural, though older translations had the kingdoms. There is one worldly kingdom under many governments: the whole world system, under the rule of Satan and the beast, and it has changed hands. It now becomes the kingdom of God and his Messiah. “Christ” (Christou) is the Anointed One, as in Psalm 2: the King whom God set on Zion while the nations raged.

Has become. The verb, egeneto, is past tense, a completed act, and it is the tense that makes the sentence extraordinary. Heaven does not announce that the kingdom of the world will become God’s, or is in the process of becoming his. It announces a transfer that has already happened, so certain it is described as done. This is the language of a herald reading out a result, not a forecast.

The result announced at half-time. And it is announced at the seventh trumpet, with eleven chapters of the book still to run. The dragon has not appeared yet. Neither beast has risen. Babylon has not fallen and the white horse has not ridden out. The outcome is declared before the conflict is described, which is one of the most important structural facts about Revelation. The book is not a thriller in which the ending is in doubt. It is the account of a war whose result was announced at the halfway point, and before that at an empty tomb.

What it meant to the first hearers. They were being read a document that told them the empire would get worse, that a beast would be given authority over every tribe and people, that they would be conquered and killed. And in the middle of it, loud voices in heaven saying that the kingdom of the world has already changed owner. They were not being asked to hope for a victory. They were being asked to live inside one that had not yet been made visible.

And he shall reign forever and ever. “He” is singular. God and his Christ reign as one; the Father and the Son do not have two thrones but one (22:1, 3). The reign is eternal: no thousand-year limit, no end. The song of Moses at the Red Sea ended with the same words, and the song of the Lamb takes them up.

And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God. The representatives of God’s people respond with worship. Twenty-four figures who have thrones of their own get off them and put their faces on the floor. Their response is not analysis. It is adoration.

Saying, We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was. Here is the small detail that repays every minute spent on it. The divine title in this book has been threefold from the first chapter: who is and who was and who is to come (1:4, 8; 4:8). Here it is twofold. Who is and who was, and the third term is gone. It is not an oversight. The one who is to come has come. The title had a future tense in it for as long as there was a future to wait for, and at the seventh trumpet the waiting ends and the future tense drops out of the name of God. Nothing in the chapter says more, and it is said by leaving a word out.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “and art to come” after “who is and who was”. The best manuscripts do not have it, and its absence is deliberate: at this point in the vision, God has come.

For you have taken your great power and begun to reign. “Taken” (eilēphas, perfect tense): decisively taken. Not been given, taken. “Begun to reign” (ebasileusas): entered on your reign. God has always been sovereign, but now his reign is openly established over all opposition. What was hidden is revealed; what was contested is settled. The one who is and who was has stopped being patient.

Where Christians differ: does Christ’s kingdom come gradually or suddenly? Postmillennialists believe that the gospel will gradually transform the world until most of humanity is Christian, and then Christ will return. Premillennialists believe Christ will return to set up a thousand-year earthly kingdom. Verdict: Christ already reigns now, at the Father’s right hand (1:5; Ephesians 1:20–22), and his kingdom grows through the gospel. But the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of Christ in full only at his return, at the last trumpet, when he judges the living and the dead. There is no thousand-year interval between the last trumpet and the eternal reign; he will reign for ever and ever from the moment of his return.

What it does not mean. God did not lack power before. The words describe the open, public, final display of the reign he always had.

If Christ reigns now, why does the world look the way it does? Because his reign is real now but not yet visible to all. He sits at the Father’s right hand with all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18), and he is gathering his people through the gospel and restraining evil within limits he has set. But he is patient, and he allows the outer court to be trampled for the appointed time. Hebrews says it exactly: at present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:8–9). We live by what we see in him, not by what we see in the headlines. At the last trumpet the two will match.

In a sentence. Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and loud voices in heaven proclaimed: The rule over the world now belongs to our Lord and to his Messiah, and he will reign for ever and ever; and the twenty-four elders, seated on their thrones before God, fell face down and worshipped God, saying: We thank you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, because you have taken up your great power and begun your reign.

On a Tuesday. Live today as a citizen of the kingdom that has already won. When the news makes it look as though the kingdom of the world belongs to whoever is loudest or cruellest, say to yourself the sentence heaven has already said: it has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. That does not make you careless about the world; it makes you unafraid in it. Give thanks, as the elders did, before you see it, because the thanksgiving of the faithful is always ahead of the evidence.

For worship. Hallelujah, for the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. The kingdom of the world, with all its empires and its beasts and its proud cities, has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign for ever and ever. He who is and who was is no longer the one who is to come; he has come, he has taken his great power, and every throne in heaven is empty because its occupant is on his face. The song of Moses at the sea and the chorus of the elders are one song, and its last line is the same: for ever and ever. Sing it with understanding. One day, every kingdom of this world will belong to Christ, and he will reign for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth." Then God's temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth.” Then God’s temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.

The setting. Psalm 2:1, 5 says the nations rage, but God speaks to them in his wrath. The ark of the covenant, the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law, stood in the Most Holy Place, the place of God’s throne on earth, where the high priest sprinkled atoning blood once a year (Exodus 25:10–22; Leviticus 16). It disappeared when Babylon destroyed the temple in 586 BC. Jewish tradition said Jeremiah hid it, and it would reappear when God gathered his people again (2 Maccabees 2:4–8).

The nations raged, but your wrath came. The nations raged is a quotation. Psalm 2 opens with it, asking why the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain, and goes on to describe kings setting themselves against the LORD and against his Anointed, and God laughing, and installing his King on Zion. Revelation has been quoting that psalm since 2:27. Here it reports it in the past tense. The raging is over. It was answered. And the two verbs share a root: “raged” (ōrgisthēsan, were angry) and “wrath” (orgē). The nations’ anger against God is met by God’s anger against them. Their rage is futile; his is just and final. It is stated in a single clause and not dwelt on, in a book that has spent six chapters on judgement. The point of the list lies elsewhere.

And the time for the dead to be judged. “Time” is kairos, the appointed moment. The final judgement of all the dead (20:11–15). Everyone, without exception, including everyone who died believing the matter was closed. Nothing has been filed away.

And for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great. This is the longest clause in the verse, and its generosity is the point. “Rewarding” is literally giving the wages, dounai ton misthon. Three overlapping groups, prophets, saints, and simply those who fear your name, and then a phrase that refuses to let anybody be ranked out of it: both small and great. There is no tier system at this reward. No one is too insignificant to be noticed and rewarded; not even a cup of cold water given to one of these little ones will lose its reward (Matthew 10:42). The two witnesses who shut the sky and the widow who kept praying and never told anybody are in the same sentence.

Reward and grace. God intends to give things to people for what they did, and the New Testament is entirely unembarrassed about that (Matthew 6:4; 1 Corinthians 3:14; Hebrews 11:6). But the reward is grace, not wages earned (22:12). The servants were bought before they ever served; their works were prepared by God beforehand (Ephesians 2:10); and when he rewards them he is crowning his own gifts. Grace is not the abolition of reward. It is the reason a reward is possible at all.

And for destroying the destroyers of the earth. “Destroying” (diaphtheirai) is ruining, corrupting, and the same root is used twice, which the English preserves. A fitting justice: those who ruin the earth, morally and physically, by violence, idolatry and corruption, will be ruined. Babylon is said to have corrupted the earth (19:2). Nothing arbitrary is happening: the sentence is the crime, said back. God made the earth good, and he will judge those who destroy it, and renew it.

Then God’s temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. Stop at that, because for a Jewish reader it would have been the most astonishing sentence in the chapter. “Opened” (ēnoigē). The ark stood in the Most Holy Place, behind the veil, and only the high priest saw it, once a year. It disappeared when Babylon destroyed the temple and was never seen again; Jeremiah had said the day would come when people would no longer say the ark of the covenant of the LORD, nor miss it (Jeremiah 3:16). For centuries the holiest object in Israel’s worship had simply been gone. Here it is. In the temple in heaven, in plain view, with the doors open.

What the ark means. The ark was the chest that held the covenant, the tablets of the law, under a lid where blood was sprinkled once a year. To see it standing there is to be told that the covenant was never lost when the building fell, that God has kept his side of it, and that the place where blood was applied for a nation’s sin is still in the room. The Most Holy Place, once closed to all but the high priest once a year, is opened. God’s presence is accessible. The covenant promises, sealed with blood, are kept. And the chapter that began by measuring a temple and leaving part of it to be trampled ends by opening the real one.

There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail. John’s standing signal that God has acted, used at 4:5 with three elements, at 8:5 with four, and here with five; the same sign, intensified again, ends the bowls (16:18–21). It grows each time. The nations raged; his wrath came; the covenant stands open in the light; and the last sound in the chapter is thunder over an ark that nobody had seen for centuries.

What it does not mean. The seventh trumpet does not end the book because Revelation is not a straight timeline. Chapter 12 will go back to the birth of Christ and show the same age again, from the angle of the spiritual war behind it.

Does the open temple mean I can come to God now, or only at the end? Now. The vision shows what is true in heaven at all times and will be visible to all at the end. When Christ died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51), and Hebrews says we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us (Hebrews 10:19–22). You do not need a priest, a pilgrimage or a special state of feeling. You come through Christ, in prayer, at any hour, and you are welcome. The ark in heaven is the guarantee that the covenant under which you come will never be broken.

In a sentence. The nations were furious, but now your anger has come, and the time has come to judge the dead, to reward your servants the prophets, your people and all who fear your name, the unimportant and the important alike, and to destroy those who destroy the earth; then God’s temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant could be seen inside it, and there came lightning, rumbling, thunder, an earthquake and a great hailstorm.

On a Tuesday. If you are one of the small, unnoticed servants, the one who visits, prays, sets out the chairs, cares for an elderly parent, and is never thanked, read this verse slowly: both small and great. God has seen it, and he intends to reward it. And if you are carrying guilt today, remember where the ark is: in the open, in heaven, with the mercy seat where the blood was sprinkled. Go to God through Christ now, not after you have cleaned yourself up.

For worship. Worship the God who keeps his covenant. The ark is in heaven, and the way into God’s presence is open through Christ’s blood. The nations raged and he laughed; they plotted and he set his King on his holy hill. He judges the dead with perfect justice, and he rewards the least of his servants with a generosity no one deserved. What men thought was lost in the ruins of Jerusalem was never lost at all: the covenant stands in the light of heaven, the mercy seat is sprinkled with better blood than that of bulls and goats, and the doors are open. Thunder rolls over it, and it is the sound of a God who has kept every promise he ever made.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, “Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there,<sup>2</sup>but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.<sup>3</sup>And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth.”<sup>4</sup>These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.<sup>5</sup>And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed.<sup>6</sup>They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.<sup>7</sup>And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them,<sup>8</sup>and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.<sup>9</sup>For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb,<sup>10</sup>and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.<sup>11</sup>But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them.<sup>12</sup>Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, “Come up here!” And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.<sup>13</sup>And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.<sup>14</sup>The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.<sup>15</sup>Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.”<sup>16</sup>And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God,<sup>17</sup>saying, “We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.<sup>18</sup>The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth.”<sup>19</sup>Then God’s temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.

12.title: The Woman, the Dragon, and the War in Heaven
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is the theological heart of Revelation. Everything that has come before — the seals, the trumpets, the witnesses — and everything that follows — the beasts, the bowls, Babylon’s fall — is explained here. We are shown the cosmic backstory: the war between the dragon and the woman, the birth of the child who will rule all nations, the war in heaven that cast Satan down, and the dragon’s fury against the woman’s offspring. This is the explanation for why the church is persecuted: the dragon, having failed to destroy the child, turns his fury on those who “hold to the testimony of Jesus.”

The great sign in heaven — the woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars — draws on Genesis 37:9 (Joseph’s dream where the sun, moon, and eleven stars bowed down to him, representing his family) and on the Old Testament imagery of Israel as the bride/mother of God’s people (Isaiah 54; Jeremiah 6:2). The woman is not Mary (though the imagery encompasses the incarnation). She is the messianic community — Israel who gave birth to the Messiah, and the church who is the continuation and expansion of that community. She is clothed with cosmic glory; she is in labor.

The great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns and seven diadems is Satan himself, identified explicitly in v. 9: “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world.” His seven heads and ten horns anticipate the beast of chapter 13, which mirrors the dragon’s appearance — the beast is the dragon’s instrument, Rome as the embodiment of satanic opposition to Christ. The dragon’s tail sweeping down a third of the stars has been interpreted as the fall of the angels who followed Satan in the primordial rebellion.

The cosmic war of vv. 7–12 is one of the most dramatic scenes in Revelation: Michael and his angels fight the dragon and his angels; the dragon is thrown down. The war in heaven is won. The announcement that follows is the theological explanation: they conquered “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.” The cross — not Michael’s sword — is the decisive weapon. The dragon is thrown down because the Lamb was slain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Woman and the Dragon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a great sign — John says so before he describes anything — a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, a crown of twelve stars, pregnant and screaming in labour. The sun, moon and twelve stars come from Joseph’s dream, where Jacob himself supplies the key (Gen. 37:9–10): this is the covenant people, from whom the Messiah comes.

Verses 3–4: another sign, a great red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven diadems — royal crowns, not the victor’s wreath the woman wears, and the crowns that belong by right to the rider of 19:12. His tail sweeps down a third of the stars, and he stands in front of the woman waiting to devour the child.

Verse 5: she bears a male child who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron (Ps. 2:9) — and the child is caught up to God and to his throne. Between the birth and the throne there is nothing: no Galilee, no cross, no empty tomb. Thirty-three years pass in a comma, because from the dragon’s side there is nothing to report but total failure.

Verse 6: the woman flees into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, to be nourished for 1,260 days. The child is safe on the throne; the mother is in the desert — which is the position of the church between the ascension and the end.
verseByVerse.theology:
The War Behind the War

The woman — the covenant people, Israel and the church — bears the Messiah, while the dragon waits to devour the child. The child is caught up to God’s throne, and the woman is kept and fed in the wilderness for a measured time.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Every attack on the promised line, from Pharaoh to Herod, was the dragon at the woman’s feet.

Now: The church’s wilderness is hard, but it is a place prepared by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth.

Meaning first. Revelation 12 goes behind the scenes of history to show the spiritual war that explains why the church suffers. A woman clothed with the sun, crowned with twelve stars, cries out in labour (vv. 1–2). A great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns, whose tail sweeps down a third of the stars, waits to devour her child (vv. 3–4). She gives birth to a son who will rule the nations with a rod of iron; he is caught up to God’s throne, and she flees to the wilderness, where God nourishes her for 1,260 days (vv. 5–6). War breaks out in heaven; Michael and his angels defeat the dragon, who is the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan, and he is thrown down to earth with his angels (vv. 7–9). A voice in heaven rejoices: the accuser has been thrown down, and believers have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, loving not their lives even unto death; but woe to the earth, for the devil has come down in great fury, knowing his time is short (vv. 10–12). The dragon pursues the woman, but she is given eagle’s wings to escape to the wilderness, and the earth swallows the flood he sends after her (vv. 13–16). Furious, he goes to make war on the rest of her offspring, those who keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus (v. 17). The chapter explains the church’s situation: Satan is a defeated enemy, beaten at the cross, enraged because his time is short, and taking out his fury on God’s people, who are protected by God and who conquer him through Christ’s blood and their faithful witness.

The setting. In Joseph’s dream, the sun, moon and eleven stars bowed down to him, representing his father, mother and brothers, the family of Israel (Genesis 37:9–10). The prophets picture Israel, or Zion, as a woman in labour, longing for deliverance (Isaiah 26:17–18; 66:7–9; Micah 4:10; 5:3). In Genesis 3:15, God told the serpent that the offspring of the woman would bruise his head, and that he would bruise his heel. Ancient myths told similar stories: in the Greek myth, the dragon Python pursued the goddess Leto, pregnant with Apollo, who later killed the dragon. The emperors identified themselves with Apollo. Revelation tells the true story behind the myths: the real child is Christ, and the real dragon is Satan.

The war behind the war. The book turns here. Chapters 1 to 11 have shown what happens on earth and in heaven as the scroll is opened; chapter 12 pulls the curtain back further and shows why. From here to chapter 20 the reader is looking at the dragon, his two beasts and their city, and this chapter introduces all of it. And it begins, not with the dragon, but with a woman and a child. Before we are shown the enemy, we are shown the one he cannot defeat.

And a great sign appeared in heaven. The word is sēmeion, a sign: something that stands for something else. It is the first time Revelation uses the word, and John says so before he describes anything, which is his standing courtesy to the reader. This is a sign; read it as one. John tells us directly that this is a symbol.

A woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. Who is she? The imagery answers it. Joseph dreamed of the sun, the moon and eleven stars bowing down to him, and his father understood it at once: the sun was Jacob, the moon was his mother, and the stars were his brothers. Add Joseph, and you have twelve. The sun, the moon and twelve stars is Israel, the covenant people from whom the Messiah comes. She wears glory, authority and heavenly identity. The twelve stars are the twelve tribes of Israel, and also, as the book will show at the end, the twelve apostles (21:12–14). She is the people of God, the messianic community from which the Messiah comes and which continues as the church.

She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth. “Birth pains” (ōdinousa). This is the suffering of God’s people in the Old Testament as they waited for the Messiah: the long years of Israel’s history, under oppression, longing for the promised offspring. John does not soften it. The word for her cry is the word for a person crying out aloud.

Glory and agony at once. She is clothed in glory and she is in agony, both at once, and that combination is the whole doctrine of the people of God in one picture. Seen from heaven, the church is clothed with the sun and crowned with stars. Seen from the street, she is a woman in labour, crying out, with something enormous waiting for her. Both are accurate. A believer who has only been shown the first picture will not recognise his own church; one who has only seen the second will not believe there is anything else to see.

Pain with an outcome. Birth pain in Scripture is never merely suffering. It is suffering with an outcome. Isaiah used it of Israel in exile; Jesus used it of the troubles before the end: all these are but the beginning of the birth pains (Matthew 24:8); Paul used it of the whole creation groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now (Romans 8:22). Nobody labours for nothing. The pain is real, it is severe, and it is going somewhere.

Where Christians differ: is the woman Mary? Roman Catholic tradition has long identified the woman with the Virgin Mary, and has used this passage in support of Marian devotion and of her bodily assumption into heaven. Verdict: the woman is the people of God, Israel and then the church. There is a secondary allusion to Mary, who literally gave birth to the Messiah, and she belongs to the people of God. But the woman’s experiences cannot be Mary’s: she is persecuted in the wilderness for 1,260 days after her child ascends (v. 6), and she has other offspring who keep God’s commandments and hold the testimony of Jesus (v. 17), who are believers. The twelve stars point to the twelve tribes. Nothing here supports praying to Mary, or her being given a special role in salvation.

What it does not mean. The woman is not the church only in the New Testament sense, as if the Messiah were born from the church. She is the one people of God across both covenants, from whom Christ came, and who continues in the church.

How should Protestants think of Mary, then? With great honour, and without worship. She was a real woman of faith, chosen by grace to bear the Son of God, and she called herself the Lord’s servant and God her Saviour (Luke 1:38, 47). All generations call her blessed, and rightly. But she was a sinner saved by her Son like everyone else, and Scripture never asks us to pray to her or through her. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). The best way to honour Mary is to do what she said at Cana: whatever he says to you, do it (John 2:5).

In a sentence. Then a great sign appeared in the sky: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head; she was pregnant and crying out in the pain and agony of giving birth.

On a Tuesday. You belong to a people with a long story, stretching back through Israel to Eve. God’s promise of a Saviour was carried through centuries of pain, and it was kept. So when the church seems weak and noisy and in distress, and your own Christian life feels more like labour than glory, remember that heaven sees her clothed with the sun. Your pain, borne in faith, is not wasted. It is going somewhere.

For worship. Blessed be the God who made a promise at the gate of Eden and carried it through every century of Israel’s groaning. He clothed a weak and suffering people with the sun, and out of their long labour brought forth the Son who would crush the serpent’s head. He did not abandon the woman in her agony. He made her agony the way the Saviour came. And the same God is bringing his whole creation through its birth pains to a new world, where the crying will stop for ever.
verseByVerse.note: The sun, moon and twelve stars recall Joseph’s dream of Israel’s family. The woman seems to be the people of God, from whom the Messiah came.

verseByVerse.quote: And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems. His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems. His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.

The setting. In the Old Testament, the sea monster or dragon (Leviathan, Rahab) is a symbol of chaos and of evil powers opposed to God, and of empires such as Egypt (Isaiah 27:1; 51:9; Psalm 74:13–14; Ezekiel 29:3). Daniel 7 describes four beasts, the fourth with ten horns, representing world empires. Daniel 8:10 describes a horn that grew great and threw down some of the stars to the ground and trampled them. At Christ’s birth, King Herod tried to kill him by slaughtering the infants of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:13–18).

And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon. A sign again, and John says so again. This is not what Satan looks like; it is what Satan is, rendered in a picture. “Dragon” (drakōn) is a great serpent, identified in verse 9 as the devil, Satan. The dragon in the Old Testament is the chaos monster of the deep, Leviathan, Rahab, the twisting serpent that God alone can master, and Ezekiel called Pharaoh the great dragon lying in the midst of his streams. “Red” (pyrros) is fiery red, the colour of bloodshed, like the second horseman (6:4). He was a murderer from the beginning (John 8:44).

With seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems. Every detail is a counterfeit of something already seen in this book. Seven heads: seven is God’s number of completeness, and the dragon wears it, a picture of complete cunning or power. Ten horns: horns are power, and ten is fullness of a lesser kind, great strength, as in Daniel’s fourth beast. And the sharpest detail is the diadems (diadēmata), royal crowns, not victors’ wreaths. The woman wears a stephanos of stars, the crown of victory; the dragon wears seven royal crowns. Satan claims royal authority over the world (Luke 4:5–6; John 12:31). He is claiming a sovereignty he does not hold. The beast of chapter 13 will look like him, because the beast is his agent.

Who the crowns belong to. At 19:12 the rider on the white horse will appear wearing many diadems, and that settles the question. The dragon’s crowns are borrowed, or rather stolen, and the true King will come wearing more of them than the usurper ever counted.

His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. Stars can represent angels (1:20; 9:1). This probably refers to the angels who fell with Satan, the demons (v. 9). Or it pictures his destructive power and his attack on God’s people, like the horn in Daniel 8:10. A third is the same fraction that ran through the trumpets. Even in the account of his greatest success the dragon gets a limited portion. Two thirds stayed.

And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it. “Devour” (kataphagē) is eat up. That single sentence is the plot of the Old Testament. Immediately after the fall God promised enmity between the serpent and the woman, and between his offspring and hers, and said, he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel (Genesis 3:15). Everything after that is the serpent trying to get to the child first. Cain kills Abel. Pharaoh orders every Hebrew boy thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1). Athaliah destroys the whole royal family of Judah and misses one baby hidden in a bedroom (2 Kings 11:1–3). Haman obtains a decree to destroy every Jew in the empire (Esther 3). When the child is finally born, Herod sends soldiers to Bethlehem to kill every boy under two (Matthew 2:16). And finally there is the cross. Every one of those is the dragon standing in front of the woman with his mouth open. Matthew reports Herod’s massacre as history; John shows what was underneath it.

The second layer. That is what this chapter offers that no other part of Scripture offers quite so directly. The events are real, a real decree, a real sword, real children, and there is something behind them that is also real, and hostile, and personal, and has been at this for a very long time. Paul said the same thing without the picture: we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness (Ephesians 6:12).

How little he does. Note where he is standing, though, and how little he achieves. He stands before the woman, waiting. He has seven crowns he did not earn and a mouth open for a child not yet born. In the next verse the child is taken to the throne of God, and the dragon does not lay a finger on him.
