What it does not mean. The dragon’s crowns do not mean his rule is legitimate or unlimited. He is a usurper, and his crowns are claims, not rights. Christ wears many diadems (19:12).

Is the devil a real person, or a symbol for evil? He is real. The dragon is a picture, but it is a picture of someone, as the lion is a picture of Christ. Jesus spoke to him in the wilderness, named him a liar and a murderer, and spoke of his fall (Matthew 4:1–11; John 8:44; Luke 10:18). He is a created spirit, a fallen angel, not God’s equal and not everywhere at once. He has intelligence, a will and a strategy. That is why Scripture tells us to be sober and watchful (1 Peter 5:8). But it never tells us to be fascinated by him or terrified of him. Resist him, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:9), and he will flee from you (James 4:7).

Does every bad thing happen because of Satan? No. Scripture names three enemies: the world, the flesh and the devil (Ephesians 2:1–3). Much evil comes from our own sinful desires (James 1:14), and much suffering comes simply from living in a fallen world. Blaming the devil for every sin can become a way of avoiding repentance. But this chapter does warn us not to be naive. Behind the great persecutions and the great lies of history, and sometimes behind the attacks on a single believer’s faith, there is a personal enemy. Take sin seriously as your own, and take the devil seriously as real, and keep your eyes on the child who went past him to the throne.

In a sentence. Then another sign appeared in the sky: a huge red dragon with seven heads and ten horns, with a royal crown on each head; his tail dragged a third of the stars out of the sky and flung them down to earth; and the dragon stood in front of the woman as she was about to give birth, ready to devour her child the moment it was born.

On a Tuesday. Behind the evil you see in the world is a real enemy with a real strategy. Do not be naive about him, but do not be afraid either: he failed to devour the child. When you read of persecution, of children harmed, of attempts to silence the church, recognise the old pattern. Pray against it, act against it where you can, and remember that the dragon has stood with his mouth open many times before and gone away hungry.

For worship. The dragon stood before the woman with all his crowns and all his power, and he could not touch the Child. The Lord who broke the heads of Leviathan in the waters, who brought Israel out of the reach of Pharaoh and hid the infant Joash from Athaliah’s sword, guarded his promise through every century until the Son was born in Bethlehem. Herod’s soldiers found nothing. The cross, which looked like the dragon’s meal, was his defeat. All the diadems the usurper claims belong to the Lamb, and on the day he rides out, he will wear them all.

verseByVerse.quote: She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne, and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne, and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.

The setting. Psalm 2:9 says that God’s Son, his anointed King, will break the nations with a rod of iron. After the exodus, God led Israel into the wilderness, where he fed them with manna and protected them for forty years (Exodus 16; Deuteronomy 8:2–4). Elijah fled into the wilderness and was fed by ravens and an angel (1 Kings 17:2–6; 19:4–8). The holy family fled into Egypt to escape Herod (Matthew 2:13–15).

She gave birth to a male child. “Male child” is literally a son, a male (huion arsen), echoing Isaiah 66:7, where Zion gives birth to a son before her labour pains. The child is clearly Christ.

One who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron. The identification is settled by the quotation. It is Psalm 2:9, the coronation psalm of the Messiah, which this book has already applied to Christ and to those who conquer (2:27) and will apply again at 19:15. Christ is the Messiah-King.

But her child was caught up to God and to his throne. And here is the most extraordinary compression in Scripture. Between she gave birth and caught up to God and to his throne there is nothing. No childhood, no Galilee, no Sermon on the Mount, no miracles, no cross, no empty tomb. More than thirty years and the entire Gospel narrative pass in a comma. The whole life of Jesus, his ministry, death and resurrection, is compressed into a single moment between birth and ascension.

Why the compression? Because of what this chapter is showing. It is not telling the story of Jesus; it is telling the story of the dragon’s attempt on him, and the point being made is that the attempt failed completely. From the dragon’s side there is nothing to report between the birth and the throne except a total defeat. He stood there with his mouth open and the child went straight past him to the seat of God. Christ was not devoured; he was exalted to God’s throne.

Caught up. The verb is hērpasthē: snatched, seized with force. It is the word Paul uses of the man caught up to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2) and of believers caught up to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). Its sense is a rescue performed at speed. Whatever the dragon intended, the child was removed out of his reach.

The cross was not avoided. Be clear about what the compression does and does not mean, because it can mislead. It does not mean the cross was skipped. The cross is in this book everywhere: the Lamb standing as though slain is the central image of the whole vision, and a few verses on the saints conquer the dragon by the blood of the Lamb. It means the cross was not a victory for the dragon. The cross, which seemed to be Satan’s victory, led to Christ’s enthronement. He devoured nothing. The child he was waiting for went to the throne, and the route ran through a grave that could not hold him.

And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God. The child is safe on the throne; the mother is in the desert. That is the position of the church between the ascension and the end, and every word of the sentence is chosen with care. “Wilderness” (erēmon) is desert. In Scripture, the wilderness is a place of testing but also of God’s protection and provision. It is where Israel went after the exodus, the place of danger and of no resources, where a nation was fed for forty years by bread that arrived each morning. It is where Elijah was fed by ravens and by an angel. It is a hard address, and it is not abandonment.

A place prepared. “Prepared by God” (hētoimasmenon apo tou theou) uses the same verb as the place Christ has gone to prepare for his people (John 14:2). The desert was not an accident of flight; the accommodation was booked. The church, after Christ’s ascension, lives as in the wilderness: not yet in the promised land, exposed to hardship, but protected and provided for by God.

In which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days. “Nourished” (trephōsin) is fed, sustained, and the verb is passive, done by somebody not named. As God fed Israel with manna, he sustains his church by his word and Spirit. 1,260 days is the same period as the witnesses’ prophesying and the trampling of the holy city (11:2–3): the whole age between Christ’s ascension and return. The church in this age is a woman in a desert, fed by an unseen hand, for a period that has already been measured.

What it does not mean. The church in the wilderness does not mean the church is hidden or withdrawn from the world. It means the church lives as pilgrims and exiles (1 Peter 1:1; 2:11), protected by God in the midst of hostility.

How does God feed his church in the wilderness? By the ordinary means he has appointed. He feeds us through his word, read and preached; through prayer; through the Lord’s Supper and baptism; and through the fellowship of believers who bear one another’s burdens. That is our manna, and like manna it comes daily and must be gathered daily; yesterday’s portion will not do for today. So if you are feeling starved, ask first whether you have been at the table. The church that neglects the word and gathered worship is not being left hungry by God. It has stopped coming to where he lays the food.

In a sentence. She gave birth to a son, a boy who is to rule all the nations with an iron rod, but her child was snatched up to God and to his throne, and the woman fled into the desert to a place God had prepared for her, where she would be cared for during 1,260 days.

On a Tuesday. The church is in the wilderness, between Egypt and the promised land. Expect hardship, and expect God’s daily provision. He feeds his people. If you are in a dry stretch of life, with no prospects, no company and no visible progress, this verse tells you what that place is. It is not where God loses track of his people. It is where he feeds them himself, with the bread that comes down from heaven.

For worship. The Child is on the throne. He who was born in weakness was caught up in power; he who was laid in a manger sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high, and the nations are his inheritance. And the God who seated him there has not forgotten the mother. He prepared her place before she fled; he numbered her days before they began; he feeds her every morning in a land where nothing grows. The Shepherd of Israel, who rained down manna and set a table in the wilderness, is the Shepherd of his church, and she shall not want.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Satan Thrown Down to Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 7–8: war in heaven, Michael and his angels against the dragon and his; the dragon fights back, is defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. Michael appears in Scripture only in Daniel, Jude and here — the great prince who has charge of your people (Dan. 12:1), and the archangel who would not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against the devil but said The Lord rebuke you (Jude 9).

Verse 9 gives him four names in one sentence, and each is a job description: the great dragon, raw destructive power; that ancient serpent, the same one, from the garden; the devil, diabolos, slanderer; and Satan, Hebrew for adversary or accuser. Two of the four mean the same thing. He is also the deceiver of the whole world, and the verb thrown down is repeated three times in the verse.

Verse 10 explains it, and the explanation is a court case: the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. Verse 11 defines the book’s central verb in three clauses — they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Verse 12 gives the two reactions: heaven rejoices, earth and sea are warned, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Accuser Thrown Down

Satan, the accuser who stood as prosecutor before God, is thrown down. The saints conquer him by the blood of the Lamb, by the word of their testimony, and by not loving their lives even to death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Congregations that had buried martyrs were told those deaths were victories.

Now: The voice reciting your record has lost its standing, because the charges were paid. His fury is the fury of one whose time is short.

verseByVerse.quote: Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back, but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back, but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.

The setting. In Daniel 10:13, 21 and 12:1, Michael is the great prince who has charge of God’s people. In Jude 9 he is called the archangel. In Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3:1, Satan appears before God to accuse God’s people. Jesus said, when the seventy-two returned from their mission, I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18), and, as the cross approached, now will the ruler of this world be cast out (John 12:31).

Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. Michael’s name is Hebrew for who is like God? He is named in Scripture only in Daniel, Jude and here: the protector of God’s people, and an archangel who, disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgement but said, the Lord rebuke you (Jude 9). He is a creature, and a careful one. And notice that it is Michael, not God or Christ, who fights the dragon. Satan is not God’s equal rival but a creature defeated by another creature. The real victory has already been won by the Lamb (v. 11); Michael’s victory in heaven reflects Christ’s victory on earth.

And the dragon and his angels fought back, but he was defeated. “Defeated” is literally he was not strong enough, ouk ischysen. Satan is powerful, but not powerful enough. That phrase is the whole of his career.

And there was no longer any place for them in heaven. Which raises a question a thoughtful reader will already have: what was Satan doing in heaven at all? The Old Testament answers it plainly, and the answer is the key to the whole chapter. In Job he presents himself among the sons of God and accuses a righteous man to God’s face: does Job fear God for no reason (Job 1:9)? In Zechariah he stands at the right hand of the high priest to accuse him, and the priest is wearing filthy garments, and the accusation is true (Zechariah 3:1–4). Satan’s place in heaven was never a throne. It was a prosecutor’s bench. He lost his position as accuser before God (v. 10). After the cross, his accusations have no standing.

And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent. Four names in two verses, and each one is a job description. The great dragon: the chaos monster, raw destructive power. That ancient serpent (ho ophis ho archaios): and the adjective is doing work. This is the same one, the serpent of Eden who deceived Eve (Genesis 3:1), the one whose head the woman’s offspring would crush (Genesis 3:15). John expects the reader to make the connection without help.

Who is called the devil and Satan. “Devil” is diabolos, slanderer, accuser. “Satan” is the Hebrew satan, adversary, accuser. Two of the four names mean the same thing, and the next verse will make that the point. Dragon, serpent, devil, Satan: all his identities are exposed.

The deceiver of the whole world. “Deceiver” (ho planōn) is the one who leads astray. That is his method, and it has not changed since the first conversation in the garden, which was not a threat but a question: did God actually say? Deception is his main weapon, from Eden onwards: the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, and he disguises himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 4:4; 11:3, 14). He deceives the nations through the beast and false prophet (13:14; 20:3, 8). He is not mainly described in this book as a torturer or even a tempter. He is a liar with a legal practice.

He was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him. “Thrown down” (eblēthē) three times in one verse: thrown down, thrown down, thrown down with him. Decisive defeat. He did not withdraw, resign, or lose interest. He was removed, by force, and the sentence will not stop saying so. His sphere is now the earth, where he rages against the church (v. 12).

Where Christians differ: when was Satan thrown down? Some place this at Satan’s original fall before creation, linking it with Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28; others at a future point in the last days, at the midpoint of a seven-year tribulation. Verdict: the context places it at Christ’s death, resurrection and ascension. The child has just been caught up to God’s throne (v. 5), and the voice in heaven says that salvation and the kingdom have now come, because the accuser has been thrown down, and that believers conquered him by the blood of the Lamb (vv. 10–11). The cross is where Satan was defeated (John 12:31–32; Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14). His original rebellion lies behind this, and his final destruction lies ahead (20:10), but his decisive defeat happened at Calvary.

What it does not mean. Being thrown down does not mean Satan is powerless now. He is defeated but still dangerous, like a wounded animal, and the next verses show his fury. But he is a beaten foe.

If Satan was defeated at the cross, why is he still so active? Because a defeated enemy is not yet a removed enemy. Think of a war in which the decisive battle has been won, but fighting goes on in the provinces until the final surrender. The outcome is settled; the danger is real. Satan has lost his place as accuser and his hold on the nations (20:2–3), so that the gospel now goes freely to every people. But he can still tempt, deceive and persecute, within limits God sets. That is why Peter calls him a roaring lion and in the same breath tells you to resist him, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:8–9). You fight a real enemy from the side that has already won.

In a sentence. Then war broke out in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon, and the dragon and his angels fought back, but they were not strong enough and lost their place in heaven; the great dragon was thrown down, the ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, who leads the whole world astray; he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels with him.

On a Tuesday. When you face temptation or accusation, remember that the devil is a defeated enemy. He lies, and his greatest lie is that he is winning. Learn to recognise his voice: it usually sounds like a question about God’s goodness (did God really say? does God really care?) or a verdict on your worth (you will never change; you are not really his). Answer it with what God has actually said. Jesus met every temptation in the wilderness with it is written.

For worship. Who is like God? Not the dragon, with all his heads and crowns; he was not strong enough. Not even Michael, whose very name is a confession that there is none like the Lord. The ancient serpent who deceived our first parents has been thrown down, because the seed of the woman came and crushed his head at the cost of his own bruised heel. The Lord Jesus disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them in the cross. He saw Satan fall like lightning, and he has the final word over him. Glory to the Lamb, before whom the accuser has no place.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, "Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, “Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!”

The setting. In Zechariah 3:1–5, Satan stands at the right hand of Joshua the high priest to accuse him; the LORD rebukes Satan and removes Joshua’s filthy garments, clothing him in pure clothes. Paul asks who shall bring any charge against God’s elect. It is God who justifies; who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died, and who intercedes for us (Romans 8:33–34).

Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come. “Now” (arti) is at this moment. Heaven explains what has just happened. With Christ’s victory, the kingdom of God has come. It is not only future: it arrived at the cross and resurrection, and Christ now has all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18).

For the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. The explanation is entirely about a court case. The dragon is not called the tempter here, or the destroyer, or the ruler of this world. He is the accuser of our brothers, katēgōr, the prosecutor, and the participle is present and continuous: who accuses them day and night before our God. Satan accuses believers before God, pointing to their sins and arguing that they deserve condemnation. And he accuses them in their own consciences.

The file is accurate. Take that as literally as it is written, because it explains something a great many Christians experience and cannot name. There has been, in the presence of God, a voice reciting a list. And it was not inventing the charges; that is the terrible part. The prosecutor’s file in Zechariah 3 was accurate, and the high priest really was standing there in filthy clothes. The accusations against you are, on the whole, true. And they were being read out, day and night, for as long as the accuser had standing in the room. He has been thrown out. Not because the charges were false, and not because God stopped listening. He has lost his case because Christ has paid for every sin, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).

And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb. This is the definition of the book’s central verb, and everything in the seven letters depends on it. “Conquered” (enikēsan) has been promised to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea. Here is what it consists of, in three clauses. First, by the blood of the Lamb, and it is the ground of the other two. The accuser was not defeated by an argument, and certainly not by the saints’ record. He was defeated because the charges were paid. Satan’s accusations are answered by Christ’s death in our place. The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). A prosecutor whose every allegation has already been settled by somebody else has nothing to do in the room. That is why he is outside: there is no case left to bring. This is the heart of the gospel, and the foundation of every victory over Satan.

And by the word of their testimony. Second, and it follows from the first. “Testimony” (martyrias) is witness: holding to and speaking the truth about Jesus. What they said, not what they achieved. They say the true thing about Christ in front of people who do not want to hear it, and that saying is a weapon. The deceiver is defeated when the truth is told.

For they loved not their lives even unto death. Third, and it is the cost. “Loved not” (ouk ēgapēsan) does not mean they hated living. It means that when it came to a choice between their lives and their testimony, the testimony won. Some of them died for it. Satan’s last weapon is the threat of death, and it has no power over those who do not cling to their lives (Hebrews 2:14–15). A person who is not holding on to his own life has nothing left that can be threatened. Jesus said that whoever loses his life for his sake will find it (Matthew 16:25).

The shape of Christian courage. Read those three clauses in order and the shape of Christian courage appears. It does not begin with bravery. It begins with a verdict already delivered in blood, produces speech, and only then costs something. Nobody in this verse is asked to be fearless first. You are asked to stand on the blood, to open your mouth, and to trust God with what it costs.

Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! “You who dwell” is hoi skēnountes, you who tabernacle, who pitch your tent there. Heaven rejoices because the accuser is gone. Believers, whose real home is in heaven, share this joy. And notice the contrast with those who dwell on the earth elsewhere in the book: God’s people, even while they walk the earth, are counted among those whose tent is pitched in heaven.

But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath. “Great wrath” (thymon megan) is fury, rage. His defeat makes him more furious, not less. The same event produces opposite reactions in the two places, and John holds both. Heaven celebrates; earth is warned.

Because he knows that his time is short! “Short” is oligon kairon, a little time. The whole age between Christ’s ascension and return is Satan’s short time, the same as the 1,260 days. He knows he is doomed. The persecution of the church is the rage of a defeated enemy. That single clause reframes a great deal of Christian experience. The pressure a believer feels is not the pressure of an advancing enemy; it is the fury of one who has been thrown out of the courtroom, has read the timetable, and has very little left. A cornered animal is dangerous precisely because it is cornered. And short here is short as heaven measures it, which is not always short as a suffering church measures it, and is short nonetheless.

What it does not mean. Conquering by the blood of the Lamb does not mean using the phrase as a magic formula, as in some deliverance practices. It means trusting in Christ’s finished work as the answer to every accusation.

What do I say when my conscience accuses me? First, be honest: if the accusation is true, do not argue with it. Confess the sin to God plainly, and where needed put it right with the person you wronged. Then answer the accusation with Christ. Not, it was not so bad; but, it was worse than that, and Jesus died for it. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9), and Christ himself is our advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1). Learn the difference between the Spirit’s conviction, which is specific and leads you to Christ, and the accuser’s condemnation, which is vague, endless and drives you away from him. The first is a mercy. The second has been thrown out of court.

Does loving not my life mean I must be ready to die? Yes, in principle every Christian is called to love Christ more than life itself (Luke 14:26), and in some places that is a daily reality. But for most believers it is lived out in smaller deaths first: not loving your comfort, your reputation, your career or your safety more than your testimony. The man who will not risk a colleague’s scorn is not yet ready for a lion. Do not try to manufacture courage for a martyrdom that may never come. Be faithful in today’s small cost, and trust God to give you dying grace if he ever asks you to die.

In a sentence. Then I heard a loud voice in heaven say: Now God’s salvation, power and kingdom have come, and the authority of his Messiah, because the one who accused our brothers and sisters before our God day and night has been thrown down; they defeated him through the blood of the Lamb and the testimony they gave, because they did not cling to their lives even when faced with death; so celebrate, you heavens and all who live there; but how terrible for the earth and the sea, because the devil has come down to you, full of fury, knowing that his time is short.

On a Tuesday. When your conscience accuses you, or the devil reminds you of your sins, answer with the blood of the Lamb. Christ has paid; the case is closed. Then open your mouth for him somewhere today, in a kind word about him, an honest answer, a refusal to pretend you are not a Christian. And when you feel the pressure of the world against you, remember what it is: the rage of one who knows his time is short.

For worship. Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. The accuser stood before the throne day and night with a true list of our sins, and the Lamb answered every line of it with his blood. Now the prosecutor’s bench is empty, the case is closed, and heaven rings with joy. Salvation and power and the kingdom belong to our God, and authority to his Christ, who loved not his life unto death so that his people might conquer through him. Let the heavens rejoice. Before this throne there is no condemnation, only the blood that speaks a better word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — The Dragon Pursues the Woman
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 13: when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down, he pursued the woman. The logic matters — he goes after the mother because he cannot reach the child, who is on the throne, and cannot go back to the courtroom.

Verse 14: the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle to fly into the wilderness, to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time. The wings are the exodus — I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself (Ex. 19:4; cf. Deut. 32:11; Isa. 40:31) — and the time is Daniel 7:25, the third form of the same number John has now used three ways in two chapters.

Verses 15–16: the serpent pours a river out of his mouth to sweep her away, and the earth came to the help of the woman and swallowed it — as the ground opened on Korah (Num. 16:31–33) and the sea closed over Pharaoh’s chariots.

Verse 17: the dragon, furious, goes off to make war on the rest of her offspring — reaching back to Genesis 3:15 — defined by exactly two marks: those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And the chapter ends on a quiet, ominous line: And he stood on the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Complete Exodus

Thrown down, the dragon pursues the woman, but she is given eagle’s wings and carried to the wilderness to be fed. The flood from his mouth is swallowed by the earth, and he turns on her children — those who keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The church under Rome was living inside the story of Exodus, and knew how it ended.

Now: Persecution is the rage of a defeated accuser, and the wilderness is where God feeds his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child. But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child. But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.

The setting. God told Israel at Sinai, you have seen how I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself (Exodus 19:4). Deuteronomy 32:11 pictures God as an eagle that stirs up its nest and carries its young on its pinions. Isaiah 40:31 says those who wait for the LORD shall mount up with wings like eagles. Daniel 7:25 speaks of the saints given into the hand of the persecuting king for a time, times and half a time.

And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman. “Pursued” (ediōxen) is persecuted, chased. Catch the logic of the verse. He goes after the woman because he has been thrown down. He cannot reach the child, who is on the throne. He cannot go back to the courtroom. So he turns on the mother. Having failed to destroy the child, Satan turns on the child’s people, the church. Persecution of the church is Satan’s revenge on Christ.

What persecution means. That does not make the persecution less real, and this book never pretends it does. What it does is settle what persecution means. It is not evidence that the dragon is gaining ground. It is evidence that he has lost the only ground that mattered and has nowhere else to go. Jesus said it on the Damascus road: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me (Acts 9:4)? To strike the church is to aim at Christ, and to miss.

But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle. “Was given”: God’s provision. She does not grow the wings or buy them. The image is the exodus, and John expects it to be recognised at once. As God carried Israel out of Egypt on eagles’ wings, he carries his church through the wilderness of this age. Isaiah made the same promise to exhausted people: they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles.

The exodus all over again. The chapter now has a complete exodus in it: a tyrant trying to kill the children, a child rescued, a flight, a wilderness, a place prepared, food from an unseen hand, eagles’ wings, and in the next verses a flood that the enemy intended for the woman and the ground swallowing it. This is not decoration. John is telling seven congregations under Roman pressure that they are living in the book of Exodus, and that they already know how it ends.

So that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished. As in verse 6. God protects and feeds his people. This is the second time the wilderness has been described as a place of nourishment rather than exposure. The desert is where the dragon cannot follow and the food arrives anyway.

For a time, and times, and half a time. From Daniel 7:25 and 12:7: one year, two years and half a year, three and a half years. The same period as 1,260 days (v. 6) and forty-two months (11:2): the whole church age, a time of persecution limited by God. John has now used all three forms interchangeably within two chapters, which is itself a strong argument that he means one thing by them.

What it does not mean. Protection in the wilderness does not mean individual believers will never suffer or die. The rest of her offspring are attacked (v. 17), and some are killed (13:7). It means the church as a whole will never be destroyed. The gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18).

If the church is protected, why do some churches die out? Because the promise is to the church of Christ as a whole, not to every congregation or denomination. The seven churches of chapters 2 and 3 have long since disappeared from most of their cities, and Jesus warned Ephesus that he would remove its lampstand if it did not repent (2:5). Churches can lose the gospel and die. But the people of God has never died out, and never will: when the church declined in one land, it grew in another, and today it is found in nearly every nation on earth. Pray for your own church to be faithful. Rest in the promise that Christ’s church cannot fail.

In a sentence. When the dragon realised he had been thrown down to the earth, he went after the woman who had given birth to the boy; but the woman was given the two wings of a great eagle, so that she could fly away from the serpent to her place in the desert, where she would be cared for, out of his reach, for a time, times and half a time.

On a Tuesday. If you feel the pressure of the enemy against your faith, your family or your church, do not read it as a sign that God has lost hold of you. Read it as a sign that you belong to the child the dragon could not reach. And when you have no strength left, remember who gives the wings. Waiting on the Lord is not passive. It is turning to him in prayer and in his word when you would rather give up, and finding, again and again, that he carries you.

For worship. Thank God that he carries his people on eagles’ wings. However fierce the attack, the church will not be destroyed. He bore Israel out of Egypt and brought them to himself; he stirs up the nest and spreads his wings beneath his young; he gives power to the faint and strength to those who have no might. The dragon pursues, and the Lord lifts his people beyond reach. He who numbered the days of the trampling feeds his people every one of them, and the place he prepared is waiting at the end of the desert.

verseByVerse.quote: The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood. But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth. Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And he stood on the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood. But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth. Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And he stood on the sand of the sea.

The setting. In the Psalms, floods and many waters picture overwhelming danger and the attacks of enemies (Psalm 18:4, 16; 32:6; 124:4–5). At the Red Sea, God opened a path through the waters for Israel, and the waters swept away Pharaoh’s army (Exodus 14–15). When Korah rebelled against Moses, the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the rebels (Numbers 16:30–32). In the song of Moses, Israel sang, you stretched out your right hand; the earth swallowed them (Exodus 15:12).

The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood. Two mouths, and the whole passage turns on them. The dragon’s mouth pours out a river; the earth’s mouth swallows it. “Out of his mouth” (ek tou stomatos autou): the flood comes from his mouth, and what comes out of the dragon’s mouth is what has always come out of it. He was called the deceiver of the whole world six verses ago, and his one method is speech. The flood is lies, deception, false teaching, slander and propaganda. As the witnesses’ fire is their word (11:5), so Satan’s flood is his. He tries to drown the church in falsehood.

A flood of words. In the Psalms, overwhelming waters are the standard image for hostile speech and danger: save me, O God, for the waters have come up to my neck (Psalm 69:1–2). And a flood is a good picture of how a reputation is destroyed, or a truth buried. Not one accusation, which can be answered, but a volume of it arriving faster than anybody can respond, until the truth is simply under water.

But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river. The rescue comes from the least likely quarter. The earth in this book is usually where the trouble is: the earth-dwellers, the beast from the earth, the outer court given over to be trampled. Here it opens its mouth and swallows a river, as the ground opened and swallowed Korah and his household, and as the sea closed over Pharaoh’s chariots. God uses even his creation to protect his people. God is not restricted to the instruments a believer would have expected. He has used a pagan king’s decree, a famine, a shipwreck and an earthquake in a prison to protect his people, and here he uses the ground. The flood of lies does not succeed. Throughout history, persecutions and heresies have risen and been swallowed up, while the church has survived.

Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring. “Furious” (ōrgisthē). Frustrated at the mother, he turns on the children. “The rest of her offspring” (tōn loipōn tou spermatos autēs, the rest of her seed) reaches straight back to Genesis 3:15 and the enmity between the serpent’s offspring and the woman’s. Christ is her first offspring; believers are her other children, Christ’s brothers and sisters (Romans 8:29; Hebrews 2:11–13). If the church as a whole is protected, individual believers are still attacked.

On those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. John pauses to define them, and there are only two marks. They keep the commandments of God: obedience, ordinary and unglamorous, in the things God has actually commanded rather than the things a person would prefer to be judged on. And they hold to the testimony of Jesus: confession; they have not let go of what they say about him. This is the definition of a true believer in Revelation, obedience to God and loyalty to Jesus (14:12), and these are Satan’s targets.

How short the list is. There is a quiet challenge in it. Not those who understand this book. Not those who identified the beast correctly. Not those who never suffered. Obedience and confession, held on to. That is what the dragon goes to war against, and that is all it takes to be on his list.

And he stood on the sand of the sea. The chapter ends with a sentence that is quietly ominous. The dragon takes his stand at the seashore, ready to call up his ally from the sea (13:1). He walks down to the shoreline and stands there, looking out at the water, and the very next sentence in the book is: and I saw a beast rising out of the sea. Satan works through human agents and systems. That is the last image of chapter 12 and the first of chapter 13, and it is a single movement.

Textual note. The last sentence is numbered 12:18 in some Bibles and 13:1 in others. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “I stood on the sand of the sea”, making John the subject. The best manuscripts read “he stood”, referring to the dragon.

Watching without panic. The reader has now been given everything he needs to watch what comes next without panic. The child is on the throne. The accuser has been thrown out and has no case to bring. The woman is fed in a place prepared for her. The saints conquer by blood already shed and words already spoken. And the dragon standing on that beach, about to summon the worst thing in the book, is a defeated prosecutor with a short time, doing the only thing left to him.

What it does not mean. Satan’s war on believers does not mean God has abandoned them. They are her offspring, and God protects the woman. But they are on the front line, and they must keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus.

How do I keep from being swept away by the flood of lies? Know the truth well enough to recognise the counterfeit. Bank clerks learn to spot forged notes by handling real ones. So read the whole Bible regularly, sit under faithful preaching, and learn the great truths of the faith, perhaps through a good confession or catechism. Be slow to believe what you hear about fellow Christians, and test every teaching by Scripture, as the Bereans did (Acts 17:11). Notice which voices make God seem less good, sin less serious or Christ less necessary, and turn them off. And stay close to the church: a flood sweeps away the one standing alone far more easily than a people holding on together.

In a sentence. Then the serpent spewed water like a river from his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away in the flood; but the earth helped the woman by opening its mouth and swallowing the river the dragon had spewed out; then the dragon was enraged with the woman and went off to wage war against the rest of her children, those who obey God’s commandments and hold firmly to their testimony about Jesus; and he stood on the seashore.

On a Tuesday. Satan floods the world with lies. Hold to the truth, keep God’s commandments, and hold the testimony of Jesus. That is what makes you his target, and that is how you overcome. Look at your week: where does the flood reach you most, through a screen, a conversation, a fear? Decide what you will put in its place. And take the two marks as your daily aim: obey God in the plain things today, and do not let go of what you say about Jesus.

For worship. The Lord sits enthroned over the flood; the Lord sits enthroned as king for ever. The dragon poured out a river of lies, and the God who split the Red Sea and opened the ground under Korah made the earth itself swallow it. He commands sea and land and every creature to serve his people. And the children the dragon hunts are the brothers and sisters of the Son, whom he is not ashamed to call his own. Not one of them can be swept out of his hand. The dragon stands on the sand. The Lamb stands on Mount Zion, and the next time the curtain opens, his people are standing with him.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.<sup>2</sup>She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth.<sup>3</sup>And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems.<sup>4</sup>His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.<sup>5</sup>She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne,<sup>6</sup>and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.<sup>7</sup>Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back,<sup>8</sup>but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven.<sup>9</sup>And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.<sup>10</sup>And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, “Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God.<sup>11</sup>And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.<sup>12</sup>Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!”<sup>13</sup>And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child.<sup>14</sup>But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.<sup>15</sup>The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood.<sup>16</sup>But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth.<sup>17</sup>Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And he stood on the sand of the sea.

13.title: The Two Beasts: The Dragon's Earthly Instruments
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is the political theology chapter of Revelation. The dragon, standing on the seashore, summons two beasts — one from the sea, one from the land — and delegates to them his authority, his throne, and great power. Together the dragon and the two beasts form a Satanic trinity that parodies the Holy Trinity: the dragon parodies the Father, the beast from the sea parodies the Son (including a parody death and resurrection), and the beast from the land parodies the Spirit (pointing away from itself to the first beast, as the Spirit points away from himself to the Son). The unholy trinity is the political and religious power structure of every totalitarian system that demands ultimate allegiance.

Interpretive flag — The Beast from the Sea: This is the third major structural decision point. The preterist reading identifies the beast as Nero Caesar — and the gematria (numerical value of letters) of “Nero Caesar” in Hebrew adds up to 666. The mortal wound that was healed (v. 3) refers to the Nero redivivus myth: rumors after Nero’s death in AD 68 that he had survived and would return from the east with the Parthian army. The historicist reading has identified the beast with various historical powers including the papacy. The futurist/dispensational reading sees a still-future individual world ruler, a literal Antichrist who will arise in the last days, be given global political power, and demand global worship. The idealist/amillennial reading understands the beast as the pattern of totalitarian political power that demands ultimate allegiance in every age — with Rome as the first-century embodiment and every subsequent empire that makes similar demands as its successor. The idealist position is followed here, while the specific Nero/Rome referent is fully acknowledged as the primary first-century layer.

Interpretive flag — 666: Three readings predominate. (1) Gematria: “Neron Kaisar” in Hebrew letters (nun-resh-vav-nun / qoph-samek-resh) adds to 666; the spelling without the final n adds to 616, which is the reading of some early manuscripts. The specific first-century referent. (2) The number of incompleteness: six is one less than seven (the number of divine completeness); 666 is the triple intensification of falling short of the divine — the beast is humanity at its most grandiose, still falling short of the glory of God. (3) The number of humanity: six was associated with humanity in some traditions (created on the sixth day). The beast is the ultimate expression of humanity’s totalitarian self-divinization. All three readings illuminate the symbol; none is exhaustive.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a beast rises out of the sea with the dragon’s own features — seven heads, ten horns, royal diadems — and blasphemous names on its heads, which is what Roman coins and inscriptions actually gave the emperors. It is like a leopard, with a bear’s feet and a lion’s mouth: Daniel’s four beasts (Dan. 7:2–7) compressed into one. And the dragon gave it his power, his throne and great authority — the offer Christ refused in the desert (Luke 4:6).

Verses 3–4: one head has a mortal wound that was healed, and the whole earth marvels. The Greek uses the same participle used of the Lamb at 5:6, so the parody is deliberate. The world worships dragon and beast together, chanting Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it? — the song of the exodus (Ex. 15:11) with a different object, and the meaning of the name Michael turned to the wrong address.

Verses 5–6: the beast was given a mouth of haughty and blasphemous words and was allowed authority for forty-two months (cf. Dan. 7:8, 25). It blasphemes God’s name and his dwelling — and John glosses the dwelling himself: that is, those who dwell in heaven.

Verses 7–8: it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them, with authority over every tribe and people and language and nation; and all the earth-dwellers worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain. Verses 9–10 turn to the reader: If anyone has an ear, let him hear — captivity to captivity, sword to sword (cf. Jer. 15:2) — Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Beast from the Sea

The dragon gives the beast his power, throne and authority. It mimics the Lamb’s death and resurrection, wins the world’s worship because it seems unbeatable, and is allowed to speak blasphemies and make war on the saints for forty-two months.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Rome’s emperors bore divine titles on coins and inscriptions.

Now: Worship of power begins as a calculation that resistance is pointless. The saints’ calling is endurance and faith; their names are in the Lamb’s book.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, with ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads. And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear's, and its mouth was like a lion's mouth. And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, with ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads. And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear’s, and its mouth was like a lion’s mouth. And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.

Meaning first. Revelation 13 introduces the dragon’s two allies, the instruments through which Satan makes war on the saints. A beast rises from the sea, with ten horns and seven heads like the dragon, combining features of Daniel’s four beasts, and the dragon gives it his power, throne and authority (vv. 1–2). One of its heads seems mortally wounded but is healed, and the whole world marvels and worships both the dragon and the beast: who is like the beast? (vv. 3–4). It speaks blasphemies against God for forty-two months, makes war on the saints and conquers them, and everyone whose name is not written in the Lamb’s book of life worships it (vv. 5–8). The saints are called to endure: captivity and death may come, and they must not resist with the sword (vv. 9–10). A second beast rises from the earth, with horns like a lamb but speaking like a dragon; it promotes the worship of the first beast, performs deceptive signs, sets up a speaking image of the beast, and has those who refuse to worship it killed (vv. 11–15). It forces everyone to receive a mark on the right hand or forehead, without which no one can buy or sell (vv. 16–17). The number of the beast is 666, the number of a man (v. 18). The chapter unmasks the political and religious powers that demand total loyalty in place of God. In John’s day that was Rome and its emperor cult; through the age it takes many forms; and it will reach a final climax before Christ returns. And all through the chapter, under every boast of the beast, runs a quiet refrain: it was given, it was allowed. The throne above the dragon has not moved.

The setting. In Daniel 7, four beasts rise from the sea: a lion, a bear, a leopard and a terrifying fourth beast with ten horns, representing four world empires, usually understood as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome. A little horn on the fourth beast speaks great things, makes war on the saints and prevails for a time, times and half a time, until the Ancient of Days judges it and gives the kingdom to the saints. For John’s readers, Rome came from across the sea, and Roman governors arrived in Asia by ship. The emperors claimed divine titles: the coins called Augustus son of god, and Domitian liked to be addressed as lord and god.

What the dragon calls up. The dragon is standing on the beach at the end of chapter 12, looking out to sea. This is what he calls up.

And I saw a beast rising out of the sea. “Beast” (thērion) is a wild animal, a monster. The sea in this book is the ancient image of chaos and of the unmanageable, the realm of evil (Daniel 7:2–3) and of the abyss (11:7). That is why the throne room has it frozen flat as glass (4:6), and why the new creation is announced with the words and the sea was no more (21:1). Empires come up out of the churn. The beast is a power from below, given human form. And to a congregation on the coast of Asia, the sea was also the direction Rome arrived from.

With ten horns and seven heads. Count the features against the dragon of 12:3, because the correspondence is exact and deliberate: seven heads, ten horns, and royal crowns. The beast is the dragon’s image. What comes out of the water is what the dragon looks like when he takes a form that can hold public office. In 17:9–12 the seven heads are seven mountains and seven kings, and the ten horns ten kings.

With ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads. Two differences from the dragon, and both are pointed. The dragon wore seven diadems on his heads; the beast wears ten on its horns: more crowns, and worn on the instruments of force rather than on the seat of thought. And the beast carries blasphemous names (onomata blasphēmias) on its heads: titles that belong only to God. That detail was not a metaphor to a first-century reader. Coins and inscriptions across the province of Asia gave the emperors titles such as divine, son of god, saviour of the world, and lord and god. The beast is wearing them.

And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear’s, and its mouth was like a lion’s mouth. This is Daniel 7, and John expects it to be recognised at once. Daniel saw four beasts come up out of the sea: a lion, a bear, a leopard, and a fourth beast terrifying and dreadful with ten horns. Four beasts, four kingdoms. John names three of them in reverse order and gives their features to one animal. What Daniel saw as a succession of empires, John sees gathered into a single creature. It sums up all the godless empires of history in one.

One beast in many costumes. The point is not chronology. It is that there has only ever been one beast, wearing different national costumes. Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome are not four different problems; they are four appearances of the same thing, and it appears again in every century. It is not just one empire but the spirit of every empire that sets itself against God. Any reader who has decided the beast is one particular regime should notice that John has just merged four of them.

And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority. “Gave” (edōken). The beast’s power comes from Satan, a grim parody of how the Father gives authority to the Son (2:27). Three nouns, and they answer an offer Christ was made in a desert. The devil showed him all the kingdoms of the world and said, to you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me (Luke 4:6). Christ refused. The beast accepts. And that is the whole difference between the two kingdoms in this book: one of them takes a throne from the dragon, and the other takes a cross from his Father.

The chain of permission. Notice the verb again. The dragon gave, and everything the dragon has, he was permitted to have. Again and again in this chapter the beasts are given or allowed something (vv. 5, 7, 14, 15). The chain of permission runs upward past the dragon to the throne, and the reader who has been paying attention since chapter 6 knows who sits there.

Where Christians differ: who is the beast? Preterists identify the beast with the Roman Empire and the emperor Nero. Historicists, including many Reformers, identified it with the papacy. Futurists see a single future world dictator, the Antichrist, at the end of history. Verdict: the beast is the persecuting power of the state, or any human system, that claims divine authority and demands worship, empowered by Satan. In John’s day it was clearly the Roman Empire and its emperor cult; through history it has reappeared in many forms, whenever a power demands the total loyalty that belongs to God alone; and Scripture expects a final, intensified manifestation before Christ returns, the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3–10). Many Reformers were right to see beastly features in the persecuting medieval church, but the beast is wider than any one institution. This combined view honours the first readers, every generation, and the end.

What it does not mean. Not all government is beastly. Paul teaches that governing authorities are instituted by God for good (Romans 13:1–7). The state becomes the beast when it oversteps its role, claims divine authority and demands worship, and persecutes those who refuse.

How do I tell when a government has become beastly? Look for the marks this chapter gives. A beastly power claims what belongs to God: titles of divinity, final authority over conscience, the right to define good and evil without reference to him. It demands worship, not merely obedience: total loyalty, public affirmation, the bowing of the mind. And it punishes those who will not give it, by exclusion or by force. A government can be unjust, corrupt or foolish without being the beast, and Christians must still honour it and obey it in everything lawful (1 Peter 2:13–17). But when it commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

In a sentence. Then I saw a beast coming up out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, a royal crown on each horn and blasphemous names on its heads; it looked like a leopard, with feet like a bear’s and a mouth like a lion’s, and the dragon handed over to it his own power, his throne and great authority.

On a Tuesday. Respect the authorities God has placed over you, and pray for them. But give your ultimate loyalty only to Christ. When any power demands what belongs to God, the Christian must refuse. Pay your taxes, keep the law, speak honourably of rulers, and pray for them by name. And keep one thing back that no government may have: your worship, your conscience and your confession that Jesus is Lord.

For worship. The beast came up out of the sea with ten crowns and a mouthful of blasphemies, and the sea it came from is the sea that God will one day abolish. The dragon gave it a throne, but the dragon has no throne of his own except the one he stole, and the Lamb is in the midst of the true throne for ever. The Son of God refused the kingdoms of the world from Satan’s hand and received them instead from his Father’s, by way of a cross. Blessed be the King who would not bow, and who now holds the authority the beast only borrows.
verseByVerse.note: This beast combines the four beasts of Daniel 7 — leopard, bear, lion and the ten-horned beast.

verseByVerse.quote: One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound, but its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast. And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, "Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound, but its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast. And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, “Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?”

The setting. After Nero’s suicide in AD 68, the empire fell into civil war, with four emperors in one year, and seemed about to collapse, until Vespasian restored order. Rumours spread that Nero had not really died and would return from the east with a Parthian army (the Nero redivivus myth). In the Old Testament, Who is like you, O LORD? is a cry of praise to God (Exodus 15:11; Psalm 35:10; Micah 7:18); the name Michael means Who is like God?

One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound. “Seemed” (hōs) is as though. “Mortal wound” (esphagmenēn eis thanaton) is literally slain to death, and the word is the same one that describes the Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, at 5:6. John does not use that word loosely. The beast imitates Christ’s death.

But its mortal wound was healed. “Healed” (etherapeuthē). A parody of Christ’s resurrection: a figure bearing a death wound and alive anyway, demanding the worship that belongs to the one who really died and really rose. The beast’s power seems to be destroyed, then revives. Godless powers often seem to fall, only to reappear in new forms.

Satan invents nothing. That is the key to this chapter and the two that follow. Everything the dragon produces is an imitation. A beast with a resurrection. A second beast with horns like a lamb. A mark on the forehead. An image that breathes. A city called great. Satan creates nothing; he copies, and the copies are close enough to be mistaken for the original by people who have not looked carefully. Which is why the best protection against the counterfeit is close acquaintance with the real thing.

What the wound refers to. What the wound refers to historically is disputed. Some point to Nero, whom many in the eastern provinces refused to believe was dead, expecting him to return from beyond the Euphrates, a rumour that produced several impostors. Some point to the empire itself, which came close to disintegrating in the civil wars of AD 68 to 69, when four emperors ruled in a single year, and then recovered completely under Vespasian. Some hold it is still future. What is not disputed is the effect. The wound is what makes the beast credible.

And the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast. “Marveled” (ethaumasthē) is was amazed. “Followed” is literally went after (opisō), as disciples follow a master. The world follows the beast as the church follows the Lamb wherever he goes (14:4). Everyone is following someone.

And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast. Worshipping the beast is really worshipping Satan. All idolatry has a demonic source: what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God (1 Corinthians 10:20). People who would never knowingly kneel to the devil kneel to him anyway, through the thing he has dressed up for them.

And they worshiped the beast, saying, Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it? Two things about that chant, and both would have landed hard on a Jewish ear. First, it is a parody of the song of the exodus. When Israel came through the sea, Moses and the people sang, who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness (Exodus 15:11)? The world’s worship uses the same sentence with a different object. Second, the name Michael, who threw the dragon out of heaven in the previous chapter, means who is like God? The beast’s worshippers are chanting the archangel’s name at the wrong address. And the answer to their question has already been given: Michael, Who is like God, has already defeated the dragon (12:7–9), and the Lamb will conquer the beast, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings (17:14).

Worship of sheer power. The second half of the chant is the more revealing: who can fight against it? That is not a statement about the beast’s goodness. Nobody in the verse claims the beast is kind, or just, or true. They worship it because it cannot be beaten. The world admires and fears power. This is worship of sheer power: the reasoning of a person who has decided that whatever is strongest must be right, or at least must be obeyed, which in practice comes to the same thing.

The first act of worship is a calculation. Be honest about that, because it is not an exotic sin. Very few people consciously decide to worship a tyrant. What they do is conclude that resistance is pointless, that the thing is too big to be opposed, and that a sensible person accommodates himself to it. That conclusion, reached quietly and without ceremony, is what the verse describes. It happens in a nation and it happens in an office, a school, a family: the moment someone decides that the strongest voice in the room must be obeyed because it is the strongest.

What it does not mean. The healed wound is not a prediction that a particular leader will be assassinated and then come back to life. It is a parody of Christ’s death and resurrection, showing that the beast is a counterfeit Christ, and that evil powers revive after apparent defeat.

When evil seems to have been beaten and then comes back, what should I think? That this is exactly what Revelation told you to expect. Godless powers rise, fall and revive in new forms throughout this age, because the beast has a healed head. Do not put your final hope in any political victory, as though one election or one revolution could finish evil off; and do not despair when the old evil returns in new clothes. Only one death and resurrection is final, and it is not the beast’s. The Lamb was really slain and really lives, and he alone will bring evil to its end, at his coming.

In a sentence. One of the beast’s heads looked as if it had been fatally wounded, but the deadly wound had healed, and the whole world was astonished and went after the beast; people worshipped the dragon, because he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshipped the beast too, saying, Who can compare with the beast? Who can fight against it?

On a Tuesday. Watch what amazes you. The world is dazzled by power, success and strength. Be amazed instead by the Lamb who was slain and rose again. Notice where in your own life you have quietly decided that something is too big to oppose, a habit, an expectation at work, a voice in the culture, and that going along is simply realism. Then ask who you are following, and whether that is the one you would call Lord out loud.

For worship. Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders? The beast has a scar and a counterfeit life; the Lamb has the marks of the nails and an endless life. The world marvels at the copy. Heaven marvels at the original, the one who was dead and is alive for evermore and holds the keys of death and Hades. There is no one like our God, and the question the beast’s worshippers asked has only one answer, sung by Moses at the sea and by the redeemed before the throne: none is like you.

verseByVerse.quote: And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words, and it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months. It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words, and it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months. It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.

The setting. In Daniel 7:8, 11, 20, 25, the little horn has a mouth speaking great things, and speaks words against the Most High. Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Greek king who persecuted the Jews in 167–164 BC, called himself God manifest, desecrated the temple, and is often seen as a forerunner of the antichrist (Daniel 11:36; 1 Maccabees 1).

And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words. “Was given” (edothē) comes four times in verses 5 to 7. The beast did not acquire its mouth; it was given one. It does nothing except by permission. God sets its limits. “Haughty” is megala, great things, arrogant boasts, the very phrase of Daniel’s little horn. These divine passives are the reason a Christian can read this chapter without despair.

And it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months. It did not seize its term of office; it was allowed one. Whatever authority it exercises is on licence, and the licence has an expiry date printed on it. Forty-two months is the same period as the trampling of the holy city (11:2), the witnesses’ prophesying (11:3), and the woman’s protection in the wilderness (12:6, 14): the whole church age, between Christ’s comings. The beast’s rule and the church’s witness run side by side, for the same limited time. The same clock governs the persecution and the preserving.

It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven. “Blaspheming” (blasphēmēsai) is slandering, insulting. Three objects, and the third repays attention. It blasphemes his name, his character, who God is. It blasphemes his dwelling, skēnēn, his tabernacle, and then John adds his own explanation in case anybody imagines a building: that is, those who dwell in heaven. God’s tabernacle is his people (21:3), and those who dwell in heaven are believers, whose citizenship is there and who are seated with Christ in the heavenly places (12:12; Ephesians 2:6). So the beast mocks and slanders the church.

To slander the church is to slander God. John states it as a simple equivalence. That is the logic of the voice on the Damascus road: not, why do you persecute my followers, but Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me (Acts 9:4)? What is done to the body is done to the head. A believer who is mocked for Christ is not alone in being mocked.

The beast’s chief weapon is its mouth. Notice what its activity actually is. It has ten horns and the authority of the dragon and a mortal wound that healed, and the verses describing what it does are entirely about its mouth. It talks. It utters. It blasphemes. That should adjust how a believer expects the pressure to come. The great opposition to the church in this book is not chiefly a police force; it is a story about reality, repeated with enormous confidence and reach, in which God is small and his people are contemptible and the beast is the only realistic option. Christians who are braced for a knock at the door are sometimes overwhelmed instead by forty years of being told, pleasantly, that what they believe is ridiculous.

Against a mouth, a mouth. And against a mouth, the church has been issued a mouth. That is its whole armament: the word of their testimony (12:11), and behind it the sharp sword that comes from the mouth of Christ (1:16; 19:15). The beast’s words are loud. Christ’s word is true, and it will have the last say.

What it does not mean. Forty-two months is not a literal three and a half years at the end of history. It is Daniel’s symbolic period of persecution, which Revelation applies to the whole time of the church’s witness.

How do I stay steady when everything around me mocks my faith? Expect it, so it does not unsettle you; this chapter told you it would come. Then keep your mind full of the truth, because constant mockery works by slow erosion more than by argument. Spend more time with God’s voice than with the voices that belittle him: in Scripture, in worship, in the company of believers. Remember that the mockery is aimed at God first, and he is not threatened by it. And refuse to answer contempt with contempt. A gentle, unashamed, cheerful faith is itself a reply the beast’s mouth cannot answer.

In a sentence. The beast was allowed to speak arrogant and blasphemous words, and was permitted to exercise its authority for forty-two months; it opened its mouth to blaspheme God, insulting his name and his dwelling place, those who live in heaven.

On a Tuesday. When the culture mocks God and his people, remember that its time is limited. Do not answer mockery with mockery; answer with faithful witness. Notice this week how much of what you hear assumes, without argument, that God is small or absent. You do not need to fight every sentence. You need to keep saying, in word and life, what is true.

For worship. The beast was given a mouth, and God gave it; the beast was allowed a season, and God numbered its days. The Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will; he laughs at the arrogant words of the little horn and appoints the hour of its judgement. And the people the beast slanders are his own tabernacle, the dwelling place he has chosen, seated with his Son in the heavenly places. No insult reaches them that does not first strike him, and he has borne insult before: he was reviled and did not revile in return. Blessed be the God whose name outlasts every blasphemy, and whose word outlasts every boast.

verseByVerse.quote: Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation, and all who dwell on earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation, and all who dwell on earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.

The setting. Daniel 7:21 says the horn made war with the saints and prevailed over them, until the Ancient of Days came and judgement was given for the saints.

Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. That is the hardest sentence in the book, and it should be read slowly rather than hurried past. The beast is permitted to make war on Christians, and permitted to win. The verb is nikaō, conquer, the same word that ends every one of the seven letters as a promise to the one who conquers, the word used of Christ at 5:5, and the word used of the saints at 12:11. Here it is used of the beast, against them, successfully, as at 11:7. Revelation will not tell the church that faithfulness guarantees survival. It says the opposite, twice. Congregations are overrun. Believers are imprisoned and executed. The beast seems to win: it kills believers.

Two kinds of victory. Hold that beside 12:11 and the two sentences interpret each other. There, the saints conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Same verb, same people, opposite outcome, and the resolution is in the last clause. In Revelation, those killed for their faith are the true conquerors (12:11; 15:2). The beast wins the battle of bodies; the saints win the battle of faithfulness. Two kinds of victory are running at once, and only one of them is visible from the street.

And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation. The fourfold phrase from 5:9, a parody of the Lamb’s redeemed from every tribe, language, people and nation. The beast’s rule seems universal. It is given, and it covers exactly the territory that has already been bought by somebody else.

And all who dwell on earth will worship it. Those who dwell on the earth is John’s technical term, established at 8:13, for the unbelieving world, people whose whole account is settled here. It is not a geographical description; the saints live on the earth too and are never called earth-dwellers. Everyone worships something. Those who do not worship God will worship the beast.

Everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain. Then the safeguard, and it is the most reassuring clause in the chapter.
