There is a register. “Written” (gegraptai) is perfect tense: it has been written and stands written. “From the foundation of the world” (apo katabolēs kosmou): before anybody had done anything to deserve entry or exclusion. The book of life of the Lamb is the Lamb’s register of his people. The only ones who resist the beast are those written in the Lamb’s book. Their names were written before creation, by God’s eternal choice. Their perseverance rests not on their own strength but on God’s election.

Where Christians differ: what does “from the foundation of the world” go with? The Greek word order allows “the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world” (as in the King James Version) or “written from the foundation of the world in the book of life” (as in the ESV). Verdict: the second is more likely, because 17:8 uses the same phrase clearly of names written in the book of life from the foundation of the world. Both truths are biblical: Christ was foreknown as the sacrifice before the foundation of the world (1 Peter 1:20), and God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). The verse teaches unconditional election: God wrote the names of his people in the Lamb’s book before they were born, not because of anything they would do, and he keeps them from worshipping the beast.

What it does not mean. Election does not make anyone’s worship of the beast excusable; people are responsible for their idolatry. Nor does it make faithfulness unimportant; the elect are precisely those who refuse to worship the beast. God’s choice is the root, and faithful endurance is the fruit.

Could I be deceived into worshipping the beast without realising it? The verse says the opposite. The people who worship are those whose names are not written; the ones whose names are written are kept. That is not a promise that a believer will never be frightened, never waver and never fail: Peter denied Christ three times in a courtyard, and was restored. It is a promise about who does the holding. Jesus said it without symbols: no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). And the book that decides it is the book of the Lamb who was slain. The register is not a list of the people who held out. It is the property of the one with the wounds, and the entries were made before the world existed.

How can I know my name is written there? Not by trying to read the book, which God has not opened to us, but by looking to the Lamb whose book it is. The names written there are the names of those who come to him; Jesus said all that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). If you are trusting Christ alone for your salvation, turning from sin, and holding to him, that is the evidence that you were chosen. Election is not a locked door to worry at. It is the foundation under the feet of everyone who has already come in.

In a sentence. It was also allowed to wage war against God’s people and to overcome them, and it was given authority over every tribe, people, language and nation; all the earth’s inhabitants will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written, since the world was founded, in the book of life belonging to the Lamb who was slain.

On a Tuesday. If you are anxious about whether you would stand firm under pressure, take your eyes off your own strength and put them on the Lamb’s book. You are not kept by your courage; you are kept by his grip. That does not make you careless. It makes you grateful, and gratitude is a far stronger defence against idolatry than fear. Pray today for believers who are being conquered in the beast’s way, that they may conquer in the Lamb’s.

For worship. Thank God that your name was written in the Lamb’s book before the world began. That is why you belong to him, and why you will not be lost. Before the mountains were brought forth, before the sea was gathered into its place, the Father wrote the names of his children, and he wrote them in the book of the Lamb who was slain. The beast may conquer bodies, but it cannot erase a single line. Blessed be the God who chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, who gave us to his Son, and whose Son will lose none of all that he has been given, but raise them up on the last day.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone has an ear, let him hear: If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes; if anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone has an ear, let him hear: If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes; if anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.

The setting. Jeremiah 15:2 and 43:11 say: those who are for pestilence, to pestilence, and those who are for the sword, to the sword, and those who are for captivity, to captivity. When Peter drew his sword to defend Jesus, Jesus said, put your sword back into its place, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52).

If anyone has an ear, let him hear. The call of the seven letters (2:7), a direct application to the church. But there is a difference here, and it is easy to miss. In chapters 2 and 3 it always ran on: let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. Here the words about the churches are gone. This call is addressed to whoever is listening, and John, having just described a beast conquering the saints, turns and says: this part is for you personally.

If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes. The saying comes from Jeremiah, and it is the language of a sentence already passed. Some believers will be imprisoned. This is under God’s sovereign plan. Accept it; do not try to escape by compromise. What it means here is not fatalism, and the last sentence of the verse rules that out. It means that a Christian facing the beast should not expect an escape route, should not spend his strength looking for one at the cost of his faith, and should not conclude when arrest comes that something has gone wrong with God’s arrangements.

If anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Some will be executed. This, too, is within God’s purpose. That sounds bleak until it is set against the alternative, which is a Christianity that promises deliverance from every hard thing and therefore leaves a believer, at the moment the door actually opens, with the conclusion that God has failed. This verse takes that conclusion away in advance. Nothing that happens to a Christian at the hands of the beast is outside what was appointed, and none of it is a surprise to the one who holds the keys.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ on the second line. Some read “if anyone kills with the sword, with the sword he must be killed”, a warning against taking up the sword, as in Matthew 26:52 and the King James Version. Others read “if anyone is to be killed with the sword, with the sword he must be killed”, a call to accept martyrdom. Either way, the lesson is the same: believers must not resist the beast by violence, but endure in faith.

Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints. That is the point of the whole passage, and it defines the Christian response to the beast. Two words. “Endurance” (hypomonē) is steadfastness, staying power, holding a position under weight; it appears throughout this book and is always used of the saints. “Faith” (pistis) is faith and faithfulness; the Greek covers both, and both fit. The church’s response to the beast is not rebellion, revolution or violence, but patient endurance and faithful trust. This is how the saints conquer.

What is not on the list. Not violent resistance. Not clever manoeuvring, not political leverage, not withdrawal into a compound. The beast has ten horns and the authority of the dragon and the worship of the whole earth, and the instruction to the church facing it is: stay where you are and keep trusting him. There is a hard-won realism in that which any Christian under long pressure will recognise. Most of what the New Testament asks of believers in trouble is not spectacular. It is the refusal to move. And the identical phrase returns at 14:12, so that twice in this book, at the two darkest points, the reader is told that what is being asked of him is endurance and faith.

What it does not mean. This does not mean Christians may never defend themselves or others, or that believers should seek martyrdom. It means that the church does not advance its cause by force, and that when persecution comes because of faith, believers accept suffering rather than deny Christ or take up arms for the gospel.

May a Christian flee persecution, or must he stay? He may flee, if he can do so without denying Christ. Jesus said, when they persecute you in one town, flee to the next (Matthew 10:23), and Paul escaped Damascus in a basket. What this verse forbids is escape by compromise: buying safety with a denial, a pinch of incense, a lie. If the way out is open and clean, a believer may take it. If the only way out runs through unfaithfulness, then captivity is the appointed road, and Christ walks it with him.

In a sentence. Whoever can hear should listen: anyone destined for captivity will go into captivity, and anyone destined to be killed by the sword will be killed by the sword; this is why God’s people need endurance and faithfulness.

On a Tuesday. When you face hostility for your faith, do not retaliate. Endure, trust God and stay faithful. That is how the church wins. Endurance is learned in small things before it is needed in great ones: in keeping your word when it costs you, in staying kind to someone who mocks you, in going on praying when prayer seems unanswered. Each small faithfulness is practice for a larger one.

For worship. The Lord has appointed the road for each of his servants, and none of them walks it alone. He who was taken captive in a garden and slain by Roman hands did not resist with the sword, though twelve legions of angels waited on his word; he endured the cross, despising the shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. His endurance is the pattern of ours and the power of ours. The saints conquer by staying where he has put them, because he stayed on the cross for them. Glory to the faithful Witness, the Author and Perfecter of our faith.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 11–12: a second beast rises out of the earth — the opposite element, so that between them the dragon has the whole world covered. It has two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon. Named three times later as the false prophet (16:13; 19:20; 20:10), its entire function is to make the world worship the first beast.

Verses 13–15: it performs great signs, including fire from heaven — Elijah’s credential on Carmel (1 Kings 18:38) — and by the signs it is allowed to work it deceives the earth-dwellers, telling them to make an image for the beast. It is allowed to give the image breath so that it speaks and orders the death of anyone who will not worship it. Behind this stands Daniel 3: an image on a plain, an order to bow at a signal, and a furnace — and three men who said But if not (Dan. 3:17–18).

Verses 16–17: it marks all — small and great, rich and poor, free and slave — on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell without the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name. Verse 18 sets the puzzle: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Beast from the Land

A second beast with horns like a lamb and a voice like a dragon makes the world worship the first. It works signs, gives the image a voice, and requires a mark — the beast’s name — without which no one can buy or sell. Its number, 666, is the number of a man.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Local notables ran the imperial cult, and refusing it cost a tradesman his living.

Now: The mark is an allegiance, not a device; nobody takes it by accident. Test teachers by what they say, not by how familiar they look.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon. It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon. It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.

The setting. Jesus warned of false prophets who come in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves (Matthew 7:15), and of false christs and false prophets who would perform great signs to deceive, if possible, even the elect (Matthew 24:24). In the province of Asia, the emperor cult was promoted by local elites: priests of the imperial temples, city councils and the provincial council (the koinon), who organised festivals, sacrifices and games in the emperor’s honour.

Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. “Earth” (gē) is land. A second beast, from the opposite element: the first came out of the sea, from far away; this one comes from the land, local and familiar. Between them the dragon has the whole world covered, which is exactly what the angel of 10:2 was answering when he planted one foot on the sea and one on the land. This beast is later called the false prophet (16:13; 19:20; 20:10).

It had two horns like a lamb. “Like a lamb” (homoia arniō). It looks harmless, even Christlike: a parody of the Lamb. It has horns like the Lamb who is at the centre of this whole book. From a distance, or on a first hearing, it is harmless and even familiar. Religious deception often looks gentle and attractive.

And it spoke like a dragon. Then it opens its mouth, and what comes out is the dragon. Its message is Satan’s. It looks like a lamb but sounds like the serpent, deceiving as he did in Eden. That single sentence is the most useful thing in the chapter for a Christian trying to recognise deception. Jesus described the same creature: sheep’s clothing, ravenous wolves. Paul said Satan disguises himself as an angel of light, so it is no surprise if his servants also disguise themselves as servants of righteousness (2 Corinthians 11:14–15). The consistent New Testament warning about deception is not that it will look frightening. It is that it will look familiar, and that the test is not appearance but speech.

A usable test. Which gives an ordinary believer something to work with. The question to ask of a teacher, a movement or a message is not whether it feels Christian, looks Christian or uses Christian vocabulary; the horns are convincing. The question is what it actually says when it speaks at length, and whether that is what the dragon says: that God is not to be taken at his word, that his commands are a cage, that sin is not so serious, that Christ is one way among many, that safety lies in accommodation.

It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence. The second beast is not a rival; it is a department. It serves the first beast, as the Holy Spirit glorifies Christ (John 16:14). Dragon, beast and false prophet form an unholy trinity, a counterfeit of Father, Son and Spirit. The dragon gives his authority to the beast, as the Father gives all things to the Son. The beast bears a death wound and lives, and receives worship. And the false prophet does not draw attention to himself at all: his entire function is to make the world worship the beast, which is precisely what the Holy Spirit does for Christ. He will glorify me, Jesus said. The counterfeit is exact.

And makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed. The false prophet’s role is religious: to promote the worship of the political power. Religion in service of the state; ideology that makes people worship power. In the province of Asia this had a very concrete shape. The imperial cult was administered by local notables, and the priests who ran it were not Romans sent from abroad but leading men of the cities: neighbours, patrons, people the church knew. The pressure to worship did not arrive only from the sea. It came up out of the local ground.

What it does not mean. The second beast is not only one future individual. It is the religious and ideological propaganda that supports godless power in every age: the imperial priesthood in John’s day, and every religion, philosophy, media or education system that persuades people to give the state, or any human power, the devotion that belongs to God.

Can the false prophet be inside the church? Yes, and that is the most sobering point here. The second beast looks like a lamb, and the most effective deceivers have always spoken from within Christian circles. The letters to Pergamum and Thyatira warned of Balaam and Jezebel, teachers inside the congregations who taught believers to compromise with idolatry (2:14, 20). Whenever a church leader tells Christians that faithfulness to Christ can wait, that the culture’s demands must be accommodated, or that the gospel needs updating to suit the powers of the day, the lamb’s horns are showing. Test teachers by Scripture, however gentle their manner (1 John 4:1).

In a sentence. Then I saw another beast, coming up out of the earth; it had two horns like a lamb’s, but it spoke like a dragon; it exercises all the authority of the first beast on its behalf, and it makes the earth and all who live on it worship the first beast, whose deadly wound had been healed.

On a Tuesday. Not everything that looks like a lamb is the Lamb. Test every message, especially gentle-sounding religious ones, by whether it leads you to worship Christ or something else. When you read, listen or scroll this week, ask of each voice: what does this make me think of God? of sin? of Christ? A message can be warm, kind and full of Christian words, and still be leading you away from him.

For worship. There is only one Lamb, and he speaks with the voice of his Father. His words are spirit and life; he never flattered, never deceived, and never asked anyone to worship any but God. And there is only one Spirit of truth, who does not speak on his own authority, but takes what is Christ’s and declares it, so that the Son is glorified. The unholy trinity can only imitate what the holy Trinity is. Blessed be the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, one God, whose glory no counterfeit can steal and whose voice his sheep know.
verseByVerse.note: This second beast is later called “the false prophet.”

verseByVerse.quote: It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people, and by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth, telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived. And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak and might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people, and by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth, telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived. And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak and might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain.

The setting. In Daniel 3, King Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden image and commanded everyone to worship it, on pain of death; Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refused. Elijah called down fire from heaven to prove that the LORD is God (1 Kings 18:38). Pharaoh’s magicians copied some of Moses’ miracles (Exodus 7:11, 22). In the ancient world, statues in temples were sometimes made to appear to speak or move by priests using hidden devices or ventriloquism. In the province of Asia, statues of the emperor stood in temples and public squares, and Christians were sometimes required to offer incense before them to prove their loyalty, as Pliny reported from neighbouring Bithynia around AD 112.

It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people. “Signs” (sēmeia) is the same word John uses throughout his Gospel for the miracles of Jesus. These are counterfeit miracles, imitating Elijah and the two witnesses (11:5). It will not do to dismiss them as mere stagecraft. Scripture is consistent that supernatural power is not by itself proof of anything. Pharaoh’s magicians copied the first plagues. Moses warned Israel that a prophet might give a sign that actually came to pass and still be leading them to other gods, and that God was testing them by it (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). Paul warned that the coming of the lawless one would be with all power and false signs and wonders (2 Thessalonians 2:9).

Fire from heaven. And fire from heaven is a pointed choice. That is Elijah’s sign on Carmel, the one moment in the Old Testament when fire falling from the sky settled who the true God was in front of a watching nation. The false prophet reproduces the credential of the greatest prophet of Israel, and the two witnesses of chapter 11 had Elijah’s powers too. Both sides in this book have fire. Only one of them has the truth.

And by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth. “Deceives” (plana) is leads astray. Deception is its main weapon, as it is Satan’s (12:9). “Allowed” (edothē): again, God’s permission and limits. Even the deceiving miracles run on a licence. The phrase in the presence of can also mean on behalf of, and both are true: the false prophet works in the beast’s presence and for its benefit.

Telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived. “Image” (eikona) is statue, likeness. Idolatry of the state, of its leader or of its ideology. Behind it stands Daniel 3, and the parallel is close enough that a first-century reader would have felt it: an image set up on a plain, an order that everyone bow at a signal, and a furnace for anyone who would not.

And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak. “Breath” is pneuma, spirit, breath: a parody of God giving breath to the witnesses (11:11). The Old Testament’s standing mockery of idols is that they cannot speak: they have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see (Psalm 115:5), and John used that psalm himself at 9:20. Here the mockery seems to be answered. This idol talks back, and what it says is a death sentence. How the image speaks is not John’s concern and should not become the reader’s. Whether the mechanism is a priest behind a wall or something genuinely uncanny changes nothing about the demand, which is the same demand made on the plain of Dura: bow, or be killed.

And might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain. As in Daniel 3. The demand for worship is enforced with death. The choice is stark: worship the beast or die. Three young men said no on the plain of Dura, and said the thing that ought to be carved over this chapter: our God whom we serve is able to deliver us, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods (Daniel 3:17–18). But if not. That is the endurance of the saints in three words.

Force and plausibility. This is the sequence the chapter has been building. The first beast supplies the force. The second supplies the plausibility: the signs, the wonders, the reasons, the respectable local men who will explain that this is only a formality. Raw power alone has never been able to command worship for long. It needs somebody with lamb’s horns to make the case.

What it does not mean. Miracles alone do not prove that a message is from God. Scripture warns that false prophets can perform signs (Deuteronomy 13:1–3; Matthew 24:24). The test is whether a message leads people to worship the true God revealed in Christ and agrees with his word.

What are the images that demand worship today? Few modern people bow to statues, but the pattern is the same wherever a human power or idea is set up to be honoured as ultimate and refusal is punished. It may be a leader whose portrait must hang in every home, an ideology that requires public affirmation of what God calls sin, or a national or tribal cause placed above Christ. Often the punishment is not death but loss: of job, standing, reputation or access. The question to ask is simple: am I being required to say or do what amounts to confessing that something other than Christ is Lord? If so, then, like the three young men, the Christian answers: we will not serve your gods.

In a sentence. It performs impressive signs, even making fire come down from the sky to the earth in full view of people; by the signs it is permitted to do on behalf of the first beast, it deceives the earth’s inhabitants, telling them to set up an image in honour of the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived; it was permitted to give breath to the beast’s image so that it could speak, and to have everyone who refused to worship the image put to death.

On a Tuesday. Do not be impressed by signs and wonders alone. Hold to the word of God, and worship Christ alone, whatever the pressure. When something spectacular is offered as proof that a teacher or movement is from God, ask what it is leading you to worship. And practise the three words now, in small matters, so they are ready in large ones: God is able to deliver me. But if not, I will still not bow.

For worship. The true fire from heaven fell on Carmel and consumed the sacrifice, the wood, the stones and the dust, and all the people fell on their faces and said, The LORD, he is God. The false fire of the beast deceives for a while; the fire of the LORD settles the question for ever. He walked in the furnace with his three servants, and the fire had no power over their bodies; not a hair of their heads was singed. The image speaks for a season and is silenced; the Word who was in the beginning speaks and worlds are made. Blessed be the living God, who has breath in himself and gives it to whom he wills, and whose servants will not bow.

verseByVerse.quote: Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.

The setting. In Deuteronomy 6:8, Israel was told to bind God’s commandments as a sign on their hand and as frontlets between their eyes, so that their actions and thoughts would be shaped by his word. In the ancient world, slaves were sometimes branded or tattooed with their owner’s mark, and soldiers with their general’s name. Trade guilds in the cities of Asia required members to honour patron gods and the emperor; refusing could exclude a Christian from work and trade (2:9, 14, 20). Roman coins bore the emperor’s image and divine titles.

Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave. Three pairs, covering every social division there was: status, wealth and legal condition. Everyone, at every level of society. Nobody is exempt by being important and nobody is overlooked for being insignificant. The demand reaches the senator and the slave in the same sentence.

To be marked on the right hand or the forehead. “Mark” (charagma) is a stamp, a brand, the impression of a seal on a document or coin. It is a counterfeit, and the original has already been shown. In 7:3 the servants of God were sealed on their foreheads before the winds were released, and in 14:1 the 144,000 have the Lamb’s name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads. Everyone in this book is marked. There is no unmarked category. Everyone bears one mark or the other: God’s name or the beast’s. The only question the book ever asks is whose name is on you.

Hand and forehead. Israel had been commanded to bind the words of God as a sign on the hand and as frontlets between the eyes. Hand and forehead: what you do, and what you think. The forehead represents the mind and identity; the right hand represents action and work. The beast demands exactly what God demanded, in the same two places, which is what makes it a parody rather than merely an atrocity. The mark means belonging to the beast and serving it, in thought and deed.

So that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark. This is where the chapter stops being theoretical for most readers, and it is the sharpest thing in it. The pressure is not only a threat of death. It is a threat to trade. You may keep your convictions and lose your livelihood, or you may make one small formal gesture and go on feeding your family. Those who refuse to give their loyalty to the beast are shut out of the economy. In John’s day, Christians who refused guild idolatry lost their livelihood (Smyrna’s poverty, 2:9). Later, under the emperor Decius in the third century, citizens had to obtain a certificate stating that they had sacrificed to the gods, and papyrus copies of such certificates survive. A piece of paper was the difference between a working life and ruin.

That is, the name of the beast or the number of its name. The mark is the beast’s name, or its number. To bear someone’s name is to belong to them. The text itself defines the mark here: not a device but a name, an identity, a declaration of who owns you and whose name you will confess.

Where Christians differ: what is the mark of the beast? Over the centuries, many things have been identified as the mark: barcodes, credit cards, identity cards, microchips implanted in the hand, even vaccines. Every generation since printing has identified it with its own newest technology, and every generation has been wrong. Verdict: the mark is not a physical device that someone might take by accident. It is a symbol of allegiance, the counterpart of God’s seal, which is also invisible (God’s name, 14:1, and his Spirit, Ephesians 1:13). To receive the mark is to give one’s worship and loyalty to the beast: to think and act as its servant. No one receives it without choosing to worship the beast (14:9–11). Christians should not live in fear of new technologies as though they might accidentally take the mark. They should watch their loyalty, and refuse to compromise their worship of Christ, whatever the economic cost.

What it does not mean. Taking part in the economy is not the mark of the beast. Christians may buy and sell, work and trade. What they may not do is give to any power, economic or political, the worship and loyalty that belong to God.

What if I take the mark by accident? Nobody in this chapter takes it by accident. It is the visible sign of a worship already given, on people who have already marvelled, already worshipped and already decided that nobody can fight against the beast. A person does not stumble into it. And the ones whose names are in the Lamb’s book, written from the foundation of the world, are not the ones at that counter. If you are afraid of having the mark, that fear is itself evidence that your heart belongs to Christ. Those who bear the beast’s mark are not worried about it; they are proud of it.

What does this look like at work? It looks like the moment when keeping your job, winning the contract or being promoted requires you to do what Christ forbids: to lie on a report, to affirm what God calls evil, to join in a ritual of loyalty to something other than him, or to stay silent about your faith when silence would be a denial. Most working days involve no such choice, and a Christian should work hard and well for ordinary employers (Colossians 3:23). But when the choice comes, the issue is not the money. It is whose name is on your hand. Settle the answer before the day arrives, and trust the God who feeds the birds to provide for you if obedience costs you your income.

In a sentence. It also forces everyone, unimportant and important, rich and poor, free and slave, to receive a mark on their right hand or on their forehead, so that no one could buy or sell anything without the mark, which is the beast’s name or the number that stands for its name.

On a Tuesday. Faithfulness to Christ may cost you a promotion, a client or your job. Be willing to pay that price. Ask whose mark is on your thinking and your work. Look at how you spend your best hours and your strongest thoughts: do they bear the name of the Lamb, or of whatever power promises to keep you comfortable? And if you know a believer who has lost work for refusing to compromise, help them. The church that shares its bread makes the beast’s economic threat far weaker.

For worship. The Lord knows those who are his, and he has written his own name on their foreheads. He sealed them before the winds were loosed; he set his Spirit in their hearts as a guarantee; he engraved them on the palms of his hands. The beast brands its slaves for a season. The Lamb marks his redeemed for ever, and in the city to come they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. Blessed be the God who does not leave his people unmarked, and who will provide for every one who would rather go hungry than bear another name.

verseByVerse.quote: This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.

The setting. In Hebrew and Greek, letters of the alphabet also served as numbers, so every name had a numerical value. The practice of adding up the letters of a name was called gematria. A graffito at Pompeii reads: I love her whose number is 545. Nero Caesar, written in Hebrew letters (nrwn qsr), adds up to 666. Spelled without the final n, as in the Latin form Nero, it adds up to 616, and some manuscripts of Revelation read 616.

This calls for wisdom. “Wisdom” (sophia) is not cleverness, but spiritual discernment, to recognise the beast for what it is (17:9). No verse in the Bible has been used more irresponsibly, so it is best to begin with what it actually says.

Let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast. “Calculate” (psēphisatō) is count up, reckon, from the word for a pebble used in counting. John is not forbidding the exercise; he is setting it as a puzzle to people who had the key. John expects his first readers to be able to work it out. It was a common game in the first century, and anyone hearing this letter read aloud would have known at once what John was asking.

For it is the number of a man. “Of a man” (anthrōpou) is of a human being. It may mean a particular man, or a human number, the number of humanity. Both are grammatically possible. The beast, for all its claims to divinity, is merely human.

And his number is 666. Six is one short of seven, the number of completeness and perfection. Three sixes: falling short again and again, a counterfeit trinity that never reaches the divine. Jesus’ name in Greek (Iēsous) adds up to 888, one beyond seven, the number of resurrection and new creation. The beast is the ultimate human pretender to deity, always falling short. The number also very likely pointed John’s first readers to Nero, the persecuting emperor, as the model of the beast.

A portrait, not only a cipher. Whatever the beast is, and whichever century it appears in, it is a magnificent, terrifying, world-conquering almost. It has seven heads it did not earn, ten crowns it was given, a resurrection it counterfeited, and it cannot reach seven. On this reading 666 is not merely a cipher hiding an identity; it is a portrait of every human power that reaches for God’s place and falls short.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts read 616 instead of 666, as the early church father Irenaeus noted around AD 180. He defended 666 as the original, which the best manuscripts support. The variant may have arisen because 616 matches the Latin spelling of Nero Caesar, which shows that early readers connected the number with Nero. A variant that changes the number by exactly the value of one dropped letter is very hard to explain as coincidence.

Where Christians differ: who is 666? The number has been applied to countless figures: popes, Muhammad, Napoleon, Hitler, various modern politicians, and titles such as the papal title Vicarius Filii Dei. Verdict: the number pointed first to Nero, the emperor who began the persecution of Christians and became the pattern of the persecuting beast; and its symbolism, six falling short of seven, describes every human power that claims to be divine. Attempts to fit it to modern figures have repeatedly failed and discredited the church. The right response is not number-crunching names in the news, but the wisdom to recognise and resist any power that demands worship.

A history of confident error. That is the pastoral caution of the verse. Every century has found its man, and the names now look faintly absurd, made to fit by ingenious arithmetic. The one thing all these identifications have shared is certainty. John asks for wisdom and understanding, not cleverness, and the two are not the same thing.

What it does not mean. The number 666 is not unlucky or dangerous in itself. Christians need not fear house numbers, phone numbers or dates containing it. Its meaning lies in what it symbolises.

So what am I meant to take from this chapter, if not a name? A recognition. The beast is whatever demands the allegiance that belongs to God, backed by force, made plausible by religion, and enforced through the ability to buy and sell. It has worn many costumes and it will wear more, until its final form before Christ returns. Every one of them is a six: gigantic, apparently unbeatable, worshipped by the whole earth, and one short of the number that belongs to the Lamb. So learn to recognise its marks, refuse its worship, endure its pressure, and keep your eyes on the one whose name is above every name.

In a sentence. This is where wisdom is needed: let anyone with insight work out the number of the beast, for it is a human number, and the number is six hundred and sixty-six.

On a Tuesday. Pray for wisdom to see through the claims of power. Every human pretender to god falls short. Only Christ is Lord. The next time a book, a sermon or a viral post claims to have identified the beast in today’s headlines, smile, close it, and open the Gospel instead. You do not need to know the beast’s name to resist him. You need to know the Lamb’s.

For worship. Every beast is a six, and the Lamb is perfect. Every empire that reached for heaven fell short and fell down; every ruler who wore the titles of God has gone to the dust, and the Lord sits enthroned for ever. The beast’s number is the number of a man, and the man Christ Jesus, who is also God over all, has the name that is above every name. At that name every knee will bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. Wisdom is to see it now.
verseByVerse.note: Letters also served as numbers. Many think 666 spells “Neron Caesar” (the Greek form) in Hebrew letters; some manuscripts read 616, which fits the Latin spelling of the name. Others see 666 as falling short of seven again and again.

And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.<sup>3</sup>One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound, but its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast.<sup>4</sup>And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, “Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?”<sup>5</sup>And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words, and it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months.<sup>6</sup>It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.<sup>7</sup>Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them.
