It had two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon.<sup>12</sup>It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.<sup>13</sup>It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people,<sup>14</sup>and by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth, telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived.<sup>15</sup>And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak and might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain.<sup>16</sup>Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead,<sup>17</sup>so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.<sup>18</sup>This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.

14.title: The Lamb, the Harvest, and the Three Angels
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is a triptych of three visions, each answering the terror of chapter 13 with a counter-vision of divine certainty. First: the Lamb on Mount Zion with the 144,000 — the redeemed in their completeness, standing where the beast could not reach them. Second: three angels flying in midheaven, each with a message that together constitute the gospel, the judgment, and the warning. Third: the great harvest of the earth — the grain harvest of the redeemed and the grape harvest of the wicked, two harvests that together depict the final judgment in all its terrible binary clarity.

The chapter is the hinge of Revelation. Behind it lies the cosmic backstory (chapters 12–13) and the long unfolding of the seals and trumpets (chapters 6–11). Before it lies the bowl judgments, Babylon's fall, the Rider on the white horse, and the new creation. Chapter 14 stands at the center and declares: the outcome is certain. The Lamb is on Mount Zion. The harvest is coming. The one who endures to the end will be saved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Lamb and the 144,000 on Mount Zion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 13 ended with a mark on the hand or forehead and a number; chapter 14 opens with a different forehead and a different name. Verse 1: on Mount Zion stands the Lamb, and with him the 144,000 sealed in chapter 7, complete, wearing his name and his Father’s. Everyone in this book is marked; the alternative to the beast’s mark is not an unmarked crowd.

Verses 2–3: a voice like the roar of many waters and loud thunder — and, in the same breath, like harpists playing on harps. They sing a new song before the throne, and no one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth. Not because the words are difficult, but because a song about being ransomed cannot be sung truly by someone who has not been.

Verses 4–5 describe them: they have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins; they follow the Lamb wherever he goes; they are firstfruits (aparchē, the first sheaf that both belongs to God and guarantees more is coming); and in their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless — language taken from the servant of Isaiah 53:9 and the remnant of Zephaniah 3:13, and amōmos, the word for a sacrificial animal without defect.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lamb on Mount Zion

Against the beast’s mark stand the 144,000 with the Lamb’s name on their foreheads, singing a new song only the redeemed can learn. They follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and are blameless because they were bought.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Not one of those sealed in chapter 7 is missing.

Now: Ask whether the song of the cross is a statement you admire or your own account.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and behold, on Mount Zion stood the Lamb, and with him 144,000 who had his name and his Father's name written on their foreheads. And I heard a voice from heaven like the roar of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder. The voice I heard was like the sound of harpists playing on their harps, and they were singing a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and before the elders. No one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I looked, and behold, on Mount Zion stood the Lamb, and with him 144,000 who had his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads. And I heard a voice from heaven like the roar of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder. The voice I heard was like the sound of harpists playing on their harps, and they were singing a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and before the elders. No one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth.

Meaning first. Revelation 14 answers the terror of chapter 13 with a series of visions of hope and judgement. The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with the 144,000, who bear his and his Father’s name, not the beast’s mark, and sing a new song only the redeemed can learn (vv. 1–3). They are pure, follow the Lamb wherever he goes, are firstfruits redeemed from humanity, and no lie is in their mouths (vv. 4–5). Three angels then fly overhead. The first proclaims an eternal gospel to every nation: fear God, give him glory and worship the Creator, for the hour of judgement has come (vv. 6–7). The second announces that Babylon the great has fallen (v. 8). The third warns that anyone who worships the beast and receives its mark will drink the wine of God’s wrath and be tormented for ever, with no rest day or night (vv. 9–11). So the saints must endure, and a voice from heaven blesses those who die in the Lord: they rest from their labours, and their deeds follow them (vv. 12–13). Finally, two harvests: one like a son of man on a white cloud reaps the earth with a sickle (vv. 14–16), and an angel gathers the grapes of the earth into the great winepress of God’s wrath, from which blood flows for 1,600 stadia (vv. 17–20). The chapter sets the two destinies side by side: the Lamb’s people, safe and singing; the beast’s worshippers, judged; and it calls everyone to choose now whom they will worship.

The setting. Mount Zion was the hill of Jerusalem where David’s city and the temple stood, and it became a name for God’s dwelling and his people. Psalm 2:6 says God has set his King on Zion, his holy hill. Joel 2:32 says that in Mount Zion there shall be those who escape, and among the survivors those whom the LORD calls. Hebrews 12:22 tells believers that they have come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.

A different forehead and a different name. Chapter 13 ended with a mark on the right hand or the forehead, and a number. Chapter 14 opens with a different forehead and a different name, and the juxtaposition is the whole point. What the reader is shown now is the alternative, and it is not an unmarked crowd. It is a marked one, wearing a different name in the same place.

Then I looked, and behold, on Mount Zion stood the Lamb. “Stood” (hestos): firm and victorious, in contrast to the dragon standing on the sand of the sea (12:17). The beasts rose from the sea and the earth; the Lamb stands on Zion, the place of God’s King, where God installs him in the teeth of the raging nations (Psalm 2:6). Zion here is the heavenly Zion, where the church already belongs; you have come to Mount Zion, Hebrews says, not you will come. In 5:6 the Lamb was standing as though slain. Here he is simply standing, and the company with him is counted and complete. This is the place where the King stands and the enemy does not.

And with him 144,000 who had his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads. The same 144,000 as in 7:4, the whole people of God, sealed. Not one is missing: after all the beast’s war on the saints, the full number stands with the Lamb. The sealing worked. And their seal is now revealed: the name of the Lamb and the Father, in contrast to the beast’s name on its followers (13:17). The beast conquered bodies in chapter 13. In chapter 14, every name is accounted for.

Who are the 144,000? They are the same as in chapter 7: the complete people of God, redeemed and sealed with the name of the Lamb and his Father. They are not a literal number from ethnic Israel, and not the special class of “anointed” taught by Jehovah’s Witnesses. The number is twelve times twelve times a thousand: the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles, the whole people of God of both covenants, multiplied to fullness. If you belong to Christ, you are in this number. Not one of his people is left out of the count, and none is counted twice.

And I heard a voice from heaven like the roar of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder. Three comparisons follow, and they should not be flattened into one. The roar of many waters is how the voice of the risen Christ was described at 1:15, and how Ezekiel described the sound of the glory of God returning to the temple (Ezekiel 43:2). Thunder is the voice of God at Sinai. Overwhelming, like Christ’s voice and God’s.

The voice I heard was like the sound of harpists playing on their harps. And then, in the same breath, harps, the most delicate sound in the ancient world. Powerful and also beautiful, music rather than noise. Hold that combination. It is overwhelming and it is beautiful, at the same volume. Nothing in human music does both; a waterfall is not tender, and a harp cannot be heard over one. This is what the worship of heaven sounds like, and any picture of it that is merely soothing has lost half of it, as any picture that is merely loud has lost the other half.

And they were singing a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and before the elders. “New song” (ōdēn kainēn), as in 5:9: the song of redemption. A new song is sung in Scripture when God has done something unprecedented (Psalm 96:1; 98:1), and it was sung once before in this book, when the elders sang that the Lamb was worthy, for he was slain, and by his blood ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation. That is the subject of this song too.

No one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth. “Learn” (mathein). Only the redeemed can sing the song of redemption, because only they have experienced it. Not because the words are difficult; a song about being ransomed by blood can be printed and read by anyone. It cannot be learned, in the sense of being sung truly, by a person who has not been ransomed. Angels can praise God for salvation (7:11–12), but they cannot sing as those who have been bought with the Lamb’s blood. Peter says angels long to look into these things (1 Peter 1:12). “Redeemed” (ēgorasmenoi) is bought, purchased, as in 5:9.

A quiet test. There is a test in that for a reader, and it can be run in any ordinary service. When a hymn about the cross is sung, is it a true statement being sung, or is it your own account? The difference is not musical and it is not emotional; a person can be moved by a tune he has no part in. The 144,000 are singing something that could only have been learned by having it happen to them.

What it does not mean. The 144,000 here are not a special elite separate from other believers. They are the whole church, sealed in chapter 7, now seen safe with the Lamb after the beast’s persecution.

What if I cannot sing, or worship feels dry? The new song is not a matter of musical ability or of feeling a certain way on a Sunday. It is the confession of a redeemed heart: I was bought by the blood of the Lamb, and I belong to him. You can sing it in a quavering voice, or say it silently in a hospital bed, and heaven hears it as part of the great chorus. Dry seasons come to every believer. When they do, keep gathering with God’s people, keep singing the true words even when your feelings lag behind, and look again at the cross that the song is about. The feelings usually follow the looking.

In a sentence. Then I looked and saw the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with him 144,000 people who had his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads; and I heard a sound from heaven like the roar of a great waterfall and like loud thunder, yet like harpists playing their harps; they were singing a new song in front of the throne, the four living beings and the elders, and no one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been bought out of the earth.

On a Tuesday. Whatever mark the world wants to put on you this week, remember whose name is already written on your forehead. You are not unclaimed. When you are tempted to compromise to keep your place, your income or your friends, say to yourself: I belong to the Lamb, and his Father’s name is on me. And next Sunday, when the church sings of the blood that bought you, sing it as your own story.

For worship. You have a song that angels cannot sing: the song of the redeemed. Sing it with all your heart. The Lamb stands on Zion, and not one of those the Father gave him is missing; the beast made war and the dragon raged, and the whole company is there, counted and complete, with his name on their foreheads. Their song is like many waters and like thunder and like harps, and it is all about him: worthy is the Lamb who was slain, who bought us for God with his blood. Let heaven and earth join it. He has lost none of us.

verseByVerse.quote: It is these who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. It is these who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These have been redeemed from mankind as firstfruits for God and the Lamb, and in their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is these who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. It is these who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These have been redeemed from mankind as firstfruits for God and the Lamb, and in their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless.

The setting. Israel’s soldiers had to abstain from sexual relations during holy war (Deuteronomy 23:9–10; 1 Samuel 21:5). The 144,000 were counted like an army (7:4–8). The prophets picture God’s people as his virgin bride (Jeremiah 18:13; 31:4), and idolatry as adultery or prostitution (Hosea 1–3; Ezekiel 16). Paul told the Corinthians he had betrothed them to Christ, to present them as a pure virgin (2 Corinthians 11:2). Firstfruits were the first part of the harvest, offered to God as belonging to him, and a pledge of the full harvest to come (Exodus 23:19; Leviticus 23:10). Zephaniah 3:13 says that the remnant of Israel shall speak no lies, nor shall there be found in their mouth a deceitful tongue.

It is these who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. This is one of the hardest sentences in the book to read well, and it must not be hurried. “Defiled” (emolynthēsan) is stained. “Virgins” (parthenoi) is a word that can be used of men as well as women. In the context of Revelation, where Babylon is the great prostitute (17:1–5) and idolatry is spiritual immorality (2:14, 20), this means they kept themselves pure from the idolatry of the beast. They are the faithful bride of the Lamb (19:7–8; 21:2).

Spiritual faithfulness. Throughout the prophets, idolatry is adultery, and God’s people are a bride who goes after other lovers. This book is about to spend two chapters on a prostitute called Babylon who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality (v. 8), and it ends with a Bride. In that setting, virgins means those who did not go to bed with the beast. They kept themselves for one Lord in a world offering many.

Holy warriors. They are also like holy warriors, set apart for the Lamb’s war. The number 144,000 came out of a tribal muster in chapter 7, twelve thousand from each tribe, which is how Israel counted an army. Soldiers under a holy-war vow kept from sexual relations for the duration of the campaign: David’s men could eat the holy bread because they had kept themselves from women, and Uriah would not go home to his wife while the ark and the army were in tents (2 Samuel 11:11). On this reading John is describing consecrated troops on active service, and the language is ceremonial rather than a judgement on marriage. The two pictures say one thing together: this company has kept itself wholly for the Lamb.

Where Christians differ: does this praise celibacy? Some, from the early church onwards, have read this verse as praising literal virginity and celibacy as a higher form of Christian life, and used it to support celibate monks, nuns and clergy. Verdict: the virginity here is spiritual purity from idolatry, the faithfulness of the Lamb’s bride. Scripture honours marriage (Hebrews 13:4; Genesis 2:24), calls forbidding marriage a teaching of demons (1 Timothy 4:1–3), and says that marriage is not defiling. Celibacy is a good gift for some (1 Corinthians 7:7–8), but it is not a higher state of holiness. The 144,000 are the whole church, married and single, who refused to commit spiritual adultery with the beast.

It is these who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. “Follow” (akolouthountes) is the word for discipleship. That is the simplest definition of a Christian in the whole book, and after two chapters of dragons and beasts and numbers it is startlingly plain. Following was the first thing Jesus asked of anybody, follow me, said to fishermen at their nets, and it is the last thing he says to Peter at the end of John’s Gospel, twice (John 21:19, 22). In contrast, the world follows the beast (13:3).

Wherever. The weight is in that word. Following is easy while the road is going somewhere a person would have chosen. This book has shown where the Lamb actually goes: to a cross, and through death, and in the meantime among lampstands in difficult towns. Wherever he goes includes suffering and death. To follow him wherever is to have surrendered the veto in advance, and it is what distinguishes a disciple from an admirer.

These have been redeemed from mankind as firstfruits for God and the Lamb. “Firstfruits” (aparchē) is the first sheaf of a harvest, brought to God before the rest was gathered. Two things are true of a firstfruit: it belongs wholly to God, offered to him; and it guarantees that more is coming. The barn is not full yet. That suggests that the harvest of verse 15 is the gathering of the redeemed. James calls believers a kind of firstfruits of God’s creatures (James 1:18), and Paul calls Christ himself the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). Here the whole church is the firstfruits offered from all humanity, the pledge of a renewed creation.

And in their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless. “Lie” (pseudos). The phrase echoes the Servant of Isaiah 53:9, in whose mouth there was no deceit, and the remnant of Zephaniah. In a book whose villain is the deceiver of the whole world (12:9) and whose second beast deceives by signs (13:14), truthfulness is not a minor virtue. It is the mark of the other side. The Lamb’s people tell the truth. They did not say Caesar is Lord, and they did not deny Christ.

Blameless. “Blameless” (amōmoi) is without blemish, the technical word for a sacrificial animal without defect. It is what Peter says of Christ, the lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:19). Nobody in this company achieved it. Verse 3 has already said they were redeemed, which means bought, which means the blamelessness was purchased and given. Their blamelessness comes from his blood, in which they washed their robes and made them white (7:14), and it shows in their faithful lives.

What it does not mean. Blameless does not mean sinless perfection in this life. It means forgiven, washed and faithful, without the stain of compromise with the beast.

I have not kept myself pure. Is there a place for me here? Yes, if you come to the Lamb. Not one of the 144,000 was pure by nature; every one was redeemed, bought out of a defiled humanity. The Corinthian church Paul wanted to present as a pure virgin to Christ included former idolaters, adulterers and thieves, and he says to them: such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified (1 Corinthians 6:11). Sexual sin and spiritual unfaithfulness in your past are real, and must be confessed and turned from. But they do not bar you from the Lamb’s company. His blood makes the defiled clean, and from now on you follow him.

Does following the Lamb wherever he goes mean I must give up everything? It means you give him the right to ask for anything. Most days he asks for ordinary things: honesty, kindness, a clean conscience, faithfulness in your work and family, time with him and his people. Some days he asks for something costly: a relationship you must end, a career move you must refuse, a reputation you must lose for his sake. The disciple does not decide in advance which roads he will take with Christ and which he will not. And he is never asked to go anywhere the Lamb has not gone first.

In a sentence. These are the ones who have kept themselves pure and not been defiled with women; they are virgins; they follow the Lamb wherever he goes; they were bought from among humanity as the first part of the harvest offered to God and the Lamb, and no lie was found in their mouths; they are without blemish.

On a Tuesday. Follow the Lamb wherever he goes. Keep yourself from the idols of the age, and speak the truth, even when a lie would be easier. Notice the small lies you tell to smooth a day: the excuse at work, the exaggeration, the pretended agreement. The people of the Lamb are known by their mouths. Speak truly today, and follow him one step further than is comfortable.

For worship. The Lamb without blemish has made his people without blemish. He bought them out of a defiled world, washed them in his blood, and presented them to himself as a pure bride. He walks ahead and they follow, wherever he goes, and every road he leads them on he has already walked: the road to Jerusalem, the road to the cross, the road out of the tomb. There was no deceit in his mouth, and he has put a true song in theirs. They are the firstfruits, and the harvest is coming. Blessed be the Lamb, who makes the unfaithful faithful and the stained clean.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 6–7: an angel flies directly overhead — at the zenith, where everyone can see — with an eternal gospel for every nation and tribe and language and people, and calls out three imperatives: fear God, give him glory, and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water, because the hour of his judgment has come. The list is deliberate: those are the four things the first four trumpets struck (8:7–12).

Verse 8: a second angel announces Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great — Isaiah’s watchman’s cry (Isa. 21:9; cf. Jer. 51:8) — she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality. Babylon is announced as finished three chapters before she is even described.

Verses 9–11: a third angel warns that whoever worships the beast and takes its mark will drink the wine of God’s wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger, and be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb; and the smoke of their torment goes up for ever, and they have no rest, day or night.

Verse 12 turns to the reader with the sentence already used at 13:10: Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus. Verse 13 gives the second of the book’s seven beatitudes, and one of the few sentences John is specifically commanded to write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on — with the Spirit adding a comment of his own: that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Gospel, Fall, and Warning

An angel flies overhead with an eternal gospel: fear God and worship the Creator. A second announces Babylon fallen. A third warns that worshippers of the beast will drink God’s wrath unmixed. Then: blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The empire was at its height when its fall was announced in the past tense.

Now: Fear God rather than the beast; the warning is given so that the saints endure, and their deeds follow them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another angel flying directly overhead, with an eternal gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people. And he said with a loud voice, "Fear God and give him glory, because the hour of his judgment has come, and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw another angel flying directly overhead, with an eternal gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people. And he said with a loud voice, “Fear God and give him glory, because the hour of his judgment has come, and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water.”

The setting. The eagle flew overhead crying woe (8:13); now an angel flies overhead with good news. Paul preached to pagans at Lystra and Athens that they should turn from vain things to the living God who made heaven and earth and the sea (Acts 14:15; 17:24–31), and that God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world. Jesus said that this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come (Matthew 24:14).

Three angels, three announcements. Three angels follow one another through these verses with three announcements, and they arrive in the order the gospel always arrives: an appeal, a warning about the world, and a warning about the alternative. God does not judge without first calling.

Then I saw another angel flying directly overhead. “Directly overhead” (en mesouranēmati) is in mid-heaven, at the zenith, the position of the eagle in 8:13: where all can see and hear at once. Nobody will be able to say the message was hard to come by.

With an eternal gospel to proclaim. “Eternal gospel” (euangelion aiōnion) is everlasting good news. It is the only time Revelation uses the noun gospel. It is eternal because it never changes and its effects last for ever. Even in the midst of judgement, God proclaims good news. Some have questioned whether what follows is the gospel at all, since it contains no mention of the cross. But this is a book in which the announcement of the cross has already been made at great length; the whole of chapter 5 is the gospel, and the Lamb who was slain has been at the centre of every scene since. And to people under a beast, the news that the true God is still calling them to himself is good news of the most concrete kind.

To those who dwell on earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people. The audience is those who dwell on earth, John’s standing term for the people who have settled for this world. To the same people who worship the beast (13:8), God offers the gospel. The fourfold list of all humanity again. The good news is proclaimed to precisely the group that has been refusing it for chapters.

And he said with a loud voice, Fear God and give him glory. “Fear” (phobēthēte) is reverence, awe. “Give him glory”: worship him, and repent (11:13; 16:9). The call is to turn from the beast to the true God. And the first command is the one modern readers find hardest. Fear God does not mean cringing terror, and it does not mean a mild respect either. It means taking God seriously as what he actually is: the settled, awed recognition that there is someone there of a different order altogether. Proverbs calls it the beginning of knowledge (Proverbs 1:7).

Fearing the right thing. Note who it is aimed at here: people who have spent the whole book being terrified of a beast. The remedy for fearing the wrong thing is not fearlessness. It is fearing the right thing, which turns out to set a person free from everything else. Jesus said it plainly: do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell (Matthew 10:28). The one who fears God need fear no one else.

Because the hour of his judgment has come. “Hour” (hōra). The good news includes the warning. Judgement is near, so turn now. Good news that ignored the judgement would not be good; it would be a lie told to people walking towards a cliff.

And worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water. The Creator, who alone deserves worship (4:11), echoing the fourth commandment (Exodus 20:11). And the list is deliberate: heaven, earth, sea and fresh water are the four realms struck by the first four trumpets (8:7–12). The one who made them all is the one to worship, not the beast who rose from the sea and earth. This is the argument Paul made to pagans who had no Bible. Where there is no shared Scripture there is still a shared sky, and every human being already owes his existence to someone. The first angel makes that case to the whole earth at once.

Where Christians differ: is this a last chance after death, or a different gospel? Some have read the eternal gospel as a final chance for salvation given after the church’s age, or even as a gospel different from that of Christ, without the cross. Verdict: the eternal gospel is the same gospel of Jesus Christ preached throughout this age, summed up here in the call to turn from idols to the living God, which was the first step of the apostles’ preaching to pagans (1 Thessalonians 1:9–10). Paul says there is no other gospel (Galatians 1:6–9). It is proclaimed to the living, before the hour of judgement, not after death (Hebrews 9:27). The angel pictures the worldwide preaching of the gospel by the church before the end.

What it does not mean. Angels do not replace the church’s task of preaching the gospel. The angel symbolises the gospel going to all nations, which Christ has entrusted to his people (Matthew 28:18–20).

How do I share the gospel with someone who does not believe the Bible? Start where the angel starts and where Paul started: with the God who made them. Every person lives in a world they did not make, with a conscience they did not invent, and a longing for meaning and justice they cannot explain away. Talk about the Creator who gave them life, the sin that has turned us from him, the judgement that is coming, and the Saviour he has sent. Do not hide the cross, because it is the heart of the message; but you need not begin with a debate about the Bible. Begin with the shared sky, and let the word of God do its own work as you open it.

In a sentence. Then I saw another angel flying high overhead with an eternal gospel to announce to the people who live on the earth, every nation, tribe, language and people; he shouted: Fear God and give him glory, because the time has come for him to judge; worship the one who made heaven, earth, sea and springs of water.

On a Tuesday. The gospel is still for everyone, even those who seem most committed to the beast. Share it with urgency: the hour of judgement is coming. Think of one person who seems furthest from God, and pray for them by name. Then look for one natural opening this week to speak of the God who made us and the Christ who saves us. And check your own fears: what are you more afraid of than God? Bring that fear to him.

For worship. Blessed be the God who sends good news to his enemies. He made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water, and every creature owes him its breath; yet when the world had bowed to the beast, he did not answer first with fire, but with a gospel flown at the height of heaven where every eye could see it. His mercy is everlasting, and his gospel is eternal. Fear him, and give him glory; he alone is worthy, for he created all things, and by his will they existed and were created, and by his Son he has redeemed a people from every nation under heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: Another angel, a second, followed, saying, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Another angel, a second, followed, saying, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality.”

The setting. Babylon was the great empire that destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC and took God’s people into exile. It became the Bible’s symbol of human pride and rebellion against God, from the tower of Babel (Genesis 11) onwards. Isaiah 21:9 cries, fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground. Jeremiah 51:7–8 says Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD’s hand, making all the earth drunken; the nations drank her wine, therefore they went mad; suddenly Babylon has fallen. Peter calls Rome Babylon (1 Peter 5:13).

Another angel, a second, followed, saying, Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great. Babylon appears here for the first time, in a single verse, announced as already finished. Chapters 17 and 18 will describe her at length; this is the headline running ahead of the story. The words are Isaiah’s, spoken by a watchman on a wall about the empire that had swallowed the world. The doubling is the sound of a herald, the way news of a great collapse actually gets shouted in the streets.

The grammar of certainty. “Fallen” (epesen) is past tense, twice. Babylon has not fallen yet in the narrative; she is not even described for three more chapters. The angel announces the collapse of an empire that is, at the moment of speaking, at the height of its power. Prophets do this constantly; it is sometimes called the prophetic perfect, and it is the grammar of certainty. What God has decided is reported as though it had already happened, because from his side it has. Which is exactly what a Christian in Ephesus needed. The empire in front of him was not wobbling. It was collecting his taxes, running his courts and threatening his trade. And the message read out in his congregation used the past tense.

Who is Babylon? The historical Babylon had been a ruin for centuries when John wrote, so the name is being used as Sodom and Egypt were at 11:8, as a type. In John’s day, Babylon was Rome, the great city built on seven hills (17:9, 18), the city that had destroyed the temple, as Babylon had; and Peter sends greetings from she who is at Babylon (1 Peter 5:13). But the name is older than Rome and outlives it. Babylon in Scripture begins at a tower built so that a people could make a name for themselves (Genesis 11:4), and that project has never closed. It stands for every proud human civilisation organised without God: its economics, culture, pleasures and power, however good its roads are.

She who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality. “Passion” (thymou) can mean passion or wrath, and the double sense is deliberate. “Sexual immorality” (porneias) is prostitution. Babylon seduces the nations into idolatry and immorality, like a prostitute offering wine to intoxicate her clients. Two things in the image. It is seduction, not conquest: the nations were not forced; they were poured a drink. And it is intoxication: the loss of judgement, the inability to see straight, the cheerful certainty that everything is fine. The same wine she makes them drink becomes the wine of God’s wrath (v. 10; 16:19). Those who drink her passion will drink God’s anger.

The sword and the glass. That is how the world’s system actually recruits, and it is why the church has so often failed to notice. The beast comes with a sword and is obvious. Babylon comes with a glass, and is charming, and pays well, and does not appear to be asking for anything at all. More Christians have been lost to Babylon’s wine than to the beast’s sword.

What it does not mean. Babylon is not only ancient Rome, or one future rebuilt city in Iraq. It is the spirit of the world in every age: the seductive, proud, self-indulgent civilisation that turns people away from God. It falls in every empire’s fall, and finally at Christ’s return.

How do I live in Babylon without drinking her wine? The way the exiles did in the first Babylon: seek the welfare of the city where God has sent you, and pray for it (Jeremiah 29:7), while refusing its gods. Daniel served the king faithfully and would not eat his food or stop praying. So work hard, be a good neighbour, enjoy God’s good gifts with thanks. But watch what intoxicates you: the pull of money, status, comfort, entertainment and approval that slowly dulls your love for Christ. A useful question is what you could not give up without bitterness. Whatever that is, hold it more loosely, and hold Christ more tightly.

In a sentence. A second angel followed, saying: Fallen! Fallen is Babylon the great, who made all the nations drink the intoxicating wine of her sexual immorality.

On a Tuesday. The world’s pleasures and power look permanent, but Babylon is already fallen in God’s sight. Do not drink her wine. When the advertisements, the ambitions and the anxieties of the day press in on you, say quietly to yourself what the angel said: fallen, fallen. It will help you see straight. You are not obliged to admire, envy or fear a city whose ruin God has already announced.

For worship. The Lord has spoken, and Babylon is fallen. Every tower that men have built to make a name for themselves has come down, and every one that stands today has its date already written. Nineveh is dust, the old Babylon is a mound in the desert, and Rome that killed the apostles is a museum, while the church of the Lamb is gathered from every nation under heaven. The kingdom of God cannot be shaken, and its King says of every proud city: I have spoken, and it is as good as done. Blessed be the God whose past tense is the future of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: And another angel, a third, followed them, saying with a loud voice, "If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives a mark on his forehead or on his hand, he also will drink the wine of God's wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger, and he will be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb. And the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever, and they have no rest, day or night, these worshipers of the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And another angel, a third, followed them, saying with a loud voice, “If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives a mark on his forehead or on his hand, he also will drink the wine of God’s wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger, and he will be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb. And the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever, and they have no rest, day or night, these worshipers of the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name.”

The setting. In the Old Testament, the cup of God’s wrath is a picture of judgement (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15–16). Wine in the ancient world was usually mixed with water; to pour it full strength, unmixed, was to make it at its most powerful. Fire and sulphur destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24), and the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace (Genesis 19:28). Isaiah 34:9–10 describes Edom’s judgement: its smoke shall go up for ever. In Gethsemane, Jesus prayed that the cup might pass from him (Matthew 26:39); he drank the cup of God’s wrath for his people.

The most terrible warning. The third angel gives the most terrible warning in the New Testament, and it should be read exactly as it stands, without softening and without relish.

And another angel, a third, followed them, saying with a loud voice, If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives a mark on his forehead or on his hand. The warning is aimed at those who choose to worship the beast. Receiving the mark means giving allegiance to the beast. No one takes it by accident. And the order of the angels is the mercy of the passage: nobody arrives at verse 11 without having been flown over by verse 6. The first of these three was an eternal gospel at the height of heaven where every nation could see it.

He also will drink the wine of God’s wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger. The image answers the previous verse precisely. Babylon poured a drink; so does God. Those who drank hers will drink his. “Wrath” (thymou) is passion, fury, and “anger” (orgēs) is settled wrath. And the detail is exact: “full strength” (akratou), unmixed, undiluted. The cup of God’s wrath is an Old Testament image: in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Psalm 75:8). Here for the first time nothing has been added to soften it.

The water left out. Which is what the whole book has been saying about God’s patience. The judgements of the seals and trumpets were mixed with mercy, partial and limited: a fourth, a third, a tenth, forty-two months, a limit on the locusts, a restraint on the winds. That was the mixing. This verse is what the cup is like when the water is left out. This is God’s wrath unmixed, with no mercy left.

And he will be tormented with fire and sulfur. “Tormented” (basanisthēsetai) is tortured, in pain. Fire and sulphur is Sodom, and it is the lake of fire (19:20; 20:10; 21:8). The worst images Scripture has, to describe the worst reality.

In the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb. Not that the angels and the Lamb watch with pleasure, but that the judgement is carried out under their authority, and is just. The one who refused the Lamb’s mercy faces the Lamb as judge. Whatever else hell is, it is not a place God has forgotten. And the one present is the Lamb: the one who was slaughtered, who wept at a tomb, who prayed for the men driving in the nails. Nobody who is finally lost will be able to say that the Judge did not offer himself first.

And the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever. “Forever and ever” (eis aiōnas aiōnōn, to the ages of the ages) is the same phrase used for God’s eternal life (4:9; 15:7) and for the saints’ reign (22:5). The smoke going up for ever is Isaiah’s picture of Edom. The torment does not end.

And they have no rest, day or night, these worshipers of the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name. “No rest” (ouk echousin anapausin). In contrast with the living creatures, who have no rest from praise (4:8), and with the dead in the Lord, who rest from their labours (v. 13). Two eternities are set side by side, and the difference is what a person is doing in them. The worshippers of the beast have endless unrest. And the verse says twice who it falls on: these worshippers of the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name. Not people who were unlucky, or confused, or never called.

Where Christians differ: is hell eternal conscious punishment? Annihilationists (or conditionalists) believe the wicked are punished and then cease to exist, and read “the smoke goes up forever” as the lasting result of a destruction that is complete. Some who hold this love the Bible and are trying to be faithful to it. Universalists believe all will finally be saved. Verdict: this passage teaches eternal, conscious punishment. The wicked are tormented, they have no rest day or night, and this continues for ever and ever. Revelation 20:10 uses the same language of the devil, beast and false prophet: tormented day and night for ever and ever, which plainly cannot mean annihilation. Jesus spoke of eternal punishment in the same breath as eternal life (Matthew 25:46). This is terrible, and it should be spoken of with tears, not glee. But it is what Scripture says, and it shows both the seriousness of sin against an infinitely holy God and the greatness of Christ’s love in bearing God’s wrath for all who trust in him.

What it does not mean. This warning is not meant to make Christians afraid that they might lose their salvation. It is meant to make them refuse the beast at any cost, and to warn the world. Those who belong to the Lamb will never drink this cup, because he drank it for them.

The cup in Gethsemane. Set this verse beside the garden. On the night before he died, the Son of God fell on his face and prayed, my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will (Matthew 26:39). This was the cup. He drank it, full strength, on the cross, when the darkness came down and he cried out that God had forsaken him. Everyone who trusts in him has had their portion drunk already. The wrath that falls on the beast’s worshippers has no claim left on Christ’s people, because it fell on him.

How can a loving God punish for ever? Because his love is holy, and sin against him is infinitely serious. We measure the guilt of a crime partly by the dignity of the one wronged; to rebel against the infinitely good God who made us is no small matter. Hell is also God giving people, in the end, what they have chosen: life without him, who is the source of all light, rest and joy. And those in hell do not repent there; this book shows the lost cursing God rather than turning to him (16:9, 11). Above all, remember who is the Judge. It is the Lamb, who bore this wrath himself so that it need not fall on anyone who comes to him. No one is in hell who wanted the mercy offered.

What about someone I love who has died without Christ, as far as I know? Scripture does not tell us the destination of any individual, and it never invites us to pronounce on the dead. You did not see every moment of their last days or the whole of their heart, and God is merciful beyond our knowledge. What you can do is leave them in the hands of the Judge of all the earth, who will do right (Genesis 18:25), and grieve honestly. And for those still alive, Scripture tells us that the Judge is the Lamb, that the gospel is still being flown overhead, and that intercession is the very work you were made a priest to do (1:6). Pray, and keep praying. Saul of Tarsus stood guarding the coats at Stephen’s death.

In a sentence. A third angel followed them, shouting: If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives its mark on the forehead or the hand, that person will also drink the wine of God’s fury, poured undiluted into the cup of his anger, and will be tormented with fire and sulphur in front of the holy angels and the Lamb; the smoke of their torment rises for ever and ever, and there is no rest day or night for those who worship the beast and its image, or for anyone who receives the mark of its name.

On a Tuesday. Take God’s warnings seriously, for yourself and for those you love. And thank Christ, who drank the cup of wrath so that you never will. Let this verse make you more urgent, not more harsh: more willing to speak of Christ to a friend, more earnest in prayer for the lost, and more grateful every time you take the cup of blessing at the Lord’s table, knowing whose cup made it possible.

For worship. The cup of wrath was full, and it was poured unmixed, and the Son of God took it from his Father’s hand and drank it to the dregs. He was made sin for us who knew no sin; he went down into the darkness that should have been ours; he bore in his body on the tree the fire we had earned. Holy and true is the Judge of all the earth, and his judgements are just. And holy and true is the Lamb who stands between the cup and his people, and says: it is finished. Now there is no condemnation for those who are in him. To him be glory for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus. And I heard a voice from heaven saying, "Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on." "Blessed indeed," says the Spirit, "that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus. And I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on.” “Blessed indeed,” says the Spirit, “that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!”

The setting. This is the second of Revelation’s seven beatitudes (1:3). Isaiah 57:1–2 says the righteous man perishes, and no one lays it to heart, but he enters into peace; they rest in their beds who walk in their uprightness. Hebrews 4:9–11 speaks of a Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God.

Here is a call for the endurance of the saints. “Endurance” (hypomonē) is staying under the weight. The same sentence appeared at 13:10, and it appears both times immediately after the darkest material in the book: there after the beast conquering the saints, here after the cup of undiluted wrath. Twice John writes something almost unbearable and then turns to the reader and says: this is what it is for. Because the stakes are eternal, believers must endure, refusing the beast, whatever it costs. The warning of verses 9 to 11 is a reason to stay faithful.

Those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus. “Faith in Jesus” (tēn pistin Iēsou) can mean faith in Jesus, or the faithfulness of Jesus. As in 12:17, obedience and faith together mark the true believer. The list has not grown, and it will not.

What the warning is for. There is something important in what this call does not ask. After three verses about hell, the response sought is not panic, and it is not a campaign. It is endurance. The knowledge of judgement in this book is never given to make Christians frightened. It is given to make them able to keep standing when the beast has all the advantages, because they know how the accounts are finally settled.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying, Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on. This is one of the few sentences in the book that John is specifically commanded to write down (compare 19:9; 21:5). Most of what he writes is on standing orders; this sentence gets its own instruction. Heaven wanted to be certain it was recorded. And look at what it is. Not blessed are the strong, or the victorious, or those who escape. Blessed are the dead. To a congregation that had buried people and expected to bury more, at the exact point in the book where the beast is killing anyone who will not take the mark, God stops the vision to dictate a sentence about the ones who did not survive.

In the Lord. “In the Lord” (en kyriō) is united to Christ by faith, and the qualifier carries everything. Death is not blessed in itself; Paul calls it the last enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26), and this book throws it into the lake of fire (20:14). What is blessed is dying in him, the same phrase Paul uses of the dead in Christ whom he expects to rise (1 Thessalonians 4:16). “From now on” (ap’ arti) means from this point in history, as persecution intensifies, or from the moment of death. Those who die faithful, perhaps as martyrs, are not to be pitied. They are blessed. The world calls them losers; heaven calls them blessed.

Blessed indeed, says the Spirit, that they may rest from their labors. Then the Spirit himself adds a comment, which happens almost nowhere else in the book. “Indeed” (nai) is yes: the Spirit adds his confirmation. “Rest” (anapaēsontai). “Labors” (kopōn) is toil, hard work, the exhaustion of service and suffering. It is the rest the martyrs under the altar were told to take in 6:11. Whatever heaven is, it is first described here as the end of being tired. In contrast with the restless torment of the beast’s worshippers (v. 11), the dead in Christ rest.

For their deeds follow them! “Deeds” (erga) is works. “Follow” (akolouthei) is accompany. Not go before them as a credential, and not stay behind as a legacy. They follow, like servants walking behind their master into a house. Their faithful works are not lost; they go with them into God’s presence, as evidence of their faith and as the basis of their reward (22:12). Nothing done for Christ is wasted; your labour is not in vain in the Lord (1 Corinthians 15:58). The visits nobody recorded, the giving that cost something, the years of raising children in the faith, the prayers said in an empty kitchen: all of it walks in behind the person who did it.

Where Christians differ: do believers go to purgatory, or rest? Roman Catholic teaching holds that many who die in God’s grace must still be purified in purgatory before entering heaven. Others hold that the soul sleeps until the resurrection. Verdict: the dead in the Lord are blessed from the moment of death, and they rest. There is no purging of sin after death; Christ’s blood has cleansed them completely (1 John 1:7; Hebrews 10:14), and to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Their rest is conscious enjoyment of Christ (6:9–11), not unconscious sleep. They wait for the resurrection of the body, but they are already with him.

What it does not mean. Their deeds following them does not mean they are saved by their works. They died in the Lord, which means united to Christ by faith. Their works follow them; they do not go before them to buy them entry.

What should I say at the funeral of a believer? Say this verse. It was written down at heaven’s express command for exactly that moment. Grieve, because death is an enemy and the loss is real; Jesus wept at Lazarus’s tomb. But grieve as those who have hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The one you loved is not lost, not sleeping in the dark, not being purged somewhere. They are with Christ, resting, conscious, at home. Their work is finished and none of it is forgotten. And one day their body, laid in the ground, will be raised in glory. Say that to the widow, the orphan, the friend. It is the truest comfort there is.

What if I feel my life has accomplished very little for Christ? Then this verse is for you. The deeds that follow the dead in the Lord are not only the public ones. They include every hidden kindness, every faithful year in a small place, every prayer for a child, every temptation resisted that nobody saw. God sees what no one records, and he forgets nothing done in his name, not even a cup of cold water. You are not asked to be impressive. You are asked to be faithful, and the Lord who works in you to will and to work for his good pleasure will see that what he has done through you follows you home.

In a sentence. This is why God’s people, who keep his commandments and hold on to their faith in Jesus, must endure; and I heard a voice from heaven say: Write this down: from now on, how happy are those who die belonging to the Lord! Yes, says the Spirit, they will rest from their hard work, for what they have done goes with them.

On a Tuesday. If you are worn out by faithful service, caring for a sick relative, holding a struggling church together, working hard for little thanks, this verse promises you rest, and promises that none of it is lost. Do the next faithful thing today. And if you know someone who is dying in the Lord, read them this verse, slowly.

For worship. Read this verse at Christian funerals. Those who die in the Lord are blessed and at rest, and nothing they did for him is lost. Blessed be the God who stopped the vision of the end to write down a word for the bereaved. He holds the keys of death; he has made the grave a place of rest for those who are his; he receives his tired servants home and says, well done. Christ has tasted death for them and taken its sting away. The Spirit says yes. The dead in the Lord are resting in the presence of the Lamb, and all their faithful works are following them in, every one remembered, every one rewarded by grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — The Harvest of the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 14–16: one like a son of man (Dan. 7:13; cf. Rev. 1:13) is seated on a white cloud with a golden crown and a sharp sickle. An angel comes out of the temple with word that the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe, and he swings his sickle and the earth is reaped — in a single sentence, with no resistance recorded.

Verses 17–19: a second angel with a sharp sickle comes out of the temple, and a third comes from the altar, having authority over the fire, and orders the vintage: gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe. The grapes are thrown into the great winepress of the wrath of God (cf. Isa. 63:3; Joel 3:13).

Verse 20: the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress, as high as a horse’s bridle, for 1,600 stadia — about a hundred and eighty miles, roughly the length of Palestine, and four times four times a hundred, four being the number of the earth in this book. The figure means the whole world, completely.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Harvest of the Earth

One like a son of man reaps the ripe harvest, and the vintage of the earth is trodden in the winepress of God’s wrath outside the city. The timing is set by the one who has watched the field.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The order for the vintage came from the altar where the martyrs’ prayers were received.

Now: The delay was never indifference but patience; the judge who reaps is the one who was trodden outside the city for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and behold, a white cloud, and seated on the cloud one like a son of man, with a golden crown on his head, and a sharp sickle in his hand. And another angel came out of the temple, calling with a loud voice to him who sat on the cloud, "Put in your sickle, and reap, for the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe." So he who sat on the cloud swung his sickle across the earth, and the earth was reaped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I looked, and behold, a white cloud, and seated on the cloud one like a son of man, with a golden crown on his head, and a sharp sickle in his hand. And another angel came out of the temple, calling with a loud voice to him who sat on the cloud, “Put in your sickle, and reap, for the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe.” So he who sat on the cloud swung his sickle across the earth, and the earth was reaped.

The setting. Joel 3:13 says: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe; go in, tread, for the winepress is full. The vats overflow, for their evil is great. Daniel 7:13 shows one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven. Jesus told parables of harvest at the end of the age: the wheat gathered into the barn and the weeds burned (Matthew 13:24–30, 36–43), and the angels sent to gather his elect from the four winds (Matthew 24:31). He said the harvest is plentiful (Matthew 9:37–38), and that the fields are white for harvest (John 4:35).

Then I looked, and behold, a white cloud, and seated on the cloud one like a son of man. One like a son of man coming with the clouds is Daniel 7:13, and it is the phrase this book used of the risen Christ in its first chapter (1:13). This is Christ, coming on the clouds (1:7).

With a golden crown on his head, and a sharp sickle in his hand. “Crown” (stephanon) is the victor’s crown: he has conquered. And in his hand, instead of a sword or a sceptre, a farm implement. “Sickle” (drepanon) is the curved blade for harvesting grain.

And another angel came out of the temple, calling with a loud voice to him who sat on the cloud, Put in your sickle, and reap. Some have taken the figure on the cloud as an angel, on the grounds that here an angel tells him to start reaping, which seems an odd thing for a creature to say to the Son of God. The objection is fair and should be stated. But the angel brings the message from God’s presence, the temple: the Father has fixed the hour. Christ himself said that of that day or that hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father (Mark 13:32; Acts 1:7). The angel does not command Christ; he conveys the Father’s timing. A message from the sanctuary saying the hour has come is exactly what the Son said he was waiting for.

For the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe. The timing is stated twice. “Fully ripe” (exēranthē) means has become dry, over-ready: grain that has stood in the field until it is at the point of being lost. That is a farmer’s judgement and it repays a moment. Anyone who has waited on a crop knows there is a right day. Cut too early and the grain is green and worthless; wait too long and it shatters on the ground and the season’s work is gone. There is one hour, and knowing it is the whole art. The point of the image is not the violence of reaping. It is that a decision about timing is being made by someone who has been watching the field.

The answer to how long. This answers the question that has run through this book since 6:10. The delay was never indifference and never a failure of nerve. It was a harvest not yet ready, and Peter says exactly what was ripening: the Lord is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9).

So he who sat on the cloud swung his sickle across the earth, and the earth was reaped. A single, decisive act: the end of the age. One sentence. After thirteen chapters of seals, trumpets, beasts and dragons, the end arrives in a single sentence with no resistance recorded. There is no battle here, no dialogue, nothing said. The instrument that finishes the age is a sickle swung once by a man on a cloud.

Where Christians differ: is the grain harvest salvation or judgement? Some see both harvests in vv. 14–20 as judgement, following Joel 3:13. Others see the grain harvest as the gathering of the redeemed and the grape harvest as the judgement of the wicked. Verdict: the grain harvest is most likely the gathering of God’s people at Christ’s return. Christ himself reaps it, as he sends his angels to gather his elect (Matthew 24:31); in the Gospels, the grain harvest is regularly the harvest of salvation (Matthew 9:37–38; 13:30; John 4:35–38); and the 144,000 have just been called firstfruits (v. 4), the beginning of this harvest. Nothing is said about destroying the grain. The grape harvest, by contrast, is explicitly thrown into the winepress of God’s wrath. Together they picture the two outcomes of the last day.

What it does not mean. The harvest does not mean God waits passively until humanity ripens by itself. He sets the hour, and Christ acts. History ripens under his hand.

Is this the rapture? It is the one gathering of God’s people at Christ’s visible return, which is what the New Testament means by our being caught up to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). There is no hint here of a secret removal of the church years before the end. The Son of Man comes on a white cloud, in the sight of the world, at the hour the Father has set, and reaps the whole earth at once. That is the hope of every believer: not escape from history halfway through, but the Lord himself coming at its end to gather his harvest home.

In a sentence. Then I looked and saw a white cloud, and seated on it someone like a son of man, with a gold crown on his head and a sharp sickle in his hand; another angel came out of the temple and called loudly to the one on the cloud, Take your sickle and reap, because the time to reap has come and the earth’s harvest is ripe; so the one seated on the cloud swung his sickle over the earth, and the earth was harvested.

On a Tuesday. Christ will gather his people home. Meanwhile, pray the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers, and be one yourself. If you are tired of waiting for the Lord to come, remember why he waits: there is grain still ripening, perhaps in your own family. Use the time. And if you are anxious about the end, look at who holds the sickle: the Son of Man who loved you and gave himself for you.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest has been watching his field since the first seed fell. He has not missed a stalk, and he will not mistake the day. He comes on a white cloud, crowned as the Victor, and the sickle in his hand is the instrument of homecoming for all his people. He sowed himself into the ground, a grain of wheat that fell into the earth and died, so that he would not remain alone but bear much fruit. Now he reaps what his death has grown. Blessed be the Son of Man, who will gather his wheat into his barn, and not lose one grain.

verseByVerse.quote: Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle. And another angel came out from the altar, the angel who has authority over the fire, and he called with a loud voice to the one who had the sharp sickle, "Put in your sickle and gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe." So the angel swung his sickle across the earth and gathered the grape harvest of the earth and threw it into the great winepress of the wrath of God. And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress, as high as a horse's bridle, for 1,600 stadia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle. And another angel came out from the altar, the angel who has authority over the fire, and he called with a loud voice to the one who had the sharp sickle, “Put in your sickle and gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe.” So the angel swung his sickle across the earth and gathered the grape harvest of the earth and threw it into the great winepress of the wrath of God. And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress, as high as a horse’s bridle, for 1,600 stadia.

The setting. Grapes were trodden in a winepress, a stone vat in which people trampled the grapes, and the juice ran down a channel into a lower vat. The red juice looked like blood. Isaiah 63:1–6 shows the LORD coming from Edom with garments stained crimson, saying, I have trodden the winepress alone; I trod them in my anger, and their lifeblood spattered on my garments. Joel 3:13 says, tread, for the winepress is full. Executions were carried out outside the city (Leviticus 24:14; Hebrews 13:12). A stadion was about 185 metres (607 feet), so 1,600 stadia is about 300 kilometres (184 miles), roughly the length of the land of Israel from north to south.

Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle. This time an angel holds the sickle, carrying out the judgement. The second harvest begins, and the order to begin it comes from an unexpected address.

And another angel came out from the altar, the angel who has authority over the fire. The reader has been at that altar before. It is where the prayers of all the saints were offered with incense (8:3–4). It is where the fire came from that was thrown down on the earth (8:5). It is where the voice came from that released the sixth trumpet (9:13). And beneath it are the souls of the martyrs who cried, How long? (6:9–10). So the command to begin the vintage of God’s wrath is issued by the angel in charge of the fire at the altar where the church’s prayers have been going up for the whole book. This harvest answers their prayers. The martyrs asked; this is the answer arriving, and it comes out of the place where the asking was received.

Put in your sickle and gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe. “Vine of the earth”: in contrast with Christ, the true vine (John 15:1), and Israel, God’s vine, which yielded wild grapes (Isaiah 5:1–7). The earth’s vine is humanity in rebellion, ripe in its sin.

So the angel swung his sickle across the earth and gathered the grape harvest of the earth and threw it into the great winepress of the wrath of God. “Winepress” (lēnon). “Wrath” (thymou). The judgement is described in terms of the crushing of grapes. A first-century winepress was hard, ordinary, labour-intensive work, and its image is one of the oldest pictures of judgement in Scripture. John is quoting Isaiah and Joel at once. And Christ himself treads the winepress in 19:15.

And the winepress was trodden outside the city. “The city” is God’s city, the holy city where his people are (20:9). Judgement falls outside, where his enemies are. And this is the detail that ought to stop a Christian reader. Outside the city is where the sin offering was burned under the law, and it is where Jesus died: so Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12). He suffered outside the gate, bearing the judgement his people deserved.

Two treadings outside the city. Say that plainly, because it is the mercy hidden inside the most violent verse in the book. There are two treadings of that press outside that city. At the first, one man went in alone and the blood was his own. Everyone at the second will have refused the first.

And blood flowed from the winepress, as high as a horse’s bridle, for 1,600 stadia. Horrific, deliberately exaggerated imagery. The measurements are symbolic and the arithmetic is not hidden. 1,600 is four times four times a hundred (or forty times forty): four, the number of the earth with its four corners and four winds, squared and multiplied. A judgement covering the whole earth, completely. And 1,600 stadia is roughly the length of the land, a distance any reader could picture. Jewish writings used similar language: 1 Enoch 100:3 says the horse will walk up to its chest in the blood of sinners. Blood as high as a horse’s bridle across the length of a country is not a forecast of casualties. It is a statement of scale, and of horror, in the only register that can carry it.

What it does not mean. This is not a literal river of blood three hundred kilometres long, to be measured. It is a vivid, terrible symbol of the completeness and severity of God’s final judgement on unrepentant evil. Nor does it portray God as cruel. It is the just answer to the blood of the martyrs (6:10; 16:6; 19:2), and it falls only on those who refused his eternal gospel (v. 6).

Two harvests, one day. The chapter ends there, without comment, and that is deliberate. Revelation does not make judgement palatable and it does not apologise for it. What it does is put it a few verses after verse 13, blessed are the dead who die in the Lord, so that the reader holds the two together. The same chapter contains the gentlest sentence in the book and one of the most terrible. The grain harvest and the grape harvest are two sides of the one final coming: the harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels (Matthew 13:39).

Should I be glad about the judgement of the wicked? Glad that God will put every wrong right, yes; the martyrs pray for it, and heaven rejoices at the justice of God (19:1–2). It would be a strange love that did not long for evil to end and the oppressed to be vindicated. But never glad in a cold or gloating way, and never as though you deserved to be on the other side of the city wall. God himself takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that they turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11). Hold together justice and tears, as Jesus did when he wept over Jerusalem. And let it drive you to pray and to speak while the gospel is still flying overhead.

In a sentence. Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, also holding a sharp sickle, and yet another angel, who has authority over fire, came from the altar and called loudly to the one with the sharp sickle: Take your sharp sickle and gather the bunches of grapes from the earth’s vine, because they are ripe; so the angel swung his sickle over the earth, gathered its grapes and threw them into the great winepress of God’s anger; the winepress was trampled outside the city, and blood poured out of it, rising as high as a horse’s bridle for about three hundred kilometres.

On a Tuesday. Do not take sin lightly, yours or the world’s. God will judge it fully. And do not take the cross lightly, where Christ was trodden outside the city for all who trust him. When you hear of great evil and wonder whether anyone will ever answer for it, remember this winepress: no injustice will be overlooked. And when you are tempted to think your own sin small, remember the first treading, where the blood was his.

For worship. The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with his people, counted and complete, singing a song nobody else can learn. An eternal gospel flies overhead where every nation can see it. Babylon is announced fallen while she is still standing. The dead who die in the Lord are at rest, and their deeds are following them in. And the field has been watched by someone who knows the day. He who treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty first trod it alone, outside the gate, and the blood that ran was his own. Glory to the Lamb, whose wounded hand holds the sickle, and who will gather his wheat into the barn and make all things right.
verseByVerse.note: The 1,600 stadia (v. 20) are about 184 miles; a stadion was about 607 feet — roughly the length of the land of Israel.

21.title: All Things New: The New Heaven, New Earth, and New Jerusalem
21.overview:
Chapter 21 is the destination toward which every page of Revelation has been moving. Every sealed scroll, every trumpet, every suffering saint, every martyr’s cry of ‘How long?’ — all of it was moving toward this: “Behold, I am making all things new.” The new creation is not the consolation prize for a plan that nearly failed. It is the goal, the telos, the end for which the whole story was told.

The chapter falls into two great movements. The first (vv. 1–8) describes the new heaven and new earth from a distance — the cosmic renewal, the descent of the holy city, the voice from the throne declaring the end of tears and death, and the character of those who will inherit and those who will not. The second (vv. 9–27) zooms in: the angel takes John in the Spirit to a high mountain and shows him the new Jerusalem in breathtaking architectural detail — dimensions, gates, foundations, materials, light, temple, nations.

The key to the chapter is understanding what the new Jerusalem is. It is not primarily a city in the architectural sense; it is a person — “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.” The new Jerusalem is the church, the bride of Christ, dwelling with God in the fullness of the covenant relationship that all of redemptive history has been building toward. The city and the bride are the same reality: the people of God in their final, perfected, glorified state, living in the presence of God as his dwelling place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The New Heaven and the New Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a new heaven and a new earth, and the sea was no more; and the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. The word for new is kainos, which usually means new in kind, renewed. And the direction is downward.

Verses 3–4: the dwelling place of God is with man — skēnē, a tent — with the covenant formula complete: they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. Then four abolitions: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore (cf. Isa. 25:8).

Verses 5–6: God the Father speaks in the first person for the second and last time in the book — Behold, I am making all things new; Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true; It is done!; I am the Alpha and the Omega; and the offer, to the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment (cf. Isa. 55:1; John 4:14).

Verses 7–8: the last promise to the conqueror — I will be his God and he will be my son, the Davidic promise of 2 Samuel 7:14 handed to anyone who holds on — and then the eight excluded categories, beginning startlingly with the cowardly and ending with all liars, whose portion is the second death.
verseByVerse.theology:
All Things New

A new heaven and earth — renewed, not replaced — and the holy city coming down as a bride. God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear; death, mourning, crying and pain are gone. He gives the water of life freely to the thirsty.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: John, cut off by the sea from his churches, hears that the sea will be no more.

Now: God answers grief not by explanation but by removal, with his own hand on the face.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.

Meaning first. Revelation 21 shows the goal of all history: the new creation, where God lives with his people for ever. John sees a new heaven and a new earth, with no more sea, and the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God like a bride (vv. 1–2). A voice from the throne announces that God’s dwelling is now with humanity: he will be their God, wipe away every tear, and end death, mourning, crying and pain (vv. 3–4). God says, I am making all things new; it is done; I am the Alpha and the Omega; he gives the water of life freely to the thirsty; the one who conquers will inherit all this and be his child, but the cowardly, faithless and wicked will have their part in the lake of fire (vv. 5–8). Then an angel shows John the bride, the new Jerusalem, shining with God’s glory (vv. 9–11). It has twelve gates bearing the names of the twelve tribes, and twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles (vv. 12–14). It is a perfect cube, twelve thousand stadia on each side (vv. 15–17), built of jasper and pure gold, its foundations adorned with twelve precious stones, its gates of pearl (vv. 18–21). It has no temple, because God and the Lamb are its temple, no sun or moon, because God’s glory is its light and the Lamb its lamp; the nations walk by its light and bring their glory into it; its gates are never shut; and nothing unclean enters, only those written in the Lamb’s book of life (vv. 22–27). The chapter is the answer to every fear and sorrow in the book: Babylon has fallen, and the bride has come; the world’s glory passes away, and God’s glory fills everything. And at the centre of it all is not a place but a Person: God himself with his people, and the Lamb as the lamp of the city.

The setting. Isaiah 65:17–25 and 66:22 promise new heavens and a new earth, where the former things shall not be remembered, and there will be no more weeping.
