Isaiah 54:11–12 promises a city built with sapphires, rubies and jewels. Ezekiel 40–48 describes a restored city and temple, ending with the name of the city: The LORD is there (Ezekiel 48:35). Abraham looked forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God (Hebrews 11:10). Peter says we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). Paul says creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption (Romans 8:19–23).

Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth. The whole Bible has been travelling toward this sentence. It opened with In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1:1), and it now says it again with one word changed. And which word matters. “New” (kainon) usually stresses newness of quality rather than mere recency: new in kind, fresh, renewed. John uses the same word here, in verse 5, and of the new Jerusalem, the new name and the new song. That is not a technicality. It is the difference between God scrapping his creation and God renewing it. Not a different world replacing this one, but this world made new. God does not abandon what he made; he restores and transforms it.

The pattern of the resurrection body. Paul says the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Romans 8:21): set free, not replaced. The risen body of Jesus is the pattern. It was the same body that was laid in the tomb, transformed and glorified, with the wounds still in the hands. So a Christian’s hope is not that he will escape the material world into something vague and vaporous. It is that this world, soil, water, weather, bodies, work, cities, will be put right. God does not abandon what he made. He never has.

For the first heaven and the first earth had passed away. “Passed away” (apēlthan, gone away). The first creation, under the curse of sin, has gone (20:11). Its old order, marked by sin, death and decay, is over. What passes away is the first form of things, the fallen form, not the handiwork of God itself.

And the sea was no more. This one troubles people who love the sea, and it should be answered rather than passed over. John is not making a statement about oceanography. In this book the sea has a settled meaning. It is the ancient image of chaos, which is why the throne room has it lying flat as glass under God’s feet (4:6); it is where the beast comes up from (13:1); it is what swallowed the dead who had no graves (20:13). And there is a personal edge to it that John’s first readers would have felt at once. He is writing from an island, and the sea is the thing keeping him from his churches. The promise is not that there will be no water; the next chapter has a river. It is that there will be nothing left that separates, threatens or devours: no more chaos, danger, evil or separation.

And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God. “Holy city” (tēn polin tēn hagian). “New Jerusalem”: the fulfilment of all God’s promises to Zion. “Coming down” (katabainousan): it comes from God; it is his gift, not human achievement. Watch the direction, because almost every popular picture of the Christian hope gets it backwards. The city comes down. Nobody is going up. Babel tried to build up to heaven (Genesis 11:4); the new Jerusalem comes down from heaven. The last movement in the Bible is not humanity being evacuated to the sky; it is heaven arriving on a renewed earth, which is what Christians have always prayed for without noticing: your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven (Matthew 6:10).

Prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. “Prepared” (hētoimasmenēn). “Adorned” (kekosmēmenēn, beautifully dressed; our word cosmetics comes from it). The city is the bride (v. 9), the people of God. Not a bride’s residence: the city and the bride are the same thing, which verse 9 will make explicit when an angel offers to show John the Bride and then shows him a city. The dwelling place turns out to be the people. The new Jerusalem is not only a place; it is a people, God’s people in their perfected community, in contrast to Babylon the prostitute. Two women, two cities, and the book has been asking since chapter 17 which one a reader has been dressing for.

Where Christians differ: will this earth be destroyed and replaced, or renewed? Some Christians, reading 2 Peter 3:10 (the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the earth and the works on it will be burned up), believe the present creation will be annihilated and replaced with something entirely new. Others think of eternity as a purely spiritual existence in heaven. Verdict: Scripture teaches that this creation will be renewed and transformed, not discarded. Paul says creation will be set free from bondage (Romans 8:21); Jesus speaks of the renewal of all things (Matthew 19:28); Peter speaks of the restoration of all things (Acts 3:21). The fire of 2 Peter 3 purifies, as metal is refined, and the earth is laid bare to judgement. Just as our bodies will be raised and transformed, not replaced, so creation will be raised and transformed. The final hope of believers is not disembodied existence but resurrection life on a new earth, with God.

What it does not mean. The new Jerusalem is not a literal city of particular dimensions to be mapped. It is a vision, full of symbols, of the perfect, eternal dwelling of God with his people. But what it describes is real: a real new creation, with real resurrected people, and God truly present.

Is heaven now the same as the new earth? Not yet. When a believer dies, he goes to be with Christ in heaven, conscious and at rest (Philippians 1:23), and that is far better than this life. But it is not the end of the story. The end is the resurrection of the body at Christ’s return and life with God on the new earth. So there are two stages of the Christian hope: with Christ in heaven at death, and with Christ in the new creation, bodily, for ever. When Christians speak of going to heaven, they are speaking truly of the first. This chapter is about the second, and it is better still.

Will we be ourselves, and will we know each other? Yes. Resurrection means the same person raised, not a stranger. The disciples recognised the risen Jesus, and Moses and Elijah were known on the mountain (Matthew 17:3). Paul says we shall know fully, even as we have been fully known (1 Corinthians 13:12). Jesus does say that in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matthew 22:30), because the marriage every human marriage pointed to, Christ and his bride, has arrived. But nothing good in the love between husband and wife, parents and children, friends in Christ, will be lost. It will be taken up into something larger, not cancelled.

In a sentence. Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, because the first heaven and the first earth had gone, and there was no longer any sea; and I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared and dressed like a bride beautifully adorned for her husband.

On a Tuesday. Your future is not an endless cloud, but a renewed earth. Care for God’s creation now, and live in hope of its renewal. The garden you tend, the work you do well, the body you look after, the city you seek the good of: these are not meaningless because this world is passing. They are the first form of things God intends to make new. And if you are weary of a broken world, a broken body, a broken family, look up. What is coming is not an escape from all that God made, but all that God made, mended.

For worship. The God who said, Let there be light, has not given up on his world. He made the heavens and the earth, and sin spoiled them, and he sent his Son into the spoiled world, into a body, into a grave, and brought that body out again glorified. What he did for Jesus’ body he will do for the whole creation. The sea that separated John from his churches is gone, and the city comes down from God, dressed for her husband, beautiful because he has made her so. Blessed be the Maker of heaven and earth, who will not rest until he has made them new.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away.”

The setting. The heart of God’s covenant promise throughout Scripture is: I will be your God, and you shall be my people, and I will dwell among you (Leviticus 26:11–12; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 37:27). God walked with Adam in the garden (Genesis 3:8), dwelt in the tabernacle and temple, and became flesh and tabernacled among us in Christ (John 1:14). Now his presence is complete. Isaiah 25:8 promises that God will swallow up death for ever and wipe away tears from all faces. Isaiah 35:10 and 65:19 promise that sorrow and sighing shall flee away, and no more shall be heard the sound of weeping.

And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. “Dwelling place” (hē skēnē, tent, tabernacle). God’s tabernacle, his presence, is now permanently with humanity. What Eden had, and sin lost, is restored and surpassed.

He will dwell with them. “Dwell” (skēnōsei, tabernacle, pitch his tent), as in 7:15. God will pitch his tent with them. Follow that one word through the Bible and the whole story is on a single thread. God walked with the man and the woman in a garden in the cool of the day, and they were sent out. He told Moses, let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst (Exodus 25:8), and a tent was pitched in the middle of the camp. Solomon built a house and the glory filled it, and Ezekiel watched that glory leave. Then the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, pitched his tent among us, and John, who is writing this, is the man who wrote that sentence (John 1:14). Then the Spirit came and made a temple out of ordinary people (1 Corinthians 3:16). And here is the end of it: no tent in a camp, no house on a hill, no veil, no exclusions. God with man, permanently, in the open.

And they will be his people. “People” (laoi, plural, peoples, in the best manuscripts). The many nations of the redeemed, now one people of God. The promise once made to Israel now includes all nations. And the covenant formula that runs through the whole Old Testament arrives complete. It was said to Abraham, to Israel at Sinai, through Jeremiah and Ezekiel, always as a promise. Here it is reported as a fact.

And God himself will be with them as their God. “God himself” (autos ho theos). Note the three words. Not an angel, not a representative, not glory at a safe distance. Not merely his gifts, but God himself. Immanuel, God with us, in full. The thing the whole Bible has been arranging is not improved circumstances for human beings. It is his presence.

He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. This is the second time the promise is made in this book (7:17), and both times it says the same extraordinary thing: God does it himself, with his hand, on a face. Not an angel with a cloth. Not time healing it. Isaiah promised it first: he will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces (Isaiah 25:8). God personally comforts his people.

And death shall be no more. Then four abolitions, and they should be taken one at a time rather than blurred into a general improvement. Death shall be no more: the thing that has taken everyone a reader has ever loved, and will take him. Gone, and 20:14 has already shown how: thrown into the lake of fire. The last enemy destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26).

Neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore. Mourning is the loud public grief of a funeral, the thing you do at the graveside. Crying is the private version, the sound a person makes alone in a car. Pain covers both the body’s pain and the labour that wears a person out, which takes the reader back to the curse in Genesis 3 and undoes it. Every result of sin and the curse is gone. And every one of them is answered by removal, not by explanation. Nobody in this verse is told why it happened. The promise is not that the tears will finally make sense. It is that they will be wiped off a face by God, and that the thing that caused them will be dead.

For the former things have passed away. “The former things” (ta prōta, the first things). The old order of sin and suffering is gone for ever. This is the verse to hold when the reason for a grief has never arrived and probably never will. God does not, in the end, argue with a bereaved person. He comes over and attends to the face.

What it does not mean. No more tears does not mean we will forget everything about this life, or that our relationships and history will be erased. It means every sorrow will be healed and every loss made up, so that nothing will cause pain any more.

Will we remember those we loved who are lost? Scripture does not explain how, and we should not claim to know more than it says. But it does say that we will be ourselves, known and knowing (1 Corinthians 13:12), and that God himself will wipe away every tear. We will see as God sees, and share his perfect justice and his perfect love. Whatever we remember, nothing will spoil the joy he gives. And that is a reason now to pray and to speak to those we love while there is time.

Is it wrong to grieve now, if this is coming? No. Jesus wept at the grave of Lazarus, minutes before he raised him (John 11:35), so tears and hope can stand side by side in the same heart. Paul does not tell the Thessalonians not to grieve, but not to grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief is love that has lost its object for a while; this verse does not shame it, it promises it an end. So weep honestly, at the graveside and in the car. Then bring the tears to the God who has promised to wipe them away himself, and let him be the one who comforts you.

In a sentence. And I heard a loud voice from the throne say: Look, God’s home is now among people; he will live with them, they will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God; he will wipe every tear from their eyes; there will be no more death, no more grief, no more crying and no more pain, because the old order of things has gone.

On a Tuesday. Read this at funerals, in hospitals and in grief. Learn it by heart, so that it is ready when the phone rings. Sit with someone this week who is mourning, and do not try to explain their loss; simply be present, as God will be present, and if the moment is right, read them these two verses. And when your own pain comes, chronic illness, an empty chair at the table, the child who will not speak to you, say to yourself: this is one of the former things, and the former things are passing away.

For worship. The God who walked in Eden, who lived in a tent in the desert, who filled the temple with glory, who took flesh and pitched his tent among us in Jesus, will live with his people for ever, with nothing between. He will not send someone else to comfort them. He will come himself, and with his own hand wipe the tears from every face. The Lord Jesus, who wept at a grave and then emptied it, will see to it that death, mourning, crying and pain are all thrown out of his world. Blessed be God, our dwelling place in all generations, who will make his dwelling with us.

verseByVerse.quote: And he who was seated on the throne said, "Behold, I am making all things new." Also he said, "Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true." And he said to me, "It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he who was seated on the throne said, “Behold, I am making all things new.” Also he said, “Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true.” And he said to me, “It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment.

The setting. This is only the second time in Revelation that God himself plainly speaks directly (the first was 1:8). Isaiah 43:19 says, behold, I am doing a new thing. Isaiah 55:1 calls: come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat; buy wine and milk without money and without price. Jesus offered living water to the Samaritan woman (John 4:10–14) and cried out at the feast, if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37).

And he who was seated on the throne said, Behold, I am making all things new. This is one of only two places in the whole book where God the Father is plainly named as speaking in his own voice in the first person. The first was at 1:8, where he said who he is. This is what he does. Two sentences, twenty chapters apart, bracketing the dragon and the beast and the bowls and the burning city. And every word repays attention. “I am making” (poiō) is present tense: it is happening, not merely scheduled. All things, with nothing excepted. And the object is not what most people assume. He does not say I am making all new things. He says I am making all things new: renewal, not replacement. The same things, this world, these people, the bodies in the ground, are being made new. God’s work of renewal has already begun in Christ, in whom anyone is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), and it will be completed.

Also he said, Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true. “Trustworthy” (pistoi, faithful) and “true” (alēthinoi). A guarantee. The new creation is certain. And this is the third and last time John is told to write a particular sentence, and the pattern of the three repays a look. At 14:13: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. At 19:9: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. And here: I am making all things new. Every one of the three is a promise a suffering church would find nearly impossible to believe, and every one of them is given its own command to record it and its own guarantee of truthfulness.

And he said to me, It is done! “It is done” (gegonan, they have happened), the same word as at the seventh bowl (16:17). The whole plan of God is complete. And it echoes the cry from the cross, It is finished (John 19:30). The finished work on the cross made the final victory certain, and the same voice now says it over a finished world.

I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. The title from 1:8, and it has waited twenty chapters to be used again. God began everything and brings everything to its goal. He was the first letter when there was nothing yet to write, and he is the last one now that everything has been written. Nothing in history has slipped out from between those two letters.

To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment. And here, at the very summit of the book, after the great white throne and the lake of fire, comes an offer. Not a reward, not a settlement, not a wage. A drink, given away. “Thirsty” (tō dipsōnti, the one who is thirsting). “Water of life” (tou hydatos tēs zōēs): eternal life, God himself. “Without payment” (dōrean): as a gift, freely, for nothing, the same word Paul uses of being justified by his grace as a gift (Romans 3:24). Salvation is free. No one can buy it or earn it. And note the only qualification named: the thirsty. Not the deserving, not the improved, not the people who worked it out. The single requirement for the water of life is wanting it, knowing that you need it, and the book will make the same offer one last time in its final chapter with the doors held open (22:17).

What it does not mean. “Without payment” does not mean salvation is cheap. It cost the Lamb his blood. It is free to us because Christ paid in full.

What if I do not feel thirsty? Then ask God to make you thirsty, and notice that you are already asking. Thirst is not a strong religious feeling; it is need, and need is there whether you feel it or not. The restless dissatisfaction that no achievement fills, the guilt you cannot shake off, the fear of death, the longing for something you cannot name: these are thirst. Many come to Christ not burning with desire but simply tired of drinking from wells that do not satisfy (Jeremiah 2:13). Come as you are. The offer is to the thirsty, and the Spirit who makes people thirsty is the same Spirit who brings them to the spring.

In a sentence. Then the one seated on the throne said, Look, I am making everything new! and he told me, Write this down, because these words are reliable and true; then he said to me, It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end; to anyone who is thirsty I will give water from the spring of the water of life as a free gift.

On a Tuesday. If you are thirsty for meaning, forgiveness or life, come to Christ. The water is free. And offer it freely to others. Notice this week where you go when you are dry: the screen, the shopping, the drink, the approval of others. Each of them is a well that runs out. Bring that thirst to Christ in prayer instead, and drink from his word before you drink from anything else. And when someone tells you their life is empty, do not lecture them. Tell them where the spring is, and that it costs nothing.

For worship. The One who sits on the throne, who spoke the first word of creation and will speak the last, uses his voice at the end of all things to say, I am making all things new. He is the Alpha, before the first star, and the Omega, after the last tear. And this God, who owes no one anything, holds out a cup at the end of history and gives it away. The spring of the water of life flows from his throne because his Son was thirsty on the cross, so that we would never thirst again. Blessed be the God who gives himself freely to all who thirst.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers will have this heritage, and I will be his God and he will be my son. But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, as for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who conquers will have this heritage, and I will be his God and he will be my son. But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, as for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death.”

The setting. God promised David that his son would be God’s son: I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son (2 Samuel 7:14). The New Testament applies this to Christ (Hebrews 1:5), and Paul applies it to all believers: I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me (2 Corinthians 6:18). The seven letters each ended with a promise to the one who conquers (chapters 2–3); here is the sum of them all.

The one who conquers will have this heritage. “Heritage” (klēronomēsei, will inherit). The last of the promises to the conqueror, and the reader should hear the whole series close. Seven times in chapters 2 and 3 something was promised to the one who conquers: the tree of life, escape from the second death, hidden manna and a white stone, authority over the nations and the morning star, white garments and a name confessed before the Father, a pillar in the temple, a seat on the throne. Here is the final one, and it is not a thing at all. The meek shall inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5). Believers are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17).

And I will be his God and he will be my son. “Son” (huios): an heir, with full rights. The most intimate relationship. That sentence was said in the Old Testament about one man’s heir: God said it to David about the son who would sit on his throne. It is the promise that made the royal line, and it was fulfilled in Christ. And here it is handed, without qualification, to anyone who conquers, which chapter 12 defined as anyone who holds on to Christ at cost: they conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony (12:11). Through Christ, the Son, believers become sons and daughters of God by adoption (Galatians 4:4–7). Which means the final reward of this book is not real estate. It is adoption. Everything else on the list, the tree, the crown, the stone, the throne, turns out to have been describing what belongs to a son in his father’s house.

But as for the cowardly. “Cowardly” (deilois, timid, fearful). Eight kinds of people, and the first will stop any honest reader: the cowardly. Not the murderers, not the idolaters. The cowardly, listed first, in a book written to people who had every reason to be frightened. Heading the list: those who, out of fear, deny Christ under persecution. The opposite of the one who conquers. Not the fearful who still trust Christ, but those whose fear leads them to abandon him.

Fear and cowardice. That has to be handled carefully, because it will land on the wrong person if it is not. The word does not mean a Christian who is afraid. If fear disqualified, the list would include Elijah under a broom tree, Peter in a courtyard, and every one of the apostles on the night of the arrest. Christ said, fear not, to John in the first chapter of this book precisely because John was on his face and terrified (1:17). What the word names, in this setting, is the person whose fear made the decision: who denied the name, took the mark, said the words about Caesar and went home safe, and never came back. Cowardice here is not an emotion; it is apostasy carried out for the sake of safety. So a believer who reads verse 8 and is frightened by it is, by that very reaction, showing that it is not describing him. And Peter, who denied Christ three times with oaths, was given breakfast on a beach and a commission (John 21).

The faithless. “Faithless” (apistois, unbelieving, unfaithful). Those who refuse to trust and obey Christ.

The detestable. “Detestable” (ebdelygmenois, polluted with abominations), linked with Babylon’s abominations (17:4).

As for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars. The sins of Babylon and the beast’s worshippers (9:21; 22:15). “All liars”: those who belong to the father of lies (John 8:44) and the false prophet. And the last item on the list closes a loop that has run through the whole book. The dragon is the deceiver of the whole world; the second beast deceives by signs; Babylon deceived the nations by her sorcery. And of the redeemed on Mount Zion John wrote, in their mouth no lie was found (14:5). Two companies, and one of the things that finally separates them is whether they belong to the truth.

Their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death. “Portion” (meros, share, part), as in 20:14–15. The heritage of the conqueror and the portion of the faithless stand side by side in two verses: an inheritance in the Father’s house, or a share in the lake. There is no third place.

What it does not mean. This list does not mean that anyone who has ever committed these sins is beyond salvation. Paul lists similar sins and then says, and such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). The list describes those who persist in these sins without repentance, refusing the free water of life (v. 6). Even a murderer or an idolater who comes thirsty to Christ will be given the water of life.

Does all liars mean that any lie damns, so that a Christian who has lied is lost? No. The list describes the settled character of those who belong to the lie and reject the truth (22:15), not believers who have sinned and repented. Every believer has lied; the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). The warning is for those who make falsehood their way of life, and a call to everyone to come to Christ.

Do I have to be a hero to be one who conquers? No. In Revelation conquering is not winning a battle by strength but holding on to Christ when it costs you, and the Lamb is the model: he conquered by being slain (5:5–6). The one who conquers is the ordinary believer who keeps trusting Christ through illness, mockery, temptation and loss, who falls and gets up, and who does not give Christ up. It is the persevering faith that God himself works in his people and keeps alive to the end (Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). If you are still clinging to him today, however weakly, you are among the conquerors, and the inheritance is yours.

In a sentence. The one who conquers will inherit all this, and I will be his God and he will be my son; but the cowards, the unbelieving, the vile, the murderers, the sexually immoral, those who practise magic, the idolaters and all liars will have their place in the lake that burns with fire and sulphur, which is the second death.

On a Tuesday. Take courage: God calls you his child and heir. And if any sin on this list still grips you, bring it to Christ today, who washes and makes new. Be especially watchful over the two sins that sound smallest: cowardice and lying. Where are you tempted this week to keep quiet about Christ to stay safe, or to shade the truth to look better? Say the true thing, kindly. Owning the name of Christ in a small moment is how conquerors are made.

For worship. The God who said to David, I will be a father to your son, has said it to every one of his people through his own Son. The heir of all things, who had every right to the inheritance, went to the cross so that rebels, cowards and liars could be washed and adopted and given his name. Peter, who lied and cursed by a charcoal fire, was restored by another charcoal fire, and the same mercy reaches us. The final reward is not a mansion but a Father. Abba, Father: blessed be the God who makes sons and daughters of the unworthy, and gives them all things with his Son.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 9–11: one of the seven bowl angels — the same rank, and almost the same words, as 17:1 — says Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb, and carries John to a great high mountain (17:3 was a wilderness). He promised a Bride and shows a city: the people are the place. It has the glory of God, radiant like jasper, clear as crystal — the description of the one on the throne at 4:3.

Verses 12–14: twelve gates, three on each side, bearing the names of the twelve tribes (cf. Num. 2; Ezek. 48:30–35); twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles (cf. Eph. 2:19–20). Verses 15–17: the city is measured with a golden rod — 12,000 stadia, about fourteen hundred miles, its length and width and height are equal — and its wall 144 cubits, twelve times twelve.

Verses 18–21: a wall of jasper and a city of gold like clear glass; twelve foundation stones named one by one, most of them from the high priest’s breastpiece (Ex. 28:17–21); twelve gates each made of a single pearl; and a street of gold like transparent glass.

Verse 22: And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb. Verses 23–25: no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God is its light and its lamp is the Lamb (cf. Isa. 60:19); the nations walk by that light and the kings bring their glory in; the gates never shut, and there is no night. Verses 26–27: they will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations — and nothing unclean, detestable or false enters, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Bride, the City

The Bride is shown as a city coming down from God, bearing the names of the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles. It is a cube — the Most Holy Place enlarged — with no temple, for its temple is God and the Lamb; no sun, for the Lamb is its lamp; gates that never shut; and only those written in the Lamb’s book inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What the high priest carried over his heart once a year is now the city’s foundation, and every gate is a pearl.

Now: Nobody will be nearer to God than anybody else, and there will be no night.

verseByVerse.quote: Then came one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues and spoke to me, saying, "Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb." And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God, having the glory of God, its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then came one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues and spoke to me, saying, “Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb.” And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God, having the glory of God, its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal.

The setting. In 17:1–3, one of the seven bowl angels said, come, I will show you the judgement of the great prostitute, and carried John in the Spirit into a wilderness. The parallel is exact and deliberate: two women, two cities, two destinies. Ezekiel was brought in visions of God to a very high mountain, on which was a structure like a city (Ezekiel 40:2). Isaiah 2:2 says the mountain of the LORD’s house shall be lifted up above the hills. Moses saw the promised land from a mountain (Deuteronomy 34:1–4). Satan showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world from a very high mountain (Matthew 4:8).

Then came one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues. John records the angel’s job description at length, and the reason is that he wants the reader to make a connection. At 17:1 it was one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls who said, Come, I will show you the judgement of the great prostitute. The same rank, the same opening word, and a different woman. Those who carried out judgement now reveal glory. The hands that poured out the bowls of wrath are the hands that draw back the curtain on the bride.

And spoke to me, saying, Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb. “Bride” (nymphē) and “wife” (gynaika). The marriage of 19:7 has happened. The church is now the Lamb’s wife. Every wedding in the Bible, from Adam waking to find Eve, to the wedding at Cana where the wine ran out, has been a rehearsal for this.

And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain. The fourth “in the Spirit” of the book (1:10; 4:2; 17:3). And the locations answer each other. To see the prostitute, John was carried into a wilderness (17:3). To see the Bride, he is carried to a great, high mountain, the place of revelation and of God’s dwelling, which is where Ezekiel was taken to be shown a city (Ezekiel 40:2). One woman is seen in a desert; the other from a height. And there is a contrast with another mountain: the devil once took Jesus up a very high mountain to show him the kingdoms of the world and their glory. Jesus refused that glory, went to the cross instead, and here is what the Father gives him.

And showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God. He promised a Bride and produced a city, and John does not treat that as a change of subject. The city is the bride. The people are the place. That is the same identification the New Testament makes everywhere: the church is a building, a temple, a body, a household, a bride. And it is why the measurements that follow can be enormous without being absurd. And the direction is stated for the second time in nine verses: coming down out of heaven from God. It is not built up from the earth. Babylon began at a tower whose builders said, let us build ourselves a city and make a name for ourselves (Genesis 11:4). Every proud human city since has been that project. This one is lowered into place, finished, by Someone else.

Having the glory of God. “Glory” (doxan). The first thing said about the city is not its size or its gates. It is that it has the glory of God: the weight of God’s presence, the shekinah glory that filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter, and the temple so that the priests could not stand to minister (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:11; Ezekiel 43:2–5). God’s presence makes the city what it is. The thing that had to be curtained off is now the city’s ordinary lighting.

Its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal. “Radiance” (phōstēr, light, brilliance). “Jasper”: as in 4:3, where it describes the appearance of the one seated on the throne. The city looks like him. “Clear as crystal”: pure, transparent, nothing hidden. A bride wearing her husband’s likeness is not a bad definition of what the church is finally for, and it is what Paul meant by being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18).

What it does not mean. The bride is not a separate entity from the city, or from the believers who make it up. All the descriptions of the city describe the glorified people of God, and the place where they live with him.

How can the church I know be this bride? The church you know is quarrelsome, slow, sometimes hypocritical, and you are part of the problem. Christ knows that better than you do, and he loves her anyway. He gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, and present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). The bride is not beautiful because she made herself so; she shines with the glory of God. What you see now is the bride on the way to the wedding, dusty from the road. Do not despise what Christ is making beautiful. Stay in her, serve her, and pray for her.

In a sentence. Then one of the seven angels who had held the seven bowls filled with the seven last plagues came and said to me, Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb; and he carried me away in the Spirit to a huge, high mountain and showed me the holy city, Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, shining with God’s glory, its brilliance like a rare jewel, like jasper, as clear as crystal.

On a Tuesday. Love the church now as Christ does. Before you criticise your congregation this week, pray for it by name: the elders, the struggling family, the difficult member. Then do one quiet thing to serve it. And ask which woman you are dressing for. Babylon offers her adornment now, at a price; the bride receives hers from her husband, at his cost. Every choice of what to love and what to want is a choice of which city you belong to.

For worship. The church, which now seems weak and flawed, will shine with the glory of God. The bride of the Lamb, gathered from the slums and the palaces of every age, who was so often unfaithful and so often forgiven, is shown at last wearing the likeness of the One on the throne. He refused the glory of the world’s kingdoms on the high mountain, and went to the cross for her; now from a great, high mountain the angel shows the glory the Father has given him: a people radiant with God. Glory to the Lamb, who has made his bride beautiful.

verseByVerse.quote: It had a great, high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed— on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates. And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It had a great, high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed—on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates. And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.

The setting. Ezekiel 48:30–35 describes the restored Jerusalem with twelve gates, three on each side, named after the twelve tribes. Israel camped around the tabernacle in the wilderness, three tribes on each side (Numbers 2). Paul says the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20).

It had a great, high wall. “Wall” (teichos). Start with the wall, because it is named first and it is the strangest thing here. A wall in the ancient world had one purpose: to keep an army out. This city has no army to fear. The last enemy was dealt with a chapter ago and thrown into the lake of fire (20:10, 14), and in a few verses John will say the gates are never shut anyway (v. 25). So what is a wall doing in the new creation? It is not there out of fear. It is there because a wall says that this place has an inside, and verse 27 will state the boundary plainly: nothing unclean will ever enter it. The wall marks the city as safe and distinct.

A good thing that cannot be spoiled. Measure that against everything you have ever loved. Every good thing you have known could be got at: the marriage, the friendship, the church, the health, the work of a lifetime. Something always found a way in and spoiled it, and usually from the inside. Here at last is a good thing with a boundary that holds. The wall is not the anxiety of a city under siege. It is the settled fact of a city that will never be spoiled again.

With twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels. “Gates” (pylōnas). The first time angels are posted anywhere in the Bible, they are cherubim outside a garden with a flaming sword, and their work is to keep people out (Genesis 3:24). Here twelve of them stand at twelve gates that never close (v. 25). Nothing about the posting has changed except what it is for. The sentries are still at their stations, and there is nothing left for them to do but watch the nations walk in.

And on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed. Old Testament Israel is part of the city. God’s promises to Israel are fulfilled. Twelve gates, three on each side, is the layout of the camp of Israel in the wilderness, where three tribes camped on each side of the tabernacle (Numbers 2), and it is the plan of Ezekiel’s city, which ends with twelve gates named for the twelve tribes (Ezekiel 48:30–35). Every believer who enters the city enters through a gate with an Israelite name over it, because salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22).

On the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates. Access from every direction. People will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God (Luke 13:29). And the gates face all four directions, which is the point of listing them. A city with gates on one side has a preferred approach and a back door. This one can be entered from anywhere: from the east where the exiles went, from the north where the invasions came, from the south where Egypt was, from the west where Rome was. Nobody arrives at the wrong side.

And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. “Foundations” (themelious). The apostles, who laid the foundation of the church by their witness to Christ. Twelve tribes on the gates and twelve apostles in the foundations: Israel and the church, built into one structure, and neither of them is an extension bolted on to the other. Together they form one city, the one people of God across both covenants. This is the clearest confirmation that the twenty-four elders (4:4) represent Israel and the church together. Paul said the same thing without the architecture: the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:19–20).

Names in the foundations. There is something quietly astonishing about names in foundations. Twelve men are named in the stonework of the eternal city, and every reader knows what those twelve were like: fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot, a man who denied Christ with oaths, and a man who would not believe the resurrection without putting his hand in the wound. Their names are cut into the foundations of the new creation. Set that beside the city they are being contrasted with. Babylon’s great ones were her merchants (18:23). This city’s great ones are twelve provincial nobodies, most of whom suffered and many of whom died for saying that a crucified man had come back. Grace builds with unlikely stones.

What it does not mean. Israel’s names on the gates and the apostles’ names on the foundations do not mean there are two peoples of God, one Jewish and one Christian, with different destinies. There is one city, one bride, one people, built on Christ.

Then does God still have a purpose for the Jewish people? Christians differ on the details, and the question deserves care. Many Reformed readers, from the Puritans onward, have understood Romans 11:25–29 to promise a future turning of many Jews to Christ before the end, because the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable; others read all Israel there as the whole elect people of God, Jew and Gentile. Both agree with this chapter: whatever God does for Israel, he does through faith in Jesus the Messiah, and into the one city. So pray for Jewish people to know their Messiah, honour the people through whom the Scriptures and the Saviour came, and reject every form of contempt for them.

In a sentence. It had a massive, high wall with twelve gates, with twelve angels at the gates, and the names of the twelve tribes of Israel were written on the gates, three gates on the east, three on the north, three on the south and three on the west; the city wall had twelve foundation stones, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.

On a Tuesday. You belong to a city built on the apostles’ witness. So build your life on the same foundation: their teaching, written in the New Testament, is the ground on which the church stands, and nothing newer replaces it. Read the apostles this week as men who were there. And look around your church at the people who seem least impressive. If God put a tax collector and a denier into his foundations, he can do great things with them, and with you.

For worship. Thank God for the whole people of God through history, Israel and the church, one city with one Lord. The God who wrote the names of Jacob’s sons over his gates and the names of Galilean fishermen into his foundations does not choose the impressive; he makes the chosen glorious. The cherubim who once barred the way to the tree of life now stand at gates that never close, because the Lamb has opened the way by his blood. From east and west, north and south, the redeemed walk in, and no one arrives at the wrong side. Blessed be Christ, the cornerstone, on whom the whole city rests.

verseByVerse.quote: And the one who spoke with me had a measuring rod of gold to measure the city and its gates and walls. The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width. And he measured the city with his rod, 12,000 stadia. Its length and width and height are equal. He also measured its wall, 144 cubits by human measurement, which is also an angel's measurement.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the one who spoke with me had a measuring rod of gold to measure the city and its gates and walls. The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width. And he measured the city with his rod, 12,000 stadia. Its length and width and height are equal. He also measured its wall, 144 cubits by human measurement, which is also an angel’s measurement.

The setting. The Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple was a perfect cube, twenty cubits long, wide and high, overlaid with pure gold (1 Kings 6:20). Ezekiel saw an angel measuring the new temple and city (Ezekiel 40–48). A stadion was about 185 metres (607 feet), so 12,000 stadia is about 2,220 kilometres (1,380 miles), roughly the distance from London to Athens, or the width of the known Greek world. A cubit was about 45 centimetres (18 inches), so 144 cubits is about 65 metres (216 feet).

And the one who spoke with me had a measuring rod of gold to measure the city and its gates and walls. Measuring, in this book, means claiming and protecting. John was given a rod at 11:1 and told to measure the temple, the altar and the worshippers, and expressly not the outer court, which was given over to be trampled. The measuring there was partial, and it was a mercy. This one is total: the city, its gates and its walls, all of it, with a rod of gold, fitting for a golden city. Measuring shows that the city is complete, secure and belongs to God.

The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width. “Foursquare” (tetragōnos, square). Perfect, complete. Nothing is lopsided, unfinished or left over.

And he measured the city with his rod, 12,000 stadia. Its length and width and height are equal. Two things, and both are enormous. The size first. Twelve thousand stadia, about 2,220 kilometres, is a city the width of the Mediterranean world, and it is that in every direction, including up. Nobody is meant to picture this successfully. What the figure does is answer a fear that few Christians like to admit: whether there will be room. 12,000 is 12 × 1,000: the people of God (twelve) in fullness (a thousand). The size, vast beyond imagining, shows there is room for the great multitude no one can count. Then the shape, and this is the detail everything in the chapter has been building toward. Its length and width and height are equal. The city is a perfect cube.

There is one cube in the Bible. In Solomon’s temple, the inner sanctuary, the Most Holy Place, was twenty cubits long, twenty wide and twenty high (1 Kings 6:20). It was the place where the ark stood behind the veil, which one man entered once a year with blood, having washed, and did not linger in. The new Jerusalem is that room, expanded to the size of a continent, with everybody living inside it. The whole city is the Most Holy Place: God’s presence fills it all, and all God’s people dwell where once only the high priest could enter once a year. That is the single most important fact about the city, and it explains verse 22 in advance: there is no temple in the city because the city is the temple, and there is no veil because there is nothing left to keep anyone out.

He also measured its wall, 144 cubits by human measurement, which is also an angel’s measurement. 144 is 12 × 12, the number of God’s people, as in the 144,000 (7:4). “By human measurement, which is also an angel’s measurement”: the angel uses ordinary units, but their meaning is symbolic. John is telling the reader that the figures are not given in some other currency that would come out differently in heaven. And the proportions are deliberately impossible. A wall of about 65 metres around a city over two thousand kilometres high would not keep anything out and could not be seen from most of the city. Which is the point. The wall, compared with the city, is small: protection is no longer needed. It is a boundary, marking what is inside as holy, and its gates never close.

What it does not mean. The dimensions are not a blueprint for a literal cube-shaped city 2,220 kilometres high. They are symbols of perfection, completeness and the holiness of God’s presence, drawn from the Most Holy Place and from the numbers of God’s people.

If the numbers are symbols, is the new creation real? Yes, entirely. Symbols in Scripture are not a way of saying less than the truth but more than plain words can carry. The cube tells you something no floor plan could: that every one of God’s people will live in the immediate presence of God, as near as the high priest ever was, and nearer. The new creation is as real as the risen body of Jesus, which could be touched and ate fish (Luke 24:39–43). What the symbols do is stop us shrinking it to the size of our imagination. Whatever it is like, it is not less than this.

In a sentence. The angel who talked with me had a gold measuring rod to measure the city, its gates and its wall; the city was laid out as a square, as long as it was wide; he measured the city with the rod, and it was twelve thousand stadia, about 2,200 kilometres, in length, width and height alike; he measured its wall too, and it was 144 cubits thick, by the human measure the angel was using.

On a Tuesday. Worship now as one who will one day dwell in the Most Holy Place. When you pray, you are not shouting through a closed door; through Christ you already have access to the Father (Hebrews 10:19–22). Come in boldly this week, and come often. And if you have feared that there will be no room for you, because of your past, your weakness or your failures, look at the size of the city. God did not build it small.

For worship. In the new creation, all God’s people will live in the Most Holy Place, in his presence. The room that only one man could enter, once a year, trembling, with blood, has become a city the size of the world, full of people who walk in it every day without fear. The veil was torn from top to bottom when the true High Priest offered himself, and the golden rod measures a city in which there is no outer court and no one left outside who belongs within. Blessed be the Lamb, whose blood has opened the holiest place to the whole family of God.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes give 12,000 stadia as about 1,380 miles; 144 cubits is about 216 feet. The city is a perfect cube, like the Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple.

verseByVerse.quote: The wall was built of jasper, while the city was pure gold, like clear glass. The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. The first was jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald, the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst. And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each of the gates made of a single pearl, and the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wall was built of jasper, while the city was pure gold, like clear glass. The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. The first was jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald, the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst. And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each of the gates made of a single pearl, and the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.

The setting. The high priest’s breastplate held twelve precious stones, each engraved with the name of one of the tribes of Israel, worn over his heart when he entered God’s presence (Exodus 28:15–21, 29). Isaiah 54:11–12 promises Jerusalem foundations of sapphires, battlements of agate, gates of carbuncles and walls of precious stones. The king of Tyre, in Eden, was covered with every precious stone (Ezekiel 28:13). The prostitute Babylon was adorned with gold, jewels and pearls (17:4).

The wall was built of jasper. Jasper: the appearance of God (4:3). The wall reflects God’s glory.

While the city was pure gold, like clear glass. “Pure gold” (chrysion katharon), like the gold-covered Most Holy Place (1 Kings 6:20). Gold that light goes through. It is not a description of a material anybody has ever handled, and John says something similar about the street. Gold so pure it is transparent, a kind of gold unknown on earth: purity and glory together. Whatever this city is made of, its most precious substance has stopped being opaque. Nothing in it casts a shadow or hides what is behind it.

The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. Twelve stones on twelve foundations, as twelve stones on the high priest’s breastplate. The high priest of Israel wore a breastpiece set with twelve stones in four rows, one for each tribe, and he bore the names of the sons of Israel on his heart when he went into the Holy Place, as a memorial before the LORD (Exodus 28:29). Most of John’s stones correspond, as far as ancient names can be matched, to those on the breastplate, and several of the names differ only because the Greek translation of the Old Testament rendered them differently. So the foundations of the city are the high priest’s breastpiece, laid out flat and built into the ground. What one man carried over his heart into the holy place is now the foundation everybody walks on. The whole people of God, precious to him, now in his presence for ever.

The first was jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald, the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst. Twelve stones, listed one by one, with their positions numbered. John takes a verse and a half to do it, and the slowness is the effect. This is a man walking along a wall naming colours. A rainbow of colour: clear, blue, green, red, golden, purple. The exact identity of ancient gem names is uncertain. The point is overwhelming beauty and variety, reflecting God’s glory in many colours, like the many nations of the redeemed. And jasper and carnelian, the first and sixth stones here, are the two John used of the one seated on the throne (4:3).

And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each of the gates made of a single pearl. Pearls were among the most valuable things in the ancient world (Matthew 13:45–46). Gates made of a single pearl are beyond imagination; this is the source of the phrase pearly gates. And a pearl is the one precious thing in the ancient world that is not mined or cut. It is made by an oyster, slowly, in response to an injury: a grain of grit that could not be expelled, covered over layer by layer for years until the wound is the treasure. Jesus told a parable about a merchant in search of fine pearls who found one of great value and sold all that he had to buy it. The gates into the eternal city are pearls, every one a single stone, and every one began with a wound. No one enters this city except through a wound: the wounds of the Lamb.

And the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass. “Street” (plateia, main street, broad way). The most valuable substance the ancient world knew, used for the surface people walk on. Babylon’s cargo list began with gold and silver and jewels and pearls (18:12), and merchants wept when they could no longer sell it. Here the same materials are paving. That is not a statement that wealth is unimportant. It is a statement about proportion. Everything the world killed for turns out, in the only city that lasts, to be pavement, and a reader who has spent a lifetime arranging his affairs around such things is being shown what they are for.

What it does not mean. The gold and jewels do not mean heaven is about wealth. They are symbols of beauty, glory, permanence and preciousness. What Babylon used to seduce and adorn herself is, in God’s city, given freely as the setting for his people’s life with him. The greatest treasure in the city is God himself (22:4).

Does this mean God wants me rich now? No. This is the opposite of a prosperity gospel. The gold is in the street, under feet, precisely so that no one in the city will ever want it again. Jesus warned that a man’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions (Luke 12:15), and Paul that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:10). God gives some of his people wealth to steward, and many of his people poverty to bear, and he loves both the same. What this verse promises is that the poorest believer will one day walk on what the richest unbeliever spent his life chasing.

In a sentence. The wall was made of jasper, and the city of pure gold, as clear as glass; the foundation stones of the city wall were decorated with every kind of precious stone: the first jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald, the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth and the twelfth amethyst; the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each gate made from a single pearl, and the main street of the city was pure gold, transparent as glass.

On a Tuesday. Hold the things of this world loosely. In God’s city, gold is pavement. Set your heart on the treasure that lasts. Look at one purchase you are planning, or one financial worry that keeps you awake, and ask how it looks from a street paved with gold. Then give something away this week, generously and quietly, as a person who knows where real wealth is stored (Matthew 6:19–21).

For worship. The great High Priest carries the names of his people on his heart, not on a breastpiece of stones but in the wounds of his hands and side, and he has built them into the foundations of a city that shines with every colour of God’s glory. The gates are pearls, and every pearl began with a wound, and every one of the redeemed enters through his. Gold that the world fought over lies in the street, clear as glass, and the only treasure anyone in the city looks at is the face of God. Blessed be the Lord, the true treasure of his people, who makes the riches of the world into the pavement of his house.
verseByVerse.note: The twelve jewels recall the stones on the high priest’s breastpiece, engraved with the names of the tribes.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.

The setting. For Israel, the temple was the centre of life: the place where God dwelt and where sacrifices were offered. Ezekiel’s vision of the restored city centred on a new temple (Ezekiel 40–48). Jesus told the Samaritan woman that the hour was coming when true worshippers would worship the Father in spirit and truth, not on a particular mountain (John 4:21–24). He called his own body the temple (John 2:19–21). The temple in Jerusalem had been destroyed by the Romans in AD 70, and many Jews hoped it would be rebuilt.

And I saw no temple in the city. “Temple” (naon, sanctuary). One sentence that overturns the whole religious history of the world. A startling statement for a Jewish reader: everyone would expect the new Jerusalem to have a glorious temple, and Ezekiel spent nine chapters on one. But there is none. Consider what a temple is. Every civilisation has built them, and every one of them answers the same problem: God is holy and people are not, so there must be a designated place, a mediating class, a set of rules for approach, and a barrier between the god and the worshipper. Israel’s was the most carefully regulated of them all. There was a court the nations could enter, a court beyond that for Israel, a court beyond that for men, a court beyond that for priests, and behind a curtain a room one man entered once a year with blood in his hands.

For its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb. There is no temple, not because worship has ended, but because the arrangement a temple exists to manage has ended. A temple was needed because God’s presence was limited to one place, and sin kept people at a distance. The problem a temple solves, how sinful people can be near a holy God without being destroyed, has been solved somewhere else, by Someone, and the verse names him. Now God’s presence fills the whole city, and nothing separates his people from him. The temple was always a pointer to this: God himself living with his people. God and the Lamb together are the temple: the Son shares the Father’s presence and glory.

There is no temple because there is a Lamb. The last two words are the answer. When Jesus died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51): from the top, by Someone reaching down. This verse is that tearing carried to its conclusion. He is not merely the priest and not merely the sacrifice. He is the building. Which is also why the city is a cube. The Most Holy Place was the one room in the world where God’s presence was unveiled, and the whole city is now that room. Everybody lives inside the holy of holies. There is no outer court, no restricted section, no closer and further; nobody is nearer to God than anybody else, and nobody is waiting outside for a priest to come back and tell him it went well.

What it does not mean. No temple does not mean no worship. The whole city is a temple, and all of life is worship. It also confirms that there will be no rebuilt temple with renewed sacrifices in God’s final plan; Christ’s sacrifice has fulfilled them all.

Then do church buildings and Sunday worship matter now? Yes, but not as temples. A church building is a meeting place, not a holy house where God lives and elsewhere he does not; the temple of God now is his people (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22), and the Lord meets them wherever two or three gather in his name (Matthew 18:20). Gathering on the Lord’s Day still matters greatly, because God commands it (Hebrews 10:24–25) and because it is a rehearsal for the city: his people together before his face. But no place, priest or ritual stands between you and God. Through Christ you may draw near anywhere, at any hour, and on that day there will be nowhere that is not his presence.

Every Christian who has ever felt it. Every Christian who has ever felt that God is available in certain places and at certain times, that some people have better access, that the holy is somewhere he visits rather than somewhere he lives: this verse is the end of all of it. The final condition of the redeemed is not going to a holy place. It is living inside one, with the One who made it standing in the middle.

In a sentence. I did not see any temple in the city, because its temple is the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb.

On a Tuesday. Through Christ, you can come into God’s presence now, anywhere: at the kitchen sink, in the car, on the hospital ward, in the office. Practise it this week. Turn to him in the middle of an ordinary task and speak to him, with no ceremony and no fear. And refuse the thought that some Christians are closer to God by rank or office. Pastors and elders serve; they do not stand between you and God. The way is open to every believer by the blood of Jesus.

For worship. For centuries the people of God stood at a distance while one man went in behind the curtain. Then the Lamb of God died outside the city, and the curtain tore from top to bottom, and the way into the holiest was opened for ever. In the city to come there is no temple, because God himself is there, and the Lamb is there, and his people live in the light of his face without a veil. The temple was always him. Blessed be the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb, the temple, the priest and the sacrifice, in whose presence we shall dwell for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb. By its light will the nations walk, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it, and its gates will never be shut by day—and there will be no night there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb. By its light will the nations walk, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it, and its gates will never be shut by day—and there will be no night there.

The setting. Isaiah 60:1–3, 11, 19–20 promises Jerusalem: arise, shine, for your light has come; nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising; your gates shall be open continually, day and night they shall not be shut; the sun shall be no more your light by day, but the LORD will be your everlasting light. Jesus said, I am the light of the world (John 8:12). In ancient cities, gates were shut at night for protection.

And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it. The second thing missing, after the temple: the sun. Genesis 1 gives two great lights on the fourth day, and Isaiah promised a day when the sun would no longer be the light by day, nor the moon give brightness, but the LORD would be an everlasting light (Isaiah 60:19). Not that the sun and moon no longer exist, but that they are not needed. A greater light outshines them. A lamp is not a criticism of the sun; it is simply irrelevant at noon. The sun and moon have been doing a job on loan for the whole of history, and the owner has arrived.

For the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb. “Glory” (doxa). “Lamp” (lychnos). The word is a household lamp, the small clay dish with a wick that lit a single room after dark. God’s glory is the light, and the Lamb is the lamp through which it shines. That is precisely what he has been since the first chapter, where his face was like the sun shining in full strength (1:16), and precisely what he said of himself: I am the light of the world. We see the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). No one in the city will ever see God’s glory except through the Lamb; and no one will ever need to see it any other way.

By its light will the nations walk. “Nations” (ethnē). The redeemed from every nation, living in God’s light. Their national and cultural diversity is preserved in the new creation. This is Isaiah 60 again: nations shall come to your light. Babel scattered the nations in confusion; the Lamb gathers them, not into one language and one culture, but into one light.

And the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it. “Kings of the earth”: the same phrase used of those who committed immorality with Babylon (17:2; 18:9). It is startling in a book that has spent nineteen chapters on the kings of the earth making war on the Lamb. What John is describing is not an amnesty for Babylon but the redemption of the nations as nations. Some kings, who once rebelled, are redeemed. The good things of human culture, its achievements, beauty and treasures, cleansed of sin, are brought into the new creation.

What is their glory? The text does not list it, and guessing is a poor substitute for reading. But the phrase does imply that what the peoples of the earth have made and been is not simply erased. Something is carried in. That is a real word to anyone who has wondered whether ordinary human work has any future: whether the making of music, the building of things, the raising of crops and children and languages and cities is all going into a fire. This verse says the gates are open, and something is being brought in through them.

And its gates will never be shut by day, and there will be no night there. Gates open because there is no danger. No night, because God is the light. Perfect safety and perfect welcome. A gate is shut for one reason. Every walled city in the ancient world closed its gates at sundown, and that was the moment the day’s safety ended: after dark, whatever was outside stayed outside, and anybody who had not got home was not getting home. This city has gates that never shut, and John gives the reason: there will be no night there. The two clauses are one thought. The gates stay open because the hour at which a gate is shut never comes. Anyone who has lain awake at three in the morning knows what is being taken away. Night in Scripture is not simply darkness; it is when the thief comes, when the enemy moves, when a person is alone with what he has done, when the sick get worse and the frightened get more frightened. There is none of it, ever again.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “the nations of them which are saved shall walk in the light of it”, adding “of them which are saved”. The best manuscripts simply read “the nations”. The addition explains correctly who the nations are.

Where Christians differ: does this mean the nations outside are finally saved? Some read the nations and kings coming into the city as unbelievers being saved after the final judgement, so that all will eventually enter. Verdict: the nations here are the redeemed nations, the great multitude from every nation (7:9), who come into the city because their names are written in the Lamb’s book (v. 27). The lake of fire is final (20:15; 21:8), and outside the city are those who practise wickedness (22:15). The passage shows that the redeemed include people from every nation, and that the best of human culture is brought in, purified. It does not teach a second chance after death.

What it does not mean. No night does not mean no rest. It means no darkness, no danger, no fear, no evil.

Will there still be different nations and cultures? It seems so. John sees nations walking by the light, and earlier a multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language (7:9). The new creation is not a grey sameness in which every trace of who we were is dissolved. Just as each believer will be himself, made perfect, so the peoples of the earth seem to be there as themselves, cleansed of pride and hostility, every tongue confessing that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:11). So love believers whose culture is not yours. You will be living with them for ever, and their way of praising the Lamb will be part of the glory.

Will we be busy, or bored? Neither tired nor bored. Scripture pictures the age to come not as endless idleness but as reigning, serving and worshipping (22:3, 5), with bodies that do not wear out and hearts that do not drift. Boredom is the soul running out of interest, and in the presence of an infinite God that can never happen; there will always be more of him to know and enjoy. If the thought of worship for ever sounds dull, that is because our worship now is so thin. Ask God this week to give you a taste of it, and read Revelation 4–5 aloud.

In a sentence. The city does not need the sun or the moon to shine on it, because the glory of God gives it light, and the Lamb is its lamp; the nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their splendour into it; its gates will never be shut during the day, and there will be no night there.

On a Tuesday. The good work you do in your culture, art, science and service, done for God’s glory, is not wasted. Its glory, purified, may yet be brought into the city. So do this week’s ordinary work well, the spreadsheet, the lesson plan, the meal, the repair, as unto the Lord (Colossians 3:23). And when night comes, literally or in your soul, the sleepless hour, the dark diagnosis, remember that night has an end, and the city is coming where the Lamb is the lamp and the gates are never shut.

For worship. The sun was lit on the fourth day, and it has been holding the light on loan ever since. In the city to come, the owner of the light is there himself, and the glory of God shines through the Lamb like a flame through a lamp, and no shadow falls anywhere. The Light of the world, who was put out on a cross at noon while darkness covered the land, shines for ever over the nations he redeemed. The kings who once made war on him walk in carrying gifts, and the gates stand open at what would have been midnight. Glory to the Lamb, the lamp of the city, in whose light we shall see light.

verseByVerse.quote: They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations. But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb's book of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations. But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.

The setting. Isaiah 52:1 says that the uncircumcised and the unclean shall no more come into Jerusalem. Isaiah 60:5, 11 says the wealth of the nations shall come to Zion. Haggai 2:7 says the treasures of all nations shall come in and God will fill his house with glory.

They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations. “Glory” (doxan) and “honor” (timēn), as in verse 24. The two verses have to be held together, because each guards the other. Verse 26 is the widest sentence in the chapter: the glory and the honour of the nations, not of one nation, and not of the church only. All that is good and beautiful in the world’s peoples is gathered into God’s city. The multitude of chapter 7 came from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, and they do not arrive empty-handed.

But nothing unclean will ever enter it. “Unclean” (koinon, common, defiled, profane). The city is wholly holy. Nothing that defiles can enter. And verse 27 immediately shuts the door on any sentimentality about verse 26. The gates are always open, and they are not unguarded. This is not a city where everything is welcome; it is a city where everything that is welcome has been made clean. Unclean is the ceremonial word, what could not come into the sanctuary, and it fits a city that is all sanctuary.

Nor anyone who does what is detestable or false. “Detestable” (bdelygma, abomination, especially idolatry) and “false” (pseudos, lie). The sins of Babylon and the beast. Detestable is the word used all through the Old Testament of idolatry, and it was written on the prostitute’s forehead in 17:5. False closes the loop one final time: the dragon deceived, the false prophet deceived, Babylon deceived, and the redeemed are the ones in whose mouth no lie was found (14:5).

But only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life. Look at how the sentence actually ends, because the criterion is not a moral audit. The one qualification for entry: belonging to the Lamb. Not good works, not nationality, not religious heritage, but the Lamb’s choice and the Lamb’s blood. Those whose names were written before the foundation of the world (13:8; 17:8). That is the last mention of the book in Revelation, and it lands exactly where it did at the great white throne (20:12, 15): not on what a person achieved but on whether his name is in a register belonging to a Lamb who was slain.

How the unclean become clean. The two halves of these verses are not in tension at all. Nothing unclean enters, and the whole book has been showing how the unclean become clean, in the most impossible image it could find: they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14).
