Nobody walks in on his own record. Everybody who walks in has had something done to him first.

What it does not mean. The exclusion of the unclean does not mean that sinners can never enter. All who enter were once unclean, and were washed in the Lamb’s blood (7:14; 22:14). The city is closed to sin, not to sinners who have been cleansed.

Will I still sin there? No. The struggle every believer knows, wanting to do right and finding sin still close at hand (Romans 7:21), will be over. Those who enter are not only forgiven but made perfect in holiness (Hebrews 12:23), and when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Nothing unclean will ever enter, and that includes the remnants of sin in you. This is one of the sweetest promises in the chapter for a tired Christian: not only no more sorrow, but no more sinning. You will love God as you have always wanted to, without anything dragging you back.

How can I be sure my name is written? Not by searching for it in a secret register, but by looking to the Lamb whose book it is. The names written there are the names of those who trust him, and Jesus said, whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). If you are resting on Christ alone, and not on your record, you may be sure. Assurance grows as you see the Spirit’s fruit in you, as you walk in obedience, and as the Spirit bears witness with your spirit that you are a child of God (Romans 8:16). If you are not sure, do not try harder to feel sure. Come to him again.

In a sentence. The glory and honour of the nations will be brought into it; but nothing impure will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is shameful or deceitful, only those whose names are written in the Lamb’s book of life.

On a Tuesday. If your name is written in the Lamb’s book, the gates of pearl are open to you. Live clean in the light of that day. Is there anything you are doing in secret that would not belong inside that city? Put it out of your life this week; confess it, and ask for help from a trusted brother or sister if you need it. Not to earn your entry, which the Lamb has already paid for, but because you are going to live in a city of light, and you may as well start getting used to it.

For worship. So the chapter closes with the door open and the qualification stated. A city two thousand kilometres high, made of the Most Holy Place, with the glory of God for daylight and the Lamb for a lamp, its foundations set with the stones a high priest wore over his heart and its gates each made from a single pearl that began as a wound; and the gates never close, and the only people inside are the ones whose names were written in a book before the world was made. God himself is with them. There is no temple, because he is there. There is no sun, because he is there. There is no night, because he is there. And there are no tears, because he has come over and attended to their faces with his own hand. To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood be glory for ever.

21.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more.<sup>2</sup>And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.<sup>3</sup>And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.<sup>4</sup>He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away.”<sup>5</sup>And he who was seated on the throne said, “Behold, I am making all things new.” Also he said, “Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true.”<sup>6</sup>And he said to me, “It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment.<sup>7</sup>The one who conquers will have this heritage, and I will be his God and he will be my son.<sup>8</sup>But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, as for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death.”<sup>9</sup>Then came one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues and spoke to me, saying, “Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb.”<sup>10</sup>And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God,<sup>11</sup>having the glory of God, its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal.<sup>12</sup>It had a great, high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed—<sup>13</sup>on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates.<sup>14</sup>And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.<sup>15</sup>And the one who spoke with me had a measuring rod of gold to measure the city and its gates and walls.<sup>16</sup>The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width. And he measured the city with his rod, 12,000 stadia. Its length and width and height are equal.<sup>17</sup>He also measured its wall, 144 cubits by human measurement, which is also an angel’s measurement.<sup>18</sup>The wall was built of jasper, while the city was pure gold, like clear glass.<sup>19</sup>The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. The first was jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald,<sup>20</sup>the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst.<sup>21</sup>And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each of the gates made of a single pearl, and the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.<sup>22</sup>And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.<sup>23</sup>And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb.<sup>24</sup>By its light will the nations walk, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it,<sup>25</sup>and its gates will never be shut by day—and there will be no night there.<sup>26</sup>They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations.<sup>27</sup>But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.

22.title: Come, Lord Jesus: The River, the Tree, and the Final Invitation
22.overview:
The final chapter of Revelation — and of the entire Bible — has the quality of a great symphony resolving into its final chord. Everything that has been promised, everything that has been anticipated, every thread of the biblical story, gathers here and arrives. The river of the water of life. The tree of life with twelve kinds of fruit. The servants of God seeing his face. His name on their foreheads. No more night. And then, three times: ‘I am coming soon.’ And the great response of the church across all the ages: ‘Come, Lord Jesus.’

The chapter is framed by the river and tree (vv. 1–5) and the final testimony and invitation (vv. 6–21). The garden returns — but infinitely elevated. Eden had a river flowing from it (Genesis 2:10); the new Jerusalem has a river flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. Eden had the tree of life (Genesis 2:9); the new Jerusalem has the tree of life bearing twelve kinds of fruit, one each month, its leaves for the healing of the nations. What was lost in the garden is restored in the city, but the city is greater than the garden: the tree is no longer guarded by cherubim with flaming swords (Genesis 3:24) — it stands in the middle of the street, its fruit available to all.

The closing testimony of the book weaves together three voices: the angel confirming the truth of what has been shown, Jesus speaking in the first person (‘I, Jesus, have sent my angel...’; ‘I am coming soon’), and the Spirit and Bride together issuing the great invitation: ‘Come.’ The book ends not with explanation but with longing — the longing of the church for her Lord, the longing of the Lord for his people, the longing of the Spirit for the consummation of all things. This is the last word of the Bible, and it is the word the whole church has been praying for two thousand years: Come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The River and the Tree of Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb down the middle of the street; and on either side of it the tree of life, bearing twelve crops a year, and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations (cf. Ezek. 47:1–12). The Bible has been away from a river and a tree since Genesis 3, where cherubim with a flaming sword were set to guard the way to the tree of life (Gen. 2:9–10; 3:24). The promise made to Ephesus in the first letter (2:7) is being kept.

Verse 3: No longer will there be anything accursed — the sentence of Genesis 3:17–19 lifted — but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. Verse 4: They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. Verse 5: no night, no need of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The River and the Tree

The river of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life stands open with fruit every month and leaves for the healing of the nations. The curse is gone, and his servants will see his face.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The way to the tree, guarded since Eden, stands open in the middle of the street.

Now: Heaven is not first a place but a face — seen at last, and lived through.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the middle of the street of the city; also, on either side of the river, the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit each month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the middle of the street of the city; also, on either side of the river, the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit each month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.

Meaning first. Revelation 22 finishes the vision of the new creation and closes the book, and the whole Bible. The angel shows John the river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and the Lamb, and the tree of life on both banks, bearing fruit every month, with leaves for the healing of the nations (vv. 1–2). There is no more curse; God’s servants will worship him, see his face, bear his name, live in his light and reign for ever (vv. 3–5). Then the epilogue: the angel assures John that these words are trustworthy and true, and Christ says, I am coming soon; blessed is the one who keeps the words of this book (vv. 6–7). John falls to worship the angel again and is told, worship God (vv. 8–9). He is told not to seal up the book, for the time is near; people will go on as they are (vv. 10–11). Christ declares that he is coming soon with his reward, that he is the Alpha and the Omega, and blesses those who wash their robes, who may enter the city, while outside are the wicked (vv. 12–15). Jesus himself speaks: he sent his angel for the churches, and he is the root and descendant of David, the bright morning star (v. 16). The Spirit and the bride say, Come, and everyone who is thirsty is invited to take the water of life freely (v. 17). A solemn warning forbids anyone to add to or take away from the book (vv. 18–19). And the book ends: Surely I am coming soon. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all (vv. 20–21). The Bible that began in a garden with a tree of life ends in a garden-city with the tree of life, God’s people seeing his face, and the prayer for Christ to come. And its last word, after all the thunder of this book, is grace.

The setting. In Eden, a river flowed out to water the garden, and the tree of life stood in the midst of it (Genesis 2:9–10). After the fall, the way to the tree of life was barred by cherubim (Genesis 3:22–24). Ezekiel 47:1–12 describes a river flowing from the temple, growing deeper, bringing life wherever it goes, with trees on both banks whose fruit does not fail, bearing every month, and whose leaves are for healing. Zechariah 14:8 promises living waters flowing out from Jerusalem. Jesus promised that out of the heart of the one who believes in him will flow rivers of living water, meaning the Spirit (John 7:38–39).

A river and a tree. The Bible has been away from these two things for more than eleven hundred chapters, and here they are again. Genesis 2 has a river flowing out of Eden to water the garden, and the tree of life in the midst of the garden. Genesis 3 ends with the man and the woman put out, and cherubim with a flaming sword set to guard the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24). From that verse to this one, nobody eats from it. The whole of Scripture happens in the interval between a tree being fenced off and a tree being handed back.

Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal. “River of the water of life” (potamon hydatos zōēs). Eternal life, abundant and flowing. “Bright as crystal” (lampron hōs krystallon): pure, clear, shining. The promise of 7:17 and 21:6 fulfilled: the Lamb will guide them to springs of living water, and the thirsty will drink without payment. What was a cup offered in the last chapter is a river here.

Flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. One throne, two names, and John does not pause to explain how. One throne shared by God and the Lamb. Life flows from God’s rule; the source of all life is God himself, through the Lamb, by the Spirit (John 7:39). And what flows out of the throne is not judgement but water. Ezekiel saw the same thing: water trickling from under the threshold of the temple, deepening as it went until it was a river nobody could cross, with trees on both banks whose leaves would not wither (Ezekiel 47:1–12). In this book thunder and lightning came from the throne (4:5); at the end, a river does.

Through the middle of the street of the city. The river runs down the main street. Life is at the centre of the city’s life. Babylon’s streets were full of merchants and their cargoes; this street carries the water of life past every door.

Also, on either side of the river, the tree of life. “Tree of life” (xylon zōēs). What Adam and Eve lost is restored, as promised to the first of the seven churches: To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God (2:7). Ephesus was told that in a letter. Here is the tree. “On either side”: perhaps a whole avenue of trees of life, or one tree spanning the river. It is impossible to draw and easy to understand: wherever a person walks, it is on both sides of him. The word for tree (xylon, wood) is also used of the cross (Acts 5:30; 1 Peter 2:24); by the tree on which Christ died, we have access to the tree of life.

Not simply Eden reopened. The differences are the point. Eden was a garden; this is a garden inside a city, with the river running through the middle of the street, so that all the work and culture of humanity is gathered around the tree rather than exiled from it. Eden had one tree of life; here it lines both banks. Eden could be lost; this cannot. God does not restore his people to the place they started. He takes them somewhere better than the place they started, and the road ran through a cross.

With its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit each month. Constant abundance. Twelve: the number of God’s people. Fruit every month: no more seasons of want or scarcity. Ezekiel 47:12 says its fruit will not fail. Anyone who has grown anything knows that fruit trees rest; there are months with nothing on them. This one does not stop.

The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations. “Healing” (therapeian, health, healing; our word therapy comes from it). The phrase puzzles readers, and rightly: there is no sickness in this city, and the previous chapter has just abolished pain. Ezekiel is the source again: their fruit will be for food, and their leaves for healing (Ezekiel 47:12). The word can mean care and tending as much as cure. Not that there is sickness in the new creation, but that the leaves sustain the full health and wholeness of the nations; the life of the city is continually supplied, not merely started. All the wounds of history, between nations and peoples, are healed. And the word nations has been a hostile word for most of this book: the nations raged, the nations drank Babylon’s wine, the beast had authority over every nation. Here the nations are the ones being tended. The long wound in human history, peoples divided at a tower, scattered and at each other’s throats ever since, has leaves growing for it.

What it does not mean. The healing does not mean there will be illness or injury in the new creation that needs curing. There is no more pain (21:4). It means the nations enjoy perfect, lasting wholeness, the healing of all that sin had broken.

Could we ever lose the tree of life again? No. Adam stood on probation, able to fall, and fell. The redeemed stand in Christ, who has already passed every test for them and cannot fail. The curse is gone (v. 3), the serpent is in the lake of fire (20:10), and those who enter the city are made perfect in holiness, confirmed in a love for God that will never cool. The tree that was guarded by a sword is now given as a right (v. 14), and what Christ gives by right he never takes back. There will be no second fall, because there will be no second serpent and no unrenewed heart.

What about the wars and hatreds between peoples now? This verse is God’s answer, and it should shape how Christians live meanwhile. The divisions of race, nation and tribe that have caused so much blood are not permanent; they are among the things the leaves of the tree will heal. So the church is meant to be a foretaste of that healing now: Jew and Gentile, rich and poor, one in Christ (Galatians 3:28; Ephesians 2:14–16). If there is someone of another background in your church you avoid, or a people you have been taught to despise, this verse says you will spend eternity with the redeemed of them. Begin now.

In a sentence. Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, sparkling like crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb down the middle of the city’s main street; on each side of the river stood the tree of life, producing twelve crops of fruit, a fresh crop every month, and its leaves are for the healing of the nations.

On a Tuesday. You are not waiting for the river to start; its first streams are already given. Jesus said whoever believes in him will have rivers of living water flowing from within, by the Spirit (John 7:38–39). So drink today: come to him in prayer and in his word before you go to anything else. And let what flows to you flow on: forgive the person who wronged you, cross the divide to the neighbour who is not like you, bring some healing where you can. You are practising the life of the city.

For worship. What Adam lost, Christ restores, and more. The tree that was guarded by a flaming sword is given back, by the One who was hung on a tree in our place and bore the sword himself. The river runs from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and it has never once run dry; the fruit comes every month; the leaves heal nations that once tore each other apart. Paradise is not merely reopened but surpassed, a garden in a city, a tree on both banks, a gift that can never be lost. Blessed be the Lamb, who has opened to us the tree of life by the tree on which he died.
verseByVerse.note: Eden’s river and tree of life return, now in a city.

verseByVerse.quote: No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. And night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. And night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever.

The setting. After the fall, God cursed the ground because of Adam’s sin (Genesis 3:17). Zechariah 14:11 promises that there shall never again be a decree of utter destruction (curse) on Jerusalem. Moses asked to see God’s glory and was told, you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live (Exodus 33:20). The high priest’s blessing asked that the LORD make his face shine on his people (Numbers 6:24–26). Jesus said, blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matthew 5:8). John wrote that when Christ appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

No longer will there be anything accursed. “Accursed” (katathema, curse, anything under a curse). One clause, and it reaches back to the third chapter of the Bible. When the man and the woman were sent out, God said the ground was cursed because of the man; in pain he would eat of it, thorns and thistles would come up, and the man would return to the dust (Genesis 3:17–19). Everything hard about human existence, the labour that exhausts, the ground that resists, the body that fails, has stood under that sentence. And it is lifted. Not managed, not compensated for, not explained: removed. Everything that sin brought, death, pain, toil, decay, enmity, is gone.

Two trees. The removal was accomplished by Someone becoming a curse for us, for it is written, cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Galatians 3:13). There are two trees at the end of this book. On one of them the curse was absorbed; from the other the fruit is handed out twelve times a year.

But the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it. God reigns at the centre of the new creation. His rule is the source of its life and peace. The throne has been the fixed point of the vision since chapter 4, and it has always been in heaven. Now it is in the city, on the renewed earth, at the end of the street with the river running out of it.

And his servants will worship him. “Servants” (douloi). “Worship” (latreusousin, serve as priests, worship). “Him” (singular): God and the Lamb together as one. Eternal life is worship and service, freely and joyfully given. John has spent the book watching heaven worship; now the redeemed on the new earth join in for ever.

They will see his face. “See his face” (opsontai to prosōpon autou). Stop there, because nothing in Scripture is bigger than this. The highest blessing in all of Scripture: the beatific vision, seeing God face to face. Moses, who spoke with God as a man speaks to his friend, asked for exactly this one thing, and was told no man could see God’s face and live. He was put in a cleft of the rock and covered with a hand and shown God’s back (Exodus 33:18–23). The high priest went behind a veil once a year and saw nothing but smoke. Isaiah saw the train of a robe and cried out that he was undone. In chapter 6 of this book, kings and generals begged mountains to fall on them and hide them from the face of him who is seated on the throne (6:16). And here, without ceremony, in a short clause: they will see his face. Ordinary people, a slave from Laodicea, a widow from Thyatira, a man who once denied Christ in a courtyard, looking directly at God, and living. To see his face is to know him fully, be fully known, and be fully accepted (1 Corinthians 13:12).

That is what heaven is. Not a location with good weather; not a reunion, though there will be one; not the end of trouble, though trouble ends. It is a face. John wrote the same promise in a letter, and admitted he could not fill it in: what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Everything else in these two chapters, the gold, the jewels, the river, the open gates, is furniture in a room where that is happening.

And his name will be on their foreheads. As in 3:12, 7:3 and 14:1. The last of the marked foreheads in this book, and the counterfeit has been eliminated. The seal of 7:3, the Lamb’s name at 14:1, and the beast’s mark at 13:16 have all been leading here: everyone is labelled, and these are labelled with him. They belong to him completely, publicly and for ever. Like the high priest, who wore Holy to the LORD on a gold plate on his forehead (Exodus 28:36–38), all God’s people are priests in his presence.

And night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light. As in 21:23–25, said for the second time in a few verses, which is John’s way of underlining. God himself is their light.

And they will reign forever and ever. “Reign” (basileusousin). Not for a thousand years only, but for ever and ever. The promise of Daniel 7:18, 27 that the saints of the Most High will possess the kingdom for ever. Adam was made to rule over creation under God (Genesis 1:26–28); redeemed humanity will finally fulfil that calling. And the last word of the description is reign: the promise made to Laodicea, the weakest church on the road, that the one who conquers would sit with Christ on his throne (3:21), arriving in full.

What it does not mean. Reigning for ever does not mean believers become rulers over one another, or over God. They reign with Christ, under God, over a renewed creation, as God always intended.

How can we see the face of God, who is spirit? Scripture does not explain the mechanics, and we should not pretend to. But two things are clear. First, we will see God in Christ. Jesus said, whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:9), and the glory of God shines in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). The risen Lord, in his glorified body, will be before our eyes. Second, the seeing will be more than sight: knowing God directly, with nothing between, in a way we cannot now imagine. What Moses could not survive, we will be able to bear, because we will have been made like him.

Will there be work in the new creation? Yes, but not toil. His servants will serve him, and they will reign; serving and reigning are active words. The curse made work painful and frustrating, thorns, sweat, futility, but work itself came before the fall (Genesis 2:15). What is lifted is the curse, not the calling. Imagine work that never fails, never wearies you, never goes to waste, and is done entirely for the joy of God. That is not boredom. That is what you were made for, and what every good day of work now is a faint taste of.

In a sentence. There will be no more curse; the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in the city, and his servants will worship him; they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads; there will be no more night, and they will not need lamplight or sunlight, because the Lord God will shine on them, and they will reign for ever and ever.

On a Tuesday. If seeing God’s face is the goal of everything, then the most important thing you do this week is seek his face now (Psalm 27:8), in his word and in prayer. Ask what in your life is competing with that longing: ambition, comfort, a relationship, a grievance. And when the curse bites, the aching back, the job that frustrates, the illness that does not lift, remember that it is one of the last things on its way out. You will one day work without thorns and rest without fear, and look up into his face.

For worship. The curse that fell on the ground in Eden fell at last on the Son of God, hanging on a tree, and it was absorbed there and never returned. So the throne of God and of the Lamb stands in the city, and his servants serve him without weariness, and they see his face. What Moses longed for and could not have, what the high priest never saw behind the veil, what the kings of the earth fled from in terror, is given to forgiven sinners, and they do not die of it; they live by it. Blessed be God, who makes his face shine upon us, and who will let us look on him for ever.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 6–7: the vision is over and the book begins closing itself by matching its own opening — the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place (cf. 1:1). Then the speaker changes without warning: And behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book — the sixth beatitude, almost word for word the first one at 1:3.

Verses 8–9: John falls down to worship the angel a second time and is stopped a second time, in almost the words of 19:10 — I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God.

Verses 10–11: Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near — the exact reverse of what Daniel was told (Dan. 12:4, 9) — followed by the hardest verse in the chapter: Let the evildoer still do evil… and the holy still be holy.

Verses 12–13: the second I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done (cf. Isa. 40:10), and three pairs of titles: Alpha and Omega, first and last, beginning and end. Verses 14–15: the seventh and last beatitude — Blessed are those who wash their robes — and the list of those outside, ending with everyone who loves and practices falsehood. Verse 16: I, Jesus, have sent my angel… I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Testimony of Jesus

The book closes as it opened: blessed is the one who keeps its words. The angel refuses John’s worship again — Worship God. The book is left unsealed, for the time is near. Jesus, the Alpha and Omega, root and descendant of David, the bright morning star, is coming soon; blessed are those who wash their robes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The whole vision was given for the churches, to be read aloud in small rooms.

Now: While the door is open, ask which way your life is already heading.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "These words are trustworthy and true. And the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place." "And behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to me, “These words are trustworthy and true. And the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place.” “And behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.”

The setting. The epilogue (22:6–21) echoes the prologue (1:1–8): the chain of revelation, the angel, the servants, what must soon take place, the blessing on those who keep the words, and Christ’s coming. The book ends where it began.

And he said to me, These words are trustworthy and true. As in 21:5. The whole book is guaranteed. The vision is over. From here to the end, the book is closing itself, and it does so by going back to its first sentence. Compare 1:1: the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place, made known by sending his angel to his servant John. The same chain, the same phrase, the same servants. John is signing off by matching the letterhead.

And the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets. “Spirits of the prophets” (tōn pneumatōn tōn prophētōn). An unusual title, doing specific work. It says that the same God who spoke through Isaiah and Ezekiel and Daniel, whose words have been echoed on nearly every page of this book, is the one who has spoken here. God, who inspired the prophets, has inspired this book. Revelation stands in the line of the Old Testament prophets, with their authority (2 Peter 1:21). It is not a new departure. It is the last chapter of a document that has been in progress for some fifteen centuries.

Has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place. As in 1:1. The revelation is for all God’s servants, not a spiritual elite. It was meant to be read aloud in ordinary congregations, by ordinary believers, and understood well enough to be obeyed.

And behold, I am coming soon. “Coming soon” (erchomai tachy). The speaker changes without warning: the angel has been talking, and suddenly it is Christ himself. He will say this three times in this chapter (vv. 7, 12, 20), and it is the drumbeat the book ends on. The great hope of the church.

Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book. The sixth beatitude, almost word for word the first one (1:3). “Keeps” (tērōn, obeys, holds fast). The book opens and closes with a blessing on the same person: not the one who understands every symbol, or charts it, or identifies the beast, but the one who keeps it. Revelation is to be obeyed, not merely studied. Whatever else a reader takes from it, that is the bracket he is being asked to live inside.

What it does not mean. “Soon” does not mean Christ was mistaken about the timing. From God’s point of view, the end has been near since the resurrection, and his apparent delay is patience (2 Peter 3:8–9). Every generation is to live as though he may come in its lifetime.

Soon, after two thousand years? The honest answer has three parts. First, the word stresses that his coming is the next great event in God’s plan, sure and sudden, not that it will come within a set number of years; nothing stands between now and then that must happen first in the way the cross had to happen. Second, the New Testament dates the last days from the resurrection (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2): we have been living at the edge of the end ever since. Third, Peter answered this very objection while it was fresh: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and he is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but patient (2 Peter 3:8–9). The delay is not indifference. It is mercy, and somebody is being brought in during it, perhaps someone you love.

How do I keep a book so full of symbols? You keep what it plainly asks, which is a great deal and not hard to see. Worship God alone, and refuse every rival, whether Caesar, money or comfort. Hold to Jesus when it costs you. Do not compromise with the sins the letters to the churches name. Endure suffering without giving up the faith. Tell the truth. Long for Christ’s coming, and invite others to come to him. You do not need to settle every question about the seals and the beast to obey that, and many believers who never solved a single symbol have kept this book perfectly.

In a sentence. The angel said to me, These words are trustworthy and true; the Lord, the God who inspires the prophets, sent his angel to show his servants what must soon happen; and Jesus says: Look, I am coming soon! How blessed is the one who obeys the words of the prophecy in this book!

On a Tuesday. Ask what Revelation calls you to do, not only what it predicts: worship God alone, refuse the world’s idols, endure, witness and long for Christ. Pick one of those and act on it today. And if you have been drawn into arguments about the end times that have made you anxious or proud, lay them down for a while. Read the book again for its commands and its comfort, and let Christ’s promise, I am coming soon, be the thing that shapes your week.

For worship. The God who spoke by the prophets has not fallen silent at the end of the story. He has sent his angel, he has guaranteed every word, and his Son has promised, in his own voice, that he is coming soon. The Lord of history is not slow; he is patient, waiting while the last of his people are gathered in. Blessed be the faithful God, whose words are trustworthy and true, and blessed be the Lord Jesus, who is on his way.

verseByVerse.quote: I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I heard and saw them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who showed them to me, but he said to me, "You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I heard and saw them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who showed them to me, but he said to me, “You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God.”

The setting. John made the same mistake in 19:10. In ancient law, a matter was established by eyewitness testimony (Deuteronomy 19:15). John’s Gospel and first letter stress eyewitness testimony: we have heard, we have seen with our eyes, we have touched (1 John 1:1–3; John 19:35; 21:24).

I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. John signs his testimony as an eyewitness. He did not invent these visions; he received them. The man who leaned on Jesus at the Last Supper and stood at the foot of the cross puts his name to this book too.

And when I heard and saw them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who showed them to me. A second time. He did it at 19:10, was stopped in almost these words, and here at the very end of the book, with the correction already in his own manuscript three chapters earlier, he goes down again. That is not flattering to John, and he wrote it down anyway, which is itself a kind of testimony. He is not presenting himself as a man who has learned his lesson. Even an apostle could make this mistake, and he records it honestly to warn us. And notice when it happens. Not in the middle of the terror, not at the dragon or the beast or the lake of fire, but immediately after the river and the tree and the face. It is the beauty that undoes him. The instinct is right; only the direction is wrong. A man overwhelmed by glory reaches for the nearest thing that is holding it.

A comfort in a repeated fault. It should be a comfort to anyone who has repeated a sin he had already repented of: the last recorded action of the apostle who wrote this book is a mistake he had made before. God did not withdraw the revelation. The angel corrected him and the book went on. Repeated failure is a reason to be humble and watchful, not a sign that God has given up on you.

But he said to me, You must not do that! The same urgent warning as in 19:10. There is no pause, no softening, no acceptance of the honour for a moment before declining it.

I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Angels, prophets and all obedient believers are fellow servants of God. No created being deserves worship. And look at how the angel describes himself, because the list is longer than it was at 19:10. He is a fellow servant with John, with the prophets, and, this is new, with those who keep the words of this book. That last group is the reader. An angel of God has just put himself in the same category as an ordinary Christian who reads Revelation and does what it says.

Worship God. Two words, among the shortest complete instructions in Scripture. Twenty-two chapters of visions, and this is the summary. The book’s last command about worship, and its central message. Throughout Revelation, the choice has been whom to worship: God and the Lamb, or the dragon and the beast. Worship God alone. And notice what this does to the Lamb. All through the book the Lamb has been worshipped with the same worship as God, by angels who would never accept it themselves (5:8–14). The angel refuses worship because he is a creature; the Lamb receives it because he is not.

What it does not mean. Respect for God’s messengers, human or angelic, is right (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13). Worship is not. Revering a teacher, preacher or spiritual experience so highly that it takes the place of God is idolatry.

Is it wrong, then, to pray to angels or saints? Yes. If the angel who showed John the new Jerusalem would not accept even a bow of worship, no angel or departed saint may be prayed to or venerated. Scripture gives us one Mediator, Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and through him we come straight to the Father (Hebrews 4:14–16). We may thank God for the saints and follow their faith (Hebrews 13:7). But we pray only to God, through Christ, by the Spirit. Anything else, however well meant, gives a servant what belongs to the Master.

In a sentence. I, John, am the one who heard and saw all this; and when I had heard and seen it, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who had been showing me these things; but he said to me, Do not do that! I am a servant like you and your brothers the prophets, and like all who obey the words of this book; worship God!

On a Tuesday. The permanent danger in the church is that the people through whom God speaks, preachers, writers, movements, worship leaders, receive what belongs to God, and the danger is greatest when what they bring is genuinely glorious. The remedy is not to think less of the messenger. It is two words: worship God. Notice this week whom you quote most, whose approval you most want, what spiritual experience you chase. Thank God for them. Then look past them to him.

For worship. Worship God. Not your experiences, not your leaders, not even the good gifts he gives. Him alone. The mighty angel who showed John the city of gold bows beside him as a fellow servant, and the whole of heaven turns in one direction, toward the throne of God and of the Lamb. He alone is worthy; he made all things and redeemed his people with his own blood. Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty, and to him and to the Lamb be blessing and honour and glory for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near. Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to me, “Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near. Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy.”

The setting. Daniel was told to shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end, because his visions concerned the distant future (Daniel 8:26; 12:4, 9). Daniel 12:10 says many shall purify themselves, but the wicked shall act wickedly, and none of the wicked shall understand. Ezekiel 3:27 says, he who will hear, let him hear; and he who will refuse to hear, let him refuse.

And he said to me, Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near. “Do not seal” (mē sphragisēs). The exact reverse of what Daniel was told. Daniel’s vision was for the far future; John’s is for now. The last days have begun. The book must be open, read and obeyed by the churches. And it is the reverse of what John himself was told at 10:4, when the seven thunders spoke and he was reaching for his pen: seal up what the seven thunders have said. There is exactly one sealed sentence in Revelation, and we do not have it. Everything else in the book is open, on purpose, by instruction. Which should settle the way this book is approached. It is not a locked document awaiting a key, and it never was. Its blessing falls on the person who keeps it rather than the person who cracks it.

Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy. This is the hardest verse in the chapter, and it must not be softened into something comfortable. Read carelessly it sounds like God shrugging, a permission slip for wickedness and a verdict that nobody changes. It is not a command to keep sinning, but a solemn warning. Time is short, and character is being fixed. Those who persistently refuse God’s call harden themselves, and when Christ comes, there will be no more opportunity to change. The present choices settle eternal destinies.

Three things settle what it means. First, its position. It comes immediately after the time is near and immediately before I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me. It is bracketed by urgency on both sides, which is the opposite of fatalism. Second, its form. It is a prophetic announcement, like the word given to Ezekiel when Israel had stopped listening (Ezekiel 3:27). What it says is that a moment arrives after which character is fixed, that there is a point beyond which a person’s direction of travel becomes his destination. Everyone knows this is true of habits within a lifetime; the verse says it is finally true of lives. Third, and most importantly, what it does to the reader. It is placed in front of somebody holding a book, at the point where the book is nearly finished, and its effect is to ask: which of these four descriptions fits the direction you are already going? The door is open now, and the invitation is six verses away, but it will not be open for ever.

And the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy. An encouragement: keep on in righteousness and holiness. Do not give up because the end seems delayed or the world seems to win. Holiness, too, is a direction that becomes a destiny, and the righteous who keep on will find that what they practised in weakness here is what they will be in glory.

What it does not mean. This is not fatalism, as if people cannot change. The very next verses invite everyone to come and drink (v. 17). It means that time is short, and that a life’s direction, if persisted in, becomes permanent. Today is the day to turn.

Is it too late for someone I love? While a person is alive, the invitation stands, and you must not treat anyone as beyond reach. The thief on the cross turned in his last hours; Manasseh, one of the worst kings Judah ever had, repented after a lifetime of evil (2 Chronicles 33:12–13). Paul called himself the foremost of sinners, saved as an example of Christ’s patience (1 Timothy 1:15–16). This verse warns that the door will close at Christ’s coming or at death, not that it has already closed on your son or your friend. So keep praying for them, keep loving them, and keep telling them the truth. It is the very urgency of this verse that makes your prayers matter.

In a sentence. Then he told me, Do not seal up the words of the prophecy in this book, because the time is near; let the one who does wrong go on doing wrong, and the vile go on being vile; let the one who does right go on doing right, and the holy go on being holy.

On a Tuesday. Your daily choices are shaping who you will be for ever. Keep doing right and keep being holy, by God’s grace, even when it seems to make no difference. The small kindness, the resisted temptation, the honest answer, the hour in prayer: these are not lost; they are the grain of the person you are becoming. And if you know a direction in your life is wrong, do not wait for a better moment to turn. The verse’s whole message is: today.

For worship. The God who could have sealed this book and left us in the dark has opened it and set it in every church, so that no one may say he was not warned or not invited. His patience holds the door open while the time is near. He makes the righteous persevere and the holy grow holier, keeping them by his power for the day of Christ. Blessed be the Lord, who does not trifle with souls, and who calls today, while it is still today.
verseByVerse.note: Daniel was told to seal his book until the end; John is told not to, because the time is near.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.”

The setting. Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11 say, behold, the Lord GOD comes with might, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him. Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12 say, I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god. Jesus said the Son of Man will come with his angels in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay each person according to what he has done (Matthew 16:27).

Behold, I am coming soon. The second of the chapter’s three announcements, and this one has the reward already in his hand.

Bringing my recompense with me. “Recompense” (misthos, wages, reward). Bringing it with him: not sent for afterwards, not calculated on arrival. Isaiah said it first of the coming of God: his reward is with him. Christ brings with him the reward of his people and the judgement of the wicked.

To repay each one for what he has done. “What he has done” (to ergon, his work). Singular: the whole pattern of a life. As in 20:12–13. The book has raised this twice already, to Thyatira at 2:23 and at the great white throne at 20:12, and the answer has not moved. A record has never yet admitted anybody into the city, and it has never yet failed to show whose a person is. It is the evidence of whom a man belongs to, and the measure of what he is given afterwards. Nobody will be standing in that scene holding an invoice. And hold on to each one. In a scene involving every human being who has ever lived, nothing is averaged. The visits nobody recorded, the giving that hurt, the cup of cold water: each one, by name.

I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. All three titles together, and they gather up everything the book has said about who is speaking. God said Alpha and Omega in 1:8 and 21:6. Christ said first and last in 1:17 and 2:8, and it is Isaiah’s exclusive divine self-identification: I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god (Isaiah 44:6). Now Christ claims all of them. The clearest statement in Revelation that Jesus shares the identity of the one God. The titles move between the Father and the Son through this book without a seam and without an explanation, and that is not carelessness. Revelation never argues for the deity of Christ; it simply speaks as though the question could not arise. The one who began all things will end them.

What it does not mean. Repaying each one for what he has done does not mean believers earn eternal life. The free gift of the water of life is offered without price (v. 17). The reward Christ brings is a gift of grace that crowns the works his grace produced (Ephesians 2:8–10).

But what if I have nothing to bring? There is a fear on the other side of this verse, and it keeps quiet Christians awake. A man converted at sixty, or a woman who has spent twenty years ill in a back bedroom, reads repay each one for what he has done and thinks: there is nothing of mine to bring. Two things answer him. The first is that what gets rewarded is not what he achieved but what Christ produced in him, and Christ does not fail to produce: the vine bears the fruit and the branch only carries it (John 15:5). Patient suffering, quiet prayer and faithfulness in small things are works too. The second is the parable Christ told about precisely this complaint: the men hired at the eleventh hour were paid the same as those who had borne the burden of the day, and the owner wronged nobody (Matthew 20:1–16). Nobody will stand in that scene feeling short-changed, and nobody will stand in it thinking he earned what he is holding.

Will some in heaven be happier than others? Scripture does teach rewards that differ: the servant with ten minas and the one with five are given different charges (Luke 19:16–19), and some works survive the fire while others are burned up (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). But no one in the city will be unhappy, envious or lacking. An old picture helps: a thimble and a bucket can both be full. Every vessel will be filled to the brim with God, and every redeemed person will rejoice in the honour given to the others. And every crown will be cast at the feet of the One who earned them all (4:10).

In a sentence. Look, I am coming soon! I bring my reward with me, to repay everyone according to what they have done; I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.

On a Tuesday. Live this week as someone whose Lord is bringing his reward with him. Do the unseen faithful thing, the visit, the gift, the patient answer to a difficult child, without needing anyone to notice; he notices. And if you have wasted years, do not despair of the time left. Begin today. The Lord of the vineyard is still hiring at the eleventh hour.

For worship. The One who was there before the first word of history, and will be there after the last, is coming soon, and his reward is with him. He is the first and the last, the God of Isaiah beside whom there is no other, and he is the Lamb who was slain. He will not forget a cup of cold water given in his name; he will not overlook the widow’s mite or the hidden prayer. Every good thing his people did, he did in them first, and then he rewards it as though it were theirs. Worship Jesus as the Alpha and the Omega, God himself, who began your story and will bring it to its end.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and that they may enter the city by the gates. Outside are the dogs and sorcerers and the sexually immoral and murderers and idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and that they may enter the city by the gates. Outside are the dogs and sorcerers and the sexually immoral and murderers and idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.

The setting. In Jewish usage, dogs were scavengers, unclean animals, and the word was a term of contempt for the immoral and for Gentiles (Deuteronomy 23:18, where a male cult prostitute is called a dog; Matthew 7:6; Philippians 3:2). Sinners were cast out of Israel’s camp (Leviticus 13:46).

Blessed are those who wash their robes. The seventh and last beatitude of Revelation, and it lands on the one act the whole book has been describing. Not blessed are those who understood it. Not blessed are those who suffered, though many did. Blessed are those who wash their robes, and 7:14 has already said in what: they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. “Wash” (plynontes, present tense: keep washing). The one who trusts in Christ’s blood for cleansing, continually.

So that they may have the right to the tree of life. “Right” (exousia, authority, right of access). What was barred in Genesis 3:24 is now open to those cleansed by the Lamb. The tree guarded by cherubim with a flaming sword since the fall is now available by right rather than by trespass.

And that they may enter the city by the gates. Through the pearly gates, always open (21:25). A strangely ordinary phrase after everything that has come before: not carried in, not admitted by a side door, but walking through the front gates like a citizen coming home.

Outside are the dogs and sorcerers and the sexually immoral and murderers and idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood. “Outside” (exō). As in 21:8. Those who persist in sin without repentance are excluded. Dogs was not a term of affection in the ancient world; these were scavengers in the street, and the law used the word of what was excluded from the sanctuary. Paul used it of men who insisted on adding requirements to the gospel (Philippians 3:2). “Loves and practices falsehood”: the followers of the father of lies. Two verbs, and the first is the sharper. Not merely tells lies: loves them. The dragon has been the deceiver of the whole world since 12:9, and the redeemed on Mount Zion were described in one clause: in their mouth no lie was found (14:5). At the very end, the line between the two companies runs through whether a person loved the truth. This does not mean they are just beyond the walls in the new creation; it means they are shut out of God’s presence, in the lake of fire (21:8).

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “Blessed are they that do his commandments” (poiountes tas entolas autou) instead of “Blessed are those who wash their robes” (plynontes tas stolas autōn). The two phrases look similar in Greek capital letters, and a tired copyist could slip from one to the other. The best and earliest manuscripts read “wash their robes”, and this fits 7:14 exactly. The difference is significant: access to the tree of life comes by cleansing in Christ’s blood, not by law-keeping. One reading makes the entrance depend on obedience; the other makes it depend on being washed. The manuscripts favour the second, and so does every page of Revelation from chapter 5 onward.

What it does not mean. Those outside are not a permanent group of people looking in. It is a vivid way of saying they have no part in the city. Nor are the sins listed beyond forgiveness: anyone who washes their robes in the Lamb’s blood, whatever their past, may enter.

What does it mean to keep washing my robes? It means living by daily repentance and faith. You were washed once for all when you first trusted Christ: justified, forgiven, declared clean (1 Corinthians 6:11). But you still sin, and Jesus told Peter that one who has bathed needs only to wash his feet (John 13:10). So each day you bring your fresh sins to him, name them honestly, and trust his blood again, not to be saved again but to walk in the joy of being saved. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9).

In a sentence. How blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they have the right to the tree of life and can go through the gates into the city! Outside are the dogs, those who practise magic, the sexually immoral, murderers, idolaters and everyone who loves and practises lies.

On a Tuesday. Keep washing your robes: bring every sin to Christ, daily, and trust his blood to cleanse you. That is the way into the city. Make it a habit this week to end each day by naming before God where you failed, and thanking him by name for the blood that covers it. And love the truth: in what you say, what you watch, what you believe. The people of the city are the people who loved the truth, because they loved the One who is the Truth.

For worship. The tree that was guarded by a flaming sword is given by right, and the gates that were shut on Adam stand open to his children, and the only thing that makes the difference is the blood of the Lamb. Sinners from every list in this chapter, sorcerers, the immoral, liars, idolaters, have walked through those gates, because they washed their robes in a fountain opened for sin and uncleanness. Blessed be the Lamb, whose blood makes the filthy clean and gives the outcast the right to come home.
verseByVerse.note: The last of the seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation. Some manuscripts read “do his commandments” for “wash their robes” (ESV note) — the reading of the King James Version.

verseByVerse.quote: "I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches. I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches. I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star.”

The setting. Isaiah 11:1, 10 promises a shoot from the stump of Jesse, the root of Jesse, who will stand as a banner for the peoples. Numbers 24:17 says a star shall come out of Jacob, and a sceptre shall rise out of Israel. Jesus asked how the Messiah can be David’s son if David calls him Lord (Matthew 22:41–45). Peter speaks of the morning star rising in our hearts (2 Peter 1:19).

I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches. “I, Jesus” (egō Iēsous). The name at last. It is the only place in Revelation where Jesus names himself this way, and it comes after twenty-one chapters of titles: the Lamb, the faithful witness, the first and the last, the Word of God, King of kings. At the end he uses the name his mother used, the human name given to a carpenter’s son in a village. He personally guarantees the whole book. “To you” (plural): to all the churches. “For the churches”: Revelation is a letter to the church, for every congregation in every age. This enormous vision, thrones and dragons and bowls and a city two thousand kilometres high, was produced for congregations, to be read aloud in rooms. The book ends where it began, at 1:11, with seven small assemblies on a road in Asia.

I am the root and the descendant of David. “Root” (rhiza): the source of David, as God, David’s Lord. “Descendant” (genos, offspring): the son of David, as man, born in his line. Both divine and human. As in 5:5. Both at once, and the pairing is deliberate. To be David’s descendant is to come after him, the promised son of the royal line, born in David’s town. To be David’s root is to be what David grew out of; a root is not produced by the tree, it produces the tree. Jesus once set that riddle himself, in the temple, and nobody could answer it: if David calls the Christ Lord, how is he his son? (Matthew 22:41–45). This verse is the answer, given by the man who asked the question. He is David’s son by birth and David’s Lord by nature, and the two belong to one person.

The bright morning star. “Morning star” (ho astēr ho lampros ho prōinos): Venus, the brightest star in the sky before dawn, heralding the new day. Christ is the sign that the long night of this age is nearly over and the day of the new creation is about to dawn. As promised to Thyatira (2:28), the conqueror receives Christ himself. That promise, made to a church in the least important town on the road, was never explained. Here it is: the morning star is himself. Behind it stands the prophecy of Balaam, of all people: a star shall come out of Jacob. And the morning star rises when the sky is at its darkest and the night has gone on longest. It does not announce more night. It means the sun is on its way. Which is what this book has been saying to frightened congregations from its first page. It never promises that the dark will be short. It promises who is standing in it.

What it does not mean. The morning star title does not compare Christ with Lucifer, the day star of Isaiah 14:12, as some have confused it. Christ is the true light; the fallen king of Babylon was a false one.

Why does it matter that he is both David’s root and son? Because only such a Saviour could save us. If Jesus were only David’s son, a good man of the royal line, he could not bear the infinite weight of our sin or give eternal life. If he were only David’s Lord, God but not man, he could not stand in our place, die our death or sympathise with our weakness. He is both, one person, true God and true man (Westminster 8.2). That is why he can be the Lamb who was slain and the Alpha and the Omega in the same chapter, and why you can trust him with everything.

In a sentence. I, Jesus, have sent my angel to give you this testimony for the churches; I am the root and the offspring of David, the bright star of the morning.

On a Tuesday. When your night feels long, a grief that will not lift, a prayer still unanswered, a church in decline, look for the morning star. Christ does not promise that the dark is short; he promises that he is in it, and that he is the sign of the coming day. Say his name this week in the hard moment: Jesus. It is the name he chose to sign this book with, and it means the LORD saves.

For worship. At the end of all his titles, he gives us his name: Jesus. The Lord of David, before whom David bowed, became the son of David, born in David’s town, laid in a manger, nailed to a cross under a sign that called him King. He is the root from which the whole royal line grew and the shoot that sprang from its stump. He is the bright morning star, rising over the darkest hour of history, and his rising means the night is nearly over. Worship Jesus as David’s Lord and David’s son, the morning star whose rising means the day is coming.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 17: The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come.” And let the one who hears say, “Come.” And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price (cf. Isa. 55:1; John 4:14; 7:37). Verses 18–19: the covenant scribe’s closing warning against adding to or taking from the words of the prophecy (cf. Deut. 4:2; 12:32; Prov. 30:5–6), with penalties that fit the offences exactly.

Verse 20: He who testifies to these things says, “Surely I am coming soon.” — the last recorded words of Jesus Christ in the Bible — and the church’s answer, Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! Verse 21: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.
verseByVerse.theology:
Come

The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come”; whoever hears is to say it too; whoever is thirsty may take the water of life without price. The book is not to be added to or taken from. Jesus says, “Surely I am coming soon,” and the church answers, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!”
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The earliest church prayed Marana tha — Our Lord, come.

Now: The most terrifying book in Scripture ends with grace, offered to all.

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit and the Bride say, "Come." And let the one who hears say, "Come." And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come.” And let the one who hears say, “Come.” And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price.

The setting. Isaiah 55:1 invites: come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat. Jesus stood up at the Feast of Booths and cried out, if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). He said, come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28).

The last invitation. This is the last invitation in the Bible, and it is the widest sentence in the most frightening book in Scripture. After the dragon and the beast and the lake of fire and the great white throne, one of the last things God says to the human race is, come and have a drink. Four movements, and they should be taken in order, because the sentence is built like a chain.

The Spirit and the Bride say, Come. “Come” (erchou). The Holy Spirit and the church speak together, with one verb between them. They pray to Christ, Come (as in v. 20), longing for his return. And they invite the world to come to Christ. The church, filled with the Spirit, both prays for Christ’s coming and calls sinners to come to him. That is the entire mission of the church in a few words, and it settles the relationship: the church does not invite people on its own authority, and the Spirit does not work around the church. They say it together.

And let the one who hears say, Come. Everyone who hears this book read in church (1:3) is to join the prayer and the invitation. The invitation is handed on. Anyone who has heard it becomes one of the people saying it, and there is no interval and no qualification: not the one who has matured, not the one who has been trained. The person who has just heard is immediately in the chorus.

And let the one who is thirsty come. “Thirsty” (dipsōn). Now the direction reverses. The first two clauses were the church calling out; this one is somebody walking in. The invitation is to anyone who knows their need. Thirst is the only qualification: not worthiness, not understanding, not improvement.

Let the one who desires take the water of life without price. “Desires” (thelōn, wants, wills). The last clause takes away even the word thirsty, which might sound like a condition, and replaces it with the one who desires: whoever wishes, whoever will. Then the price is stated, and it is the same word used at 21:6. “Without price” (dōrean, as a free gift). The book of judgement ends with an open invitation. The last offer in the Bible is free grace. Isaiah shouted it seven hundred years earlier; Jesus shouted it on the last and greatest day of the feast; and he said it quietly to one woman at a well at noon (John 4:14).

Where the verse is placed. Two verses earlier the dogs and sorcerers and murderers were outside the gate. One verse later comes a solemn warning about tampering with the book. And in between, unfenced, is the freest offer in Scripture. That is not carelessness. It is the last word on the character of the God who has been running this entire book: the One whose judgements filled sixteen chapters ends by holding out a cup and asking nothing for it. So the answer to the question raised at 20:15, whether a name is written in the book of life, is not, have I done enough? Nobody has. It is whether a person is thirsty, and whether he will come and take what is being handed to him for nothing.

Where Christians differ: if salvation depends on God’s choice, is this invitation sincere? Some argue that if God has chosen who will be saved, a universal invitation is meaningless; others argue that the invitation proves people have free will to come in their own power. Verdict: the gospel invitation is sincere and is to be offered freely to everyone without exception. Whoever wants to may come, and no one who comes will be turned away (John 6:37). At the same time, no one comes unless the Father draws them (John 6:44), and those who come are those whose names were written in the Lamb’s book (13:8). God’s sovereign grace does not make the invitation less real; it makes it effective. The Spirit who says Come is the Spirit who gives the thirst and the will to come.

What it does not mean. “Without price” does not mean without cost to God. It cost the Lamb his life. It is free to us because it was paid in full by him.

What if I am not sure I am chosen? Then come anyway, because the invitation is not addressed to the chosen; it is addressed to the thirsty, and to whoever desires. You do not need to read the Lamb’s book before you drink. You learn that your name is written there by coming, not before coming. No one has ever come to Christ and been told, sorry, you were not on the list. Jesus promised the opposite: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). Election is a comfort to those who have come, not a barrier for those still thinking about it. If you want the water, take it.

How do I actually invite someone? Simply, honestly and personally, as one beggar telling another where the bread is. Pray first for the person by name, and ask God for an opening. Live in a way that raises questions. When the moment comes, speak of Christ himself, not only of church: who he is, what he did on the cross, and that the water of life is free. Ask, would you like to read one of the Gospels with me? or, can I tell you why I trust Jesus? Invite them to hear the word preached. And leave the results with the Spirit, who says Come alongside you.

In a sentence. The Spirit and the bride say, Come! and everyone who hears should say, Come! Let anyone who is thirsty come, and anyone who wants it take the water of life as a free gift.

On a Tuesday. Join the Spirit and the bride: invite someone this week to come to Christ. The water of life is still free. And say Come in the other direction too: pray for the Lord’s return, today, in your own words. A church that prays Come, Lord Jesus and a church that says to the world, Come to Jesus, are the same church, and you belong to it.

For worship. After the seals and the trumpets and the bowls, after the fall of Babylon and the lake of fire and the great white throne, the last thing the God of all the earth does in his book is open his hand and hold out a cup. The Spirit says Come, and the bride says Come, and the water is free, because the Son was thirsty on the cross so that we would never thirst again. No book has ever ended with such a door left open. Blessed be the God of all grace, who does not merely permit sinners to come but calls them, draws them and satisfies them with himself.

verseByVerse.quote: I warn everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book, and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are described in this book.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I warn everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book, and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are described in this book.

The setting. Moses warned Israel: you shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it (Deuteronomy 4:2; 12:32). Proverbs 30:6 says, do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar. In the ancient world, authors and copyists sometimes added curses to their writings to prevent tampering, and covenant documents ended with such a clause. Revelation was the last book of the New Testament to be written, and it stands at the end of the Bible.

I warn everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book. “Warn” (martyrō, testify, solemnly declare). Probably Jesus himself speaking (v. 20: he who testifies to these things). “Everyone who hears”: every congregation and every reader. The warning is severe, and it is not unprecedented. It is the standard closing formula of an ancient covenant document, and Moses used it twice. John is doing what a covenant scribe did when the text was finished: sealing it against tampering.

If anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book. A play on words: add to the book, and God will add its plagues to you. Adding to God’s word means claiming new revelation, new teaching with divine authority, or twisting the book with false prophecy: supplying what God did not say, the date, the identity, the extra requirement, the private revelation that completes what Scripture left open.

And if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and in the holy city. Taking away means removing, denying or ignoring parts of God’s word: its warnings, its judgements, its demands or its promises, quietly setting aside the judgement, or the exclusivity, or the return, because it is unpopular or uncomfortable. The penalty is the loss of eternal life itself. Such a person shows they never truly belonged to the Lamb. And the penalties fit the offences exactly, as everything in this book does. Add to the words, and what is added to you is the plagues; take away from the words, and what is taken from you is the tree and the city. In each case a person receives the operation he performed.

Where Christians differ: does this verse close the whole canon of Scripture? Strictly, the warning applies to the book of Revelation. Some therefore argue it says nothing about the rest of the Bible, while others claim continuing revelation through prophets, popes, councils or new scriptures, such as the Book of Mormon. Verdict: the direct reference is to Revelation, but it applies the principle of Deuteronomy 4:2 to the final book of the New Testament, written by the last living apostle, and it fittingly closes the whole canon. With the death of the apostles, the foundation was laid (Ephesians 2:20), and the faith was once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3). God has spoken his final word in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). Scripture is complete and sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17). No later revelation, vision, tradition or book may be added to it with equal authority, and no part of it may be removed. This app holds that the canon is closed and Scripture alone is our final authority.

What it does not mean. The warning does not condemn faithful copying, translation or teaching of the Bible. It condemns deliberately adding false teaching to it or cutting out what we do not like. Comparing manuscripts to establish what John actually wrote is the opposite of tampering with what John wrote: it is the effort to make sure nothing has been added or lost. The textual notes in this commentary are that work being done honestly and in the open.

Can a true believer lose his salvation by taking away from this book? No. The warning describes those who falsify God’s word, and shows that such people never truly belonged to Christ: they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). Christ’s sheep will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28). For believers the warning is a solemn reason to handle Scripture with reverence, and one of the means God uses to keep them faithful. A Christian who misunderstands a verse, or struggles to believe a hard one, is not what this describes. It describes the person who sets himself above the word and edits God.

What about Christians who hear words from God today? This app holds, charitably, that the gifts of new revelation ceased with the apostles, because the foundation has been laid and Scripture is complete. Many dear brothers and sisters believe God still gives prophetic words, and most of them would agree that no such word can add to Scripture, bind the conscience or carry its authority. That agreement is what matters most here. Test every impression, dream or prophecy by the written word (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21; 1 John 4:1). If anything claims to add a new doctrine, a new requirement or a new date, this verse says: do not receive it. The Bible is enough.

What about the extra books in some Bibles? The books called the Apocrypha, found in Roman Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, were not part of the Hebrew Scriptures that Jesus and the apostles received, and they are never quoted in the New Testament as Scripture. The Reformed confessions say they are not inspired, and are no part of the canon, though they may be read as human writings with some historical value (Westminster 1.3).
