The sixty-six books of the Old and New Testaments are the whole of God’s written word. This is not the church deciding what God said, but the church recognising the books God gave.

In a sentence. I solemnly warn everyone who hears the words of the prophecy in this book: if anyone adds anything to them, God will add to that person the plagues described in this book; and if anyone takes away anything from the words of this book of prophecy, God will take away from that person his share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are described in this book.

On a Tuesday. Take the whole Bible seriously: do not add to it with your own ideas, and do not skip the parts you find hard. Let all of it shape you. Very few readers will ever publish an edition of Revelation, but a great many are tempted to do to it privately what the verse forbids publicly: to add a chart the text does not authorise, or to subtract the parts that are hard to hear. Which passages do you avoid? Read one of them this week, slowly, and ask God to make you willing to receive it.

For worship. The God who spoke in many times and many ways by the prophets has spoken his last word in his Son, and he has given his church a book that is finished, sufficient and true. He guards it with his own warning, because it is the bread of his people and the voice of their Shepherd, and he will not let it be poisoned or stolen. Nothing needs to be added to Christ, and nothing in him can be taken away. Blessed be God for his perfect word, which endures for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: He who testifies to these things says, "Surely I am coming soon." Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who testifies to these things says, “Surely I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.

The setting. The earliest Christians prayed in Aramaic, Maranatha, which means Our Lord, come! (1 Corinthians 16:22; Didache 10:6). Paul ended his letters with a grace blessing, and Revelation ends as a letter, as it began (1:4).

He who testifies to these things says, Surely I am coming soon. “He who testifies” (ho martyrōn): Jesus, the faithful witness (1:5). “Surely” (nai, yes, truly). The third and final I am coming soon in this chapter, the last recorded words of Jesus Christ in the Bible. Not a command, not a warning, not a doctrine. A promise about arriving. Everything he is has been unfolded across twenty-two chapters: the one who walks among the lampstands, the Lamb who was slaughtered and is standing, the rider with a sword out of his mouth, the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star. And the last thing he says is that he is on his way and will not be long.

Amen. So be it. John responds for the church. It is the only appropriate reply, and it is barely a word: an agreement.

Come, Lord Jesus! “Come” (erchou). And then a request. The church’s answer to Christ’s promise, the Greek form of Maranatha. In Aramaic, the language the first congregations prayed in before Greek took over, it was one word: Marana tha, Our Lord, come. Paul dropped it untranslated into a letter to Corinth, which means it was already a prayer people said without needing it explained. The final prayer of the Bible. The prayer of a bride for her bridegroom, of a persecuted church for its deliverer, of a groaning creation for its renewal (Romans 8:22–23). This is how Christians should feel about Christ’s return: not fear, but longing. That is the state of the church between the two comings, and it is the answer to everything the book has shown. Not a strategy. Not a timetable. A prayer that Someone would come, said by people who cannot make him come and are certain he will.

A gentle test. It is a fair test of a Christian’s actual condition, gently applied. A person who says Come, Lord Jesus and means it is a person who has nothing here he would be unwilling to have interrupted. That is not a rebuke to anybody who finds the prayer harder than he expected; it is simply what the prayer measures. And Revelation was written to people who could say it because they had already lost most of what a person might have wanted to keep.

The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. “Grace” (charis): God’s undeserved favour in Christ. And the last verse of the Bible is a benediction. Consider what this book has contained. Four horsemen. A third of mankind dead. A dragon waiting to devour a child. A beast given authority over every tribe and people and language and nation. Bowls of wrath. A city drunk on the blood of the saints, burned in a single hour. A great white throne with the books opened and no place found for earth or sky. It is, by a distance, the most terrifying document ever written. And the last word is grace. Not a warning, though there have been many. Not a summary of the judgements. Not instructions for a final generation. The same word Paul ended every one of his letters with, unearned favour given to people who have nothing to bring. The book of judgement ends with grace, as the whole Bible does. Everything in it, from the first word to the last, rests on the grace of the Lord Jesus.

Amen. The last word of the Bible. It means it is firm; it is so.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ on the last line. Some read “with all”; others, “with all the saints” (followed by the ESV footnote); others, followed by the King James Version, “with you all”. The meaning is essentially the same: grace for all God’s people. Some manuscripts omit the final Amen.

What it does not mean. “With all” does not mean that grace will save everyone regardless of faith. The blessing is for those who hear and keep the words of this book (1:3), the church to which it is addressed.

So the Bible closes. It opened with a garden, a river and a tree, and a man and a woman walking with God in the cool of the day; and it closes with a city, a river and a tree, and a countless multitude out of every nation looking directly at his face. Between the two lies the whole of human history, and at the centre of it a Lamb standing as though slaughtered, who took a scroll nobody else was worthy to open, and opened it.

What if I find it hard to pray Come, Lord Jesus? Nothing need be wrong with you; you are being honest, and honesty is where prayer starts. Many believers love this world’s good gifts, a marriage, children, a calling, and fear losing them, or fear the judgement itself. Bring both to God. Remember that his coming does not take away any good thing; it gives every good thing back, perfected, with him at the centre. Remember that the Judge is your Saviour, so you need not fear condemnation. And ask him to make you long for him more than his gifts. Pray the prayer even when it is small; desire grows by being exercised, and he is pleased with the smallest true longing.

How should I live while I wait? Watchfully, not anxiously; busily, not idly. Jesus told parables of servants who were found working when the master came (Matthew 24:45–46), and Paul rebuked those who stopped working to wait for the end (2 Thessalonians 3:10–12). So do your work well, love your family, serve your church, tell others about Christ, and keep your hope fixed on his coming (Titus 2:13). Do not try to set dates; do not let the delay make you careless. Live every day as one of his servants who may be called to give account tonight, and who would be glad of it.

In a sentence. The one who gives this testimony says, Yes, I am coming soon; Amen, come, Lord Jesus! May the grace of the Lord Jesus be with all of you. Amen.

On a Tuesday. Make this your prayer every day: Come, Lord Jesus. Say it in the morning before you look at your phone, and at night when you lie down. Say it at the graveside and in the hospital, and when the news is bad. And rest in his grace until he does. You do not have to hold yourself together until he comes; his grace is with you, and it will be enough for every day between now and then.

For worship. He is the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. He was dead, and behold, he is alive for evermore, and he has the keys of Death and Hades. He walks among his churches, he holds the stars in his right hand, he opened the scroll no one else could open, and he is coming soon. The last thing he says to his people is a promise, and the last thing he leaves with them, after everything, is grace. To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honour and glory and might for ever and ever. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: “Come, Lord Jesus” matches the Aramaic prayer Maranatha that Paul quotes.

The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.<sup>3</sup>No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him.<sup>4</sup>They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.<sup>5</sup>And night will be no more. 15.title: The Song of Moses and the Lamb
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is the shortest chapter in Revelation — eight verses — but it is one of the most carefully constructed. It serves as the vestibule to the seven bowl visions of chapter 16, doing what chapters 4–5 did before the seals and what chapters 8:1–5 did before the trumpets: grounding the coming sequence in the worship and sovereignty of God before a single bowl is poured. Before heaven acts in judgment, heaven first breaks into song.

The chapter presents two contrasting scenes held in deliberate tension. The first (vv. 1–4): the victorious on the sea of glass, harps in hand, singing the Song of Moses and the Lamb. The second (vv. 5–8): seven angels emerge from the heavenly temple dressed for a solemn task, given seven golden bowls by one of the four living creatures, while the temple fills with the glory of God so completely that no one can enter until the seven bowls are finished. Praise and solemn purpose belong together. The song is not premature celebration; it is the theological foundation without which the coming acts of God would be misread.

The Song of Moses and the Lamb is one of the richest theological moments in the book. It binds together the two great saving acts of God — the Exodus and the cross — into a single song of praise. The God who opened the Red Sea is the God who opened the tomb. The Lamb who was slain is the LORD who drowned Pharaoh’s army. The song the victorious sing is drawn almost entirely from the Psalms, Jeremiah, and Deuteronomy — the whole Hebrew Scripture gathered into the church’s final praise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Song of the Victorious
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: another sign in heaven, great and amazing — the third and last of the book’s three signs, after the woman (12:1) and the dragon (12:3). Seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished. The verb is from teleō, the same root as the word from the cross, It is finished (John 19:30).

Verse 2: the sea of glass of 4:6 is now mingled with fire, and standing beside it are those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, holding harps — a direct contradiction of 13:7, where the beast was allowed to conquer them. The position is the far shore of the Red Sea with Egypt behind it.

Verses 3–4: they sing the song of Moses… and the song of the Lamb — one song under two names. Its words are not from Exodus 15 but are a mosaic of Scripture: Great and amazing are your deeds (Ps. 111:2), Just and true are your ways (Deut. 32:4), Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? (Jer. 10:7), All nations will come and worship you (Ps. 86:9). Four clauses, and every one is about God — not one word about the beast, the persecution, or their own endurance.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Song of Moses and the Lamb

Seven angels hold the last plagues, and with them God’s wrath is finished — it has an end, as his mercy does not. Beside the sea of glass, those who conquered the beast sing one song of Moses and the Lamb, made of Scripture and entirely about God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those the beast conquered in the street are standing on the far shore with harps.

Now: Faithfulness that consists in refusing to bow still counts as conquering.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.

Meaning first. Revelation 15 is the shortest chapter in the book, and it does one job: it gets the reader ready. It prepares for the seven bowls of chapter 16, the last plagues, which complete God’s wrath (v. 1). Before the plagues fall, John sees those who conquered the beast standing beside a sea of glass mixed with fire, holding harps (v. 2). Like Israel beside the Red Sea, they sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb, praising God’s great deeds, his just and true ways, his holiness, and the coming worship of all nations (vv. 3–4). Then the heavenly sanctuary, the tent of witness, opens, and seven angels come out dressed as priests (vv. 5–6). One of the living creatures gives them seven golden bowls full of God’s wrath, and the sanctuary fills with smoke from God’s glory, so that no one can enter until the plagues are finished (vv. 7–8). The chapter places the final judgements inside worship: the redeemed praise God’s justice before it is displayed, and the judgements come out of his holy presence. Chapter 16 will pour out seven bowls in twenty-one verses, faster and heavier than anything in the book, and these eight verses are the deep breath before it. Before a single drop falls, heaven has already sung that every one of God’s ways is just and true.

The setting. The bowl judgements follow the pattern of the plagues on Egypt even more closely than the trumpets did: sores, water turned to blood, darkness, frogs, hail. And the scene by the sea of glass recalls Israel singing beside the Red Sea after God destroyed Pharaoh’s army (Exodus 15). The new exodus is complete. John’s first readers, small congregations in Asia under the shadow of Rome, would have heard the whole story of their own deliverance in the shape of the one their Bible began with: a tyrant who would not let God’s people go, plagues that broke his power, a sea, a far shore, and a song.

Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing. The word is sēmeion, sign, and John has used it of signs in heaven twice before, both times in chapter 12: the woman clothed with the sun (12:1) and the great red dragon (12:3). This is the third, and the only other. A woman, a dragon, and seven angels with the last plagues: the mother, the enemy, and the end. The book has been telling one story all along, and this sign announces its final movement.

Great and amazing. It is an odd pair of words for a plague, and John will use them again in two verses about God’s deeds (thaumaston, marvellous, a thing to wonder at). What is being described is not merely dreadful. It is astonishing, in the way something enormous and long expected is astonishing when it finally begins. The plagues are not the collapse of God’s plan. They are one of his works, and heaven looks at them the way it looks at creation and redemption: with wonder.

Seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last. The word for plagues (plēgas) means blows, strokes, the wounds left by striking. And they are the last (eschatas): the final series. The seals struck a quarter of the earth (6:8), the trumpets a third (8:7–12); the bowls strike everything. Each series has been wider than the one before, like a doctor who first warns, then insists, and finally operates.

For with them the wrath of God is finished. This is the clause that governs the whole of chapter 16. The verb is etelesthē, from teleō, to bring to an end, to complete, to carry to its goal. It is the same root as the word Jesus spoke from the cross: it is finished (John 19:30, tetelestai). Something is being brought to its appointed completion, and the sentence says so before a single bowl is lifted.

The wrath of God has an end. That is a strange and necessary thing to be told at this point in the book. A reader who has come through six chapters of dragons and beasts and marks might reasonably fear that the wrath of God is a reservoir with no bottom to it, that once it starts it simply continues. This verse says the opposite. God’s wrath is not endless rage in history; it has a goal and an end. The end is in view from the moment it begins, and there is a last plague after which there are no more. When the bowls are poured out, God’s judgement on this age is complete.

His mercy has no last plague. And that is not true of his mercy, which is the point of the contrast. Scripture says again and again that his steadfast love endures for ever, and it never once says that of his anger. His anger is for a moment and his favour for a lifetime (Psalm 30:5). He does not keep his anger for ever, because he delights in steadfast love (Micah 7:18). Judgement in the Bible always has a stopping point written into it. Grace does not.

Two places where wrath is finished. There is one more thing in the word finished. If the wrath of God against sin is a thing that can be completed, the question worth asking is where it was completed for a Christian, and the answer is the cross, where the same verb was used by the same author about the same wrath. There, God’s wrath against his people’s sin was finished, borne in full by Christ in their place. Here, his wrath against the unrepentant world is completed. There are two places in John’s writings where the wrath of God is brought to its end. One of them is a hill outside Jerusalem, and for everyone who trusts in Christ it happened before any of this began.

What it does not mean. “Last” does not necessarily mean the bowls happen after the seals and trumpets in strict time. They are the last in John’s sequence of visions and in their intensity, describing the final outpouring of God’s judgement, which the earlier series also reached in their own way (6:12–17; 11:15–19). Revelation tells the story of the age between Christ’s first and second comings several times over, each time from a new angle and with mounting force, and each time arriving at the end.

Does finished mean the wicked stop being punished? No. The wrath of God is finished in the sense that his judgements on this present age reach their goal: the plagues stop, history is wound up, and Christ returns. But Revelation is plain that the punishment of those who refuse him is conscious and without end (14:10–11; 20:10, 15). What is finished in chapter 16 is the series of warning blows in history, the last chances given to a rebellious world. After that comes not a pause and a fresh start but the final judgement. That is exactly why the word finished is such good news for a Christian and such a solemn one for anyone else.

How can a God of love have wrath at all? Because love that is never angry at what destroys the beloved is not love but indifference. God’s wrath is not a bad temper or a loss of control. It is his settled, holy opposition to evil, the same holiness that makes him faithful and kind. A father who felt nothing when someone harmed his child would not be more loving for it. And the gospel does not say that God set his wrath aside to love us. It says that he loved us so much that he bore his own wrath in his Son (Romans 3:25–26; 1 John 4:10). The cross is where love and wrath meet, and neither is diminished.

In a sentence. Then I saw another great and astonishing sign in heaven: seven angels holding the seven last plagues, the last because with them God’s anger is brought to completion.

On a Tuesday. When the news is full of disaster and the world seems to be coming apart, remember that nothing in it is beyond God’s measuring. Even his judgements are counted: seven, and the last. If you are a Christian, the wrath that hung over your sins was finished at Golgotha, and nothing in chapter 16 is aimed at you. So you can look at the worst headlines without despair. And when you think of friends who do not know Christ, let the word last move you. The blows will not go on for ever, and the time to turn is now.

For worship. God’s judgement has an end, and he wrote the end into it before the first bowl was lifted. His anger is for a moment; his steadfast love is for ever. And the same God who will finish his wrath on a world that refuses him has already finished it for his people, in the body of his Son, on a cross outside the city, where a single word declared that nothing was left to pay. It is finished: no sentence has ever been more full of mercy, and it was spoken by the one who bore the wrath himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.

The setting. Israel crossed the Red Sea and stood on the far shore, safe, while the waters closed over Pharaoh’s army (Exodus 14:26–31). Then Moses and Israel sang (Exodus 15:1–18), and Miriam led the women with tambourines (Exodus 15:20–21). The sea of glass first appeared before God’s throne in 4:6, flat and still and clear as crystal.

And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire. In chapter 4 the sea of glass was stretched out in front of the throne, calm and transparent: the sea, which in the Bible stands for chaos and the place the beast came up from (13:1), frozen solid and lying subdued under God’s feet. Now there is fire in it (memigmenēn pyri, mixed with fire). Something has changed in the eleven chapters between, and the fire is judgement: the same fire that was taken from the altar and thrown down on the earth (8:5), or the reflection of God’s blazing holiness. The floor of heaven has begun to glow.

And also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name. Stop at the verb, because it directly contradicts something the reader was told two chapters ago. At 13:7 the beast was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. Here the same people are the conquering ones (nikōntas). The same verb, nikaō, in the opposite direction, about the same encounter.

Both statements are true. Holding them together is the single most important thing this book asks of a suffering Christian. From the street, the beast won: the believers were arrested, tried and killed, and there is no version of events in which that did not happen. From the sea of glass, they won: they are standing, with instruments in their hands, and the beast is not in the room. And 12:11 has already explained how a defeat becomes a victory: they conquered by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they did not love their lives even to death. The winning was not survival. It was refusing to let go, and the losing of the life was part of the victory rather than a failure of it.

A victory made of refusals. Note what they conquered, listed in three parts: the beast and its image and the number of its name. Not an army, but a demand. They were not asked to defeat anything. They were asked to bow, to worship an image, and to take a number that would have let them keep buying and selling (13:16–17). Their whole victory consists of things they did not do. Say that plainly to any Christian who suspects his faithfulness is too quiet to count. The company standing on the sea of glass did not storm anything. They declined. They said no to a formality, again and again, at rising cost, and heaven files that under conquered.

Standing beside the sea of glass. The preposition (epi) can mean beside or upon, and the picture is Israel on the far shore of the Red Sea with the water behind them and Egypt at the bottom of it, which is exactly what the next verse makes explicit. They have come through the great tribulation (7:14) and stand safe. The people who came through are standing on the far bank, and the first thing they do is sing.

With harps of God in their hands. Harps given by God for his worship (5:8; 14:2). Even the instruments are his gift. The people who were stripped of everything on earth, their freedom, their trade, their lives, are handed something in heaven, and what they are handed is a way to praise him.

What it does not mean. The conquerors are not a special group of martyrs only. All who refuse the beast’s worship and remain faithful to Christ, whether or not they are killed, are conquerors. Revelation’s promises to the one who conquers are made to every faithful believer in the seven churches (2:7, 11, 17, 26; 3:5, 12, 21).

What is the beast today, and what is its mark? In Revelation the beast is the power of the state or culture when it sets itself up as God, demanding the loyalty that belongs to Christ alone; Rome was its form in John’s day, and it takes new forms in every age until the end. Its mark is not a microchip or a tattoo that someone could receive by accident. It is the stamp of belonging, seen in what a person thinks (the forehead) and does (the hand), the opposite of the seal of God on his servants (7:3; 14:1). So the question is not whether you have been scanned but whom you worship, and whether you will keep your loyalty to Christ when it costs you.

I have never been persecuted. Am I really among the conquerors? If you belong to Christ and are holding fast to him, yes. Conquering in this book is not measured by how dramatic the pressure was but by whether faith held. For most believers the beast’s demands come quietly: the colleague who expects you to laugh along, the promotion that requires a lie, the cultural script that says your faith must stay private, the slow pull of comfort and money. Every time you choose Christ over those, you are refusing the image and the number. And the strength to do it is his gift, not your achievement. He keeps his people, and every one of them will stand on that shore (John 10:28–29).

In a sentence. And I saw what looked like a sea of glass mixed with fire, and standing beside it, holding harps given by God, were those who had won the victory over the beast, its image and the number of its name.

On a Tuesday. Notice the small refusals this week: the joke you did not tell, the figure you did not fudge, the compromise you did not make so as to fit in. They feel like nothing. Heaven calls them conquering. And when a fellow believer is losing something real for Christ, a job, a friendship, a reputation, tell them what this verse tells you: from the street it looks like defeat, but from the sea of glass it is victory.

For worship. Christ is the conqueror who makes conquerors. He was arrested, tried and killed, and from the street it looked as if Rome had won; three days later the grave was empty, and the defeat turned out to be the victory of the ages. Everyone who is his shares in that pattern. The beast can take their lives, and it cannot take them, because the Lamb has written their names in his book. And on the far shore, with the sea of fire behind them, he puts a harp into hands that were once in chains. He loses none of his own, and every one of them will sing.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, "Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, “Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed.”

The setting. The song of Moses in Exodus 15 celebrated God’s victory over Pharaoh: who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness? (Exodus 15:11). Deuteronomy 32, another song of Moses, says that God’s work is perfect, that all his ways are justice, that he is a God of faithfulness, without iniquity, just and upright (Deuteronomy 32:4). The words of this new song are drawn almost entirely from Old Testament praise: Psalm 86:9 (all the nations shall come and worship before the Lord and glorify his name), Psalm 98:1–2, Psalm 111:2, Psalm 139:14, Psalm 145:17, Jeremiah 10:6–7 (who would not fear you, O King of the nations?), and Malachi 1:11.

And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb. Not two songs but one. The grammar allows a single song called by two names, and the content proves it: what follows is sung by both at once, because there is only one deliverance and it has two chapters. The song of Moses is Exodus 15, sung on the far side of the sea with Pharaoh’s army drowned behind them. That is why John has just put these people beside the sea. Israel came out of Egypt through water; these have come out of the beast’s empire through fire and death; and the song is the same song, because the God who did the first did the second. As Moses led Israel out of Egypt through the sea, the Lamb has led his people out of the world’s bondage through his blood. The first exodus and the final exodus are celebrated together.

Moses the servant, Christ the Lamb. Moses is called the servant of God, which is his great title in the Old Testament (Numbers 12:7; Joshua 1:2). The letter to the Hebrews draws the line exactly: Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6). The servant led the people through the sea; the Lamb led them through death by going into it first. The redeemed sing both names because the whole Bible is one story, and Moses was always pointing to the one whose song this finally is.

The redeemed sing in quotations. Here is something surprising. The words that follow are not from Exodus 15 at all. They are a mosaic of the Psalms and the prophets, stitched together. Great and amazing are your deeds (Psalm 111:2; 139:14). Just and true are your ways (Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 145:17). Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? (Jeremiah 10:7). All the nations shall come and worship (Psalm 86:9). The worship of heaven is made out of the Scriptures God’s people were given on earth, which is a quiet argument for filling a mind with them now. The Bible you read this morning is the hymnbook of eternity.

Every line is about God. Look at what the song is about, because it is not what a persecuted church would have been expected to sing. There is not one word in it about the beast, about the persecution, about what they suffered, or about their own endurance. Four clauses, and every one of them is about God: his deeds, his ways, his name, his righteous acts. The singers have forgotten themselves entirely. That is what heaven does to people: it makes them so taken up with God that their own story becomes a footnote to his.

Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! His deeds (erga, works) in creation, redemption and judgement. Almighty (pantokratōr), as in 1:8, the one who holds all things. The beast seemed to rule the world for forty-two months; the singers know who was holding it the whole time.

Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! Just (dikaiai, righteous) and true (alēthinai, faithful, genuine, real). Before the bowls are poured out, the redeemed declare that God’s ways are just. His judgements are not arbitrary or cruel; they are right. And King of the nations means not Caesar, but God. This is the sentence these particular singers are qualified to say. Anybody can affirm the justice of God from a comfortable chair. These people were killed for refusing a number, they have come out the other side, and the first thing they say about the way God ran history is that it was just. No complaint. Not because the question was never asked: it was asked, loudly, under the altar in 6:10, how long, O Lord? But it has been answered.

Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? The question is rhetorical and expects the answer nobody: everyone ought to fear him and give him glory. To fear God here is not to cower but to stand in awe, to take him with the seriousness he deserves. The song has just praised his justice and now calls the whole world to respond to it.

For you alone are holy. The ground given is not power but holiness. The word is hosios, devout, pure, holy, used of God in Revelation only here and in 16:5. You alone: there is one of him, and the beast that demanded worship for forty-two months is not in the category. Every rival claim to ultimate loyalty, ancient or modern, is answered by those four words.

All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed. This is the widest sentence in the chapter, and it is startling in a book so full of judgement. The nations who raged (11:18), who drank Babylon’s wine (14:8), over whom the beast was given authority (13:7), will come and worship. It is Psalm 86:9 quoted almost straight, and it is the promise made to Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Righteous acts (dikaiōmata) are God’s just deeds, his judgements and his saving acts. And notice what finally brings the nations in: not that God overwhelmed them, but that his righteous acts were seen clearly. This looks to the great multitude from every nation (7:9) and to the nations walking by the light of the new Jerusalem (21:24–26). God will have the nations, and the multitude is not a consolation prize.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ on God’s title in v. 3. The best manuscripts read “King of the nations”; others read “King of the ages”; later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “King of saints”. All three are true of God; “nations” fits the song’s theme of all nations coming to worship.

Where Christians differ: will all nations, and so all people, be saved? Universalists sometimes cite “all nations will come and worship you” as proof that everyone will finally be saved. Verdict: “all nations” means people from every nation, not every individual in every nation. The great multitude comes from every nation, tribe, people and language (7:9), but Revelation is clear that those who worship the beast and refuse to repent are judged for ever (14:9–11; 21:8; 22:15). The song celebrates the worldwide scope of God’s salvation, fulfilling his promise to Abraham, and the universal acknowledgement of his justice. Every knee will bow (Philippians 2:10–11), but not every knee bows in love.

What it does not mean. The redeemed do not praise God’s justice because they are hard-hearted toward the lost. They praise it because they see clearly, as we often cannot, that every one of his ways is right.

How can people in heaven praise God for judging people they loved? Because in heaven they will see what we only believe now: that God has been perfectly fair to every person, that no one is condemned who did not freely refuse him, and that his patience was longer than anyone deserved. Our hesitation comes partly from our love, which is good, and partly from our limited sight and our sense that sin is not so bad, which is not. The redeemed will not love less. They will love as God loves, and see as God sees. Until then, the right response to the thought of the lost is not to doubt God’s justice but to plead with people while there is time, and to trust the Judge of all the earth to do right (Genesis 18:25).

Should we still sing of God’s justice in church? Yes. The songs of heaven are full of it, and a church that sings only of God’s comfort and never of his holiness and justice is singing a smaller God than the one who is there. It matters especially for persecuted and wronged believers, for whom the justice of God is not a threat but a hope: no evil will go unanswered. Songs like this teach us to rest in his rule. And it should always be sung with the cross in view, because the justice that will judge the world is the justice that was satisfied for us in Christ.

In a sentence. They sing the song of God’s servant Moses and the song of the Lamb: Great and wonderful are your works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are your ways, King of the nations; who will not fear you, Lord, and give glory to your name? You alone are holy; all nations will come and bow down before you, because your just acts have been made plain for all to see.

On a Tuesday. When you cannot understand what God is doing, in your own life or in the world, say this song before you say anything else: your ways are just and true. You may still bring the question; the martyrs did. But bring it as someone who already knows how the song ends. And make the Psalms your own now, because they are the words you will sing for ever. Learn a line of one this week and pray it back to him.

For worship. You alone are holy, Lord God Almighty. Your works are great and amazing: you made the sea and you dried it; you broke Pharaoh and you broke the beast; you led your people out of Egypt by the hand of your servant and out of death by the blood of your Lamb. Your ways are just and true, and the people who suffered most under them are the first to say so. The nations that raged against you will come and bow, from every tongue and tribe, because your righteous acts have been revealed. And the greatest of those acts was the day your justice and your mercy met on a cross, when the Lamb was slain and by his blood ransomed a people for God.
verseByVerse.note: As Israel sang beside the sea after the exodus, so God’s redeemed sing after their deliverance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — The Sanctuary Filled with Smoke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 5: the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened. The phrase is the Old Testament’s name for the tabernacle, the tent that housed the ark, which housed the tablets called the testimony because they are God’s witness against a people who agreed to keep them (Ex. 38:21; Num. 1:50). The bowls come out of the place where the covenant is kept.

Verse 6: out come the seven angels, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests — priestly dress (Lev. 16:4; Dan. 10:5), and precisely how the risen Christ was described at 1:13.

Verse 7: one of the four living creatures — the beings nearest the throne, who never cease to say holy, holy, holy — hands over seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God. The word is phialē, a shallow libation dish that empties in a moment, not a jug.

Verse 8: the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgement as Liturgy

The bowls come out of the tent of witness, carried by angels in priestly linen and handed over by a worshipper. The golden bowls that once held prayers now hold wrath, and the sanctuary is closed until the plagues are finished.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The judgement rests on the covenant kept since Sinai.

Now: The sanctuary is open today, with a high priest interceding inside it — pray while it is.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened, and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened, and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.

The setting. The tabernacle in the wilderness was called the tent of witness or testimony (Numbers 17:7; 18:2), because it held the ark containing the tablets of the law, the testimony of God’s covenant (Exodus 25:16; 31:18; 38:21; Numbers 1:50). The priests wore white linen when they entered the holy place (Leviticus 16:4). Christ in 1:13 wore a golden sash around his chest, and Daniel’s heavenly man was clothed in linen with a belt of fine gold (Daniel 10:5).

After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened. The sanctuary (naos) is the inner shrine, the holy place itself. The tent of witness (tēs skēnēs tou martyriou) is the heavenly reality of which the earthly tabernacle was a copy (Hebrews 8:5). The phrase is precise and old. The ark held the two tablets of the law, which are called the testimony because they are God’s witness to the covenant, and his witness against a people who agreed to keep it and did not.

Wrath from the place where the covenant is kept. So the bowls of wrath come out of the place where the covenant is kept. Not out of an armoury and not out of a prison, but out of the tent that holds God’s law. That is the difference between the judgements of this book and mere destruction. What is coming has a legal basis, and the document it rests on has been in the same box since Sinai. The judgements that follow come from God’s holy law, which the world has broken.

Opened twice. At 11:19 the temple in heaven was opened and the ark of the covenant was seen. Here the sanctuary opens again, and something comes out of it. Twice in five chapters the doors of heaven’s holy place stand open, and the second time it is not to show the reader something but to release seven angels.

And out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues. They come from God’s very presence. The judgements are holy acts, carried out by those who stand before God.

Clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests. They are dressed as priests. Linen (linon) was what the priest wore into the holy place (Leviticus 16:4), and a golden sash across the chest is exactly how the risen Christ was dressed in the first chapter of this book (1:13). The sashes show their dignity and their connection with him. And the linen is pure and bright: the second word is the one used of the Bride’s dress at 19:8. Nothing that comes out of that door is dirty. Whatever a reader has to say about the severity of chapter 16, he will not be able to say that the hands carrying it were.

Judgement as liturgy. That combination should stop a reader, because it refuses two easy pictures at once. These are not demons let loose, and they are not soldiers. They are ministers in priestly dress, coming out of a sanctuary, carrying out a service. The judgement of God is not a loss of control, and it is not something he hands off to others to do in a manner unlike himself. It is worship. The same holiness that is praised in the song is carried out in the plagues.

What it does not mean. The angels are not acting on their own initiative. They come out of the sanctuary; they serve God’s will.

Why does God’s law still matter if Christians are not saved by keeping it? Because the law is the expression of God’s own holy character, and it is the standard by which the world is judged (Romans 2:12–16; 3:19–20). It cannot save us; it shows us our need of Christ, who kept it perfectly and bore its curse for us (Galatians 3:13). But for the believer it remains the good and holy rule of life, now written on the heart by the Spirit (Jeremiah 31:33; Romans 8:4). The tent of witness in heaven tells us that God has not lowered his standard. What he has done is meet it himself, in his Son.

In a sentence. After this I looked, and the inner shrine of the tent of the testimony in heaven was opened, and the seven angels holding the seven plagues came out of it, dressed in pure, shining linen, with gold sashes around their chests.

On a Tuesday. God’s law is not a dead letter. It stands at the centre of heaven, and its testimony will be upheld. Take it seriously in your own life: not as a ladder to climb to God, but as the shape of the life he is making in you. Read the Ten Commandments this week and ask, honestly, where your heart is out of step with them. Then take each failure to the one who kept them all for you.

For worship. Our God is holy in his law and holy in his judgements, and even his wrath comes dressed in white. He has never broken his covenant, and his testimony has stood in the heart of heaven since the day he wrote it with his finger on stone. And the same law that will be upheld against a rebellious world was upheld for us in a different way: the Son of God was born under it, kept it in every thought and deed, and bore its curse in our place. In him, the testimony that was against us has become the ground of our peace.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever, and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever, and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.

The setting. Golden bowls were used in the temple for carrying incense and the blood of sacrifices (1 Kings 7:50; 2 Chronicles 4:22). The golden bowls of 5:8 were full of incense, the prayers of the saints. When the tabernacle and the temple were dedicated, God’s glory filled them as a cloud, so that Moses and the priests could not enter (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11). In Isaiah’s vision, the house was filled with smoke (Isaiah 6:4).

And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls. The handover is made by one of the four living creatures, the beings nearest the throne, full of eyes, who have been saying holy, holy, holy day and night without ceasing (4:8). The worshippers are the ones who pass the bowls. Nothing in this chapter allows judgement to be handled by anybody outside the worship of God. And a living creature, representing creation, hands them over: creation itself has been groaning for its liberation (Romans 8:19–22).

A bowl, not a trumpet. The word for bowl is phialē, a shallow, wide dish used for pouring out an offering, not a jug or a jar. It empties in a moment. Compare the trumpets: a trumpet is a warning, blown to be heard, giving time to respond. A bowl is tipped once, and it is gone. The instrument itself says that the time of warnings is running out.

The same bowls. The reader has seen golden bowls in this book before, and the connection is deliberate and almost unbearable. At 5:8 the elders held golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. The same vessels, in the same throne room. Golden bowls went up full of prayer; golden bowls come down full of wrath. God’s judgement is the answer to his people’s prayers. The martyrs asked how long? and these are the vessels in which the answer is delivered.

Full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever. Full (gemousas), filled to the brim. The eternal God’s wrath is not a passing temper. It is his settled, holy opposition to evil, and it belongs to the one who lives for ever and ever, which means no tyrant can outlive it and no evil can wait it out.

And the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power. Smoke (kapnou) filling the sanctuary is an old and glorious sight. When the tabernacle was finished, the cloud covered the tent of meeting, the glory of the LORD filled it, and Moses was not able to enter (Exodus 40:34–35). When Solomon dedicated the temple, the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house (1 Kings 8:10–11). Isaiah saw the house filled with smoke and cried, woe is me (Isaiah 6:4–5). It is God’s glory and power in overwhelming holiness, as at Sinai.

And no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished. In every one of those earlier cases the smoke meant God had come to dwell, and the exclusion was brief and joyful. Here it means something colder. Consider what the sanctuary is for. It is where a priest goes in to intercede, where blood is brought and pleading is done and mercy is asked for somebody else. And for the duration of the seven bowls, nobody goes in. No one can intercede now. The time for mediation is past; judgement must run its course. This is the most solemn moment in the book: the door of intercession closes. It should not be softened. There comes a point at which the door is shut, not because God has become unwilling to hear, but because the case has been closed, the warnings have been given, and the answering has begun.

Until. But note the exact wording, because it is also the mercy in the verse: until. The closure has a limit, and the limit is the one given in verse 1, when the wrath of God is finished. Even the shutting of the sanctuary has an end date, and beyond it lies the new creation, where the dwelling of God is with man (21:3) and no one is ever shut out of his presence again.

What it does not mean. This does not mean that today it is too late to pray or to turn to God. The scene describes the final judgement at the end of history. Today is still the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2), and Christ still intercedes for all who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25).

Should I pray for God to judge my enemies? Pray first, as Jesus commanded, for their good and their salvation (Matthew 5:44), as Stephen did for the men stoning him (Acts 7:60). That is the Christian’s first prayer. Yet it is also right to pray for God’s kingdom to come and for evil to be ended, and the martyrs’ cry for justice is not rebuked (6:9–11). The answer is to leave vengeance with God (Romans 12:19). He will judge rightly, and he may answer your prayer for justice by turning your enemy into a brother, as he did with Saul of Tarsus. Either way, you do not have to carry the score.

Could it already be too late for me? If you are worried that you have gone too far, that worry is itself a sign that the door is still open. The people shut out in this verse are not anxious seekers; they are those who refused every warning to the end. As long as you are alive and Christ is still offered to you, the sanctuary is open and the High Priest is inside it, praying for those who come to God through him. No one who comes to Christ is ever turned away (John 6:37). Do not wait to feel ready. Come now.

In a sentence. Then one of the four living beings gave the seven angels seven gold bowls filled with the anger of God, who lives for ever and ever, and the temple was filled with smoke from God’s glory and power, so that no one could go into it until the seven plagues of the seven angels were over.

On a Tuesday. There will come a day when it is too late. Today it is not. The sanctuary is standing wide, and there is a great high priest inside it who always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). While that is true, pray: for yourself, and for the people whose names you would not want read out on the day the smoke fills the room. Write down two or three of those names this week, pray for them by name, and look for one opportunity to speak to one of them about Christ while the door is open.

For worship. The God of this chapter lives for ever and ever, and his glory fills his temple so completely that no creature can stand in it. Yet that same God opened the way into his presence for sinners. When his Son died, the curtain of the temple was torn from top to bottom, and a great High Priest passed through the heavens with his own blood. He is in the sanctuary now, and he always lives to intercede. The prayers of his people rise in golden bowls, and not one of them is lost. Glory be to the one who shuts the door at the end, and who has held it open for so long, at such a cost, for us.

15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.<sup>2</sup>And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.<sup>3</sup>And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, “Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations!<sup>4</sup>Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed.”<sup>5</sup>After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened,<sup>6</sup>and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.<sup>7</sup>And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever,<sup>8</sup>and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.

16.title: The Seven Bowls: The Completion of Divine Justice
16.overview:
Chapter 16 is the third and final series of seven judgments in Revelation, and it is the most intense. Where the seals affected a quarter of the earth and the trumpets a third, the bowls are poured on the whole earth without fraction. The escalation is deliberate: the time for partial warning has passed. These are the last plagues, and with them the response of God to the accumulated rebellion of history reaches its completion.

The bowl series follows the Exodus plague pattern more closely than either the seals or the trumpets. Bowls one through five draw on the Egyptian plagues, though not in their order: sores (bowl 1, cf. Exodus 9:8–11), water turned to blood (bowls 2–3, cf. Exodus 7:17–21), darkness (bowl 5, cf. Exodus 10:21–23). The Exodus pattern is not decorative. It carries a theological message: the God who liberated Israel from Egypt is the same God who now acts in the final Exodus. The pattern of redemptive history repeats at the cosmic scale.

The chapter reaches its climax at the seventh bowl: a loud voice from the throne declares ‘It is done!’ and the greatest earthquake in human history splits the great city into three parts. Babylon is remembered before God and given the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. Every island flees, every mountain disappears. The chapter ends not with despair but with the certainty that the one who declared ‘It is done’ from the cross has declared it again from the throne — all things are now moving irresistibly toward the new creation of chapters 21–22.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: a loud voice from the temple — almost certainly God’s own, since 15:8 has just closed the sanctuary to everyone else — orders the seven angels to pour. Verse 2: the first bowl brings harmful and painful sores on those who bore the mark of the beast and worshipped its image (cf. Ex. 9:8–11).

Verse 3: the sea becomes like the blood of a corpse and everything in it dies — against the second trumpet, which killed a third (8:8–9). Verse 4: the rivers and springs become blood, as the Nile did (Ex. 7:20–21).

Verses 5–7 stop the sequence and defend it. The angel in charge of the waters — whose department has just been ruined — declares Just are you, O Holy One… they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve! And then the altar itself answers: Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!

Verses 8–9: the fourth bowl turns the sun up, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory. Verses 10–11: the fifth falls on the throne of the beast and its kingdom goes dark (cf. Ex. 10:21–23); people gnaw their tongues in anguish and curse the God of heaven for their pain and sores, and did not repent of their deeds.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Same Ground, Undiluted

The bowls strike earth, sea, rivers, sun and the beast’s throne — the trumpets’ targets, now without limit. The angel of the waters and the altar itself declare God’s judgements true and just. Those struck curse God and do not repent.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The plagues of Egypt return in one chapter, and the mark becomes the wound.

Now: Suffering drives some to their knees and hardens others; it depends which way a person was already facing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard a loud voice from the temple telling the seven angels, "Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God." So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I heard a loud voice from the temple telling the seven angels, “Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God.” So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.

Meaning first. Revelation 16 pours out the seven bowls of God’s wrath, the last and fullest judgements on a world that has chosen the beast. The first bowl brings painful sores on the beast’s worshippers (vv. 1–2); the second turns the sea to blood (v. 3); the third turns the rivers and springs to blood, and the angel of the waters and the altar declare God just, for those who shed the saints’ blood are given blood to drink (vv. 4–7). The fourth scorches people with the sun, and they curse God and do not repent (vv. 8–9). The fifth plunges the beast’s kingdom into darkness, and still they curse God and do not repent (vv. 10–11). The sixth dries up the Euphrates for the kings of the east, and three frog-like demonic spirits from the mouths of the dragon, beast and false prophet gather the kings of the whole world for battle on the great day of God, at the place called Armageddon; in the middle, Christ warns that he comes like a thief, and blesses those who stay awake (vv. 12–16). The seventh bowl brings the voice from the throne, It is done!, with the greatest earthquake ever known: Babylon splits apart and drains the cup of God’s wrath, islands and mountains vanish, and huge hailstones fall, and still people curse God (vv. 17–21). Like the seals and trumpets, the bowls reach the end of history; unlike them, they are complete, not partial. They show God’s justice against those who persecute his people, and the terrible hardness of hearts that will not repent. And standing over all of it is the God whom heaven calls holy, true and just, who has heard every prayer of his suffering people and answers them all.

The setting. The bowls follow the plagues on Egypt closely: sores (the sixth plague, Exodus 9:8–12), water turned to blood (the first, Exodus 7:17–21), darkness (the ninth, Exodus 10:21–23), frogs (the second, Exodus 8:1–15), and hail (the seventh, Exodus 9:22–26). Five of the ten, in one chapter. The empire is Egypt, and the God who broke Egypt has not changed his methods. As Pharaoh hardened his heart, so do the beast’s worshippers. And the trumpets and bowls run in parallel: both strike earth, sea, rivers, sun, the realm of darkness and the Euphrates, and both end with the final judgement. But the trumpets struck a third; the bowls strike all.

Three things that govern the chapter. Before the first bowl is tipped, three things should be set out, because they govern all twenty-one verses. First, the targets are the same as the trumpets, in the same order: compare 8:7–12 and 9:13–14, and the correspondence is almost item for item. What has changed is the extent. That parallel is one of the strongest arguments for reading the three sevens as recapitulation, the same ground covered again at greater intensity (see on 6:1). Second, Egypt is here again, more densely than anywhere else in the book. Third, and this is the drumbeat of the chapter: three times John records that the people struck by these plagues cursed God and did not repent (vv. 9, 11, 21).

Then I heard a loud voice from the temple telling the seven angels. Nobody in the previous chapter could enter the sanctuary (15:8), and the voice comes out of it anyway. It is almost certainly God’s own: the temple is full of the smoke of his glory and closed to everybody else. Whoever else is involved in what follows, the order to begin is given by the one on the throne.

Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God. The verb (ekcheete, pour out) is the word for drink offerings and for blood poured out at the base of the altar. Psalm 79:6 prayed for exactly this: pour out your anger on the nations that do not know you. The prayer of the psalmist and the prayers of the saints in 5:8 are being answered.

So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth. The land, first, as with the first trumpet.

And harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image. The word for sores (helkos, an ulcer, a festering wound) is the word used in the Greek Old Testament for the boils on the Egyptians. Harmful and painful (kakon kai ponēron) is literally bad and evil. The sixth plague on Egypt was boils breaking out in sores on man and beast (Exodus 9:8–11), and it is the one the magicians could not stand up to: they could not stand before Moses because the boils were on them too. Whatever else Egypt’s wisdom could imitate, it could not imitate health.

The mark becomes the wound. Note precisely who is struck: the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshipped its image. The bowls are not indiscriminate. Chapter 13 said that anyone who refused the mark could not buy or sell; the mark was the ticket to a working life. Here those who took the beast’s mark bear another mark on their bodies. What was taken as a passport turns out to be the wound. That removes the sense of arbitrariness, because it is how judgement usually works in Scripture. God rarely invents a punishment unconnected to the offence. He hands people over to what they insisted on having: God gave them up, three times in one paragraph (Romans 1:24, 26, 28).

What it does not mean. The bowls are not aimed at believers. As in Egypt, where the plagues did not touch Israel in Goshen, God’s people are not the targets of his wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9). They may still suffer from the beast, but not from God’s anger.

Are the bowls still future, or happening now? Both, in a sense. Revelation shows the whole age between Christ’s comings several times over, and the bowls are the final and fullest view, pressing hard toward the end. The kinds of judgement they picture, sickness, disaster, the collapse of proud powers, recur throughout history as warnings, and they will reach their climax in the last days before Christ returns. So we should neither treat every disaster as one specific bowl, nor imagine that the God of these bowls is idle now. He is ruling history, and its end is already written.

If disaster strikes everyone, how are believers protected? Christians live in the same world and can suffer the same illnesses, floods and wars as their neighbours, and sometimes the beast’s hatred besides. The protection promised is not that nothing will touch us, but that nothing that touches us is God’s wrath. For the believer, the same events are a Father’s discipline, a trial of faith, or a share in Christ’s sufferings, and all of them are working for good (Romans 8:28). The sealed belong to God (7:3), and no plague can separate them from his love (Romans 8:35–39).

In a sentence. Then I heard a loud voice from the temple telling the seven angels, Go and pour out the seven bowls of God’s anger on the earth; so the first angel went and poured his bowl on the land, and ugly, painful sores broke out on the people who had the beast’s mark and worshipped its image.

On a Tuesday. Whatever mark people choose, they will bear its consequences. Think of what you are tempted to take on in order to keep up: a habit, a dishonesty, a loyalty that crowds out Christ. Every such mark promises to open doors and ends by festering. Choose today to belong to the Lamb, and ask him to show you any mark you have been carrying that is not his.

For worship. The God who breaks Egypt has not changed. He is the same LORD who struck Pharaoh with boils and brought his people out with a mighty hand, and he will not let the beast keep them either. His wrath is exact, falling where it is deserved and nowhere else. And for those who belong to the Lamb, it will not fall at all, because the wound it should have made was made already, in the hands and side of the Son of God. By his wounds we are healed.
verseByVerse.note: The bowls are the last and fullest judgments; unlike the trumpets, they are not limited to a third.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became like the blood of a corpse, and every living thing died that was in the sea. The third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became like the blood of a corpse, and every living thing died that was in the sea. The third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood.

The setting. The first plague on Egypt turned the Nile and all Egypt’s waters to blood, so that the fish died and the river stank (Exodus 7:17–21). The second trumpet turned a third of the sea to blood (8:8–9) and the third made a third of the rivers bitter (8:10–11).

The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became like the blood of a corpse. The comparison is deliberately revolting: not bright blood from a wound but the blood of a corpse (haima hōs nekrou, blood as of a dead man), dark, thickened, going bad. Anyone who has been in a room with a body knows what is being described. It is a horrifying image of death, and it is meant to be.

And every living thing died that was in the sea. Every (pasa). Set it against the second trumpet, which turned a third of the sea to blood and killed a third of its creatures (8:8–9). Here there is no fraction. The restraint that has governed every judgement since chapter 6, a fourth, a third, a tenth, forty-two months, a fence around the winds, is gone. Not a third, as with the trumpets, but all. The bowls are complete.

The third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood. Fresh water, essential for life, is gone. The first plague on Egypt turned the Nile to blood so that the Egyptians could not drink from it (Exodus 7:20–21), and the Nile was the river into which Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew boy thrown (Exodus 1:22). The river was given back to Egypt in the condition Egypt had put it in. And the world that rejected the living water (7:17; 21:6) loses even ordinary water.

What the world lives on and lives by. Take the two bowls together and notice what has been removed. The sea is where the beast came from (13:1) and where the world’s trade ran; the rivers and springs are where a settlement gets its drinking water. Between them they are everything wet on the planet, commerce and survival, and both are now blood. And the springs have been touched once before. At the third trumpet a star called Wormwood made a third of them bitter (8:10–11). Bitter water can still be drunk by a desperate man. Blood cannot. The trumpet made the water unbearable; the bowl makes it impossible, and the distance between the two is the distance between a warning and a verdict.

Everything belongs to somebody. There is a plain and uncomfortable observation here, and it runs through the whole book. The sea a merchant sails on, the spring a village was built around, the sun a farmer plants by: none of it is neutral machinery that happens to be reliable. It is upheld, moment by moment, by the one whom the world is cursing (Colossians 1:17; Hebrews 1:3). A civilisation can spend centuries assuming the water will be there, and be right every single day, and still be wrong about why.

What it does not mean. These are not predictions of a particular ecological disaster, though disasters in nature are real and serve as warnings. They are pictures of God’s final judgement on a world that has turned its back on the Creator, in which the creation that sustained it turns against it.

Is every natural disaster a judgement on the people it strikes? No, and Jesus forbids that conclusion. When a tower fell and killed eighteen people, he said they were not worse sinners than anyone else, and then turned the question round: unless you repent, you will all likewise perish (Luke 13:1–5). Disasters are signs that the whole world lies under the curse of sin and that God’s final judgement is coming, and they call every one of us, not just the victims, to repent. They are never a licence to point at a particular town or person and say God is punishing them. The right response to a flood on the news is compassion, help and self-examination.

In a sentence. The second angel poured his bowl into the sea, and it turned into blood like that of a dead body, and every living creature in the sea died; the third angel poured his bowl into the rivers and springs, and they turned to blood.

On a Tuesday. Every glass of clean water is a gift from God. Thank him for it, and do not take his goodness in creation for granted. Next time you turn on a tap, let it be a small act of worship: the God who could withhold everything is giving you this, today, though you did not earn it. And remember the Christians in places where clean water is scarce, and do something practical for them.

For worship. Our God upholds the sea and the springs by the word of his power, and every river that has ever run clear has run because he willed it. He gives rain on the just and the unjust, and fills the hearts of his enemies with food and gladness. And when the world refused his goodness, he offered it something better than water: the spring of the water of life, without price, to anyone who is thirsty. Christ is that spring, and he still stands and cries out: if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the angel in charge of the waters say, "Just are you, O Holy One, who is and who was, for you brought these judgments. For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve!" And I heard the altar saying, "Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I heard the angel in charge of the waters say, “Just are you, O Holy One, who is and who was, for you brought these judgments. For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve!” And I heard the altar saying, “Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!”

The setting. Jewish writings spoke of angels with charge over different parts of creation, such as fire (14:18), winds (7:1) and waters. The principle of fitting judgement runs through Scripture: whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed (Genesis 9:6). Isaiah 49:26 says God will make the oppressors drunk with their own blood. Psalm 19:9 says the rules of the LORD are true, and righteous altogether. Pharaoh had the Hebrew boys thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1:22); God turned the Nile to blood.

Heaven answers whether this is fair. John does something here that he does nowhere else in the bowl sequence. He stops. The fourth bowl does not follow the third; three verses of worship follow instead, because heaven has something to say about whether this is fair. These verses are the theodicy of the book, the place where Revelation answers the question a reader has been carrying since chapter 6. And the answer is not given by an argument. It is sung, in the middle of the plague.

And I heard the angel in charge of the waters say, Just are you, O Holy One. Just (dikaios, righteous). Holy One (hosios, as in 15:4). The detail should not be missed. The angel in charge of the waters is the one who has just watched every river and spring under his care turn to blood. If anybody in the universe had grounds to file an objection, it is him. He does not complain. He declares God just.

Who is and who was. As in 11:17, the threefold name has lost its third term. The words and is to come are missing, because now he has come in judgement. And the attribute picked out is holy. Not powerful. The angel is not saying God has the right to do this because he is strong enough. He is saying it is consistent with what God is.

For you brought these judgments. The verb (ekrinas) is simply you judged. God is the judge, and he judges in person.

For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. The grounds are stated in one sentence, and it is the oldest principle of justice there is. The punishment fits the crime: it is the crime, served back. Egypt drowned Hebrew children in a river and had to drink the river. These people made the earth run with the blood of God’s people, and now there is nothing else to drink. Nothing arbitrary is being done. What God does to the wicked is what the wicked did, returned. This is the answer to the martyrs’ cry (6:10).

It is what they deserve! Two words in Greek (axioi eisin, they are worthy), and they are not comfortable. They are a grim echo of the praise of the Lamb: worthy are you (5:9, 12). The Lamb is worthy of glory; the persecutors are worthy of judgement. But notice who is not saying them: no human being in this book ever pronounces that sentence over another. The martyrs under the altar asked how long? and left the verdict to God (6:10). Vengeance is God’s, and the reason it is his alone is that only he can be trusted to get it exactly right (Romans 12:19).

And I heard the altar saying, Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments! The altar speaks. It is a strange sentence and John lets it stand, and any reader who has been following will know why the furniture is given a voice. Under that altar are the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God, who cried, O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood? (6:9–10). From it the saints’ prayers rose (8:3–5). They were given white robes and told to rest a little longer. This is the altar answering its own question. The same words come back, holy and true there, true and just here (alēthinai kai dikaiai, as the redeemed sang in 15:3), and the verdict of the people who actually paid for the injustice is yes. Not at last, and not it took long enough. Yes.

Nobody in heaven thinks God has overdone it. That is the most important thing this chapter has to say to a Christian who finds these plagues hard to look at. The one group whose opinion might be thought to carry most weight, the murdered, who waited for this, are the ones who declare it just when it comes. Nobody in heaven, seeing the whole file, thinks God has gone too far.

Textual note. In v. 5 the King James Version reads “which art, and wast, and shalt be”, following a late reading; the best manuscripts read “who is and who was, the Holy One”. In v. 7, the King James Version reads “I heard another out of the altar say”, but the best manuscripts read simply “I heard the altar saying”.

What it does not mean. Praising God’s judgement is not rejoicing in suffering for its own sake. It is the recognition that God has put things right, that evil has not had the last word, and that the blood of the innocent has not been forgotten. Without God’s justice, the world’s victims would have no hope.

How does this fit with loving my enemies? Perfectly, once we see who does what. Our task is to love, bless and pray for those who wrong us (Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:14), and to leave vengeance entirely to God (Romans 12:19–21). We can do that precisely because we know God will judge. If there were no judge, every wrong would either have to be avenged by us or swallowed as if it did not matter. Because there is a just God, we can forgive without pretending evil is nothing. And we pray, meanwhile, that our enemies will be saved, as many persecutors have been. The praise of this verse belongs to the day when God himself has acted.

In a sentence. Then I heard the angel who has charge of the waters say: You are just, Holy One, who is and who was, in judging like this; they poured out the blood of your people and your prophets, and you have given them blood to drink, which is what they deserve; and I heard the altar answer: Yes, Lord God Almighty, your judgements are true and just.

On a Tuesday. When you see injustice that is never put right in this life, the abuser who is never charged, the regime that is never toppled, the lie that is never exposed, bring it to God in prayer, and trust that his judgements will be true and just. Name it to him honestly. Then put it down, and do good to the people in front of you. You are not the judge, and you do not need to be.

For worship. Just are you, O Holy One. No wrong done to your people has ever slipped your notice, and no tear of theirs has fallen without your seeing it. You keep the blood of the martyrs in your book, and you will answer every cry from under the altar. Your judgements are true and just, and the people who suffered most will be the first to say yes. And your justice is the same justice that was satisfied at the cross, where the Lamb was slain and his blood was shed for sinners, so that those who deserved to drink the cup of wrath might drink the cup of salvation instead.

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire. They were scorched by the fierce heat, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire. They were scorched by the fierce heat, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory.

The setting. The fourth trumpet darkened a third of the sun (8:12). The redeemed are promised that the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat (7:16).

The fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire. It was allowed (edothē, it was given).
