Even here, at full strength, with the limits off, the divine passive holds. Nothing in this book acts on its own authority, and the sun is no exception. To scorch (kaumatisai) is to burn. The sun, which God made to give light and life, becomes an instrument of judgement.

Two companies, one sun. The fourth trumpet darkened the sun; the fourth bowl turns it up. And the reversal is pointed, because the great promise made to the multitude in 7:16 was that the sun would not strike them, nor any scorching heat. For the sealed it is shaded by the tent of God spread over them; for these it is a furnace. What the redeemed are spared, the beast’s worshippers suffer. The same created thing behaves differently depending on whose you are.

They were scorched by the fierce heat. Fierce heat (kauma mega, great heat).

And they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. Then the sentence that is repeated three times in this chapter, and it is one of the most sobering diagnoses in the New Testament. They cursed (eblasphēmēsan, blasphemed, slandered): the same verb used of the beast’s mouth in 13:6. Under the plague they have started to sound like the thing they worshipped. And they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. This is the extraordinary part. They know. There is no ignorance here, no confusion about the source, no atheism. They have correctly identified who is doing this and they curse him for it. Suffering has not hidden God from them; it has revealed him, and they have decided against him with the evidence in front of them.

They did not repent and give him glory. Did not repent (ou metenoēsan), as in 9:20–21. And notice what repentance is called here: repent and give him glory. Not repent and feel sorry. To give God glory is the response called for by the eternal gospel (14:7), and given by some in 11:13. To repent is to hand God back the glory that was given to something else, which is precisely what these people will not do, because they gave it to a beast and they are not taking it back.

Pain does not produce repentance. This is the answer, given for the second time in the book, to a hope most people carry quietly: that if things got bad enough, people would turn. Chapter 9 said it after a third of mankind died. Chapter 16 says it three times more. Pain reveals what was already there, and it hardens as reliably as it softens. There is a warning in that for a believer, and it is not chiefly about other people. Every Christian meets small versions of this: the illness, the loss, the disappointment that could go either way, and the direction it goes is not decided by the size of the trouble. Two men lose the same thing in the same week, and one is driven to his knees and the other never prays again. The difference is not the weight. It is which direction a person was already facing when it landed.

What it does not mean. The plagues are not the reason they refuse to repent; their hard hearts are. Judgement reveals what is already in the heart. Pharaoh, too, hardened his heart under the plagues, and God also hardened it (Exodus 8:15; 9:12).

Is it fair for God to harden hearts? Scripture holds two things together, as Exodus does with Pharaoh. People harden themselves: they see God’s hand, refuse him, and are fully responsible for it. And God, as judge, confirms them in the path they chose, giving them over to it (Romans 1:24; 9:17–18). He never hardens a soft heart that is seeking him; he hands a rebellious heart over to its own rebellion. So no one in this chapter is a seeker who wanted to repent and was not allowed. If you want to turn to God, that desire is the sign he is softening you, not hardening you. Follow it now.

Why do some people turn to God in suffering and others away from him? Because suffering does not create faith; it tests and exposes what is there, and only the Spirit of God makes a heart new (John 3:5–8; Ezekiel 36:26). That is why we must pray for people in suffering, not merely wait for the trouble to bring them round. And it is why a Christian who is hurting should run to God with the hurt, as the Psalms do, rather than away from him. Lament, honest complaint, even confused anger brought to God in prayer is the very opposite of the cursing in this verse. The cursers turn their backs; the lamenter turns his face.

In a sentence. The fourth angel poured his bowl on the sun, and the sun was allowed to burn people with fire; they were seared by the intense heat, and they cursed the name of God, who had power over these plagues, but they refused to repent and give him glory.

On a Tuesday. Suffering can soften or harden a heart. When hardship comes, turn toward God, not away from him. Tell him the truth about how it feels, and then give him glory anyway: say what is still true of him, even if it is only one line, that he is good, that he is with you, that Christ died for you. The direction you face in small troubles is the direction you will face in large ones, so practise it now.

For worship. The sun rises every morning at the command of the God who made it, and he has spread his tent over his people so that no scorching heat will strike them. He shelters the multitude by day and leads them to springs of living water. And when the full heat of God’s anger against sin fell on a human being, it fell on the Son, who hung under a darkened sun and cried out in the dark. He bore the burning so that his people could stand in the shade. He alone deserves the glory these people would not give.

verseByVerse.quote: The fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues in anguish and cursed the God of heaven for their pain and sores. They did not repent of their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues in anguish and cursed the God of heaven for their pain and sores. They did not repent of their deeds.

The setting. The ninth plague on Egypt was a darkness that could be felt, three days in which nobody rose from his place, but all the people of Israel had light where they lived (Exodus 10:21–23). Jesus spoke of the outer darkness where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 8:12; 22:13).

The fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast. The first four bowls fell on creation: earth, sea, rivers, sun. The fifth falls on a government. And it is aimed with precision: not at the beast’s subjects, or its armies, but at the throne of the beast (ton thronon tou thēriou), the seat of its power, given by the dragon (13:2). The reader last heard of such a throne in Pergamum, where Satan’s throne is (2:13). Christians had been living under its shadow for the whole book. It goes dark.

And its kingdom was plunged into darkness. The word (eskotōmenē) is simply darkened. In Egypt the god being judged by the darkness was the sun, the head of the Egyptian gods, whose son Pharaoh claimed to be. To darken the empire is to show that its god cannot keep a lamp lit. That is what makes the fifth bowl different from the four before it. The others damaged the world; this one exposes the regime. Every empire that demands worship rests on an appearance of permanence: the lights are on, the courts sit, the coins are minted, and it is inconceivable that any of it should stop. One bowl, and the kingdom is in the dark. The beast’s kingdom, which seemed so dazzling, collapses into darkness. All human empires that defy God end this way.

People gnawed their tongues in anguish. Gnawed (emasōnto, chewed); anguish (ponou, pain). Gnawing the tongue is a small, physical, entirely credible detail: what a person does with pain he cannot get away from and cannot usefully cry out about.

And cursed the God of heaven for their pain and sores. The sores are the ones from the first bowl, still there. The plagues in this chapter accumulate; nothing has healed. And notice what they curse God for: for their pain and sores. Not for anything they have thought about, and not for any account of who he is. The entire content of their complaint is their own discomfort. It is possible to spend a life measuring God only by how one feels, and this is what that comes to in the end.

They did not repent of their deeds. The third time this refusal is mentioned (9:20–21; 16:9), with one word changed. In verse 9 they did not repent and give him glory. Here they did not repent of their deeds. The first is about worship, the second about behaviour, and together they cover the ground: they will not change what they adore and they will not change what they do. Their hearts are set.

What it does not mean. The darkness does not mean God is unable to reach them. It means he gives them what they chose: they loved darkness rather than light (John 3:19), and now they have it.

Is it wrong to be angry with God? It depends what you do with it. Scripture is full of believers who brought anger, confusion and grief to God: Job, Jeremiah, the psalmists (Psalm 13; 88). They argued with him, but they argued with him, to his face, in prayer, and they did not let go of him. That is faith in pain. What this verse describes is different: cursing God and refusing to turn, with no desire to know him, only resentment that life is uncomfortable. If you are angry with God, tell him so, ask him to help you understand, open the Psalms, and talk to a mature Christian. Do not let anger become a wall.

In a sentence. The fifth angel poured his bowl on the beast’s throne, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness; people bit their tongues in agony and cursed the God of heaven because of their pains and sores, but they did not turn from what they had done.

On a Tuesday. Every kingdom built against God ends in darkness. Invest your life in the kingdom of light. And run a test now rather than at the fifth bowl. When you last had a grievance against God, what was it actually about? If the honest answer is that he had not arranged your comfort as you would have arranged it, that is the same complaint, at a survivable scale, and there is still time to tell him so and turn.

For worship. God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. Thrones rise and fall at his word, and the empires that demanded worship cannot keep their own lamps lit when he withdraws his hand. In Egypt the darkness could be felt, and in Goshen there was light; so it is still. He has called his people out of darkness into his marvellous light, and in the city to come there will be no night, for the Lord God will be their light, and the Lamb is its lamp. The beast’s kingdom ends in the dark. His kingdom ends in a morning that never fades.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — The Sixth and Seventh Bowls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 12: the sixth bowl dries the Euphrates to prepare the way for the kings from the east — and when Cyrus took Babylon his engineers diverted that river and his troops walked in up the empty bed, exactly as Isaiah had said (Isa. 44:27–28). Verses 13–14: three unclean spirits like frogs (Ex. 8:6) come out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet — the unholy trinity together for the first time — and go to the kings of the world to assemble them for battle.

Verse 15 interrupts, in brackets, in Christ’s own voice: Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed! — the third of the book’s seven beatitudes. Verse 16 names the muster point: Armageddon, its only occurrence in the Bible.

Verse 17: the seventh bowl is poured into the air, and a loud voice from the temple and the throne says It is done! — gegonen, a perfect tense, the completion promised at 15:1. Verse 18: the storm signs at full strength, with an earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth.

Verse 19: the great city splits in three, the cities of the nations fall, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. Verse 20: every island flees and no mountains are found (cf. 6:14). Verse 21: hailstones of about a hundred pounds fall (Ex. 9:24) — and they cursed God, for the third time in the chapter, which is the last thing humanity does in it.
verseByVerse.theology:
It Is Done

The Euphrates is dried, and frog-like spirits from the mouths of the dragon, beast and false prophet gather the kings to Armageddon. Christ breaks in: stay awake. The seventh bowl brings the voice from the throne, It is done!, the great earthquake, and Babylon remembered for judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Babylon had fallen once before when its river was diverted.

Now: Stay awake and clothed in Christ; ask how much of what you lean on can be shaken.

verseByVerse.quote: The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, to prepare the way for the kings from the east. And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs. For they are demonic spirits, performing signs, who go abroad to the kings of the whole world, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, to prepare the way for the kings from the east. And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs. For they are demonic spirits, performing signs, who go abroad to the kings of the whole world, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.

The setting. God dried up the Red Sea and the Jordan for Israel (Exodus 14:21; Joshua 3:14–17). Cyrus the Persian took Babylon in 539 BC by diverting the Euphrates and marching his army along the riverbed into the city, as the Greek historian Herodotus records (compare Isaiah 44:27–28; Jeremiah 50:38; 51:36). The second plague on Egypt was frogs (Exodus 8:1–15). In the Old Testament, frogs were unclean animals (Leviticus 11:9–12). The prophets foretold a final gathering of the nations against God and his people, which God would defeat (Joel 3:2; Zechariah 12:3; 14:2; Ezekiel 38–39).

The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up. The Euphrates was the eastern frontier of the empire and the direction every invasion of Israel had come from, and the reader has been here before: at the sixth trumpet four angels were released who had been bound at this same river (9:14). Now the river itself goes. The barrier that held back invasion is removed.

A road cleared by God. A dried-up river is one of Scripture’s standard pictures of God clearing a road. He dried the Red Sea for Israel to walk through (Exodus 14:21) and the Jordan for them to enter the land (Joshua 3:16). And when Cyrus took Babylon, his engineers diverted the Euphrates and his troops walked into the city up the empty riverbed, which is what Isaiah had prophesied when he named Cyrus and said that God would dry up the deep (Isaiah 44:27–28). A first-century reader hearing that the Euphrates had been dried for kings from the east knew exactly how the last great Babylon fell. Babylon is about to fall again.

To prepare the way for the kings from the east. From the east (apo anatolēs hēliou) is literally from the rising of the sun. In John’s day the Parthians beyond the Euphrates were the empire’s nightmare. Here they stand for the forces of the world gathering against God. And the irony is that the water is removed to make an invasion easier. God is not defending the beast’s kingdom; he is opening the gate for the thing that will destroy it. Even the enemies of God’s people serve his purposes without knowing it, as in 17:16–17, where the beast and the ten kings turn on the harlot because God has put it into their hearts.

And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs. The unholy trinity of chapters 12 and 13 (12:3; 13:1, 11) appears together for the first time, and notice what all three do. They speak. Three mouths, and one thing comes out of each: their words, lies and propaganda. The dragon is the deceiver of the whole world (12:9); the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words (13:5); the false prophet deceives by signs (13:13–14). The entire arsenal of evil in this book is talk.

Like frogs. Unclean spirits (pneumata tria akatharta), and like frogs, which is the second plague on Egypt (Exodus 8:6) and, to a Jewish reader, unclean by law (Leviticus 11:10–12). It is also, deliberately, ridiculous. Everything about this book’s villains has been magnificent so far: seven heads, ten diadems, a mortal wound healed, the worship of the whole earth. And when their propaganda is finally shown, it hops and croaks. Deception is loud and persistent, but worthless. Evil is never as grand as it looks.

For they are demonic spirits, performing signs. Demonic (daimoniōn). The signs are deceptive wonders, as in 13:13–14. Lies rarely travel alone; they come with something impressive enough to make them believed.

Who go abroad to the kings of the whole world, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty. The frogs are a diplomatic service. They go to the kings of the earth, they perform signs, and they assemble a coalition. To assemble (synagagein) is to gather together, and the battle (polemon, with the article in Greek) is the battle, the final one. The great day of God the Almighty is the day of judgement. This is how the last war begins in Revelation: not with a mobilisation but with a persuasion campaign, and the persuading is done by demons who look absurd and are believed anyway. The rulers of the world think they are gathering to fight; in fact God is gathering them to be judged. The same battle is described in 19:19 and 20:8.

The real battlefield is belief. Set that beside the way people usually imagine spiritual warfare. The decisive struggle in this book is not fought with weapons and is not chiefly about power. It is about what the world is told and whether it believes it. The dragon’s one method, from a conversation in a garden to the last coalition on earth, is to say something untrue convincingly. And the church’s one weapon is the word of truth, the testimony of Jesus (12:11; Ephesians 6:17).

Where Christians differ: who are the kings from the east? John’s readers feared the Parthian armies beyond the Euphrates. Futurist readers expect a literal army from the east, often identified with a modern nation. Verdict: the more likely reading is that John uses that ancient fear as a picture of the nations gathered by the dragon for the final battle (v. 14), not a prediction of a particular invasion.

What it does not mean. The kings from the east are not a coded prediction about any modern nation, such as China. The Euphrates and the east are symbols drawn from Israel’s history and the Roman world’s fears.

How do I recognise the frogs’ voice today? Look for the marks this chapter gives. It comes from mouths: it is talk, often loud, repeated and everywhere. It is backed by signs: success, spectacle, numbers, things that look like proof. And it always gathers people against God, persuading them that Christ is the enemy of their freedom and that his people are the problem. It can come from a government, a movement, a media culture, or a false teacher in the church. The test is the same: does it confess Jesus Christ as Lord, and does it agree with Scripture (1 John 4:1–3; Isaiah 8:20)? Fill your mind with God’s word, and the croaking becomes easier to hear for what it is.

In a sentence. The sixth angel poured his bowl on the great River Euphrates, and its water dried up to open the way for the kings from the east; then I saw three unclean spirits that looked like frogs coming out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet; they are demonic spirits that perform signs, and they go out to the kings of the whole world to gather them for the battle on the great day of God Almighty.

On a Tuesday. Demonic deception often comes through words and propaganda. Measure what you hear by God’s word, and refuse lies, however loud. Before you share, repeat or believe a message about God, his people or what is right and wrong, ask where it came from and whether it agrees with Scripture. And notice how much of your day is filled with other voices. Give the word of God the first word in the morning, so that it has the loudest voice in your head.

For worship. The God of this chapter rules even the plans of his enemies. He dries a river, and the kings who think they are marching on his people are marching into his court. The dragon, the beast and the false prophet can gather the whole world, and they cannot gather it one step beyond where God has appointed. And the one who will meet them is the Word of God himself, the Truth in person, who has only to speak and every lie is silenced. Their mouths produce frogs. His mouth holds a sharp two-edged sword, and with it he will judge the world in righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: ("Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!") And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
(“Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!”) And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.

The setting. Megiddo was a fortified city overlooking the plain of Jezreel (Esdraelon) in northern Israel, on the main route between Egypt and Mesopotamia, and the site of many decisive battles. There Deborah and Barak defeated Sisera (Judges 5:19), Ahaziah died (2 Kings 9:27), and King Josiah was killed fighting Pharaoh Neco, and all Judah mourned (2 Kings 23:29–30; 2 Chronicles 35:22–25; Zechariah 12:11). Nearby Mount Carmel was where Elijah defeated the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18). Jesus said he would come like a thief (Matthew 24:43–44), as he warned Sardis (3:3), and he told Laodicea to buy white garments to cover the shame of its nakedness (3:18).

Christ interrupts his own book. In the middle of a sentence about demonic frogs assembling the kings of the world, a different voice cuts in, and the ESV rightly marks it with brackets. Christ has scarcely spoken in his own voice since chapter 3, and will not again until chapter 22; here, at the darkest point of the story, he breaks in without introduction to speak directly to his church. The interruption is itself the message. The armies are gathering, the frogs are going out to the kings, the last battle is being assembled, and the Lord’s concern at that exact moment is a Christian in Thyatira staying awake and keeping his clothes on. The cosmic scale of this chapter never once displaces the person reading it.

Behold, I am coming like a thief! He said it to Sardis in the same words (3:3) and on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24:43), and Paul and Peter both repeat it (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10). The point of the image is never stealth. A thief does not sneak so much as arrive on a night nobody expected. It is unpredictability, and its practical consequence is that there is no point in a person planning to get ready later. His coming will be unexpected for those who are not watching.

Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on. The third of the book’s seven beatitudes. Stays awake (grēgorōn) means keeps watch. Keeping his garments on (tērōn ta himatia autou) is literally guarding his clothes. The image would have made a Christian in Asia smile before it made him think. The captain of the temple guard in Jerusalem went round at night, and a Levite found asleep at his post could be beaten and have his clothes burned, as the later Mishnah records. Being caught asleep meant public shame.

That he may not go about naked and be seen exposed! Exposed (tēn aschēmosynēn) is shame, disgrace. And garments in this book have a settled meaning: white robes given to those who conquer (3:4–5), robes washed and made white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14), the fine linen of the Bride which is the righteous deeds of the saints (19:8). Laodicea was told to buy white garments so that the shame of its nakedness might not be seen (3:18), the same phrase. The garments are the righteousness of Christ received by faith, and the faithful life that flows from it. To be found unprepared at Christ’s coming is to be shamed.

Not complicated and not heroic. So the instruction is simple. Stay awake. Keep your clothes on. That is what is asked of a Christian while the kings of the earth are being assembled for Armageddon: not that he do anything about the coalition, but that he be found alert and dressed.

And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon. This is the only occurrence of the word in the Bible, and an enormous popular literature rests on one verse. Honesty requires saying that its meaning is not certain. The likeliest derivation is har Megiddo, the mountain of Megiddo. Megiddo was a fortress town guarding the pass into the plain of Jezreel, and the most fought-over place in the land. To say Megiddo was to say the battlefield. The difficulty is that there is no mountain of Megiddo, only a plain and a mound (a tel). Some therefore connect it with Mount Carmel nearby, or read mountain of assembly, the phrase Isaiah puts in the mouth of the fallen day star who says he will sit on the mount of assembly (Isaiah 14:13). John says it is called this in Hebrew, a signal to look for its meaning. It fits a book that has already told the reader that Sodom, Egypt and Babylon are all names for one city (11:8).

Where Christians differ: is Armageddon a literal battle in northern Israel? Many futurists, including premillennial and dispensational Christians, expect the armies of the world to gather literally in the valley of Megiddo for a final war in the Middle East, before Christ returns. Verdict: Armageddon is a symbolic name for the final conflict between the powers of the world and God, drawn from Israel’s history of decisive battles at Megiddo. The battle is described three times in Revelation (16:14–16; 19:17–21; 20:7–10), and each time no battle is actually fought: the enemies are gathered and then destroyed instantly by Christ at his coming. It is the same final event, seen from different angles. It may involve a literal gathering of hostile powers, but its location and form are not the point; its outcome is. Christ wins without a fight.

The shortest battle in the book. What is not uncertain is who wins, and how little of a battle it turns out to be. The kings are assembled here in chapter 16 and nothing happens; the end is described in 19:19–21, it lasts a few lines, and the only weapon is a sword out of a mouth. Armageddon is the most famous battle in the world’s imagination and the shortest in the Bible.

What it does not mean. “Armageddon” in Revelation does not mean nuclear war or a global catastrophe caused by human beings, as the word is often used today. It means the day when God judges the world’s rebellion.

Does coming like a thief mean a secret rapture? No. The thief image is about timing, not visibility: his coming will be unexpected for those who are not watching, not invisible. Revelation says every eye will see him (1:7), and Jesus said his coming will be like lightning flashing across the sky (Matthew 24:27). Paul uses the thief picture in the same passage where the Lord descends with a cry of command and the sound of the trumpet (1 Thessalonians 4:16; 5:2). There is one return of Christ, public and glorious, at the end of the age, when he raises the dead, gathers his people and judges the world. Notice too that here, in chapter 16, the church is still on earth being told to stay awake.

If he comes like a thief, can anyone know when? No. Jesus said that no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), and every attempt to set dates has failed and done harm. But Paul adds that believers are not in darkness, for that day to surprise them like a thief (1 Thessalonians 5:4). The difference is not that Christians know the date but that they are ready whatever the date. A watchman does not know when the attack will come; he simply does not fall asleep.

In a sentence. (Look, I am coming like a thief! How blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his clothes on, so that he will not have to walk around naked and be seen in his shame!) And the spirits gathered the kings together at the place called in Hebrew Armageddon.

On a Tuesday. Do not speculate about Armageddon; prepare for Christ’s coming. Stay awake, keep your garments clean, and live as one who will meet him. Practically, that means keeping short accounts with God, confessing sin the day you see it; keeping your hope fixed on Christ’s righteousness and not your own; and living each ordinary day, at the desk, the sink or the hospital bed, as if he might come before evening. Ask yourself: is there anything I would want to be found doing, or not doing, if he came tonight?

For worship. The Lord Jesus is coming, and his coming is certain. While the kings of the earth are gathered against him, he stops to speak to one sleepy believer, because he loses none of his own. He clothes the naked in his own righteousness, robes washed white in his blood, so that no one who trusts him will ever stand exposed before God. And the battle the world dreads will be no battle at all: the King of kings will appear, and his enemies will fall at a word. Blessed is the one who watches for him, and more blessed still the one who watches for us.
verseByVerse.note: Armageddon probably means “mountain of Megiddo,” a hill fortress overlooking the plain where many of Israel’s famous battles were fought.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, "It is done!" And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, and a great earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth, so great was that earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, “It is done!” And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, and a great earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth, so great was that earthquake.

The setting. On the cross, Jesus said, It is finished (John 19:30). The same signs of lightning, thunder and earthquake ended the seals (8:5) and the trumpets (11:19), and here they reach their climax. Daniel 12:1 speaks of a time of trouble such as never has been since there was a nation.

The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air. The last bowl is poured into the air (aera), the one element the first six left alone, and the one nobody can stand outside of. Paul calls the devil the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:2), the realm where demonic powers operate. The final judgement falls on the atmosphere the whole world has been breathing, the whole environment of human life.

And a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, It is done! The voice comes from the temple and from the throne, which in this book means God himself. Two words in English and one in Greek: gegonen, it has happened, it has come to pass, it stands accomplished. The tense is perfect: a completed act whose result is permanent.

Three announcements of completion. The cry echoes two others, and they are the frame of everything. On the cross, Jesus said it is finished (John 19:30), a different verb with the same force. At 21:6, on the throne, God says of the new creation it is done, the same word as here. Three announcements of completion: the cross, the end of wrath, and the beginning of the new world. Christ’s word on the cross accomplished salvation; God’s word here completes judgement; and the same word opens the new creation. What was accomplished at the first makes the second bearable and the third certain.

What exactly is done? Chapter 15 said it in advance: with them the wrath of God is finished (15:1). This is that sentence arriving. There is no eighth bowl. God’s judgement on this age has a stopping point, and the seventh angel has just reached it.

And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder. John’s standing signal that God has acted, and it has been growing all through the book. At 4:5 it was three elements, coming out of the throne. At 8:5, when the censer of the saints’ prayers was thrown down, an earthquake was added. At 11:19, when the ark was seen, hail was added. Here it is the full list, with the earthquake described in a clause of its own.

And a great earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth, so great was that earthquake. The description is a superlative: nothing like it since there were human beings. The prophets had promised exactly this, and the letter to the Hebrews quotes it to make the point Christians most need from this verse. God said through Haggai that he would shake the heavens and the earth (Haggai 2:6), and Hebrews comments that the words yet once more mean the removal of things that are shaken, so that the things that cannot be shaken may remain; therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:26–28). That is what the greatest earthquake in history is for. It is not demolition for its own sake. It is a sorting: everything that can be shaken is being shaken, so that what is left standing afterwards is only what was never going to fall.

What it does not mean. “It is done” does not mean that nothing more happens in Revelation. Chapters 17–20 go back and describe the fall of Babylon and the final defeat of the beast and Satan in detail. It means that God’s judgement on this age has reached its end.

What counts as shakeable in my life? Anything that belongs only to this age: money and property, reputation, health, career, national power, the approval of others, even the outward shapes of church life. None of them is evil, and many are God’s good gifts, but none can bear the full weight of a soul. What cannot be shaken is God himself, his word, Christ’s finished work, the kingdom he gives, and the people he has made his own. A believer’s honest question on reading this verse is therefore not, will I survive this? but, how much of what I am leaning on is in the shakeable category? Hold the first loosely and the second with both hands.

In a sentence. The seventh angel poured his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, It is done! and there came lightning, rumbling, thunder and a massive earthquake, greater than any since human beings have been on earth.

On a Tuesday. This week, when something you rely on wobbles, a bank balance, a relationship, your health, let it remind you which kingdom you belong to. Thank God for the gifts, and then deliberately rest your weight on what cannot move: tell him that Christ is enough, and that his finished work is your security. People who have already settled what they stand on are the calmest in an earthquake.

For worship. Worship the God whose word is final. He speaks, and it is done. His Son spoke from the cross, and the work of salvation was finished, never to be repeated or added to. He will speak from the throne, and his judgement on this age will be complete. And he will speak once more over a new heaven and a new earth, and they will stand for ever. What Christ finished on the cross and what God completes at the end are both sure. The heavens and the earth will be shaken, and we have received a kingdom that cannot be shaken; let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.

verseByVerse.quote: The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. And every island fled away, and no mountains were to be found. And great hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, fell from heaven on people; and they cursed God for the plague of the hail, because the plague was so severe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. And every island fled away, and no mountains were to be found. And great hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, fell from heaven on people; and they cursed God for the plague of the hail, because the plague was so severe.

The setting. The seventh plague on Egypt was the worst hailstorm the country had ever seen (Exodus 9:18–26). God threw great hailstones from heaven on the Amorite kings fleeing from Joshua (Joshua 10:11). Ezekiel 38:22 promises hailstones, fire and sulphur against Gog. A talent (talantiaia) weighed about 45 kilograms (100 pounds).

The great city was split into three parts. The great city is Babylon (v. 19; 17:18), the phrase used at 11:8 of the place that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified. Split into three: completely shattered. Ezekiel was told to divide his hair into three parts as a sign of Jerusalem’s ruin (Ezekiel 5:1–2).

And the cities of the nations fell. Every human city and civilisation built without God collapses with Babylon. They were all built on her plan, and they all fall with her.

And God remembered Babylon the great. The phrase carries more weight than any other in the verse. Remembered (emnēsthē). In Scripture, God remembering never means that something had slipped his mind. It is covenant language, and it always means that he is about to act on what he has long known. God remembered Noah, and the waters went down (Genesis 8:1). God remembered his covenant with Abraham, and the exodus began (Exodus 2:24). The thief on the cross asked to be remembered, and was told that today he would be with Christ in paradise (Luke 23:42–43). So the sentence means that a file which has been open for a very long time has come to the top of the pile. God had not forgotten her sins (18:5). Delayed judgement is not cancelled judgement.

The hinge between announcement and account. Babylon was announced fallen in 14:8 and described nowhere. Chapters 17 and 18 will do nothing else. This verse is the hinge between the announcement and the account.

To make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. The verb is exact: to make her drain the cup. Not sip it, not drink from it, but drain it to the bottom. It is the cup of 14:10, poured full strength, and it is the cup Babylon herself had been passing round, she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality (14:8). She poured; she drinks; and she finishes the cup.

And every island fled away, and no mountains were to be found. Two things that do not move. The sixth seal had already said that every mountain and island was removed from its place (6:14), and at the final judgement earth and sky flee from God’s presence (20:11), which is more evidence that the seals and the bowls are covering the same ground. Islands and mountains are what people steer by and shelter behind, and there are none. The old creation passes away.

And great hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, fell from heaven on people. Enormous, crushing, deadly: the final blow. A hundred pounds is roughly a talent, the largest standard weight in the ancient world. And stones falling on people from above has one other meaning in the law: stoning was the penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16). The chapter has recorded three times that these people blasphemed. The sky returns the sentence.

And they cursed God for the plague of the hail, because the plague was so severe. To the very end, they curse God rather than repent. Not they cried out, not they fell down. The final act of humanity in this chapter, with the sky falling on it, is to curse. The last word of the bowls is not repentance but blasphemy. This is the true horror of sin: it hardens until it cannot turn.

What changes people. That is where the bowls end, and the placement is deliberate. Revelation gives its reader no consoling picture of a world that finally comes round under pressure. It has now said four times that judgement by itself changes nobody. What changes people is what was shown at 11:13, where the two witnesses were killed and raised and the rest of the city gave glory to the God of heaven, and what was announced at 14:6, an eternal gospel flown where every nation could hear it. The bowls are the answer to the question how long?, and they are not the instrument of anybody’s salvation. That instrument is a Lamb who was slain, and he has been in the middle of the throne since chapter 5, and while the door of the sanctuary is open he is still saving.

What it does not mean. The persistent cursing does not mean God failed to give them opportunity. He sent warnings, judgements, witnesses and the eternal gospel. They chose, again and again, to refuse. God gave them what they chose.

Could a Christian end up like this? A true believer will not, because God keeps his own and finishes what he began in them (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29). But Scripture warns Christians about hardness precisely as one of the means by which he keeps us: exhort one another every day, so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Hebrews 3:13). Hardening is gradual: one sin excused, one warning ignored, one prayer neglected. So if your heart feels cold, do not despair and do not drift. Confess it, go back to God’s word and God’s people, and ask him to soften you. A heart worried about being hard is not yet the heart in this verse.

In a sentence. The great city split into three parts, and the cities of the nations collapsed; God remembered Babylon the great and made her drink the cup filled with the wine of his furious anger; every island disappeared and the mountains could no longer be found; huge hailstones, each weighing about forty-five kilograms, fell from the sky on people, and they cursed God because of the hail, because the plague was so terrible.

On a Tuesday. Do not harden your heart today. If God is calling you to repent of something, turn now, while your heart can still be softened. Name the thing to him, take the first concrete step away from it, and tell a trusted Christian friend if you need help to keep going. And keep telling others the gospel: judgements will not save your neighbours, but the good news of the Lamb can.

For worship. God remembers. He remembered Noah in the flood, Abraham’s children in Egypt, and a dying thief on a cross, and he will remember Babylon. Nothing evil escapes his memory, and nothing done for his name is forgotten. And for those who are in Christ, he has made a promise that turns the whole chapter on its head: their sins and lawless deeds he will remember no more. The cup Babylon must drain to the bottom, the Son of God drained first, in Gethsemane and at Golgotha, for everyone who trusts him. There is no wrath left in it for us. There is only a cup of blessing, and a feast waiting at the wedding of the Lamb.

It is what they deserve!”<sup>7</sup>And I heard the altar saying, “Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!”<sup>8</sup>The fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire.<sup>9</sup>They were scorched by the fierce heat, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. People gnawed their tongues in anguish<sup>11</sup>and cursed the God of heaven for their pain and sores. They did not repent of their deeds.<sup>12</sup>The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, to prepare the way for the kings from the east.<sup>13</sup>And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs.<sup>14</sup>For they are demonic spirits, performing signs, who go abroad to the kings of the whole world, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.<sup>15</sup>(“Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!”)<sup>16</sup>And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.<sup>17</sup>The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, “It is done!”<sup>18</sup>And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, and a great earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth, so great was that earthquake.<sup>19</sup>The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath.<sup>20</sup>And every island fled away, and no mountains were to be found.<sup>21</sup>And great hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, fell from heaven on people; and they cursed God for the plague of the hail, because the plague was so severe.

17.title: Babylon the Great: The Seductive City
17.overview:
Chapter 17 introduces one of Revelation’s two great female figures: the great prostitute who sits on many waters, dressed in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold and jewels, holding a golden cup full of abominations. She is the counterpart to the bride of the Lamb (chapters 19 and 21) — two women, two cities, two ways of organising human life. The bride is pure, faithful, clothed in the righteousness of the Lamb. Babylon is seductive, unfaithful, clothed in the luxury of empire. Every human being in history has been drawn toward one or the other.

The identity of Babylon is both specific and universal. In the first century, every reader knew who she was: Rome. The seven hills (v. 9), the woman drunk with the blood of the saints, the city that rules over the kings of the earth (v. 18) — all of this pointed unmistakably to the imperial city on the Tiber. Preterists and idealists agree on this much. Where they differ is on what Rome represents: preterists see primarily the historical Rome of Nero and Domitian; idealists see Rome as the type of every civilisation that organises itself around wealth, power, and the seduction of the nations away from the living God. The idealist position is followed here: Babylon is Rome, and Babylon is every Rome.

The chapter falls into two movements: the vision of the woman on the beast (vv. 1–6) and the angel’s interpretation (vv. 7–18). The interpretation is deliberately cryptic — ‘this calls for a mind that has wisdom’ (v. 9) — and the details about the seven kings and the eighth king have generated more interpretive proposals than almost any other passage in Revelation. The main options are presented honestly here rather than forcing a specific identification that the text itself refuses to make definitive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Woman on the Beast
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: one of the bowl angels — tying this chapter to 16:19, where God remembered Babylon — invites John to see the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters (cf. Jer. 51:13). The kings committed immorality with her; the dwellers on earth merely got drunk on her wine. The same invitation will come from the same rank of angel at 21:9: Come, I will show you the Bride.

Verses 3–4: carried in the Spirit into a wilderness (the Bride is shown from a high mountain, 21:10), John sees a woman riding the scarlet beast of chapter 13 — seven heads, ten horns, blasphemous names. She is arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding a golden cup full of abominations (cf. Jer. 51:7; Matt. 23:25).

Verse 5: a name on her forehead, in a book where that is never incidental (7:3; 13:16; 14:1) — Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes and of earth’s abominations, which the ESV prints in capitals. Verse 6: she is drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus — and John, seeing her, marveled greatly, using the verb this book twice uses of the world’s reaction to the beast (13:3; 17:8).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Great Prostitute

John is shown Babylon, magnificent in purple and gold, riding the beast, holding a golden cup full of abominations, drunk with the blood of the saints. She is Rome for the first readers, and the mother of every city built to make a name for itself.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Kings made the arrangements; ordinary people simply drank what was poured.

Now: The cup always looks better than its contents — and even an apostle had to be asked why he marvelled.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said to me, "Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality, and with the wine of whose sexual immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said to me, “Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality, and with the wine of whose sexual immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk.”

Meaning first. Revelation 17 zooms in on Babylon, whose fall was announced in 14:8 and 16:19, and shows her as a great prostitute. An angel invites John to see her judgement: she sits on many waters, the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the world is drunk on her wine (vv. 1–2). In the wilderness John sees her riding a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns, dressed in purple, scarlet and jewels, holding a golden cup full of abominations, with her name on her forehead: Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes; and she is drunk with the blood of the saints (vv. 3–6). The angel explains: the beast was, is not, and will come up from the abyss and go to destruction, and the world will marvel at it (vv. 7–8). Its seven heads are seven hills where the woman sits and seven kings; the beast is an eighth king, belonging to the seven (vv. 9–11). Its ten horns are ten kings who rule briefly with the beast and make war on the Lamb, but the Lamb conquers them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and his people are called, chosen and faithful (vv. 12–14). The waters are the peoples of the world, and in the end the beast and the kings will turn on the prostitute and destroy her, because God put it in their hearts to fulfil his purpose (vv. 15–17). The woman is the great city that rules the kings of the earth (v. 18). The chapter exposes the seductive glamour of the world system, the economic, cultural and religious power of Rome in John’s day and of every godless civilisation since, and shows that evil turns on itself, while the Lamb wins. Over the whole glittering scene stands one sentence that cannot be shaken: the Lamb will conquer, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings.

The setting. The prophets called cities that lured others into idolatry and greed prostitutes: Nineveh (Nahum 3:4), Tyre (Isaiah 23:15–17), and even Jerusalem when unfaithful (Ezekiel 16; 23). Ancient Babylon was built on the Euphrates with canals around it, and Jeremiah addressed it as you who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures (Jeremiah 51:13). In John’s day, Rome was the centre of a vast trading empire, rich, luxurious, and the seat of the emperor cult; Roman writers themselves called it a city of vice. The goddess Roma was worshipped in Asia, and a coin of Vespasian showed her seated on Rome’s seven hills.

Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said to me. The guide is one of the bowl angels, which ties this chapter to the last. In 16:19 God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup, and no further detail was given. Chapters 17 and 18 expand on the seventh bowl: they are that detail.

Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute. Judgement (krima) is the verdict, the sentence. The same invitation will be issued once more, four chapters later, by another bowl angel in almost identical words: come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb (21:9). Two women, two cities, two invitations from the same rank of angel: Babylon and the new Jerusalem. That is the architecture of the rest of the book, and the frame this chapter must be read in. Every human being is finally a citizen of one of two cities and belongs to one of two households, and Revelation is going to describe both so that a reader can tell them apart.

Why a prostitute? The word (pornēs, harlot) is not chosen for shock. It is the settled prophetic word for covenant unfaithfulness, and it is used most often of the people of God themselves: Israel is the wife who played the whore (Jeremiah 3:6–10; Ezekiel 16; Hosea 1–3), and Isaiah opens a lament over the faithful city that has become a whore (Isaiah 1:21). It was also used of pagan cities. Nineveh and Tyre are both called prostitutes for selling themselves to whoever would trade (Nahum 3:4; Isaiah 23:15–17). The point of the word is transaction. A prostitute offers what belongs inside a covenant, without the covenant, for a price. That is what Babylon does with every good thing there is, beauty, security, belonging, significance, and it is why she is a more dangerous enemy than the beast. The beast demands. She offers.

Who is seated on many waters. Verse 15 will interpret it: the waters are peoples, multitudes, nations and languages. She rules over the world. But the image comes first from Jeremiah’s oracle against the original Babylon, which literally sat on the Euphrates and its canals: you who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come (Jeremiah 51:13). John takes a geographical fact about one city and makes it a statement about influence.

With whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality. The kings have joined her in idolatry and in the pursuit of wealth and power: political and economic alliances with the godless world system. This is the deal made at the top, the arrangement between power and money that every empire runs on.

And with the wine of whose sexual immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk. Drunk (emethysthēsan). Two groups, and the distinction matters. The kings committed immorality with her; the dwellers on earth merely got drunk, the ordinary population who never signed anything and simply drank what was poured. That is a fair description of how a civilisation actually corrupts the people in it. Very few of them are in the room where the arrangements are made. What reaches them is a mood: what everyone assumes, what is obviously worth having, what only a strange person would refuse. And the effect named is drunkenness, intoxication by her luxury, pleasures and values, which is not primarily wickedness but the loss of judgement: the inability to think clearly about God, or to walk in a straight line while being quite certain that you are.

What it does not mean. The prostitute is not a picture of women or of sexuality as such. It is a prophetic image for seductive unfaithfulness to God, as the Old Testament used it for cities and nations.

What does Babylon look like where I live? Wherever a culture offers you everything good, comfort, pleasure, status, security, belonging, without God, and then asks for your heart in return, you are looking at her. In a modern Western city she rarely persecutes with swords. She advertises. She tells you that you are what you own, that your worth is your success, that sex is a right without a covenant, that a sensible person keeps religion private, and that the good life is always one purchase away. She is in the shopping centre, the screen in your pocket, the career ladder and the endless feed. None of those things is evil in itself. The question is whether they are being offered to you as substitutes for God.

In a sentence. Then one of the seven angels who held the seven bowls came and said to me, Come, I will show you the punishment of the great prostitute who sits enthroned over many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed sexual immorality, and with whose immoral wine the people of the earth got drunk.

On a Tuesday. The world’s seductions are attractive. Ask what intoxicates you, and whether it draws you away from Christ. One honest test: what do you assume, without ever having thought about it, that a good life must include? Write down three things. Then ask where you learned them, from the word of God or from the wine everyone else is drinking.

For worship. There are two women in this book and two cities, and the Lamb has made sure his people can tell them apart. He did not leave us to be seduced in the dark; he sent his angel to show us what Babylon is before her glitter could fool us. And he did more than warn. He loved an unfaithful bride, as Hosea loved Gomer, went down into the market and bought her back at the price of his own blood, and is washing her clean to present her to himself in splendour. The prostitute sells herself and is destroyed. The Bride was bought, and will be loved for ever.
verseByVerse.note: “Many waters” recalls ancient Babylon, built on the Euphrates and its canals.

verseByVerse.quote: And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns. The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns. The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality.

The setting. Purple dye was extremely expensive, made from shellfish, and was worn by royalty and the very rich. Scarlet was also costly. Jeremiah 51:7 calls Babylon a golden cup in the LORD’s hand, making all the earth drunk. Jeremiah 4:30 pictures unfaithful Jerusalem dressing in scarlet and adorning herself with gold to attract lovers.

And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness. In the Spirit (en pneumati), as in 1:10 and 4:2: the third of John’s four times in the Spirit (1:10; 4:2; 17:3; 21:10), each marking a new section. And the location is deliberate. To see the Bride he will be carried to a great, high mountain (21:10); to see the prostitute he is taken into a desert. The wilderness is where the woman of chapter 12 fled and was fed for 1,260 days (12:6). The same landscape shelters the true woman and exposes the false one. From the wilderness, the place of the faithful church, John sees Babylon clearly for what she is. The church sees the world most clearly when it is not living inside her palace.

And I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast. Sitting on (kathēmenēn epi): riding, supported by, controlling. It is the beast of chapter 13, political power empowered by Satan, and she is riding it. That single image says more about the relationship between a culture and its government than a chapter of analysis could. Babylon, the world’s culture and economy, rides on the back of political power. She does not own the beast; she is carried by it. Her whole position depends on a creature she does not control, and verse 16 will show what that arrangement is worth.

That was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns. As in 13:1. The scarlet of the beast matches the scarlet of the woman, and of the dragon (12:3). They are dressed for each other.

The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls. She is magnificent, and that must be said plainly or the chapter will be misread. Purple dye came from a Mediterranean shellfish and was fabulously costly; a purple garment was the mark of an emperor. Scarlet was the next most expensive colour there was. Gold, precious stones and pearls are exactly the list that will reappear in chapter 18 as the cargo the merchants of the earth weep over (18:12, 16). This is not a squalid figure in a doorway. She is the best-dressed woman in the world.

Nobody is seduced by something repulsive. That is the point of the whole picture. The beast is frightening and can be recognised by a child; Babylon is beautiful, expensive, cultured and hospitable, and it takes a prophet in the Spirit to see what she is. The church has always found it easier to resist persecution than prosperity, and this chapter knows it.

A counterfeit Bride. Her finery is a parody of the Bride, who wears fine linen, bright and pure (19:8), and of the new Jerusalem, adorned with gold, jewels and pearls (21:18–21). Babylon offers a counterfeit glory. Compare the two women while the picture is fresh. John stops to say what the Bride’s linen is: the righteous deeds of the saints, and it was given her to wear (19:8). One woman is covered in what she bought; the other is dressed in what was given her.

Holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality. Abominations (bdelygmatōn) are detestable things, especially idols; impurities (akatharta) are unclean things. Outwardly golden, inwardly filthy. It is precisely the charge Jesus laid against the Pharisees: they cleaned the outside of the cup while inside it was full of greed and self-indulgence (Matthew 23:25). Jeremiah said of the first Babylon that she was a golden cup in the LORD’s hand, making all the earth drunk (Jeremiah 51:7).

The vessel is worth more than the contents. Nobody would drink from a cup that looked like what is in it. That is the entire mechanism of temptation, and it has not needed updating in nineteen centuries. The vessel is always worth more than the contents, and the contents are always worse than they look.

What it does not mean. Beauty, wealth and fine clothes are not evil in themselves; the new Jerusalem is glorious. Babylon’s sin is using them to seduce people away from God and to serve herself.

How can I enjoy good things without being seduced by them? By receiving them as gifts and not as gods. Everything God made is good and to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4), and Paul tells the rich not to set their hopes on riches but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). The danger signs are when a good thing begins to define you, when you cannot imagine being content without it, when getting or keeping it bends your conscience, or when it crowds out God and his people. A simple safeguard is generosity: give freely of what you most enjoy. A thing you can give away has not yet captured you.

In a sentence. Then the angel carried me away in the Spirit to a desert, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast covered with blasphemous names, with seven heads and ten horns; the woman was dressed in purple and scarlet and glittered with gold, precious stones and pearls, and she held a gold cup filled with detestable things and the filth of her immorality.

On a Tuesday. Do not be dazzled by the glitter of the world. Look at what is in the cup. Next time an advertisement, a lifestyle or a career path makes your heart race, ask what is actually being poured: what it will cost your soul, your family, your devotion to Christ. Then look at the other woman, the Bride, and remember what you are being dressed for.

For worship. The Lord Jesus is the true treasure, and every glittering thing in Babylon is a cheap copy of glories that are his by right. The gold, the jewels and the pearls belong to the city he is building, where the streets are gold and the gates are pearls, and he gives them freely to his Bride. He clothes her not in purple bought with blood but in fine linen washed white in his own blood. He opens our eyes in the wilderness to see through the world’s glamour, and he fills our cup, not with abominations, but with himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And on her forehead was written a name of mystery: "BABYLON THE GREAT, MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH'S ABOMINATIONS." And I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. When I saw her, I marveled greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on her forehead was written a name of mystery: “BABYLON THE GREAT, MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH’S ABOMINATIONS.” And I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. When I saw her, I marveled greatly.

The setting. Roman writers mention that prostitutes in Rome sometimes wore a headband bearing their name. Jeremiah 3:3 tells unfaithful Israel that she has the forehead of a prostitute and refuses to be ashamed.

And on her forehead was written a name of mystery. A name on a forehead, in a book where that is never incidental. The servants of God are sealed on the forehead (7:3); the 144,000 carry the Lamb’s name and his Father’s there (14:1); the beast’s worshippers take its mark in the same place (13:16). The forehead shows identity, and everyone is labelled. Mystery (mystērion) means a name with a hidden meaning that must be understood spiritually. Babylon is not literally the ancient city on the Euphrates, which was in ruins in John’s day.

BABYLON THE GREAT. The ESV prints the name in capital letters, and it is not decoration; it is how a placard reads. Babylon is the city of pride and rebellion, from Babel onward, the destroyer of Jerusalem. Babylon in Scripture begins at a tower built by people who said, let us make a name for ourselves (Genesis 11:4), and that project has never once closed. John is using the name the way he used Sodom and Egypt at 11:8, as a type. In John’s day she was Rome (1 Peter 5:13), and in every age she is the human city organised against God.

MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH’S ABOMINATIONS. Mother: the source, the origin. All the world’s idolatries and corruptions flow from her. She is not one city but the source of a family of them, reproducing in every generation. Rome was a daughter. So was Babylon itself. There will be others.

Who is she? For John’s first readers she is unmistakably Rome. Verse 9 says the seven heads are seven mountains, and Rome was famous throughout the empire as the city on seven hills. Verse 18 calls her the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth, which in the AD 90s named exactly one place. Peter, writing from the same city, sends greetings from she who is at Babylon (1 Peter 5:13). A minority reading, held by some preterists, takes her as apostate Jerusalem, pointing to verse 6 and to Jesus’ words that Jerusalem kills the prophets (Matthew 23:37). It has real evidence behind it, but it does not explain the seven mountains or verse 18 as naturally.

And I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. She has been serving a cup all chapter, and now the reader is told what she has been drinking. The word is drunk, not merely stained: she has killed God’s people in great numbers, and revels in it, past the point where it serves any purpose. Martyrs (martyrōn) is the word for witnesses. Nero blamed Christians for the fire of Rome in AD 64 and had many killed horribly, and Peter and Paul died in Rome.

When I saw her, I marveled greatly. Stop at that, because the angel does. The Greek is emphatic (ethaumasa … thauma mega, I wondered with a great wonder), and it is the same verb used twice in this book of the world’s reaction to the beast: the whole earth marvelled (13:3), and the dwellers on earth will marvel to see the beast (17:8). John, an apostle, in the Spirit, on assignment, has just had the reaction that the earth-dwellers have. What exactly he marvelled at the text does not say. It may have been horror. It may have been that a figure so magnificent was so foul. It may, uncomfortably, have been fascination. The world’s glamour can fascinate even believers. The next verse opens with a rebuke, why do you marvel?, which suggests he should not have.

Where Christians differ: who is the prostitute? Many Reformers and later Protestants identified the prostitute with the Roman Catholic Church and the papacy, seeing in her purple and scarlet the robes of cardinals, and in her drunkenness the blood of the persecuted Reformers. Others see her as apostate Christianity in general, or a future one-world religion. Preterists see first-century Jerusalem. Verdict: the prostitute is Rome, the great city of John’s day (v. 18), seen as the centre of a seductive world system of wealth, idolatry and persecution; and she stands for the godless world system in every age, the culture, commerce and false religion that seduce people from God and persecute his people. Wherever a church becomes rich, worldly and persecuting, as the Reformers saw in their day, it takes on Babylon’s features. But the image is wider than any one church: she is the whole seductive world, which Christians are called to come out of (18:4).

The Reformers’ reading. It is worth understanding why Luther, Calvin, Knox and the Westminster divines read the chapter as they did. They lived under a church seated in Rome, clothed in purple and scarlet, enormously rich, allied with kings, and burning Bible-believing Christians. They rightly saw that a church can become a harlot, as Israel did. Their reading is not foolish; it is too narrow. Babylon was already there before the papacy, and she is still there wherever Christ’s people are seduced or persecuted.

What it does not mean. Seeing Babylon in the world does not mean Christians should withdraw from society, hate their cities, or treat individuals as enemies. They are called to seek the welfare of the city where they live (Jeremiah 29:7), while refusing its idols.

Will ancient Babylon in Iraq be rebuilt? Some popular teachers expect the literal city on the Euphrates to be rebuilt as a world capital. The text itself rules that reading out as its main point: the name is a mystery, to be understood spiritually, and the angel identifies her as the great city that ruled the kings of the earth in John’s day, on seven hills (vv. 9, 18). The ruins in Iraq are not the issue. The issue is the spirit of Babel, which is alive in every capital and every heart that says, let us make a name for ourselves.

Can a Christian be fascinated by Babylon? Yes, and John shows it. It is possible to spend a great deal of time appalled by a culture and still be more interested in it than in God: reading every outrage, watching every scandal, knowing every detail of the world’s sin and very little of God’s word. The line between prophetic concern and simple fascination is thinner than it looks, and an apostle needed to have it pointed out to him. If you find your mind full of Babylon, turn it deliberately to the Lamb. You become like what you gaze at.

In a sentence. On her forehead was written a name with a hidden meaning: BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF ALL THE EARTH’S DETESTABLE THINGS; and I saw that the woman was drunk with the blood of God’s people, the blood of those who bore witness to Jesus; and when I saw her, I was utterly astonished.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the persecuted church. And beware of being fascinated by the culture that persecutes it. This week, pray by name for one country where Christians are suffering for their faith, and for one believer there if you know of one. Then notice how much time you spend looking at the world’s glamour, or at its scandals, and give at least as much to looking at Christ.

For worship. The blood of the martyrs is precious in the sight of the Lord. Babylon drinks it; God counts it, every drop. Not one witness of Jesus has died unnoticed or in vain. And their witness was to a better blood, the blood of the Lamb, shed not by a city drunk on cruelty but by the Son of God giving himself freely for sinners. Babylon’s name is a mystery of iniquity. His name is the mystery of godliness: God manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 7–8: the angel rebukes the marvelling and explains — and vv. 7 to 18 are the most explicitly interpretive passage in the book, saying this is or these are six times. The beast was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction, and those who marvel at it are those whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world.

Verses 9–11: this calls for a mind with wisdom — the seven heads are seven mountains and also seven kings, five fallen, one is, one still to come who must remain only a little while; and the beast is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.

Verses 12–14: ten horns are ten kings (cf. Dan. 7:24) who receive authority for one hour and hand their power to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.

Verses 15–16: the waters are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages; and the ten horns and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire (cf. 2 Kings 9:36; Lev. 21:9). Verse 17: they do it because God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose… until the words of God are fulfilled. Verse 18 closes: the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lamb Will Conquer

The beast was, and is not — a parody of God’s name — and goes to destruction. The seven kings cannot be identified with certainty, but their time is short. The kings make war on the Lamb and lose, and the beast turns on the woman it carried; God put it in their hearts.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those with the Lamb are called, chosen and faithful — in that order.

Now: Evil is not loyal: whatever you ride for safety will one day devour its passengers.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to me, "Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her. The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast, because it was and is not and is to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the angel said to me, “Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her. The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast, because it was and is not and is to come.

The setting. God is the one who is and who was and who is to come (1:4, 8). The beast has a counterfeit title. The Nero redivivus legend held that Nero, who died in AD 68, would return.

But the angel said to me, Why do you marvel? A gentle rebuke. The world’s power and glamour should not impress the people of God. They should see through it. And the cure for staring at Babylon is being told what she is, which the angel supplies for the rest of the chapter.

I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her. Mystery here means what it always means in the New Testament: not a riddle nobody can solve but a secret now disclosed. Verses 7 to 18 are the most explicitly interpretive passage in Revelation; again and again the angel says this is, or these are.

The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. Read that clause slowly against the divine name in this book. God is him who is and who was and who is to come (1:4, 8; 4:8). The beast was, and is not, and is about to rise. It is a parody of the eternal name, and a bad one, because the middle term has collapsed: where God says I am, the beast can only say is not. It is also a counterfeit of Christ’s death and resurrection (13:3). Its comings and goings, its apparent defeats and revivals, all end in destruction (apōleian, perdition). The beast appears in one empire, falls, reappears in another, and finally rises for a last time before its end.

Evil has no being of its own. That is the most concentrated theological statement about evil in the book. Whatever the beast is, it does not have being in the way God has being. It was; it is not; it will make an appearance; and its journey ends at one destination which the sentence names before the journey starts: and go to destruction. Four verbs, and the last one is the only certainty among them. Historically, the phrase almost certainly plays on the Nero legend, an emperor who died and whom much of the eastern empire expected back. John takes the popular rumour and turns it into a theological joke.

And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast. The same safeguard as 13:8, and it is the counterweight to everything alarming in the chapter. There is a register. It belongs to the Lamb. The entries were made from the foundation of the world, before anyone had done anything to earn or forfeit a place. Those not written in the Lamb’s book are fascinated by the beast. Those whose names are written are protected from its deception. Election protects.

Because it was and is not and is to come. Its ability to revive after apparent death astonishes the world. Persecuting powers seem to die, and then the same spirit rises in a new form, and the world is impressed every time.

Am I in danger of being taken in? That is the fear this chapter is most likely to produce in a sincere reader, and the answer should be given plainly. The verse does not say the enrolled are cleverer or more discerning than others. It says they are written, and it says who wrote them, and it says when. John himself marvelled and had to be corrected. The security is not in his reaction but in the register. Jesus said that the false christs would lead astray, if possible, even the elect (Matthew 24:24), and the words if possible are the point: it is not possible. The Lamb keeps those the Father gave him.

How can I know my name is in the book of life? Not by looking into the book, which no one can do, but by looking to the Lamb whose book it is.
