Scripture gives election not as a puzzle to solve but as a comfort to those who believe. If you have come to Christ, trusting him alone for forgiveness, and you love him and want to follow him, however weakly, that is the evidence that God chose you (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5; John 6:37). The Father draws, the Son receives, and none of them is lost. Make your calling and election sure (2 Peter 1:10), not by anxious introspection but by continuing to trust and follow him.

What it does not mean. The beast’s revival does not mean that a specific dead person, such as Nero, will literally return. It means the beastly power that persecuted the church in Rome will rise again in other forms, and finally in a last great form before Christ’s return.

In a sentence. But the angel said to me, Why are you so amazed? I will explain to you the secret meaning of the woman and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her: the beast you saw once was, now is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss and go to its destruction; and the people of the earth whose names have not been written in the book of life since the creation of the world will be amazed when they see the beast, because it once was, now is not, and yet will come.

On a Tuesday. When evil seems to revive after defeat, do not be amazed or afraid. It is heading for destruction. Christ alone was dead and is alive for ever. When the news makes you anxious that the church is losing, read 1:17–18 aloud: the one who died and is alive holds the keys of death and Hades. And when you feel too weak to resist deception, rest in the fact that your safety is written in his book, not in your strength.

For worship. God is the one who is. He was before the mountains were born, he is now, and he is coming, and there is no gap in his being, no weakening, no is not. The beast flickers into history and goes to destruction; God endures for ever. And the Lamb, who was dead and is alive for evermore, wrote the names of his people in his book before the foundation of the world, before they had done good or evil, out of nothing but his own love. No beast can rub them out. They will not be dazzled for ever, for he will open their eyes to see him as he is.

verseByVerse.quote: This calls for a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated; they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while. As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This calls for a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated; they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while. As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.

The setting. Rome was known throughout the ancient world as the city on seven hills (the Palatine, Capitoline, Quirinal, Viminal, Esquiline, Caelian and Aventine). Roman writers such as Virgil, Horace and Cicero refer to it this way, and an annual festival, the Septimontium, celebrated the seven hills. The emperors from Augustus to Domitian were Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, Nero, then Galba, Otho and Vitellius (in AD 68–69), then Vespasian, Titus and Domitian.

This calls for a mind with wisdom. As in 13:18, where the number of the beast was set as a puzzle, spiritual discernment is needed. Both times John invites calculation, and both times readers have been more confident than the evidence allows. Honesty is more useful here than ingenuity.

The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated. A clear reference to Rome, the city on seven hills. The first readers could not have missed it. Seven mountains would have settled the geography for anyone in the empire: it was the city’s name in ordinary speech, celebrated in a festival and stamped on coins.

They are also seven kings. The symbols have more than one meaning: the heads are both hills and kings. Seven is completeness, the full line of rulers of the beastly empire.

Five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while. This is where certainty has to stop. Many attempts have been made to match these to specific emperors, but they depend on where one starts counting and whether one includes the three short-lived emperors of AD 68–69, and no scheme fits perfectly. Start at Julius Caesar or at Augustus? Include or omit Galba, Otho and Vitellius? Depending on the choices, the sixth, the one who is, can be made to come out as Nero, or Vespasian, or Domitian, and each reconstruction requires decisions the text does not authorise. More likely, John’s point is that most of the beast’s rule is already past, the present ruler is in power now, and only a short time remains. Five have fallen, one is, one is to come means what it always means when a prophet says it: most of it is already over. History is nearer its end than its beginning.

Only a little while. And this is the practical point. The angel says the seventh must remain only a little while. Whatever the count, the message is that the sequence is nearly finished and the last of them is brief.

As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction. An eighth: one beyond the seven, a final ruler, yet belonging to the same line and spirit. Possibly a reference to the expectation of Nero returning in a new form; possibly Domitian, often seen as a second Nero. In biblical symbolism, eight is the number of new beginning, the day of resurrection; the beast’s eighth is a counterfeit resurrection, heading only for destruction. The beast is not a new thing; it is the seven again, one more time, wearing a new number. That is what chapter 13 said by giving one animal the features of all Daniel’s four beasts. Empires are not a series of separate problems. They are one problem with a changing letterhead.

The destination, twice. And it goes to destruction, for the second time in three verses. The angel has now given the beast’s past, its present, its future and its destination, and he has mentioned the destination twice as often as anything else. A reader who cannot reconstruct the emperor list, and nobody can with certainty, has still been given the one piece of information the chapter most wants him to have. The angel’s emphasis is not on who the kings are but on how long they last: a little while, and then destruction.

What it does not mean. The seven kings are not a code for predicting modern political leaders or nations, as many have tried. The symbolism shows the beast’s line of rulers, its limited time, and its sure end.

Should I try to work out who the kings are? It is not wrong to study the history, and it helps to see how clearly the first readers would have recognised Rome. But be very wary of anyone who claims certainty, and still more of anyone who matches the kings to present-day leaders. Every such scheme in church history has failed, and many have damaged faith when the dates passed. The wisdom John calls for is not cleverness with lists but the spiritual insight to recognise the beast’s character in any age, refuse its claims, and remember that its time is short.

In a sentence. This needs a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven hills on which the woman sits; they are also seven kings: five have fallen, one is reigning now, and the other has not yet come, and when he comes he must stay only a short time; the beast that once was and now is not is an eighth king, yet it is one of the seven, and it is going to its destruction.

On a Tuesday. Rulers come and go, and the beast’s time is short. Do not put your hope in any political leader, and do not despair over any either. When an election or a regime fills you with fear or with excitement, put the name of the leader alongside this verse: one is, another is to come, a little while, and then destruction. Pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2), obey what is lawful, and keep your hope where it cannot be voted out.

For worship. Kings rise and fall, and the Lord sits enthroned for ever. He counts the reigns of emperors as a man counts the fingers of his hand: five fallen, one now, one brief. He gave Rome its hills and its little while, and he took them away. The true eighth day belongs to Christ, who rose on the first day of a new week and began a new creation that will never pass away. His throne is for ever and ever, and of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end.
verseByVerse.note: Rome was famous as the city on seven hills.

verseByVerse.quote: And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast. These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast. These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.”

The setting. Daniel 7:24 says that the ten horns of the fourth beast are ten kings. Deuteronomy 10:17 calls the LORD God of gods and Lord of lords. Daniel 2:47 calls him God of gods and Lord of kings. The title King of kings was used by Babylonian and Persian emperors.

And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power. The ten horns come from Daniel 7, where the fourth beast had ten horns and the interpretation given was ten kings (Daniel 7:24). Ten in this book is a large, complete number, a full set of a lesser kind: the devil throws some into prison for ten days (2:10). So this is most likely the complete roster of the beast’s client rulers, future from John’s point of view, rather than a list to be filled in with names.

But they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast. One hour (mian hōran): a very short time. It will be used three more times in the next chapter, each time of Babylon’s ruin: in a single hour your judgement has come (18:10, 17, 19). These kings get the same hour they destroy her in. Whatever authority they receive is measured out in the smallest unit John has.

These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast. One mind (mian gnōmēn): one purpose, a single settled opinion. They unite with the beast against God, the nations of the world united in rebellion (Psalm 2:2). And nobody takes anything from them. They give away the one thing a king exists to hold. That is what every totalitarian arrangement in history has actually looked like from the inside: not a conquest of the powerful, but a queue of them agreeing to hand something over in exchange for a share.

They will make war on the Lamb. Make war (polemēsousin). The final battle of 16:14 and 19:19. Ten kings, the full authority of the empire, a beast with seven heads and the dragon’s throne behind it, against a Lamb. John does not switch to the Lion for the battle. The word he uses (arnion) is the one he uses of Christ throughout, the Lamb standing as though it had been slain.

And the Lamb will conquer them. Here is the sentence the chapter exists for. Conquer (nikēsei). The Lamb, who conquered by his death (5:5–6), conquers his enemies at his return. And there is no description of the fighting: they are simply defeated. The reason given is not a strategy or a weapon or a number of troops. It is a title.

For he is Lord of lords and King of kings. The outcome follows from who he is. Nothing has to happen for this to be true, which is why the verse can state it before the event. The title is the highest there is, an Old Testament name for God: the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords (Deuteronomy 10:17; Psalm 136:2–3). And it is applied here to the Lamb without a word of explanation, as this book does everything else concerning his deity. It will be written on his robe and his thigh at 19:16, in reverse order. Every emperor’s claim is answered. The Babylonian and Persian rulers who called themselves king of kings were borrowing a title that belongs to him.

And those with him are called and chosen and faithful. Three words describing believers, almost in passing, and the order is the whole doctrine. Called (klētoi): summoned by God’s effective call (Romans 8:30). They did not volunteer; God summoned them. Chosen (eklektoi, elect): chosen by God before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). Behind the calling is a choosing, and behind the choosing is nothing but God’s own decision. Faithful (pistoi): trusting and loyal to the end. This is the one they do, but it comes third. God calls and chooses, and those he calls and chooses prove faithful. Their faithfulness is the visible end of a chain whose first two links were forged before they existed. Jesus said many are called, but few are chosen (Matthew 22:14), using call there for the outward invitation; here it is the inward, effectual call.

What it does not mean. Those with the Lamb do not fight with weapons. They share his victory, won by his word (19:15). Their part is to be faithful.

Outnumbered, and on the winning side. This is the answer for a Christian who reads the chapter and feels outnumbered, which is the correct arithmetic and the wrong conclusion. Ten kings, one beast, the whole world drunk, and a handful of congregations meeting in houses. The verse does not encourage them by disputing the numbers. It tells them who is at the front and who put them there.

What is the difference between being called here and in Matthew 22? In Matthew 22:14 the call is the gospel invitation, which goes out to everyone who hears it and which many refuse. In Revelation 17:14, as in Romans 8:30, the called are those whom God has effectually drawn, whose hearts he has opened so that they come (John 6:44; Acts 16:14). The first is the voice of the preacher; the second is the voice of God through the preacher, raising the dead. So we must offer Christ freely to all, and we can be confident that God’s sheep will hear his voice.

I do not feel faithful. Am I really with the Lamb? Faithfulness here is not a feeling or a flawless record but a heart that keeps trusting and returning to Christ. Peter denied him three times and was restored; Thomas doubted and was met. If you are still holding to Christ, still confessing your sins to him and wanting to follow him, you are with the Lamb. And remember the order: you are faithful because you were called and chosen, not the other way round. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

In a sentence. The ten horns you saw are ten kings who have not yet begun to reign, but they will receive royal authority for one hour, together with the beast; they have one purpose, and they will hand over their power and authority to the beast; they will wage war against the Lamb, but the Lamb will defeat them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are his called, chosen and faithful followers.

On a Tuesday. When you feel that your faith is small and the world’s power is huge, say these three words over yourself: called, chosen, faithful. Then say who the Lamb is: Lord of lords and King of kings. Your loyalty this week, at work, at home, online, is not a lonely stand. You are standing with him, and he has already won.

For worship. If you are with the Lamb, you are called, chosen and faithful by his grace. Worship him as King of kings and Lord of lords. The kings of the earth gather against him and give their power to the beast for one hour, and he does not even need to describe the battle. He conquered by being slain, and he will conquer by appearing. Before the world was made he chose a people; in time he called them by name; and to the end he keeps them faithful. Every crown on earth is borrowed from his, and every one will be cast at his feet.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to me, "The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages. And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the angel said to me, “The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages. And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire,

The setting. Ezekiel 23:25–29 describes how the lovers of unfaithful Jerusalem would turn on her, strip her naked and leave her bare. Jezebel’s flesh was eaten by dogs (2 Kings 9:36). In AD 68–69, Rome itself was torn apart in civil war, and the Capitol was burned by rival Roman armies. The fire of AD 64 had already destroyed much of the city.

And the angel said to me, The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages. The angel interprets his own image, and the fourfold phrase is the one used since 5:9 of the whole human race (5:9; 7:9), the same people the Lamb ransomed. Babylon’s influence is worldwide, and her seat is popular support. She rules by being wanted.

A throne set on water. Water in this book is not solid ground. The sea is chaos; a river was poured out of the dragon’s mouth to sweep the woman away (12:15); the Euphrates dried up in a single bowl (16:12). A throne set on water is a throne set on a mood, and a mood can go out as fast as it came in, which is what the next verse describes.

And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. Hate (misēsousin). This is the turn of the chapter and it is the last thing a reader expects. Babylon is not destroyed by the armies of heaven. She is destroyed by the beast she was riding and the kings who were her clients. The beast and its allies turn against the woman who rode on them.

They will make her desolate and naked. Desolate (ērēmōmenēn): laid waste, made a wilderness. Naked: stripped of her finery and exposed, the woman in purple and scarlet and gold with nothing on.

And devour her flesh and burn her up with fire. Like Jezebel, eaten by the dogs by the wall of Jezreel (2 Kings 9:36); like a city sacked and burned. Under the law, burning was the penalty for a priest’s daughter who became a prostitute (Leviticus 21:9). The four verbs escalate, and every one of them was a clause in her own contract. She sold beauty and is left desolate; she traded on being clothed and is stripped; she drank the blood of the saints and is eaten; she offered a cup of fire and is burned.

Evil is not loyal. The underlying observation is one of the most useful things this book says about evil, and it should be stated plainly because it is not obvious. Evil has no loyalty. It has no capacity for it. Political power eventually destroys the culture and economy that supported it. The godless world system is self-destructive. The alliance between the corrupt system and the brute power that carries it holds only while both are getting something, and when it stops paying, the beast eats the woman. History is monotonous on this point: the collaborators are purged, the financiers are shot, the useful men are tried by the regime they installed. Nobody who has ever climbed onto the beast has been carried all the way.

What it does not mean. The beast destroying Babylon does not make the beast good. It shows that evil destroys evil, and that God uses even the wicked to judge the wicked.

Should Christians ever seek political power or allies? Christians may serve in government and should seek justice and the good of their city (Jeremiah 29:7; Romans 13:1–7). Joseph and Daniel served pagan kings faithfully. The warning here is against climbing on the beast: making an alliance that requires us to compromise Christ’s truth, or trusting a political power to secure the church’s future. Whenever the church has bought favour by silence or sold its witness for protection, it has eventually been devoured. Serve honestly, speak truthfully, and never make any party, ruler or nation your saviour.

In a sentence. Then the angel said to me, The waters you saw, where the prostitute sits, are peoples, crowds, nations and languages; and the ten horns you saw and the beast will come to hate the prostitute; they will strip her bare and leave her ruined, eat her flesh and burn her up with fire.

On a Tuesday. The world’s alliances and pleasures do not last; those who serve them are eventually devoured by them. Find your security in Christ alone. If you are tempted this week to make a small accommodation for the sake of safety, a silence to keep your place, a compromise to keep the peace with someone powerful, remember that the thing you are riding to keep your position has an appetite, and it is not sentimental about passengers.

For worship. The Lamb is faithful to the end. The beast devours its friends, and the world consumes those who love it, but Christ has never once betrayed one who trusted him. He was the one who was stripped and made desolate, numbered with the transgressors, so that the unfaithful could be clothed and kept. He laid down his life for his friends while they were still his enemies. His love is not a contract that ends when it stops paying; it is a covenant sealed in his blood, and he will never leave nor forsake his own.

verseByVerse.quote: for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled. And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled. And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.”

The setting. Scripture often shows God using the free actions of wicked people to accomplish his purposes: Joseph’s brothers (Genesis 50:20), Assyria (Isaiah 10:5–7), Cyrus (Isaiah 45:1–4), and above all those who crucified Jesus, who did what God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:27–28). Proverbs 21:1 says the king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will.

For God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose. The verse explains the one before it, and it is the most audacious sentence in the chapter. Put it into their hearts (edōken eis tas kardias autōn, gave into their hearts); purpose (gnōmēn, mind, plan). The reason the kings agreed, the reason they handed everything to the beast, and the reason the beast turned on the woman, is that God has put it into their hearts. God is sovereign even over the evil intentions of the beast and its kings. They act freely and wickedly, and they are responsible for what they do; yet God directs it to his own ends.

Free, wicked, and directed. Not that God tempted anybody, and not that anybody in this chapter is innocent; every one of them is doing exactly what he wants and will answer for it. But the deepest cause of the collapse of Babylon is a decision taken in heaven, carried out through the free and wicked choices of men who thought they were serving themselves. Scripture says this repeatedly and without embarrassment. God hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and Pharaoh hardened his own heart, and both are stated in the same narrative. He turned the hearts of the Egyptians to hate his people (Psalm 105:25). Assyria was the rod of his anger and did not know it (Isaiah 10:5–7). And Peter said of the worst act in human history that Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and in the same breath that lawless men crucified him (Acts 2:23).

By being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast. Even their alliance with the beast serves God’s plan. The very unity they formed against him is the instrument he uses.

Until the words of God are fulfilled. Fulfilled (telesthēsontai, completed). God’s word sets the limit. Nothing happens apart from it. There is an end point, and it is not the exhaustion of the kings or the collapse of the system. It is the completion of what God said. The permission runs exactly as far as the promise and not one hour further.

And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth. Has dominion (echousa basileian): has a kingdom, rules. In John’s day there was only one city that ruled the kings of the earth: Rome. The angel makes the identification as clear as it could safely be made in a letter that might fall into Roman hands. But the description is about what she does rather than where she is, and the office has never been vacant for long. Babylon is whatever, in a given century, sits on the peoples, trades with the kings, dresses beautifully, offers everything a person wants without the God who made it, and is prepared to shed blood to keep its position.

Where Christians differ: is God the author of evil? Some worry that saying God put it into their hearts makes God responsible for their sin, and so they soften the verse to mean only that God permits it. Verdict: Scripture teaches that God ordains all that comes to pass, including the evil acts of creatures, without himself being the author of sin, and without taking away their responsibility (Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). He does not tempt anyone to evil (James 1:13), nor infuse wickedness into their hearts; but he directs their evil desires to fulfil his good purpose. This mystery is not a reason for fear but for comfort: even the beast’s schemes serve God’s plan.

What it does not mean. God’s sovereignty does not excuse the beast and the kings. They are judged for what they do (19:19–21).

How does this help a persecuted church? The practical weight of it is considerable, and it is why the verse is here rather than in a theological appendix. A believer watching a hostile power arrange itself has two possible accounts. Either history is a contest whose outcome depends on whether the good side can hold out, or the arrangements being made against the church are themselves the means by which God dismantles what is arrayed against her. The second is harder to look at and is the only one with a floor under it. It means that no plot against you is outside his plan, and none can go one hour beyond his word.

Two women, side by side. So the chapter ends where it began, with an angel showing John a woman. There will be another woman, and another angel, and another invitation in the same words (21:9). Both are cities and both are brides, and a reader is asked to look at them side by side and see which he has been dressing for. One is arrayed in purple and scarlet and gold, rides a beast she does not control, and is stripped and burned by the thing she was sitting on. The other is clothed in fine linen, bright and pure, and comes down out of heaven from God, and her husband is the Lamb who was slain and is Lord of lords and King of kings.

In a sentence. For God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose, by agreeing together to hand their royal authority over to the beast until God’s words are fulfilled; and the woman you saw is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth.

On a Tuesday. When world events seem out of control, remember that God directs even the plans of the wicked. Trust him, and pray. Pray specifically: for rulers to be restrained, for the persecuted to be kept, for enemies of the gospel to be converted, and for God’s words to be fulfilled. Then go about your ordinary duties in peace. The king’s heart is in the LORD’s hand, and so is yours.

For worship. Our God rules the hearts of kings. He turns them like streams of water, and he turns even their rebellion into the fulfilment of his word. He did it at the cross, where the rulers gathered against his Anointed and did only what his hand and plan had determined, and out of the worst crime in history came the salvation of the world. If he could make the murder of his Son the means of our redemption, there is no scheme of the beast he cannot overrule. And the Lamb will conquer, because of who he is, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful, in that order, and the first two were settled before the world was made.

17.text: <sup>1</sup>Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said to me, “Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters,<sup>2</sup>with whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality, and with the wine of whose sexual immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk.”<sup>3</sup>And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns.<sup>4</sup>The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality.<sup>5</sup>And on her forehead was written a name of mystery: “BABYLON THE GREAT, MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH’S ABOMINATIONS.”<sup>6</sup>And I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. When I saw her, I marveled greatly.<sup>7</sup>But the angel said to me, “Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her.<sup>8</sup>The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast, because it was and is not and is to come.<sup>9</sup>This calls for a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated;<sup>10</sup>they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while.<sup>11</sup>As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.<sup>12</sup>And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast.<sup>13</sup>These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast.<sup>14</sup>They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.”<sup>15</sup>And the angel said to me, “The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages.<sup>16</sup>And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire,<sup>17</sup>for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.<sup>18</sup>And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.”

18.title: Fallen, Fallen Is Babylon the Great
18.overview:
Chapter 18 is Revelation’s sustained lament over the fall of the great city. It is one of the longest chapters in the book, and it is deliberately literary in character — structured like the great prophetic dirges of the Old Testament (Isaiah 13–14 over Babylon; Ezekiel 26–28 over Tyre; Ezekiel 27 especially, whose cargo list John adapts in vv. 12–13). The chapter uses the Old Testament’s own poetic forms to announce the end of the Old Testament’s great enemy.

The chapter moves through three distinct movements. First (vv. 1–8): the angelic announcement of Babylon’s fall and the call for God’s people to come out of her. Second (vv. 9–20): the threefold lament of the kings, merchants, and seafarers — three groups whose wealth depended on Babylon, each mourning from a safe distance as the city burns. Third (vv. 21–24): the millstone sign and the sixfold silence — the total, irreversible end of the city that made the nations drunk with her wine.

The economic detail of chapter 18 is one of its most striking features. The cargo list of vv. 12–13 is specific, comprehensive, and damning — ending with ‘slaves, that is, human souls.’ Babylon’s economy is built on everything, including people. The city that offered the nations luxury and culture and wealth was also the city that traded in human beings as commodities. This is Revelation’s most direct indictment of the economics of empire, and it is not limited to the Roman slave trade: every economic system that treats human beings as means rather than ends falls under the same indictment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Announcement and the Call
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: an angel with great authority comes down and the earth was made bright with his glory (cf. Ezek. 43:2). Verses 2–3: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! — the announcement of 14:8 now given twenty-four verses instead of one. She becomes a haunt of demons and unclean birds, which is exactly what the prophets said of the first Babylon (Isa. 13:21–22; Jer. 50:39). And three groups are named who will structure the chapter: the nations who drank, the kings who traded, and — new here — the merchants, who grew rich from the power of her luxurious living.

Verses 4–5: Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues (Jer. 51:45; Isa. 52:11; cf. 2 Cor. 6:17), for her sins are heaped high as heaven — a tower again (Gen. 11:4) — and God has remembered her iniquities.

Verses 6–8: repay her double in the cup she mixed; and Babylon speaks in her own voice, quoted from Isaiah’s taunt against the original city (Isa. 47:7–8): I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see. The three things she says she will never see are the three that arrive: death and mourning and famine, all in a single day.
verseByVerse.theology:
Come Out of Her

Babylon is fallen and left a haunt of unclean things. God’s people are called to come out of her — not by emigrating but by refusing to share her sins. She said she would never see mourning; death, mourning and famine come in a single day.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What the beast enforced by law, Babylon sustained by trade.

Now: Coming out of Babylon happens in small daily refusals; beware the unspoken belief that your comforts will simply go on.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory. And he called out with a mighty voice, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast. For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory. And he called out with a mighty voice, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast. For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living.”

Meaning first. Revelation 18 is a funeral song over Babylon, the world city of wealth, luxury and persecution, written in the style of the Old Testament prophets’ laments over Babylon and Tyre. A glorious angel announces that Babylon has fallen and become a haunt of demons, because she seduced the nations, kings and merchants with her wealth and immorality (vv. 1–3). A voice from heaven calls God’s people to come out of her, so as not to share her sins or plagues, and calls for her to be repaid double for her pride and self-glorification, for she said, I sit as a queen, and her plagues will come in a single day (vv. 4–8). Then three groups lament from a distance: the kings who shared her luxury (vv. 9–10), the merchants who grew rich from her trade in every luxury, and even in human beings (vv. 11–17a), and the sailors whose wealth came from her shipping (vv. 17b–19). Each cries, alas, in a single hour she is ruined. But heaven, the saints, apostles and prophets are told to rejoice, because God has judged her for them (v. 20). Finally, a mighty angel throws a great millstone into the sea: so Babylon will be thrown down, and music, craft, the mill, lamplight and the voices of bride and groom will be heard in her no more, because her merchants were the world’s great ones, she deceived the nations by sorcery, and in her was found the blood of the prophets and saints (vv. 21–24). The chapter exposes the hollow glory of a civilisation built on greed, luxury and exploitation, warns the church not to be entangled in it, and assures the suffering that God will judge it completely. Chapter 17 showed Babylon as a religious and political power; chapter 18 shows her as an economy, and the charge sheet is a cargo list. And over the smoking ruin, heaven is told to rejoice, because the God who hears his people has judged their case.

The setting. The chapter draws heavily on Isaiah 13, 21 and 47, Jeremiah 50–51 (oracles against Babylon) and Ezekiel 26–28 (the laments over Tyre, the great trading city of the ancient world). In John’s day, Rome imported vast quantities of goods from across the empire, by sea through its port at Ostia, to supply the luxury of its elite, and the wealth of the provinces flowed to it. Roman writers such as Pliny the Elder complained about the extravagance of Roman luxury and its drain on the empire.

After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority. Great authority (exousian megalēn). Babylon claimed great authority; this angel’s is greater. And it is the authority of one sent, coming down from heaven, which is where every true authority in this book comes from.

And the earth was made bright with his glory. The detail is easy to miss and it sets the tone of the chapter. This angel is bright enough that the whole earth lights up as he descends. Ezekiel saw the same thing when the glory of God returned to the temple: the earth shone with his glory (Ezekiel 43:2). The city about to be described as the most magnificent in the world is about to be lit by something that makes it look like a candle at noon. And the contrast runs to the end of the chapter, where Babylon’s lamps go out (v. 23).

And he called out with a mighty voice, Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! The announcement made in one verse at 14:8 is made again, and this time the chapter does not move on: twenty-four verses of it. The words are Isaiah’s watchman on the wall (Isaiah 21:9). And they are in the past tense: so certain that it is as good as done.

She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast. This is exactly what the prophets said would happen to the first Babylon, and John is quoting deliberately. Isaiah said that wild animals would lie down there, howling creatures fill its houses, hyenas cry in its towers and jackals in its pleasant palaces (Isaiah 13:21–22; also 34:11–14 of Edom; Jeremiah 50:39). Consider what that means as a picture. It is a ruin at night. The great houses are still standing; the streets are still laid out; and what moves in them are owls and jackals. Anyone who has walked through an abandoned town knows the effect. The buildings are what make it terrible, because they were built for people and there are no people. The glittering city becomes a desolate ruin, and her true nature, demonic all along, is revealed.

A prison for unclean things. The word haunt (phylakē) is literally a prison, a place of keeping, a lair. The city that offered the whole world its freedom has become a cage for unclean things.

For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality. As in 14:8 and 17:2. The nations drank what she poured, and lost their judgement.

And the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living. Three groups shared her sin and will lament her fall: kings, merchants and sailors (vv. 9–19). This verse is the chapter’s table of contents. And notice the new group. In chapter 17 the parties to Babylon’s business were the kings and the drunken population. Here the merchants arrive (emporoi, wholesale traders), and from verse 11 onward they dominate the chapter. That is the most striking thing about the two chapters read together. Chapter 17 showed a prostitute demanding worship, riding a beast, drunk on the blood of the saints. Chapter 18 shows a market. And they are the same city, which is the point: what the beast enforces by law, Babylon sustains by trade. Political power and economic profit were bound up with her idolatry.

The power of her luxurious living. The last phrase names the mechanism precisely. The word (strēnous) means arrogant luxury, excess, wantonness, the strength that comes from having far more than is needed. Babylon’s hold on the merchants is not that she threatened them. It is that she made them rich.

What it does not mean. Trade and commerce are not evil in themselves. Babylon’s sin is luxury pursued in pride, at the expense of others, as a substitute for God, and built on idolatry and exploitation.

Has Babylon already fallen? In John’s day Babylon was Rome, and Rome did eventually fall, but slowly, over centuries, not in a single hour (v. 10). Some expect a literally rebuilt city of Babylon. The more likely reading is that Babylon is the world system of wealth, power and false worship that Rome embodied, which has risen and fallen in many forms, and whose final fall comes at Christ’s return. Every collapse of a proud empire in history is a rehearsal of this chapter, and the last one will be the performance.

Is it wrong for a Christian to be wealthy? No. Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly, and Paul does not tell the rich to give up everything but to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share, and to set their hope on God rather than on uncertain riches (1 Timothy 6:17–19). The danger is real, though: Jesus said it is hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom (Mark 10:23–25), because wealth so easily becomes the thing we trust. The questions to ask are how you got it, what you trust in, whether you are generous, and whether you could lose it and still praise God.

In a sentence. After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven with great authority, and the earth was lit up by his splendour; he shouted with a powerful voice: Fallen! Fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a home for demons, a lair for every unclean spirit, every unclean bird and every unclean and hated animal, because all the nations have drunk the wine of her passionate immorality, the kings of the earth committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth grew rich from her extravagant luxury.

On a Tuesday. Ask how much of your life is shaped by the pursuit of luxury. Babylon’s glory ends in ruins. Look at your diary and your bank statement for the past month, and ask what they show you are living for. Then choose one concrete way this week to live more simply or give more generously, as a small declaration that you belong to another city.

For worship. The glory of God lights the whole earth, and every human glory is a candle before it. Babylon’s lamps go out, and her palaces are left to jackals, but the city of God needs no sun or moon, because the glory of God is its light and the Lamb is its lamp. Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and standing, for ever, is the throne of the one who was rich and for our sake became poor, so that we, through his poverty, might become rich.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, "Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues; for her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, “Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues; for her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.

The setting. The prophets called the Jewish exiles to flee from Babylon before its fall: go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of the LORD! (Jeremiah 51:45; also 50:8; 51:6; Isaiah 48:20; 52:11). Lot was urged to flee Sodom before its destruction (Genesis 19:12–22). Paul quoted Isaiah 52:11 to the Corinthians: go out from their midst, and be separate from them (2 Corinthians 6:17). The tower of Babel was built to reach the heavens (Genesis 11:4); Babylon’s sins now pile up to heaven.

Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, Come out of her, my people. Come out (exelthate). The command is quoted from the prophets almost word for word, and Paul used the same line to a church living in a Greek port. And notice the possessive: my people. God’s people are still in Babylon, in the world system, living among its temptations, and he claims them there. They are called to come out.

Lest you take part in her sins. Take part (synkoinōnēsēte): share, have fellowship with. The danger is not just living in Babylon, but sharing her sins: idolatry, greed, luxury, immorality, injustice.

Lest you share in her plagues. Those who share her sins will share her judgement. It is a warning rather than a threat. When a system falls, the people who were profiting from it fall with it, and they do not get a separate hearing on the grounds that they were only doing what everyone did.

It is not emigration. Two things need saying about what the command means, because it has been misused in both directions. It cannot mean physical withdrawal, and the New Testament settles that. Christians stayed in Rome; Paul greeted a congregation there and told them to pay their taxes (Romans 13:6–7). Jesus prayed that the Father would not take his disciples out of the world, but keep them from the evil one (John 17:15). Paul told the Corinthians that avoiding immoral people altogether would require leaving the world entirely (1 Corinthians 5:9–10). Whatever coming out of Babylon is, it is not a compound in the hills.

It is non-participation. The verse itself says what it is, twice, in two parallel clauses: lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues. A Christian lives in the city, works in it, pays for it and prays for it, and does not join in what it does, and does not want what it wants. That is far harder than moving house, and far more searching. Nobody has to decide whether to leave a country. Everybody has to decide, repeatedly and in small instalments, whether to make the arrangement that everyone makes: the invoice adjusted, the thing not mentioned, the standard that quietly relaxes because it is costing too much. Coming out of Babylon happens on Tuesday afternoons, and nobody photographs it.

For her sins are heaped high as heaven. Heaped high (ekollēthēsan): glued together, piled up. The image is a tower of sins stacked up until they reach the sky, and it takes the reader straight back to where Babylon began, at a tower whose builders wanted its top in the heavens (Genesis 11:4). She always did want to reach heaven. She has managed it at last, and it is her record that arrived. God’s patience has an end.

And God has remembered her iniquities. As in 16:19. In Scripture that never means something had slipped his mind. It is the language of a file coming to the top of the pile, and of a God who is about to act on what he has known all along. God’s delay is not forgetfulness.

Where Christians differ: does this mean Christians should withdraw from society? Some groups, such as some Anabaptists and monastic movements, have taken such passages to call for physical separation from the world, forming separate communities. Others have used the verse to call believers out of particular churches they regard as Babylon. Verdict: coming out of Babylon is mainly spiritual and moral: refusing to share the world’s idolatry, greed and sin, while still living in the world as salt and light. Jesus prayed not that his disciples would be taken out of the world, but that they would be kept from the evil one (John 17:15). Paul told the Corinthians not to leave the world, but not to share the sins of professing believers (1 Corinthians 5:9–11). Sometimes faithfulness will require leaving a particular job, relationship or even church that demands compromise. But the call is to holiness, not withdrawal.

What it does not mean. Coming out of Babylon does not mean God’s people can lose their salvation if they are found in the city when it falls. It is a call to be what they are: God’s holy people, not Babylon’s.

What does coming out look like on an ordinary day? It looks like honesty in your accounts when everyone else rounds up; refusing to laugh at what degrades people; keeping sex within marriage when the culture treats it as recreation; turning off what fills your mind with greed or lust; paying fairly and giving generously; and speaking of Christ when silence would be safer. It also means rhythms that keep your heart in the other city: the Lord’s Day, the church gathered, the word of God and prayer. You come out of Babylon not by moving away but by belonging somewhere else while you live there.

When should a Christian actually leave something? When staying would require you to sin, or when you cannot remain without being drawn into sin you have repeatedly failed to resist. A job that requires dishonesty, a relationship that pulls you from Christ, a business deal that depends on exploitation, or a church that has abandoned the gospel itself, not merely one with faults: these are places where coming out may mean walking out. Seek counsel from mature believers, pray, and act with humility rather than pride. But do not stay in sin because leaving is costly.

In a sentence. Then I heard another voice from heaven say: Come out of her, my people, so that you will not share in her sins or suffer any of her plagues; for her sins are piled up as high as heaven, and God has remembered her crimes.

On a Tuesday. Where are you being drawn into the world’s sins, at work, online or in your spending? Come out of her, not by leaving the world, but by refusing her ways. Name one specific arrangement you have quietly made with Babylon, and end it this week.

For worship. God calls his people my people, even while they live in Babylon’s streets. He does not abandon them to the city or wait for them to find their own way out; he calls them, as he called Lot out of Sodom and Israel out of Egypt and the exiles out of Babylon. He remembers the city’s sins, and he remembers his people’s names. And he provided the way out at the cost of his own Son, who suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood. Here we have no lasting city; we seek the city that is to come, and its builder and maker is God.

verseByVerse.quote: Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed. As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, 'I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.' For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed. As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, ‘I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.’ For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her.”

The setting. Jeremiah 50:15, 29 says of Babylon: repay her according to her deeds; do to her as she has done. In Isaiah 47:7–9, Babylon says that she will be mistress for ever, that she will not sit as a widow or know the loss of children; but God replies that these two things will come to her in a moment, in one day: the loss of children and widowhood. Double repayment was a principle of restitution in the law (Exodus 22:4, 7, 9), and Isaiah 40:2 and Jeremiah 16:18 speak of double punishment.

Pay her back as she herself has paid back others. Pay back (apodote): render, give back. The imperatives are plural and unattributed, addressed perhaps to the agents of God’s judgement, and the reader should not assume they are the church, because 17:16 has already said who actually destroys Babylon: the beast and the ten kings. Whoever is being commanded, no Christian in this book ever repays anybody. This is the principle of just retribution: what she did to God’s people will be done to her.

And repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed. Double (diplōsate ta dipla, double the double). That raises a fair question about justice. If the punishment is twice the crime, is it just? The way the prophets use the word answers it: double can mean the full corresponding measure, a matching copy, rather than twice as much. Isaiah promised Israel a double that plainly meant full payment rather than excess (Isaiah 40:2; 61:7). And the rest of the sentence makes it explicit: mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed. It is her own cup, her own recipe, folded back on her. Nothing new has been added. Her judgement fits her sin precisely and completely.

As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning. Glorified herself (edoxasen hautēn): the root sin is pride, taking the glory that belongs to God. Lived in luxury (estrēniasen). Self-glorification and self-indulgence go together. The measure of her judgement is the measure of her self-exaltation.

Since in her heart she says, I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see. Here is Babylon in her own words, and the boast is quoted from Isaiah’s taunt against the original city (Isaiah 47:7–8). Three claims, and each is a denial of something ordinary. I sit as a queen: permanent authority. I am no widow: she will not be left; nothing she depends on can die. Mourning I shall never see: she is exempt from grief. This is pride and false security. She thinks she is untouchable and permanent, the city that called itself eternal (Roma aeterna). Every proud civilisation thinks the same.

The assumption of every prosperous society. That is not chiefly arrogance. It is the settled, unexamined assumption of every prosperous society that has ever existed, and it is why a comfortable church finds this chapter so hard to feel. The claim is not, I am better than others; it is, this will go on. Anyone who has never seriously reckoned with the possibility that his country, his savings, his health or his arrangements might simply stop has said this sentence in his heart without ever putting it into words. And Laodicea said the same thing in different words: I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing (3:17). The sentence can be said inside a church as easily as inside an empire.

For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine. In a single day (en mia hēmera): sudden collapse. The three-part list echoes the horsemen (6:8). And the three things she said she would never see are the three things that arrive. She will not be a widow, and death comes; she will never see mourning, and mourning comes; she lived in luxury, and famine comes. The judgement is her own boast, itemised and reversed. And the chapter will say in a single hour three more times (vv. 10, 17, 19). Something built over centuries goes in an afternoon, which is how these things actually happen: slowly, then all at once.

And she will be burned up with fire. As in 17:16.

For mighty is the Lord God who has judged her. Mighty (ischyros). Babylon was called the mighty city (v. 10), but the Lord God is mightier. Her strength was borrowed and temporary; his is his own and eternal.

What it does not mean. The call for repayment is not a call for Christians to take revenge. It is God’s own sentence on Babylon, carried out by his agents. Believers are forbidden to repay evil for evil (Romans 12:17–19); they leave vengeance to God, who will repay.

How do I know if I am saying I sit as a queen? Watch for the signs of quiet self-sufficiency: you rarely pray except in crisis; you assume your income, health and comfort will continue; you plan your future without reference to God (James 4:13–16); you feel little need of the church; and other people’s suffering seems far away. The cure is not anxiety but humility: thank God daily for what you have as gifts that could be withdrawn, hold your plans with if the Lord wills, and let the needs of others interrupt your comfort.

In a sentence. Give back to her as she has given, and pay her back double for what she has done; in the cup she mixed for others, mix her a double portion; give her as much torment and grief as the glory and luxury she gave herself, because in her heart she boasts, I sit enthroned as a queen; I am not a widow; I will never mourn; so her plagues will overtake her in a single day, death, mourning and famine, and she will be burned with fire, for the Lord God who judges her is mighty.

On a Tuesday. Watch for the thought, I am secure, nothing can touch me. Pride goes before a fall. Find your security in God, not in wealth or status. When you make plans this week, say out loud, if the Lord wills. It is a small phrase, and it is the opposite of Babylon’s boast.

For worship. Mighty is the Lord God who judges. He sees through every boast and brings down every throne that exalts itself against him. Yet the same mighty God took the lowest place. Christ, who truly was King, did not cling to his glory but emptied himself, became a servant, and humbled himself to death on a cross, and drank a cup he had never mixed, the cup of our sin. Babylon glorified herself and was brought low. He humbled himself, and God has highly exalted him and given him the name above every name.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Three sets of mourners in descending rank, modelled on Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre (Ezek. 26–28). Verses 9–11: the kings weep and wail, stand far off, in fear of her torment, and cry Alas! Alas! You great city… For in a single hour your judgment has come; and the merchants mourn since no one buys their cargo anymore.

Verses 12–13 give the manifest: twenty-eight items in seven groups, running downward from precious metals and stones through fabrics, fine furniture, spices, food and livestock — and ending and slaves, that is, human souls. Verse 14 speaks to the city directly: the fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you… never to be found again.

Verses 15–16: the merchants stand far off and describe her as a dressed body — linen, purple, scarlet, gold, jewels, pearls, nearly the wording of 17:4. Verses 17–19: shipmasters, seafaring men and sailors stand far off, throw dust on their heads (cf. Ezek. 27:29–32), and cry What city was like the great city? and in a single hour she has been laid waste.

Verse 20 opens a window in the middle of the funeral: Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!
verseByVerse.theology:
The Threefold Lament

Kings, merchants and sailors stand far off and weep — for their trade, not for her. The cargo list ends with slaves, that is, human souls. Heaven and the saints are called to rejoice because God has given judgement for them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The whole Roman world was arranged to supply one city.

Now: Ask whose hands made what you hold, and whether your deepest grief would be for a person or for a market.

verseByVerse.quote: And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning. They will stand far off, in fear of her torment, and say, "Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come." And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning. They will stand far off, in fear of her torment, and say, “Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come.” And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore,

The setting. Ezekiel 26:16–18 and 27:29–36 describe the princes of the sea, merchants and sailors lamenting the fall of Tyre, the great trading city, standing on the shore, crying bitterly, throwing dust on their heads. Revelation 18 follows the same pattern with three groups of mourners.

The funeral. Now the funeral, and it has three sets of mourners in descending order of rank: the kings, the merchants and the sailors. The whole passage is modelled on Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre, where the same three groups stand off and wail over a burning port, and John expects the echo to be heard.

And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her. The first group of mourners: political rulers who shared her idolatry and luxury.

Will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning. Weep (klausousin) and wail (kopsontai, beat their breasts). Their grief is for themselves, for what they have lost. Not one of them grieves for her victims or repents.

They will stand far off, in fear of her torment. Far off (apo makrothen). The detail that governs all three laments is in this clause, and it is repeated at verses 15 and 17. Nobody goes near. Nobody attempts a rescue. These are her lovers, her business partners and her carriers, and every one of them watches from a safe distance, afraid of sharing her fate. Their loyalty was only to what she could give them. That is the exact measure of what Babylon’s relationships were worth. She had the kings of the earth and the merchants of the earth and every shipmaster afloat, and at the end not one of them will cross the road. Set that beside the promise made to the poor, persecuted church of Smyrna in chapter 2: be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life (2:10), said by someone who did come near, all the way to death.

And say, Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! Alas (ouai) is the same word as woe: the double cry of lament.

For in a single hour your judgment has come. Single hour (mia hōra), repeated three times (vv. 10, 17, 19). The suddenness of her collapse is astonishing: centuries of power undone in an hour. And read the laments carefully for what is absent from all three. Not one word of repentance. Not one word about the blood of the saints, which verse 24 says was found in her. Not even any real sympathy for Babylon herself. They weep because they are afraid, and because their trade is finished.

And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore. The second group: the traders. There it is, said outright, and John gives the reason in the same breath as the tears. Their grief is openly economic. They mourn the end of the market, not the city. The most honest sentence in the chapter is put in the mouth of the mourners, and they do not appear to notice what they have admitted.

What it does not mean. The mourners’ distance does not mean they were innocent. They shared her sin. They are simply trying to escape her punishment.

Is it wrong to work in business or finance? No. Trade, banking and enterprise can be honourable callings that serve neighbours and glorify God; the woman of Proverbs 31 considers a field and buys it, and Lydia was a dealer in purple cloth (Acts 16:14). The merchants here are condemned because they grew rich from Babylon’s sin, did not care whom they hurt, and loved the market more than God or people. A Christian in business serves God by dealing honestly, paying fairly, refusing exploitation, and treating profit as a means of serving others rather than as the measure of a life.

In a sentence. When the kings of the earth who committed immorality with her and shared her luxury see the smoke rising from her burning, they will weep and mourn over her; terrified by her torment, they will stand at a distance and cry: How terrible, how terrible for you, great city, mighty city of Babylon! In one hour your judgement has come; and the merchants of the earth weep and mourn over her because nobody buys their goods any more.

On a Tuesday. Notice who mourns Babylon: those who profited from her. Ask what you would grieve if the world’s economy collapsed tomorrow, and whether your treasure is in heaven (Matthew 6:19–21). If the thing you would find hardest to lose were taken away, would the grief be for a person or for a market? The kings and merchants are not condemned for feeling loss. They are shown up by the reason for it.

For worship. The world’s friends stand far off when the end comes. Christ came near. He did not watch our ruin from a safe distance, afraid of sharing it; he entered it, took our judgement on himself, and was forsaken so that we would never be. Every other loyalty in Babylon lasts only while it pays. His lasts to the end and beyond, and he has promised never to leave nor forsake us. Blessed be the friend of sinners, who crossed the road.
verseByVerse.note: The laments echo Ezekiel’s dirge over the trading city of Tyre.

verseByVerse.quote: cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth, all kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble, cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth, all kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble, cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls.

The setting. This list closely matches the luxury imports of first-century Rome, which drew goods from across the known world: gold and silver from Spain, pearls from the Indian Ocean, silk from China, citron wood from North Africa (prized for expensive tables), ivory from Africa and India, marble from Greece, cinnamon and spices from India and Arabia, wine from Italy and Greece, wheat from Egypt (Rome depended on Egyptian grain), horses and chariots from many provinces. Rome had an enormous slave population, perhaps a third of the city, bought and sold in markets across the empire. Ezekiel 27:12–24 contains a similar list of Tyre’s trade, which also included human beings (Ezekiel 27:13).

Read it as a list. Then the cargo manifest, and it must be read as a list rather than skimmed, because John has arranged it with great care and the last item is the point of the whole chapter. There are twenty-eight items, in groups: precious metals and stones, fabrics, materials for fine furniture, spices and perfumes, foodstuffs, livestock, and finally people. The order runs downward from the most luxurious to the most basic, which is itself a comment: the list begins with what nobody needs and ends with what everybody does. The whole world was arranged to supply one city.

Cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls. Precious metals and stones, the adornments of the prostitute (17:4). The list opens with exactly what she was wearing. And in the new Jerusalem, gold, jewels and pearls are the building materials (21:18–21), freely given. What Babylon traded at a fortune, God paves the streets with.

Fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth. Luxury fabrics. Silk came overland from China along the trade routes and was enormously expensive; under Tiberius the Roman Senate forbade men to wear it, as Tacitus records, on the grounds that it was effeminate extravagance.

All kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble. Materials for luxurious furniture and buildings. Scented wood (xylon thyinon) is citron wood from North Africa, whose grained table tops could sell, Pliny says, for the price of an estate.

Cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense. Exotic spices and perfumes, some used in worship, brought up the incense road from Arabia or by sea from India. Frankincense and myrrh were among the gifts brought to the infant Jesus (Matthew 2:11). The same goods that were laid at the feet of the true King were burned in Babylon for her own pleasure.

Wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep. Food, from luxury (fine flour) to staples (wheat). Rome imported hundreds of thousands of tonnes of grain a year from Egypt and North Africa because it could not feed itself.

Horses and chariots. Chariots (rhedōn) are four-wheeled carriages, a Latin word borrowed into Greek. Transport and luxury.

And slaves, that is, human souls. Here, at the very end, after the horses and carriages, is the climax of the list and its deepest condemnation. The word translated slaves (sōmatōn) is literally bodies, the trade term for slaves, and the manifest of a Roman merchant ship really would list bodies after livestock. Then John adds words of his own that no manifest ever carried: that is, human souls (psychas anthrōpōn, lives of human beings). It is a correction inserted into somebody else’s paperwork. The market says bodies, in the same column as the cattle, priced by weight and condition. The apostle stops the list to say what they actually are: people, made in God’s image. Babylon’s economy treated human beings as commodities, and her wealth was built on the exploitation of persons. It is the last thing named before the lament resumes, and it is the charge that hangs over the entire economy.

Every generation has its own version. That is why this chapter is not merely about ancient Rome, and why a modern reader should not read it comfortably. The sin named here is not wealth. It is an arrangement in which human beings appear on the manifest, where the accounting is done in a way that makes people into a line item, and where the profitability of the arrangement is reason enough not to enquire too closely into who is at the far end of it. Every generation has found its own version difficult to see while it was running. The question the manifest puts to a reader is not whether he owns anyone. It is whether he knows whose hands made what he is holding, and whether he has ever wanted to.

What it does not mean. The list does not condemn trade in these goods as such. God gives food, wine and oil to gladden human hearts (Psalm 104:15). It condemns an economy driven by greed and luxury, that devours people and puts profit above persons.

What can an ordinary Christian do about modern slavery and exploitation? More than nothing. Slavery still exists, in forced labour, trafficking and debt bondage, and it touches ordinary supply chains. Pray for the enslaved and for those who rescue them. Learn where common goods come from, and where you reasonably can, buy from companies that treat workers justly, even if it costs more. Support Christian and other agencies that fight trafficking. Treat the people who serve you, cleaners, delivery drivers, shop workers, as souls rather than services. And remember that the gospel itself is the great liberator: Christians like William Wilberforce opposed the slave trade because they believed that every human being bears God’s image.

In a sentence. No one buys their cargoes of gold, silver, precious stones and pearls; fine linen, purple, silk and scarlet; every kind of fragrant wood and articles of ivory, expensive wood, bronze, iron and marble; cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh and frankincense; wine and olive oil, fine flour and wheat; cattle and sheep; horses and carriages; and human bodies and souls sold as slaves.

On a Tuesday. Ask where the things you buy come from, and whether people were exploited to make them. Babylon’s economy treats people as cargo; God’s people must not. Pick one thing you buy regularly, coffee, clothes, a phone, and find out this week who made it and how they were treated.

For worship. Babylon priced souls by weight. God values them beyond all the gold in the manifest, because he made them in his image, and because he bought them back at a price no market could pay: not with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish. The Son of God was sold for thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave, so that slaves could become sons. In his kingdom no one is cargo. Every name is written, every soul is known, and the redeemed are his treasured possession.
verseByVerse.note: The cargo list ends with human beings — the slave trade on which Rome’s economy depended.

verseByVerse.quote: "The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you, and all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again!" The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment, weeping and mourning aloud, "Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls!
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you, and all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again!” The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment, weeping and mourning aloud, “Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls!

The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you. A single verse spoken directly to the city, breaking into the merchants’ lament, and it contains the most penetrating phrase in the chapter. Fruit (opōra) is ripe fruit, the late summer harvest; longed (epithymias) is craving, desire, lust. The Greek is the fruit of the desire of your soul. It is not a word about trade. It is a word about appetite, and it says that all of this, the silk, the citron wood, the frankincense, the bodies, was never really about commerce at all. It was about wanting. The whole system was built to feed a longing, and the longing was in the soul. What she craved most is gone.

A diagnosis of prosperity. That is the most useful thing this chapter has to say to a reader in a wealthy society, and it is not an attack on prosperity. It is a diagnosis of what prosperity is usually being asked to do. Nobody accumulates in order to have more objects. People accumulate because something in them is hungry and the objects are what is nearest. Augustine said it in a sentence at the start of his Confessions: God made us for himself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in him. Babylon is that restlessness, organised, with a shipping fleet.

And all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again! Delicacies (ta lipara) are rich, fat things, luxuries; splendours (ta lampra) are bright, glittering things. Never (ouketi ou mē) is the strongest negative Greek has: never again, not ever. Not merely lost, but unfindable, a phrase that will toll over the city several more times before the chapter closes. Everything the world prizes is temporary. The fruit her soul longed for did not last, and could not have lasted, and was never going to satisfy the longing even while she had it.

The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment. As the kings did (v. 10). Once more the phrase that runs through all three laments: far off. The merchants who grew rich from her, watching from a distance, mourning aloud, and not moving.

Weeping and mourning aloud, Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls! The second lament is put in almost the words used of the woman in 17:4. The merchants describe her as a dressed body: linen, purple, scarlet, gold, jewels, pearls. Six items, and every one of them was for sale in the manifest they have just lost. So their eulogy for a civilisation is a description of her clothes. Their lament is for her appearance and wealth, the surface glitter, and for their lost profits. They knew her wardrobe and nothing else. There is no mention of anything she did, made, believed or was, and there is nothing else to say, because there was nothing else there.

What it does not mean. Enjoying good things is not sin. The problem is a soul that longs for them above God, so that when they are gone, nothing is left.

Why do the things I want never satisfy for long? Because you were made for God, and every created good, however lovely, is too small to fill a space shaped for him. C. S. Lewis observed that if we find in ourselves a desire no experience in this world can satisfy, the most probable explanation is that we were made for another world. The answer is not to stop desiring but to desire rightly: to receive good things with thanks as signposts, and to bring the deepest longing to Christ, who said that whoever comes to him will never hunger (John 6:35). Contentment is learned, Paul says (Philippians 4:11–13), and it is learned in him.

In a sentence.
