The fruit you longed for is gone from you; all your luxury and splendour have vanished, and you will never find them again; the merchants who sold these things and grew rich from her will stand far away, terrified by her torment, weeping and mourning: How terrible, how terrible for the great city, dressed in fine linen, purple and scarlet, glittering with gold, precious stones and pearls!

On a Tuesday. What does your soul long for? If it is anything this world offers, one day it will be gone. Long for Christ, who is never lost. Next time you feel the pull to buy, scroll or indulge to fill an empty moment, stop and name the hunger underneath, and bring that hunger to God in a short prayer before you reach for anything else.

For worship. Christ is the fruit that never fails. The tree of life in the city of God bears its fruit every month, and its leaves are for the healing of the nations. In his presence is fullness of joy, and at his right hand are pleasures for evermore. Babylon’s splendours are lost, never to be found again; but those who have found him have found what can never be lost, a treasure in heaven where moth and rust do not destroy and thieves do not break in. He satisfies the longing soul, and the hungry soul he fills with good things.

verseByVerse.quote: For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste." And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, "What city was like the great city?" And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned, crying out, "Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste.” And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, “What city was like the great city?” And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned, crying out, “Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.

The setting. Throwing dust on the head was a sign of grief and mourning (Joshua 7:6; Job 2:12; Ezekiel 27:30, where the sailors throw dust on their heads over Tyre). Rome’s grain and luxury goods came by sea, through the port of Ostia and the Bay of Naples.

For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste. Laid waste (ērēmōthē): made desolate, turned into a wilderness. The second single hour.

And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea. The third group of mourners, and the humblest: not kings and not merchant princes, but captains, crews and dockworkers, everyone whose living came off the water. The whole economy of the sea was bound up with Babylon. Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre has the same cast standing on the shore, throwing dust on their heads and crying, who is like Tyre? (Ezekiel 27:29–32).

Stood far off and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, What city was like the great city? That question is a parody, and it is the third time this book has used the form. Israel sang at the Red Sea, who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? (Exodus 15:11). The worshippers of the beast chanted, who is like the beast? (13:4). And here sailors on a beach ask it of a burning city. It is the question of worship, and it keeps being asked of the wrong subject. They had made the city their god.

And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned. As the sailors mourned Tyre. Dust on the head is the ancient sign of grief that has no words left.

Crying out, Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! Grew rich (eploutēsan). Again, their grief is for their own losses, stated in the plainest possible terms. Three social classes, three laments, and one reason between them. Nobody mourns Babylon. They mourn their share of her.

For in a single hour she has been laid waste. The third and final single hour, from the third group. All three laments say it, which means all three have understood the one thing that actually frightens them: not that Babylon was wicked, but that she was quick. Consider what that means for anybody whose confidence rests on something built. These are men who spent their working lives on a trade route, and it took an hour. The chapter is not saying that wealth is evil or that trade is wrong. It is saying that everything in the manifest, and the city that consumed it, and the fleet that carried it, belongs to the category of things that can end between breakfast and lunch.

What it does not mean. Sailors and traders are not singled out as especially wicked. They represent everyone whose livelihood and identity were wrapped up in Babylon’s economy.

Should a Christian save, invest or plan for the future? Yes, wisely. Scripture commends the ant that stores up in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8) and the person who provides for his family (1 Timothy 5:8). The problem is not prudence but trust. Saving is wise; making savings your security is idolatry. Jesus called the rich man a fool not because he had barns but because he was rich toward himself and not toward God (Luke 12:16–21). So plan, save and work hard, but give generously, hold it all loosely, and remember that it could all be gone in an hour, while what you have given to Christ is kept for ever.

In a sentence. In a single hour all this wealth has been wiped out! And every ship’s captain, every seafarer, all the sailors and everyone who makes a living from the sea stood far off, and when they saw the smoke of her burning they cried out, Was there ever a city like this great city? They threw dust on their heads and shouted, weeping and mourning: How terrible, how terrible for the great city, where everyone with ships at sea grew rich from her wealth! In one hour she has been ruined!

On a Tuesday. If your whole identity is tied to your work, your income or the economy, you will be devastated when they fail. Build your life on Christ. Try finishing this sentence honestly: I would not know who I was if I lost my... Whatever completes it is the thing to hand to God this week, thanking him for it and telling him that he, not it, is your life.

For worship. Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders? Not the beast, and not the great city; their glory goes up in smoke in a single hour. You alone are God, and your kingdom does not end. The sailors of Babylon lost everything in an afternoon, but those who trust in you have a treasure that no fire can touch and an anchor for the soul, sure and steadfast, fixed in the heavens where Jesus has gone as our forerunner.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!”

The setting. Jeremiah 51:48 says that the heavens and the earth, and all that is in them, will sing for joy over Babylon. Deuteronomy 32:43 calls the nations to rejoice with God’s people, for he avenges the blood of his children. This verse leads into the great hallelujahs of 19:1–5.

Rejoice over her, O heaven. Rejoice (euphrainou): be glad, celebrate. One verse, and it stands in the middle of the funeral like a window opened in a closed room. Three groups have been weeping; heaven is told to do the opposite. The kings, merchants and sailors weep; God’s people celebrate.

And you saints and apostles and prophets. All God’s people, and especially those who led and suffered: apostles, such as Peter and Paul, killed in Rome, and prophets. Their blood was found in her (v. 24). These are the people she killed. Nobody who has not been wronged is invited to this celebration, and there is a great difference between a victim relieved that justice has finally been done and a bystander enjoying somebody’s ruin.

For God has given judgment for you against her! The Greek is a legal phrase (ekrinen ho theos to krima hymōn ex autēs): God has judged your case against her. The saints brought their case to God’s court (6:10), and he has ruled in their favour. Babylon condemned them; now God has condemned her and vindicated them. What is being celebrated is not suffering, and not destruction as such, but a verdict.

Where Christians differ: is it right to rejoice over judgement? Many Christians are uneasy with this verse, feeling that rejoicing over anyone’s destruction contradicts Christ’s command to love our enemies. Scripture does say, do not rejoice when your enemy falls (Proverbs 24:17). Verdict: the joy here is not delight in suffering, nor personal revenge. It is joy that God has kept his promise, that justice has been done, that evil has been defeated, and that the persecuted have been vindicated. God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11), and neither should we. But when the judgement is final, his people will see clearly that it was right, and rejoice in God’s justice. Now, before that day, we love our enemies, pray for them and seek their salvation, leaving vengeance to God (Romans 12:19–21).

The alternative is worse than it looks. A universe in which the murder of the innocent is finally shrugged at, in which the blood in the foundations of every great city is never mentioned again, is not a kinder universe; it is one in which nothing matters. To be unable to rejoice that wrong has been put right is not compassion. It is a failure to believe that the wrong was real.

The rejoicing follows the judgement. And this is the safeguard: the rejoicing follows the judgement; it never produces it. No Christian in this book lifts a hand against Babylon. They pray, they endure, they refuse the mark, they die, and God settles the account. The joy of verse 20 is the joy of people who were told to leave it with him and did.

What it does not mean. Christians should not rejoice now at the misfortunes of unbelievers, or wish for their destruction. The rejoicing is over the final, completed judgement of an unrepentant world system.

What about the wrong done to me that was never put right? This verse has a quiet pastoral word for anyone still carrying something unresolved: a crime nobody was charged with, a reputation destroyed by someone who prospered afterwards, an abuse that was covered up, a person who died and was never accounted for. A day is coming when heaven will name your case out loud and tell you to be glad. Not because you were owed revenge, but because you were owed a verdict, and it will be delivered. Meanwhile, you may seek justice through proper means, the courts, the church’s discipline, the authorities God has appointed (Romans 13:4), and you may bring your grief to him. You are not required to pretend it did not matter. It matters to God.

In a sentence. Celebrate over her, heaven, and you saints, apostles and prophets, because God has judged her for the way she treated you.

On a Tuesday. Pray this week for a persecuted church by name, and for one person who has wronged you. Ask God to bring the persecutors to repentance, as he did Saul of Tarsus, and to vindicate his people. Then rest: the case is in the right court.

For worship. Thank God that he hears the cries of his persecuted people, and that he will vindicate them. He is the Judge of all the earth, and he will do right. Not one martyr’s case has been lost in his files, not one apostle’s blood forgotten, not one prophet’s word left unanswered. And the verdict he gives for his people rests on a greater verdict: the Judge himself took the sentence we deserved, so that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. He was condemned so that we could be vindicated, and on that day heaven will rejoice, and so shall we.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–24 — The Millstone and the Sixfold Silence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 21: a mighty angel throws a stone like a great millstone into the sea — the act Jeremiah commanded of Seraiah, who tied a stone to the scroll of Babylon’s doom and threw it into the Euphrates saying Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more (Jer. 51:59–64). A millstone is the heaviest ordinary object in an ancient town and the last thing in the world that floats.

Verses 21–23 toll a sixfold silence, six things heard or found no more: Babylon herself; the sound of harpists and musicians, flute players and trumpeters; a craftsman of any craft; the sound of the mill; the light of a lamp; and the voice of bridegroom and bride. Jeremiah listed the same three — millstones, lamp, bridegroom and bride — as the sum of what a judged city loses (Jer. 25:10). Two reasons are given: your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery (pharmakeia, as at 9:21).

Verse 24 gives the indictment: And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Millstone and the Silence

An angel throws a millstone into the sea: so Babylon sinks. Music, craft, the mill, the lamp, and the voice of bride and bridegroom are heard in her no more — and in her is found the blood of the prophets and saints.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jeremiah had sunk Babylon’s doom in the Euphrates; John’s angel repeats the sign.

Now: The ordinary goods of life — bread, lamplight, weddings — were always worth more than the cargo. Nothing hidden stays unlooked-for.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, "So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more; and the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more, and a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more, and the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more, and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more, for your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery. And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, “So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more; and the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more, and a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more, and the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more, and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more, for your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery. And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth.”

The setting. In Jeremiah 51:59–64, Jeremiah had his prophecy against Babylon written on a scroll, and told his messenger Seraiah, when he had read it aloud in Babylon, to tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates, saying that so Babylon would sink, to rise no more. A great millstone could weigh several tonnes and was turned by a donkey. Jesus said it would be better to have a great millstone fastened around one’s neck and be drowned in the sea than to cause one of his little ones to sin (Matthew 18:6). Jeremiah 25:10 says God will banish from Judah the voice of mirth, the voice of the bridegroom and the bride, the grinding of the millstones and the light of the lamp.

Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea. A great millstone (mylinon megan). A dramatic acted prophecy, borrowed from Jeremiah, and John expects it to be known. A millstone is the right object for it. It is the heaviest ordinary thing in an ancient town, the stone an animal turned all day to grind the community’s grain, and it is the last thing in the world that floats. When it goes into deep water there is one splash and then nothing at all. It sinks instantly and is never recovered.

Saying, So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more. Violence (hormēmati): with sudden force. Found no more (ou mē heurethē eti). Her destruction is total and permanent.

The sixfold silence. Then comes the most beautiful and most desolating passage in the chapter. Six things will be heard or found no more (ou mē … eti), and the phrase itself tolls six times.

And the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more. Music goes first. No concerts, no weddings, no processions, nobody practising badly through an open window. Music and celebration silenced. The city of entertainment is quiet.

And a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more. No workshops. Nobody making anything. Work and skill ended. The particular satisfaction of skilled hands producing something that did not exist before is gone from the whole city.

And the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more. The daily grinding of grain for bread: ordinary life ended. In an ancient town the grinding of the handmills began before dawn and was the ordinary background of being alive, the sound that told you the day had started and there would be bread. Jeremiah listed its ending among the worst things God would do (Jeremiah 25:10).

And the light of a lamp will shine in you no more. Not a public illumination: a lamp, the small light in one room where a family sits after dark. Every window in the city, black. No home is lived in. In the new Jerusalem, God is the light (21:23; 22:5).

And the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more. This is the last and the heaviest. No more weddings, no more joy, no future: nobody is being married, so nobody is being born, so there will be no next generation. Jeremiah used exactly this group of images together, the voice of the bridegroom and the bride, the sound of the millstones and the light of the lamp, as the sum of everything a judged city loses (Jeremiah 25:10). And in contrast, the marriage of the Lamb is about to be announced (19:7).

Where Babylon’s true wealth was. Stand back and see what has been listed. Not palaces, armies, temples or treasuries. Music, craftsmanship, bread, lamplight and weddings. The things named are the ordinary goods of human life, and the chapter that has spent twelve verses on gold and silk and ivory ends by mourning the loss of the mill and the lamp. That is where Babylon’s true wealth was the whole time, and she spent it on cargo.

For your merchants were the great ones of the earth. The first reason for her judgement: her merchants were exalted and wealth was worshipped. Isaiah 23:8 says of Tyre that her merchants were princes. The traders had become the aristocracy, which is a precise description of what happens when a society decides that money is the only real rank.

And all nations were deceived by your sorcery. Sorcery (pharmakeia): magic, drugs, enchantment, the word used at 9:21. The second reason: she bewitched the nations, intoxicating them with her seductive power so that they could not see the truth. It is manipulation, the technique that bends people without their consent.

And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth. The third and deepest reason: murder. The last verse is the indictment, and it is enormous. Not merely the blood of the martyrs she killed herself, but of all who have been slain on earth. Jesus said something with the same reach over Jerusalem: that on that generation would come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from Abel onward (Matthew 23:35). The logic is not that one city committed every murder. It is that Babylon is the name for the whole arrangement, the human project of building without God, in every century and every place, and every drop of innocent blood ever spilled was spilled somewhere inside it. The account is presented to the system that produced it.

Found. And a single word in that verse should not be passed over. Babylon did not report it. Somebody looked, and it was there. This is a city that ran the greatest concealment operation in history, brilliant, cultured, generous, beautifully dressed, and at the end the search was conducted anyway and the blood was in the foundations. Nothing was ever really hidden. It was only unlooked-for.

What it does not mean. The end of music, work, food, light and marriage in Babylon does not mean that God hates these good things. They are his gifts, and they will be restored and perfected in the new creation. Babylon loses them because she abused them and rejected the Giver.

Will there be music, work and marriage in the new creation? Music, certainly: heaven in this book is full of harps and new songs (5:8–9; 14:2–3; 15:2–3). Meaningful work too, it seems: the nations bring their glory into the city (21:24–26), and his servants will serve him (22:3). Marriage is different. Jesus said that in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matthew 22:30), because the marriage that every human marriage pointed to will have arrived: Christ and his Bride, the church (Ephesians 5:31–32; Revelation 19:7). Nothing good is lost. Every true joy is either kept or fulfilled in something greater.

In a sentence. Then a powerful angel picked up a boulder the size of a huge millstone and threw it into the sea, saying: With this kind of violence Babylon the great city will be hurled down, never to be found again; the music of harpists, musicians, flute players and trumpeters will never be heard in you again; no craftsman of any trade will ever be found in you again; the sound of a millstone will never be heard in you again; the light of a lamp will never shine in you again; the voices of bridegroom and bride will never be heard in you again; your merchants were the world’s great men, and your magic spells led all the nations astray; and in her was found the blood of prophets and of God’s people, and of all who have been killed on the earth.

On a Tuesday. Enjoy God’s gifts of music, work, food, light and love, and thank him for them. Give him the glory, so that what you enjoy is never Babylon’s, but his. Tonight, when you switch on a lamp, eat bread, or hear someone you love laugh, say thank you to the Giver. Those small, ordinary gifts were Babylon’s real wealth, and she lost them by forgetting where they came from.

For worship. Every good and perfect gift comes down from the Father of lights. The song and the craft, the bread and the lamp, the voice of the bridegroom and the bride: all of them were his before Babylon ever touched them, and all of them will be his when Babylon is a millstone at the bottom of the sea. He will not leave his gifts in the hands of those who despised him. He will gather them into a new creation where the music never stops, where the Lamb is the lamp, where his servants work with joy, and where the voice of the Bridegroom is heard calling his Bride home to the marriage supper. Nothing hidden will stay hidden, and nothing good will be lost.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah had a scroll against Babylon tied to a stone and thrown into the Euphrates.

18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory.<sup>2</sup>And he called out with a mighty voice, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast.<sup>3</sup>For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living.”<sup>4</sup>Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, “Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues;<sup>5</sup>for her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.<sup>6</sup>Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed.<sup>7</sup>As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, ‘I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.’<sup>8</sup>For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her.”<sup>9</sup>And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning.<sup>10</sup>They will stand far off, in fear of her torment, and say, “Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come.”<sup>11</sup>And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore,<sup>12</sup>cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth, all kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble,<sup>13</sup>cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls.<sup>14</sup>“The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you, and all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again!”<sup>15</sup>The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment, weeping and mourning aloud,<sup>16</sup>“Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls!<sup>17</sup>For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste.” And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off<sup>18</sup>and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, “What city was like the great city?”<sup>19</sup>And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned, crying out, “Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.<sup>20</sup>Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!”<sup>21</sup>Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, “So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more;<sup>22</sup>and the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more, and a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more, and the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more,<sup>23</sup>and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more, for your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery.<sup>24</sup>And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth.”

19.title: Hallelujah! The Wedding and the Rider
19.overview:
Chapter 19 is the great pivot of Revelation — the hinge between Babylon’s fall and the new creation. It opens with the loudest sound in the book: the fourfold Hallelujah chorus of heaven celebrating the justice of God and the arrival of the marriage supper of the Lamb. It closes with the appearance of the Rider on the white horse, whose name is Word of God, whose robe is dipped in blood, who strikes the nations with the sword of his mouth, and who is named King of kings and Lord of lords.

The chapter falls into two movements that mirror each other. The first (vv. 1–10) is pure celebration: heaven erupts in praise, the twenty-four elders and four living creatures worship, the great multitude shouts like the roar of many waters, and the Bride has made herself ready in fine linen bright and pure — the righteous deeds of the saints. The second (vv. 11–21) is the appearing of the Rider: heaven opened, white horse, faithful and true, eyes of flame, many diadems, name unknown, Word of God, armies following, sharp sword from his mouth, King of kings. The beast and the false prophet are captured and thrown into the lake of fire.

The relationship between the two movements is crucial. The praise precedes the appearing; the wedding supper is announced before the battle is described. This is Revelation’s consistent pattern: the outcome is declared before the outworking. Heaven celebrates the marriage of the Lamb while the final confrontation with the beast is still being described. The sequence is not chronological; it is theological. The Lamb has already conquered. What the Rider on the white horse depicts is the visible manifestation of a victory already secured.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Hallelujah and the Marriage Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–3: a great multitude cries Hallelujah! — Hebrew, untranslated, the great word of the psalter, and used in the New Testament only in these six verses, four times. The grounds are given: his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute… and has avenged on her the blood of his servants — the two verbs the martyrs asked for at 6:10, now in the past tense. And the smoke from her goes up forever and ever (cf. Isa. 34:10).

Verses 4–5: the elders and living creatures, in their last appearance in the book, fall down and say two Hebrew words — Amen. Hallelujah! (cf. Ps. 106:48). Then a voice from the throne: Praise our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, small and great.

Verses 6–8: the last hallelujah, in a voice like many waters and thunder — the Lord our God the Almighty reigns (cf. Ps. 93:1; 97:1) — and the announcement the book has been travelling toward: the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready; it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure — for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.

Verses 9–10: the fourth beatitude, and one of the few sentences John is told to write down (cf. 14:13; 21:5) — Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. John falls down to worship the angel and is stopped: You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you… Worship God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Hallelujah and the Wedding

Heaven’s hallelujahs answer the martyrs’ prayer: God has judged and avenged. The marriage of the Lamb has come; the Bride is granted fine linen, which is the righteous deeds of the saints. Blessed are those invited — and worship God, not his messengers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The prayer under the altar was not lost; it was answered.

Now: The hidden faithfulness of ordinary believers is being woven into the Bride’s dress.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude in heaven, crying out, "Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God, for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality, and has avenged on her the blood of his servants." Once more they cried out, "Hallelujah! The smoke from her goes up forever and ever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude in heaven, crying out, “Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God, for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality, and has avenged on her the blood of his servants.” Once more they cried out, “Hallelujah! The smoke from her goes up forever and ever.”

Meaning first. Revelation 19 moves from Babylon’s fall to the Lamb’s wedding and Christ’s return. Heaven bursts into hallelujahs: God’s judgements are true and just, for he has judged the prostitute and avenged his servants’ blood (vv. 1–3). The elders and living creatures say Amen, Hallelujah, and a voice from the throne calls all God’s servants to praise him (vv. 4–5). A great multitude, like thunder, sings: the Lord our God the Almighty reigns; the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his bride has made herself ready, clothed in fine linen, which is the righteous deeds of the saints (vv. 6–8). The angel blesses those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb; John falls to worship him and is told: do not, worship God (vv. 9–10). Then heaven opens, and Christ rides out on a white horse, Faithful and True, with eyes like fire, many crowns, a robe dipped in blood, named the Word of God, followed by the armies of heaven (vv. 11–14). From his mouth comes a sword to strike the nations; he treads the winepress of God’s wrath; and on his robe and thigh is written King of kings and Lord of lords (vv. 15–16). An angel summons the birds to the great supper of God (vv. 17–18). The beast and the kings gather to make war on him, but the beast and the false prophet are captured and thrown alive into the lake of fire, and the rest are killed by the sword from his mouth (vv. 19–21). The chapter shows the two suppers at the end of history: the marriage supper of the Lamb for his bride, and the great supper of God for his enemies, and Christ’s single, glorious, victorious return. Chapter 18 ended with a millstone in the sea and a city gone silent. This is the reaction in heaven, and it is the loudest worship in the Bible.

The setting. Hallelujah is a Hebrew word meaning praise the LORD (hallelu, praise; Yah, the short form of God’s name). In the New Testament it occurs only in this chapter, four times. In the Psalms it often begins or ends a psalm, especially Psalms 104–106, 111–117 and 146–150. Psalms 113–118, the Hallel, were sung at Passover, and Jesus and his disciples sang a hymn, probably from these psalms, after the Last Supper (Matthew 26:30). Psalm 104:35 is the first Hallelujah in the Psalter: let sinners be consumed from the earth, and let the wicked be no more! Bless the LORD, O my soul! Praise the LORD!

After this I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude in heaven. Great multitude (ochlou pollou), as in 7:9: the redeemed, from every nation, tribe, people and language, more than anyone could count.

Crying out, Hallelujah! Praise the LORD. Hallelujah is Hebrew, not Greek, and it is left untranslated. It is the great word of the Psalter, where it opens and closes the final psalms, and every Jewish Christian hearing this read aloud would have heard his own liturgy. Four times in these six verses, and never again in the New Testament. And in contrast with the earth’s alas, alas (18:10, 16, 19), heaven sings hallelujah. Earth’s last word over Babylon is a groan; heaven’s is praise.

A hallelujah at a funeral. The thing it is shouted over is the fall of a city, and that takes some facing. The word most associated with Christian praise makes its only New Testament appearance at the funeral of an empire. But look at the reasons given, because the verses supply them at once, and they are not what a modern reader fears.

Salvation and glory and power belong to our God. As in 7:10 and 12:10. All credit belongs to God. The praise is for the character of God, not for the suffering of anybody. Three nouns are said to belong to him, and Babylon had claimed all three, offering security, glamour and influence to whoever would drink with her. Every one of them turns out to have been his.

For his judgments are true and just. As the redeemed (15:3) and the altar (16:7) declared. God’s justice is the ground of their praise. Three times now heaven has said the same two words about his judgements, before the bowls, during them, and after Babylon’s fall, and it has never once had to take them back.

For he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality. Corrupted (ephtheiren): ruined, destroyed. She was destroying the earth (11:18), and now she is destroyed.

And has avenged on her the blood of his servants. Avenged (exedikēsen). That is the answer to a question asked thirteen chapters ago, and the reader who has come this far should hear it land. Under the altar in 6:10 the souls of the martyrs cried, O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? They were given white robes and told to rest a little longer. Here are the same two verbs, judged and avenged, in the past tense, in the mouth of a multitude nobody can number. Prayer answered.

Nothing was forgotten. That is the whole content of the first hallelujah, and it is the thing a persecuted church most needs and most doubts. The prayer prayed under the altar was not filed and lost. It was answered, in order, at the time appointed, and the answer is being sung about.

Once more they cried out, Hallelujah! The smoke from her goes up forever and ever. As with Sodom (Genesis 19:28) and Edom, where the smoke of the land goes up for ever (Isaiah 34:10). It is the language of a verdict that will not be reversed: no rebuilding, no restoration, no second edition. Her judgement is final and permanent. She will never rise again. The city that said, I sit as a queen and mourning I shall never see (18:7), got the permanence she asked for, but not the kind she wanted.

What it does not mean. The hallelujahs are not gloating. They praise God because his justice has been done, and evil will never again corrupt the earth or kill his people.

Does smoke for ever mean that the punishment of the lost is eternal? Yes. The same phrase, for ever and ever, is used of the worship of God (4:9–10; 5:13) and of the torment of those who worship the beast (14:11) and of the devil (20:10). The fall of Babylon as a system is final, and the punishment of those who belonged to her and refused to repent is conscious and without end (Matthew 25:46). That is a terrible truth, and it should make us tremble and plead with people. But it is also why the hallelujah is right: evil is never coming back, and nothing will ever again corrupt God’s world.

In a sentence. After this I heard what sounded like the roar of a huge crowd in heaven, shouting: Hallelujah! Salvation, glory and power belong to our God, because his judgements are true and just; he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality, and he has avenged the blood of his servants that she shed; and again they shouted: Hallelujah! The smoke from her rises for ever and ever.

On a Tuesday. Next time you pray about an injustice that seems to have gone unanswered for years, remember that the martyrs waited from chapter 6 to chapter 19, and that their prayer was not lost. Keep praying, and add a hallelujah before the answer comes: praise the LORD, because his judgements are true and just.

For worship. Sing Hallelujah with understanding: praise the LORD, because he is just and true, and he hears his people’s cries. Salvation is his: he planned it, purchased it and applies it. Glory is his: no city, empire or beast will ever share it. Power is his: he raised Christ from the dead and will raise all who are his. He keeps every prayer of his people in golden bowls, and not one cry from under the altar has gone unanswered. Hallelujah, for the Lord our God has judged, and his judgements are true and just.
verseByVerse.note: “Hallelujah” means “praise the LORD” (Hebrew). In the New Testament it appears only here, four times in this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who was seated on the throne, saying, "Amen. Hallelujah!" And from the throne came a voice saying, "Praise our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, small and great."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who was seated on the throne, saying, “Amen. Hallelujah!” And from the throne came a voice saying, “Praise our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, small and great.”

The setting. Psalm 106:48 ends: and let all the people say, Amen! Praise the LORD! Psalm 115:13 says the LORD will bless those who fear him, both the small and the great. Psalm 135:1, 20 calls all the servants of the LORD to praise him.

And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who was seated on the throne. This is the last appearance of the elders and living creatures in Revelation. They have been there from the first throne vision (4:4–11), and they close the worship of this age. And they fell down. These are figures with thrones of their own who have spent this book throwing their crowns on the floor (4:10). The posture has not changed.

Saying, Amen. Hallelujah! Amen means it is true, it is firm, so be it. Hallelujah means praise the LORD. Two words, both Hebrew, and it is the oldest congregational response there is: Psalm 106 ends with let all the people say, Amen! Praise the LORD! (Psalm 106:48). The beings closest to the throne of God add nothing original. They agree. The entire contribution of the highest creatures in the universe at this moment is to say that what the multitude has just said is true. They confirm the multitude’s song.

And from the throne came a voice saying, Praise our God, all you his servants. A voice from the throne, and the striking thing is the pronoun: our God. Whoever is speaking stands alongside the worshippers, which is why the speaker is taken to be Christ, or an angel near the throne. Either way, the summons to worship comes from inside the company rather than being shouted down onto it. Servants (douloi): all believers.

You who fear him, small and great. Fear (phoboumenoi) means revere. Small and great means everyone, whatever their status, and the phrase appears several times in this book, always to refuse a ranking. It was used of the beast’s mark, which reached both small and great (13:16); it is used at 11:18 of the servants God rewards; and it will be used of the dead standing before the throne (20:12). In God’s presence, distinctions of rank disappear; all praise him together.

No back row. Stop on that, because a great deal of Christian discouragement comes from a suspicion that there are tiers. The people summoned here are described in exactly two ways: they serve him and they fear him. Not those who did notable things. Not those who understood this book. The choir is assembled by a single qualification, and the smallest voice in it is not standing at the back.

What it does not mean. Fearing God does not mean being terrified of him. It means reverent awe, the humble worship of those who know who he is.

Will there be degrees of reward in heaven? Scripture does speak of rewards for faithfulness (Matthew 25:21; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15; 2 Corinthians 5:10), and many Reformed teachers have held that capacities for joy may differ, as vessels of different sizes may all be full. But there are no degrees of acceptance. Every believer is welcomed on exactly the same ground, the righteousness of Christ, and every one is equally a child, a servant and a member of the Bride. Rewards themselves are gifts of grace, God crowning his own work in us. No one in heaven will feel second-class, and no one will want anything but to praise.

What am I saying when I say Amen? You are saying, this is true, and I put my weight on it. It is not a way of ending a prayer but a confession of faith. In the early church the whole congregation said it aloud after prayers and readings (1 Corinthians 14:16), and Christ himself is called the Amen, the faithful and true witness (3:14), because every promise of God is yes in him, and through him we say our Amen to God for his glory (2 Corinthians 1:20). So say it on purpose.

In a sentence. The twenty-four elders and the four living beings fell down and worshipped God, who sits on the throne, saying, Amen! Hallelujah! Then a voice came from the throne: Praise our God, all you his servants, all who fear him, from the least to the greatest!

On a Tuesday. Whoever you are, small or great, God calls you to praise him. If you feel unimportant in your church, or in the world, read verse 5 again: you are on the guest list in exactly the same words as everyone else. And this Sunday, when the congregation says Amen, say it out loud, and mean it.

For worship. Whoever you are, small or great, God calls you to praise him. Say Amen and Hallelujah today. Our God is worthy of the worship of the highest creatures in heaven, who fall on their faces before him and add nothing but their agreement. And he is gracious enough to want the voice of the smallest of his servants in the same choir. The Son, who calls him our God, is not ashamed to call us brothers; in the midst of the congregation he sings his Father’s praise, and he brings us with him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters and like the sound of mighty peals of thunder, crying out, "Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready; it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure"—for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters and like the sound of mighty peals of thunder, crying out, “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready; it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure”—for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.

The setting. In the Old Testament, God is Israel’s husband (Isaiah 54:5–6; Hosea 2:16–20). Jesus called himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19–20) and told parables of wedding feasts (Matthew 22:1–14; 25:1–13). Paul says Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, to present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). A Jewish wedding had two stages: betrothal, a binding commitment, and then, after a period of preparation, the wedding itself, when the groom came to take his bride to his home, followed by a feast. Isaiah 61:10 says, he has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.

Then I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters and like the sound of mighty peals of thunder. The fourth and last hallelujah, and the volume is described in three ways: a multitude, a waterfall and thunder. John reaches for the loudest things he knows and says the sound was like all of them at once. It is overwhelming sound, like Christ’s own voice (1:15) and the song of the 144,000 (14:2).

Crying out, Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. Reigns (ebasileusen): has begun to reign, has taken up his reign. It is one word in Greek, and it is the great announcement of the Psalms: the LORD reigns (Psalm 93:1; 97:1; 99:1). The tense means a reign has begun and stands. This is what the seventh trumpet announced at 11:15–17, now sung by the whole company. God’s reign is now openly established. These are the great words of Handel’s Hallelujah Chorus.

Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory. Rejoice (chairōmen) and exult (agalliōmen, be overjoyed). As Jesus told the persecuted: rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven (Matthew 5:12). The same people who were told to rejoice in their suffering now rejoice at its end.

For the marriage of the Lamb has come. Marriage (ho gamos): the wedding. The image is not new and it is not an ornament. God is the husband of his people all through the Old Testament: your Maker is your husband (Isaiah 54:5); I will betroth you to me for ever (Hosea 2:19). Jesus called himself the bridegroom and said the guests could not fast while he was with them (Mark 2:19). Paul told husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church, and then said the whole arrangement had been about Christ and the church all along (Ephesians 5:25–32). This is the goal of all history: the union of Christ with his people, perfect and permanent. Betrothed now by faith (2 Corinthians 11:2), the church will be united with Christ at his return. The book that opened with seven struggling congregations on a postal road in Asia ends with those congregations getting married.

And his Bride has made herself ready. Bride (gynē, wife, woman), in contrast with the prostitute. Made herself ready (hētoimasen heautēn). The church prepares for Christ by faithful living, holiness and perseverance. One woman was dressed by her lovers and stripped by them; this one has been waiting for one husband.

It was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure. This is one of the most carefully balanced sentences in the New Testament, and both halves have to be held or it collapses. It was granted (edothē, it was given). The dress was given. She did not buy it, weave it or earn it, and the divine passive that has governed this whole book governs the Bride’s wedding clothes too. She clothes herself, but only with what is given her. Set it beside Laodicea, who was counselled to buy white garments from Christ (3:18), and beside the multitude who washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14). Nobody in this book is wearing anything he produced. Fine linen (byssinon), in contrast with the prostitute’s purple and scarlet, gold and jewels (17:4). The bride’s beauty is purity.

For the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints. And yet the dress is made of something. John stops the sentence to say what the fabric is, and it is not an abstraction. Righteous deeds (dikaiōmata, righteous acts): the plural is concrete, the deeds themselves, the faithful lives of believers, their works of obedience and love. Their deeds follow them (14:13).

Where Christians differ: is the bride’s righteousness her own deeds or Christ’s? Some read “righteous deeds of the saints” as meaning that believers are made acceptable to Christ by their own good works. Others, emphasising imputed righteousness, are uneasy with the phrase. Verdict: both grace and works are in the verse. The linen was given to her (granted), and her robes were washed white in the Lamb’s blood (7:14): her standing before God rests wholly on Christ’s righteousness credited to her by faith (2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). And the linen is her righteous deeds, the fruit of that grace, the good works God prepared beforehand for her to walk in (Ephesians 2:10). Justification by faith alone is the root; sanctification is the fruit, and both are gifts. The bride is dressed by her bridegroom.

Both clauses are true. Neither may be dropped. The righteousness that admits a sinner to the wedding is Christ’s and is given; the life that follows from it is truly his people’s own, and it is truly theirs to wear. Paul held the same two together without difficulty: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:12–13).

Textual note. The King James Version reads “the Lord God omnipotent reigneth”, following later manuscripts. The best manuscripts read “the Lord our God the Almighty reigns”. The meaning is the same.

What it does not mean. The marriage does not mean that individual believers are each married to Christ in a romantic sense. The bride is the church together, the whole people of God.

If God already reigns, why does it say he has begun to reign? God has always been King over all; nothing has ever been outside his rule (Psalm 103:19). But in this fallen world his reign has been resisted and hidden, and his people have prayed, your kingdom come. What begins here is the open, undisputed exercise of his rule, when every rival is removed and every knee bows. It is like a rightful king who has ruled from exile and now enters his capital and is crowned in public. He was always King; now everyone sees it.

My life seems to have produced so little. What will I have to wear? There is great comfort in this verse for a believer who suspects his life has amounted to nothing. The visits nobody recorded, the giving that hurt, the years of patience with a difficult person, the prayers for a wayward child, the refusal to say the profitable untrue thing: those are not evaporating. They are being woven. Nothing done for Christ is wasted (1 Corinthians 15:58; Matthew 10:42). And remember the first half: the dress is granted. Your place at the wedding does not depend on the size of your contribution but on the Bridegroom who washed you. When the Bride finally appears, what you did in his name will be part of what she has on.

In a sentence. Then I heard what sounded like a great crowd, like the roar of rushing waters and like loud thunder, shouting: Hallelujah! For our Lord God Almighty has begun to reign; let us celebrate and be glad and give him the glory, because the wedding of the Lamb has come and his bride has got herself ready; she has been given fine linen, shining and clean, to wear; for the fine linen stands for the righteous acts of God’s people.

On a Tuesday. The church is preparing for her wedding. Every act of faithfulness and love today is part of the bride’s dress. Live in a way that gets her ready. That includes how you treat the church herself: her unity, her purity and her members. A bride being prepared for her husband is not someone to gossip about or walk away from lightly. Do one thing this week to build up your local congregation.

For worship. The Lord our God the Almighty reigns, and the marriage of the Lamb has come. Before the foundation of the world the Father chose a bride for his Son; in the fullness of time the Son came to win her, not with gifts but with his blood; and through the ages the Spirit has been calling her, washing her and clothing her. Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle. He found her in rags and dressed her in fine linen. He will not be ashamed of her on the day of the wedding, and she will never stop singing hallelujah.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to me, "Write this: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb." And he said to me, "These are the true words of God." Then I fell down at his feet to worship him, but he said to me, "You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who hold to the testimony of Jesus. Worship God." For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the angel said to me, “Write this: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” And he said to me, “These are the true words of God.” Then I fell down at his feet to worship him, but he said to me, “You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who hold to the testimony of Jesus. Worship God.” For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.

The setting. Isaiah 25:6–8 promises that the LORD will make for all peoples a feast of rich food and well-aged wine, and swallow up death for ever. Jesus said many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom (Matthew 8:11), and at the Last Supper said he would not drink wine again until he drank it new in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29). Colossians 2:18 warns against the worship of angels.

And the angel said to me, Write this: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. The fourth of the book’s seven beatitudes (1:3; 14:13; 16:15), and one of the few sentences John is specifically told to write down (14:13; 21:5). Each time the command is given, it is given over something a suffering church would find hard to believe. Invited (keklēmenoi) is called, the same word as in 17:14: the called. Marriage supper (deipnon tou gamou) is the wedding feast. The feast pictures the joy of the new creation, fellowship with Christ, and the fulfilment of the Lord’s Supper, which looks forward to it (1 Corinthians 11:26).

The least deserved document in the world. The wording is exact: blessed are those who are invited. Not those who earned a place, or arranged one, or arrived early. A wedding invitation is the least deserved document in the world; it says only that somebody wanted you there. Jesus told a parable about a wedding feast where the invited guests would not come, and the servants were sent into the streets to bring in whoever they found, both bad and good (Matthew 22:9–10).

Bride and guests. Notice the strange double position of the church. She is the Bride in verse 7 and the guests in verse 9. The bride and the guests are the same people seen from two angles. The picture will not resolve into a single photograph, and it is not meant to. The point is not staging but relationship: the same people are both married to him and welcomed by him.

And he said to me, These are the true words of God. True (alēthinoi): genuine, reliable. A guarantee: this promise will happen. And the guarantee is aimed at the reader. Nobody needs to be assured that the beast is real when the beast is at the door. It is the wedding that strains belief.

Then I fell down at his feet to worship him. Overwhelmed, John makes a mistake, and he records it honestly. He does it again in 22:8. An apostle, in the Spirit, who has already seen the throne and the Lamb and the sea of glass, twice goes down in front of a messenger. That should be a comfort as well as a warning, because it shows how easily this particular mistake is made. It is not a stupid mistake. The angel is truly glorious, has truly brought the word of God, and has just said something overwhelming. The instinct to worship is right; only the direction is wrong.

But he said to me, You must not do that! You must not (hora mē): see that you do not. An urgent warning.

I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who hold to the testimony of Jesus. Fellow servant (syndoulos). Angels, however glorious, are servants like us (Hebrews 1:14). Not senior. Alongside.

Worship God. Worship belongs to God alone. This is crucial evidence for Christ’s deity: the angel refuses worship, but the Lamb receives it (5:8–14). The book that forbids worshipping the highest angel shows the whole of heaven falling down before the Lamb, and no one tells them to stop.

A permanent hazard for the church. It is recorded twice because it is a permanent danger. The people through whom God speaks are always in danger of being given what belongs to God: the preacher whose congregation depends on him rather than on Christ, the writer quoted more readily than Scripture, the movement that becomes the thing believed in. The angel’s answer settles it: worship God. And his self-description is the one every faithful minister has to make: I am a fellow servant with you.

For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy. The testimony of Jesus (hē martyria Iēsou) is the testimony that Jesus gave, and the testimony about Jesus; both are true in this book. The spirit of prophecy is its essence, its heart. All true prophecy bears witness to Jesus. And the sentence explains why the angel refused: everyone who holds the testimony of Jesus is in the prophetic company, so the apostle on the floor and the angel standing over him are colleagues. The angel, John and the church share one task: witnessing to Christ. There is one rank in that room above them both, and neither of them holds it.

Where Christians differ: does this mean prophecy continues in the church? Some read “the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy” as meaning that every witnessing believer has a gift of prophecy, so that new revelations continue today. Verdict: the verse teaches that the heart of all prophecy is witness to Jesus, and that every believer who bears that witness shares in the prophetic calling of the church (11:3). It does not promise new revelation. The prophetic word that John received is now written and closed (22:18–19). Today, the church bears the testimony of Jesus by proclaiming the completed Scriptures, which this app holds, with charity, is how the prophetic gift functions now.

What it does not mean. The angel’s refusal of worship is not false modesty. Worshipping anyone or anything other than God, whether angels, saints or images, is idolatry.

Am I invited to the marriage supper? If you will come, yes. The invitation of the gospel goes out to everyone who hears it: the Spirit and the Bride say, come, and let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price (22:17). You do not need to qualify first, clean yourself up, or prove you are chosen. You come by trusting Christ, the Bridegroom who paid for the feast. Those who are truly called are those who accept the call, and no one who comes to him will be turned away (John 6:37). The only people missing will be those who refused.

How is the Lord’s Supper connected to this? The Lord’s Supper is a foretaste and a promise of the marriage supper. Every time the church eats the bread and drinks the cup, it proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26), looking back to the cross and forward to the feast. Jesus said he would not drink the cup again until he drank it new with us in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29). So come to the Lord’s Table as a guest rehearsing for a wedding: humbled by what it cost him, and glad about where it is leading.

In a sentence. The angel said to me, Write this: How blessed are those who are invited to the wedding banquet of the Lamb! And he added, These are the true words of God; I fell at his feet to worship him, but he said, Do not do that! I am a servant just like you and your brothers and sisters who hold to the testimony about Jesus; worship God! For the testimony about Jesus is the heart of all prophecy.

On a Tuesday. At the Lord’s Supper, look forward to the marriage supper of the Lamb. And worship God alone, giving no creature the honour that belongs to him. Ask yourself honestly whether there is a preacher, author or Christian leader you lean on more than on Christ himself. Thank God for them, and then make sure your Amen goes to him.

For worship. Blessed are those who are invited. The King of heaven has prepared a wedding feast for his Son, and sent out his servants into the streets and lanes to bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame. He did not wait for worthy guests; he made them worthy, washing them in the blood of the Lamb whose wedding it is. And at that table the Lamb himself will serve: he has promised that he will dress himself for service, have them recline at table, and come and serve them. These are the true words of God. Worship him alone, the God who invites, and the Lamb who is both the Bridegroom and the price of the feast.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — The Rider on the White Horse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 11–13: heaven opens — not a door this time — and a rider comes out on a white horse, called Faithful and True (cf. 1:5; 3:14), and in righteousness he judges and makes war (cf. Isa. 11:3–4). His eyes are a flame of fire (1:14); on his head are many diadems, against the dragon’s seven and the beast’s ten; he has a name written that no one knows but himself; he is clothed in a robe dipped in blood; and he is called The Word of God — John’s own title for him (John 1:1).

Verses 14–16: the armies of heaven follow, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure — the Bride’s dress from v. 8, in the same words. From his mouth comes a sharp sword (1:16; Isa. 11:4); he will rule with a rod of iron (Ps. 2:9); he treads the winepress (Isa. 63:3). And on his robe and thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords (cf. Deut. 10:17; Rev. 17:14).

Verses 17–18: an angel standing in the sun calls the birds to the great supper of God (Ezek. 39:17–20), to eat the flesh of kings, captains, mighty men, horses and riders, both free and slave, both small and great. Verses 19–21: the beast and the kings gather to make war — and the beast was captured, with the false prophet, and both are thrown alive into the lake of fire; and the rest are slain by the sword from the rider’s mouth.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Rider on the White Horse

Faithful and True, crowned with many diadems, robed in blood, named the Word of God and King of kings and Lord of lords, the Rider strikes the nations with the sword of his mouth. The beast and false prophet are captured without a battle and thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The churches had no army; the armies of heaven ride out in wedding clothes and strike no blow.

Now: There are two suppers in this chapter: at one people are guests, at the other they are the meal.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse! The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war. His eyes are like a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems, and he has a name written that no one knows but himself. He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and the name by which he is called is The Word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse! The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war. His eyes are like a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems, and he has a name written that no one knows but himself. He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and the name by which he is called is The Word of God.

The setting. Roman generals celebrated victory in a triumph, riding into Rome on a white horse, followed by their army, displaying captives and spoil. Isaiah 63:1–3 describes the LORD coming from Edom in crimson garments, stained from treading the winepress of his wrath. Psalm 45:3–6 describes the king riding out victoriously for the cause of truth and righteousness. John’s Gospel begins: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1).

Then I saw heaven opened. Heaven has been opened once before in this book, at 4:1, when a door stood open and John was called up. This time it is not a door. Heaven itself is opened, and something comes out. This is Christ’s return.

And behold, a white horse! The horse of victory, the horse a Roman general rode in his triumph. A reader will remember a white horse from 6:2, and the two must not be confused; that rider was a counterfeit conqueror. The differences are deliberate and decisive. That rider had a bow; this one has a sword from his mouth. That rider was given a crown, a single stephanos, a victor’s wreath; this one wears many diadems, royal crowns, and nobody hands them to him. That rider was unnamed; this one has four names in six verses.

The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True. As in 3:14, where Christ introduced himself to Laodicea as the faithful and true witness, and 1:5. The rider coming out of heaven with a sword is the same person who wrote the seven letters. Christ keeps every promise and speaks only truth. His coming is the fulfilment of God’s word.

And in righteousness he judges and makes war. Righteousness (dikaiosynē). The sentence has to be heard in full. Every war ever fought has been declared righteous by the people fighting it, and history is a graveyard of holy causes. This is the one case in which the claim is true, and it is true because of who is making it. Unlike human wars, his war is perfectly just. Isaiah promised a shoot from the stump of Jesse who would judge the poor with righteousness and strike the earth with the rod of his mouth (Isaiah 11:3–4).

His eyes are like a flame of fire. As in 1:14 and 2:18: the eyes that saw what Sardis and Laodicea could not see about themselves. He sees through everything. No disguise survives his gaze, and no faithful act goes unseen by it.

And on his head are many diadems. Many diadems (diadēmata polla). The dragon wore seven (12:3) and the beast ten (13:1). This rider wears an uncounted number, and every crown either of them claimed is on his head. His authority surpasses all. He is King of kings.

And he has a name written that no one knows but himself. Three names are given in these verses and another is withheld, which is one of the most restrained things in the book. There is a depth in Christ that no creature fully comprehends: no one knows the Son except the Father (Matthew 11:27). He is not exhaustively knowable. After every doctrine has been correctly stated there is something in Christ that no creature has been given, and Revelation says so at the moment of his greatest self-disclosure. He is more than all his titles.

He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood. Dipped (bebammenon): dipped, soaked. Here is the crux of the scene, because the battle has not been fought yet. He is already covered in blood before a single enemy appears in verse 19. Whose blood is it? The immediate source is Isaiah 63, where a figure comes from Edom in crimson garments and explains that he has trodden the winepress alone, and their lifeblood has spattered his garments (Isaiah 63:1–3). John quotes the winepress two verses later, so Isaiah is unmistakably in view, and on that reading the blood is his enemies’, before the battle has even begun, pointing to his certain victory. Or it is his own blood, shed on the cross, by which he conquered (5:9; 12:11).

His own blood, most likely. Revelation regularly reinterprets Old Testament war imagery in the light of the cross, and the robe is mentioned before any battle, so his own blood is most likely, with a hint of judgement as well. The whole book has turned on a Lamb standing as though it had been slain (5:6), and every victory in Revelation has been won by blood already shed: they conquered him by the blood of the Lamb (12:11). Whichever way the image is weighted, the rider arrives already bloodied, and the outcome of the battle was settled before the battle began. The one who judges is the one who was slain.

And the name by which he is called is The Word of God. The Word of God (ho logos tou theou). The one writer in the New Testament who uses that title of Christ is the man writing this, in the first sentence of his Gospel: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God (John 1:1, 14). It is his signature, and it identifies the rider beyond argument. He is God’s final self-revelation and speech. And it explains the weapon: the conqueror whose name is the Word fights with his mouth (v. 15).

Where Christians differ: is this Christ’s return before a millennium, or his final coming? Premillennialists read 19:11–21 as Christ’s return to defeat the antichrist, followed in chapter 20 by a thousand-year reign on earth before the final judgement. Verdict: this is Christ’s one, final, visible return, which brings the last battle, the final judgement and the new creation. Revelation is a series of parallel visions, and chapter 20 goes back to describe the whole church age again from another angle. The same final battle appears in 16:14–16, 19:19–21 and 20:7–10, described in the same words, drawn from Ezekiel 38–39 (the birds’ feast here, the fire there). There is one return, one battle, one final judgement.

The pattern of going back. This is not special pleading for chapter 20. Revelation has done it before: chapter 12 goes back to the birth of Christ after chapter 11 has reached the end (11:15–18), and the seals, trumpets and bowls each reach the end in turn. So the return of Christ in chapter 19 is the end of the thousand years, not the start of them, and chapter 20 shows the same age from the side of Satan bound and the saints reigning with Christ.

What it does not mean. Christ’s warfare is not a call for Christians to wage holy war. He fights alone, with his word, and the victory is entirely his.

How can the Prince of Peace make war? Because there can be no lasting peace while evil is free to destroy. The Christ who came the first time as a Lamb, to suffer and to offer peace to all who will receive it, comes the second time as Judge, to end the rebellion of those who have refused it (Acts 17:31). His war is not against the weak but against the beast, the false prophet and those who make war on him and his people. It is the war that ends all wars, and it is fought with perfect justice, by one who himself bore the judgement for every enemy who repents. The same hands that hold the reins bear the marks of the nails.

In a sentence. Then I saw heaven standing open, and there was a white horse, whose rider is called Faithful and True; he judges and wages war with justice; his eyes are like blazing fire, on his head are many royal crowns, and he has a name written on him that no one knows except himself; he wears a robe soaked in blood, and his name is the Word of God.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to think that evil is winning, or that God has forgotten his promises, picture heaven opened and the rider called Faithful and True. Every promise he has made to you, he will keep. Choose one of them this week, perhaps John 14:3 or Hebrews 13:5, write it down, and carry it with you.

For worship. Worship Christ as the Faithful and True, the Word of God, King of many crowns. The one who was crucified will return in triumph. He is the Word who was with God in the beginning and was God, by whom all things were made; the Word who became flesh and dwelt among us; the Word who spoke from the cross and said it is finished. He wears every crown the dragon and the beast pretended to, and many more. He carries a name no creature can fathom, and he wears a robe dyed in the blood that bought his people. Heaven will open, and he will come, and every eye will see him.

verseByVerse.quote: And the armies of heaven, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure, were following him on white horses. From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron. He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the armies of heaven, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure, were following him on white horses. From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron. He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords.

The setting. Zechariah 14:5 says the LORD will come, and all the holy ones with him. Jesus said the Son of Man will come in his glory, and all the angels with him (Matthew 25:31). Paul says Christ will come with his saints (1 Thessalonians 3:13) and with his mighty angels (2 Thessalonians 1:7). Isaiah 11:4 and 49:2 speak of the Messiah’s mouth like a sharp sword, striking the earth with the rod of his mouth. In the ancient world, a name or title might be written on a statue’s thigh, or on the part of a rider’s robe that covered the thigh, where it would be seen as he rode.

And the armies of heaven, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure, were following him on white horses. Armies (strateumata). Stop at what this army is wearing, because John has just told the reader what fine linen means: the righteous deeds of the saints (v. 8). This is the same fabric in almost the same words. The armies of heaven are dressed as the Bride, and those with the Lamb are the called, chosen and faithful (17:14). They include his saints and his angels. Which means the church rides out to the last battle in its wedding clothes. Not armour, not uniform: linen.

They carry no weapons. Notice: they carry no weapons and do not fight. They simply follow. Nothing in these verses says the army does anything at all. It strikes no blow; it is not said to do anything after this verse. Its entire role in the greatest battle in Scripture is to be present and to be with him. That is the last word of this book on Christian militancy. The saints have been told to endure, to hold fast, to keep their garments on, and to conquer by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony. They have never once been told to fight, and when the fighting finally happens they are spectators in white.

From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations. Sword (rhomphaia), as in 1:16 and 2:16: his word. He conquers by speaking, as God created by speaking (Genesis 1). One word from him, and his enemies fall: the Lord Jesus will kill the lawless one with the breath of his mouth (2 Thessalonians 2:8). In a chapter full of horses and armies and a coming slaughter, the conqueror carries nothing in his hands. What kills is what he says. That has been true since the first chapter, and it is why the church’s only weapon in this book has been the word of its testimony. The weapon the saints have been using all along is a small version of the one he will finish with.

And he will rule them with a rod of iron. As in Psalm 2:9, quoted at 2:27 and 12:5. The Son whom the kings of the earth set themselves against is the one who breaks them.

He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. As in 14:19–20 and Isaiah 63:3. Christ himself carries out God’s final judgement. The Father has given all judgement to the Son (John 5:22), and the one who drank the cup of wrath for his people now treads the winepress for his enemies.

On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords. The supreme title, as in 17:14, where the order is reversed. Here the greater word comes first. It is placed where a rider’s thigh is visible above the horse to everyone standing on the ground: a title worn where it can be read. And it is God’s own title. Moses said the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords (Deuteronomy 10:17). Every emperor, king and lord is under him. Domitian’s claims are answered once and for all.

What it meant to the first hearers. Consider what those words meant to the seven congregations who first heard them read out. They lived in a province where the emperor was called lord, where his image was on every coin they handled, and where their neighbours had been asked to say a few words about him that they could not say. Somebody in that room had a relative in prison for it. And into that room came a sentence written on the thigh of a rider coming out of an open heaven: King of kings and Lord of lords. Not a hope, not a slogan, and not a consolation. A name, already written, on someone already riding.

What it does not mean. The armies of heaven do not fight. The battle belongs to Christ alone. The church does not establish Christ’s kingdom by force. Its weapons now are the word and prayer, and at his coming he alone wins the victory.
