Will I be in that army? If you belong to Christ, yes. The armies are dressed in the Bride’s linen, and the Bride is the whole church. Paul says that when Christ appears, we will appear with him in glory (Colossians 3:4), and that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:14). Believers who have died are with Christ now, and will come with him; believers still living will be caught up to meet him (1 Thessalonians 4:17). There is one coming, and the whole people of God, living and dead, will share in it, not as soldiers who win the victory but as the Bride who shares it.

In a sentence. The armies of heaven, dressed in fine linen, white and clean, were following him on white horses; out of his mouth comes a sharp sword to strike down the nations, and he will rule them with an iron rod; he treads the winepress of the furious anger of God Almighty; and on his robe and on his thigh he has this name written: King of kings and Lord of lords.

On a Tuesday. Whoever has power over you, Christ has more. Live under his lordship today, whatever any lesser lord demands. When an employer, a government or the culture demands something Christ forbids, remember the name on his thigh. Be respectful and obedient wherever you can, but where you cannot, say graciously and firmly that you belong to a higher Lord, and leave the outcome to him.

For worship. King of kings and Lord of lords: the title is written where everyone can see it, and one day everyone will. He needs no army to win, yet he will not ride out without his Bride. He conquers with a word, the same word that called light out of darkness and Lazarus out of the tomb. He rules the nations with a rod of iron, and he leads his own people gently, like a shepherd. Every crown on earth is held on loan from him, and every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and with a loud voice he called to all the birds that fly directly overhead, "Come, gather for the great supper of God, to eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of captains, the flesh of mighty men, the flesh of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all men, both free and slave, both small and great."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and with a loud voice he called to all the birds that fly directly overhead, “Come, gather for the great supper of God, to eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of captains, the flesh of mighty men, the flesh of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all men, both free and slave, both small and great.”

The setting. Ezekiel 39:17–20 describes God summoning the birds and wild beasts to a great sacrificial feast on the bodies of Gog’s defeated armies, to eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of the princes of the earth. In the ancient world, to be left unburied, eaten by birds, was the ultimate disgrace (Deuteronomy 28:26; 1 Kings 14:11). Jesus said, wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather (Matthew 24:28).

Then I saw an angel standing in the sun. Blazing, visible to all, at the highest point. The position is chosen so that the summons reaches everything with wings.

And with a loud voice he called to all the birds that fly directly overhead. Directly overhead (en mesouranēmati): in mid-heaven, at the zenith, the same phrase used of the eagle in 8:13 and the gospel angel in 14:6. Three times in this book something is announced from the highest point of the sky where nobody can miss it: a warning, a gospel, and now this. The birds are birds of prey, vultures.

Come, gather for the great supper of God. The great supper of God (to deipnon to mega tou theou). The scene is Ezekiel 39, almost word for word, and John’s readers knew the passage. And the placement is the horror of it. Eight verses ago an angel told John to write: blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (v. 9). Here is the other supper, and the invitation goes out to carrion birds. There are two suppers at the end of history: one where the redeemed feast with Christ, and one where his enemies become the feast. Everyone will be at one supper or the other. That is the arrangement the chapter is built on, and it should not be softened into a mere figure of speech. At one, people are the guests. At the other, they are the meal.

To eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of captains, the flesh of mighty men, the flesh of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all men, both free and slave, both small and great. The word flesh five times, and a list that starts at the top: kings, commanders, strong men, cavalry, the whole apparatus of power. Every class of people who opposed Christ is here, as at the sixth seal (6:15). Then the phrase that has run through this book refusing every ranking: both small and great. As the redeemed include small and great (v. 5), so do the lost. Rank gives no protection.

The last word on human greatness. To be left unburied and eaten by birds was, in the ancient world, the most complete disgrace there was, the fate David threatened Goliath with (1 Samuel 17:46), and the thing every army feared more than dying. A king in that condition is indistinguishable from a slave. And that is the last thing this book says about human greatness built against God. The chapter has just given a rider four names and an army in wedding linen; it now takes the rival aristocracy, kings, captains, mighty men, and lists them by their flesh. Whatever is being built on the strength of rank, and however permanent it looks, this is where it is heading if it is built against him.

What it does not mean. This is not a literal description of birds eating corpses at the end of the world, to be imagined in detail. It is a vivid, shocking symbol, drawn from Ezekiel, of total and shameful defeat for those who fight against God.

Why would Scripture use such a shocking image? Because we need to be shocked. We easily think of God’s judgement as a polite disappointment, and of rebellion against Christ as a harmless difference of opinion. The image strips away the illusion: to set oneself against the King of kings is to choose utter ruin and disgrace. It is also deliberately placed beside the marriage supper, so that no reader can miss the choice. God does not show us this to frighten us into despair, but to drive us to the other table while the invitation is still open (Ezekiel 33:11).

In a sentence. Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and he called out loudly to all the birds flying high overhead: Come, gather for God’s great supper, to eat the flesh of kings, military commanders and powerful men, of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all people, free and slave, unimportant and important.

On a Tuesday. There are two suppers. Make sure you have accepted the invitation to the Lamb’s, and urge others to accept it too (Luke 14:16–24). Think of one person you know who has not yet come to Christ, and pray for them by name every day this week. Ask God for an opening, and when it comes, tell them about the wedding.

For worship. There are two suppers, and the Lamb has done everything to bring us to the right one. He took the shame of the cross, stripped and exposed, so that we would not be exposed on the last day. He was given up to death outside the city, so that we could be welcomed into it. The God who could have left us all for the birds sent his Son to bring us in as guests, and as his Bride. Rank gives no protection at the great supper of God, and none is needed at the marriage supper of the Lamb; there the small and the great sit down together, saved by grace alone.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies gathered to make war against him who was sitting on the horse and against his army. And the beast was captured, and with it the false prophet who in its presence had done the signs by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur. And the rest were slain by the sword that came from the mouth of him who was sitting on the horse, and all the birds were gorged with their flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies gathered to make war against him who was sitting on the horse and against his army. And the beast was captured, and with it the false prophet who in its presence had done the signs by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur. And the rest were slain by the sword that came from the mouth of him who was sitting on the horse, and all the birds were gorged with their flesh.

The setting. Psalm 2:2 says the kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD and his Anointed. The gathering was announced in 16:14–16 (Armageddon) and 17:14. Daniel 7:11 says the beast was killed and its body destroyed and given over to be burned with fire. Korah, Dathan and Abiram went down alive into Sheol (Numbers 16:33).

And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies gathered to make war against him who was sitting on the horse and against his army. Gathered (synēgmena), as in 16:14, 16 and 20:8. This is the muster of 16:14–16 arriving, the kings assembled by three frog-spirits at the place called Armageddon. All the forces of evil gathered in one place. The most famous battle in the world’s imagination has finally been joined, and the reader should watch how long it lasts.

And the beast was captured. Captured (epiasthē): seized. That is the battle. There is no engagement, no exchange, no struggle, no contest, and no account of the fighting at all. The verb is passive, and the beast that was worshipped by the whole earth (13:4), that was given authority over every tribe and people and language and nation, that made war on the saints for forty-two months, is simply taken. John has built thirteen chapters of dread and then refuses to give the confrontation a single sentence of drama. That is not carelessness; it is the argument. A thing that requires no fight was never the equal of the one who ends it, and every reader who has been frightened by the beast is being told what the beast actually weighs when the rider arrives.

And with it the false prophet who in its presence had done the signs by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. The second beast of 13:11–17. He is named by the charge sheet: deception is what he is arrested for. In a book whose enemy is the deceiver of the whole world, that is the charge that matters.

These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur. Alive (zōntes). Lake of fire (tēn limnēn tou pyros): the place of final, eternal punishment, first mentioned here. Later the devil is thrown there (20:10), then death and Hades, and all whose names are not in the book of life (20:14–15). It was prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41). Alive is deliberate: this is not annihilation on a battlefield.

And the rest were slain by the sword that came from the mouth of him who was sitting on the horse. By his word alone. The armies of heaven do nothing; Christ speaks, and it is over. Not one member of the army in fine linen is recorded as having lifted a hand.

And all the birds were gorged with their flesh. Gorged (echortasthēsan): filled, satisfied. The great supper of God (v. 17) has been served.

Where Christians differ: are the beast and false prophet persons, and is the lake of fire eternal? Some say that since the beast and false prophet are symbols of systems, not individuals, the lake of fire may mean only their abolition, not eternal punishment. Verdict: the beast and false prophet represent systems of persecuting power and deception, and also, finally, the persons who lead them. Their being thrown into the lake of fire shows the total end of those systems, and the eternal punishment of the persons who embody them, together with all who follow them. Revelation 20:10 says the devil, the beast and the false prophet will be tormented day and night for ever and ever: the punishment is conscious and endless. Christ’s victory over every evil power is complete and permanent.

What it does not mean. The final battle is not a long war in which the outcome is uncertain. It is over the moment Christ appears. Evil is no match for him.

Is the lake of fire literal fire? The language is picture language, and Scripture uses several pictures for hell: fire, outer darkness, the worm that does not die (Mark 9:48; Matthew 8:12). Fire and darkness cannot both be literal at the same time in the ordinary sense. But the pictures do not soften the reality; they point to something worse than any image can convey: conscious, unending separation from the goodness of God, under his just wrath. The right response is not curiosity about its physics but fear of God, gratitude to Christ who bore that wrath for all who trust him, and urgency in warning others.

What the seven churches were being told. This is the final answer of the book to a question the seven churches were living inside. They had no army, no legal standing, no leverage, and no way of resisting the power arranged against them. Nothing in Revelation ever tells them to acquire any of those things. It tells them to endure, to keep their garments on, to hold the testimony, and to conquer by blood already shed. And then it shows them the end, in which they ride out in wedding clothes behind someone who does not need them, and wants them anyway.

In a sentence. Then I saw the beast, the kings of the earth and their armies gathered to wage war against the rider on the horse and his army; but the beast was captured, along with the false prophet who had performed signs on its behalf, by which he had deceived those who received the beast’s mark and worshipped its image; the two of them were thrown alive into the lake of fire burning with sulphur, and the rest were killed by the sword that came from the mouth of the rider on the horse, and all the birds ate their fill of their flesh.

On a Tuesday. The powers that seem invincible today will be taken without a fight. Stay with the Lamb; he has already won. When you feel outnumbered, at work, in your family, in a culture hostile to Christ, do the things this book asks of you: endure, keep your garments clean, hold to the testimony of Jesus. You do not have to win the battle. You only have to be found with him when he wins it.

For worship. His eyes are a flame of fire and there are more crowns on his head than anyone has counted. He is called Faithful and True, and the Word of God, and King of kings and Lord of lords, and there is another name that no one knows but himself. He came out of an open heaven already covered in blood, and the war the whole earth had been assembling for was over before it started, and the only weapon he used was his mouth. The beast that terrified the world is seized like a thief, and the deceiver is silenced for ever. And the King who ends it all is the Lamb who was slain for us, who loved us and freed us from our sins by his blood. To him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

20.title: The Thousand Years and the Great White Throne
20.overview:
Chapter 20 contains the most debated passage in the most debated book of the Bible: the millennium. The thousand-year reign of Christ with his saints (vv. 1–6) has divided serious, Scripture-loving Christians for two thousand years and continues to do so. The amillennial position is followed here as the Reformed mainstream, with all four major views presented with genuine respect and fairness. The stakes in this debate are high — but the non-negotiables that all four views share are higher: Christ will return, the dead will be raised, the wicked will be judged, the righteous will be glorified, and God will be all in all.

The Four Positions — Stated Fairly: Dispensational Premillennialism (MacArthur, Walvoord, Ryrie, Swindoll): After the pre-tribulation Rapture and the seven-year tribulation, Christ returns bodily to earth and establishes a literal thousand-year kingdom centred in Jerusalem, with a rebuilt temple and a restored national Israel fulfilling the Old Testament covenants. Satan is literally bound in the abyss. The martyred saints and tribulation believers are resurrected to reign with Christ. At the end of the millennium, Satan is released, defeated, and cast into the lake of fire. Then the Great White Throne judgment and the eternal state. Historic Premillennialism (Ladd, Grudem): Similar to dispensational, but without the pre-trib Rapture — the church goes through the tribulation. Christ returns, binds Satan, raises the martyrs (the first resurrection), and reigns on earth for a literal thousand years. Postmillennialism (Jonathan Edwards, Charles Hodge, Warfield in some respects): The thousand years represents the gospel era of expanding Christian influence, gradually Christianising the world through the preaching of the gospel, before Christ returns to a world largely won for the kingdom. The binding of Satan is the progressive restriction of his power through the gospel. Amillennialism (Augustine, Calvin, Vos, Berkhof, Hoekema, Beale — the position followed here): The thousand years is the entire period between the first and second comings of Christ — the church age. The binding of Satan (vv. 1–3) was accomplished at the cross (John 12:31; Colossians 2:15; Luke 10:18) and restricts his ability to deceive the nations so the gospel can go to all peoples. The first resurrection (vv. 4–6) is the spiritual resurrection of souls reigning with Christ in heaven now, or the new birth through which believers participate in Christ’s resurrection life. The thousand years is a symbolic number (10 x 10 x 10 = complete fullness) for the complete church age. Satan’s release at the end (vv. 7–9) represents the brief intensification of opposition immediately before Christ’s return. The Great White Throne (vv. 11–15) is the final universal judgment of all the dead.

The chapter divides into two sections: the millennium and Satan’s career (vv. 1–10) and the Great White Throne (vv. 11–15). Both sections are eschatologically essential and both are theologically clear on the matters that count: no one escapes the final judgment, no name not written in the book of life survives it, and the last enemies — Death and Hades themselves — are thrown into the lake of fire. Whatever one believes about the millennium, these outcomes are certain.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–3: one angel with a key and a chain seizes, binds, throws, shuts and seals the dragon — named with the four names of 12:9 — for a thousand years, and the binding is given a stated purpose: so that he might not deceive the nations any longer. After that he must be released for a little while, using the word of divine necessity.

Verse 4: thrones, with authority to judge committed to those on them; the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and those who had not worshipped the beast or taken its mark; they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. Verses 5–6: the rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection. Then the fifth beatitude: Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him.

Verses 7–8: Satan is released, deceives the nations at the four corners of the earth — Gog and Magog (Ezek. 38–39) — and gathers a host like the sand of the sea. Verses 9–10: they surround the camp of the saints and the beloved city, fire comes down and consumes them, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire where the beast and false prophet already are.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Thousand Years

An angel binds the dragon so that he may no longer deceive the nations; those who refused the beast reign with Christ; and after a brief release Satan’s last host is consumed and he is thrown into the lake of fire. Premillennial, amillennial and postmillennial readers differ on the timing, and agree on all that the creeds require.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The people the world beheaded and shut out of the market are seen on thrones.

Now: Over those who share in the first resurrection the second death has no power — on that there is no dispute.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding in his hand the key to the bottomless pit and a great chain. And he seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and threw him into the pit, and shut it and sealed it over him, so that he might not deceive the nations any longer, until the thousand years were ended. After that he must be released for a little while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding in his hand the key to the bottomless pit and a great chain. And he seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and threw him into the pit, and shut it and sealed it over him, so that he might not deceive the nations any longer, until the thousand years were ended. After that he must be released for a little while.

Meaning first. Revelation 20 is the only passage in the Bible that speaks of a thousand years, and it shows Satan’s defeat and the final judgement. An angel binds Satan with a chain and seals him in the abyss for a thousand years, so that he can no longer deceive the nations, after which he must be released for a little while (vv. 1–3). John sees thrones and those given authority to judge, and the souls of those beheaded for Jesus and those who refused the beast; they come to life and reign with Christ for a thousand years (v. 4). This is the first resurrection; those who share in it are blessed, the second death has no power over them, and they are priests reigning with Christ (vv. 5–6). When the thousand years end, Satan is released and gathers the nations, Gog and Magog, as numerous as the sand, to surround the camp of the saints and the beloved city; but fire from heaven consumes them, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire with the beast and false prophet, to be tormented for ever (vv. 7–10). Then John sees a great white throne, from which earth and sky flee; the dead, great and small, are judged according to their works recorded in the books; the sea, Death and Hades give up their dead; Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, the second death; and anyone not found in the book of life is thrown in too (vv. 11–15). In the amillennial reading this app follows, the chapter goes back to the beginning of the church age once more: Satan was bound at Christ’s first coming so that the gospel could go to the nations; the martyrs and faithful dead now reign with Christ in heaven; at the end Satan is released briefly for a final assault; and then Christ returns, once, to raise all the dead and judge all people. And the whole chapter, read rightly, is a hymn to the Lamb: the serpent of Genesis 3 is finished, death itself is thrown away, and the only thing that decides anyone’s destiny is a name written in the Lamb’s book.

The setting. Jesus said no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man (Matthew 12:29), and he did this by casting out demons through the Spirit of God, showing that the kingdom of God had come. On the eve of the cross he said, now will the ruler of this world be cast out, and I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself (John 12:31–32). Through death he destroyed the one who has the power of death, the devil (Hebrews 2:14), and disarmed the rulers and authorities, triumphing over them in the cross (Colossians 2:15). Jude 6 speaks of angels kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgement. When John hears of a chain and a pit, his readers would have heard all of this behind it.

Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven. “Then I saw” (kai eidon) is John’s regular formula for a new vision. It marks the order of the visions, not necessarily the order of events. John has already done this more than once: chapter 12 went back to Christ’s birth after the seventh trumpet had announced the end of the world. A man who tells you what he saw next is not always telling you what happened next.

Three things everybody agrees on. Before a word is said about the thousand years, three things in these verses should be noticed, because they are agreed by every reader and they are easy to lose in the argument.

Holding in his hand the key to the bottomless pit and a great chain, he seized the dragon. First, the arrest is effortless. One angel, one key (kleida), one chain (halysin), and five verbs done to the dragon: seized, bound, threw, shut, sealed. This is the creature who had seven heads and ten diadems, who gave the beast its throne, who made war on the woman and on the rest of her offspring, and who deceived the whole world. He is handled by a single unnamed angel with a set of keys. Nobody in this chapter has to fight him. A spiritual being cannot literally be chained; the key and the chain are pictures of authority and restraint, and they say that Satan’s power is limited by God, whenever and however God pleases.

That ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan. Second, the four names are the ones from 12:9, in the same order: the dragon, the ancient serpent, the devil, Satan. The same enemy, all his titles read out at his arrest. John is deliberately reaching back to the garden, to the serpent who spoke to Eve, and closing the file that was opened in Genesis 3. The Bible’s first villain is about to receive the Bible’s last sentence, and the promise that the woman’s offspring would crush his head (Genesis 3:15) is about to be seen in full.

And bound him for a thousand years. “Bound” (edēsen) is the same word Jesus used of binding the strong man (Matthew 12:29). The Lord had told his disciples what he was doing in his ministry, and John now shows it from heaven’s side. “A thousand years” (chilia etē; millennium is simply Latin for a thousand years). In Revelation numbers are symbolic: seven lampstands, twelve thousand from each tribe, a woman nourished for twelve hundred and sixty days. A thousand is ten cubed, the number of completeness raised to its fullest. A long, complete period, its length set entirely by God.

And threw him into the pit, and shut it and sealed it over him. “Sealed” (esphragisen) is the word used of the tomb of Jesus, when the authorities sealed the stone to keep a dead man in (Matthew 27:66). That seal failed, because the man inside was the Lord of life. This one holds, because the one who placed it is the same Lord.

So that he might not deceive the nations any longer. Third, and this is the clause that decides the whole chapter, the binding is given a stated purpose. Not so that he could do nothing at all. The text says: so that he might not deceive the nations any longer, until the thousand years were ended. Whatever the binding is, John defines it himself, and it is specific. It does not mean Satan is inactive in every way; he still prowls (1 Peter 5:8), tempts and persecutes. It means he cannot prevent the gospel from going to the nations, or gather the nations for the final assault on the church until God permits. Before Christ, the nations sat in darkness, with only Israel knowing the true God. Since Christ, the gospel has gone to every continent, and people from every nation have been turned from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God (Acts 26:18). That is precisely what a dragon prevented from deceiving the nations would look like.

A dog on a chain. Here is the honest picture. A chained dog is still dangerous to anyone who wanders within reach of it; you would not put your hand near its mouth. But it cannot stop the house being plundered, and it cannot follow the plunderers down the road. Satan can still bite, and Christians are told to resist him firm in the faith (1 Peter 5:9). What he cannot do is keep the nations locked in his house while Christ carries his captives out of it, one by one, from every people on earth.

Until the thousand years were ended. After that he must be released for a little while. “Must” (dei) is the divine must that has governed this book since 1:1, the things that must soon take place. Even the release is on a permission and has a term. “A little while” (mikron chronon) is a short time at the end of history, a final outburst of deception and persecution before Christ returns (2 Thessalonians 2:3–12). Nothing the dragon does, including his final rampage, is outside the timetable God has written.

The thousand years: three readings. Now the most argued-over paragraph in Scripture. The phrase occurs six times in six verses, and this is the only place in the Bible that speaks of a thousand-year reign. Godly readers have understood it in three main ways, and all three deserve to be set out with what genuinely favours each, rather than one asserted and the others waved away.

The premillennial reading. This takes the chapter in the order it is written. Christ returns at the end of chapter 19; then Satan is bound; then Christ reigns on the earth for a thousand years; then Satan is released, the last rebellion is crushed, and the final judgement follows. Two forms of it are held. Historic premillennialism (George Eldon Ladd, Wayne Grudem) has the church go through the tribulation before Christ returns. Dispensational premillennialism (John Walvoord, Charles Ryrie, John MacArthur and the Scofield tradition) adds a rapture of the church before a seven-year tribulation, and understands the millennium as the period in which God’s promises to national Israel are fulfilled. What favours it is considerable and should not be minimised. The narrative flows straight on from chapter 19 with then I saw. The Old Testament promises of a messianic kingdom on the earth, a wolf lying down with a lamb, a child playing over a snake’s hole, a man building a house and living in it (Isaiah 11:6–9; 65:20–25), are given somewhere to land. And the strongest argument is at verse 5, where the same verb used of the martyrs coming to life is used of the rest of the dead, whom everyone agrees are raised bodily.

The postmillennial reading. This holds that the gospel will succeed so widely that a long era of Christianised civilisation follows, and that Christ returns at the end of it. It was held by Jonathan Edwards and Charles Hodge, and today by writers such as Kenneth Gentry. What favours it is the trajectory of Jesus’ own parables, a mustard seed becoming the largest of garden plants and leaven working through the whole lump (Matthew 13:31–33), along with Psalm 2, Psalm 72 and Isaiah 2:2–4, the sheer scope of the Great Commission, and Paul’s statement that Christ must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25). Its difficulty is the New Testament’s equally consistent expectation of apostasy and tribulation before the end (Matthew 24:9–13; 2 Timothy 3:1–5), and the final deception described in this very chapter.

The amillennial reading. This takes the thousand years as the whole period between the first and second comings: the age the church is in now. On this view Satan was bound at the cross, in exactly the sense verse 3 specifies: he can no longer keep the nations in the dark. The reign of the saints is their reign with Christ in heaven, which is why verse 4 says John saw souls. Christ returns once, at the end, and there is one resurrection and one judgement. This is the position of Augustine, the Reformers broadly, Geerhardus Vos, William Hendriksen and G. K. Beale, and it is the position followed here. What favours it is also considerable. Numbers in this book are symbolic throughout. The chapter never says Christ is on the earth during these years, and never mentions his physical presence at all. And Jesus described his own ministry in exactly this image of binding the strong man.

Where Christians differ: what is the thousand years? Premillennialists, including dispensationalists, hold that Christ will return before (pre-) a literal thousand-year reign on earth, during which Satan is bound and Christ rules from Jerusalem; then Satan is released, defeated, and the final judgement follows. Postmillennialists hold that the gospel will gradually triumph in the world, bringing a long golden age of Christian influence, after (post-) which Christ returns. Amillennialists hold that the thousand years is a symbol for the present church age, between Christ’s first and second comings: Satan is now bound so that he cannot stop the gospel; believers who have died reign with Christ in heaven; and Christ’s return brings the end, with no separate earthly millennium. Verdict: the amillennial view fits Revelation best. Revelation repeatedly goes back over the same period in parallel visions, and chapter 20 does so again. The binding of Satan is what Jesus and the apostles say happened at the cross. The reign is with Christ, who already reigns from heaven. The final battle of 20:7–10 is the same as 16:14–16 and 19:19–21, all drawn from Ezekiel 38–39, and gathered in the same words. And the rest of the New Testament teaches one return of Christ, bringing the resurrection of both righteous and wicked together (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15), the final judgement and the new creation (2 Peter 3:10–13), with no interval of a thousand years. Premillennial and postmillennial believers are brothers and sisters in Christ, and this is a matter where Christians may charitably differ; but the amillennial reading is the most faithful to the text.

What all three agree on. Now the honest part, and it matters more than the schemes. All three hold everything that the historic creeds require, and they agree on far more than they dispute. Every one of them affirms that Christ has decisively defeated Satan; that he will return bodily, visibly and personally; that the dead will be raised; that there will be a final judgement; that the wicked will be condemned and the redeemed will live in a new creation; and that the church’s duty now is faithfulness under pressure. The disagreement is about the timing and sequence of things all three are certain will happen. Some of the most godly men who have ever lived have been on each side, and none of them was able to convince the others. The right response to a brother who reads it differently is not suspicion but an open Bible and a warm handshake.

What it does not mean. Satan’s binding does not mean evil has disappeared. Evil is everywhere, and Satan still tempts and attacks. It means his power to keep the nations in darkness has been broken, and the gospel advances in spite of him.

If Satan is bound, why does the world look so dark? Because the binding is specific, not total. John never says the world will become pleasant; the same book that binds the dragon has the beast making war on the saints. What has changed is that the gospel cannot be stopped. Look at the map: in John’s day the church was a few scattered congregations in one corner of the Roman Empire, and today there are believers in nearly every nation, worshipping in thousands of languages. That did not happen with Satan free to keep the nations blind. So when the news is grim, read it inside this verse. Darkness is real, but it is no longer in charge of who hears about Christ.

But does the rapture not come before all this? This app holds that there is no secret rapture. The New Testament knows one coming of Christ, and it is anything but secret: the Lord descends with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel and the sound of the trumpet of God (1 Thessalonians 4:16). Believers who are alive are caught up to meet him, and the dead in Christ rise first, but this is the public meeting of the King, not a quiet removal years before the end. Christians who hold a pre-tribulation rapture are brothers in Christ, and many of them love the Lord’s appearing more than we do. But the church should expect to go through trouble, as it always has, and to be kept in it rather than taken out of it (John 17:15).

Does it matter which view I hold? It matters, but not as much as some arguments make it seem. It matters because how you read this chapter shapes how you read the whole of Revelation, and whether you expect the world to get better, worse or both. It does not matter in the sense of dividing Christians. You can belong to a church whose pastor reads it differently, pray with brothers who disagree, and sing the same hymns about the coming King. What you must not do is let the chart replace the Christ. All three views wait for the same person.

In a sentence. Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding the key to the abyss and a huge chain in his hand; he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years; he threw him into the abyss, locked it and sealed it over him, so that he could not deceive the nations any more until the thousand years were over; after that he must be set free for a short time.

On a Tuesday. Share the gospel with confidence. Satan cannot stop it reaching the nations; he has been bound. The colleague who seems hardest, the neighbour who mocks, the relative who has refused for thirty years: none of them is beyond the reach of a gospel the dragon cannot block. Pray for missionaries by name this week, and for the unreached people groups who have still not heard, because the binding of the strong man is the reason those prayers are not in vain. And when you are tempted, remember that the one tempting you is on a chain, and the chain is held by Christ.

For worship. The dragon who deceived the whole world is arrested by one angel with a key. He does not fight; he cannot. The Son of God walked into the strong man’s house, took the strong man captive at the cross, and has been carrying his captives out ever since: from Ethiopia and Rome, from the islands of the sea and the cities of the north, men and women from every tribe and tongue walking out of darkness into the light of the Lamb. The serpent who opened the Bible’s first sorrow is sealed in a pit by the command of the Lamb who was slain, and the gospel runs free across the earth. Worthy is the Lamb, who binds the strong man and plunders his house.
verseByVerse.note: The thousand years (the millennium) is read in three main ways: Christ’s present reign from heaven through the church age (amillennial); a future reign on earth after his return (premillennial); or a golden age of gospel success before his return (postmillennial).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw thrones, and seated on them were those to whom the authority to judge was committed. Also I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw thrones, and seated on them were those to whom the authority to judge was committed. Also I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.

The setting. Daniel 7:9 and 22 say thrones were placed, and judgement was given for the saints of the Most High, and the time came when the saints possessed the kingdom. Jesus promised the Twelve that they would sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes (Matthew 19:28), and the overcomer that he would sit with Christ on his throne (3:21). Paul asked the Corinthians, apparently expecting them to know, whether they did not know that the saints will judge the world (1 Corinthians 6:2). Beheading with a sword was the Roman method of executing citizens, and tradition says Paul died this way.

Then I saw thrones, and seated on them were those to whom the authority to judge was committed. Thrones, plural, and John does not say at once who is on them. “Thrones” (thronous): in Revelation, thrones are almost always in heaven, and the word appears forty-seven times. “Authority to judge” (krima edothē autois, judgement was given to them) can mean either that they were given authority to judge, or that judgement was given in their favour, as in Daniel 7:22, vindicating them. Both are true of the same people. They were judged by earthly courts; now heaven’s court has found for them, and they sit with the Judge.

Also I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God. “Souls” (psychas): the same word as 6:9, the souls under the altar. These are believers who have died, now alive in God’s presence. They were killed on earth; now they reign in heaven. “Beheaded” is a specific word, execution by the axe or sword. John does not merely say killed. He says how, because he wants us to see the cost.

And those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands. Two groups, or one company described twice? The Greek allows either, and it may well be one company seen from two sides: those who died for refusing, and those who lived without yielding, all who conquered the beast (15:2). If so, the reign belongs to everyone who did not take the mark, not to a sub-class of martyrs. And there is a phrase here the reader has met before. Chapter 13 said nobody could buy or sell without the mark. These people could not buy or sell, and here they are on thrones.

They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. Everything turns on that verb. The Greek is ezēsan, and it means simply they lived, or they came to life. It is not their bodily resurrection, which comes at the end (1 Corinthians 15:23, 52), but their entry into life with Christ when they died. Though their bodies were killed, they live and reign with him, for God is not God of the dead but of the living, for all live to him (Luke 20:38; John 11:25–26). “Reigned with Christ” (ebasileusan meta tou Christou): sharing his rule from heaven, where he reigns now (Ephesians 1:20–22). This is the answer to 6:9–11. The martyrs who waited under the altar, crying how long, are now seen on thrones.

Where Christians differ: is this a bodily resurrection to rule on earth? Premillennialists read “came to life” as a bodily resurrection of believers at Christ’s return, followed by a literal thousand-year reign on earth, and their argument from verse 5 is the strongest single argument in the debate: the identical verb is used one sentence later of the rest of the dead, and nobody disputes that their coming to life is bodily. Some amillennial readers take the coming to life of the new birth, for God made us alive together with Christ and seated us with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:5–6), and Jesus said the hour is coming and is now here when the dead will hear his voice and live (John 5:25). Verdict: John sees souls, not bodies, on thrones, which in Revelation are in heaven. The scene is the heavenly reign of believers who have died, during the present age, while Satan is bound on earth. The same word for living is used of the beast who was and is not (13:14), and of Christ who was dead and is alive (1:18; 2:8); life after death is meant. The bodily resurrection of all believers comes at Christ’s single return at the end (1 Thessalonians 4:16). This is the great comfort of the passage for persecuted believers: those who die for Christ are not defeated; they reign with him now.

The verdict reversed. Whatever a reader concludes about the verb, what the verse is for is not in dispute at all. Look at who is reigning. Not one of them held any office. They were beheaded, boycotted, shut out of the market, unable to buy bread, tried in courts that found against them and buried by people who were afraid to say why. The world’s verdict on them was delivered and recorded and is still on file. And John sees them on thrones, with the authority to judge committed to them, reigning with Christ. That is what this verse is doing in this book, and it is what the whole book has been doing since chapter 1. It reverses the verdict. The people the world disposed of are the people on the thrones, and the arrangement is already in force.

What it does not mean. Reigning with Christ does not mean that the dead in Christ rule the earth now in a political sense, or that we should pray to them. They share his heavenly reign and await the resurrection.

What happens to a Christian the moment he dies? He goes at once to be with Christ, conscious, at rest and full of joy. Paul calls it far better (Philippians 1:23), and to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). The thief on the cross was told, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). There is no purgatory where the believer must pay off what Christ left unpaid, and no sleep of the soul in which he knows nothing until the last day: John sees souls who are alive and reigning. The body rests in the grave until the resurrection; the person is with the Lord (Westminster 32.1). That is why Christians may grieve at a graveside, but not as those who have no hope.

Do my loved ones in heaven see me, and should I talk to them? Scripture does not tell us what the departed see of earth, and it is wise not to build on guesses. It does tell us where they are and what they are doing: they are with Christ and reigning with him, and that is enough to know. We should not pray to them or seek to speak with them; the Bible forbids consulting the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), and the one Mediator between God and men is Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Speak to the Lord about them, thank him for them, and look forward to the morning when you will see them again in a body that cannot die.

In a sentence. Then I saw thrones, and those seated on them were given authority to judge; I also saw the souls of those who had been beheaded because of their testimony about Jesus and because of the word of God, those who had not worshipped the beast or its image or received its mark on their foreheads or hands; they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.

On a Tuesday. When standing for Christ costs you something, a promotion passed over, a friendship cooled, a family member’s contempt, remember where the story ends for people like you. The world files its verdict, and heaven overturns it. And when you stand at the grave of a believer, say it out loud to yourself: they are not lost, they are reigning. Grief is right, but it is grief for a parting, not for a defeat.

For worship. The souls who waited under the altar are seated on thrones. Men who were beheaded, women who could not buy bread because they would not bow, are reigning beside the King who was himself condemned by a Roman court and hung outside the city. He was the first to have the world’s verdict reversed, on the third day, and every one of his people shares his vindication. Death did not defeat them; it delivered them to him. Blessed be the Lord Jesus Christ, who turns executions into coronations and makes the despised of the earth kings and priests with him.

verseByVerse.quote: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.

The setting. Jesus said that an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgement (John 5:28–29). He also said, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life; he does not come into judgement, but has passed from death to life (John 5:24). Paul says believers have been raised with Christ and seated with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6; Colossians 3:1).

The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. “The rest of the dead”: unbelievers. They do not share the life and reign with Christ during the present age; they come to life only to be judged, at the end (vv. 12–13). One sentence, and it carries the weight of the argument set out at verse 4. On the premillennial reading the parallel is decisive: two groups, two comings to life, a thousand years apart, and the same verb for both. On the amillennial reading John distinguishes them by calling only one of them the first resurrection, and by reserving for the other the plain statement that it happens at the end.

This is the first resurrection. “First resurrection” (hē anastasis hē prōtē). The phrase occurs only here. If there is a first resurrection, there is implicitly a second: the bodily resurrection at the end. Just as there is a first death (physical) and a second death (eternal), so there is a first resurrection (spiritual, entering life with Christ, at conversion and at death) and a second (bodily, at Christ’s return). Believers share both resurrections and only the first death; unbelievers share both deaths and only the second resurrection, to judgement.

First and second of different kinds. There is a feature of John’s vocabulary in this very passage that bears on it. He speaks of a second death in the next verse and again at verse 14, and the second death is plainly not a death of the same kind as the first: the first is a body in a grave, the second is a lake of fire. If second death can name something of a different order from the first death, then first resurrection may name something of a different order from the second. That is the amillennial answer, and it is a real one. A premillennial reader will reply that the parallel with verse 5 is closer than the parallel with the deaths. The reader should weigh both, with an open Bible.

Textual note. One important early manuscript (Codex Sinaiticus) and some others omit the first sentence, “The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended”. Most manuscripts include it, and it is probably original.

Where Christians differ: are there two bodily resurrections a thousand years apart? Premillennialists read the first resurrection as a bodily resurrection of believers before the millennium, and the second as a bodily resurrection of unbelievers after it. Verdict: the rest of the New Testament teaches one bodily resurrection of both righteous and unrighteous at the same time, on the last day (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15; Daniel 12:2). Jesus says he will raise up believers on the last day (John 6:39–40, 44, 54), which leaves no room for a thousand years after their resurrection. The first resurrection is the believer’s sharing in Christ’s resurrection life, beginning at new birth and carried into heaven at death, while the body awaits the last day.

Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! The fifth of the book’s seven beatitudes, and the only one that adds a second adjective. Not merely blessed: blessed and holy (hagios), set apart, belonging to God. Three things are said about this person, and they should be taken one at a time, because they are among the great promises of Scripture.

Over such the second death has no power. Not they will probably escape it, and not they will be forgiven at the trial. It has no authority over them. The word is exousia, a legal term. The second death has no jurisdiction; it cannot bring a case. “Second death”: the lake of fire (v. 14). Smyrna was promised this in almost the same words: the one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death (2:11). And that is the answer to the deepest fear underneath everything in this chapter. A Christian may reasonably be uncertain about the timing of the millennium; he may not reasonably be uncertain about this. Whatever is coming at the great white throne, one kind of person is outside its reach altogether, and the reason is not their record. It is that their names are in a book that belongs to a Lamb who was slain.

But they will be priests of God and of Christ. “Priests” (hiereis): the kingdom of priests of 1:6 and 5:10, arriving. A priest has access, offers worship, and carries other people’s names into the presence of God. That is what these people will be doing: not standing about being rewarded, but serving in the nearest place there is. And notice the phrase of God and of Christ. Christ is served with the same priestly service as God. No creature is ever worshipped in this book; the Lamb is, because he is God.

And they will reign with him for a thousand years. “Reign” (basileusousin). The reign is with him, which is the qualifier that keeps it from being a fantasy of revenge. Nobody in this chapter reigns on his own account or over his own patch. The whole substance of the thousand years is being where he is and doing what he does. And note the two offices together: priests, and reigning. That is the combination Israel was promised at Sinai, a kingdom of priests (Exodus 19:6), and never managed. It is held in one person only, the one who is both King of kings and the Lamb who was slaughtered. His people get both because they are with him.

What it does not mean. The first resurrection is not a special reward for martyrs only. All believers share in it (Ephesians 2:5–6).

How do I know I share in the first resurrection? If you have been born again, you have. The first resurrection begins when the Spirit makes a dead heart alive and joins it to the risen Christ, and you know it by its fruit: you trust Christ for your salvation and not your record, you love him and want to obey him, you hate the sin you once enjoyed, and you love his people (1 John 3:14). None of that is perfect in anyone. But none of it grows naturally in a dead soul either. If those things are in you, however weakly, the second death has no claim on you, and Christ will not lose you (John 10:28).

Does reigning with Christ start only after I die? In its full form, yes; but it has already begun. Paul says God has raised us up with Christ and seated us with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6), present tense. A believer on earth already shares Christ’s victory: sin no longer has dominion over him (Romans 6:14), he may come boldly to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16), and his prayers are part of how Christ rules the world (8:3–5). The reign John sees in heaven is what this becomes when the struggle is over. So reign now, by saying no to sin and yes to God, and by praying as one who has the King’s ear.

In a sentence. The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were over; this is the first resurrection; how blessed and holy are those who share in the first resurrection! The second death has no power over them; they will be priests of God and of Christ and will reign with him for a thousand years.

On a Tuesday. If you are in Christ, you have already passed from death to life, and the second death has no power over you. Live today as a priest and king with him. As a priest: bring someone’s name before God today, a colleague in trouble, a child who has wandered, the persecuted church. As a king: refuse one sin today that used to rule you, and know that you are refusing it from a throne, not begging for mercy from a cell.

For worship. The second death has no jurisdiction over the people of the Lamb, because the Lamb went under the judgement in their place. He died the death that was theirs, rose with the life that is his, and shares that life with every one of them from the day he calls them out of the grave of sin. He is Priest and King together, the one Israel longed for and never saw, and he makes his people priests and kings with him, not because they earned a throne, but because they are joined to the one who sits on it. Blessed and holy are they, and all the blessing and holiness is his.
verseByVerse.note: The fifth of the seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released from his prison and will come out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released from his prison and will come out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea.

The setting. In Ezekiel 38–39, Gog of the land of Magog leads a vast coalition of nations from the far north against God’s restored people Israel, living securely in unwalled villages; God destroys them with fire and brimstone, and the birds and beasts feast on their bodies (Ezekiel 39:4, 17–20). In Jewish tradition, Gog and Magog became names for the final enemies of God’s people. Revelation 19:17–21 used the birds’ feast from Ezekiel 39; 20:7–10 uses the fire from Ezekiel 38:22. Both describe the same final battle, told twice.

And when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released from his prison. “Released” (lythēsetai), the passive again, and 20:3 has already said he must be, using the word of divine necessity. Even the last rebellion is on a licence issued from the throne. God allows a final, brief period of satanic deception and persecution at the end of the age, which Jesus and Paul also foretold (Matthew 24:21–24; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–12).

And will come out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth. “Deceive” (planēsai). Released from restraint, he goes straight back to the work he was bound to stop doing. The verb has defined him since 12:9, where he was named the deceiver of the whole world. Nothing has been learned, nothing has changed, and after a thousand years in a sealed pit the first thing he does is start talking. That should be said plainly, because it settles a question people ask about the devil’s end. He does not repent, negotiate or reconsider. Evil in this book has no capacity for growth; it only ever repeats itself with a larger audience. “Four corners”: the whole world, every direction at once.

Gog and Magog. In Ezekiel, Gog is a ruler and Magog his land. Here both are names for the nations. John compresses two entire chapters of Ezekiel into two words and expects them to be recognised. And he uses them the way he has used every other name in this book: as a type rather than an address. Babylon was not the city on the Euphrates; Sodom and Egypt in chapter 11 were not Sodom and Egypt; here Gog and Magog is not a country but the last coalition of everything opposed to God. The clue is that these nations are at the four corners of the earth, which is not a place either.

To gather them for battle. “The battle” (ton polemon, with the definite article): the battle already described in 16:14 and 19:19, in nearly identical words. The same event, seen a third time. John has been showing us the last day from different windows, and this is the last window.

Their number is like the sand of the sea. Countless. The church will seem overwhelmed. And the phrase is one of the most loaded in the Old Testament, because it is the promise God made to Abraham about his offspring: I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore (Genesis 22:17). The enemy assembles a counterfeit of Abraham’s promise. That is the last thing the dragon does in Scripture, and it is what he has done at every stage: a beast who parodies the Lamb’s resurrection, a false prophet with horns like a lamb, a mark answering a seal, a prostitute answering a bride, and now a countless host answering the countless family promised to a childless old man standing outside his tent at night.

Two uncountable crowds. A Christian looking at the numbers is being told something he needs at the end of this book as much as at the beginning. The last enemy army is beyond counting, and the multitude before the throne in chapter 7 was also one that no one could number. Two uncountable crowds. Only one of them lasts, and the other is about to be dealt with in a single verse.

Where Christians differ: is Gog and Magog a specific nation, such as Russia? Some popular prophecy teachers identified Gog and Magog with Russia, linking Rosh (Ezekiel 38:2, in some translations) with Russia and Meshech with Moscow. Verdict: those connections are based on sound-alike words, not on language or history; Rosh is a Hebrew word meaning chief, and Meshech and Tubal were peoples in what is now Turkey. In Revelation, Gog and Magog are explicitly the nations at the four corners of the earth: not one nation but the whole world in rebellion. The point is not geography but the final, worldwide assault on God’s people, and its sure defeat.

What it does not mean. Satan’s release does not mean God has lost control. He is released by God’s permission, for God’s purpose: to expose the persistence of human rebellion and to bring all evil into the open for final judgement.

Why would God let Satan out at all? Scripture does not give every reason, but it gives enough. The release shows that the human heart, left to itself, does not become good with time or better surroundings: after a whole age of the gospel going out, the nations still gather against God the moment the deceiver speaks. It brings every hidden rebellion into the open, so that the final judgement is seen by all to be just. And it shows the church, one last time, that her safety never rested on Satan being chained but on God himself. A God who can chain the dragon with one angel loses nothing by letting him go for a little while.

How should I read prophecy headlines? With a calm mind and an open Bible. Every generation has had preachers who named the nation of Gog, the identity of the beast and the year of the end, and every one of them has been wrong, and their wrong guesses have made the church look foolish and left believers frightened or cynical. Jesus said no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36). What we know is enough: opposition to God will gather, it will be worldwide, and it will be destroyed by Christ at his coming. So watch the news without fear, pray for persecuted believers, and be found faithful whenever he comes.

In a sentence. When the thousand years are over, Satan will be let out of his prison and will go out to deceive the nations in every corner of the earth, Gog and Magog, and gather them for battle, as numerous as the sand on the seashore.

On a Tuesday. If you see opposition to the gospel growing, do not panic. The final assault was foretold, and its end is certain. When a law changes against Christians, or a friend tells you the faith is dying out, remember that the numbers have always looked like this from the inside of the camp. Count the promises, not the enemies. And notice the deceiver’s method, which has not changed: he still works by lies. The best defence of your soul this week is not cleverness but truth: read the Bible, believe what it says about God, and refuse what it does not say.

For worship. The devil’s last campaign is a copy of a promise God made to Abraham, because the devil has never had an original idea in his existence. Everything he builds is a counterfeit of something God made first. And God, who made the promise, keeps it: the true seed of Abraham is Christ, and in him a multitude like the sand of the sea from every nation is gathered, not to make war on the city but to live in it. The Lord who numbered the stars for Abraham knows every one of his own by name, and not one of them will be lost in the last storm.
verseByVerse.note: Gog and Magog come from Ezekiel’s vision of a last great attack on God’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: And they marched up over the broad plain of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city, but fire came down from heaven and consumed them, and the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur where the beast and the false prophet were, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they marched up over the broad plain of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city, but fire came down from heaven and consumed them, and the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur where the beast and the false prophet were, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.

The setting. Ezekiel 38:22 says God will rain upon Gog torrential rains and hailstones, fire and sulphur. Fire came down from heaven on Sodom (Genesis 19:24), on Elijah’s sacrifice at Carmel (1 Kings 18:38), and at Elijah’s word on soldiers sent against him (2 Kings 1:10–12). Psalm 87:2 says the LORD loves the gates of Zion. Israel camped around the tabernacle in the wilderness, tribe by tribe, with the presence of God in the middle (Numbers 2).

And they marched up over the broad plain of the earth. “Broad plain” (to platos tēs gēs, the breadth of the earth). Spreading over the whole world. This is not a march on one valley in the Middle East but a tide covering every land.

And surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. Two images for the people of God in one clause, and they should be separated. “The camp” (parembolēn) is Israel in the wilderness: tents, no walls, a people on the move, defended by nothing but the presence in the middle of them. “The beloved city” is Jerusalem, Zion, the city God loves (Psalm 78:68; 87:2), here the people of God, the new Jerusalem in its present form, the church. Pilgrim camp and settled city held together, which is what the church always is: on the way, and already home. Not a literal city in one location, since the nations come from all over the world; the church throughout the world is surrounded and threatened. And they are surrounded. Not attacked at one point but encircled on every side, by a host like the sand of the sea. If John had wanted to describe a hopeless military position he could not have done it more completely.

But fire came down from heaven and consumed them. That is the battle. One clause, no engagement, and the saints do not lift a hand, exactly as in chapter 19, where the armies of heaven rode out in white linen and struck no blow. Instant destruction, as in 19:20–21. God acts alone. This is Christ’s return: the Lord Jesus revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8). The image is Ezekiel again, and behind it Sodom, and behind that Elijah. And it is the one thing James and John once wanted to call down on a Samaritan village, and Jesus rebuked them for it (Luke 9:54–55). The fire is real, and it is not the church’s to call.

The posture of the saints. This is the whole posture the book has been teaching for twenty chapters. The saints are surrounded and do nothing. They have no weapons, no strategy and no plan of breakout, and they are not rebuked for the lack of one. What they are asked for, from the first letter to the last battle, is endurance and faith. And then the sky opens over the heads of the people who came to finish them.

And the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur where the beast and the false prophet were. The beast and false prophet were thrown there in 19:20, the same final event; now their master joins them. The unholy trinity is together for the last time. And the dragon is described one last time by what he does rather than what he is: the devil who had deceived them. That is his epitaph. Not the great red dragon with seven diadems, not the accuser of the brothers, not the prince of the power of the air: the one who told lies, thrown into a lake, in the passive voice, by someone the verse does not even bother to name.

And they will be tormented day and night forever and ever. “Tormented” (basanisthēsontai). “Day and night forever and ever” (hēmeras kai nyktos eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn). Conscious and endless. John notes, with no comment at all, that the beast and false prophet are still there: the lake of fire is not an incinerator and not a momentary end. The devil’s defeat, begun at the cross, is completed. So the serpent that spoke in a garden in Genesis 3 has said his last word here. He was cast out at the cross, thrown down to the earth, given a short time, bound in a pit, released for a little while, and is now finished. And the head that was promised to be crushed (Genesis 3:15) is under the heel of the child the dragon once stood waiting to devour (12:4).

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “fire came down from God out of heaven”. The meaning is the same.

Is this the same battle as 19:19–21? The more likely reading is yes. Both draw on Ezekiel 38–39, both gather the nations for the battle with the definite article, and both end at once with God’s judgement, without any fighting. Premillennial Christians see two battles a thousand years apart, one before the millennium and one after it. But John has shown the end of history several times already, at the sixth seal, the seventh trumpet and the seventh bowl, and this is one more view of the same day. It is not a literal siege of the city of Jerusalem but the world’s final assault on the camp of the saints and the beloved city, God’s people wherever they are.

Does this teach that punishment is conscious and unending, for lost people as well as the devil? Yes. For ever and ever is the strongest phrase for duration in the New Testament, the same phrase used of God’s own life (4:9–10) and of the reign of the saints (22:5). And the lost share the same lake of fire (v. 15; 14:10–11), the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41). Some evangelicals hold that the wicked will finally be destroyed and cease to exist, and that the torment is only for the devil and his agents; they are often moved by real compassion. But Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence (Matthew 25:46), and if one is endless, so is the other. The punishment of the lost, like that of the devil, is conscious and without end.

How can a loving God punish for ever? This is a real question, and it deserves a real answer, not a shrug. First, sin is not a small thing made large; it is rebellion against an infinitely holy and good God, and its seriousness is measured by the one sinned against. Second, those in the lake of fire do not become sorry there; the devil goes in still deceiving, and the impenitent go on refusing God (16:9, 11). Third, the punishment is just, according to what each has done, with no one punished beyond what he deserves. And fourth, the clearest proof that God is loving is not that hell is empty but that his own Son went to the cross to bear it for sinners. The same Jesus who spoke most about hell wept over Jerusalem and opened his arms on the cross.

What it does not mean. The saints do not defend themselves in this battle. They are surrounded and helpless, and God delivers them. The church’s safety at the end, as always, is God himself.

In a sentence. They marched across the whole breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of God’s people, the city he loves; but fire came down from heaven and burned them up, and the devil, who had deceived them, was thrown into the lake of burning sulphur, where the beast and the false prophet had already been thrown, and they will be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

On a Tuesday. When you feel surrounded, by illness, by opposition at work, by a family that mocks your faith, by a culture that seems to have closed in, you are standing where the saints stand in this verse. You are not asked to break out by your own strength. You are asked to stay in the camp, near the presence, and trust. And refuse the temptation to want fire called down on your enemies. Pray for them instead (Matthew 5:44). Judgement is the Lord’s business, and he will do it perfectly; your business is to love them while there is still time.

For worship. The camp of the saints is surrounded, and the people in it have nothing in their hands, and they do not need anything. Fire falls from heaven, and the battle that the whole world assembled for is over in a single clause. The serpent who whispered in Eden, who accused the brothers day and night, who stood before the woman to devour her child, is thrown down for ever by a Saviour who never once had to raise his voice against him. The seed of the woman has crushed the serpent’s head, and the bruise on his own heel is the wound that saved us. Praise the God who loves the gates of Zion, and who has never yet lost a single tent in the camp.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 11: a great white throne, and one seated on it whom John does not describe — as he refused to describe the one on the throne in chapter 4. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them.

Verse 12: the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done (cf. Dan. 7:10).

Verse 13: the sea gives up its dead, and Death and Hades give up theirs, and they were judged, each one of them. Verse 14: Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire. Verse 15: And if anyone’s name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judged by Works, Saved by a Name

Before the great white throne earth and sky flee, and all the dead, great and small, are judged by what is written in the books. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, and anyone whose name is not found in the book of life follows them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Even the sea gives up its dead; nobody is missing, and each is judged by name.

Now: The question is not whether you have done enough, but whether your name is in the Lamb’s book — and the water of life is offered without price.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done.

The setting. Daniel 7:9–10 says thrones were placed, the Ancient of Days took his seat, his throne was fiery flames, the court sat in judgement, and the books were opened. Psalm 62:12 says God will render to a man according to his work. Jesus said the Father has given all judgement to the Son (John 5:22), and that he will sit on his glorious throne and all the nations will be gathered before him (Matthew 25:31–32). Paul says we must all appear before the judgement seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10).

Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it. The book has been full of thrones since chapter 4: the throne, twenty-four thrones, the throne of the beast, the thrones of verse 4. This is the last one, and it is described with two adjectives. “Great” (megan), so that its size settles who is in charge. “White” (leukon), which in this book is the colour of purity, holiness and verdicts: white robes, white linen, white horses. “Him who was seated on it”: God, who judges the world through Christ (Acts 17:31; Romans 2:16). The Father and the Son share one throne (22:1, 3). John does not describe him, exactly as he refused to describe the one on the throne in chapter 4. He says instead what happens in his presence.

From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them. “Fled away” (ephygen). Stay with that for a moment, because it is the most quietly terrifying sentence in the chapter. Nothing is said to be destroyed. The universe simply cannot remain in the room. The ground under a reader’s feet and the sky over his head, the two things that have always been there, the very definition of what is permanent, get up and leave, and there is nowhere for them to go. The old creation passes away before God’s holiness (2 Peter 3:10; 21:1). Nowhere to hide (6:14–16). Which means the last judgement has no scenery. Every human court sits somewhere: a room, a building, a country whose laws apply. This one has no location, because the location has gone. There is nothing in the frame but a throne, the one seated on it, and the people standing.

And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne. “The dead”: all humanity, raised for judgement. “Great and small” for the last time in this book, and it flattens the last hierarchy there is. Emperors and slaves, the men whose statues filled the forum and the women whose names were never written down anywhere, standing on the same floor. No one is too important to be judged or too insignificant to be overlooked. Nobody is represented by a lawyer, and nobody has a better seat.

And books were opened. Books, plural, and then a book, singular, and the distinction is the gospel. Daniel saw the same scene: the court sat in judgement, and the books were opened (Daniel 7:10). “Books” (biblia): records of every person’s deeds. God knows everything people have done, said and thought (Ecclesiastes 12:14), and Jesus said every careless word would be accounted for on the day of judgement (Matthew 12:36). Nothing is missing from them.

Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. The Lamb’s book (13:8; 21:27), with the names of those chosen before the foundation of the world (17:8). Two kinds of books: the books of deeds, and the book of life. The first shows what each person deserves; the second shows who belongs to the Lamb. The book of life is not a second, better record of the same kind. It is a register of names, and verse 15 says it is the only thing that finally decides anything.

And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done. “According to what they had done” (kata ta erga autōn, according to their works). The judgement is perfectly just, based on the evidence. No one will be condemned unfairly.
